RealSci_Nano Tweets

Every tweet posted by the curators of @RealSci_Nano, 2019 to 2024, by year and curator.

RealSci_Nano was a rotation curation account. Each week, a new materials or nanoscientist took over the account and shared their research, their life in the lab, and their questions. It ran alongside the Under the Microscope podcast, and many curators were also podcast guests.

In 2024 I closed shop on Twitter/X and moved to Bluesky, so the account now lives on as Under the Microscope. This page keeps every post the curators wrote, grouped by year and curator, so the work doesn’t disappear with the platform. For the full story, see the RealSci_Nano project page.

Tuesday has rolled around, and I thought I'd talk about #ConductingPolymers A rather unique material with a mix of properties between polymers, semiconductors and metals. https://t.co/z8IzlAbGG1

30.09.2019 · Tweet

Interestingly the polymer properties can be modified by inserting or removing dopant ions from its structure. They can be made insulating through to conductive.

30.09.2019 · Tweet

Many researchers exploit this for applications - not just conductivity. Think electrochromics, thermoelectrics, sensing, bioelectronics, optoelectronics.

30.09.2019 · Tweet

An example of this is work we are doing with @SentekTech around sensing for agriculture Here's an explainer (20 min mark onwards) from my colleague @DrSamRudd about our #AgTech https://t.co/YjDspVXXeJ

30.09.2019 · Tweet

@SentekTech @DrSamRudd Another behaviour we study is their optical switching behaviour - electrochromics. This property is driven by low power, and we get different colours by changing polymers. My colleague @Zuber_Kamil studies the nanoscale mechanisms behind this. https://t.co/l4pQXAJ4RU

This morning I thought I'd talk a bit about the science behind our materials. And how we study them. The core of this is the interplay of chemistry and structure on various properties.

01.10.2019 · Tweet

For eg, our metal alloy films (40-ish nm layer) we use X-ray Diffraction (XRD) and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) to look at the atom arrangement and orbital interaction. This dictates a lot of the mechanical, optical and electrical properties. https://t.co/fmXaRSM2p7

01.10.2019 · Tweet

Similarly we use these to look at how structure and chemistry define properties of conducting polymers. https://t.co/J4k995dZf4

01.10.2019 · Tweet

Understanding how molecules and atoms arrange and interact on the nm scale is key to designing materials. From that different properties can be achieved. We then use that to make new devices with industry. Linking them together is an exciting space. https://t.co/HRMRptNqe4

01.10.2019 · Tweet

In another study we used techniques to get details on the electrical properties of our materials. Such as studying the density of states and charges in a polymer. From this we uncovered semimetallic polymers. https://t.co/vUW3bBNNmg

01.10.2019 · Tweet

More recently this has led us into looking at how different anions influence the properties of the polymers. Not totally sure yet what's happening, but appears to be specific ion effects. https://t.co/zb5HYBuYFL

01.10.2019 · Tweet

This opens the door to exploring sensing. As we have done with nitrate using a polymer called PEDOT. https://t.co/VlLtKF4eaH

One big aspect of making our materials is understanding how they form. A technique we use is Vapour Phase Polymerisation (VPP). http://dx.doi.org10.1016/j.pmatsci.2017.01.004

02.10.2019 · Tweet

There's more to it than simply polymerising a monomer. On the molecular scale we have controlled reactions at the liquid-vapour interface. The interface is structured using non-ionic copolymers.

02.10.2019 · Tweet

This is a trick borrowed from colloid chemistry. In one form used to make mesoporous metal oxides. We use the structure to direct how the conducting polymer grows directly on the substrate. By changing the structure we can drastically change the polymer properties.

02.10.2019 · Tweet

The nice thing about this process is we can (somewhat) control; - how the polymer forms on the nanoscale - over large areas (up to m2) This works for oxidative polymerisation of any volatile monomer.

02.10.2019 · Tweet

Understanding processes like this helps us bridge the fundamental science with commercial manufacture. We do a similar level of work on magnetron sputtering and chemical vapour deposition.

02.10.2019 · Tweet

For example, understand how processing of dielectric films can enhance their properties for certain applications. https://t.co/EF2vObMRZa

03.10.2019 · Tweet

Fun fact: We name our coating equipment after objects in our solar system. We do sputtering in Saturn, Mars and Jupiter. Yes, Jupiter is the big machine. We do conducting polymer coatings in Callisto, Io and Europa. Our thermal evaporator is called Mercury. https://t.co/TtuzSn0OtF

Great thread 👇 Traveling for work............ https://t.co/sZwO0dYFRr

03.10.2019 · Tweet

It's Friday. I figured I'd raise a challenge facing many researchers - work with industry or do fundamental research? More specifically, can you do one only? Or both? What does it mean for your career, and meeting the 'metrics' for promotion?

03.10.2019 · Tweet

Many industry engaged projects have a long lead time to publish, if at all. Considering intellectual property, confidentiality, trade secrets, and so on. This poses a challenge when an academic researcher needs publications.

03.10.2019 · Tweet

This is particularly relevant for Early Career Researchers. They are less likely to have other avenues to publish. But also less likely to have employment length to see an industry project through.

03.10.2019 · Tweet

So what to do? One thing to note is research is done in teams. Get a good group of people around you. Together you'll figure out how to do it. Also, make an end-user is part of that group. Someone who can help you shape your research to be relevant to industry.

03.10.2019 · Tweet

This still doesn't answer whether you can do both. I found that early in my career it is very hard to do. But not impossible. It takes a lot of time to plan strategically how it all goes together. What is core fundamental and what is applied research?

03.10.2019 · Tweet

Then comes the next step - who pays? Neither funding agencies or business have endless money to fund research. So make an assessment of which to focus on first. You can't do everything from day one.

03.10.2019 · Tweet

A key thing I have learnt is that the path from idea to products is not linear. Some of my best (IMO) fundamental research came from questions in an industry project. So maybe think backwards about products and ideas. Working with industry may spawn your basic research.

05.10.2019 · Tweet

Time...... How do you balance it? How do you allocate it?

05.10.2019 · Tweet

As I try to get out with my kids to do the grocery shopping; I've spent several hours of Saturday morning working. After a week predominantly spent doing admin, and helping others at work....I find the time to do 'my stuff' gets pushed out of hours when I want to be not working.

05.10.2019 · Tweet

Many academic roles have scope creep. The slow expansion of your tasks, including increased contribution to the greater sector. Boards, committees, panels, etc. All worthy things. But does it impact your day job? Time for teaching or research?

05.10.2019 · Tweet

Or even more importantly, is it forcing you into decisions about out of work hours choices? Everyone is different. Everyone balances things differently. How to manage the expectation to 'do it all'?

05.10.2019 · Tweet

I've been lucky these past years that out of hours work is infrequent. Others are not so lucky. This is a challenge I see for the sector. A research career should not have to contain sacrifices (unless you want to).

05.10.2019 · Tweet

Is this something people in your local area discuss? Keen to hear how others manage this in their situation.

05.10.2019 · Tweet

08.10.2019 · Tweet

Autocorrelation measurement is used to measure the length of ultrashort pulses. This is often achieved by using the pulse itself through a nonlinear optical effect, usually Second Harmonic generation (again harmonics 😉).

08.10.2019 · Tweet

Infact you cannot use a simple electronic device to measure a femtosecond (10^-15 sec) pulse since you would need some 100 THz electronics, which simply does not exist.

08.10.2019 · Tweet

Introducing the Tandem lab! This is where I do my experiments. The Tandem lab is named after our biggest machine - our tandem accelerator. The photo shows me in front of it! https://t.co/eGfpqwPZzv

14.10.2019 · Tweet

Here’s a short video following the beam line from the accelerator to the end stations. You can see in the end how the initial beam line splits up into 6 different ones. We have a range of different set-ups for different analysis methods and the Tandem provides ions for them all. https://t.co/4G50n3VJuV

14.10.2019 · Tweet

So, why do we need so many different set-ups? First, I should explain that the Tandem lab’s a Swedish National research infrastructure. That means that not only people from my group do experiments here but that researchers from all over Sweden (and abroad) can apply for beam time

14.10.2019 · Tweet

That means that research questions and samples vary quite a bit - from coating materials to steel used in fusion research to DNA samples to backing materials for solar cells.

14.10.2019 · Tweet

Additionally, all analysis methods have their strengths and weaknesses so often a combination of several is needed for complete characterisation of a sample.

14.10.2019 · Tweet

When I say characterisation what do I actually mean? Here are some examples of what you can do with ion beams based methods: - find out which chemical elements are contained in a sample - and in which concentration

14.10.2019 · Tweet

- atomic structure (is the sample crystalline?) For thin films (that means nanometre up to about 1 micrometre for us): - thickness, position or concentration gradient of layers

15.10.2019 · Tweet

Now I want to tell you bit more about some basic methods and how they work in principle. We start with maybe the most basic ion beam analysis method - Rutherford Backscattering Spectrometry!

15.10.2019 · Tweet

Quick note on the side: Researchers love acronyms! So, we would just say RBS instead of Rutherford Backscattering Spectrometry for obvious reasons. However, please stop me if I should start throwing around acronyms and you don't get their meaning!

15.10.2019 · Tweet

The principle of backscattering spectrometry can be understood as some kind of atomic billiards. We have a material that consists like all matter of atoms and we shoot an ion onto it. https://t.co/E6KD4KmZT7

15.10.2019 · Tweet

If the ion and an atomic nucleus of the target material come close enough to each other, the positive charges repell each other and the ion gets scattered. https://t.co/k2INw5LX6Q

15.10.2019 · Tweet

Like in billiards, the direction in which the ion gets scattered depends on the incident angle. In backscattering spectrometry we look as the name says only at particles scattered in a backwards direction.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

Unlike in the game in our experiments the masses of our two atoms don't have to be the same. The masses of the atoms, the energy of our incoming ion (determined by the accelerator) and the geometry of the experiment all determine the energy of the ion after the collision. https://t.co/pDYC92mXRt

15.10.2019 · Tweet

And this energy is what we measure! Since we know the beam we send in (energy and mass) and the geometry of our set-up, we can then calculate the mass of the atomic nucleus from which the ion scattered. And thereby we identify chemical elements in a sample!

15.10.2019 · Tweet

@vynisle Thanks ☺️

15.10.2019 · Tweet

This afternoon I had a meeting with the doctoral board of @uppsalauni. I’m one of the vice-chairs of the board for this year and I’d like to talk a bit about being active in student representation and why I think it’s important.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

To start this conversation one has to have a look at the Swedish law on higher education. This laws guarantees students a vote in all decision making organs of a Swedish university. This means students have representatives on all level from department to the university board.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

PhD students are full students from a legal point of view in Sweden (we’re also employees so we get the best from both worlds like a salary and student discounts 🙃) so we also have representatives and get a say in university matters.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

I think this is super important. A university is so much more than just tenured professors and management! And all the voices need to be heard to create a learning + researching environment where everyone can thrive.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

@uppsalauni PhD students are organised in PhD boards both at faculty and at university wide level to speak as the voice for the respective group of PhD students. These boards also appoint the representatives to university boards I was talking about earlier.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

They also organise and support different kind of events from seminars to afterwork to help PhD students to connect to others.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

A PhD can look very differently depending on the field. The doctoral board is there to have a voice for all PhD students at the university no matter their specific situation. We therefore consist of representatives from all faculties.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

To wrap this up: The situation of PhD students in Sweden is probably a lot better than in other countries (in terms of rights and employment benefits). However, I think it's important not to take these rights too much for granted.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

An example: Allowing scholarships instead of employment is a current (and reoccurring) discussion topic, which would not really be in our interest.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

Additionally, it's not always straightforward to know and claim your rights especially when you're maybe in a stressful situation. The PhD boards (and ombudsman) are also there to give support and information.

15.10.2019 · Tweet

Getting engaged in student representation has also been a lot of fun for me. I've been working together with a diverse group of nice people plus I learned tons about how a big organisation such as a university is working. I really recommend it!

16.10.2019 · Tweet

Good morning! If you folllowed along yesterday you might have noticed that I did a lot of things other than research. Yes, doing a PhD often entails more things than just standing in the lab! I honestly find it hard sometimes to balance out all my activities. Any tipps?

16.10.2019 · Tweet

I should add though that I'm actually only teaching one course running for around 2.5 months every year so the rest of the time it's one thing less and more time for research

16.10.2019 · Tweet

Today I'm going to focus more on physics though! https://t.co/xUcDzje7aL

16.10.2019 · Tweet

Yesterday I explained how we can use scattering to identify the elements contained in a sample: https://t.co/amOr0XGFQs

16.10.2019 · Tweet

You might have noticed that in my explanation I only talked about one part of the sample atoms - the atomic nuclei. The thing is that these are actually very small even compared to the size of the whole atom. So atoms are mostly "empty"!

16.10.2019 · Tweet

That also means that it's actually quite rare that an ion is backscattered from the first layer (or any layer) like shown in my illustration. More likely it travels further into the material. In this case we will need to look at the other parts of the sample atoms - electrons!

16.10.2019 · Tweet

The ion also collides with the electrons. But cause electrons are much lighter than the ion (even hydrogen is 1836 times heavier), it doesn't change direction much and only loses a tiny bit of energy in every collision. https://t.co/QU4uXAg9Lg

16.10.2019 · Tweet

But since they're many electrons and many collisions, this process noticably slows down the ion. Eventually the ion will stop inside the material if it is thick enough (how thick is thick enough depends on the ion energy and mass and the sample material)

16.10.2019 · Tweet

Alternatively, the ion meets an atomic nucleus before it has lost too much energy and is scattered in the same way as from the surface. It can then travel back through the sample and we can detect it! https://t.co/88tsXcVAII

16.10.2019 · Tweet

With enough understanding of the ion-electron interaction we can translate the energy lost to the electrons to information about depth. For example: we can determine the thickness of a layer or calculate the depth in which the ion will stop.

16.10.2019 · Tweet

We call the average energy loss by the ion per distance travelled the stopping power. Since it's such an important quantity, all measurements of it are collected in a big data base: https://t.co/YIIntSxqOL

16.10.2019 · Tweet

17.10.2019 · Tweet

I first talked a bit about how ions interact with electrons. https://t.co/WIf32PcgPO

17.10.2019 · Tweet

In this context I introduced the stopping power. The thing is that the strength of this quantity (you can think of it as a force that slows down the ion) depends strongly on ion energy. Here is an example: https://t.co/99ON1O72fM

17.10.2019 · Tweet

For various reasons (physics,technical, historical...) we understand much more about the high energy region of this graph. This is why my PhD project focusses on slow ions and how they interact with electrons.

17.10.2019 · Tweet

Side note: this is also why I measured my samples at the high-energy set-up the other day. I characterise my samples (mainly their thickness and composition) first with a well-established method before I use them to learn about interactions at low energies.

17.10.2019 · Tweet

These are super good questions because they very much lead to why interactions of slow ions are more complicated. I try to answer as good as I can. Please continue asking if something stays unclear. https://t.co/JXwTHgbuiM

17.10.2019 · Tweet

1. The easiest case to consider is this: The ion is much faster than the electron in the atom and they get relatively close to each other. Then the Coulomb force between them is acting and momentum is transferred to the electron.

17.10.2019 · Tweet

If it would be a free electron, the interaction would be like in the scattering case more or less billiard like. However, the electrons usually are bound and they have discrete binding energies in the atom.

17.10.2019 · Tweet

So, if the energy transferred is not enough for the electron to leave the atom, it might still be transferred to a different energy shell --> the atom gets excited.

17.10.2019 · Tweet

So far so easy. But there is more that can happen: If the ion is slow and/or heavy (i.e. has a high nuclear charge) it has a rather high chance to capture an electron. That means the electron becomes part of the travelling ion/atom (it might become neutral).

17.10.2019 · Tweet

I try to explain this process in this tweet here: https://t.co/EnZRzkEnX9

17.10.2019 · Tweet

Note that the reverse process is also possible, i.e. that the ion transfers an electron to the solid and becomes (higher) charged. This process depends strongly on how close the ion gets to the target atoms though cause the two electron levels needs to be resonant with each other

17.10.2019 · Tweet

Then there is a process called "molecular orbital formation". Which means that the ion is so slow that for a time it seems like it's forming a molecule with a target atom. That has again an influence on the electron energy levels and thereby on the energy loss.

17.10.2019 · Tweet

Considering this question: "Could we even discriminate between these possibilities, even theoretically?" Theoretically we can look at single events. Experimentally, we always look at the average of many collisions. There are some tricks though...

17.10.2019 · Tweet

I pause here since I have teaching now. I leave you with this pretty image of one of my samples. I promise it has a lot to do with what I've been talking about in this thread and the trick I've just mentioned... https://t.co/A4S0Cbo2O3

Ready for experiments tomorrow! https://t.co/7GzkH2s6O7

27.10.2019 · Tweet

Before I start in on the research, I should tell you how I became a scientist. I knew I wanted to go into science at age 12 because of Star Trek. I watched TNG as an impressionable lad, and I was captivated by all the sciencey solutions to the problems of the week.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

I say "sciencey" because once I started studying science for real, I discovered that all the Treknobabble was quite literally babble.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

The character I identified with most was Wesley. I've met Wil Wheaton at a couple of cons and told him that, and he was absolutely thrilled. (I didn't tell him that the reason I identified with Wes was that I was the obnoxious kid that nobody liked.)

27.10.2019 · Tweet

Poor guy's had to deal with a lot of undeserved grief over the years because of how terribly his character was written.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

I didn't zero in on chemistry until grade 11. I had a great teacher, and something about balancing reactions and finding out what things are made of at the atomic level appealed to me.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

I knew before I finished high school that I was going to take chemistry at university.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

I did a Bachelor's degree in Kelowna, British Columbia, Canada at Okanagan University College, now called UBC Okanagan. I got interested in zeolites, which are essentially rocks with tiny channels in them where interesting chemistry happens.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

I went to grad school at the University of Ottawa, because there was a prof there working with zeolites. I got accepted into his lab, and turned up on my first day to be given a project involving...not zeolites.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

Instead, it was a project investigating oxidative stress in...something or other. I can't remember, because I was only on the project two days before discovered a paper describing exactly that project.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

I couldn't do something that was already published, so my boss switched me to a different oxidative stress project...with the same result.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

The third time turned out to be the charm. My boss found a paper describing making silver nanoparticles using light. He was a photochemist, and had done work on a photochemical system that would be much better at making nanoparticles.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

I'm going to leave it there for today, because it's a little weird tweeting under someone else's name and picture. Tomorrow I'll describe my nanoresearch, and the trials and tribulations along the way.

27.10.2019 · Tweet

#NewProfilePic

28.10.2019 · RT

RT @sciencenotscary: I tried to throw a neutrino pumpkin through the detector, but it just smashed on the outside of the support structure…

28.10.2019 · Tweet

OK, nano-time.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

I started my Masters in December of 2003. Was that really 16 years ago?

28.10.2019 · Tweet

I took an overnight flight to Ottawa from the other side of the country, and got no sleep.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

When I got to campus, I went looking for the lab and was confronted by a sign that said "authorised personnel only." I stopped for a second, then thought "wait a minute, I'm authorised personnel."

28.10.2019 · Tweet

As I mentioned yesterday, the first two projects I was assigned quickly proved to be already published. I can't remember exactly what they were, but they weren't nano, so they aren't important.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

The third project was the charm. My supervisor was Tito Scaiano, who at that point had not had any interest in nano-anything. He was a photochemist, and had spent a lot of his career finding rate constants for various photochemical reactions.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

He read a paper describing the production of silver nanoparticles in thin polymer films using light. The process took two hours, and resulted in an unpleasant brown colour. Tito figured he could do better.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Incidentally, explaining why the state of the art is terrible and you're so amazing is pretty standard in writing grant proposals.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Anyway, this paper described how their polymer film had molecules dissolved in it that would produce ketyl radicals in it that would convert silver salts into silver nanoparticles when hit by light. Cool. What does all that mean?

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Let's start with radicals. Most organic molecules are held together by bonds between adjoining atoms. Each atom contributes an electron, and those two electrons are shared between the two atoms and form the bond. This is covalent, a term that might be familiar from highschool.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Generally, all of the electrons in the molecule will be paired up, either in a bond or just hanging out on one atom. Radicals are what happens when one of those pairs is sundered.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

A radical is an unhappy molecule, generally, and it spreads that unhappiness around with a shovel. It wants its electrons to be paired, so it starts stealing electrons from other molecules. Which then makes more radicals. The circle of life.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

The particular type of radical in this study is derived from ketones, hence the name ketyl (ket + -yl suffix). Great, what's a ketone? Hang on, let me find a picture. (Public domain image from Wikipedia user Benjah-bmm27) https://t.co/rGCDXzshIK

28.10.2019 · Tweet

The big R groups simply represent chunks of molecule we aren't bothering to specify. The important part is the C=O, which represents a double bond between carbon and oxygen.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

That's a carbonyl. This time the suffix is -onyl, and represents a double bond to oxygen. It's also pronounced differently. Here the y sounds like a long e (neel), and in ketyl it sounds like a short i (till). There's no rhyme or reason to this.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Anyway, when you have a double covalent bond, the electrons in the second bond are a lot more playful than those in the first. In addition, the oxygen has two more pairs of non-bonded electrons, so there are lots of options to steal one to make a radical.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Alternately, the plain ketone can steal an electron from another molecule and make itself a radical. This is where photochemistry comes in.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Electrons live in orbitals, which are mathematical descriptions of where electrons can be found 95% of the time. There's a lot of uncertainty about where an electron is at any given time, hence the elaborate math and stats involved.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Each orbital can hold two electrons...which is also the number in a covalent bond. This isn't coincidental. For the purposes of this discussion, the covalent bonds between atoms can be considered molecular orbitals.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Everybody keeping up? Do I need to go back and explain something in more detail?

28.10.2019 · Tweet

OK, all of these orbitals exist at different energy levels, usually expressed relative to some arbitrary zero points. It's nearly impossible to measure absolute energies, so we just pick some point we can measure and call it zero. Everything else is relative to that.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

All of these orbitals contain 2 electrons...but there are a bunch of empty ones as well. Whether or not they actually exist if they're empty is a question for the philosophers, but they're real enough that an electron can jump into one.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

That's jump between orbitals is a quantum leap, if you're wondering where that term came from.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

A quantum leap can only happen if an electron suddenly receives exactly enough energy to make that jump. Too much or too little, and it's not happening. In organic molecules with C=O double bonds, that energy can be delivered by UV light.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

That's the basis of photochemistry right there: light carries energy, and molecules can absorb that energy if it matches the difference between one of its full and one of its empty orbitals. After that, chemistry happens.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

So where does the nano come in? Patience, I'm getting there.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

(This story is quickly becoming How I Met Your Nanoparticle.)

28.10.2019 · Tweet

If that ketone absorbs a photon of light, one of the playful electrons in the C=O double bond gets booted up to a higher orbital. Once it's there, it can grab a hydrogen atom from a C-H bond of another molecule, and drag along one of the electrons from that bond.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Now that C=O is a C-OH, and that other poor molecule is now a radical, with the remaining electron from that C-H bond sitting sadly on the C. But what about the other electron left behind when the photon kicked the other one upstairs to start this process?

28.10.2019 · Tweet

It's still there, also unpaired, sitted forlornly on the C of the C-OH. That's the ketyl: a radical derived from a ketone. Took a while, but we got there eventually.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

After all that, why did we care about these ketyl radicals? It turns out that unhappy radicals can also make themselves happy by giving away that unpaired electron, if it results in something stable.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

If our ketyl gives away its unpaired electron, now there's a big empty hole on that carbon atom. That hole can be filled by remaking that C=O bond. Currently it looks like this: +C-OH, where the + is the positive charge caused by the loss of the radical electron.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

There are two electrons in the O-H bond. If the H takes off and leaves behind its share of the bonding electrons, those two can then pivot around and slam down into the hole on the carbon. C=O H+ There's a + on the H because now it's got a positive charge.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Clear as mud?

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Half the reason the ketyl can give away its electron is because this stable, happy non-radical molecule is the product. Reactions generally want to end up stable and happy. However, the other half depends on finding something stable and happy to give the electron to.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Enter silver. Silver is a metal, and metal chemistry is quite unlike non-metal chemistry. For starters, metals tend not to* form covalent bonds. * - OK, some do under very particular circumstances, but not in the system we're considering.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Metals generally form ions by losing electrons. If you've seen corroded steel or copper, that's what's happened. The metal atoms in the solid metal chunk lost their electrons and were dissolved into any nearby moisture as freefloating ions.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Because the universe is electrically neutral, those positive ions need negative partners, which are usually formed during the corrosion process. Compounds made of these positive-negative ion pairs are called salts.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Silver is quite difficult to convince to become a salt, and quite eager to go back to its metallic state. It will accept an electron from any ready source. It will also do so if exposed to enough light, but that's not helpful to the reaction at hand.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Actually, it's actively unhelpful, which I'll get to when I talk about what happens when things go wrong.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Silver salts will accept that electron from the ketyl radical to become metallic silver...and that's where things get nano.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

If you shine light on a ketone that's in a mixture of some sort with silver salts, you generate ketyl radicals which give electrons to silver ions that make silver metal, and those silver metal atoms glom together and grow into nanoparticles.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

It was a long walk, but we got there in the end. Anyone still with me?

28.10.2019 · Tweet

Tomorrow I'll carry on with my particular research project, and some pictures as well. As interesting as wall-of-text tweet threads are, metal nanoparticles are way too colourful not to show you.

28.10.2019 · Tweet

As of 2012, the jury was still out, and I haven't heard of a verdict being returned since then. Best guess is local oxidation of surface gold atoms by the sulphur forming a covalent bond. tl;dr, <elaborate shrug> https://t.co/aPEydDGx8h

If you're just tuning in, I did nanoresearch between 2004 and 2006 at the University of Ottawa. I haven't quite got to exactly what I did yet, because I was explaining how radicals worked.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

If you take a covalent organic molecule and slice a bond such that each fragment gets one of the electrons in that bond, you end up with radicals: molecules with an unpaired electron.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Things with unpaired electrons tend not to be happy, and they spread that unhappiness around with a shovel.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Normally this unhappiness is manifested by the radical shredding another molecule in search of electrons to pair with. This just results in the formation of another radical from the wreckage.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Sometimes two radicals will find each other and peacefully combine their unpaired electrons to form a new bond. This stops the make-a-new-radical chain reaction and is called the termination step. These two things are common in reactions that grow long-chain polymers.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Finally, and most relevant to the discussion at hand, a radical can sometimes give away its unpaired electron to something else, if both resulting molecules end up happy and stable.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

A radical can give away its electron if it can rearrange itself afterwards to fill the hole left behind. This usually requires the formation of double bonds, and requires a source of mobile electrons within the structure of the molecule.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

I covered this in detail in yesterday's thread. Let me go find and retweet the starting point.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

This is where I describe giving away an electron to form a stable molecule. I, uh, don't know how to weld it into the existing thread. Sorry. https://t.co/katmLWmZUg

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Having a stable product left over is good, but you also need something that wants to take the electron. Silver is a metal that really wants electrons, and will do it quite readily. It will grab them some other metals, or whatever else it can find.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

It does need a bit of help to get started. That help can come in the form of light. Silver salts are photosensitive. The entire pre-digital photography industry was built on this premise. Film and photographic paper were coated with light-sensitive silver.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

If you put silver salts in close contact with these radicals, you can grow nanoparticles quickly and easily. Well, I say quickly and easily, but it still took me a year and a half to figure out how to do it.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

OK, let's pick up where we left off: growing silver nanoparticles.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

But first, tea, Earl Grey, hot.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

There are a bunch of ways to grow nanoparticles. The simplest brute-force approach is to smash a chunk of bulk copper into nano-sized pieces. This is a lot harder than it sounds, and highly discouraged.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

(If you're following this account, I'll assume you're already reasonably familiar with nano-related concepts, so I'm not going bother with the usual comparisons to some miniscule fraction of the width of a human hair.)

29.10.2019 · Tweet

A much better way is a ground-up approach, where you start with silver in salt form and convert it into metallic silver, which then self-assembles into nanoparticles. There are several ways of doing it.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

A simple chemical way is to throw something at it that will do that reaction spontaneously. You have to do it in a controlled manner, otherwise you'll end up with a mirror on the inside of your beaker.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

This is an old way to test for the presence of a class of organic compounds called aldehydes: Tollen's test, or the silver mirror test. It's also how they used to make actual mirrors: take a slab of glass and spray silver salt and aldehyde on the back of it.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

I need to digress into some fundamental chemistry again. I've been talking about metallic silver and silver salts. Going from the salt form to the metallic form is called reduction, which is the opposite process as oxidation. Everyone remember LEO the lion says GER?

29.10.2019 · Tweet

That works too. https://t.co/k9D6jid9wx

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Silver in salt form has a charge of +1, and in the metallic form it's 0. These also correspond to the oxidation state. When it gains the electron, the state is reduced from 1 to 0, hence reduction.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

"Oxidation" is a holdover term from the early days of chemistry, when the compounds they were studying got more oxygen atoms glommed onto them. The term it more broadly applied now to any reaction where the oxidation state increases.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Anyway, making nanoparticles from salts is a reductive process, and requires a reducing agent, some other chemical that serves as a source of electrons.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Making silver mirrors is as simple as throwing them together. Making nanoparticles requires some way of persuading them to grow to nano-size and then stop. We usually add yet more chemicals called capping agents, because they cap the growth.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Something like sodium citrate acts as both reducing and capping agent, and is readily available and fairly inexpensive, so it's a popular choice.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

The citrate molecule physically binds to the surface of the growning nanoparticle, stopping its growth and preventing it from agglomerating with any other nanoparticles. You get a nice golden-yellow solution rather than brown crud.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

I've made both. The yellow stuff is much prettier.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

It's one of life's little ironies that silver nanoparticles are gold coloured, and gold nanoparticles can be just about any colour except gold.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

True. One of my successors in the Scaiano lab managed to grow a whole variety of different colours due to size and shape with selective illumination of previously synthesised AgNPs. https://t.co/f1vMT7WKa3

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Incidentally, it's surprisingly hard to find good images of silver nanoparticles in solution. I know there's one in my thesis, but I'm not currently anywhere near the computer that the document is stored on.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

I took this image from @ScaianoGroup 's website. It's from the work of Kevin Stamplecoskie, who's now a chemistry professor at @QueensChem. The shapes above each vial are the shapes of the nanoparticle responsible for each colour. https://t.co/rZcT8iqV6l

29.10.2019 · Tweet

The numbers are the wavelength of light he used to irradiate the starting nanoparticles. For those interested, I'll put the paper citation in the next tweet.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

K.G. Stamplecoskie and J.C. Scaiano, “Light Emitting Diode Irradiation Can Control the Morphology and Optical Properties of Silver Nanoparticles”, J. Am. Chem. Soc., 132 (6), 1825-1827 (2010); DOI: 10.1021/ja910010b.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

The particles they grew ended up absorbing at the wavelength of light used to grow them. This was a surprise to Tito, because generally in photochemistry, if you irradiate something that absorbs at a specific wavelength, that thing goes away (this is called photobleaching).

29.10.2019 · Tweet

But I'm getting ahead of myself. I haven't talked about my research yet, and I've skipped to work that built on it.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Where was I? Oh yeah, capping. Another way of capping particles is to make them in a polymer film. If the polymer is made up of subunits that can double as capping agents, you have plenty of things around to stop the growth.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

It's also harder for the particles to float around and find each other, so agglomeration is slowed. This is about a page away from where I enter the story. Tito, my https://t.co/4ASfUWWicg. supervisor, read a paper describing the photosynthesis of AgNPs in a polymer film.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

(AgNP is just a shorthand for silver nanoparticle. The same pattern is used for gold nanoparticles, AuNP).

29.10.2019 · Tweet

It took them2 hours of irradiation to make an ugly brown film. Turns out polymers aren't great at stopping agglomeration after all. Tito knew he could do better, and he had a new Master's student in need of a project.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

(That was me.)

29.10.2019 · Tweet

He showed me that paper, and one he's published in the early 80s about making ketyl radicals in micelle cages. That other paper had used ketyl radicals as their reducing agent, but not very efficiently. I talked about ketyls yesterday.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

He suggested I try making AgNPs using his micelles. Wait, what's a micelle? I made a video about it: https://t.co/teRVNRuwlW

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Word of advice for anyone who may want to make videos: if your nose is itching, you may want to take care of that before you hit record.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Did I forget to mention that in addition to being a chemist, I'm also a science communicator? I'm a science communicator. Won a trophy for it, but that's a story for another day. <Ted Moseby's kids sigh and roll their eyes>

29.10.2019 · Tweet

@upulie Cats are legendarily curious. There's even a saying about it that I'm carefully not quoting.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

As the source of my ketyl radical, I used benzophenone (public domain image). The O on a stick in the middle is the ketone part, and the two hexagons are benzene rings, which are great for stabilising radicals. https://t.co/JqlXqhbULu

29.10.2019 · Tweet

I dissolved the benzophenone inside the soap micelles, then threw light at it to make the ketyl radical. Yesterday I talked about how there needs to be some other molecule around with C-H bonds to make the radical. The long chains on the micelles served this purpose, but poorly.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

I could make AgNPs, but they weren't pretty golden ones. My solution turned brown, indicating that they were clumping together. I didn't have a capping agent.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

The system from the 80s also used a molecule called 1,4-cyclohexadiene (image made by me). Instead of grabbed a hydrogen and electron from the micelle cage, the benzophenone could more readily grab it from here. https://t.co/1ydf2v8t9r

29.10.2019 · Tweet

See those two double bonds on either side of the ring? Remember, double-bond electrons are playful and can move around. If you generate the radical at the carbon between the bonds, you can smear it around the double bonds. Smearing makes unstable things happy.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

It's the same reason the benzene rings on the benzophenone (BP) made the ketyl radical happy: you could smear it around the rings.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Not only did 1,4-CHD make it easier to make ketyl radicals, it also served as a capping agent. This was completely unforseen, and is one of my contributions to the sum total of human knowledge.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

This is why scientists do science: to find things out that nobody knew beforehand. If I took a brown agglomerated sample and added CHD to it, the clumps would break up and it would turn yellow(ish).

29.10.2019 · Tweet

With CHD, the reaction went faster, too. After 30 seconds of shining a light on the system, it changed from colourless to bright yellow. If you recall, the paper Tito read that started all this took 2 hours to make brown stuff.

29.10.2019 · Tweet

Granted, it took me 18 months to get to this part. A year and a half of trial and error (mostly error). The day it succeeded, I went running down the hall to my boss's office with a vial of yellow liquid.

Good morning Americas, good afternoon Europe, good evening Asia. (Australia, go to bed, it's a school night.)

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Yesterday I got as far as running from the lab to my boss's office with a little vial of yellow victory.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

I used to describe my research as shining a light on water and making it turn yellow. Every single person said "I can do that too, and I don't need the light." Three years of my life condensed down to a pee joke.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

I had succeeded in making silver nanoparticles suspended in water, and had capped them so that they floated around by themselves and didn't all glom together. I even discovered a new capping agent. I should have been done, right? Nope. I still needed to turn on the magnet.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

I'll explain about that after lunch.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

@svenja_lohmann @OlgainAus @sciencenotscary [admin] "Growing nanoparticles with magnets" 🎙️podcast episode #10 out now: https://t.co/vceKPNJG1A

30.10.2019 · Tweet

I'm back in the chair now and ready to carry on, but first I need to fortify myself with some hot chocolate. Because I'm 12.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Someone left a bunch of packets of mint-flavoured hot chocolate powder in the break room, so of course I'm going to have one. Because I'm 12. Anyone who thinks scientists are boring and stuffy has clearly never met a scientist.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

So far this week, I've described using light to create a radical that can donate an electron to a silver salt and reduce it to silver metal. These metallic silver atoms can then grow into nanoparticles, provided something stops them glomming together or turning into a mirror.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

The process of growing nanoparticles is more complicated that simple throwing stuff together. There are two main phases, and the being able to influence them allows greater control over the final product.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

The first phase is nucleation. This is where silver atoms are formed from the salt and first come together in clusters. These are the nuclei that the particles grow around.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

The same principle happens to snowflakes: water crystallises around something (usually dust particle or some other tiny piece of schmutz) and grows in a regular hexagonal pattern.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Controlling the speed and duration of nucleation allows you control over what the final product looks like. A fast burst of nucleation means you have fewer nucleation sites, which means you end up with fewer nanoparticles, but they tend to be larger.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

A longer nucleation phase has the opposite effect: you have oodles of sites competing for a limited amount of growth material (in this case, silver), so they don't get as big. Controlling this during chemical synthesis is very difficult.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

It's much easier to control if you can just turn a lamp on and off. Because reduction of silver only happens while the light is shining, you can start and stop nucleation with a flick of a switch. I usually gave it 15-30 seconds.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Photochemistry is just better than regular chemistry*. * - in this particular set of circumstances, under these conditions, offer not valid during months with an R in the name

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Incidentally, if you're enjoying my irreverent sense of humour, you can find much more of it at @sciencenotscary, as well as videos about how science isn't scary. Oh, and neutrinos.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

After nucleation comes growth. This can start happening before the end of nucleation In systems where all the growth material already exists, it can keep happening after the end of nucleation. For example, snowflakes will keep growing as long as there's moisture.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

In my AgNP system, growth should stop as soon as the light shuts off and stops making silver metal, right? No, because of subtleties I haven't told you about. I hate trick questions, especially ones that rely on withholding information.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

There's a minimum size that nanoparticles need to achieve in order to be stable and happy. If they're smaller than this, they simply fall apart, and the material is incorporated into larger particles in a process called Ostwald ripening.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Put another way, the big ones eat the small ones. In the nanorealm, it's survival of the fattest.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

This is how you can get growth in silver nanoparticles even after the light has shut off. As long as there's a capping agent present, they'll stop growing before they pass out of the nanoscale and stay suspended in solution.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

After 800 tweets with no pictures, I bet you're wondering what they look like up close. Wonder no more. Those are AgNP I made, imaged with an electron microscope. https://t.co/AnJ6zrNP86

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Each of those dots is the top of a stack of silver atoms. Now you can say you've seen atoms.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

You can see by the regular rows of atoms that the particles are crystalline. That's the definition of crystal: having a regular repeating pattern to its atoms. "Crystal" isn't a substance, it's a property of substances.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Saying something is made of crystal makes as much sense as saying a window is made of square.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

If you look at the large particle right in the centre, you can see that the rows don't all go the same way. This one wasn't grown from a single nucleation site. Instead, a bunch came together and joined to make one nanoparticle, possibly during Ostwald ripening.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

This is my favourite image from my thesis. I made the particles, and while I didn't acquire the image myself, I sat next to the guy who operated the electron microscope and watching him zoom in.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

So where do the magnets come it? When I made my nanoparticles, it only took 30 seconds. If I did it with the vial sitting next to a magnet, it took 15. Taking 15 seconds off the synthesis time may not seem like much, but it made it go twice as fast. That's not trivial.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Why did the magnet make it go faster? We need to go back to radicals and their unpaired electrons.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

An electron has a property called spin. This spin can point up or down. I didn't fully understand what that meant during my Masters, and I'm not sure I understand it now.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

I once heard a particle physicist describe spin as "a property particles have." I'm not sure they fully understand it either, or what it represents.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

It's usually shown graphically as an arrow stuck through a ball. The ball is the electron, and the arrow is the axis that the electron spins around. If the electron was a globe, the arrow would be sticking out of the North Pole.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

This explanation is just simple enough to be a useful metaphor while simultaneously being completely wrong.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

When two electrons form a bond or occupy the same orbital, the spins need to point in opposite directions. Why? Because. That's why.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

This paired-up state is called a singlet. The name comes from the way electronic systems like this were studied. When something with no unpaired spins emits a photon, the resulting spectrum has a single line.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

When something with a single unpaired electron emits a photon, the spectrum has a doubled line, or doublet. If we can get two unpaired spins, we get a triplet. The pattern is # of unpaired spins + 1.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Why? <embarrassed pause> Like I said, I didn't fully grok it then, and I've never had cause to come back and learn it properly.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Anyway, the important thing here is the triplet. I described how ketyl radicals form when an excited ketone rips a hydrogen and electron off another molecule, resulting in two radicals.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Those two radicals form a radical pair, especially if they're caged in micelles and can't get away from each other. The cage is important. The two spins can either point in opposite directions and form a singlet, or the same direction and form a triplet.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

If they're a singlet, they can easily recombine and go back to the starting materials. Remember, two electrons can only occupy the same orbital if the spins point in opposite directions.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

If they're a triplet, the spins point the same way, and they can't do this. This means the ketyl lives long enough to wander around, find its way out of the cage and meet up with a silver atom outside.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

The more triplets there are, the more often this happens.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Thing is, the spin direction is not set in stone. The triplet can flip back to the singlet, which then results in recombination. However, it can only do this is the triplet and singlet states are reasonably close in energy.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

This is where the magnet comes in. It turns out there are three different triplet substates, based on how the spins line up. If you can't picture that based on the arrow-in-a-ball picture, this is why I said it was completely wrong.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

I can't actually describe how this works, so you'll just have to go with me on this one. I am deeply sorry.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

Anyway, when you put this triplet radical pair in a magnetic field, one of the substates is raised in energy, one is lowered, and one stays the same. The corresponding singlet is unaffected.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

What this does is move two thirds of the triplet substates far enough away from the singlet that they can't flip over and recombine. You've basically made two thirds of the triplet molecules immortal.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

This means they have all the time in the world to float out of the cage and go play with the silver outside. More triplets getting out means the reduction reaction happens faster, which is why it only takes half as long to get nice nanoparticles.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

But if 2/3 of the triplets are immortal, why is it twice as fast? Shouldn't those numbers match up better? Don't try to read too much into it. My irradiation times were fairly arbitrary, and I didn't try to accurately measure reaction rates.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

If anyone wants to revisit this, go right ahead. Just remember to cite me.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

This magnetic effect on the triplet state requires the two radicals to be caged together, hence the blob of soap molecules.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

We made it to the end! And just in time for the end of the work day. If anyone wants anything clarified, please let me know. I'm pretty sure I glossed over a bunch of things.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

There's no such thing as a stupid question. If you don't understand something, there are probably dozens of other people who also don't understand it, and you're all too shy to ask. Go ahead and ask. It might be because I didn't explain something clearly enough.

30.10.2019 · Tweet

31.10.2019 · Tweet

Yesterday I brought my research story to its end: making silver nanoparticles with photochemistry, with a little help from a nearby magnet. If anyone wants anything explained in more detail, let me know.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

Later today I'm going to talk about what happens when things don't go smoothly in grad school.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

Research is hard. You're trekking into the unknown, often without a map or procedure to follow. Half the time you have to make it up as you go, and you don't know what you're going to find.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

That's the exciting part. If we already knew what the answer was, there'd be no point in doing it. Finding out things that nobody else knew is one of the reasons I went into science. It's exciting.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

It can also be incredibly frustrating, when you find yourself in your fifth blind alley in four weeks and feel like you're wasting your life in grad school.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

Meanwhile all your friends are getting real jobs and buying cars and houses and starting families, while you're still a broke student at 28.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

"A grad student is someone who forgoes short-term earnings in order to forgo long-term earnings later." In short, it's rough. I've been there.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

I wasn't the most talented or assiduous researcher, either. The science I described this week should have taken about a month to sort out. I was a year and a half into my degree before I got good results.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

My entire thesis was written from four months of data at the end. It was 100 pages of near-identical spectra.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

I was having trouble getting consistent results. I'd make up my solutions, shine the light on them, and then take an absorbance spectrum to examine the yellow colour.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

None of the squiggles in the spectra of the various tests lined up. If I was making the same thing every time, they should have all come out the same. A lot of of the times they would come out as near-random gibberish.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

My boss was not happy. I set a date for myself that if I didn't get good results by then, I'd withdraw from the program. I pulled it off at the 11th hour. The stars aligned, and everything worked.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

But it was nerve-wracking as hell getting to that point.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

My PhD, which wasn't nano-related and is beyond the scope of this account, was even worse. I couldn't get any publishable results at all. I failed two meetings with my thesis committee. I ended up having to leave the program, which is why I'm not Dr. Steve.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

At the time, I was trying to write up while teaching in a little town in Ontario. They'd hired me on the assumption that I'd eventually get a PhD. I don't think I told them I withdrew, and they didn't seem to care.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

The job was covering someone's maternity leave, and my first year chemistry class had 7 people in it, so I don't think they wanted to go to the trouble of finding someone else mid-semester.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

Anyway, 2013 was a low point for me. My PhD imploded, my personal life collapsed and I was living in a slum in small-town Ontario, earning peanuts despite having a graduate degree. It turned around.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

At the end of my contract, as I was starting the jobhunt all over again, a great job fell into my job through the Knowsaguy Network. (As I, I know a guy who knows a guy who knows a guy...)

31.10.2019 · Tweet

For the past five years, I've been a chemist on a neutrino experiment at @SNOLABscience in Sudbury. This is the coolest and weirdest job I've ever had.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

@SNOLABscience There isn't a lot of nano involved, so I won't go into much detail, except to mention that at one point we thought we might be making tellurium oxide nanoparticles (spoiler: we weren't, although I would have been uniquely qualified to look into them if we had.)

31.10.2019 · Tweet

@SNOLABscience The point I'm getting at here is that leaving grad school is not the end of the world. Definitely stick with it as long as you can, if for no other reason than to be able to tell yourself that you gave it everything you could.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

I was lucky in that both my advisors were supportive and genuinely wanted me to succeed. There are a lot of abusive PIs in academia who will work you to the bone and then discard you. If you're in that situation, you don't have to stay. There's a better place for you.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

Grad school is also tough if you have obligations outside of it, like a family to support. Health and financial security also make it hard to succeed. Academic culture makes unreasonable demands and expectations.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

14-hour days, 7 days a week sound like commitment to science, but really it's a good way to cause rapid burnout. Your work quality suffers drastically after about 8 hours. Anything more is counter-productive.

31.10.2019 · Tweet

Good luck convincing your overbearing PI of this, though.

There aren't a lot of jobs for professional science communicators, either. You need to already have a high-profile job, and then do it in your spare time.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

Even in dedicated scicomm orgs like science centres, all of the actual scicomm is done by people at the bottom of the pyramid: part-time employees or volunteers. Meanwhile, all the admin staff have permanent jobs and benefits.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

This is the same thing that happens in universities. The people who actively perform the work associated with the institute's mission are treated like garbage, while the bureaucracy exists mostly to sustain itself.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

Let me describe my #SciComm credentials.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

I am the 2013 winner of the Flame Challenge, awarded by the @AldaCenter for Communicating Science. The center was founded by and named after Alan Alda from M*A*S*H and The West Wing.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

The premise of the first Flame Challenge was for actual scientists to explain to actual 11-year-olds what a flame is, because of Alan's dissatisfaction with the answer he got when he asked the question of his teacher when he was 11.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

The entries were judged by Grade 5 and 6 classrooms. That was in 2012. After the first year, the kids themselves started picking the questions for the following contests.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

The year I entered, the question was What Is Time? This was a little daunting, because I'm a chemist and this is a physics question. Of course, the previous year was a chemistry question and a physicist won.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

Anyway, I pressed on regardless and made a little video. It had terrible production values, and it won. This be it: https://t.co/ACzl5kT6Ni

02.11.2019 · Tweet

It's just me in front of a horrible orange wall for four minutes. The other two finalists had fancy animations and cartoon dinosaurs, but mine was the only one where the audience could see the person talking to them.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

Lesson 1: don't get caught up in bells and whistles if you don't have a clear message. You can do a lot more with simple clarity and charisma than you can with 10 hours in an editing suite.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

I spoke in a conversational style, rather that using a stiff, formal lecturing mode of speech. I also aimed it at an 11-year-old audience. It's very easy to get that last bit wrong. Do not aim too low, because that will come off as condescending.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

I remember being 11 (dimly), and I always hated it when grownups talked down to me. These kids are on the cusp of their teenage years. You don't need to talk to them like they're toddlers.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

I tend to use humour in my videos, because it's impossible for me to not try to be funny. That said, humour isn't mandatory. Being funny isn't as easy as it looks. If you aren't a natural joker, best leave it to the professionals and talented amateurs.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

So how do you explain your nanoscience to the uninitiated? The standard comparison is expressing a nanometre in some unfathomable fraction of the width of a human hair.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

Thing is, the human mind has a hard time comprehending how big a nanometre is, and saying it's one millionth of a millimetre isn't really all that helpful.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

You could say it's bigger than an atom but smaller than a virus, assuming your audience has any sort of conception of the relative sizes of those two things.

02.11.2019 · Tweet

When you're not talking to a technical audience, mathematical precision doesn't really matter.

03.11.2019 · Tweet

What really matters, and this is true of any scicomm, is to lead with why your audience should care about your work. Why is it important, why is it exciting, how does it matter to them?

03.11.2019 · Tweet

Take them through the story of what you did. Even when you're writing for an audience in your field, your article should have a narrative describing the process of your work. The same idea applies outside your field as well.

03.11.2019 · Tweet

If you've giving an outreach talk, formal or otherwise, remember to wrap up by recapping the important points you want them to remember.

03.11.2019 · Tweet

I never spell a word wrong, I just spell the wrong word right.

Hi everyone, I'm back. And today I plan to talk about thin film deposition. And if I say thin films, what do I mean? Well a thin film is a continuous layer of material that is, for my research, anywhere between a single atomic layer and a few micrometers in thickness.

05.11.2019 · Tweet

generally, for me I grow a film to be between 50 nanometers (5*10-6mm) and 2 micrometres (0.002mm), depending on the application. When you consider that a human hair is around to be around 0.05 millimetres thick, I think we can say it is fairly thin. (for me, 0.05mm is huge!)

05.11.2019 · Tweet

There are a lot of ways to make a thin film. Most of the techniques I use fall under physical vapour deposition (PVD). These techniques create a vapour of material that coalesces on a substrate material (the material we are growing the film on).

05.11.2019 · Tweet

Mostly, PVD techniques grow films under vacuum. I tend to use high vacuum, with a ballpark figure of around 6*10-3 mbar, or 0.6 Pascals (Pa) in SI units. The atmosphere is around 100 kPa and space can be taken as around 1*10−11 Pa.

05.11.2019 · Tweet

My vacuum chambers (the box inside which I grow my films) will pump overnight to the range of between 1*10-6 and 1*10-8mbar, depending on the system and vacuum pumps. This is important as is removes air, water and other materials that may contaminate our process from the system.

05.11.2019 · Tweet

We need to start at low vacuum as our vapour material can easily react with a residual gasses in the vacuum. For example, if we have an aluminium vapour, it reacts very readily with oxygen to form aluminium oxide. If we want aluminium, then this is not good!

05.11.2019 · Tweet

Another benefit of vacuum is that if we have a higher pressure, our vapour will collide with atoms, molecules, etc in our chamber and change direction. When we deposit, we generally want the vapour created to travel to our substrate directly. Collisions may cause it to 'miss'

05.11.2019 · Tweet

If playing snooker we want the ball we hit to travel in a specific direction. When it hits another ball, the direction is changed. If this is unintended, our ball misses where we meant to place it such as eg, in a pocket in the snooker table.

05.11.2019 · Tweet

The same is true for our vapour which is, basically, atoms, ions and molecules acting as 'balls' and the substrate is the pocket. How we 'strike the ball' and control the angle depends on the technique, and I'll discuss more details in my next batch of tweets!

05.11.2019 · Tweet

However I mentioned earlier that for example, aluminium would react with oxygen if it was in our chamber. It may be that we want aluminium oxide (AlOx) so we would introduce (pure) oxygen to the chamber and create an AlOx vapour.

05.11.2019 · Tweet

Ok, so I spent far too long making pictures, but hopefully I can explain one of the techniques we use, Pulsed laser deposition. We have two of these systems in our lab, sharing one laser. These are pretty new to us! https://t.co/X1aamFKitt

05.11.2019 · Tweet

The laser, an invisible pulse class 4 laser bounces around a long beam path, reflecting off mirrors (and all encased in what looks like a fish tank!) https://t.co/t6oyG2HNbj

05.11.2019 · Tweet

Finally, we focus this through a magnifying glass, through a window in our vacuum chamber and by the time it hits our target, the material that we vaporise, it is highly focused and knocks of atoms of the material https://t.co/CbpPoCHW0w

05.11.2019 · Tweet

And here are a series of pictures, to visualise the process! https://t.co/3BGEaIRYwG

05.11.2019 · Tweet

https://t.co/RnbuPbLtIV

05.11.2019 · Tweet

https://t.co/tf6ySi5nGO

05.11.2019 · Tweet

Whilst this is happening quickly, and atoms are small, we do see the laser hitting the larget as a flash which I think is pretty cool! https://t.co/uXGZSMF9Y3

06.11.2019 · Tweet

[admin] Listen to the episode #11 podcast as @ClaraMBarker candidly explains her research: https://t.co/gJ8eZ8Xa48 https://t.co/C1O8dM9dRB

06.11.2019 · Tweet

Ok. So I promised snooker with atoms. This is my main area of expertise. SO how do we turn a vacuum chamber with little inside to something that glows like in the picture? https://t.co/LCr53XVqaZ

06.11.2019 · Tweet

We start, similar to PLD. However, this time we have a mangetic field behind the target. https://t.co/p6Y8U7Eni2

06.11.2019 · Tweet

We then add a low of argon gas to the system (other gases can be used, but argon is inert and does not react with our vapour) We also apply a large voltage to our target. Electrons are generated in the chamber and some get trapped in the magnetic field behind the target. https://t.co/TakXy85E7c

06.11.2019 · Tweet

As argon bounces around the chamber, it may collide with one of the electrons https://t.co/RAS1Hwx0Kd

06.11.2019 · Tweet

And when it does, the collision can cause it to loose an electron, becoming an argon ion. The positive charge of the ion is attreacted to the negative voltage behind the target, and thus it is attracted to the target with high energy. https://t.co/Fl0txlhnUl

06.11.2019 · Tweet

When the high energy ion hits the target, a cascade collision can happen of the target atoms. Some of these collisions may cause an atom of the target material to be ejcted from the target, travelling through the vacuum. https://t.co/rvxBqJOwXc

06.11.2019 · Tweet

Meanwhile, the argon atom may then collide with an electron, recombine and become an atom again. During this time, we are continually pumping the chamber, so some argon will leave the chamber thus we continue to flow the argon in. https://t.co/CF4NxLMSJD

06.11.2019 · Tweet

Meanwhile, the target atom may have travelled around the chamber and, if we are lucky, landed on the substrate. https://t.co/pxEgZ7l7gy

06.11.2019 · Tweet

Lots of these collisions are happening, so a lot of energy means that we great a plasma discharge, which has a bright glow in the chamber. And the arriving target atoms on the substrate may have enough energy to 'clump' together and form a continous thin film. https://t.co/fenS73nXmF

06.11.2019 · Tweet

The plasma is brightest in the area confined by the magnetic field. There are lots of electrons bouncing around this area and some of them have enough energy to cause collisions also leading to target atoms to be ejected! Pictured is a zinc target with an argon atmosphere. https://t.co/iV7bWfXzLm

06.11.2019 · Tweet

Depending on the gas used, the target material and the energy of the system, we can change the colour and brightness of the plasma, as different wavelengths of photons are released. Pictured is a titanium taget in an argon and oxygen atomsphere (as i made titania) https://t.co/putKrKA8tR

06.11.2019 · Tweet

We can actually measure the individual wavelengths with the right equipment, so we know what we have in the system. With enough collision energy some of the target material may become ions, and this can cause the film to grow in different ways!

06.11.2019 · Tweet

And boom, we have played snooker with atoms (and ions!) Of course, it is a little more complicated than described, but it captures the principals 😀 Pictured, a lithium composite target with an argon and nitrogen atomsphere. https://t.co/XJC1nUJgWs https://t.co/3XqDyL9dsA

07.11.2019 · Tweet

07.11.2019 · Tweet

Morning all. I had hoped to follow up my chat about magnetron sputtering but didn't have the images I wanted to share. So I will continue this now, with a little more in-depth look at sputtering.

07.11.2019 · Tweet

Sputtering has various properties that we can control. The pressure, partial pressure of the gas, power to the target, the magnetic fields behind the target, the distance between the substrate and target and more. I'm not sure there is any such thing as a 'controlled experiment'

07.11.2019 · Tweet

But we control and fix what we can in order to have usable data. With power, we can actually supply the voltage to the target in different ways. Most common in research is probably DC power, a fixed power to the target. In industry, it can be common to supply the ower as AC

07.11.2019 · Tweet

DC is great, it is fairly easy to fix and we can manipulate the makeup of the power, i.e. the voltage and current. However, if a material is not conducive, we run into problems. And sputtering from ceramics is not uncommon (such as using a lithium oxide composite target)

07.11.2019 · Tweet

Thus, using an RF power supply is a good way to get around this. You can set an RF offset to the power, or have a net-zero power level. In this way we can sputter materials that otherwise would act as an insulator and prevent us from striking a plasma.

07.11.2019 · Tweet

During my PhD and post-doc positions, I made use of an emerging type of power generation, HiPIMS (high power impulse magnetron sputtering). In the technique, we pulse the DC power, having an on-time of 100-200 microseconds, and long off time, in frequencies of 50 - 100 Hz https://t.co/BlWNbKKEmf

07.11.2019 · Tweet

This is compared to the frequencies of RF, which is commonly 13.56 kHz and an RMS voltage of zero, or 50 V). As a result, we get duty cycles of around 1%. Which may seem pretty low, but the trade off is that we can generate very high voltages and current during this time. https://t.co/34VnnzXgTS

07.11.2019 · Tweet

Note, in the above image the on time is the sharp spike voltage. (The system had grounding issues initially, this the odd offset during the off-time. This was when I started working with HiPIMS, in 2007!)

07.11.2019 · Tweet

Having currents of the magnitude of 100 A is not uncommon with associated voltages of 1000 V. Below is a real IV curve that I used frequently during my PhD. Compared to common DC systems, where we use maybe 2 A and 400 V. https://t.co/69nQwG72oW

07.11.2019 · Tweet

During my post-docs, I had access to a power supply that could shape these pulses even further. I spent a lot of time 'chopping' the on-pulse of HiPIMS into smaller 'micro-pulses'. I called this c-HiPIMS, chopped HiPIMS, but we still had low duty cycles with long off-times. https://t.co/SjAUQ1K17C

07.11.2019 · Tweet

With HiPIMS, we experience a phenomenon called gas rarefaction. The high on-pulses ionise all the gas close to the target, and cause lower partial pressure at the target. Because we use this working gas to cause collisions, we quickly 'run out' of gas and our current drops. https://t.co/YA1fTsHEBO

07.11.2019 · Tweet

However, I saw indications that if the time between micro-pulses was long enough, gas was able to refill this area. My indication of this was the peak current of each micro-pulse, where the peak current was much lower for later pulses when the time between them was small https://t.co/XWRtRHsZZd

07.11.2019 · Tweet

Of course, this is a balancing act. Once the micro-pulses become too spread out, we can lose the long-off time between the pulse-trains. Once this happens, we lose some benefits for our growing film with these long off-times.

07.11.2019 · Tweet

And I'll talk a more about these benefits in my next 'pulse-train' of tweets, finally showing a little of why I spend so much time playing with these conditions 🙂

07.11.2019 · Tweet

So, why do we want to play around with the run conditions during sputtering? Well, the vapour, or flux as we tend to call it, of the target material travels to the substrate and grows our think film. However, not all arriving flux is equal!

07.11.2019 · Tweet

Depending upon the energy it arrives, and the rate at which it arrives, means that the way the film grows can end up looking very different. In the picture below we have a film grown using DC magnetron sputtering. This is a titanium film, grown to 2 micrometres thickness https://t.co/jfUuKiBi3T

07.11.2019 · Tweet

Compared to a film grown using HiPIMS. We have the same pressure, average power and target material, but the additional energy as the flux arrives means that it grows more densely, with fewer spaces between grains. These differences can change the properties of the film we grow. https://t.co/GH9ZBoM4wc

07.11.2019 · Tweet

eg in titania films we can change the crystal structure and phases, which in turn can affect the photocatalytic properties of the film. These properties can be used when we create solar cells or self-cleaning glass, so optimising these properties is key https://t.co/LBefvO9Egy

07.11.2019 · Tweet

In the paper above, we also highlight the effective heat load at the substrate. Whilst HiPIMS has very high powers, the long off-time means that there is lower average heating of the substrate than with DC, allowing us to deposit on thermally sensitive substrates such as plastics

07.11.2019 · Tweet

However, one downside of using HiPIMS compared to DC is that the growth rate, or deposition rate measured as growth in Angstrom/second, A/s, can be significantly lower which can be an issue if you are trying to produce these coatings on an industrial scale https://t.co/17lDqejC87

07.11.2019 · Tweet

When using our modified c-HiPIMS, we showed an increase in the deposition rate for the right conditions (different c-HiPIMS conditions are shown in the green line). https://t.co/GEMHGO8gB3

07.11.2019 · Tweet

Yet we still had the dense films for these experiments https://t.co/5Mpi6R3A4c. As gas is used to cause cascades, releasing the flux from our target, it makes sense that if we lose gas through rarefaction, as discussed previously, our growth rate drops. c-HiPIMS mitigates this. https://t.co/LnxEvssNWs

07.11.2019 · Tweet

As for why we have higher energy, well this can be partially explained by the ratio of ions to atoms of the target material that we release. This starts to get complicated, other people can explain this better. However, more ions at the substrate means higher energy for growth

07.11.2019 · Tweet

So whilst DC grows faster, HiPIMS and c-HiPIMS have higher ion to atom ratios, as in the example below for Ti. & remember yesterday I said we can measure the wavelengths in a plasma glow, well we can even differentiate ions and atoms of the same material https://t.co/j57JX3ItaD https://t.co/x86wWCrkLL

07.11.2019 · Tweet

Randomly just found a picture of the magnetron deposition rig that I used to get my PhD at @ManMetUni! It had the original design drawings, and they were dated 1979 - the same year I was born! whoever said 'memories of cobbling equipment together' were right! https://t.co/FuoJjFmGuv

@ManMetUni Which makes me want to give my old group, and most importantly my PhD director a shout out. Pete was an amazing supervisor, I was lucky to have him. Without his support, I would not have been able to finish my project due to poor mental health at the time https://t.co/Ysknw2gjeN

@ManMetUni A great supervisor like Prof Pete Kelly important. PhDs are hard work. Having a supervisor who can manage people makes such a difference. We must get away from this 'work all hours' ethic & improve #ResearchCulture as highlighted by the @royalsociety https://t.co/wjJxTujOIX
