Hi everyone, busy morning in the lab! Finally, I have some time to tweet'n'eat. I thought I would continue my comments from yesterday, on how we need to improve research culture. Why? Well, because we push people out. Science is not for all: careers are not only judged on merit

08.11.2019 · Tweet

Various stats show similar trends, and I'll try and pull out example studies/results to highlight what I say (many from UK studies). Starting with (binary)gender. Despite making up around 50% of the population, women make up a small number of STEM workers https://t.co/VtoHh07dC0

The numbers vary by various factors, such as industry https://t.co/h86vjXCnLe

And some fields are worse than others: https://t.co/L0fKXYFJzr https://t.co/Ti2YltN34y

Generally, it is fair to say, there is a discrepancy, especially in certain fields. https://t.co/PSMBGhw8fx We have an issue. https://t.co/fCejLJFlFp

As of 2018, Nobel Prizes have been awarded to 853 men, 51 women (Marie Curie won it twice) twelve have won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine five have won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry three have won the Nobel Prize in Physics Why fewer women?

I have seen newspaper headlines just this year suggesting that women don't like STEM subjects, that woman are less good at physics than men. Men seem to have made a lot of the discoveries throughout history - is there something in it? Quite frankly, no.

It is not that long since women have been 'officially allowed' to study science. A quote on the wki for Dorothy Hodgkin says: "where she was one of two girls allowed to study chemistry." https://t.co/GLCBDJO9xu

Cambridge University did not allow women to take degrees until 1947! (It was 1920 in Oxford). If you are not allowed to study, how on earth are we able to make those big discoveries?

Also, if we look to other diversities, BME men are less likely to work in STEM than white men. 62% of black men have suffered discrimination in their STEM workplace because of their race. https://t.co/2R1apWcf03

In the UK, of 14,205 male professors, more than 12,000 are white, while only 90 are black and of 4,735 female (a third the number for males) professors, more than 4,000 are white, while only 25 are black https://t.co/FTLvys0XZW

1 in 3 US physicists have been advised to stay in the closet (LGBT Climate in Physics, APS March 2016) and LBT students are ~10% less likely to enter STEM subjects, additional to other factors Hughes, Science Advanced 2018)

08.11.2019 · Tweet

Is it all bad? Well, we are starting to gather data on these issues. Our learned societies and institutions are acknowledging that there is an issue, and this is a fantastic start. We should not be pushing people out of science because of who they are.

08.11.2019 · Tweet

And this does happen. A recent, in depth report by the @RoySocChem @IOPDiversity and @RoyalAstroSoc https://t.co/QFX2ySsuVd showed that LGBT+ scientists often consider leaving their workplace due to the climate https://t.co/ojhln4NJDB

08.11.2019 · Tweet

@RoySocChem @IOPDiversity @RoyalAstroSoc If we say that science is for all, how can we reconcile people who are pushed out of their field by the way they are treated. This isn't theoretical, I talk to people all the time who feel this way.

08.11.2019 · Tweet

@RoySocChem @IOPDiversity @RoyalAstroSoc I am one of those trans people who did leave. I was looking at new careers and stopped publishing my results, did not apply for fellowships when I should have. I was done. I only applied for my current job to prove a transwoman would not be given the job. Turns out, I was wrong.

08.11.2019 · Tweet

A big part of this is having role models. I met 2 LGB scientists in 13 years, no trans ones. I assumed there were no trans scientists because we were unwelcome. Sure, I have faced discrimination but generally I feel very welcome. The idea is we can only be what we see.

08.11.2019 · Tweet

Now I know better. There are many amazing groups out there. And having support from others like you is really important. I'll include a few great group accounts I know of: @500womensci @BlackWomenSTEM @500QueerSci @STEMGamechange @PrideinSTEM @tigerinstemm. There are many more!

08.11.2019 · Tweet

Science is not for the few. Yes, you have to be smart, hard-working and somewhat apt at science. However, that does not mean you should be excluded because of who you are. It is a right to feel accepted at work.

08.11.2019 · Tweet

You don't need to be friends with everyone, but you should not have people who hate you because of who you are, who go out of their way to exclude you.

08.11.2019 · Tweet

It is actually good for your groups' output to be diverse too. When everyone can be themselves, they can be creative, work their hardest and will be able to come up with new ideas thanks to a different perspective. Recent reports show there is a benefit to the output of the group

08.11.2019 · Tweet

https://t.co/T7tmhj113x and https://t.co/7AZKTYHeFJ https://t.co/roOQIG1I7t

08.11.2019 · Tweet

In business, they are starting to see that diversity can improve profit: Business case for diversity: https://t.co/3taC6GB5ZR and https://t.co/rUpYiX6xzA

08.11.2019 · Tweet

Of course, we should do it because it is the right thing to do, not because it is profitable for us. But it does help to have extra incentives. A diverse group can lead to diverse ideas, new creativity to solve problems.

08.11.2019 · Tweet

And if we really want to say that we have the best minds in science, we need to make sure that is true. If we exclude a whole bunch of people for their sexuality, gender, race etc, then we are lying. We do not have the best minds. We have the best minds of those who fit in.

09.11.2019 · Tweet

Hi everyone. I want to talk briefly about outreach and working with young people. For those who don't know, I run a youth organization that has youth groups for LGBTI+ young people. It takes up a lot of my spare time, but it is the most valuable thing I do.

09.11.2019 · Tweet

Today I was popped by my core group (and it was a quite session - I blame the weather!) but on a busy week we can have up to 40 young people attend. And we have an awesome bunch of volunteers also, who give up their afternoons and evenings to be there.

09.11.2019 · Tweet

I am of the thought that my youth groups are important - that there are a lot of young people that need the support we provide. So I am doing everything I can to provide that.

09.11.2019 · Tweet

Normally I would attend for the entire session, but I was asked to speak at a youth conference, delivering a work shop for other youth organizations and run by the amazing Oxfordshire Youth. As usual, there were loads of other amazing youth organisations in attendance.

09.11.2019 · Tweet

This workshop was for LGBTI+ inclusion in youth services. I'm so glad that people come to my sessions and they do so because they want their organisations to be more inclusive of all. That they give their time to come and listen, to improve their services

09.11.2019 · Tweet

As a youth organisation my success is to become obsolete. I don't want LGBTI+ young people to only be able to come to LGBTI+ groups. I don't run arts or sports groups. I want them to be able to attend groups for the activities, not because it is the only place they feel safe.

09.11.2019 · Tweet

Again, that so many people come to my sessions, want to be inclusive of LGBTI+ young people is amazing. And those people running the groups will shape the future, we do shape the minds and values of the people we work with.

09.11.2019 · Tweet

So to all my volunteers, my employees, those who I collaborate (and support/guide me) with who attend my training and the young people I do and have worked with - thank you. You are all AMAZING

09.11.2019 · Tweet

Continuing with young people, on Wednesday I was part of an outreach event designed to get young women into studying STEM subjects, We went to a school, there was an amazing show (with a pyrotechnic) and then a panel made up of mixed backgrounds and fields.

09.11.2019 · Tweet

I think back, and I know I never thought I could be trans and be a scientist. I never had those role models. I never saw people like me in science. Heck, I never saw scientists who were covered in tattoos and for those who know me, I do like my tattoos!

09.11.2019 · Tweet

So going out, doing outreach in schools and at festivals or in community / shopping centers is really important. @SoapboxScience and similar projects are really influential. We want people to know that scientists do not have to fit a stereotype, that anyone can be one.

09.11.2019 · Tweet

@SoapboxScience The session on Wednesday was part of the (as of Tuesday award winning!) SeeMe project https://t.co/YrZETsEYX0, with @SiemensUKNews @GSAUK , amazing and fiery science show by @Frans_facts and with the wonderful @Sarah_Cosgriff on the panel once again

09.11.2019 · Tweet

@SoapboxScience @SiemensUKNews @GSAUK @Frans_facts @Sarah_Cosgriff Outreach is important. To inspire others. And to show that the preconceptions I held for all those years, that I could not be a scientist because of who I am, is wrong. Again, let's make science for all.

09.11.2019 · Tweet

So what is graphene? You may have heard about it in the news... https://t.co/NbgUZU9FSK

18.11.2019 · Tweet

Graphene is one of the many forms ("allotropes" if you want a fancy chemistry word) pure carbon can take. In fact, this image shows 8 allotropes of carbon. https://t.co/bK5SCrQ0Es

18.11.2019 · Tweet

The top left and top center show the forms we're most familiar with in our normal macroscopic lives - the top left is how carbon is arranged in diamond, and the top center is graphite.

18.11.2019 · Tweet

And if you look closely at graphite, you can see that it is made up of pretty distinct layers of atoms. The carbons are all covalently bonded (the kind where atoms share electrons) to other atoms in the same layer. These individual layers are graphene! https://t.co/M4GqpYLrhb

18.11.2019 · Tweet

At first, this was just theoretical. Physicists were referring to the graphene layers within graphite since around the 1950s, as a useful concept and shorthand.

18.11.2019 · Tweet

But in 2004, researchers not only showed that they could isolate a single layer of graphene in real life, they were able to characterize its properties. And that was so impressive they won the Nobel prize just a few years later in 2010.

18.11.2019 · Tweet

I have to take a break for a meeting, but more graphene fun facts will be coming later today! https://t.co/j7MDNA1NvY

18.11.2019 · Tweet

As a bit of an aside, it turns out carbon has tons of allotropes. There's now a database dedicated to tracking them all to improve consistency, and it lists over 500! https://t.co/yh2Wle4oQy

18.11.2019 · Tweet

And new ones still have surprising properties. "U-carbon" was just announced and may be ferromagnetic at room temperature, which has never been seen in other carbon allotropes. https://t.co/3GyOGELnIa

18.11.2019 · Tweet

Carbon is like the Meryl Streep of elements: You can try it in any role at least once. (Though it may not always be as great as Meryl Streep) https://t.co/DCqmMaQHGq

19.11.2019 · RT

RT @svenja_lohmann: Moving to 2D materials (e.g. graphene) now allows to study what happens IN the surface only! #IISC23

19.11.2019 · Tweet

Outside of work, I'm really involved with @scipolnetwork! Tonight, the Communications Committee is having its monthly meeting. Shout-outs to @CaitlinAShort,@VivaceBelles, @_sindhu42, @MeredithSchmehl https://t.co/hjAHuMwgTd

19.11.2019 · Tweet

@VivaceBelles @scipolnetwork I feel like every photo I ever take in a webcam looks like I'm tired or perplexed.

19.11.2019 · Tweet

Good afternoon everyone! I want to pick up where I left off yesterday discussing graphene, and this will be a good segway to talking about colloids today! GIF below: also a good segway https://t.co/qmDoh7TPeZ

19.11.2019 · Tweet

As I mentioned, "graphene" is what we call an individual layer of carbon atoms in graphite, and the image below shows the crystal structure of 3 layers in graphite. https://t.co/1VrHJN9crD

19.11.2019 · Tweet

So how do we get an individual layer (or in technical terms, a monolayer)? I mentioned that a group managed to isolate monolayer graphene in 2004, and characterize it well enough to discover its properties.

19.11.2019 · Tweet

This actually surprised some people, b/c while physicists had theoretically discussed graphene for decades, several thought it was impossible for a free-standing, single atom thick material to be stable on practical time scales.

19.11.2019 · Tweet

For those interested in history #HistSci #HistSTS, this leads to some neat discussion about who "discovered" graphene. One of the graphene laureates, Andre Geim, has written on the "pre-history" of graphene before 2004 (unfortunately, this is paywalled https://t.co/xvOYuT8ch0 )

19.11.2019 · Tweet

Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov actually used Scotch tape in their Nobel-winning work. They donated their tape dispenser, some graphite, and a graphene transistor to the Nobel museum! https://t.co/aL73UDUBgr

19.11.2019 · Tweet

Here you can show the "Scotch tape method" being demonstrated by researchers in their lab: https://t.co/tiKnJEffJa

19.11.2019 · Tweet

Also, don't Google "Scotch tape method" without mentioning graphite or graphene, otherwise you might end up finding really gross things about tapeworms you weren't expecting to learn. Or at least that happened to me a few years when I was working on my lit review.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

You can also see in the graphene Scotch tape video that you can't really make a lot at a time. It's great for research - it makes high-quality material to test out new devices. But it's now how we're going to mass produce graphene to make the wonder products of the future. https://t.co/vGb2DJQlI4

20.11.2019 · Tweet

Also, you might be wondering why we even want graphene. That's a good question! It turns out to be a really impressive material and illustrates some neat concepts in nano and materials science when you compare it to graphite. https://t.co/YbR3CqFKTY

20.11.2019 · Tweet

For instance, graphene is the strongest material humans have discovered (~100x stronger than steel). And you might think that's wild because we use graphite to write because it's so easy to break off pieces. But the difference is what's under stress.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

The bonds between carbon atoms in the graphene plane are incredibly strong (stronger than diamond!). When we're breaking up graphite, you're breaking it up between layers, and those bonds are very weak.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

Graphene's also really conductive, but even more impressive is its "mobility" - how fast the electrons carrying charge move - which is 100 times faster than that of electrons or holes in silicon (e.g. our current computer chips).

20.11.2019 · Tweet

While graphite is reasonably conductive, it's not as impressive because it turns out even the weak bonds between graphene layers disrupt this electron motion.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

So with those superlative properties, we want to use graphene for a lot of things: https://t.co/A4OwlEoj0b Sometimes we want to use graphene straight-up, but we can also add graphene to other materials to improve their properties! https://t.co/uSSFkLam0d

20.11.2019 · Tweet

For instance, adding less than 0.1 percent (by weight) of graphene to the plastic PET (which you may know as Dacron or Terylene) increased its strength by 40% Source: https://t.co/wNGLRMIgsu https://t.co/kCgSTrKMo9

20.11.2019 · Tweet

@StemCorps @MatSciMatt [admin] "graphene smoothie" podcast episode #16, conversation with @MatSciMatt is out now. find it here: https://t.co/Bl59fITFc7

20.11.2019 · Tweet

That's a good question! The Fermi velocity of electrons in graphene is about 0.3% the speed of light, so the Lorentz factor is still really small and you don't see much change in relativistic mass. https://t.co/ds69GGWo7x

20.11.2019 · Tweet

But, it turns out the honeycomb lattice of identical atoms leads to an interesting property. The dispersion relation between electron energy and momentum is linear, so the conduction electrons actually behave like they have zero mass in graphene!

20.11.2019 · Tweet

When people say electrons behave like light in graphene, that's the linear dispersion relationship More formally, they're described by the Dirac equation as massless particles (but the speed of light needs to be replaced by their Fermi velocity).

20.11.2019 · Tweet

It turns out this works in other lattices with identical molecules. For instance, a lab at Stanford made "molecular graphene" by making a honeycomb of carbon monoxide molecules on a surface, and the electrons behaved similarly https://t.co/DExCHqPzkO https://t.co/3gpyEs7W51

20.11.2019 · Tweet

Continuing last night's discussion, what’s cool about graphene is that you can make it both starting from graphite (a “top-down” method), like with Scotch tape, or in a “bottom-up” process where you bring together carbon atoms. Image source: https://t.co/XXal860uvQ https://t.co/q1rtjmOUv6

20.11.2019 · Tweet

Check out this thread from last night on why scientists and engineers really want to use graphene! https://t.co/mMxkXWz0Pu

20.11.2019 · Tweet

The application you want graphene for is often a good guideline for how you should make it. Do you want it for electronic devices? Then you need consistent sizes and very few imperfections. Bottom-up processes enable more control over the quality. https://t.co/eTsMGvUy9p

20.11.2019 · Tweet

Do you want a lot of graphene, like to use as a filler in composites? Then you need to mass produce it, and only the top-down processes scale up. You lose some quality control, but a well-characterized distribution of sizes can be useful in these apps.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

While the Scotch tape method is a top-down technique, the techniques that will probably be used to manufacture graphene on large scales use liquids to break down graphite. The two popular ones are (1) sonication and (2) shear exfoliation.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

Sonication uses sound to make a micro-bubble bath. If you’ve seen a cleaning bath for glasses or jewelry, they’re a kind of sonicator. https://t.co/pbAq1HrE18

20.11.2019 · Tweet

Sonicators use sound waves to create small bubbles in the liquid, and when these collapse, they generate intense pressure and shock waves that break apart the graphite. Image source: https://t.co/VfQM1eh0vT https://t.co/c9wXGIG541

20.11.2019 · Tweet

It’s a bit harder to scale up sonication than first glance might suggest. Most of the sound energy gets absorbed close to the moving surface/tip, so adding more liquid doesn’t really change the working volume. Scaling up the volume requires adding power.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

And those collapsing bubbles are really violent. They heat the surrounding area to a few thousand degrees C at rates of billions of degrees per second! The shock wave also creates pressures >1000 atmospheres! This turns out to make new defects in the graphene.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

So instead of blowing apart graphite to make graphene, why don’t we take a clue from our pencils, and peel layers off? https://t.co/WtLp3co0IX

20.11.2019 · Tweet

This is where the "graphene smoothie" comes in. In 2014, a group made graphene in a blender. First, they did try it in an industrial blender, but then they found they could make graphene even in a kitchen blender! https://t.co/j46GEXOwmu

20.11.2019 · Tweet

In the blender, the motion of the liquid peels layers of graphene off each other. https://t.co/KRYHQMtKgl

20.11.2019 · Tweet

The peeling is driven by the shear forces in the liquid. The slightly different speeds of adjacent flow can slide the graphene layers relative to each other. https://t.co/EMgXwd9ZTF

20.11.2019 · Tweet

The #graphene in a blender paper was HUGE for the community, because it showed several improvements over sonication.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

(1) It takes less energy to slide graphene layers off each other instead of pulling/blasting them apart from the bubble shock waves.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

(2) This less violent sliding process doesn't create new defects while you're peeling off the graphene.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

(3) Blending scales up better than sonication. Production in sonication is almost directly proportional to power. In the blender, it scales up with the liquid "smoothie" volume without requiring the same increase in power.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

And sometimes at the end of blending graphene, you can see some flakes that were still in the middle of sliding off each other. Image source: https://t.co/wNGLRMIgsu https://t.co/8QRftHQotO

20.11.2019 · Tweet

@StemCorps I've heard carbon nanotubes are used in rackets for a while, but I haven't heard much about graphene. There was a neat study of an alleged graphene racket, showing that the material was mainly carbon fiber with some graphite nanoplatelets. https://t.co/qplhqsf1cl

20.11.2019 · Tweet

The early blender #Graphene work is based on mixing the graphite in a liquid that has a similar surface energy. If they have the same surface energy, you don't need to add energy to make more interfaces going from a hunk of graphite to individual graphene flakes. https://t.co/Gw9YmzpjMx

20.11.2019 · Tweet

This graph shows how the graphene concentration changes as a function of the liquid's surface energy/tension (they're related values). Image source: https://t.co/h6mYeoLhq3 https://t.co/RiHJZcOhd8

20.11.2019 · Tweet

The peak around 70 mJ/sq. m reflects graphite's surface energy. But you also see that there's some spread in these values. Also, it doesn't really predict how stable the isolated graphene is in the liquid against clumping back together into graphite.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

So then work started to move on from surface energy to solubility parameters. In chemistry class, you learn that "like dissolves like". Solubility parameters are a way to quantify that to help make more rigorous predictions.

20.11.2019 · Tweet

In graphene work, it's popular to look at Hansen solublity parameters - one parameter for each of 3 important aspects in chemical bonding. (1) London dispersion (when random electron motions cause attraction) (2) the force caused by permanent dipole moments (3) hydrogen bonding

20.11.2019 · Tweet

We can think of these as making a 3D Hansen space where each liquid and solid can be plotted based on their values. This graph shows the solubility of nanotubes (shown by sphere size) at the Hansen point of several liquids. Image source: https://t.co/2h6ncZA6Nb https://t.co/lv3KEUt7ja

20.11.2019 · Tweet

We just hit 300 followers today! Thank you everyone! It's exciting to spread the word about #nano and #materials #SciComm. https://t.co/VpedbWQMPA

20.11.2019 · Tweet

You can also think of how "like" two substances as being related to their distance in Hansen parameter space!

20.11.2019 · Tweet

Although even using the more detailed parameters doesn't explain all the data we see in the field. This is a graph showing how much graphene is made in different liquids based on how far apart they are in Hansen space. Image adapted from https://t.co/OygEXFMAxi https://t.co/mD5XznAO0y

20.11.2019 · Tweet

By definition, solvents at the same distance in Hansen space from graphene should be able to disperse the same amount of material. But you can see that's not true, especially when you get REALLY close to graphene's parameters.

21.11.2019 · Tweet

@StemCorps It's also confusing because there are definitely a number of products that claim to include nanoparticles, but actually don't. @TheWilsonCenter has an inventory trying to track and verify various products touting nanomaterials. https://t.co/ILRfCTfnoj

21.11.2019 · RT

RT @cshperspectives: Where are bioRxiv preprints finally published? https://t.co/wNsnb58ItD

21.11.2019 · Tweet

So now I'm going to be talking about where I came in on the #graphene blender field and my dissertation, so I guess this is a very literal #PhDChat.

21.11.2019 · Tweet

Last night I mentioned that even the more detailed Hansen parameter framework doesn't explain all the variations seen made by blending graphite into graphene in various liquids. So what other physical properties could matter?

21.11.2019 · Tweet

If you look at the way the liquid moves, the sliding is driven by the shear force between the layers of fluid. The force is the product of the shear rate, that gradient du/dy in velocity between layers, and the viscosity η. https://t.co/NQgq2D0Ir6

21.11.2019 · Tweet

Viscosity is the technical term for what we often call the “thickness” of a liquid. A “thick” liquid like honey is more viscous than a “thin” liquid like water. Or I suppose blood is metaphorically more viscous than water.

21.11.2019 · Tweet

If you increase the viscosity at the same shear rate, you increase the force. My big hypothesis for my dissertation was that a more viscous liquid could help you exfoliate more graphene. And, yes exfoliate in the sense of a skin care routine, b/c both are peeling off layers. https://t.co/RkxCFIuwAu

21.11.2019 · Tweet

So I tried blending graphene in 3 solvents with different viscosities. 1) NMP, the common solvent used for graphene, with a viscosity like water 2) Benzyl benzoate, about 5x more viscous 3) Propylene glycol, about 25x more viscous

21.11.2019 · Tweet

However, I didn’t use a kitchen blender to test this. I used a “rheometer”, an instrument that let me precisely control the flow of graphite-liquid mixture at multiple shear rates, so the flow was identical for all three solvents.

21.11.2019 · Tweet

After centrifuging out the graphite that didn’t break up, I measured the absorbance of these dispersions of graphene in liquid, which is roughly proportional to the amount of material at low concentrations. (Thanks Beer-Lambert Law!)

21.11.2019 · Tweet

You can see that at every shear rate, the most viscous PG is more absorbent than the least viscous NMP, which is a sign of more graphene being made and which confirmed my hypothesis! https://t.co/RIyQCjBgsJ

21.11.2019 · Tweet

You might be curious about the BB/Benzyl Benzoate, which has an intermediate viscosity but does the worst. It has a very different dielectric value from the others, which we think increases the van der Waals forces between graphene flakes.

21.11.2019 · Tweet

Based on the fact that BB doesn’t even seem to consistently follow a trend within itself of greater absorbance at higher shear rates, we think the flakes are clumping back together into graphite so fast it was unstable by the time I tried measuring it.

21.11.2019 · Tweet

If you’re really interested in these tweets, they are based on my first published paper, over at @Materials_MRS https://t.co/QzBOEPaxkg

21.11.2019 · Tweet

Also, excitingly, this trend help up in a real industrial mixer! https://t.co/gPdfDnkUAG

21.11.2019 · Tweet

Here's what it looks like when I make the "graphene smoothie" in the industrial high-shear. I start with graphite mixed in with the liquid, at a concentration of 50 grams of graphite per liter. https://t.co/T7ytvSdwfv

21.11.2019 · Tweet

I don't really see much of a change before and after mixing. A concentrated graphite dispersion looks pretty similar to a concentrated graphite/graphene dispersion to the naked eye. https://t.co/GZ4wDk4QqL

21.11.2019 · Tweet

Also, even with the graphite, these mixtures are still pretty thin, so I've never been able to pull off some graphite-based #LatteArt as #SciArt. https://t.co/ftMpixmj8j

21.11.2019 · Tweet

However, while this may not be the prettiest #SciArt image, I am really proud of this electron micrograph of my #graphene. There's so many neat things here! https://t.co/kZiT8USNCm

21.11.2019 · Tweet

These central flakes show outlines that are slightly displaced from each other. This shows they were still sliding off, just like that one from the original blender graphene paper! https://t.co/z0HlV9NNNp

21.11.2019 · Tweet

And in the center here is what looks like true monolayer graphene, based on the lack of other edges or wrinkles! (A lot of blender graphene is actually few-layer material, say 2-5, but if you can produce a significant of monolayer, that's great.) https://t.co/rB3Fo1cQDT

21.11.2019 · Tweet

Oh, I meant to add, this image is from the propylene glycol mixture, so I found out this new solvent not only can make more graphene than NMP, but the graphene it makes it of similar quality! More bang for your buck, if you will.

The original inspiration for my dissertation was to add the graphene into polymers, which tied into my graduate lab’s study of “soft matter”. What is soft matter? Literally stuff that is soft, for the most part. Or as we say in my department, the stuff that is “squishy”.

22.11.2019 · RT

RT @realscientists: When talking about squishy materials, I often ask people if they like to cook. Because I think understanding cooking ca…

22.11.2019 · Tweet

I talked a lot about squishy materials when I got to curate partner account @RealScientists earlier this year, so let me share some highlights from there. https://t.co/YpcytLy2RY

22.11.2019 · Tweet

Most foods, except hard candy, are soft matter: https://t.co/niBrl4eW9z

22.11.2019 · Tweet

Soft matter is everywhere! Other things you may have interacted with today that are engineered soft materials: lotions, make-up, ink. You might just think these are liquids, but they’re behavior is more complicated than something just like water or even a simple solution.

22.11.2019 · Tweet

Also, for another name that describes exactly what these are, we call these systems "complex fluids". Or you can also call them #colloids, which you might remember from a #chemistry class.

22.11.2019 · Tweet

What's a #colloid? That's a great question! It's a mixture where microscopic particles of one (or more) chemical are uniformly mixed (dispersed) in another chemical (the dispersing phase), but these chemicals still exist as distinct phases.

22.11.2019 · Tweet

So sugar water is a solution - the sugar is broken up into its molecules, which each get surrounded by water molecules. (The sugar is "solvated"). But milk is an emulsion - a colloid of two insoluble liquids, in this case the milk fats and water.

22.11.2019 · Tweet

Or maybe I should just say modern milk is an emulsion. Cream would rise to the top of milk before homogenization because it wasn't a stable mixture. Homogenizing breaks up the fat into much smaller particles that are more stably mixed into the water. https://t.co/w31LEA9b9w

22.11.2019 · Tweet

This lovely table from Wikipedia classifies all the various colloid phases you get by mixing solids, liquids, and gases. https://t.co/q13CK5y9P0

22.11.2019 · Tweet

This may also answer your childhood questions of "is dough/Jello a solid or a liquid?". It turns out they're both. Jell-o is a gel, liquid dispersed in a solid. Raw dough is also a gel, but bread is a foam. https://t.co/B5XGhOOaSS

22.11.2019 · Tweet

You also may have noticed I spent most of this week using the term "dispersion" or mixture to describe my #graphene-in-liquid system. That's because it is a colloid - the liquids aren't breaking up the graphene into its constituent carbon atoms like in a solution.

22.11.2019 · Tweet

This is also why the electric properties of the liquids matter. Since the van der Waals force is a major force for colloidal particles, we can tune that through the difference in dielectric between the particles and the liquid.

22.11.2019 · Tweet

Also, following up on this, a new favorite paper I've seen actually tries to add #graphene into polymers by adopting the pressing and folding method from making croissants! https://t.co/lWIrMyusRT https://t.co/niBrl4eW9z https://t.co/fAR3Oe56si

22.11.2019 · Tweet

A vinaigrette is one way to understand composites, but for the graphene, it’s helpful to consider another food analogy https://t.co/guAYsmfb9v

22.11.2019 · Tweet

When you want to mix a really hard, compact material like graphene with wobbly polymer chains, I like to think of this like making fettuccine alfredo, but the American kind, with the extra toppings. https://t.co/an1aTA17YL

22.11.2019 · Tweet

So have ever eaten a bowl of fettucine alfredo only to find out at the end that all the chicken and broccoli fell to the bottom instead of mixing with the noodles? The noodles entangle with each other, not with the stiff edges of the toppings. This is a problem with polymers too!

22.11.2019 · Tweet

If you added chains to the surface of the topping (or filler), they could get tangled in the big mess of noodle/polymer chains and they would be strongly mixed together. Well, we're not going to do that for chicken alfredo. But you can do this for nanoparticles in plastic. https://t.co/wXMi9Dto3D

22.11.2019 · Tweet

This prevents them from separating out and makes sure they reinforce the whole material.

23.11.2019 · Tweet

To finish out my week, I'd like to briefly discuss #rheology, or the study of flow, which is very useful for understand squishy materials.

23.11.2019 · Tweet

I wrote this up two years, after I proposed my dissertation, and I think it's a fun piece. For instance, I learned that rheology may in fact be related to Rhea Perlman. https://t.co/LV3Y14B9Ue https://t.co/sjozLidloY

23.11.2019 · Tweet

I mentioned my lab's rheometer earlier this week, but didn't describe it much besides saying it enabled precise control of the flow of my graphite mixtures. Here's what it looks like in action! This the set-up I used to break down graphite into #graphene. https://t.co/2PcmSZuGaX

23.11.2019 · Tweet

This is essentially two slightly differently sized concentric cylinders, and the inner one rotates at speeds to apply the shear force or shear rate I want. This geometry is really nice because it prevents turbulence, which simplifies the experiment https://t.co/bjazX29FRq

23.11.2019 · Tweet

And here's a video. This geometry is also useful for me because it lets me apply a very high force to low viscosity colloids. https://t.co/psL4vNlIGD

23.11.2019 · Tweet

Here's a different geometry, with a cone and a flat plate. For really small angles α, the shear force is uniform for the whole sample. This set-up is useful for studying very viscous materials. I was using it to study when the graphite-liquid mixture became gel-like. https://t.co/Z7VHpJYt50

23.11.2019 · Tweet

When you're studying soft/squishy materials, you learn that many don't have a single viscosity and that they're "non-Newtonian fluids". This means they're viscosity depends on the stress being applied and/or the history of that stress over time.

23.11.2019 · Tweet

Many polymer mixtures are shear thinning - they get less viscous as more stress in applied. This is because the chains will first start to untangle from each other, and then they start to line up with each other, making it easier to move. https://t.co/l4piPynTks

23.11.2019 · Tweet

Ketchup is (in)famously "thixotropic". When you agitate a thixotropic material, you disrupt the bonds between molecules and becomes weaker, but it will start to recover over time. This is why you often need to tap a ketchup bottle to start pouring it out.

23.11.2019 · Tweet

And "oobleck", that fun mixture of cornstarch and water, is shear-thickening - it actually becomes more viscous under stress. https://t.co/gGVOYlGPsu

23.11.2019 · Tweet

Why is oobleck shear-thickening? Good question! We're still not completely sure. A study published just last month seems to have come very close, suggesting that higher shear rates cause the particles to lose the lubrication between them. https://t.co/6IhxEf7xm5

Hi Everyone! Let me start by introducing myself! I’m Rachel Oliver (@ProfRachelGaN) Professor of Materials Science at Cambridge University and Director of the Cambridge Centre for Gallium Nitride. I’m going to be talking nitrides and nano this week!

02.12.2019 · Tweet

Why nitrides? Well, the nitride materials I work on are used in light emitting diodes or LEDs, the technology at the heart of energy efficient LED light bulbs. Any RealSciNano followers got LED bulbs installed at home? https://t.co/Nz3JDYqlqC

02.12.2019 · Tweet

If you have, I bet it’s because of how energy efficient these bulbs are! As much as 6 times more efficient than a traditional incandescent bulb and also better than a compact florescent. Also, they have really long lifespans, up to 50,000 hours. Good, huh?

02.12.2019 · Tweet

Inside a typical LED bulb, is a yellow hemisphere of a phosphor material, which converts some of the blue light which comes from the LED into other colours, to make white light. The LEDs themselves are pretty tiny – a few mm across or less. https://t.co/9TNjqBU6eK

02.12.2019 · Tweet

That’s not exactly nano though! Later today, I’ll delve into the insides of an LED bulb and show you the much smaller structures from which the light is actually emitted!

02.12.2019 · Tweet

OK! Just grabbing a quick coffee, so I’ve got a couple of minutes to take you inside an LED. Here’s an optical microscope picture of a single LED chip: https://t.co/s1ZUeS1PGd

02.12.2019 · Tweet

All we can really see here is the metal electrodes which are used to connect the LED to a power source, so let’s dig down under the surface a bit and have a closer look using a scanning electron microscope: https://t.co/QwMUqZiDDO

02.12.2019 · Tweet

There's material labelled “n” and “p”. In the family of materials we call “semiconductors” which includes gallium nitride, electrical current can flow via the movement of either negative or positive charge carriers. We call the two sorts of material “n-type” and “p-type”.

02.12.2019 · Tweet

When we apply a voltage across the LED, it forces negative and positive charge carriers towards one another. When they meet and combine, light is given out. That’s how we make light in an LED!

02.12.2019 · Tweet

(This is very different to how we get light out of an incandescent bulb. There we use a metal wire. Current flowing makes it hot, so it glows to get rid of some heat. We have to create a lot of heat energy & that makes incandescents inefficient. LEDs don’t have to get hot).

02.12.2019 · Tweet

If we only use the n-type and the p-type semiconductor, we find that the negative and positive charges don’t often meet one another and combine to give out light. We need to find a way to trap them together in a really small space to make them more likely to meet.

02.12.2019 · Tweet

We create a trap for the charges using something called a “quantum well” – and this is where we hit the nanoscale! Quantum wells are layers of one semiconductor material sandwiched between layers of another. The quantum well layers may only be 2 nm thick!

02.12.2019 · Tweet

For nitride LEDs, the quantum wells are made of indium gallium nitride – gallium nitride with some of the gallium replaced by indium. We can’t see the quantum wells with an optical microscope, or even an SEM. We need to use a transmission electron microscope: https://t.co/BRgNzS0Mhm

02.12.2019 · Tweet

I’ll explain the importance of these InGaN quantum wells a little more! We need to get the positive and negative charges to meet. Imagine that I want to meet a friend in Cambridge… how can I increase the probability of that happening?

02.12.2019 · Tweet

If I say to my friend: “Let’s meet in Cambridge” we’re pretty unlikely to find eachother. However, if I say “Let’s meet in front of the Chronophage clock” that get’s the two of us into a much smaller volume and we’re much more likely to find one another. https://t.co/pIKUCtvDA9

02.12.2019 · Tweet

It’s the same with the charge carriers: by squeezing them into a tiny space in the few nanometre quantum well, we make it much more likely they will meet, and when we increase that probability, we make the device more efficient. Hooray for nano!

02.12.2019 · Tweet

I'll talk more tomorrow about the importance of nanostructures in nitride LEDs. Later today, I'll also post some more resources about these devices, in case you want to dig into the topic a bit more deeply!

02.12.2019 · Tweet

Earlier I promised a few more resources on all things LED. My group does a lot of outreach, so here are a few things we've developed over the years...

02.12.2019 · Tweet

Our youtube channel has a few videos about our research. This one is a longish watch - but in it I talk a lot about what's inside an LED, and also how we make and study these fascinating little devices: https://t.co/a5x5gokVbt

02.12.2019 · Tweet

This infographic explains the impact LEDs can have on society: https://t.co/M5mMLivhiq

02.12.2019 · Tweet

If you're thinking about switching to using LED bulbs then you can download our app to estimate how much money you will save long-term because of their superior energy efficiency and lifetime: https://t.co/YXgtXEfqae (The app runs on android devices)

02.12.2019 · Tweet

Our second app, LED Lab, is much more in depth, and provides a lot of detail about how LEDs work, with classes at different levels and interactive online experiments. I'd love to hear feedback about it! https://t.co/YXgtXEfqae (This app runs on android).

02.12.2019 · Tweet

If you'd like to meet the people behind some of our LED research, we have researcher profiles here, where scientists at different career stages introduce themselves and talk about their interests and careers: https://t.co/hmCCW8cVnu

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Morning all! Yesterday I talked about light emitting diodes, LEDs, and I promised I’d delve more deeply into their nanoscale structure today!

03.12.2019 · Tweet

LEDs have actually been around for ages (since the 1960s), but in 2014 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for the development of blue nitride LEDs. One of the reasons that making good blue LEDs was so hard is all down to their nanoscale structure. https://t.co/gwn97Fxj8Q

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Conventional semiconductors (like Silicon) are grown as single crystals: all the atoms lie in perfect organised rows, like soldiers stood on the parade ground. Those single crystals can be taller than a person, and contains hardly any mistakes in the rows and rows of atoms. https://t.co/0d3XaDkMUA

03.12.2019 · Tweet

It’s really, really difficult to grow big crystals like that of gallium nitride (GaN). Big GaN crystals need really high pressures & temperatures to grow, & even now – about 25 years after the development of the first LEDs – we’re a long way from the scale of Silicon crystals!

03.12.2019 · Tweet

So instead, we grow GaN as layers on top of another material, most commonly sapphire. And because the spacings between the rows of atoms in sapphire doesn’t match the spacings in GaN, the GaN crystals tend to be full of tiny mistakes in how the atoms line up.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

The most important mistake (or defect) in GaN is a dislocation. It’s not really a single mistake, more a line of mistakes that runs right through the crystal. You can learn more about dislocations on DoITPoMs, a great teaching resource hosted by @cu_mat: https://t.co/UJjezczpCq

03.12.2019 · Tweet

In GaN there are really a lot of these mistakes. If you looked at 1 cm x 1 cm area of the surface of a GaN crystal, you could find the terminations of about 1 billion dislocations. (For comparison, in Silicon, a 1 cm x 1 cm area hardly ever has even one of these defects).

03.12.2019 · Tweet

For LEDs, the key thing you need to know about dislocations, is they can really mess up the performance of the device. For an LED emitting in the infra-red based on GaAs, if you have more than about 1000 dislocations in a 1 cm x 1 cm area it will very rapidly fail.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

That’s because when negative and positive charges meet at a dislocation, they combine and give out heat rather than light. The device gets hotter and hotter, and the heat eventually causes it to fail.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Because GaN is full of dislocations, most scientists thought it was a dead loss for light emitting devices. However, it turns out that GaN devices are incredibly robust to the presence of defects.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Understanding the reasons for that robustness was a really challenging puzzle to solve, and caused huge controversy in my field. I’ll come back later and tell you a bit more about that!

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Right! I’m back and ready to talk about major nitride controversies! Earlier I said that there are loads of defects in GaN LEDs and the devices survive amazingly well. How could that be? Well there are basically two options:

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Option 1: Perhaps dislocations in GaN just aren’t a problem like they are in other materials? https://t.co/hjCPqKasGC

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Sadly option 1 doesn’t hold up. We can take pictures of the light emission from GaN and when we do that we can see that dislocations and the areas around them emit a lot less light than material without defects. Dislocations do mess up the light emission in GaN.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Option 2: If the dislocations are a problem, something must stop the charge carriers from reaching them, and hence limit the damage they can do.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Option 2 has legs – there’s lots of experimental evidence suggesting that charge carriers in the InGaN quantum wells (which make up the light emitting bit of a nitride LED) can’t move around freely.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

The next big question was this: What is it about the structure of those InGaN quantum wells that prevents the charge carriers moving around?

03.12.2019 · Tweet

This is where the big controversy arose. Because there were some really interesting early electron microscopy images which suggested that the indium wasn’t spread out evenly through the InGaN quantum well layer. Instead, the indium atoms seemed to be in little clusters.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Those indium rich clusters would act to trap the charge carriers really effectively, and stop them moving to the defect sites. It sounded like a solution – but it wasn’t. Because later images, taken with other techniques showed no clusters at all.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Tomorrow, I’ll talk a bit about the different techniques that were used. The microscopy is really cool! For now, I’m going to admit that it all got a bit shouty. We scientists can be pretty passionate about our ideas. Not as calm and collected as you might expect! https://t.co/1OMCceyXh8

03.12.2019 · Tweet

In the end, most people agreed that the indium atoms were pretty evenly mixed through the InGaN quantum wells. Which meant no more fighting, but we were back where we started… not knowing what it was about the quantum wells that made the LEDs robust to defects!

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Here, it all gets a bit complicated. But basically, it turns out that you don’t need a lot of indium in a cluster to trap the carriers and keep them from moving to the defects. You just need a couple of indiums almost next to each other with a nitrogen between them.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

And that happens pretty often, even when the indiums and galliums are randomly mixed up through the crystal. It’s like if you’re throwing a dice. Throwing two sixes in a row happens quite a lot if you throw the dice a million times. https://t.co/FiLs1SDmcT

03.12.2019 · Tweet

It is in the very nature of the indium gallium nitride alloy that it can trap carriers. The natural disorder in the material is all it takes.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

That natural disorder is then vital to making LEDs work despite the prescence of loads of crystal defects. It’s a lucky throw of the dice, on which the multi-billion dollar LED industry relies.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Interestingly, the same natural disorder – and its impact on charge carriers – has also been blamed for the fact that green nitride LEDs are much less efficient than blue ones. But that’s another story!

03.12.2019 · Tweet

If you’ve made it to the end of this story, you might want to know that I talk about all this stuff in the extended version of the @RealSci_Nano podcast. Also, I’ll be giving a seminar on this and other LED topics in Bristol on Monday: https://t.co/EP1p8Hlb7N

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Tomorrow, I’ll tell you more about the microscopes we used to understand the nanoscale structure of LEDs. In the meantime, do feel free to ask me about LED technology. Other cool nitride folks on twitter who you might want to engage with are…

03.12.2019 · Tweet

From Tyndall in Cork, Ireland: @SarojPatrares who has done fantastic work on modelling the impact of nitride nanostructures on how carriers can move and combine in quantum wells.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

From Strathclyde in Scotland: @RobMartin100 – who uses scanning electron microscopy techniques to understand the effect of small scale structure of ntirides on light emission.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Also in Strathclyde these days: @FabienMassabuau who is a master of transmission electron microscopy on GaN – although he’s moving towards new wonder material gallium oxide these days!

03.12.2019 · Tweet

From Bristol: @CDTR_Bristol - The Center for Device Thermography and Reliability – who may not sound like a nitride group, but actually do excellent work on nitride electronics.

03.12.2019 · Tweet

Just looked back at my list of people to check out and realised that they’re all men. I’m sad but not surprised – gallium nitride is a very male dominated field. I’ll recommend fantastic female microscopers tomorrow!

04.12.2019 · Tweet

04.12.2019 · Tweet

If you enjoyed hearing about the controversial nature of the nanostructure in nitride quantum wells, have a listen to the extended podcast, where I talk about this story, in a lot more detail! https://t.co/zEWC02VTOl

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Good morning followers of all things nano! Today, I’m going to talk about how we characterise the nanoscale structure of nitride materials.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Yesterday – I made a really long thread about a major controversy in the nitride field about the nanoscale structure of InGaN quantum wells. You can read it here if you like: https://t.co/eWrPQF0gjv

04.12.2019 · Tweet

That controversy involved data from two amazing nanoscale microscopy techniques: transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT). I’m going to tell you a bit about each of them!

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Let’s start with TEM! TEM got a bit of a raw deal yesterday, because it resulted in some controversial observations which caused some heated debate in the field. Data from microscopes can be hard to interpret, but TEM is really an amazing technique!

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Many people will have used an optical microscope to magnify the features of a sample. Optical microscopes are great as long as the thing you want to look at is at the micrometer scale or bigger – so bigger than 1 millionth of a metre (or a thousandth of a mm). https://t.co/0X3Mvbxths

04.12.2019 · Tweet

But a standard optical microscope isn’t much use for looking at nanostructures. Light is a wave, and when the structures are smaller than its wavelength it becomes impossible to image them using a basic optical microscope.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

So, we need a wave with a shorter wavelength! And electrons (and other fundamental particles) behave as waves. If we accelerate the electrons to high speeds, they have a high energy and a very short wavelength. So we can use them to take really high resolution images. https://t.co/qrMRz8uGA0

04.12.2019 · Tweet

In a TEM, we fire the electrons through a very thin sample. This is like transmission light microscopy, where you shine a light through from below a transparent sample, and view it from above. Except in TEM we usually shine the electrons from the top and view from below.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Just like in an optical microscope, we need lenses. But we can’t use beautifully shaped pieces of glass. Instead we might use whopping great electromagnets to shape and direct the electron beam. We call them “electron lenses”. https://t.co/SMCHrPekvF

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Now steering electron beams isn’t easy, and the lenses don’t work perfectly. We call the imperfections due to the enses the lenses "aberrations", and the best TEMs have additional components called aberration correctors to deal with the problems they produce.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Once you get the electron optics right, the images can be truly astounding. This one was taken by @fabienmassabuau and you can see it on his twitter profile. It’s a picture of a GaN crystal, and every one of those white dots is a column of atoms viewed end on! https://t.co/B1MzQIiodN

04.12.2019 · Tweet

In that image, there is one mistake in the crystal – it’s a dislocation (the sort of defect I discussed yesterday) and you can see how it mucks up the regular repeating pattern of atoms. That mistake goes on, down a line, into the plane of the image.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

That raises a very important thing about TEM. We’re firing the electrons through the sample. That means that we are viewing everything in projection. And that can sometimes cause problems. https://t.co/V5JvCh7lrp

04.12.2019 · Tweet

There are techniques, like electron tomography, in which you rotate the sample and image it from multiple different angles, which seek to overcome this and get three-dimensional images.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Instead of getting into electron tomography, later on I’m going to talk about a completely different technique for nanoscale imaging in 3D: atom probe tomography. https://t.co/uumjmtoHtb

04.12.2019 · Tweet

The next nanoscale characterisation technique I want to talk about is atom probe tomography (APT), which is an amazing way of getting three dimensional compositional maps of materials.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Unlike TEM, APT bears essentially no resemblance to the traditional light microscope. For APT, we have to start with a very sharp needle of material, whose end is only about 100 nm across. These can be tricky to make, but it can be done! https://t.co/BmzvSzu2CG

04.12.2019 · Tweet

When a very sharp conductive object is raised to a high voltage, the electric field around the sharp end is huge, big enough to pull ions off the end of the spike. The process of pulling a material apart with an electric field is called “field evaporation.”

04.12.2019 · Tweet

In APT, we hold the very sharp specimen at a voltage just below the value needed to achieve field evaporation, and then add a pulse of extra energy to kick it up above that threshold very briefly.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

The extra energy can come from a pulse of additonal voltage, or a pulse of laser light focussed on the tip of the sample. For semiconductor materials, we tend to use the laser approach.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

If we’re lucky, the pulse of extra energy will evaporate one single ion. It will fly out from the end of the tip along a trajectory defined by the electric field and land on a detector.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

The position where the ion lands on the detector can be traced back to tell us where it must have come from on the specimen. That basically gives us its x and y coordinate.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Because you have to evaporate the ions at the end of the needle before you evaporate ions from lower down, the order in which the ions evaporate gives you information about the depth into the sample from which they arise: the z-coordinate.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Now, to get a compositional map, we just need to know what the ion is. We can figure that out from its mass, and we can figure out its mass from how long it took to fly to the detector. Heavier ions go slower.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

With a certain amount of mathematical jiggery pokery, we can identify where the ion came from in 3D space and what it’s mass and hence chemical identity are. So, we can build a 3D compositional map.

04.12.2019 · Tweet

Like this data on InGaN quantum wells from the first ever atom probe tomography experiment on nitride semiconductors. A classic! Turquoise dots are Ga atoms, orange dots are indium. Green is gold from where we messed up the sample prep! https://t.co/h0fUk89uVT

04.12.2019 · Tweet

APT has historically mostly been used to study metals, like in the beautiful image of steel below. But increasingly it’s used for a very wide range of materials. I’ve even met a researcher who is trying to do APT on chocolate! https://t.co/6CXhycghez

04.12.2019 · Tweet

I'll be back a bit later to introduce you to some of the fabulous microscopists who work on these types of data!

@Maryam_Eslami Thank you!!

05.12.2019 · Tweet

I’m a bit short of time today – some of my lovely collaborators are visiting to talk about current and future projects. Just time to squeeze in a quick thread before our discussions begin!

05.12.2019 · Tweet

Earlier in the week, I talked a lot about nitride light emitting diodes, which can make a huge difference to the amount of energy we spend on lighting our homes and workplaces. So GaN already does a lot for us, but what else can it help with?

05.12.2019 · Tweet

Loads of things! Power transistors based on GaN are also really efficient and can be used to make things like laptop charges more smaller efficient. (More about GaN-based chargers here: https://t.co/LE3qS3ZAkm)

05.12.2019 · Tweet

Other applications of GaN transistors include being used in amplifiers in mobile phone base stations and in power conversion in electric vehicles. (More about GaN in the automotive industry here: https://t.co/lE0B6x9hT8)

05.12.2019 · Tweet

GaN-based laser diodes are at the heart of “BluRay” technology and are also used in displays and even in industrial applications like welding.

05.12.2019 · Tweet

Ultra-violet LEDs based on GaN are being developed, and can kill or damage many of the bugs which can infect drinking water, particularly in the developing world, causing sickness and death, so GaN may in future be widely used for water purification. (https://t.co/B3uFtRIoR0)

05.12.2019 · Tweet

My group is even developing GaN LEDs which emit precisely one photon (the fundamental quantum light particle) on demand, and these single photon emitters could be used in future secure communications technologies!

05.12.2019 · Tweet

So increasingly, GaN is all around us: saving energy, cleaning water, transmitting data, and lighting up our world! And all of these applications require us to understand and engineer the nanoscale structure of this amazing material!

06.12.2019 · Tweet

When @RealSci_Nano asked me what my three wishes were to improve the world of science I said "Equality. Diversity. Inclusion." If they'd offered me a fourth wish, I would have said "Accessibility".

06.12.2019 · Tweet

I could have spent all week talking about my passion for #equality, #diversity, #inclusion & #accessibility in STEMM! However, I also wanted to talk science! If you'd like to know more about my work & passion in this area, head over to @TIGERinSTEMM or to: https://t.co/0YOqFxjoF6

06.12.2019 · Tweet

TIGERS - The Inclusion Group for Equity in Research in STEMM - is a grass roots collective which campaigns for a more inclusive future for science. We've just published a document - led by @DrJessBoland - about accessibility in STEMM, with particular focus on funding processes.

06.12.2019 · Tweet

Please do read the document, and if you have a disability, let us know what we've missed by joining the discussion on @tigerinstemm: https://t.co/6AhE2TnFsz

06.12.2019 · Tweet

Before I got involved in @tigerinstemm, I hadn't really thought about the barriers disabled people face in scientific research. The more I learn about this, the more shocked I am at how poorly we accommodate talented scientists who happen to have a disability.

06.12.2019 · Tweet

TIGERS are focused on funding processes currently, so here are just a few of the things I have learnt about accessibility issues around UK funding processes:

06.12.2019 · Tweet

1. Blind and visually impaired researchers use screen readers to access web-pages and documents. However, the main UK funder, @UKRI_News, uses a web-portal for grant submission which is incompatible with screen readers.

06.12.2019 · Tweet

2. Similarly, when @UKRI_News publishes grant guidance, they use a pdf format which is also incompatible with screen readers. 3. Sometimes grant info comes on a video instead... but those videos are not subtitled, so deaf researchers can't access them.

06.12.2019 · Tweet

4. Some grant processes require interviews. If your disability makes it difficult for you to travel to an interview, you can dial in remotely. But if the technology doesn't work within 5 minutes of the interview start time, your interview will be cancelled.

06.12.2019 · Tweet

(How often do any of us get a Skype conference working within 5 minutes? It usually takes me at least 10 minutes of swearing).

06.12.2019 · Tweet

5. If you need extra funding for accommodations for a disability, you can request that - but you have to put it in your main proposals documents. Which is a bit like writing "HEY, I HAVE A DISABILITY, DISCRIMINATE AGAINST ME!" across your Justification of Resources document.

06.12.2019 · Tweet

I could go on, but if you want to know about this stuff you'd be far better reading the TIGERS report which was written and reviewed by actual disabled people: https://t.co/6AhE2TnFsz

06.12.2019 · Tweet

So I'll stop here, but say this: whilst there are a lot of other issues facing disabled scientists, the system problems above are all really fixable. So why aren't we fixing them?? Answers on a postcard to @tigerinstemm please!

06.12.2019 · Tweet

Well folks, I hope you've enjoyed hearing a little bit about what I've been learning about the (lack of) accessibility of STEM today!

06.12.2019 · Tweet

Another part of my developing understanding of #diversity and #inclusion in STEM is that it's important that all scientists have time for themselves, their families and their other interests...

On Thursday of this week I'll talk a little more about the teaching side of what I do, and how a materials research program can fit into a place where teaching is (formally) 80% of what I do.

I did both my undergraduate and graduate work in the @UWMadisonMSE program at @UWMadison. https://t.co/3AjTqFfxqH

09.12.2019 · Tweet

@UWMadisonMSE @UWMadison One of the things that got me hooked on science & materials research was the idea that I could contribute something new to society. Early in my undergraduate career I was given the task to metallographically polish and calculate the void density of a wire cable.

09.12.2019 · Tweet

@UWMadisonMSE @UWMadison I calculated a value and brought it to my research mentor. "Is this right?" I asked him. He looked at me like I had just landed from another planet. "I don't know," he said, "no one's ever done this before."

09.12.2019 · Tweet

@UWMadisonMSE @UWMadison That was it - I was hooked. I was doing something new...was creating knowledge that had never before existed in the history of the planet. So far no one's given me a Nobel Prize for polishing that cable sample, but it started me on my journey in science.

09.12.2019 · Tweet

@UWMadisonMSE @UWMadison It just takes a nudge, folks.

09.12.2019 · Tweet

@UWMadisonMSE @UWMadison I think what was most significant to me about that was not just that I was learning something new, but that the whole world (in my mind) was going to be trusting my methodology and technique to decide "if it's right."

09.12.2019 · Tweet

@UWMadisonMSE @UWMadison I didn't really understand the whole scientific process of peer review and replication at that point, but I did understand that it was important that I sweat the details and get them right. A little responsibility can be tremendously empowering for a student.

09.12.2019 · Tweet

@UWMadisonMSE @UWMadison In graduate school I studied the chemical and mechanical properties of superconductors, an extraordinary class of materials that can conduct electricity without resistance. Here's the obligatory YouTube video on how they work: https://t.co/0U4iZS1shf

09.12.2019 · Tweet

@UWMadisonMSE @UWMadison That introductory video does a good job explaining the physics of superconductivity, but what it misses is the primarly application: to make big magnets.

09.12.2019 · Tweet

@UWMadisonMSE @UWMadison Floating a superconductor above a magnet (the Meissner effect) is a nice party trick, but what really makes them useful is the high electric current densities they can carry when in a wire form.

09.12.2019 · Tweet

@UWMadisonMSE @UWMadison Wind a superconducting wire into a solenoid or other shape, push a bunch of electricity through it, and you have a really big magnet. The largest steady-state magnets in the world are all superconducting. Much more on that tomorrow.

09.12.2019 · Tweet

10.12.2019 · Tweet

Today we're looking at applications of superconductivity. Specifically, how do nano-engineered superconducting materials enable some of the biggest science projects on the planet?

10.12.2019 · Tweet

Application of superconductivity #1: Particle physics It turns out that if you want to know what something is made of, smash it! Physicists have utilized this highly scientific idea for decades to explore the structure of the atoms that make up our Universe.

10.12.2019 · Tweet

And the biggest atom-smasher we've built so far is the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at @CERN. Here's a nice write-up on the LHC and what it does: https://t.co/NCjSqx9dHB

10.12.2019 · Tweet

@CERN There's a basic challenge with this design of particle collider...you need to move the particles, in a circle, at something approaching the speed of light. To do this without blowing a hole in the side of your very expensive device, you need to BEND and FOCUS the particle beam.

10.12.2019 · Tweet

@CERN Enter superconductivity. Superconducting NbTi wire is used to create dipole magnets that each generate around 7 Tesla (T) of magnetic field. A 1 T magnet is strong enough to lift a small car, so these things put your refrigerator magnets to shame.

10.12.2019 · Tweet

@CERN There are over 1300 of these dipole magnets in the LHC ring, and each one weighs 35 tons and is 15 meters long! Here's a short video of CERN engineers manipulating one of the dipole magnets during LHC construction. https://t.co/UlPkUyG67q

10.12.2019 · Tweet

@CERN Without superconductors, the LHC ring would have to be much larger in size (and thus much more expensive), and the energy cost to run the magnets would be prohibitive.

10.12.2019 · Tweet

@CERN So superconductivity is one important "enabling" technology for particle physics. In the 10 years it has been running, the LHC has realized a number of important discoveries, most significantly the discovery of the Higgs boson. https://t.co/NGRKBVryl5

10.12.2019 · Tweet

Application of superconductivity #2: Fusion energy! The old joke is that fusion is 30 years away....and always will be. But in fact there are a number of feasible fusion projects in construction right now, and superconductivity is a big piece of making them possible.

10.12.2019 · Tweet

The big big big fusion project is ITER (@iterorg) in southern France. This machine is attempting to generate net-positive fusion energy and (just as important), sustain the fusion reaction for 500 seconds. https://t.co/zQ8LXimzk0

10.12.2019 · Tweet

@iterorg I did a postdoc at ITER and worked on their magnet system. Enormous cables of NbTi and Nb3Sn superconducting wires are used to levitate and stir the plasma. https://t.co/VEwEK9vHvm

10.12.2019 · Tweet

@iterorg The 500 tons of Nb3Sn needed for ITER were the largest procurement of that material in history...by far! Manufacturing all that complex, composite wire involved eight manufacturers in six countries. We spent a lot of time in airplanes.

10.12.2019 · Tweet

@iterorg The key point to understand is that if you tried to generate the ITER magnetic fields with conventional (e.g. copper) magnets, you would need *many* gigawatts of electric power, and you would never achieve break-even fusion.

10.12.2019 · Tweet

@iterorg This is a theme for superconductivity: these big science projects (like the LHC or ITER) are already massive in scale. But without superconductors, their size and cost would be absurdly enormous, or (in the case of ITER), they simply could never achieve their design goal.

10.12.2019 · Tweet

Hey look at that...those big LHC superconducting magnets we were talking about earlier today? They're getting an updgrade: https://t.co/SuWWeoxJnn

11.12.2019 · Tweet

Application of superconductivity #3 - medicine! https://t.co/SN6yMVmMmz

11.12.2019 · Tweet

You've maybe spent some time inside a superconducting magnet and didn't even realize it. The largest commercial application of superconductors, by far, is in MRI machines in hospitals.

11.12.2019 · Tweet

The big doughnut of the MRI machine is a helium-cooled, NbTi superconducting magnet. https://t.co/pvqsOAN7wq

11.12.2019 · Tweet

MRI machines require a highly *stable* magnetic field. With a conventional electromagnet, the magnetic field can vary slightly due to variations ("ripple") in the voltage powering the magnet.

11.12.2019 · Tweet

But with a superconductor, you can charge the magnet, and then actually *remove* the electrical leads, and the current will continue flowing in the magnet. https://t.co/08s2mNC5t2

11.12.2019 · Tweet

This "persistence" of the superconducting current flow is a crazy physics trick, but it is also technologically critical for MRIs. Producing an accurate MRI image requires knowing the magnetic field value in the magnet bore to something like 1 part per million.

11.12.2019 · Tweet

So it's superconductors to the rescue...generating a high, stable, and uniform magnetic field that allows doctors to take that peek inside your body without having to, you know, actually take a peek. https://t.co/luOMkzF5My

11.12.2019 · Tweet

Superconductors are also being used to make proton therapy - a more precise and farr less invasive form of radiation therapy for cancer patients - more accessible. https://t.co/baU5CWa6uf

11.12.2019 · Tweet

Proton therapy requires manipulating a beam of protons so they can be deposited exactly at the tumor location in a human body. But bending and focusing proton beams takes...wait for it...big magnets.

11.12.2019 · Tweet

As a result, there are just a few dozen proton therapy clinics in the U.S. The treatment is massively expensive. Compact superconducting magnets will help make proton therapy more widely available by reducing the size of the machine and lowering the cost.

11.12.2019 · Tweet

So there's lots going on in the world of superconductivity...in physics, in fusion, and in medicine. How does this all relate to nanotechnology? Well it turns out we design these superconductors at the nanoscale to get the properties we need to enable all these advances.

11.12.2019 · Tweet

Stay tuned for more on how we do that! https://t.co/TCyyo9MPk1

11.12.2019 · Tweet

@ClaraMBarker @StemCorps https://t.co/UsZvJWizMe

11.12.2019 · Tweet

@ClaraMBarker @StemCorps [admin] "Tons of nanomaterials: Big science and little details" Extended podcast 🎙️ with Matthew Jewell @Prof_Jewell out now! Check it out: https://t.co/A8f4zCiJxk

13.12.2019 · Tweet

Superconductors are used to build some of the largest science projects on the planet. But they are also exquisitely engineered at the nanoscale. Today we'll see how!

13.12.2019 · Tweet

To help me, I'll be utilizing images from the incomparable Peter Lee at Florida State University. Check out his full gallery of superconductor microstructures here: https://t.co/vpYVFkqZId

13.12.2019 · Tweet

Let's start with the workhorse: NbTi. A high-current NbTi wire is comprised of thousands of individual Nb-47 wt.% Ti filaments in a Cu matrix. But there's a lot going on in every single one of those little strands.... https://t.co/xoj0DpRCEX

13.12.2019 · Tweet

Magnetic flux in superconductors is quantitzed, and those quanta of flux need to be "pinned", or held in place, to prevent heat generation when current flows in the superconductor. In NbTi, this is done by engineering in ribbons of alpha-Ti in the NbTi matrix. https://t.co/fa8fHJ7NGZ

13.12.2019 · Tweet

This is a great triumph of metallurgy...the alpha-Ti precipitates are strain-induced, meaning they develop as the wire is drawn. So the original billet and the desired final wire size have to be engineered to cause just the right amount of Ti precipitation.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

Too little Ti and the precipitate spacing won't match nicely the quantitized flux line lattice spacing. Too much Ti and the superconductivity starts to degrade. The LHC was able to be designed and built in the 1990s because NbTi was metallurgically optimized in the 1980s.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

Next up is my personal favorite, Nb3Sn. Nb3Sn powers the toroidal field and central solenoid magnet systems of the ITER fusion reactor, under construction in southern France. Like NbTi, Nb3Sn is used by the ton in cables that carry thousands of amps of current... https://t.co/XgewnbsPsr

13.12.2019 · Tweet

...and like NbTi, Nb3Sn is able to do it's job because it's been engineered at the nanoscale. In Nb3Sn, there are two competing forces. First, the phase itself has some significant solid solubility. In other words, it doesn't exist only at 25 at.% Sn.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

The phase can be tin deficient, down to about 18 at.% Sn. This is a problem, because the superconductivity degrades as the tin content drops off. So metallurgically we want to keep the tin content in the Nb3Sn filaments as high and as uniform as possible.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

So, metallurgy students, how do you get and maintain a high, uniform Sn content? Consult a phase diagram and a kinetics textbook, and you'll agree that what we want is a LONG and HOT heat treatment, which for Nb3Sn might be something like 700C.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

So what's the problem? Well the problem are the individual Nb3Sn grains. Here they are shown in grey, in a false-colored (red) Cu matrix. Just like in NbTi, we need to pin the quantitized flux somehow. In Nb3Sn that's done mostly via the grain boundaries. https://t.co/uarWPIxhkL

13.12.2019 · Tweet

So for maximum flux pinning, we'd like a very fine grain structure, i.e. the formation heat treatment should be as SHORT and as LOW TEMP as possible!

13.12.2019 · Tweet

That's the basic challenge with Nb3Sn. We need temperature and time to form the phase via a diffusional heat treatment with high Sn content, but all that diffusion goodness also grows the grain size. What are we to do?

13.12.2019 · Tweet

Well we put our engineer hats on, that's what. We've found a few ways to outsmart the material. For example, we can: 1. Keep the filaments small (a few microns in diameter). This reduces the diffusion distances, allowing phase formation to happen without excessive grain growth.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

2. We can introduced precipitates (artificial pinning centers, or APCs) that both help to pin the quantitized magnetic flux, and also help supress grain growth.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

3. Last, we go for lower temps and longer times in our heat treatments, since diffusion is exponential with temperature but parabolic (square root dependence) with time.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

Not every Nb3Sn conductor employs all these strategies (for example the ITER material does not utilize APCs), but together they represent a toolbox that allows us to design a micro- and nano-structure that maximizes the current we can push through the wire.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

For example, the ITER Nb3Sn wire can carry about 1,000 A/mm^2 at 12 Tesla and 4.2 K, and Nb3Sn wires designed for high energy physics applications (such as the upcoming luminosity upgrade for the LHC) can carry around 3,000 A/mm^2.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

That's some serious current density! https://t.co/cRiKvcegdq

13.12.2019 · Tweet

The materials scientists who brought you beautifully optimized NbTi and Nb3Sn figured they had earned at least a nice vacation. But those dang magnet builders are never satisfied...they just want more and more current in smaller and smaller spaces. https://t.co/LXf3JipfNX

13.12.2019 · Tweet

So now we are cooking up a whole new generation of "high" temperature superconductors ("high" is a relative term...here we typically mean that it can operate in liquid nitrogen at 77 K or higher) with even more extreme current densities.

13.12.2019 · Tweet

And - you guessed it - each of those requires carefully engineered chemistry and structures at the nanoscale to get the most out of the material. It can get...dizzying. https://t.co/5fMbMBwrsM
