All right, got busy with actual work during most of the day today, but I guess let's start talking about magnetism. But first, an important announcement in a RT to follow for my USian tweeps.

17.12.2019 · RT

RT @DrLothar: This thread! @cmclymer is rallying the troops to fight an impending regulation change to allow discrimination against our LGB…

17.12.2019 · Tweet

So if we're going to talk about magnets, we need to know about magnetism. I can't really do better by way of simple explanation that National Geographic, so I'm not going to try: https://t.co/kJWmWoqj1O

17.12.2019 · Tweet

In sum - electrons have a property called "spin," and you can think of this like spinning a basketball on your finger (SHOOSH PHYSICISTS I KNOW!). If you have one ball spinning clockwise and the other spinning counterclockwise at the same speed, the sum of the spins is 0.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

The same is true with electrons - if electrons are paired up they have opposite spins (+/- or ↑/↓ or ɑ/β) and the net spin of the system is 0. If electrons are unpaired, the net spin of the system is not zero. Non-zero spin = magnetism.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

That's the gist, anyway. Things can be more complicated than that, but for our purposes at the molecular level that's what we care about. Okay, great. Well... there's more than one kind of magnetism and that's where things start to get funky.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

I'm going to link you to the Wikipedia page on magnetism, but only because the references are okay. It's really jargony and I'm new to working a lot on magnetic systems myself. https://t.co/6lwLryKq9E

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Broke the thread because I am a foolish fool. https://t.co/eQQRwmIGYk

17.12.2019 · Tweet

So, there are several kinds of magnetism and we should talk about a few of them so we can start talking more about the magnetic properties of nanoparticles tomorrow.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Diamagnetism - we usually think of it as all the spins being paired up so the system doesn't magnetize in response to a magnet. Think of a block of wood, or a gold watch band.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Paramagnetism - there are unpaired electrons. What's that mean? Non-zero spin and therefore magnetism. They'll magnetize when exposed to a magnet, but when the magnet goes away don't remain magnetic.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Ferromagnetism - This basically means "magnetic like iron." There are unpaired spins in ferromagnetic systems just like in paramagnets, but ferromagnetic materials can be made into permanent magnets below a certain temperature.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

In ferromagnets spins near each other align parallel* to each other. ↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑ Because the spins all point in the same direction, they add together. *technically the moments of neighboring magnetic domains, but that starts to get REAL complicated.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

There's also ANTIferromagnetism. Those are systems where there are unpaired electrons but the overall spin is zero because the spins of individual unpaired electrons align anti-parallel: ↑↑↓↓↑↑↓↓↑↑

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Lastly there's ferrimagnetism. This one is the weirdest because it has properties of both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic systems depending on temperature.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Ferrimagnets, like ferromagnets, will remain magnetic after they've been exposed to a magnetic field if they are cold enough. HOWEVER like antiferromagnets, their spins tend to align anti-parallel if left to their own devices.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

This can happen because of the structure of ferrimagnetic materials - in a sense there are more spins aligned one direction than in the opposite.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Ferrimagnetism and another property called SUPERPARAMAGNETISM will be important when I talk about the nanoparticles I'm working on tomorrow.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Good morning everyone! Light I left off with a brief intro to magnetic materials written from the perspective of a chemist who is pretty new to working on magnets. https://t.co/eImttztZuA

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Today I want to get into why anybody would care about nanoscale magnets and what some of the goals of my present research are. As always, any opinions expressed are mine alone and do not reflect any position of the DoE, Sandia Lab, or NTESS.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

I mentioned superparamagnetism yesterday, and I want to take a second to explain what that means. So there's a super jargony Wiki page, like one might expect - https://t.co/KNveIZ4X5Q

17.12.2019 · Tweet

In terms that make sense to me, a person without a degree in physics and who hasn't done math more complicated than calculus in years, it's like all the spins in nanoparticles are acting like one GIANT spin.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

If you have a nanoparticle made of a ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic material - like magnetite, say - the spins will all couple up so the particle will have what we call a single magnetic domain.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

More or less that means that when you put them into a magnetic field they behave a lot like paramagnets but they respond more. Their susceptibility to external magnetic influence is higher.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Unsurprisingly, we call how much a sample responds to an external magnetic field its "magnetic susceptibility." Higher susceptibility can be important for a lot of things - data storage, medical imaging, electronics.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Susceptibility is also related to another property that can be important for how your magnets perform called hysteresis. Again, I'll give you a link to the wiki for the references: https://t.co/niE0tCRZid

17.12.2019 · Tweet

So we've talked about how magnetic materials will respond to other magnets, well, if you put them in a strong enough magnetic field the magnetic moment of your sample will align with the direction of the external field.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

It's not unlike how a magnetic compass works, but you're using a field you generated rather than the earth's magnetic field. And if you have ever used a compass, you've probably noticed that there is a delay between when you turn and the needle moving to a new position.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

If you take magnetic particles, put them in a big magnetic field, and then change the orientation of that magnetic field while observing your sample's magnetic orientation you'll see a delay as well. Your sample won't instantly realign with the field, it'll take some time.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

We measure how magnetized the sample remains as we change the field strength and orientation, and that tells us about the magnetic behavior of our particles. Sometimes you want a lot of hysteresis - like with a hard drive - in our case, we want none.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Why would particles that respond nearly instantly to the orientation of a magnetic field be useful? That's going to have to wait until I've gotten some science going in the lab.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

All right, I have my experiment going and it's going to have to run for most of the rest of the day, so let's talk about why having particles with no hysteresis can be useful. https://t.co/HLA2yW4rEq

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Transformers are a part of the electrical grid, I'm sure everyone knows this. Some hang on power poles in your neighborhood, some are huge and centralized somewhere in the grid.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Transformers change the voltage between the input and the output - for instance taking the high voltage transmission power from the lines outside down to something usable in your house. In the US residential voltage is 120/240 V.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

What does that have to do with magnetic nanoparticles? Well, a key part of a transformer is an inductor, which is basically a magnet with some wire wrapped around it. These are often called cores. Inductors store energy when current is passed through them.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Inductors also appear on circuit boards, in radios, etc, for a variety of different applications. I'm not an electrical engineer, so my knowledge of this stuff is a bit sparse, but the point is that inductors are important and that inductors are made of magnets.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

Well, because electric current and magnetism are really the same thing - the electromagnetic force (one of only four fundamental forces in the universe no matter what some cranks in Austria say), the magnetic field of an inductor responds to the field generated by current.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

As the current changes so does the field it generates, and the inductor's magnetic moment will follow it - like the compass responding to the Earth's magnetic field.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

And as we may remember from earlier, there's a bit of a delay in the response. Over time, this adds up and the inductor's magnet gets less and less synchronized with the current's field. That leads to a loss of stored energy. https://t.co/uBGFMmJ8KE

17.12.2019 · Tweet

As time passes you get a build up of magnetization in the inductor, leading to hysteresis like we talked about early. The higher the hysteresis the greater the loss of energy in your inductor, leading to worse efficiency.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

To bring this back around to nanoparticles - superparamagnetic nanoparticles have almost no hysteresis (ideally none) at ambient temperatures. So if we could make inductors out of superparamagnetic particles we could massively improve efficiency across all kinds of applications.

17.12.2019 · Tweet

The big one is large transformers in the power grid, which are something like 80% efficient if I remember correctly. The transformers in your neighborhood are about 96% efficient, but because there are so many small gains represent major energy savings.

18.12.2019 · Tweet

Today I while I have some time during the day I want to talk a bit about what I actually do. By training, I am a synthetic chemist. That means that I take molecules we don't like, and use chemistry to turn them into molecules or materials we want.

But, the reason I've spent so much time earlier in the week talking about magnets is that at the moment I'm working on magnetic iron oxide particles.

18.12.2019 · Tweet

We're interested in magnetic nanoparticles because magnets are super important to the modern world, like I mentioned yesterday. https://t.co/BPvwiuUYZH

18.12.2019 · Tweet

One problem in magnetic nanoparticle synthesis is reproducibility. Another is size control - both in terms of getting the desired size and in having a narrow size distribution.

18.12.2019 · Tweet

These two problems exist across a lot of nanoscience, but can be particularly troublesome for iron-based particles. Why? Well, FeNP synthesis is usually done at really high temperatures, like 350 °C high. At that kind of temp, all kinds of things happen, it's a mess.

18.12.2019 · Tweet

You also run into issues of thermal transport - it is really hard to keep your reaction vessel a consistent temperature when it's that high.

18.12.2019 · Tweet

So how do we overcome the temperature challenge? By using a molten metal bath! Our awesome tech (BIG UPS TO TECHNOLOGISTS & TECHNICIANS!) converts soldier pots for use with some custom software he wrote & high performance thermocouples.

18.12.2019 · Tweet

As a result, the group developed a pretty cool and very reliable synthesis of magnetite nanoparticles a few years back. https://t.co/DE3KPBjW18

18.12.2019 · Tweet

Not everyone will have access to that paper (I am happy to send a pdf if you don't, just let me know), but there are some pretty cool images I think are worth seeing. All the scale bars are 20 nm. https://t.co/iee7Qu6wfv

18.12.2019 · Tweet

These images are from a transmission electron microscope (TEM), that we use to see stuff too small for optical microscopy. As you can see the drip-feed synthesis the group developed makes very regular particles with size predictable by reaction time.

18.12.2019 · Tweet

And also in that third image look at how nice and hexagonally close packed those spheres are! Symmetry is fun.

18.12.2019 · Tweet

If you want to know more about electronmicroscopy, I can't say enough good things about Grant Jensen's lectures. He's a professor at Cat Tech, and what he's put up on YouTube is a really great way to get started (it's how I learned the basics). https://t.co/VxWTTbQIfo

18.12.2019 · Tweet

So, the group developed this extended FeNP synthesis a few years back, so what am I working on? Well, it's an update to that procedure that is easier to do. I'm also working on making particles that don't just contain iron, materials called ferrites.

18.12.2019 · Tweet

Because of my interests and experience I'm trying to control particle size in our new synthesis, figure out the best way to incorporate other transition metals, and the best ways to stick different stuff to the surfaces to make the particles better for inductor applications.

18.12.2019 · Tweet

I can't show you any of the results from those experiments for a few reasons - mostly they're not published or in a publishable state yet. But, because I work at Sandia, any photo I release has to go through an approval process that can take some time.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

ETEM is "environmental TEM" it allows us to do things like flow gas into the microscope and look at reactions in progress. 4D STEM is a technique that collects just A TON of data and lets you understand really fine details about your samples. https://t.co/L7z0wXBcBX

19.12.2019 · Tweet

Hello all, good morning, I haven't had as much time to tweet this week as I had hoped, but that's good for my life here at the science factory! As always opinions of mine do not represent SNL, DoE or NTESS.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

Yesterday one of the microscopists here got some really nice images showing that I'd made particles without any surface oxidation. They're an intermediate of our synthesis of magnetite, which is why we're interested in them. Understanding how these convert to magnetite is good.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

So the result from yesterday means today we're doing Environmental TEM on the samples. We'll be exposing these nanoparticles to gas while they're in the TEM and observing what happens. Some serious #RealTimeChem to help us understand more about our particle synthesis.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

I'm pretty excited because it took a few tries to get the particle quality we needed. I synthesized them in a molten metal bath under nitrogen, capped them, pumped them down on my hi-vacuum line, and immediately put them in our inert glove box.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

I had to build a custom nitrogen tent around the metal bath, and figure out how to get the mechanical stirrer setup so not to interfere with it and also not melt the plastic on the 350 °C metal. I wish I could post the pictures, but I'd get in a serious amount of hot water.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

The nitrogen tent was needed because you do part of the reaction with your flask open under nitrogen flow to cook off some of the stuff from the precursors, so I needed a way to have an inert atmosphere around the reaction vessel while I did that.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

After the reaction was done and I had them in the glovebox, I had to figure out how to purify them. Normally we use a centrifuge, so I had to track down a very tiny centrifuge that I pumped into the box.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

Once I had the tiny centrifuge and some tiny centrifuge tubes in the box, it was a matter of repeatedly precipitating, centrifuging, and resuspending the particles. Over the course of 10 washes I got essentially all of the stuff we didn't want off of them.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

Next our microscopist pumped a special kind of holder into the glovebox, it keeps samples inert and he used that to load our sample into the ETEM. Once it was in the instrument, it could just sit there because it's under a pretty hard vacuum.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

Today we're flowing gas to look at some surface reactions. We'll probably get some video, but it's 2 GB per second so we won't get long videos. We'll definitely get some high quality images every few minutes.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

The computer setup running this microscope (the instrument is from FEI) has a half a terabyte of RAM and a 40 TB storage setup. It can't be connected to a network for security reasons, so with huge file sizes it needs a lot of local storage.

19.12.2019 · Tweet

And now I'm off for lab cleanup day! Sandia does an official shutdown from 25 Dec to 2 Jan, so my last day of work for the year is Tuesday next week. As such, we're cleaning the labs today and tomorrow so everything is in a nice state when we get back, and safe for the break.

06.01.2020 · Tweet

06.01.2020 · Tweet

She had offered me a PhD working on multiferroics, a hot topic at the time, but I specifically requested to continue the electronic multipole project from a year earlier. She said "This is not sexy science. Few people will read your papers. But if you are passionate, then fine."

06.01.2020 · Tweet

This has informed how I talk to students who come and ask me for PhD references. It's really important to think about where the research in your project fits into the global scientific paradigm. 'Sexy' science is more likely to lead to papers which get you an academic job.

06.01.2020 · Tweet

At the same time, if you find that project boring, it wont sustain your interest for 4 LONG gruelling years. So you need to balance that tension along with how you feel about the group you work with and your supervisor.

Crystals are a pretty fascinating topic for a lot of people, but for a lot of different reasons. People recognise some things as being crystals (i.e. the image above) but not a lot of other common materials - iron / steel, rocks, many sands, etc.

06.01.2020 · Tweet

Even a lot of plants have some degree of crystallinity in their cellulose fibres! But of course, this gets to what it means to be a crystal as far as scientists think: being a crystal is about being ordered and regular at the atomic and molecular scale.

06.01.2020 · Tweet

Lets take a pretty common example: table salt! A lot of people might remember that table salt has the chemical name sodium chloride, which means it is made up of equal parts from the elements sodium and chlorine. https://t.co/KgSNgPZrfI

06.01.2020 · Tweet

Salt has another name: Halite! Theres not a huge difference between what we call salt or halite (im sure the geologists will have something to teach me on this, but im talking broad brushstrokes). https://t.co/1Nn4N7B57I

06.01.2020 · Tweet

In both cases, when you zoom in to the atomic scale, they look like this (but obviously without colour!) https://t.co/BpWGel2qhK

06.01.2020 · Tweet

The regular structure of crystals is extremely helpful for physicists like me, because it means we can mostly get away with understanding what happens in one little bit of the crystal - by the principle of symmetry it is enforced to be the same everywhere except the surface https://t.co/BlPAysaMu1

06.01.2020 · Tweet

not all materials are so simple, however. Most high temperature superconductors have a very complicated crystal structure! https://t.co/BMbIqDs1zD

06.01.2020 · Tweet

@tonyver45 There really is! The mathematics of group theory was developed mostly in the early 20th century. It has very deep applications in quantum physics but also in the study of crystal structure.

06.01.2020 · Tweet

@tonyver45 You can use group theory to show, for instance, that there are only 230 possible three dimensional crystal structures! And by relating the symmetry of properties like magnetism and the symmetry of crystals, you can tell if a given crystal can display a particular property

06.01.2020 · Tweet

@tonyver45 This has been especially useful in studying multiferroic materials, which display magnetism AND a property called ferro electricity. There are only a handful of crystal structures which can support both

06.01.2020 · Tweet

Okay, theres been a bit of a break because I had to change countries and the lack of sleep has left me a bit frazzled, but I am here to do my best to explain the phenomenon of magnetism! https://t.co/Fomslgeq6l

08.01.2020 · Tweet

To start, I will take the humble bar magnet. And then I will do terrible things to it https://t.co/ifP0fowlAZ

08.01.2020 · Tweet

What would happen if we cut our bar magnet in half? The universe does not permit the separate existence of a north and a south magnetic pole, so you must end up with two separate bar magnets! https://t.co/2zfL4ktJ57

08.01.2020 · Tweet

BUT WHAT IF WE KEEP CUTTING!?! https://t.co/hHPN5N3bg6

08.01.2020 · Tweet

It turns out that the very atoms in a bar magnet behave themselves like bar magnets! If you really wanted you could keep going beyond the level of atoms, down to electrons and subatomic particles, but this is detail that isnt necessary for us. https://t.co/SZoEl3ybRd

08.01.2020 · Tweet

This is due to a quantum mechanical feature of particles could Spin: electrons have it, and because electrons can be either paired (with an electron that has opposite spin) or unpaired, atoms with unpaired electrons will tend to have a spin and can thus show magnetism. https://t.co/vaTWfFG8Rf

08.01.2020 · Tweet

atoms having a magnetic moment like this is fairly common, so we might wonder why more materials arent magnetic. But when we look at two atoms next to each other, theres a lot of different ways they could be aligned right? Why one and not others? https://t.co/A5bV1Vsb1K

08.01.2020 · Tweet

The detailed answer requires a pretty astonishing amount of quantum mechanical calculation, but it actually turns out you can often reduce this problem to an interaction that says: the atomic magnets want to be either parallel, or antiparallel, and antiparallel usually wins!

08.01.2020 · Tweet

But this is based on a fairly simple idea where each atom only cares what the atoms right next to it are doing. What if you care about what atoms further away are doing? Well, then it gets very complex! But my favourite result is the spin spiral: https://t.co/cyqMnJl3le

08.01.2020 · Tweet

Spin spirals can happen for lots of reasons, but the simplest one is that you want to be antiparallel to your neighbour, and to your neighbours-neighbour (the next-nearest neighbour). Spin spirals happen in a lot of materials, especially one with rare-earth elements.

08.01.2020 · Tweet

Its also easy if you have simple geometries: you can be antiparallel to all of your neighbours in a chain, or on a square (or cube) but what about in a triangle? https://t.co/OM8Zped11j

08.01.2020 · Tweet

The triangle has two possibilities, depending on whether the little atomic magnets are free to rotate or not - we call this magnetic anisotropy, and it basically is just about whether there is a cost to change your direction and how large is that cost.

08.01.2020 · Tweet

When that cost is low, we get this, and everyone is happy. https://t.co/SC9Qo1aurk

08.01.2020 · Tweet

When the cost is high - when the atomic magnets can only point in a single direction and be either up or down, there is actually no nice solution at all! We call this kind of system geometrically frustrated. https://t.co/R0ZiQG6NPQ

08.01.2020 · Tweet

Although the atomic magnetic moments, and the interactions between them, i have talked about so far are of course a consequence of quantum mechanics, all of the above you can understand by treating the magnetic moments as being classical objects.

08.01.2020 · Tweet

When we get into quantum magnetism a bit later today, things will get much weirder https://t.co/eXDJjoAtXi

@schrodingerskit So this means it's less about the magnetic field due to the induced currents (which is stronger for a better metal) than it is about aligning the spins in the metal of the fridge

08.01.2020 · Tweet

Alright, its time to get weird! https://t.co/qPQeqkloBC

08.01.2020 · Tweet

Unfortunately, we have to get a *bit* mathy here, but I will try to do this as nicely as possible. In the classical world, we had two atoms which had a bar magnet each, and that bar magnet could point essentially anywhere. In the language of math, these are vectors. https://t.co/9dQL4C0xpX

08.01.2020 · Tweet

The equation that determines how these will behave is the Hamiltonian, which is an equation that tells you the energy of a system. The lowest energy state is what we call the ground state, and is where we would find the system at zero temperature. https://t.co/L6DRSnBK6L

08.01.2020 · Tweet

The simplest classical Hamiltonian that describes what our atomic magnets will do is this one: It just considers a pair of atoms, treats them like a vector, and wants to know what their dot product is (if you need a quick refresher on what that is, now is the time!) https://t.co/vpNKkavyZ0

08.01.2020 · Tweet

Based on whether J is positive or negative, the lowest energy will be when the atomic magnets are either aligned or antialigned, which are the two simple cases from before. J is usually something we would measure, because its very hard to calculate just from quantum mechanics. https://t.co/VLZ826F8Kd

08.01.2020 · Tweet

What really defines quantum mechanics is that things are quantised. Crazy, right? In the case of our atomic magnets, this means (and ill call them spins now) that they cant point in any direction, they can only point in certain directions separated by a small jump. https://t.co/diT1ShF7Mi

08.01.2020 · Tweet

We are going to consider the simplest, and most quantum case, where "spin" has a maximum value of 1/2, must also have a minimum value of -1/2, and since it can only change by 1 each time, it has no other values. Conveniently this means i can say its pointing up or down ;) https://t.co/H0t3r2pZiR

08.01.2020 · Tweet

Another consequence of us being in the quantum world is that the equation we were using before is busted. You cant use an equation based on vectors any more! Vectors have to be replaced by these things called operators, but thankfully i can just show you what they do: https://t.co/5jPrrIes1r

08.01.2020 · Tweet

each of the operators, when it acts on a spin, gives you something back. the Z operator gives you the spin back, but + and - flip the spin. If the + operator tries to flip an up spin up, nothing happens. if the + operator tries to flip a down spin up, you get an up spin. https://t.co/GT8qmDpbvn

08.01.2020 · Tweet

Another small caveat is that these operators care about who they are operating on! So where the equation above reads i and i+1, this refers so the atom on the left or the right in our picture with just two atoms. https://t.co/p9OF4v7iCy

08.01.2020 · Tweet

So, now we have to consider two cases: J is positive, and J is negative. For J > 0 we try our regular solution before, and it gives us our trial back times its energy. https://t.co/AbDbBO6ZR4

08.01.2020 · Tweet

Thats great! Thats exactly what quantum mechanics requires. https://t.co/ZOZtg3zJjL

08.01.2020 · Tweet

For the solution where the spins are antialigned though, something funny happens. https://t.co/mO1vpZ992g

08.01.2020 · Tweet

It just flips our spins! This means that what is a solution in the classical case, is NOT a solution in the quantum case. Because the quantum world is radical, we can try other things as solutions and see if they work. The most radical solution of all is this: https://t.co/md5vs5NbcT

08.01.2020 · Tweet

What we have done, is taken the quantum superposition of two different, but equally valid classical solutions, and somehow this turns out to be the right answer! But, is it still even a magnet? https://t.co/ScWnmrvhNz

08.01.2020 · Tweet

The answer is tricky, but basically: not really. This superposition takes a magnet pointing in one direction, and entangles it with a magnet pointing in the opposite direction. The superposition has to average everything out to zero, so quantum mechanics has turned off magnetism!

08.01.2020 · Tweet

This is just for two atoms though. What if we had a more realistic situation, like a chain, here we see a problem... How did we choose which atoms to pair?? https://t.co/grXbYjsFGs

08.01.2020 · Tweet

You know theres only one way we can possibly resolve this ambiguity fairly. SUPERIMPOSE THEM BOTH! [evil laugh, lightning] https://t.co/Ugbf4QWKqX

08.01.2020 · Tweet

This madness continues, of course, if you have atoms arranged on a lattice (like a crystal) instead of a slightly artificial chain https://t.co/b9N2S92f8w

08.01.2020 · Tweet

In the end the description is very hard, because the object we call the groundstate is the superposition of VERY many different states which are themselves made up of a lot of superpositions. https://t.co/FNiMPFsRLB

08.01.2020 · Tweet

But what actually is this crazy thing that ive spent a hundred tweets building towards? https://t.co/s4h4aE5qal

08.01.2020 · Tweet

We call this a Spin Liquid. It is, really, a giant quantum soup of spins which is very chaotic even at low temperatures (near absolute zero). It is a challenge to describe, but its also a big challenge to measure! Trying to measure and understand these is an ongoing problem. https://t.co/5pv6NMsBoh

08.01.2020 · Tweet

I hope you made it to the end, because if you did you now know something about condensed matter physics and magnetism that most people would graduate a physics degree without knowing!

08.01.2020 · Tweet

@NotHF That picture is actually ectoplasm from Ghost Busters 2, sadly spin liquids are nowhere near that cool! It's an example of a state of matter that can only exist parasitically on something else. Like a metal, or a magnet, they need a regular solid (or rarely liquid).

08.01.2020 · Tweet

@NotHF Most known spin liquids are based on copper, but the chemical formula are dizzyingly complex. There are some naturally occurring examples, one of which is the mineral Herbersmithite. It's also one of the prettiest!

08.01.2020 · Tweet

@C_J_Smith 😘

08.01.2020 · Tweet

@NotHF Some do! Its not a generic feature though. Some also order at very low temperatures due to nuclear spins, impurities, or other subtle effects and interactions. It's quite a fragile state.

If you were interested in what I had to say about magnetism yesterday, here is a fairly accessible essay about an extremely powerful technique in physics (called Renormalisation) which unites the study of liquids, alloys, and magnets into a single framework. Powerful *and* cool! https://t.co/ve1aYvPRmQ

Sure Majorana Fermions are interesting, but so is Majorana himself - he vanished without a trace at age 32! https://t.co/srCPgK11Wb https://t.co/STNmrZtOeQ

Made it! I missed Professor Seamus Davis' plenary on measuring magnetic monopoly noise in spin ice, but it was a tactical choice so I could catch up on the sleep i missed travelling yesterday, and I've had the opportunity to see Seamus give this talk recently

09.01.2020 · Tweet

So first up I get to see a talk on getting magnetism out of nonmagnetic materials! https://t.co/B6S4nmLRD9

09.01.2020 · Tweet

It's quite exciting because they are doing the world using metal organic frameworks, which is something I work on in collaboration with @goodwingroupox https://t.co/I8B0rXSqU3

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Theres a lot going on, because for starters they are trying to look at something similar to skyrmions, which are a peculiar magnetic phase people are looking at for magnetic memory https://t.co/CxvXgKbzdb

09.01.2020 · Tweet

But to make it more exciting/ complex, they are doing it with orbital quadrupoles instead of magnetic dipoles https://t.co/46kpTRhuUa

09.01.2020 · Tweet

They have managed to show that these phases can exist theoretically, but are yet to find any systems which realise this experimentally. Its early days yet though! This talk was by Emma Wolpert from @UniofOxford

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Next up is the man who had my current position before I did, Dr Paul McClarty of @tudresden_de https://t.co/13FDiqh0Uv

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Paul is an incredibly clever theorist, and I definitely cannot so justice to such a complex topic in tweet form, so I'll just tell you what a magnon is!

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Remember yesterday we had ferromagnets? https://t.co/RoomAgPtxL

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Well we said this is the ground state, which means there are some states which are "excited" states. If we consider our magnet to be fairly classical, these excitations are just wiggles of our atoms, a lot like vibrations

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Because what one atomic spin is doing affects what its neighboura are doing, these wiggles move along the crystal, like any other kind of wave in water, air, or a crystal vibration (which is called a phonon btw!) https://t.co/7Fmfzjig7m

09.01.2020 · Tweet

These magnets have an energy cost, and a wavelength, and these have a complicated relationship. Ones with a very long wavelength have very low cost because nobody is moving very much. Ones with a short wavelength have a higher cost because the spins are further from home.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

This gives you what we in physics call a dispersion, in this case a magnon dispersion! They give you very pretty pictures to show at conferences (cheating because this is data from a much more complex system, but it's one we saw yesterday!) https://t.co/jHzcMu3Mzm

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The following talk is also about magnons https://t.co/LzGdPK6jgY https://t.co/QV4o1g2nm9

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The kind of magnons I showed you before are what we call transverse magnons. This means that the direction the magnetic moments wobble in is perpendicular to the direction they point in.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The current case being talked about by Harry Keen from @uniofedinburgh is that of longitudinal fluctuations: this means that instead of wobbling around their axis, the spins fluctuate in size in a way that is correlated with their neighbours.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

We normally ignore this, because in a lot of materials this costs far more energy than the system has access to (generally that is set by the temperature). But there is a case where it's very important: magnetic metals!

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Side note, it was awesome to see someone cite a classic book in their talk. Importantly one that I own! https://t.co/1FeE3QhiJ5

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Understanding magnetism in metals is actually very hard. The framework we used yesterday doesnt work well - you might get something that behaves similarly, but all the numbers are wrong and you can see some behaviour (like longtitudinal magnons) that you wont see in insulators.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Now it's time for a talk from an old labmate of mine, Dr Matt Watson who has recently moved to @DiamondLightSou https://t.co/dTvfMZoZFK

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Matt's work focuses on very thin magnets, sometimes even only a few atoms thick! Thats quite thin https://t.co/1Q9fJpSIVe

09.01.2020 · Tweet

He is working on CrGeTe3, a material which has a honeycomb of Chromium atoms in its crystal structure that give rise to its magnetic properties https://t.co/J6xXeMRl48

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Matt does a technique called Angular Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy or ARPES, which basically uses the photoelectric effect to kick electrons out of a material and studies the energy and momentum of these electrons https://t.co/Apjxn29Qrx

09.01.2020 · Tweet

@MySci_PK @GrapheneCA @GrapheneLabs @2DResearch @MyGraphene I thought you could use sticky tape? ;p

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Here they see some really interesting results: while normally you expect the behaviour of electrons to be fairly unaffected by the magnetism (it's an insulator, these energy scales are fairly different), but instead they find the chromium electrons to change dramatically!

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The energy levels and the lifetimes of the chromium electrons are completely changed when the material becomes magnetic. Magnetism is a very low energy phenomenon (most things become magnetic below room temperature) but metallicity is a very high energy behaviour.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

It's a bit like you walking into an office block changing the very shape of the whole building!

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Now theres a talk from my colleague Dr Pascal Manuel at @isisneutronmuon Ans he is talking about spin liquids! https://t.co/LJFP0Sk5UI

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Most spin liquids, he reminds us, exist in systems that have triangular arrangements of atoms. This is because spin liquids are very delicate, and the triangular lattice is very good at preventing a normal magnetic order from occurring https://t.co/aQ74YBnO2Q

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Something which is very important about the material he is studying: NaYbO2, is that the crystals are very perfect. Even 0.1% of chemical impurity or disorder can wash out or even kill your spin liquid, and in some materials this just isnt possible to avoid https://t.co/bPcaxPMJYa

09.01.2020 · Tweet

This work had used a lot of different techniques because spin liquids are really tricky to understand: neutron and xray diffraction, neutron spectroscopy, heat capacity, and muon spin rotation.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

And heres the money shot, they observe only diffuse excitations showing conclusively that theres no proper magnetic order, the excitations have no gap - I.e. there are excitations which cost no energy, and this is a really nice result! https://t.co/ENR2k1akyP

09.01.2020 · Tweet

This is kind of how you look at spin liquids though. You measure EVERYTHING, and spin liquids are a weird amorphous blob that exists only in the absence of anything else.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

We now have Johnathan Bulled, also from @UniofOxford He is talking about Frustrated metal-organic magnets https://t.co/liaS3W7Yhm

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The magnet Johnathan is looking at doesnt become magnetic till a VERY low temperature: 0.2 degrees Kelvin! That's -272.95 degrees C or -459.3 F for people using freedom units :p https://t.co/X8UyDWW0Cs

09.01.2020 · Tweet

What makes this material really cool (hah) is that because of the the magnetism is very frustrated there is a lot of entropy associated with it. This means that if you play with a magnetic field, you can use it like a magnetic refrigerator - the magnetocalorcic effect!

09.01.2020 · Tweet

09.01.2020 · Tweet

First up after lunch is Dr Neil Wilson from @warwickuni walking about layers of 2D materials and their electronic properties. https://t.co/XhoVZmr4mD

09.01.2020 · Tweet

It's quite interesting that even though the layers are 2D and dont really fork chemical bonds, stacking layers of graphene on top of each other fundamentally changed their properties, even within the layer. https://t.co/ilEFyRPcHR

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Some of the interesting changes of the properties when you stack layers on top of each other are due to complicated processes that essentially amount to quantum tunneling of electrons from one layer to another. https://t.co/vjBNkRRtXs

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Neil is also using ARPES to measure the electronic properties of these materials (mainly WSe2) It's a great technique for looking at what the electrons are doing, but it requires ultra high purity samples, in an ultra high vacuum, prepared meticulously to get good results.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

They have obtained a lot of really exciting results from examining what happens if you change the number of layers that are stacked on top of each other. Remember, each layer is only about one atom thick!

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The experimental are also supported by quantum mechanical calculations performed on supercomputers https://t.co/tIUP2bsPf4

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The main thing they have found is that the effects strongly depend on how the layers are aligned relative to each other, which thankfully they are able to control to better than 0.5 degrees. In graphene this has resulted in an explosion of exciting results btw!

09.01.2020 · Tweet

You can probably guess why if you look at the Moire pattern formed by stacking two sheets of graphene on top of each other with a slightly different alignment: https://t.co/WRDDTFPTpv

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Even though graphene is (to me, anyway) quite boring, the twisted bilayers have shown magnetism, superconductivity, insulating and metallic behaviour. It's really crazy.

We have another talk on layers of graphene now, from Glenn Wagner of @UniofOxford who is a theorist. https://t.co/UANelq0edL

09.01.2020 · Tweet

He is looking at what mechanism give rise to the scattering of electrons in this material. This is based on comparing his simulations to data, and his equations are a quantum version of the Boltzmann Equation https://t.co/Z9xsqt1ThD

09.01.2020 · Tweet

They are able to show using a very clever analysis that the sub-dominant contribution to the scattering is due to phonons (vibrations in a crystal) ruling out other options. They then are able to model the electrical properties as the motion of two fluids: one made of electrons https://t.co/A8vkvNBEmb

09.01.2020 · Tweet

And one made of holes! Holes are a concept we have in physics that describes the absence of an electron. It nevertheless behaves a lot like an electron with positive charge.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

So this means that the dominant scattering is electrostatic and basically is down to the scattering of an electron fluid and a hole fluid.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Next up we have Dr Marcin Mucha-Kruczynski from @UniofBath talking about those amazing patterns you get from stacking two layers of graphene! https://t.co/YZiju4SUzW

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Moiré patterns are really fascinating generally! https://t.co/sMZ6mOjqjH https://t.co/jICHQ66vhm

09.01.2020 · Tweet

In this case the effect is to trick the electrons into thinking they are in a different crystal than the kind they really are. https://t.co/a5jy0P1EB3

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Because the crystal symmetry has a strong effect on the properties of the electrons and the way they move, this is why the formation of these patterns has a spectacular effect on the way the electrons behave! https://t.co/vH7b2lw2Ua

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The late afternoon session begins with a topic which is very big here in @BristolUni - high temperature superconductors! This talk will be by Professor Ted Forgan, head of condensed matter here https://t.co/cNMZnbDcGJ

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Superconductors are pretty amazing things- conducting electricity without resistance, expelling magnetic fields, and my favourite related effect: magnetic levitation https://t.co/AHujZgrOGa

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Superconductivity is pretty amazing, because before we understood really how it works, we still understood that it was caused by two electrons forming a pair that then conducts electricity without resistance.

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Now, given that electrons are negatively charged they should repel each other, so how could they become paired together? The surprising answer that won the 1972 nobel prize is that they are glued together by crystal vibrations! https://t.co/cdJEtNFE1H

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The way this works is a bit funny - a negatively charged electron moves along, and disturbs the positively charged atoms of the crystal. These disturbed atoms then attract a nearby electron, and it results in an effective attraction between the electrons. https://t.co/LuX1Cf0XGd

09.01.2020 · Tweet

This only works up to a point though. The normal superconductors only really work up to about 45 degrees above absolute zero, or -230 Celsius. Not very practical! https://t.co/D6tuonuSD8

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Thankfully we then discovered high temperature superconductors, which are complex and usually based on copper or iron. These can superconduct up to much more useful temperatures and form the basis for hospital MRIs https://t.co/hWiA9KAmQh

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The reason they work at a much higher temperature is because the glue between the electrons is not provided by crystal vibrations but instead by magnetism - the magnons which I spoke about earlier https://t.co/yLyVkhbrwc

09.01.2020 · Tweet

We have, however, recently made some new superconductors using ultra-high-pressure methods (and they only exist at high pressures!) based on hydrogen. https://t.co/HEPzlgOR0w

09.01.2020 · Tweet

These are again based on vibrations to provide the pairing of electrons, but because the energy of the hydrogen vibrations is so high, they work almost at room temperature (just, not at room pressure 😭)

09.01.2020 · Tweet

Charge density waves are an unusual feature exhibited by some insulating materials, where the density of electrons varies in some direction of the crystal. https://t.co/7k25DoLT7M

09.01.2020 · Tweet

A simple example of this might be an element like Cr which can be 2+ or 3+, but in Cr3O4 the average number of electrons per chromium is 2.666. There are many ways this could work out in practice, because each chromium in an insulator needs an integer number of electrons

09.01.2020 · Tweet

The charge density wave solution might have a pattern where the chromium atoms went 3 - 3 - 2 - 3 - 3 -2 - 3 - 3 - 2 The crystal symmetry would be different here than if the arangement was simply random, because the symmetry cares about what each chromium is doing!

Next up for the #LGBTSTEMinar20 @NathanWoodling is going to tell us about how fruit flies can be used to tell us about the biology of ageing and dementia. https://t.co/spDFdmqlf3 https://t.co/efkcyQG3vJ

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Nathan is, it turns out, quite the artist https://t.co/kNOl8W4U8E

10.01.2020 · Tweet

There is quite a lot of evidence that certain genes are linked to ageing, and that mutations in those Gene's can often lead to increased lifespan. In some simple animals mutating a single gene can double their lifespan! Even in human populations there is evidence for this.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

@NathanWoodling quite likes flies as a model organism because they are complex enough to have a full anatomy similar to humans (heart, brain, digestive system, etc) but they only live a very short time. And wings. They have wings. (Personally I think the eyes is the killer) https://t.co/nDYSgSdDNo

10.01.2020 · Tweet

He also has to perform a lot of brain surgery on teeny tiny fly brains https://t.co/qSIhFBkXf7

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Part of his research involves comparing genes which are involved in ageing in both flies and mice, and making sure those genes change in the same way, then testing what happens if you modify those genes one at a time in flies. https://t.co/ay4GxNRvok

10.01.2020 · Tweet

What he wants us to take away is that the same genes seem to be involved in ageing are similar across many animals, and that changing just one single gene can increase healthy lifespan in some cases!

10.01.2020 · Tweet

He also wants to remind us that having to do a PhD on the opposite side of the world to your partner can be very hard! Especially when the country you're in does not support your relationship at all. But his story has a happy ending! https://t.co/pu1kJJimaD

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Now at the #LGBTSTEMinar20 we hear from @DoriekeMG is going to tell us about how our brain connects our knowledge of landmarks to our understanding of where we are. https://t.co/d1JoEyeSPM

10.01.2020 · Tweet

There are certain cells that activate in our brain only when we are in a specific place! And because scientists are amazing at naming, those are called Place Cella https://t.co/lmxBp8UDzF

10.01.2020 · Tweet

@DoriekeMG puts mice into an amazing little virtual reality program and studies the activation of these brain cells vs where the mouse is inside the virtual environment. https://t.co/PcMF88VGVU

10.01.2020 · Tweet

The results on the mice are quite counterintuitive though, because although the mice improved at the task they were given, the cells did not behave as expected.

Final talk of the #LGBTSTEMinar20 morning seminar is Marcus Lohr talking about astrophysics https://t.co/zgjrruzpZ1

10.01.2020 · Tweet

In particular Marcus is going to talk about massive stars https://t.co/mfMUE8sKd1

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Specifically stars within the Arches cluster in the milky way galaxy https://t.co/ZQhpwRL4Af https://t.co/H0q6I8UcH5

10.01.2020 · Tweet

This is of interest because it contains a high density of massive stars, and in particular binary massive stars. We want to understand these because they will eventually lead to the binary black hole mergers we have recently observed using gravitational waves.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Nearly a third of all the observed targets in the survey met criteria that suggests they are binary stars. Thats a lot! https://t.co/7ZW6txQ7hL

10.01.2020 · Tweet

In the future Marcus will turn their giant telescope and scientific powers to study the Quintuplet cluster https://t.co/P9Y6tG4HJ9 https://t.co/ZfJTRKfpRc

First up to talk at the #LGBTSTEMinar20 after the morning break is @Sunkensie to tell us about simulating the impact of plant levels on waterways https://t.co/aWRQMltdvU

10.01.2020 · Tweet

This is important because river vegetation has a profound impact on flooding, which has increased in frequency and intensity in the UK in recent years https://t.co/sUum938f7f

10.01.2020 · Tweet

"Here is what a plant looks like in case you didnt know" https://t.co/CiOhERkvH2

10.01.2020 · Tweet

@Sunkensie's research, which uses a sophisticated 3D model of the effect of vegetation on water flow indicates that the plant coverage has a huge impact on the water flows. This has big implications for flooding in the future https://t.co/WXZf7zhVLu

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Climate change is expected to cause the amount of water plants to peak later in the year, to coincide with autumn storms, which will create a feedback loop of worsening flooding (Aligators not included) https://t.co/lQoQH7O04A

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Unfortunately the answer is not just more or less plants. Fewer plants near settlements will decrease flood risk locally, but that just means worse flooding downstream.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Now we have @Tuffers_c who is both gay and northern 😅 They will be talking to us about the origins of misalignment between stars and planets. https://t.co/FA4HQJM98n

10.01.2020 · Tweet

The way solar systems form normally, is why all if the planets are in the same plane, and that's the plane that the sun rotates in also. https://t.co/Ype5aocpnX

10.01.2020 · Tweet

But thanks to deep space imaging like Kepler, we now know that not all solar systems are like this. Some of them are... a bit wonky. https://t.co/hnkDLZtXaW

10.01.2020 · Tweet

There are a few ways this is thought to happen: the star shits alignment after the disk that will eventually become planets has formed. Something happens to a planet that changes its axis. Or the disk forms in a completely unusual way.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

The data for the alignment between stars and its planetary orbits is quite sparse, because it is hard to measure and may take decades of observation. There are only 15 extrasolar systems characterised properly.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Statistical analysis indicates that the number of misaligned systems may not be unusual, but their degree of misalignment is very difficult to understand.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Now we have a talk on autophagy and motor neurone disease, which I am glad we have after lunch, given by @mattjaywhy #LGBTSTEMinar20 https://t.co/ZwP7JN92qw

10.01.2020 · Tweet

MND or ALS is a terrible disease. Famously Professor Stephen Hawking suffered from it, but he was very lucky - he lived 55 years after his diagnosis which is far longer than most. https://t.co/Y7kC8zmlwJ

10.01.2020 · Tweet

@JostMigenda We needed the laugh 😅

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Neurons are also wild. And somehow, huge! The nerve fibres called Axons may stretch the whole length of the body https://t.co/djms6dRTKC

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Neurons are very large and long-lived cells. Autophagy is the process whereby cells eat some of the broken parts or bits which arent necessary anymore. Neurons therefore have an important balance between growing new parts and eating old or broken parts https://t.co/W32SJtCjcn

10.01.2020 · Tweet

When the balance is broken, and autophagy happens too much or in the wrong way, this can lead to diseases that affect the brain, especially ones like Motor Neurone Disease

10.01.2020 · Tweet

It's also a problem when you turn off autophagy! This can lead to neurons growing too long, which leads to other disorders.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Now the #LGBTSTEMinar20 gets some supersymmetey from @GeeknProud42 https://t.co/WkNgseuJzA

10.01.2020 · Tweet

@MarinaLogares @PRISMAciencia Sorry! This is what I thought might be the case but I was in a rush 😅

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Important note: this talk is making use of text-to-speech technology, and we had a brief technical glitch setting it up but now it's working great. A question for conference organisers: would your conference be able to support this?

10.01.2020 · Tweet

The standard model has 3 generations of fermionic particles, force carrying bosons, and the higgs. https://t.co/sx8awZDijW

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Gluons are some of the most important, because they bind quarks together into protons and neutrons and hence atoms. And are not to be confused with some warlike races from the star trek universe https://t.co/fCHNvrhe5Z

10.01.2020 · Tweet

But the standard model has to be incomplete, because it seems to account for only 5% of the universe, there is seemingly a lot of missing energy and matter. It also cannot explain why we are all made of regular matter and there isnt really any antimatter floating around. https://t.co/tgctWnWtJB

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Supersymmetry is a model which might solve some of these problems. It posits the existence of a super-partner particle for every known particle, which is almost the same as every particle but much heavier. https://t.co/svExbIU1BS

10.01.2020 · Tweet

They also have TERRIBLE names. For every particle there is a supersymmetric sparticle. For the quarks, their super-partners are the squarks, and for the top quark, there is the stop quark. https://t.co/QsssmqUS0B

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Many people hope that this would provide a complete picture of the universe, because if it isnt, we should all give up and go to the pub 😅 https://t.co/YopamuPU5T

10.01.2020 · Tweet

The final talk of this post lunch session at #LGBTSTEMinar20 is from Jon Davies talking about the variation of gene regulation in brain development and autism spectrum disorder https://t.co/1TbkluR2f4

10.01.2020 · Tweet

This talk is mainly about the phenomenon of epigenetics. If genetics is the blueprint, epigenetics is the person reading the blueprint to build an ikea table but maybe sometimes making it into a bookshelf. https://t.co/IwTnaEVAQz

10.01.2020 · Tweet

All of your cells have the same genes, but epigenetics is what determines whether a stem cell becomes a muscle cell, or a skin cell, or a brain cell, etc. This is important because twins have the same genes, but in 70% with autism spectrum disorder of twins only one has it

10.01.2020 · Tweet

This means there must be an epigenetic component. If it was just down to your genes, then it would always be both or neither. This is actually true of many diseases and conditions which are known to have a genetic component.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Terrifying takeaway from this talk: by examining your genes people can tell if you have smoked, drunk alcohol, or taken drugs. They leave a permanent mark on your body which is part of your epigenetics!

10.01.2020 · Tweet

10.01.2020 · Tweet

After the breakout panel we have @GayRollerCEng giving us the lowdown on the nuclear robots she builds today at the #LGBTSTEMinar20 https://t.co/K7HqXzbmEi

10.01.2020 · Tweet

These robots are meant to assist in fusion power plants, like the tokamak under construction at ITER https://t.co/Bd9oXeoS1H

10.01.2020 · Tweet

The heat involved in fusion power is immense, the plasma is about 15 million degrees. This is wrapped in coils of superconducting magnets at -270 degrees. That's quite a huge difference! https://t.co/TjLXEC7W53

10.01.2020 · Tweet

It's difficult enough containing that heat, but fusion also produces a lot of neutrons. When neutrons smash into materials, they dont just make them radioactive, they leave behind damage at the atomic level which makes the material brittle https://t.co/gXUwz384hi

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Theres also a lot of radiation flying around. Radiation is usually pretty bad 😅 https://t.co/RGzQue0UKe

10.01.2020 · Tweet

As a result of all this radiation, we would like to use robots to do work inside the fusion reactors! https://t.co/I75daZClXj

10.01.2020 · Tweet

These robots need to be able lift 80 tonnes, be incredibly precise, and all their parts need to be easily replaceable.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Basically: It's really hard! https://t.co/OAn101qt2X

10.01.2020 · Tweet

But its worth it. For the amount of lithium in your phone battery, and a bathtub full of seawater, you could have power for 40 years. It's also quite safe! Fusion power plants basically just stop working when they go wrong. They safely turn off. https://t.co/l1VOB53TUH

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Why do we not have fusion yet? Mostly money. ITER will cost about 20 billion, and if we spent more we could have it faster. For reference the soccer world cup in Quatar will cost 150 billion. https://t.co/11ULb8k6Ql

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Also @GayRollerCEng is REALLY funny. https://t.co/0xfA2sm5o4

10.01.2020 · Tweet

The final talk of the day for the #LGBTSTEMinar20 is by @Dr_KTaylor talking about the relationship between HIV and a heart disease https://t.co/07DyEBwJBk

10.01.2020 · Tweet

It is quite difficult for people of my generation and later to really understand what it was like living through the epidemic of the early 80s. It's also impossible to overstate the importance of activism in forcing action on the epidemic from the establishment https://t.co/OZH1vjnPo8

10.01.2020 · Tweet

It's also amazing to note that almost half of all people diagnosed with HIV are women, despite the association with gay men. Although this ignorance around infections in women led to the phrase "women dont get aids, they just die from it"

10.01.2020 · Tweet

The world has moved on greatly from this. We now have PrEP, PEP, and antiretrovirals that enable people to avoid infection or live a normal lifespan once infected. However, antiretrovirals are associated with an increased risk of heart failure.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

In order to avoid complicating lifestyle factors, @Dr_KTaylor studies blood of people who do not have HIV and how antiretroviral drugs affect blood clotting. Knowing these effects would enable therapies to be tailored to avoid damaging heard health.

10.01.2020 · Tweet

Additionally thanks to these medications (undetectable = untransmissible, and PrEP preventing infections) we are on the verge of ending the HIV epidemic

10.01.2020 · Tweet

In 2k15, we celebrated the international year of light. It marked the anniversary of many great achievements in the field of optics. It was 150 years since Maxwell came up with electromagnetism and 100 years since Einstein's General relativity. #optics #light

20.01.2020 · Tweet

We are quite familiar with the way optics work. We use glasses and mirrors on a day to day basis. Phenomena such as reflection and refraction can be seen with naked eye. #optics #light

20.01.2020 · Tweet

As time passed, the race to make a strong light source began. The light beam should be of single colour and coherent (analogous to two people walking in phase). Thus the race to make lasers began! #optics #lasers #photonics

20.01.2020 · Tweet

But that was not it. There was a necessity to carry data over long distances and hence a new form of cable was invented - fiber optic cable. It then became faster and more efficient to transmit signals over fiber optic cables than copper wire. #fiberoptics #light #data

20.01.2020 · Tweet

The field of fiber optics thus emerged - a way to guide light using fibers! Fiber optics finds application in a variety of fields such as sensing, medical diagnosis, apart from optical communication. #fiberoptics

20.01.2020 · Tweet

With the dawn of #fiberoptics emerged yet another interesting field called #photonics. Photonics is about the generation, detection, and manipulation of #photons.

20.01.2020 · Tweet

Optical fibers are capable of transmitting data over long distances and is the backbone of today's internet. Every smartphone manufacturing has something to do with Photonics. Lithography uses laser to etch out micro patterns, optics are used in display, etc.. #fiberoptics

20.01.2020 · Tweet

So what is #nanophotonics? While so far, #photonics has been used in technology to create devices, the next leap is to see what will happen if light is allowed to interact with matter at the nanoscale level.

20.01.2020 · Tweet

21st century saw the convulsion of of nanotechnology and photonics. Nanophotonics emerged and revolutionized the way we look at light. #nanophotonics #light

20.01.2020 · Tweet

So what is a nanometer? You take a meter scale and split it a billion times and then look at just one unit. That's nanoscale! #nanophotonics

20.01.2020 · Tweet

At this scale, light does not behave as it behaves at higher scales. The physical structure of the matter with which it starts interacting comes into picture. #nanophotonics

20.01.2020 · Tweet

So how do we induce interactions between light and matter at nanoscale level. There are two ways to do it. One, confine light to dimensions that are smaller than the wavelength of light and two, confine matter to nano dimensions. #nanophotonics

20.01.2020 · Tweet

Some prominent areas where nanophotonics has tremendous applications are spectroscopy, optical communication, solar cells, etc. We will look at them in more detail from tomorrow.

20.01.2020 · Tweet

In nature, we have both preys and predators. Some moths have evolutionarily developed an anti-reflective ability on the eyes, thanks to the presence of nanophotonic structures. This prevents visible light from being reflected off moths' eyes and thus helps moths to escape.

21.01.2020 · Tweet

So what is there to be inspired from the moth eyes? #nanophotonics #biomimicry https://t.co/QsYHzUAVQl

21.01.2020 · Tweet

Scientists are now designing novel procedures to construct a nano sphere monolayer using several deposition and plasma techniques. The biomimicked structure can now be applied to solar cells, monitors, and LEDs. #nanophotonics #biomimicry

21.01.2020 · Tweet

Let me give some more examples. For improving light extraction from LEDs, directionally controlled fluorescence emission in butterflies has been an inspiration. #nanophotonics #biomimicry #butterflies https://t.co/F1DarR9iXA

21.01.2020 · Tweet

Another example is that of a chameleon's skin which has a dynamically toned periodic two dimensional structure. #nanophotonics #biomimicry https://t.co/jX0UW7oIDV

21.01.2020 · Tweet

Biomimicking certain natural nanophotonic structures has avoided overheating in hot climates. For example, desert ants have surfaces covered with nanostructures which reflect off light and hence they can search for food without feeling the heat. #nanophotonics #biomimicry https://t.co/QigizY0dXJ

21.01.2020 · Tweet

But is it easy to develop these nanostructures in lab? #nanophotonics #biomimicry Not really and thus we again look into nature itself for solution.

21.01.2020 · Tweet

The answer to the question is a process called biotemplating. With this technique, researchers exploit natural biological materials for creating replica of their highly ordered morphologies. #nanophotonics #biomimicry

21.01.2020 · Tweet

Nature has also inspired the development of photonic components such as lasers and mirrors. The question we need to ask is why we need biocompatible and nanoscale photonic components? #nanophotonics #biomimicry

21.01.2020 · Tweet

21.01.2020 · Tweet

Biopolymers in thin film form can be used as cavity mirrors which are again important for creating nanoscale lasers that are biologically compatible. #nanophotonics #lasers

On monday, we talked about how photonic technologies are important for us. To better develop these systems at the nanoscale level, we need to understand the fundamental laws of quantum physics. Nanoscale quantum optics is all about that. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics #light

22.01.2020 · Tweet

These sophisticated technologies are of use for our well being such as health care, security, and economic growth. Photonic devices have gained prominent importance over other technologies, thanks to the advantages they offer at the quantum level. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics.

22.01.2020 · Tweet

Light based processes such as absorption, propagation, and even light storage can be exploited at the quantum level. But the interaction of single photons with matter at nanoscale level is very weak. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics #light

22.01.2020 · Tweet

This dearth is obstacle for creating a rapport between quantum physics and photonic devices. Nanophotonics, as as field, addresses these issues by funneling down light to nanoscale dimensions. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

22.01.2020 · Tweet

On overcoming the challenges, we can see significant breakthroughs in the field of sensing, metrology, information processing at the quantum and classical level, etc. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics #light

22.01.2020 · Tweet

Let us look at what the current scenario is like in this area of research. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics #lightmatter

22.01.2020 · Tweet

The first focus has been on the creation of novel materials like graphene, silicon, and meta materials that can be used for probing light matter interaction at the nanoscale level. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

22.01.2020 · Tweet

The next focus is on devices that will be used for facilitating and controlling strong light matter interaction. Some examples of this include photonic integrated circuits, nanofibers, plasmonic structures, and superconductors. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

22.01.2020 · Tweet

Now that we know the possible materials and devices, the next aspect is to look into quantum degrees of freedom. For this, color centers in solids, ions, and neutral atoms have been used. For single photon sources, organic molecules, 2D materials are used.

22.01.2020 · Tweet

This is an example of a fully integrated quantum circuit. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics Cred: Agio M. https://t.co/lwaMFdS9Vw

22.01.2020 · Tweet

To funnel light to nanoscale dimensions, one uses metamaterial which unlike conventional material such as glass does not possess a positive index of refraction. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

22.01.2020 · Tweet

The origin of such a behaviour for metamaterials is due to rationally designed geometry, composition, and arrangement of nanostructured building blocks. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

22.01.2020 · Tweet

By using single photons for switching and routing through the exploitation of quantum mechanical phenomena, one can have efficient computing in the future. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

22.01.2020 · Tweet

When combined with tiny optical emitters, metamaterials could make possible a hybrid technology that uses quantum light in future computers. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

22.01.2020 · Tweet

Computers that operate on quantum optics would exploit qubits which exist in both the on and off state simultaneously. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics https://t.co/3g1AY7GzLF

22.01.2020 · Tweet

The prowess of employing qubits is that it enhances the computer's power and memory, thereby increasing it's working capacity. #nanophotonics #QuantumComputing https://t.co/nGBNIyUCtY

22.01.2020 · Tweet

That is just a brief introduction to quantum optics at the nanoscale level. If you would like to know more, do let me know! Until then, bye people! #nanophotonics #quantumoptics https://t.co/dfon8NjvTi

Hey tweeps! How is the day treating you so far? I had a long day and I will be winding it up with this Twitter session. Here is what we are going to look at. Are we facing a telecommunication crunch? #nanophotonics #optics #telecommunication #data

23.01.2020 · Tweet

If you are reading tweet on your phone or your laptop, thank optical physicists. The world of internet is revolutionized by optical principles. #telecommunication #optics #data #internet

23.01.2020 · Tweet

While browsing, your computer converts the human language into electrical signals. These electrical signals are then converted into optical signal through a certain optical process. The optical signal reaches the server to collect information and returns back to the computer.

23.01.2020 · Tweet

The optical signals are light pulses generated using lasers and the medium which carry these signals back and forth are called fiber optic cables. #telecommunication #optics #data #internet #nanophotonics

23.01.2020 · Tweet

The cables carry light through total internal reflection which is a process by which light gets guided inside the fiber. The fibers are referred to as single mode fiber since they have the capacity to support just one mode of the light. #fiberoptics

23.01.2020 · Tweet

Though the information travels at the speed of light, encoding data onto light and processing them affects data speeds. #telecommunication #data #internet

23.01.2020 · Tweet

Apart from that, we do not have the capacity to meet the growing demands for faster internet and more channels. We are already at the verge of using the visible light bandwidth. #telecommunication #fiberoptics #data #internet

23.01.2020 · Tweet

So, there are two missing links to achieve ultrafast, broadband transmission. 1. To enhance the amount of data transferred and 2. To enhance the processing of signals at launch and output. #nanophotonics #telecommunication #internet

23.01.2020 · Tweet

Let us look at the issues one by one. To enhance the amount of data that can be transferred, the way is to let the optical fibers carry more modes. So instead of encoding data just on light's spectrum, it is essential to look at other properties that can be exploited.

23.01.2020 · Tweet

The oscillation or shape of light are other parameters that can be used to encode data. This way, we can make use of the several modes at the same time without any interference. #telecommunication #nanophotonics #data

23.01.2020 · Tweet

The idea is to twist the light beam into a spiral to increase its capacity. This is referred to as light in a state of orbital angular momentum. #telecommunication #data

23.01.2020 · Tweet

But how to improve the encoding process. For that, a nanophotonic chip designed by RMIT's laboratory comes into picture. #nanophotonics #data #internet

23.01.2020 · Tweet

The miniature chip is designed to separate different orbital angular momentum states of light in a continuous order and to decode the information carried by twisted light. #nanophotonics #telecommunication #internet

23.01.2020 · Tweet

Previously, this would call for instruments the size of a table which we know is not practical for telecommunication. So the researchers use topological nano sheets a fraction of a millimeter and they fit well on the end of an optical fiber. #nanophotonics #telecommunication

23.01.2020 · Tweet

Another main advantage is that the material used in the device is compatible with silicon based materials used in the telecommunication industry. #telecommunication #nanophotonics

23.01.2020 · Tweet

The technology is of high performance, low cost and tiny size and makes it a viable application for the next generation of broadband optical communications.

23.01.2020 · Tweet

It is demonstrated that the processing speed has been increased by about 100 times which is quite exciting for the telecommunication sector. #telecommunication #nanophotonics

23.01.2020 · Tweet

So yay! It is going to be all the more better soon! With this, I sign off for today. https://t.co/GoBOH3slzf

24.01.2020 · Tweet

The tweet highlights ten different areas which are promising candidates for the future of technology. #nanophotonics #optics

24.01.2020 · Tweet

1. Quantum optics, where nanophotonics can help build one-chip integrated optical circuitry for performing tasks in quantum information processing. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

24.01.2020 · Tweet

2. Telecommunications, where nanophotonic circuitry can help dramatically shrink the physical size and power consumption of devices such as modulators, switches, and lasers. #nanophotonics #telecommunications

24.01.2020 · Tweet

3. Data storage, in which plasmonics can help take magnetic storage to new levels of data density through heat-assisted magnetic recording. #datastorage #nanophotonics

24.01.2020 · Tweet

4. Medical therapies and Diagnostics, where the interaction between nanoparticles and light can be used for imaging purposes or to kill cancerous cells through localized heating or even light-induced drug delivery. #medicine #nanophotonics

24.01.2020 · Tweet

5. Nanoscale imaging involving probes, optical antennas or super-lens techniques to image beyond the diffraction limit. #nanophotonics #imaging

24.01.2020 · Tweet

6. Molecular scale sensors using nanophotonic technology to offer single-molecule detection and identification. #nanophotonics #sensing

24.01.2020 · Tweet

7. Nanotagging, in which metamaterials and nanostructured barcodes can be used to combat counterfeiting. #nanophotonics #barcodes

24.01.2020 · Tweet

8. LEDs and solar cells, where nano structuring can be used to optimize the emission and absorption of light. #nanophotonics #efficiency

24.01.2020 · Tweet

9. New processing techniques for fabrication and lithography at higher resolutions. #nanophotonics

24.01.2020 · Tweet

10. Nanophotonic materials with custom-designed optical properties. #nanophotonics #materials

I started taking part in service learning programs to better understand what it means to communicate the science that I am doing. #scicomm

I have been involved in #scicomm for the last 10 years or so. Like I started teaching school kids in schools that were devoid of enough facilities. Then in Ph.D, I started the Optical Society student chapter where the outreach programs were extended to colleges too.

25.01.2020 · Tweet

25.01.2020 · Tweet

During various occasions, I got to talk to several visually impaired students. These students generally don't have access to science education since they cannot SEE. So my main goal in #scicomm which I haven't reached so far is to take science to the visually impaired.

25.01.2020 · Tweet

Another common challenge is to convince the importance of #scicomm. Most of the time, the efforts of science communicators go unnoticed. In a university or college, professors don't appreciate the idea of their students taking part in science communication activities.

25.01.2020 · Tweet

Oftentimes, I have felt confident about concepts that I have explained school students before writing a paper. This raises another important question. How well do we write our scientific and technical papers?

25.01.2020 · Tweet

My personal opinion is that a scientific paper should read like a story instead of an agglomeration of random facts that are results of an experiment. Just ripping off content and putting them under titles such as 'introduction', 'results' doesn't make a paper appealing. #scicomm

25.01.2020 · Tweet

This is something which is usually ignored as a result of which the difficulty arises to read a lit of scientific papers. #scicomm
