Hey Twitter! Sorry I’m late to start this Monday party! I, @itskameronyall, will be curating @RealSci_Nano this week, so it’s only fair I introduce myself and tell you what I do. (A thread)

28.01.2020 · Tweet

I grew up in the heart of Cajun country, in south Louisiana. I went to my local state flagship university, @LSU (#GEAUXTIGERS). Which, by the way, let me say—public schools are important. Call your state legislators and tell them how important your public unis are!

28.01.2020 · Tweet

While I was at LSU, we faced several incredibly painful budget cuts that caused tuition to go up (RAPIDLY) and cut services on campus. I majored in biological engineering. Three major memories stick out to me, and some minor ones.

28.01.2020 · Tweet

1, I was very active in my schools LGBTQ group, @SpectrumLSU. This was a major part of our social lives in the capital of a very conservative state. Do you part to create a supportive community for those around you!

28.01.2020 · Tweet

2. It is hard to understate how jealous I was of schools with more resources (and we had decent resources!). I really wanted to major in biomedical engineering, but the major wasn’t offered. Luckily... 3. I was able to do undergrad research in a tissue engineering lab...

28.01.2020 · Tweet

...where we studied nanocomposite materials and how they interacted with cells. I learned analytical techniques like scanning electron microscopy, which lets us look at extremely small things.

28.01.2020 · Tweet

I also had the opportunity to do some cool undergraduate research in the chemistry department, where we studied how flame retardant particles were distributed in plastic, and how these particles moved and dissolved under heating.

28.01.2020 · Tweet

THE TECHNIQUE TO DO THIS WAS NUTS!!! My prof built a μ-CT using the X Ray emissions of a synchrotron at the Louisiana Center for Advanced Microstructures and Devices. This is basically a giant ring in which electrons in a vacuum tube are accelerated to a significant fraction...

28.01.2020 · Tweet

...of the speed of light. Giant electromagnets bend the electrons back into the ring. Every time the electrons get bent, they let out a stream of high energy photons called bremsstrahlung. We used these photons to take projection Xrays of our sample, then turn it a bit & repeat

28.01.2020 · Tweet

This gave us projections which were then reconstructed into micron scale 3D reconstructions. This was my introduction to computational image analysis, a set of techniques I turn to time and time again.

28.01.2020 · Tweet

Eventually, I applied to graduate schools all over the country. I knew I was interested in nano, biomedical engineering, tissue engineering, and drug delivery. I wanted to make an impact on human health.

28.01.2020 · Tweet

With some fantastic mentorship from a prof in my dept, I wrote a successful @NSFGRFP application. Before getting the fellowship, I wasn’t sure I wanted to go to grad school.

28.01.2020 · Tweet

In fact, this is a lesson I’d like to share with you: let life make some important decisions for you, and don’t fight it. If a pretty door opens, walk through it. (But think about what kind of doors you’re looking for, and keep an eye out)

28.01.2020 · Tweet

So I visit some grad schools and after a couple visits I’m told I won this fellowship. Lucky for me, I had REALLY enjoyed my visit to @VandyBME and decided to join @Duvall_Lab_VU where I got to study nanoscale drug delivery. A dream come true!

28.01.2020 · Tweet

Not only did I get to spend those years learning about self assembling polymers that form nanoscale drug delivery vehicles, but I got the opportunity to build a broad base of knowledge in several different areas.

28.01.2020 · Tweet

I think that’s about enough ancient history, let’s talk about more recent stuff. My PhD research resulted in 3 research stories, and I’ll give you the short summary.

28.01.2020 · Tweet

But first: some scientific background. A variety of molecules could be great medicines, but they’re not very effective because of specific cellular barriers that evolution has created. The one I have spent the most time thinking about is the endosomal membrane.

28.01.2020 · Tweet

You can think of the endosome as a little cell stomach. It’s the digestive system for a cell. Our craziest drugs made of nucleic acid’s and proteins get destroyed here. The focus of my PhD lab was to get those drugs out of the endosome and into the cell where they can be active

28.01.2020 · Tweet

A previous grad student had developed a nanoscale drug delivery system for peptides that worked really well. It was my job to figure out how it worked so well, and we did! We used pharmacologic techniques as well as SEM and TEM to figure out how our nanoparticles worked

28.01.2020 · Tweet

Along the way, I was really frustrated by how hard this research was. We discovered a paper another lab had published showing a protein called Gal8 works to find damaged endosomes. When we watched fluorescent Gal8, it went straight to disrupted endosomes!

28.01.2020 · Tweet

We still weren’t really satisfied with this system, so we thought about how to improve it. We then created a split Luciferase system wherein a luciferase enzyme becomes bioactive upon endosomal disruption. We can now measure endosomal disruption in even higher throughput!

28.01.2020 · Tweet

We recently submitted this manuscript as a pre-print, the first ever from that group! You can read all about it over at @biorxivpreprint !

28.01.2020 · Tweet

As I finished up my PhD (defended July 28! Woohoo!), I applied for industry jobs all over the country and eventually settled on an industry postdoc doing cutting edge research with protein therapeutics

28.01.2020 · Tweet

with @JanssenUS here in La Jolla where I have the coooooolest project, exploring new applications of our tech. Hopefully I’ll be able to share this work when we have a paper in the next couple years!

31.01.2020 · Tweet

Let's talk about intracellular drug delivery, and why it's important! Also, viruses are nanoparticles. Fight me.

31.01.2020 · Tweet

Biology is made of large molecules. DNA is used to make mRNA and mRNA is used to make proteins. Proteins fold up and do useful stuff. Cells use proteins to talk to each other. Sometimes, proteins misbehave, due to improper instructions from the DNA or the RNA.

31.01.2020 · Tweet

We've come a long way in terms of understanding what genes can cause disease, but what if there were a way to turn off diseases by turning off the bad gene?

31.01.2020 · Tweet

That's exactly what some types of intracellular-acting medicines do! Therapies like antisense oligonucleotides, small interfering RNAs, and even gene editing platforms like CRISPR, TALENS, and ZFNs can be used to reprogram cells from the inside out.

31.01.2020 · Tweet

Unfortunately, those things are stuck on the outside of cells. And if they do enter cells, they're probably stuck in an endosome. My PhD research looked at the molecular mechanisms of these processes, to understand how we could engineer smarter nanoparticles...

31.01.2020 · Tweet

to break down endosomal membranes to deliver drugs to the inside of cells. A few days ago, I asked whether you thought viruses were nanoparticles https://t.co/FrQaddOTSQ

31.01.2020 · Tweet

Personally, I think viruses are definitely nanoparticles, and they're more efficient at getting foreign DNA into our cells that anything humans have invented! Viruses are the ultimate "smart" nanoparticle.

31.01.2020 · Tweet

Viruses are used to reprogram cells for therapies, like CAR-T cells, which use synthetic lentivirus to reprogram T-cells to turn them into cancer killing machines. There are two CAR-T cell therapies on the market today! Amazing stuff!

31.01.2020 · Tweet

There are also viruses being used to give patients a shot at a normal life, by giving them a gene they were born without. Truly, truly, crazy! There are two FDA approved viruses. One delivers RPE65 gene to the retinal pigmented epithelium, which literally cures blindness!!!!!

31.01.2020 · Tweet

The other gives patients back SMN1 gene. Babes born with broken SMN1 will never sit up on their own. Most don't survive to their second birthday. In the clinical trial, 10 of the 21 patients could sit on their own for >30 seconds. AMAZING.

31.01.2020 · Tweet

So, in my opinion, viruses are some of the oldest nanoparticles on earth!

I've been thinking about this a lot lately, but I think that when peer reviewers request additional experiments "to improve impact" (rather than to support unsupported claims), authors should withdraw the manuscript and resubmit to higher impact journals.

01.02.2020 · Tweet

The editor screens for interest and impact. The peer reviewers screen for solid science, sound methods, and well-supported claims. If my paper clearly says "XYZ in mice" and reviewers ask me for data in human cells/tissue, the scope of the paper has now changed.

01.02.2020 · Tweet

Peer review is broken. Rather than focusing on whether claims are well-supported, reviewers often ask for new experiments to expand the impact/scope of the paper. Suggestions are welcome, but almost any critique of the manuscript should be addressable by either:

01.02.2020 · Tweet

1. Doing a "killer" experiment that was not performed, i.e., was the central hypothesis directly tested or not? 2. Removing / weakening the claim. If the claim is central to the paper, see 1. All too often, authors say "We show ABC" and reviewers ask "but can you show DEF?"

01.02.2020 · Tweet

This back and forth dance slows down science and cloisters results. My last published paper took ~13 months from first submission to the first journal to final acceptance in a second.

01.02.2020 · Tweet

We had 7 peer reviewers at the second journal. Their comments certainly polished the manuscript and broadened its impact. But I don't believe the additional experiments substantially strengthened the central claim.

01.02.2020 · Tweet

So, 13 months from 1st submission to acceptance. My most recent manuscript? It was about 13 months **from conception** to pre-print. Those results are there for the world to see and can stand on their own merits.

Today I’m going to attempt to answer the question “what is soft matter”? The term covers a huge variety of systems and I’m only going to touch on a few of my favourite ones. I guess the flippant answer is soft matter is condensed matter that is soft

10.02.2020 · Tweet

What do I mean by soft? It’s not very obvious. E.g., if you have a plastic bottle of liquid soap, both the packaging and the soap fall under soft matter despite seeming to have very different material properties. So what do these 2 materials have in common to both be soft matter? https://t.co/bYwlPY5TBy

10.02.2020 · Tweet

If we consider the two at the mesoscopic level, somewhere between the nanoscale (i.e. size of an atom) and micron size (i.e. visible under a microscope), they share a number of similarities. Both have physical structures on this level that determine the overall properties.

10.02.2020 · Tweet

In both cases the mesostructure can be deformed with relatively little energy, on the scale with thermal energy at room temperature. This is why the soap is “liquid”, and the bottle can be produced at easily accessible temperatures.

10.02.2020 · Tweet

These mesostructures can make it difficult to predict the physical properties from molecular composition alone – and (to me) this is what makes soft matter so interesting! The term “soft matter” can cover a huge range of materials, across all areas of our daily lives.

10.02.2020 · Tweet

From make-up to tires, even mobile phone screens, all wouldn’t be possible without soft matter somewhere. With so much variation, this is a huge and vibrant field of research. Personally, I’ve been involved with work on liquid crystals, surfactants (like in the soap) and polymers https://t.co/g3C48u4dqy

11.02.2020 · Tweet

Happy Tuesday everyone! In my opinion the worst day of the week. So to brighten it up today I’m going to talk a bit about the type of simulations I use to investigate soft matter. Simulations are basically virtual experiments that run “in silico”, i.e. on a computer. 1/13

11.02.2020 · Tweet

As with “wet” science, there is a vast range of possible approaches, so I’m just going to talk about my little corner of them. I use virtual beads to represent atoms (or groups of atoms). Deciding how to model different interactions depends on what you are interested in. 2/13

11.02.2020 · Tweet

Each bead you model costs computer processing power and it is currently not possible to model huge systems at an atomic level (i.e. one bead per atom). So you have to choose your model based on the length and time scale you are interested in. 3/13 https://t.co/qQFIDARdVg

11.02.2020 · Tweet

If you want to look at the interaction between a few molecules, it is easy to represent each atom separately. That’s what I did in this paper looking at polymer actuation. https://t.co/kcTxClez2T 4/13

11.02.2020 · Tweet

If you want to look at a much larger system, you might not care what all the individual atoms are doing and you might represent a group of atoms as a single bead. This means that instead of the atomic scale, you can look on a mesoscale. https://t.co/jm7XK2rFsy 5/13

11.02.2020 · Tweet

On an even larger scale you might not be interested in what the single molecules are doing and you model a group of molecules as a single bead. This is what I did for my PhD, we looked at micron-sized liquid crystal bubbles. https://t.co/lODKIYZwek 6/13

11.02.2020 · Tweet

Deciding the model is a very important part, you put rubbish in you get rubbish out. There are a huge number of papers purely on model (also called force field) development. 7/13 https://t.co/Gin5dryFae

11.02.2020 · Tweet

One of the trickiest things to model is water! Given the ubiquitous nature of water, a wide number of models exist (and are still being developed). No one model captures it perfectly and you have to carefully chose given what physical property you are interested in. 8/13

11.02.2020 · Tweet

With all this difficulty in selecting a model, why bother doing it at all? In the lab, we know what water is and the melting temperature of ice. There are loads of really good reasons! 1. I’d be out of a job if we did that! 9/13

11.02.2020 · Tweet

2. It is very difficult to know what is going on at the mesoscale experimentally. In the lab there may be impurities, the conditions at a specific point might not be known exactly. It’s possible to control all these things precisely in simulations. 10/13

11.02.2020 · Tweet

3. We can see how changing one specific attribute can affect the system -e.g. changing a methyl group to a t-butyl group. This is much easier to do in simulations than having to do a whole new synthesis. 11/13

11.02.2020 · Tweet

4. It gives information that might be very difficult (or even impossible) to know experimentally, such as how much energy it takes to break a micelle or how the molecules align in a liquid crystal phase. 12/13

11.02.2020 · Tweet

Phew! I’ve written more than I expected about how to use particles to model soft matter; I didn’t get on to how we use these models! I’ll try to do a thread about that later in the week. 😊 13/13

12.02.2020 · Tweet

[admin] "From Shampoo to LCD - a Theoretical Approach" extended podcast with @craywand out now Listen here 🎧🎙️ https://t.co/6enyMqtpWP

12.02.2020 · Tweet

Hi everyone! Today I’m going to talk about liquid crystals, seemingly an oxymoron. How can crystals be liquid? Well, liquid crystal is actually a term for any state of matter that flows like a liquid but has some form of long range order. 1/15

12.02.2020 · Tweet

The term liquid crystal (LC) actually covers lots of different phases. Broadly LC’s fall into two types, lyotropic and thermotropic. Today I’m going to focus on thermotropic – these are materials whose phase depends on the temperature (and pressure). 2/15

12.02.2020 · Tweet

One thing all LC molecules have in common is some form of anisotropy, shape being a common one. For example, rod-like or disc-like molecules often form LC phases. This phenomenon isn’t unique to the molecular scale, anisotropic colloids can form LC phases. 3/15

12.02.2020 · Tweet

You can even see LC ordering on a much bigger scale, a pile of coins or tree trunks floating down the river. 4/15 https://t.co/NgjBEZd7ey

12.02.2020 · Tweet

The most disordered phase is called the nematic phase where all the molecules (say) point in average in one direction but have no positional order. This long range order but low viscosity means that the nematic phase has a number of unique and interesting properties. 5/15

12.02.2020 · Tweet

For example, it is birefringent meaning it a different refractive index depending on the orientation of the molecule. This can lead to beautiful images under cross polarisers 6/15. (check out https://t.co/4CohduyQcx for some cool photos).

12.02.2020 · Tweet

The direction that the molecules tend to point in can be influenced by a number of things, including surface treatment and applying a voltage. When doped with a small amount of chiral material, it causes a helical twist; like stacking tables that start to twist as they stack. https://t.co/z6dQB9xR5C

12.02.2020 · Tweet

Now this is where things start to get even. This twist can actually guide light! And this is the basis for a lot of LCD displays. I found this awesome gif but couldn’t find who made it – if you know please tell me! 8/15 https://t.co/kqnYBBhDCL

12.02.2020 · Tweet

Here the LC is sandwiched between cross polarisers. Without a voltage there is a twist in the molecules and the light can pass through. When a voltage is applied, this causes the twist to disappear and the light can no longer pass through the second polariser, appearing dark.

12.02.2020 · Tweet

During my PhD I investigated what would happen when you confine the nematic (and chiral nematic) phase in bubbles of various geometries, including shells and toroids (donut-shaped). By confining the LC, you can induce (and hopefully control) defects in the fluid. 10/15

12.02.2020 · Tweet

With planar anchoring the molecules lay flat at the surface and it’s physically impossible to cover a sphere with rods, similarly to this spherical dog. These ‘partings’ or defects are regions of disorder that have different properties to the surrounding nematic phase. 11/15 https://t.co/JlFfSo0moK

12.02.2020 · Tweet

For example, they show up as black under cross polarisers. But remember, they are not “physical” objects and are free to move. We found that you can control the position, type and number of defects by varying in the shell thickness and the chiral pitch length. 12/15 https://t.co/RnY7fvSPR6

12.02.2020 · Tweet

One of the nicest findings from my PhD work was that I predicted a transition from 4 to 2 defects as the chiral pitch length decreased which was later confirmed from experiments. Predictions like this is one of the ultimate goals of doing simulations! 13/15

12.02.2020 · Tweet

I’ve written a short intro into this paper here: https://t.co/mEPUoNyUnB that explains the findings and importance in plain English. 14/15

12.02.2020 · Tweet

And I’m going to leave it there today. There is so much I haven’t touched on, I’ve only really talked about a small bit of the most disordered phase. I didn’t even get to put in my gif of a mood ring! (Also based on LCs!). 15/15 https://t.co/WGNwoR8x6R

13.02.2020 · Tweet

Wow, I can’t believe it is Thursday already! Today I’m going to talk about something a bit different – the importance and difficulty of working in an intrinsically interdisciplinary area of science. 1/9

13.02.2020 · Tweet

The work I do has given me a chance to work with people from a wide range of backgrounds and in a number of different departments. My degree is in chemistry, but I’m now in a chemical engineering department. 2/9

13.02.2020 · Tweet

Those don’t sound that different, but I swiftly learnt that they are! I have no idea how to design a power plant, whilst a chemical engineer will struggle with some of the stuff I know. I’ve also worked in a textile school, working with textile designers (amongst others). 3/9

13.02.2020 · Tweet

One of my favourite things about working with people from different scientific backgrounds is the number of different ways we all approach the same problem. When it works, it’s definitely better than the sum of its parts. 4/9

13.02.2020 · Tweet

But this leads me onto one of the difficulties – we all have our own vocabulary to describe things. A trivial example is Helmholtz free energy; as a chemist I write it ‘A’, but a physicist might write it ‘F’. Not a problem in itself, until I think ‘F’ is force (for example). 5/9

13.02.2020 · Tweet

I’ve learnt that communication is key, from both sides and it can work really well. It’s also important to keep expectations grounded – I have no idea* what is reasonable for an experimentalist to do or how long it will take (*= slight exaggeration). 6/9

13.02.2020 · Tweet

One thing I’m currently struggling with, and would love to hear your thoughts/experiences on the matter is how easy it is to progress from a postdoc in an inherently interdisciplinary area. Where do I fit? 7/9

13.02.2020 · Tweet

Happy Friday everyone! We’ve finally made it to the end of the week. Today I want to talk today a bit about something I’m currently working on – surfactants. They are super useful in everyday life and are found in a lot of household products. 1/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

All surfactants have the same basic molecular structure with a long water-hating (hydrophobic) tail joined to a water-loving (hydrophilic) head group. 2/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

This duality of behaviour causes surfactants to self-assemble in water. These phases can have long range order, or no order. In fact, phases with long range order are an example of the (other type) of liquid crystal phases. 3/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

These systems are called lyotropic liquid crystals, and again covers a range of different phases but I don’t want to go into that today. If you want to learn more about them, there’s a good video here: https://t.co/3QGOgEvuJ2 4/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

My current work looks at isotropic surfactant systems, that’s systems with no long range order. I work as part of @cafe4dm. The systems I’m specifically interested in are shampoo! 5/15 https://t.co/NXCAA2E47i

14.02.2020 · Tweet

One of the most common ingredients in shampoo is SLES (aka sodium laurylethoxysulfate) is one of the most important ingredients in shampoo and shower gel - pick up a bottle and it is very likely to be the second ingredient listed after water! 6/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

SLES has a charged head group, which means that the salt concentration of the liquid affects the self-assembly. We use computer simulations to investigate what the phases look like. In particular we are interested in how these affect the thickness (viscosity) of the fluid. 7/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

We recently published the phase diagram of SLES, you can read a “plain English” summary here https://t.co/ZTqJzVXOFu. Most of this work that I’m going to talk about was actually done by Maria Panoukidou, a PhD student in the group. 8/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

At low salt concentration, the surfactants assemble into spherical aggregates known as micelles, protecting the water-hating tails from the water whilst exposing the water-loving head groups to it. This complex fluid is a similar thickness to water. 9/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

As the salt concentration increases the interactions between the charged head groups decreases and they can pack closer together and the micelle starts to grow into rod-like micelles. 10/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

As the salt concentration continues to rise, the micelles continue to grow and form long, wormlike micelles. 11/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

These micelles can be up to microns in length and they can become entangled, increasing the thickness of the fluid. A good analogy of this is a plate of spaghetti, when you try to pull one strand out more come with it. 12/15 https://t.co/cFw5Sl99VS

14.02.2020 · Tweet

In shampoo the surfactants form this type of wormlike micelles. The mean micelle length and breakage time are really important, but very difficult to measure experimentally. This is where computer simulations come in handy. 13/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

As you keep adding salt to the wormlike micelles, there comes a point where branches start to form. These branches allow the stress to be relaxed in more ways and the thickness of the fluid actually decreases again. 14/15

14.02.2020 · Tweet

Again these branches are difficult to quantify experimentally which is why we use computer simulations. If you are interested in reading the full paper, you can find it here. https://t.co/jm7XK2rFsy 15/15

15.02.2020 · Tweet

Today is my last day curating here and I have to say I’ve really enjoyed it and had a great time. I didn’t really have anything planned for today, but looking over my threads this week I realised I haven’t actually talked about how to do simulations yet. 1/10

15.02.2020 · Tweet

Performing a simulation itself isn’t very difficult, there is loads of user-friendly free software available to do it. The difficult thing is picking the appropriate approach. Rubbish in = rubbish out 2/10

15.02.2020 · Tweet

I perform particle-based simulations which means I use virtual beads to represent atoms (or groups of atoms). From these we tend to be interested in averages over a large number of snapshots, or configurations. 3/10

15.02.2020 · Tweet

There are two main categories to generate these snapshots – molecular dynamics type or Monte Carlo type methods. Both have pros and cons and I’ll go through them quickly here. There are also more advanced methods that use a combination of the two but I won’t go into those. 4/10

15.02.2020 · Tweet

Molecular Dynamics a.k.a. MD. It essentially solves Newton’s equations of motion to advance the system. You* split the simulation into small time steps and calculate the change in forces, velocities and position acting on each bead. (* the computer) 5/10

15.02.2020 · Tweet

Pros of MD: + You can get dynamical information out, such as diffusion, viscosity + It is conceptually easier than Monte Carlo (MC) 6/10 https://t.co/uYXb7Noo6F

15.02.2020 · Tweet

Cons of MD: - You have to calculate the forces and store them. It may be non-trivial for non-spherical particles. - It is easy to get stuck in a meta-stable state which we are not interested in 7/10 https://t.co/KSnHbeZrZQ

15.02.2020 · Tweet

Monte Carlo a.k.a. MC. It takes a completely different approach. You make a move at random – it could be a particle translation/rotation and accepts it based on an underlying probability distribution based on the conditions of interest (temperature, pressure etc). 8/10

15.02.2020 · Tweet

Pros of MC: + Quicker than MD, you don’t need to calculate forces for the particles and so you store less information + You can perform “unphysical moves” (e.g. particle insertion) so you are less likely to get stuck in a high energy state and you need shorter simulations 9/10 https://t.co/aAyHzUndcp

15.02.2020 · Tweet

Cons of MC: - No kinetic/dynamic information (there is no concept of time in MC!) - Not as many programs readily available to use as for MD 10/10 https://t.co/V5JgIZPhuD

Hi Nano Tweeps 👋🏾! Izzy here - my turn in the hotseat talking abt how we, in the Life Sciences, watch the building 🧱s of life. We'll see some of the tiniest & coolest things we've ever shone light on, some of the latest tech & the problems that we face as Nano🧑🏻‍🔬👨🏾‍🔬👩🏼‍🔬 (0/n)

17.02.2020 · Tweet

First thing’s first [long thread] – How do we see the building blocks of life? It’s (relatively) easy. #superresolution microscopy. It’s a family of fluorescence microscopy techniques which allow us to see structures in the scale of ~ 1-200 nanometres. (1/n)

17.02.2020 · Tweet

“WHY”, you may ask. What we know is, this is the scale in which the tiniest processes of life are carried out. These range from single biomolecules (e.g. DNA, proteins) doing their own things, to tiny machines and compartments inside cells. (2/n) [GIF: Liam Neeson saying “Why”] https://t.co/njF7zXkkvv

17.02.2020 · Tweet

You might say, why not use X-ray or EM, as we have for decades. I’d say, “Aye”. If you want to watch these molecules orchestrate life, you need catch them in their natural habitats. You need to give them individual spectral signatures. Goodbye #monochrome (3/n) [GIF: conductor] https://t.co/keeeh61XyH

17.02.2020 · Tweet

Enter #fluorescence. The spectral signature we give each molecule is a fluorescent tag. There are literally 💯s of tags . They tell us where each molecule is *relative* to other molecules or structures. Modern Cell & Molecular Biology is built on this contextual info. (4/n)

17.02.2020 · Tweet

A decent microscope & a set of fluorescent tags will only get you to a resolution of ~ 200 nm. WHY: we’re rubbish at making lenses which can capture the light in the finest of diffraction patterns coming from smaller structures, as described by Abbe (not Abba) (5/n) [GIF: Abba] https://t.co/BhOEi6zeX0

17.02.2020 · Tweet

The answer to this was #superresolution. The most popular version was called localisation 🔬. And it basically involves making the fluorescent tags on *individual* markers switch ON-&-OFF. Much like the Eiffel tower here. More a bit later. (6/n) [GIF: Eiffel Tower lights] https://t.co/pwgbsSjYwY

17.02.2020 · Tweet

So, here’s how it usually works. We have a cell w. tags on a set of targets. We can either photo-activate (hit the tags with 💡 to chemically modify them) to make them visible, or we can deplete those available for fluorescence – this makes them 'blink' (7/n) [GIF: cat blinking] https://t.co/d6ISVenPiW

17.02.2020 · Tweet

This ‘blinking’ of fluorescent molecules is rapid. They are captured by a fast, sensitive camera. Here’s a movie of a typical recording (8/n): [video: fluorescent molecule photoblinking] https://t.co/PUHDPbpQhc

17.02.2020 · Tweet

By computationally-localising the centroid of each blink at sub-pixel accuracy, one frame at a time, you can build up a map which (like magic) reveal the finer features of the structure. See this fab animation by @HenriquesLab (9/n) https://t.co/W83OQkzrz4

17.02.2020 · Tweet

As Prof Henriques points out, the principles of reconstructing a #superresolution image is not unique to the nanoscale. Even a mobile phone camera can, in principle, do this: (10/n) https://t.co/6teFvjOeFS

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@HenriquesLab You are so welcome. This animation has been so useful for talks. I can now imaging - not a lot of better ways to enjoy image acquisition than pairing it with creme brûlée.

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@KLeoPullin Ooh! Good questions! This one first: The secret to sub-pixel accuracy of localising the centroids is 🥁🥁🥁🥁 curve-fitting. We know that each blink is ~ a 2D Gaussian in shape (the microscope optics and the refr. index in the sample dictate this)...

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@KLeoPullin For each 'blink', if we took a line profile across it, as you say, you would have a boxy profile (histogram with blue boxes). But because we know that the shape of the unpixelated event is Gaussian, we can fit an infinitely spooth 2D gaussian (red) using a statistical protocol... https://t.co/7gP3tjrgdj

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@KLeoPullin which allows us to pin point the centroid (essentially at the true peak of the red curve) with far greater precision than what the pixel grid alone would allow. Like magic. https://t.co/iZAHcnu9oO

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@KLeoPullin Actually, there is a limit to how accurate you can be with pinpointing the centroid. The amount of noise in the images (which create uncertainty in the curve-fitting) restrict the "precision of localisation" to a few nanometres. But that's far better than 10s or 100s of nm.

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@martinjones78 @LaineBioImaging I heard that @LaineBioImaging was better at strings than keyboard.

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@KLeoPullin Excellent-questions^2. So, localisation microscopy doesn't directly rely on wavelength because the images are not formed directly by the emitted light. For each molecule, we map its centroid (based on the curve-fitting to each 'blink')... https://t.co/RENUj7gosY

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@KLeoPullin It is the reconstruction put together from *that map of fine centroids* which can have a resolution of single-digit nanometres. So it is essentially a pointillist image. [GIF: 3D points cloud] https://t.co/8clEd9sYyu

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@KLeoPullin Ooh! YES! This is my ongoing debate with our local data managers. The primary data are the image series which contain the 'blink' events of the fluorescent tags. These are fairly big (~ 5 Gb). The really useful data are the coordinates of the centroids & the fit parameters.

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@KLeoPullin Once you have the list of coordinates and the related parameters, you can reconstruct the image it lots of different ways. There are actually lots of different rendering algorithms which have different strengths and weaknesses.

17.02.2020 · Tweet

@KLeoPullin The most common ways to display the data is to show, rather than just where the points (left) are, a smoothed (not explicitly smoothed) image which shows the local density of detected points (right). So, intensity, still would reflect density of the fluorescent tags. https://t.co/tU8LjSfMZY

Morning everyone 😃 ! Izzy *again* here. So, carrying on with the theme of #superresolution, I want to talk about what happened after 2010, because it has been a helluva ride. (1/n) [GIF: spiral rollercoaster] https://t.co/CGix1UHFA1

2010-2020 has been a golden decade for #superresolution tech because one can never have enough resolution! By 2019, we were achieving angstrom-level of localization precision and resolutions of ~ 1 nm. (2/n)

18.02.2020 · Tweet

The first thing was, methods like STORM and PALM became better. We started to better-understand & control the sample chemistry which made them more user-friendly. We also saw was the advent of newer & cleverer ways of getting #superresolution. (3/n) [GIF: teacher spills liq N2] https://t.co/zltFJid8WP

18.02.2020 · Tweet

Most of the new methods came from 3 areas: (A) Improved/innovative hardware. These included new flavours of structured illumination microscopy - more acronyms like iSIM/mSIM (4/n) https://t.co/cuNoM2CZSb

18.02.2020 · Tweet

For sheer resolution, these've been fantastic. MINFLUX is a method which scan and localise markers using a 🍩-shaped laser spot. These can give you images at ~ 1 nm in resolution. Watch this lecture by Stefan Hell on how it works (5/n) https://t.co/R12KY5Ax6S [GIF: dog with🍩] https://t.co/GCWsqJqShD

18.02.2020 · Tweet

B) The 2nd is using contextual info to improve resolution, imaging speed &/or reduce artefacts. So, we’ve got some *new* acronyms like SRRF, SOFI, 3B, HAWK. One of the 🆒 things, I think, about them is that seeing single blinks is no-longer mandatory (6/n) https://t.co/FVN8MDyQnE

18.02.2020 · Tweet

These are mostly algorithmic methods which use additional information about samples to estimate the likely structure in #superresolution without having to see the full complement of the fluorescent tags as blinks. Result = faster & more versatile imaging (7/n) [GIF: roadrunner] https://t.co/vMCxtMKHMo

A big 💩 in 📍pointing the fluorescent tags accurately, is noise. In light 🔬, noise depends on a lot of things – the 📷 you use, how fast you record images (i.e. how quick the ‘blinks’ are) & how many photons you collect from each tag. (10/n) [GIF: noise on CRT TV] https://t.co/yseGzg0979

18.02.2020 · Tweet

Classic #superresolution like dSTORM were notorious for limited control of noise. What you need, are noise-free images where the ‘blinks’ are easier to detect. Introducing: DNA-PAINT (🧬🎨). (11/n) [image: dSTORM & DNA-PAINT blinks] https://t.co/3LNVsaPHPh

18.02.2020 · Tweet

🧬🎨: We separate the fluorescent tag from the 🎯. The tag is now linked to a short diffusible single-strand 🧬. The matching 🧬-strand marks the 🎯. It is lit by a thin sheet of light. You see the tag *only* when the tag has ‘docked’ with the target (12/n) [Image: DNA-PAINT] https://t.co/bq18Se3ZHo

18.02.2020 · Tweet

You see them as lots of blinks because these dockings of the 🧬+tag are short-lived (~ 1 s). They actually looks like lots of blinks. They are not blinks #fakeblinks. But for us microscopists, these ‘blinks’ can be used the same way as blinks (13/n) [GIF: lots of eyes blinking] https://t.co/qvetG4BUwA

18.02.2020 · Tweet

So, here’s the difference 🧬🎨 makes to the images. ‘Optical’ resolution of ~ 10 nm. (14/n) [Image: comparison of TIRF, dSTORM & 🧬🎨 images of a protein cluster] https://t.co/Ll7AVk1eZH

18.02.2020 · Tweet

Fun fact: because tags are made of 🧬 & not attached physically to the 🎯s, you can use lots of unique pieces of 🧬s to image lots of diff 🎯s. You simply wash-in ➡️📸➡️ wash-out each tag to map multiple 🎯s on the same cell. (15/n) [image: 4 diff structures on same cell] https://t.co/Njmdzkwt2r

@ProfRachelGaN My non-expert expl: The 3D image is built up from single marker blinks, localised in 3D, rather than 2D. The focal vol is still relatively thick (sub-micron), so blinks can occur anywhere within it. What 4Pi gives you is *very* good confidence in localising the blinks axially.

19.02.2020 · Tweet

@ProfRachelGaN So, when you map the 3D coordinates of all the blinks coming from the imaging volume, what you get is a well-resolved 3D volume that is sub-micron in height. To sample a greater depth, one moves the focus axial and sample blinks from different depths. Hope I am making sense.

19.02.2020 · Tweet

@ProfRachelGaN I suspect the total thickness of a sample one can practically image this way however is limited (to a few microns at best, I estimate). The lattice light sheet would have much better working depth.

Atomic Force Microscopy - what's this nanoscale tool doing being bandied in the world of biology? Actually, hold up... what IS AFM? (1/6) https://t.co/OdIplyacdq

02.03.2020 · Tweet

AFM is a type of scanning probe microscopy - a technique which won Gerd Binning and Heinrich Rohrer the 1986 Nobel Prize for Physics. In its simplest form, a physical probe is scanned across a surface and a laser is used to measure deflections of the probe. (2/6) https://t.co/1Krk18WcBd

02.03.2020 · Tweet

As AFM involves 'feeling' the surface to produce an image or information, we aren't limited by the optical diffraction limit and can measure down to the picoscale (depending on your experimental set-up, of course!). (3/6)

02.03.2020 · Tweet

Additionally, the only sample preparation required is that your sample is adhered to some degree to a substrate - no loose particles or floaties allowed! (4/6) https://t.co/zEHdlH0jC1

02.03.2020 · Tweet

Finally, as this is a physical measurement, we aren't shackled by the need to dry, fix, stain, or resin mount samples. And we can perform these measurements in situ, in ambient or controlled environments. Which leads us to... (5/6)

02.03.2020 · Tweet

The ideal technique to study single living cells! ☑️ Adherent cells grow happily on a substrate ☑️ In situ measurements- living cells in media and heated to the perfect 37C ☑️ No fixing or staining required to probe the cells (6/6)

03.03.2020 · Tweet

This was a commercially pure titanium particle (5-25 micrometers in diameter) hitting a 300 series stainless steel substrate at a velocity above 600 m/s. There was no heat involved. /2

08.03.2020 · Tweet

This as my first ever experiment to make a commercially pure titanium coating. In a cold spray setup we have a powder feeder and a high pressure gas (in my case helium). We push the helium through a convergent divergent nozzle, also called a de-label nozzle like a rocket nozzle/3 https://t.co/MWMl0wKbA1

08.03.2020 · Tweet

Helium going through the nozzle accelerates the powder particles to supersonic velocities. The powder we use are small. My hair is around 100 micrometer. The powder we use are in the range of 5-20 micrometer. /4

08.03.2020 · Tweet

When the cold titanium hits the steel it deforms very quickly (strain rate of 10^9 per second of you really need to know). At that sort of conditions metal start behaving very differently. There is something called thermal softening. /5

08.03.2020 · Tweet

This very soft metal start flowing and forms a jet. This jet (see the edge of the particle) removes any oxide from the metal surface and two metals come together and weld—it’s like magic. Cold welding. This bonding is super strong, more than 100 MPa. /6

08.03.2020 · Tweet

How much is 100 MPa? You can hang my weight from a small disc and it won’t fail. This was my intro to surface engineering—a cold spray process. Those materials scientists out there would enjoy this seminal paper by Prof Assadi at Brunel https://t.co/U1l0uhFyDH /7

08.03.2020 · Tweet

👆🏼was my first journal paper that I read on cold spray in 2006. It was tough but I fell in love with materials after reading that. What is happening here is similar to hitting a wall with a flour dough and the dough sticking to the wall for a couple of sec. /8

08.03.2020 · Tweet

Now imagine being able to engineer the dough so it will not fall off. It will stick to the wall for ever! That is what I started my career on in 2006. /9

08.03.2020 · Tweet

@AaronSlepkov Close. Thanks for engaging. Titanium into steel. But there was no melting involved. The particle was travelling around 600 m/s when it hit the steel.

I am continuing the theme of cold gas spraying. 10+ years ago there was a big controversy. We all thought the bond strength of the coatings only come from metallurgical bond. My first ever journal paper introduced a concept called mechanical bonding. https://t.co/2dmF28XTl2 /1 https://t.co/q9xF4l5ujM https://t.co/6zq5b3wx9d

08.03.2020 · Tweet

We figured out the entire strength of the coatings cannot simply come from metal-metal bonds. There was someone else in play. When a particle (copper here) hits a substrate (aluminium), the substrate also deforms and it gets squeezed between particles. /2

When the bond fails, copper-aluminium contact fails as well as the squeezed bit of aluminium, which gives the additional strength. /3

Time to talk about various spray technologies. Let’s start with Arc spray. Here a pair of electrically conductive wires are melted by means of an electric arc. The molten material is atomised by compressed air and propelled towards the substrate surface https://t.co/gKPwOfT51j /1 https://t.co/yM5a1KVpbF https://t.co/1l2o6uOHGk

10.03.2020 · Tweet

Arc spray particles are travelling relatively slower and cooler but the coatings are usually denser than the wire flame sprayed coating and higher deposition efficiencies. Examples include mostly corrosion and wear coatings for large components. https://t.co/crVdVvkZwN /2 https://t.co/y9jyWdoNcz

10.03.2020 · Tweet

Aerospace companies in the U.K. uses a version of wire arc spray for metallizing polymer composites, for plane wings. These are deicing coatings based on joule heating—pass a small current and it will melt the ice. /3

10.03.2020 · Tweet

Flame spray, a low cost option, with similar particle velocities to arc spray but much higher particle temperature. Typically we use oxyacetylene flame or hydrogen flame (3000 C). Fig courtesy of Gordon England. Also known as a low velocity oxy fuel spray. /1 https://t.co/yM5a1KVpbF https://t.co/C0EvYMro1f

10.03.2020 · Tweet

We have an @OerlikonGroup combustion flame spray https://t.co/cMc7OFoROz . Instead of coating my colleague @Dr_Ifty_Ahmed uses it to make porous powder. /2

I am back talking about HVOF (High Velocity Oxy Fuel) thermal spray—the industry standard process for cermet (ceramic+metallic) coatings. The particles are travelling much faster here but temperature cooler than plasma spray. It’s essentially a rocket engine burning O2+Fuel. /1 https://t.co/XNS7rk1p0O

12.03.2020 · Tweet

The combustion here is supersonic so one can see the shock diamond in the flame. JP5000 is an industry standard HVOF torch. There two types of HVOF spray, gas fuelled and liquid fuelled. Gas fuelled torches can spray ceramic powder and the particles are injected into burner./2

12.03.2020 · Tweet

Liquid fuel or kerosene fuelled guns are much more powerful (250 kW) but the particles are much cooler as we inject the powder in after the nozzle (cooler part). Tungsten carbide cobalt and chromium carbide nickel chrome are two popular coatings for HVOF /3

12.03.2020 · Tweet

WC-Co is used for <500 C and CrC-NiCr is used >900 C in your plane engine to protect from wear. We need a finer cut powder 5-38 micron here where the carbides could be Nano sized <100 mm. /4

Where is this nano in surface engineering? Thermal spray is mostly micron scale business but nano came in 1990s and it opened a whole new world for us. We call it suspension thermal spray (STS). Instead of using powder we can use a suspension with nano particles./1 https://t.co/CRaNTM0ve3

13.03.2020 · Tweet

The benefits: finer particles result in uniform properties in all directions and the hardness can be increased significantly which is good for wear. You can see suspension thermal sprayed alumina coating here. /2 https://t.co/tyY3J2PZtu

13.03.2020 · Tweet

You can improve the wear performance of alumina by an order of magnitude by using suspension (nano) over micron sized powders you can see an AFM image showing how hard these particles can be./3 https://t.co/0agDWxvGV5

13.03.2020 · Tweet

Link to our first suspension thermal spray work https://t.co/m1Z0vS0m88

13.03.2020 · Tweet

A suspension high velocity oxy fuel thermal spray setup to spray sub-micron to nano range particles. We are spraying cerium oxide here to make surfaces super hydrophobic. /1 https://t.co/NzGCTGrPDv

13.03.2020 · Tweet

Benefits: water would roll off easily. The surface can be self cleaning. Also bugs wouldn’t grow if the water doesn’t stay there for long. For icy conditions, if water doesn’t stick there won’t be any ice—a great idea. More details here https://t.co/BVws2uFAAM /2 https://t.co/dzKzfcDCdK

14.03.2020 · Tweet

Using a spectroscopy like Raman spectroscopy one can measure the vibrational modes of the molecule which can tell us how many layers are there in the graphene nanoplatelets after the spray. Carbon has D, G & 2D peaks. More about Raman https://t.co/WDWUE7vbh4 /2 https://t.co/dF6hJox3W7

14.03.2020 · Tweet

There is a barely a scratch on the sample which was sprayed with graphene nanoplatelets, compared to the sample which was pure alumina after a wear test. Details here https://t.co/cx3ufc4aLs https://t.co/X97zwy0lKZ

Breakup of a suspension in a plasma is a beautiful process. Look here. When fine particles are injected in a plasma they behave very differently. They follow the gas trajectories. /1 https://t.co/piNLqaXpk5 https://t.co/z0vxqvJ8qa

14.03.2020 · Tweet

SPS (Suspension Plasma Spray) setup. These fine particles hit the asperities of the substrate and form beautiful columnar structure. These columnar structures are highly desirable for thermal barrier coatings for aero engines. They can expand and contract better in service/2 https://t.co/ui6JXWkFdm

14.03.2020 · Tweet

These columnar structure could only be formed using a very expensive process called EB-PVD (electron beam physical vapour deposition). We can now form these using a much cheaper SPS process—thanks to nano particles. https://t.co/Pn5vaJ2lLx /3 https://t.co/YSlhdeXwiH

Okay, first principles. The universe is made of atoms. For 'just' a moment lets forget about electrons, neutrons and protons, and say that this is it. This is the basic building block. We'll label different atoms by colour; so lets say Oxygen is red. It looks a little lonely https://t.co/aOyquV4gkh

23.03.2020 · Tweet

So the atoms stick together in groups. Here we have two carbons (grey) and 6 oxygens (white). This is quite a stable 'family unit' (Why? Because of all the electrons, neutrons and protons that I am not going to discuss). This is what a molecule is - just a stable arrangement https://t.co/qI7Czld7xN

23.03.2020 · Tweet

Some configurations become useful molecules. This is methanol - great at disinfecting surfaces and distilling into alcoholic beverages. It just has one oxygen, a couple of carbons and six hydrogens. That ONE extra oxygen has made all the difference https://t.co/iHG5enIo1S

23.03.2020 · Tweet

So, I will move on, but some great examples of functional molecules are Caffeine - the component of tea and coffee that gives you that buzz. It's 'usefulness' comes from this particular arrangement of molecules. It's still just carbon, oxygen hydrogen and now nitrogen (the blue) https://t.co/wqtcgqhn8Q

23.03.2020 · Tweet

Or, a fun favourite, Glutamate - something your body produces to regulate FEAR! This is a great molecule but it's just one simple structure. At this point we're just painting by colour https://t.co/FFgjYko1ad

23.03.2020 · Tweet

My final example of a small molecule is Vancomycin - a 'potent' antibiotic. Doctors do not like prescribing this unless they are certain it will work. Antibiotic resistance is a story for another day. All you need to take from this is 'this arrangement of atoms = bacteria death' https://t.co/mGG7BPvqvh

Yes, Hemoglobin IS smart. The more oxygen it has the more generous at sharing it is. The less it has the more choosey it is about letting that last one go. It is a conscientious delivery man - serving to where it is most needed. https://t.co/EL5Ea7YvcV

Most polymers are a mix of carbon and other atoms. Every blue or red spot on this molecule is a site that 'could' grab a water molecule. Whether it will or not? Depends on its environment https://t.co/2SrK1JqIRy

23.03.2020 · Tweet

If a polymer doesn't want to play with the water it can coil in on itself. This form of 'molecular isolation' can be inherent but some polymers can switch back and forth, changing their mind depending on the environment https://t.co/VAGy2nktyF

23.03.2020 · Tweet

Why would a polymer switch? Temperature is a common one. Think of it like stretching out to get some sun on a warm day, or coiling up into a ball to preserve heat when its cold. https://t.co/UBFxaqs4ZY

23.03.2020 · Tweet

The physics driving this (its entropy) are ridiculously complicated but the maths is sound. The polymer doesn't choose to unravel, it is responding to its environment https://t.co/ku434QdRgb

23.03.2020 · Tweet

Another influence is pH - if the water is acidic the polymer might retract. Or salts, some polymers respond completely differently depending on what else is around them https://t.co/fzTldBr97Z

23.03.2020 · Tweet

Lets take a step back. We can split out polymers into two categories with a grey area in the middle. Some polymers are 'water loving' - we call them 'Hydrophilic' https://t.co/4v6gGegD7M

23.03.2020 · Tweet

Some other polymers don't like water at all. Plastics wont dissolve and wont bond with the water molecules. We label them as 'Hydrophobic'. They 'hate' water. https://t.co/kIRj3keU2p

23.03.2020 · Tweet

We're at a point where we can 'finally' forget molecular structures and just describe things with these two terms. Water loving or water hating. Life, biology, chemistry, materials science as we know it can be essentially simplified like this. https://t.co/U9sTwUWepf

Hypothetical scenario. I have a colleague who is very smart and very worried about headaches. He has designed a drug that when it gets in the brain will sort everything out. https://t.co/iqgaY5Bb1i

23.03.2020 · Tweet

But this drug is fragile, if you swallow it then your stomach acids will destroy the perfect structure. That is 'why' we have a stomach after all, to break things down and stop anything nasty getting into our bodies. https://t.co/L63aw9s2ti

23.03.2020 · Tweet

This guy is smart but he's tried everything. Save taking a needle and injecting it straight into your skull the drug is useless. You could inject the arm and 'hope' it makes its way down the blood stream but for headaches nobody wants that https://t.co/tY94Rq1gY4

23.03.2020 · Tweet

That's where we come in! What if we had a polymer that wrapped around the drug molecule. What if it held onto it so tightly it shielded the drug from the stomach acids? The polymer (which is pretty indestructible) could act as shield helping the drug through the flash point https://t.co/NifmMEEDIt

23.03.2020 · Tweet

This kind of helping hand transport is really common, in fact 'controlled delivery' is an entire field within Pharmacy. Polymers can lend a hand to small molecules, help them get where they need to go then drop them off where they need to go. It's easy! https://t.co/w8txiXhg7i

23.03.2020 · Tweet

With the right polymers you can target delivery of your drug somewhere warm - like an infection. The body will be heating up to fight off the infection and the polymer will 'carry' the drug safely until it finds the spot https://t.co/T4RB0Wg4c8

23.03.2020 · Tweet

They are also good at fighting another problem. Your body is really, really good at getting rid of stuff it doesn't recognise. We get rid of drugs in our body the normal way we get rid of most things in our body https://t.co/ge28rgT70l

23.03.2020 · Tweet

So, a lot of the 'drug load' is lost. It never reaches your brain / heart / infection / whatever because the body pushes it out. Polymers (because they are big) hang around. Our molecular taxi can just circle round the body, dropping a little here and a little there. https://t.co/f78KUSgSnB

23.03.2020 · Tweet

But, though he codified the rules and concepts of polymer science, the origins of the discipline go back further. In fact to nearly 180 years years ago. Something happened in 1843 that codified the need for Materials Scientists. Something significant. What was it? Here's a clue: https://t.co/gte1oO9azy

In 1837 Queen Victoria became queen of England and ushered in a new age of modernity in Britain. The Industrial revolution had reshaped the world as we knew it - this was a time of thriving industry and mass manufacture. The world had changed https://t.co/wgGAzX2W5K

24.03.2020 · Tweet

24.03.2020 · Tweet

24.03.2020 · Tweet

24.03.2020 · Tweet

Rubber is an elastomer. It is soft, stretchy and flexible (great) but it also goes 'weird' if you heat it up or cool it down. Bad news if you are using it to waterproof your coaches or mailbags. Cold winters or hot summers = need to replace it every year https://t.co/mbDSkKyCp6

24.03.2020 · Tweet

Hence the need for scientists and inventors to 'modify' rubber. We knew that we had a great product here, it just needed some minor modifications to make it perfect. There was money to be made https://t.co/H6wj2KrJ7v

24.03.2020 · Tweet

And, as some of you have guessed, this is the point where someone dropped sulphur and white lead into the rubber before it was processed. It turned bright white, very sticky and very hard. It was still rubber but it was completely different https://t.co/AsksZFPIy1

24.03.2020 · Tweet

If you then heat it up (i.e. cook it) the product turned black, not sticky and much more stable. It also stopped going 'weird' if you let it get hot or cold. It was the birth of a new class of materials. It may not look like much but it really was revolutionary. https://t.co/uUIMuDgII3

24.03.2020 · Tweet

We 'think' Charles Goodyear was the first person to do this. He knew he was onto something big, he knew this was important work that could change the world. His mistake was to tell and show other people what he was working on before he was finished. https://t.co/OCVwPils0M

24.03.2020 · Tweet

Fed up of replacing his rubber British entrepreneur Thomas Hancock was keen to solve this problem. A friend of a friend showed him some 'American' samples of prototype materials and he immediately saw the potential. All efforts were rediverted to solving this issue https://t.co/SE53QRndBx

24.03.2020 · Tweet

In 1844, completely separately, both men filed a patents for the 'vulcanisation' of Rubber. First Hancock in the UK, then 8 weeks later Goodyear in the USA. They were working separately, unaware of what each other was up to, and they both wanted to change the world. https://t.co/UegbCYfPfv

These enzymes convert small molecules into other, useful, materials. However polymers are not like small molecules, they are long chains of molecules, strings of them stuck together. If you can't break the chain you can't process them. https://t.co/rGdt9FVozl

25.03.2020 · Tweet

To the average punter 'Plastic' is 'Plastic'. However, chemically, there are MANY different types of plastic and they are all completely different. Most plastics are full of carbon, making them really strong and really difficult to break. https://t.co/Ifao1lhmJi

25.03.2020 · Tweet

So if you want to break down a polymer you need to cut the string apart. Breaking polymers is not a one step process, it is several steps, and it is a very, very slow process https://t.co/CV11CIgQrM

25.03.2020 · Tweet

Tomorrow I am going to talk about 'chain length' but the important thing for now is - these long chains are very strong. If your material is wrapped up with this 'molecular rope' it's not going to go anywhere fast https://t.co/DP1UoSQp6t

25.03.2020 · Tweet

Polymers are long chain molecules, with many repeat units. Scientists are usually very good at determining 'what' a chemical is but they are not quite at adept at determining how big something could be https://t.co/3VxUpcoSFe

26.03.2020 · Tweet

The best 'size' method for the standard chemist is an instrument called a Mass Spectrometer. You may have seen these at airports - they are now routinely used to test baggage for traces of explosives. https://t.co/73UfhU0PQ5

26.03.2020 · Tweet

In its simplest form 'Mass Spec' works by flinging the molecules down a tube and seeing how far / fast they fly. For small molecules it is an incredibly sensitive method of detection - hence the use in mass spectrometers https://t.co/nUX17apSvg

26.03.2020 · Tweet

A high end mass spectrometer can spot the extra mass of one single neutron in a molecule. This means it can be used for radiocarbon dating of fossils - determining how much C14 in the molecule remains can tell you if a dinosaur if 65 or 165 million years old https://t.co/MtLtkSCBgV

26.03.2020 · Tweet

But polymers, particularly synthetic polymers have two problems. The first is they are big, and the bigger something is the less efficient they are at flying. You need a 'very' strong 'catapult' to launch these suckers. https://t.co/0NgTKQ4X4g

26.03.2020 · Tweet

And the second problem comes right back down to the way we make polymers. Broad generic statement about all Polymer Chemists. We hide it well but we're just not very good at this. 🙄 https://t.co/uvYim8Nsw6

26.03.2020 · Tweet

We can make polymers. We can make tonnes of them, our factories are literally churning them out. But here I need to explain 'dispersity' and bring back our molecular models from Monday https://t.co/3sJNXq2PXG

26.03.2020 · Tweet

I want to talk about this paper from S. Harrison in 2018 - however it isn't open access. So bear with me whilst I lay out what it's saying for those who can't open it https://t.co/O9JbakUa4i

26.03.2020 · Tweet

A polymer is a chain of repeat units. However when 'we' make long chains controlling the speed of the reaction is difficult. Synthesising long molecules takes a long time and we cannot ensure that they will 'all' be the same length https://t.co/y3sGKOdNVI

26.03.2020 · Tweet

Polymer Chemists have a term 'dispersity'. It is a measure of how 'similar' the lengths of all our pieces of string are. In an ideal world, if everything was the same length, if all our molecules were 'the same' we would have a dispersity of 1. https://t.co/ziKXY5WMIp

26.03.2020 · Tweet

The larger your dispersity the more variety you have in your sample. They are all the same polymer (type) but they are different lengths. And trying to work out if all your chains are the same length is difficult. https://t.co/fmgMosfq5M

26.03.2020 · Tweet

In traditional polymer chemistry our dispersity values would be huge - over the last 3 decades we have developed techniques bringing them down to 1.1 - 1.3 ish when we need to…. https://t.co/wwTNg5BqLv

26.03.2020 · Tweet

But, as Dr Harrison pointed out, if we applied the maths polymer chemists use to people's height... Well, this is the 4 members of family. They have an average height of 122 cm and a dispersity of 1.18. https://t.co/rhG64JRBMd

26.03.2020 · Tweet

Let that sink in. Even with a dispersity of 1.18 they had a baby (50 cm) and two fully grown adults (over 5 feet tall). Polymers are, a little like this. We, as chemists, just can't make them all the same size. https://t.co/qc6lKUrGBi

26.03.2020 · Tweet

His sample size is small but I would also point to the fact no member of the family is 122 cm tall. They have two tall people (adults) and two small people (children). This is a bimodal distribution and polymer chemistry is FULL of bimodal distributions https://t.co/toeKuH2eno

26.03.2020 · Tweet

Got annoyed last year when we bought some polymers with a stated mass of 100,000. When we tested them I don't think there was a single chain that long in the bottle. Half were approx. 50,000 and half were approx. 200,000. The dispersity was reasonable though so same difference? https://t.co/yA94QiKhwG

27.03.2020 · Tweet

I am particularly interested in what I call 'smart' polymer chains - these are materials that respond to their environment by swelling / collapsing. They can respond to temperature, pH, salts. https://t.co/zpZXvx1jBS

27.03.2020 · Tweet

When our polymers collapse they tend to group up. The 'accumulated mass' of polymers piling on top of each other means they form into particles that we can analyse fairly easily with scientific instruments. https://t.co/nWCbZKPGMT

27.03.2020 · Tweet

Here is an atomic force microscope image of some of these distorted globules. These are linear polymer chains (polyacrylic acid and polyacrylamide) that have just collapsed in on themselves because the pH is low. The individual chains are only a few nm across https://t.co/P4B3t2wWES

27.03.2020 · Tweet

Here is the same sample, if we raise the pH, shows the globules just fading away as the individual polymer chains escape back into the solution. The AFM has picked up just noise - just flakes of noise https://t.co/yzR0XVWuzW

27.03.2020 · Tweet

And here is exactly the same sample under an optical microscope - we are able to form polymer particles that form and then dissolve with just a 0.1 change in pH https://t.co/ngLG7Mpekr

27.03.2020 · Tweet

This is a great example of what we call polymer complexation - amorphous materials associating / dissociating with each other in solution. As Materials Scientists we are 'very' good at studying the collapsed particles but the stretched chains - more difficult https://t.co/D1j9jZQes4

27.03.2020 · Tweet

It's very difficult to study dissolved polymer chains as they just wont keep still. We have some brilliant techniques however that I want to pull out and show off after my next meeting https://t.co/qlCWhro1ve

27.03.2020 · Tweet

Yes, a lot of people 'describe' polymer association across the chains as a ladder effect - they are looking at DNA and thinking of each link as a rung on the ladder. It's a lovely model but for most polymers the evidence does not bear it out at all https://t.co/wiZgOzca97 https://t.co/Oidh82B6HS

27.03.2020 · Tweet

So - my go to technique for studying the movement of single polymer chains in solution? Tag them with fluorescence dyes and use light to track their movement https://t.co/FIHUjFRQRh

27.03.2020 · Tweet

Dyes are great molecules. Some of them are inorganic (metals) - you can get a lot of different and bright colours by mixing metals together. However mixing metals / polymers is a 'whole' other conversation. Things get sticky https://t.co/ZCbU722tLH

27.03.2020 · Tweet

So I stick to using organic dyes - like this one. See the double bonds (dashed lines) between the carbon atoms. It means it can absorb light and re-emit. It's a fluorescent dye and it's awesome https://t.co/7ghTxHpmzJ

27.03.2020 · Tweet

You can drop your dye into a solution of polymers to see if they interact - the dyes have a lot of carbons so they tend to seek out our polymers and stick to them. We'd call this 'hydrophobic association' https://t.co/QkryohkOXs

27.03.2020 · Tweet

But you get the most out of them by covalently attaching your dyes so they stick directly onto the polymer chain. Here is our acenapthylene molecule sitting in the middle of a polymer chain, minding it's own business. One outlier amongst a sea of acrylic acid units https://t.co/FRclp3z4X5

27.03.2020 · Tweet

The polymer doesn't know it but that 1 tiny acenapthylene unit is our eyes and ears onto what the polymer is doing. We've successfully incorporated a spy into the backbone that can report on everything the polymer does https://t.co/tAjsLA4Ecp

27.03.2020 · Tweet

So, when the polymer coils, stretches, collapses, binds, or does whatever it fancies, our spy dye sits unobtrusively in the centre. All I have to do is shine light on them and the fluorescence spectra (and lifetime) will report back) https://t.co/owdkLLEQFP

27.03.2020 · Tweet

We have a device that can count the photons in, then time how long they take to come out. If the dye is 'crowded' (i.e. in a collapsed polymer) it may take longer than if the polymer is swelled. Why does this happen? https://t.co/taOMAKLOHv

27.03.2020 · Tweet

We 'think' this is because the solvent molecules can collide with the dyes. Every molecule is moving quickly with Brownian motion - and could knock the light out of our dyes. If the polymer collapses it shields the dye, protects it, and it holds onto the light for longer https://t.co/v4xmoJ6V4S

27.03.2020 · Tweet

In this scenario remember light = energy. When the dye grabs the light it enters what we call an 'excited state'. But this isn't stable - it can't maintain this super form for very long. https://t.co/reZhHcEyGs

27.03.2020 · Tweet

And if you polarise the light going into the dye, and stick a rotating polariser to the detector, we can see how fast the polymer is moving. Polarising filters are brilliant inventions - as people with smart sunglasses may know https://t.co/lZba7hdn4R

27.03.2020 · Tweet

My go to fluorescent tag shown off this afternoon was acenaphthylene - it's a small dye and so has the least influence on the polymer chain. It sits tight to the C-C backbone and reports on molecular motion very well https://t.co/7FDhfjeuiC

Pyrene is an odd one - It emits 2 peak colours of light - and the ratio of them it emits depends on how close it can get to other pyrene molecules. And Pyrene is a fascinating reporter as you don't 'need' to actually attach it to the polymer you are inspecting. You can, and we have, but you can also just add it loose in the solution and it will provide data about how effectively your polymer chain wraps around it. https://t.co/MLY62WCLoT

NMR = Nuclear Magnetic Resonance. We drop our sample in a tube into the centre of a very powerful magnetic coil. The machine has to be insulated several times to protect people outside - even then we don't recommend pacemakers or mobile phones go near it! https://t.co/CocPiP12FB

MRI is a fantastic, non-invasive, method at looking at the chemical composition inside your body. It's safer than X-rays and gives doctors much more detail about what they are looking for. Chemists love NMR for much the same reason - although we tend not to get beautiful pictures https://t.co/3P0KKTKs6D

So - if we want to work out a molecule's size - we can watch how fast it moves. You may have heard of Brownian motion - the idea that all particles are vibrating and moving - this holds just as true for polymers https://t.co/aSOCgeeFP6

Polymers move just like any other molecule, however they are a little slower because of their size. This means using NMR to study their diffusion (speed) in solution is particularly appealing https://t.co/lCqNd4nhVx

So how does DOSY work? Well we put a magnetic pulse into the field (pointing in different direction across the tube) and then we fire a reverse pulse to bring the molecules all the way back to way they started. https://t.co/bB8eP921Io

28.03.2020 · Tweet

It sounds simple but because the molecules wont keep still they won't end up pointing in a uniform direction. It is this 'abnormality' we can measure - we can catch how fast our particles are moving by how out of line they are when we've fired our second pulse https://t.co/U1iHY7iLio

28.03.2020 · Tweet

So DOSY takes the NMR peaks (left image) that represent different protons and gives you diffusion (or size data) beneath them. And if you configure your instrument right it can provide some information about the size distribution! https://t.co/xlKaF41TJH

So our in house toolkit for measuring size of polymers includes the size exclusion chromatography, DOSY NMR and the fluorescence techniques + several other specialist techniques like light scattering, viscometery, membrane osmometry... but they are 'far' more specialised

We then used this method to assess the effect of polymer functionalisation on the enzyme activity. https://t.co/abavEE9KJX Using different polymer architectures, an enhanced enzyme activity was achieved because of the polymers on their surface. More on this later this week. https://t.co/mRpaz7qMvp

05.04.2020 · Tweet

Now more specifically, BION is looking into biogenic avenues. That is, drug carriers inspired by nature because we can learn to optimise synthetic delivery systems through this. Biogenic and Biomimetic Carriers as Versatile Transporters To Treat Infections https://t.co/Uc5jlYKt0V

So today, I will focus on antimicrobial resistance and why it is important to do research in this area (not only because of corona nowadays). Our institute is the @Helmholtz_HIPS in Saarbrücken and the first research institute in Germany fully dedicated to pharmaceutical research https://t.co/2EKFQ5owg5

06.04.2020 · Tweet

@Helmholtz_HIPS belongs to the Helmholtz Centre for Infection research @Helmholtz_HZI focusing on antimicrobial resistance development and therapies. Why? See the info-graphic below (copyright HZI). https://t.co/vRtTp5TDAQ

06.04.2020 · Tweet

According to the WHO, antimicrobial resistance is one of the major threats to humanity. An antimicrobial resistance review (https://t.co/9dIvAvsb7R) predicted that by 2050 up to ten million deaths may occur from such infections. Very interesting read with many infographics! https://t.co/8csQenL70M

06.04.2020 · Tweet

And @Helmholtz_HIPS is tightly associated with @Saar_Uni as you can see from our logo!

06.04.2020 · RT

06.04.2020 · Tweet

@FuhrmannGregor So, following up on this, in our institute we develop new antimicrobial strategies: from mining of natural products, to chemical synthesis and optimisation and finally formulation (which is what BION is doing). Just one recent example from @Helmholtz_HIPS https://t.co/yK1R9b6cPW

06.04.2020 · Tweet

How can targeted drug delivery help to enhance the efficiency of antimicrobials? “Nanoantibiotics” https://t.co/J6MlslDFiF By delivering antibiotics more selectively to the infection site, we reduce unspecific accumulation and increase local drug concentration to treat bacteria.

06.04.2020 · Tweet

Of course nanotechnology cannot overcome resistances if the mechanisms are on the molecular basis. But think of antibiotics that induce diarrhea or show kidney toxicity. If we deliver them more selectively, we reduce these side-effects

06.04.2020 · Tweet

When considering targets for nanoantibiotic carriers, it is also important to know who you are fighting against: the bacterial cell wall and membrane. Challenging to overcome. Nanomaterials and molecular transporters to overcome the bacterial env... https://t.co/LDek37vXzV

06.04.2020 · Tweet

Here is another interesting example for a very simple carrier system to deliver antibiotics. These liposomes carry oleic acid which by itself is also antimicrobial. https://t.co/G0ispq2mvt

06.04.2020 · Tweet

Just to pull out a few examples on how nanotechnology can be useful in combating resistant bacteria and what is needed in the future.

06.04.2020 · Tweet

Finally, the situation becomes even more complicated when resistant bacteria embed themselves into rigid biofilms - a very tight diffusion barrier for free antibiotics. A few persister cells survive and restart the infection: https://t.co/YODycIFzYB

06.04.2020 · Tweet

Nanotechnology may again help to tackle this challenge. Enhanced design and formulation of nanoparticles for anti-biofilm drug delivery https://t.co/HWqzwbfOoR But even for nanoparticles, they sometimes stick on the biofilm surface which requires careful nanocarrier design.

A bit later today, but I get to tweet about my favourite topic #extracellularvesicles These are small, membrane-bound phospholipid vesicles that are produce by almost any living cell; present in mammals, bacteria, fungi and even archaea To start: https://t.co/EdvLmodml6

These guidelines give an overview of how to isolate and characterise your vesicles. It also gives an overview on the nomenclature because EV is not EV. https://t.co/4YrfPpvlyd

07.04.2020 · Tweet

We are interested in #extracellularvesicles because they are natural conveyors of cell-cell communication, they are also derived from cells which makes them potentially less immunogenic than synthetic carriers. https://t.co/vR88wTVRzu

07.04.2020 · Tweet

Here are a few examples of how we characterise extracellular vesicles - this time from no-pathogenic bacteria (that usually live in the soil). Turned out that the vesicles were low in cytotoxicity but at the same time inherently antibiotic against gram-negative bacteria. https://t.co/tLUjL73Ecw

07.04.2020 · Tweet

We also showed an distinct antimicrobial activity of the vesicles against intracellular pathogens (Staphylococcus aureus). These bacteria often hide within human cells to be less recognised by our own immune system. But our vesicles find them! https://t.co/A7xFCGhFw5

08.04.2020 · Tweet

Didn't really have enough time to talk about #extracellularvesicles for therapeutic applications. I see the main challenges in the field to be 1) large scale GMP-production, 2) suitable isolation and purification methods and 3) appropriate ways to load them with drugs of choice.

08.04.2020 · Tweet

For 1), there are efforts ongoing. Especially mesenchymal stem cells are a suitable source for cell-derived vesicles with antiinflammatory potential Manufacturing of Human Extracellular Vesicle-Based Therapeutics for Clinical Use @MDPIOpenAccess https://t.co/FjcuB7pSej @BGiebel

08.04.2020 · Tweet

2) is rather difficult because of the vast number of different vesicle subpopulations which are challenging to seperate. Various approaches are followed here. For example, we try to use flow fractionation https://t.co/nL94sSrFQ3

08.04.2020 · Tweet

Finally, 3) needs physical opening of the vesicle membrane for drug loading. This works quite well for small molecule compounds, for example by electroporation or saponin treatment. Get's more difficult for larger biomacromolecules because of artifacts https://t.co/w0Bq6uTKYj

@NPL stands for National Physical Laboratory, and it is the UK's 'National Measurement Institute' (NMI). Many countries have a NMI - e.g. @NIST (US) and @NMIAustralia. NMIs do research in making precise measurements and knowing uncertainty really well.

20.04.2020 · Tweet

A lot of the research is on things like standardising units and calibrating measurement tools (rulers and stuff). How does materials research fit with this? Well - manufacturing materials w reliable properties is v important for engineering industry!

20.04.2020 · Tweet

Majority of fundamental research at @NPL is funded through @GOVUK "National Measurement System" (NMS). Research outputs don't have to make £££ immediately, but topics should still align to govt strategy & priorities. (https://t.co/Nu4FGFkg7O)

20.04.2020 · Tweet

A similar fundamental research funding route for is the European Metrology Programme (EMPIR) @EURAMET. I've not been directly involved in EMPIR projects so far, so I don't know as much about this!

20.04.2020 · Tweet

@EURAMET How about industrial research? Projects can be directly funded by businesses, or govt subsidised (e.g. 'Analysis for Innovators' scheme - https://t.co/uUNQ85xWfN) Some of these results can be published, e.g. in journal papers, but not always - it depends!

20.04.2020 · Tweet

For businesses, the fact that NPL's research doesn't have to be published is a big advantage over e.g. working w/ a university, where all research needs to be publishable.

20.04.2020 · Tweet

The same mentality also applies to fundamental research. There is less pressure to chase 'groundbreaking' 'new' science or 'sexy' fields. Instead, our research has more of a 'boring but important' flavour. Even sexy new science is underpinned by precise measurements!

Hi! Today I will be talking about one of my favourite microscopy techniques, electron backscatter diffraction #EBSD! I use EBSD mostly to measure properties of engineering materials, but it's also used by geologists and planetary scientists to look at rocks/meteorites.

21.04.2020 · Tweet

@AlexFoden, who is completing his PhD thesis on dveloping new #EBSD techniques, has a great thread explaining what EBSD is and how it works. https://t.co/TfmITG7F1i

21.04.2020 · Tweet

Fundamentally, EBSD measures the crystal structure of the material you're looking at. What's 'crystal structure'? Crystal structure describes how atoms in many materials stack together symmetrically, like the fruits here: https://t.co/dvAIgtimzr

21.04.2020 · Tweet

Most ceramics & metals are poly-crystalline - their microstructure consists of tiny crystals stuck together. @Pham_Material led some cool work that flips this concept inside out - used 3D printing to make macroscopic 'meta-crystals'. https://t.co/bN1Y58azL9

21.04.2020 · Tweet

Why do we care about crystal structure? One reason is: material properties change with crystal orientation. For the hexagonal crystal structure here - the material's strength differs depending on which direction (red/blue arrows) I push. https://t.co/jDhg21QreX

21.04.2020 · RT

RT @MySci_PK: Crystal Structure (materials scientists use this term very often) But what does it mean? 👇 https://t.co/EyHsCczOEc

21.04.2020 · Tweet

Q: Why do we care about crystal structure? A2: The size of the crystals in a material (grain size) affects its strength. Usually, small grains -> strong material. Sometimes, interfaces weaken the material! That's why turbine blades in jet engines are made of single crystals.

21.04.2020 · Tweet

Kathleen Lonsdale pioneered this field - she did the maths to describes crystal structures (which underpins not just EBSD, but all other diffraction techniques using electrons, X-rays, & neutrons). @paulcoxon has a thread about here: https://t.co/3Eiuo2FUQj
