Controlled release, be it for medicine or agriculture have a lot in common. Controlled release can achieve better delivery (medicine/fertilizer...) and avoid the peaks (too much) and trough (too little) of repeated applications. But constant release might not always be best. https://t.co/AeUEelkyxk

28.04.2020 · Tweet

Often we need multiple (not constant delivery) injections of vaccine (booster shots) to achieve immunity. Microcapsules (mc's) in a single injection could be designed to release doses at three different times, thereby matching better with how the immune system can best respond. https://t.co/FiaZKXg4aQ

Sodium nitrate is an agent to control feral pigs and the Australian possum. But it's unstable and bitter. While the initial zein coating formulation did improve compatibility and stability it wasn't sufficient. Formulation improvements were tested, some made the coat crack... https://t.co/DAc3OnYj14

29.04.2020 · Tweet

29.04.2020 · Tweet

No matter how good you do manage to coat something if there are any cracks at all the coating will fail. A typical way to address this is to make you coat extra thick (requiring more materials, time to manufacture and reducing the proportion of coated material to coat)... https://t.co/ZViB0WsjUY

29.04.2020 · Tweet

So we started thinking; could we make agricultural formulations and unlike the one in the picture here we'd use less coating material (giving a cost saving and better loading of coated material), could it be self-healing (if a crack develops can the coating fix itself)? https://t.co/MmmBsWYVES

So I mentioned we electrospin nanofibers, using the apparatus we assembled from off the shelf and 3D printed items. We have two many areas of interest; applied uses such as agriculture and more fundamental investigations of nanofiber properties. https://t.co/riOxFh4lxG

And we're looking at how choice of polymer and nanofiber structure can influence nanofiber properties. Often asessing water droplet contact angle as a measure of wet-ability https://t.co/dkZW6UZm3C

We've been looking at double layered nanofiber mats. One side we make using PEO so it can get wet and stick to a biological surface like inside the mouth. The otherside we make using PCL that's difficult to get wet. This way one side sticks the other side doesn't. https://t.co/Y0CtcPPM94

02.05.2020 · Tweet

We can access just how difficult or easy it is to wet by the measuring the contact angle of a water dropped. The flatter the droplet the easier it is to get wet. https://t.co/LyE9AAZbBs

We can calculate the contact angle using a photo of the droplet and freely available software called ImageJ with a couple of add-ons https://t.co/eBsLdf6zYs

I'd like to talk about initiating/maintaining research while dealing with big challenges like covid. In a way I was almost prepared for covid. The Christchurch earthquakes/ terroist attack, multiple management changes, poor funding/resources ... A decade of disruption in my life!

03.05.2020 · Tweet

Worrying about covid feels very much like living through the Christchurch earthquakes; poor sleep, distracted thoughts, difficulty focusing, fuzzy brain. At the time of the quakes we called it "quake brain"

03.05.2020 · Tweet

So for a few weeks leading up to and since stay at home was ordered in NZ I've expected nothing of myself or my team. We all need to deal with things in our own way; mine was making hand sanitizer and setting up a home office. Basically tidy a few things and do a little often.

03.05.2020 · Tweet

What ever the new normal is (or return to the old normal) will need to be established before we can set ourselves concert targets (not aways the attitude of management sadly). Till them I remind myself of 3 good bits of advice I've had over the years from mentors..

03.05.2020 · Tweet

1) don't worry if you can't do what you wanted to, just do something. 2) do something that you find exciting. 3) do a little often. Keep in contact with friends and if you find yourself at a road block ask around, someone will appreciate any offer of or request for assistance...

03.05.2020 · Tweet

There's always someone who needs a manuscript edited (or someone who can help you with yours). Volunteer for a committee. Start scoping a review you may never submit. Or just do nothing, sometimes this has been the hardest but most effective thing I've ever done.

03.05.2020 · Tweet

Speaking of maintaining/initiating research, ugggh funding! In NZ 10% success is a well funded scheme, so typically less that 1 in 10 applications successful. I can handle reject as well as the next person, but in NZ there's no feedback!

03.05.2020 · Tweet

I prefer applying overseas for funding; two attempts to get an @OECD fellowship, twice rejected for USDA funding. All rejections came with feedback! So very happily submitting for a 3rd time the USDA application. NZ colleagues think I'm lying, they say feedback is a myth

Hey everyone! Damien @dr_djleech here, will start as I mean to go on - with an overuse of the gif function. https://t.co/XxiDHHy3WT

A bit of background - I did my PhD on models of the interactions between stacked layers of 2D materials. With a focus on the electronic structure of graphene, particularly in a bilayer form, and moire pattern formation. https://t.co/DFOMR2UZqc

03.05.2020 · Tweet

If you've ever been remotely adjacent to work on graphene, you'll have probably seen the figure of a van der waals heterostructure represented as lego bricks. This stack of 2D materials is built layer-by-layer and has properties that depend on the stacking https://t.co/0Z4f13Gk46

03.05.2020 · Tweet

But this simple picture misses out two of most interesting parts of the problem - how adjacent layers affect one another and what happens when the periodicity of the lego bricks don't match up. https://t.co/KDCe4jrCoj

03.05.2020 · Tweet

Both graphene and hexagonal boron nitride have, yep, hexagonal structure.And this structure is very similar. So much so that hBN is the perfect substrate to place graphene onto to study the behavior of it - it's insulating so it doesn't interfere, flat, relatively easy to make... https://t.co/RHJ9JqfL9T

03.05.2020 · Tweet

But there's a lattice constant mismatch of 1.8% and, over many hexagons, this makes all the difference. A moire pattern forms and a new periodicity arises, much larger than before - this has a subtle but very real effect on the electronic structure. https://t.co/wEKQ2fbEhB

03.05.2020 · Tweet

This interaction changes depending on the materials used and orientation between them, giving us many avenues of manipulation. And vertically, we can just keep stacking - some groups are making mind-bogglingly complex stuff! https://t.co/j6zTm9hkgU

03.05.2020 · Tweet

How does bilayer graphene come into all this? Well, when your stack is built, you are mostly locked in, in terms of properties. The materials, stacking and orientation won't change. But bilayer graphene has some symmetry breaking properties that make it distinct from monolayer...

03.05.2020 · Tweet

Place bilayer graphene in a perpendicular electric field and the symmetry breaks, one layer has a differing on-site energy to the other. This causes a band gap to open, with a magnitude proportional the strength of the electric field. https://t.co/FdEGSZVGzX

03.05.2020 · Tweet

Now you have an avenue for tuning the properties of a stack externally! It can produce all sorts of strange electronic behavior, including extremely flat energy bands... https://t.co/rHODUNseyU

03.05.2020 · Tweet

One thing I always loved about 2D materials research was the ever-increasingly-obscure materials being suggested/isolated - from silicene to graphyne(?) to bismuthene(!?). It's really fascinating to keep up with! 2019 saw isolated plumbene! https://t.co/Mzpi7m9mce

03.05.2020 · Tweet

So what's the 'I knew about them before they were cool' monolayers I should be keeping an eye out for next? Because I only really enjoyed stanene's first album.

03.05.2020 · Tweet

After PhD, I moved 10 mins down the road to Bristol to work @CFPRresearch @UWEBristol on print technologies, alongside scientists, engineers, and even artists and craftspeople. It's a fascinating place! https://t.co/GYLZ079icK

03.05.2020 · Tweet

The research in the centre encompasses print in all forms - going from additive manufacture and inkjet all the way to more traditional approaches like screen printing and letterpress. All for industry, academic research and even artistic use... https://t.co/FtJzhXeVea

03.05.2020 · Tweet

This includes 3D printed ceramics, custom glassware, laser-dyed textiles, artist's books, colour perception, robotics driven design, texture mapping, jewelry production, stop-motion animation, maintaining/resurrecting dying crafts and manufacture processes... All sorts!

04.05.2020 · Tweet

So how does a materials scientist even be useful when it comes to print technology? Printers, in all sorts of forms, are complex kit that often work on the premise that the ink you put in is well defined and consistent. Lest you go all Office Space on your printer... https://t.co/YbMsoAmGMb

04.05.2020 · Tweet

Therefore ink characterisation is incredibly important and properties such as the rheology, surface tension and even colour all arise from effects on the micro/nano scale. First principles models can be really useful in determining what is going wrong! https://t.co/xTl4lETYiZ

04.05.2020 · Tweet

There's this term 'printability' that contains all the vague concepts that make an ink printable. It's not usually strictly defined - notable exception is inkjet, where it's driven by the Ohnesorge number, which gives a thin window of opportunity! https://t.co/UOjCi0048c

04.05.2020 · Tweet

By the way, 'ink' is another vague term used to describe whatever 'input material' you give the printer! It can be liquid ink, 3D printer filament, powders, chocolate...

04.05.2020 · Tweet

But what do I do? Printing has a lot of history to it - there's been plenty of methods that have come and gone and a lot of lost knowledge there. I look at forgotten 19th century print methods with unique advantages and how we can revive and modernise them (Daguerreotype, 1837) https://t.co/g4mxrMk2gn

04.05.2020 · Tweet

This time was particularly exciting as print was some sort of weird collision between print, photography, chemistry and physics. So the methods use elements of all of them. One focus is the Woodburytype - it's a relief print method that uses a gelatin and carbon black ink (1880) https://t.co/HEZVG4qq9b

04.05.2020 · Tweet

The darkest regions of the print stick out from the page further than the lighter parts, trapping more pigment - it's very intuitive in terms of optics, but not very common in print. You can read more about the process here: https://t.co/hBacHunedd

04.05.2020 · Tweet

@MaterialsDan Love this! Really fascinating read

04.05.2020 · RT

RT @MaterialsDan: @RealSci_Nano This New Yorker article about printer science is a great read https://t.co/u7BmsEDsCZ

04.05.2020 · Tweet

One aspect of updating old print processes is moving monochromatic processes to polychromatic. Colour perception is a whole field of its own that encompasses pigment chemistry, ambient optical conditions and even how the brain/eye combo reads and interprets these signals. https://t.co/3WTsdhLKQJ

04.05.2020 · Tweet

This plot represents the response of the three types of cones in the human eye. They're not uniform at all and therefore neither is our interpretation. (Side note: some people have 4 cone types! As do plenty of animal species, in this case it is usually located toward the UV end) https://t.co/QgXKwdrR21

04.05.2020 · Tweet

Using this knowledge, we can begin to map our colour perception. This horseshoe represents it, white is in the middle and colours become more purely monochromatic as you move towards the outside edges. There's a secret 3rd dimension to it, lightness, giving lighter/darker tones. https://t.co/NsFgtQlYWx

04.05.2020 · Tweet

Tracking the outermost regions of the plot that we can reach defines a colour gamut, within which contains all the possible colours from that technique. sRGB is shown here, the standard digital colour space, reproducible by 99% of all digital monitors. https://t.co/2hiHzZvGbU

05.05.2020 · Tweet

The Woodburytype has no photoactive element in the print and so very little fading occurs, giving surprisingly high-quality windows into 19th century life. Street Life of London (1876) gave 'direct communication with the people' in 'unvarnished language' https://t.co/GvmCGTM2ag

05.05.2020 · Tweet

3D Printing? That's kind of a big thing, huh? More generally known as additive manufacture, you're probably familiar with fused deposition modelling process whereby plastic is selectively extruded from a heated print-head. https://t.co/E7wHpyQHBT

05.05.2020 · Tweet

This works really well for a whole range of shapes and high-end printers are regularly getting beneath a 100 micron layer thicknesses for a handful of materials. The print is self-supporting so sometimes excess supports are added and removed after printing. https://t.co/JNOvYtPLXU

05.05.2020 · Tweet

But theres other options - stereolithography uses laser to selectively cure photopolymers and can breach sub-50 micron layer thicknesses.Still requires supports and materials must contain a photopolymerizable component. Optical methods tend to be sharper! https://t.co/VIgcKwwFUI

05.05.2020 · Tweet

Selective laser sintering spreads a 'powder' layer, uses a laser to sinter regions of it, and repeats for the next vertical layer. This means no supports! But requires an excess of the feed material and the object has to be 'excavated' from the powder. https://t.co/WWTk6jd15H

05.05.2020 · Tweet

There's all sorts of others, but some of the most interesting are hybrid manufacture. This uses additive techniques to build the main bulk and then switches to subtractive in order to give a smooth finish and smaller feature sizes. https://t.co/uC6hpXiZd4

05.05.2020 · Tweet

Additive manufacture loves three-lettered acronyms (FDM, SLA, SLS, FFF, EBM, STL...?) but usually you pick your technique based on the materials you want to print... So we'll talk about that in a bit!

05.05.2020 · Tweet

And it probably goes without saying... But if you do have access to 3D printers at the moment, please look into local groups printing PPE! There's many amazing initiatives going on at the moment!

05.05.2020 · Tweet

3D printing (FDM) typically utilises plastics like PLA and ABS - they're a standard. But some of the most fascinating research, for me, is when people use these printing platforms to print material that is 'unprintable'. Want a new coffee mug? Print one! https://t.co/QtOIsJ6mHD

05.05.2020 · Tweet

Ceramic 3D printing tends to come in two flavors - an extrudable clay is formed or a powder base is selectively bound together via light/chemical reaction. It makes structures not traditionally possible and is used in both tableware and biomedical apps https://t.co/UqEkytMl7b

05.05.2020 · Tweet

But what's really awesome here is the enthusiast community that exists for clay/ceramic printing. This wikifactory contains so much useful information, all on how you can modify your own setups and produce suitable clay inks. https://t.co/SXi6MyZB1j

05.05.2020 · RT

RT @UniofBath: For the first time, labs around the world can 3D print their own precision microscopes to analyse samples and detect disease…

Ceramics not your thing? OK, how about bioprinting? This is loosely defined as the printing of biomaterials, ranging from directly (and carefully!) printing materials loaded with cells to constructing complex scaffolds that can later be seeded with cells. https://t.co/Z274rKf6vQ

05.05.2020 · Tweet

This is an incredibly complex field, that requires expertise from a whole range of backgrounds. But the ultimate goal is the realisation of complex and biocompatible printed tissues. This paper sums it up far more eloquently than I can! https://t.co/jwAIH3i0Ur

05.05.2020 · Tweet

But surprisingly, I have to refer to the literature for this field a lot. No one understands the rheological and optical properties of gels and soft materials (and particularly gelatin) better and so my work with gelatin is often propped up by these, frankly mind-blowing, papers. https://t.co/AzTJWorF6v

This, for instance, is just exceptionally cool! https://t.co/36UM9ERroM

And this really encapsulates that interdisciplinary approach that is so necessary for these sorts of complex problems! https://t.co/RfiPTwrR9f

05.05.2020 · Tweet

Alright, how about printing chocolate instead? Fed up with delicious chocolate in simple shapes? Reprocess and print into all manner of shapes! This paper covers a custom setup for a chocolate extruder and explores the flow properties of chocolate inks. https://t.co/NWoPrAik83

05.05.2020 · Tweet

This system is particularly interesting as it turns out the key here is in the temperature control, just as much as it is in the rheological control. It represents a fascinating test case into the effects of cooling and air flow on the print process... And it's delicious.... https://t.co/jOs4TxwISF

Currently working on a similar homebrew setup and making some progress (and a lot of mess). Just need more ink making supplies from @CadburyUK! https://t.co/doxBwX8eSW

No sweet tooth? Try 3D printed mash instead! Also includes NMR analysis! https://t.co/MFaQmlxfEW

Colour from pigments is one thing, but nature explores more complex setups quite commonly. Nacre (mother of pearl) occurs on the inner layers of many mollusks. It consists of platelets bound in a matrix of biopolymers and produces the lustre seen on shells/pearls. An example below from a common flattop shell, with the upper patter scraped away. https://t.co/EJWlcfZE9w

OK science time! This is a thread about how I “painted” stem cells during my PhD with the @perrimangroup. I chemically modified proteins so that they would “stick” to cells to give them superpowers (sort of)...check it out here in @NatureComms https://t.co/P3qG0lznEQ https://t.co/QVE5aahsa1

11.05.2020 · Tweet

How did we do this? Well, cell surfaces are negatively charged, so if you make your protein positively charged then it will spontaneously bind through electrostatic interactions. Simple! But how do you go about making a protein positive...?

11.05.2020 · Tweet

Well, proteins are made of positive, neutral and negative amino acids – these usually cancel each other out and you end up with a “net charge” that is either slightly negative or slightly positive. But we can mess with this!!

11.05.2020 · Tweet

Some groups use genetic manipulation to switch out these amino acids and make #supercharged proteins. I particularly love this paper by the Liu group: https://t.co/ejFBmRPgeg

11.05.2020 · Tweet

But we did something totally different. We took proteins and used a simple chemical reaction to turn the negative amino acids into positive ones – a process called #cationization

11.05.2020 · Tweet

When we added these cationized proteins to cells, they stuck to the cell membrane! However, we could make even more protein stick by using a neat trick - attaching a surfactant to the surface of the cationized protein.

11.05.2020 · Tweet

These proteins stick to the cell membrane through hydrophobic interactions - and stayed for over a week! Here is a picture of a stem cell "painted" with surfactant labelled green fluorescent protein. We estimated that there were around 6 billion proteins per cell! https://t.co/KIyfVqyILv

11.05.2020 · Tweet

So why is this useful? Well, we wanted to see if this could address a big problem in tissue engineering - the starvation of cells in the middle of big tissues. We figured that we could use our method to "oxygenate" our cells with myoglobin...

11.05.2020 · Tweet

So together with the Hollander group, I grew lots of chunks of cartilage using either "painted" cells or "unpainted" cells... https://t.co/hUIqQatvhA

11.05.2020 · Tweet

...and to skip over a lot of work (!) this was the final result: the left column shows tissues grown with unpainted cells (big hole in the middle) while the right column shows tissues grown with painted cells (much smaller hole). https://t.co/y5N8VGePno

11.05.2020 · Tweet

This means that we could grow big* tissue constructs simply by pre-treating the stem cells! This could be potentially used in the future to replace cartilage lost through osteoarthritis or sporting injury. *big = 5 x 6 mm which is pretty big for cartilage!

11.05.2020 · Tweet

But what else can you do with this? Well the @perrimangroup attached surfactant-modified thrombin to stem cells to grow fibrin hydrogels from the cell surface, potentially offering a new route to wound healing...check it out here in @NatureComms: https://t.co/vh4fBmXRVI

11.05.2020 · Tweet

@sciborgess @Pingosaurus and others then magnetized cells using cationized magnetoferritin. This took just 1 minute, with the cells responding to an external magnet and detectable by MRI...check it out here in @nanoscale_rsc: https://t.co/k9uEwHyokn ... more on magnets tomorrow!

11.05.2020 · Tweet

I should also say that this bioconjugation method was adapted from some incredible work by @perrimangroup and @apsbrogan who used surfactants to make liquid solvent-free proteins. If you've not seen this before then definitely check it out here: https://t.co/eDQx0vSIkQ

11.05.2020 · Tweet

We can also adapt cell modification strategies for the modification of extracellular vesicles. These tiny membrane-bound particles have potentially interesting therapeutic opportunities, and surface modification can allow in vivo targeting or imaging: 10.1021/acsnano.6b07607

11.05.2020 · Tweet

This is (hopefully) a working link for the extracellular vesicle modification review, co-written with @maggieholme and published in @acsnano: https://t.co/Av9xOkw2Kf

12.05.2020 · Tweet

So today's thread is on magnetizing proteins, DNA and cells - and how you can use this to build complex tissues! https://t.co/coO8OAg9EQ

12.05.2020 · Tweet

As I mentioned yesterday, @sciborgess and I developed a new ultra-fast method for delivering #magnetic #nanoparticles to cells. These magnetized cells could be detected by MRI - offering a potential opportunity for tracking #stem #cell #therapies!

12.05.2020 · Tweet

Other people have used magnetic fields to manipulate magnetized cells - I especially like this paper in @naturecomms, which used a magnetic "microtip" to cluster and stretch stem cells - this caused them to become more like heart cells! https://t.co/5bKhBjwvm5 https://t.co/HwQysR1AOx

12.05.2020 · Tweet

However, there are problems with magnetic cell manipulation. Cells are relatively big (~0.01-0.02 mm) and to move them, you need quite a lot of magnetic nanoparticles - but lots of nanoparticles can harm the cell, or change the way it functions...

12.05.2020 · Tweet

So @sciborgess and I thought - can we magnetize growth factors instead 🤔? Growth factors are proteins that can make cells produce a certain type of tissue (e.g. cartilage, bone)...if we made magnetic growth factors then we could move them and maybe build complex tissues!

12.05.2020 · Tweet

An amazing PhD student (Chunching Li) made this reality! His secret was to cover the magnetic nanoparticles in a "sugar coating" which soaked up growth factors and then released them slowly over time. Just what we needed! Red = nanoparticle Blue = sugar Green = growth factor https://t.co/Y2K6EDGuNH

12.05.2020 · Tweet

He used a magnet to make a gradient of bone-forming growth factors across a material full of #stem #cells. After 3 weeks: - The end with growth factor - turned into bone - The end without growth factor - turned into cartilage We made an "#osteochondral" (bone-cartilage) tissue! https://t.co/PBJ8AotV65

12.05.2020 · Tweet

Why is this useful?? Well, #osteochondral tissue is often missing in damaged knees - which is incredibly painful. This is a potential way to grow replacement osteochondral tissue in the lab! Check out Chunching's @biomaterials_ paper here: https://t.co/S3u13cFCXX

12.05.2020 · Tweet

We used a bone-forming growth factor - but if we switched this out for another growth factor then we could potentially make other #gradient #tissues! Any ideas, please let me know (DM @jrmstrng)!

13.05.2020 · Tweet

[admin] "Making Cells Dance - Acoustic Tissue Engineering" @jrmstrng talking about his science on podcast episode #54, out now https://t.co/UzpvJUbbwT

Today’s #RealSci_Nano thread is all about my favourite topic and the tagline for this week – how to use sound to “make cells dance.” This is a video of cells patterned by an ultrasound wave...read on to hear more about how we can use this for #tissue #engineering! https://t.co/rpaRvMgZMx

13.05.2020 · Tweet

What is going on here? Well, what we have here is a "standing wave" which means that we have made sound waves but they are not travelling. This creates static regions of pressure - some higher than usual, some lower than usual, and some unchanged.

13.05.2020 · Tweet

This is a slightly unusual situation for cells to find themselves in! Cells in areas of high and low pressure will feel an "acoustic radiation force" which pushes them into areas of unchanged pressure. This is what we see in the video - the cells accumulate in the "nodal plane."

13.05.2020 · Tweet

What is great about this is that you don't need to modify/label the cells or the culture media in any way! This works because the cells have a different density and compressibility to the surrounding liquid.

13.05.2020 · Tweet

There are things that can mess with this - gravity, viscosity, cells sticking to things and an effect called acoustic streaming. A lot of what I do is trying to figure out how to get around these problems!

13.05.2020 · Tweet

...but when you get the conditions right, you can start to pattern cells in gels. This is an image of cells all lined up in a collagen hydrogel. This is exciting because this means we can start making a patterned tissue! https://t.co/c3BkviERVE

13.05.2020 · Tweet

We first used this to make muscle - because muscle is naturally made of parallel bundles of long cells. Using our sound waves, we were able to make something similar! If you are interested in this, see our Advanced Materials (@AdvSciNews) paper here: https://t.co/PJIdJqwE2F https://t.co/JCiwpkItgv

13.05.2020 · Tweet

The possibilities for this are endless! I worked with @sonic_bruce and his team to make these patterning devices - they are easy to use and compatible with normal cell culture. By tuning the ultrasound properties we can make all sorts of different cell patterns! https://t.co/YO1i0FVMi9

13.05.2020 · Tweet

I'm now working with my brilliant student @katya_pch to use these devices to make different patterned tissues and create smart cell culture systems!

13.05.2020 · Tweet

Others have also worked with acoustic cell patterning - my favourite is this work by Peer Fischer's group published in Advanced Materials (@advscinews): https://t.co/Uj1hjnuISo Here they cleverly used acoustic holograms to make completely customized cell patterns! https://t.co/Jl7Ck4gI4J

13.05.2020 · Tweet

If you are interested in using sound, magnets or light to build complex tissues then you can read more about it here in this @TrendsinBiotech review: https://t.co/CMZmzCVrO0

14.05.2020 · Tweet

@badz_nithin Thanks and good question! People have looked into cell separation using sound + microfluidics. There is a whole @labonachip series about this field of "#acoustofluidics" (e.g. https://t.co/6fGqei9bAy). A nice example of acoustofluidic separation: https://t.co/DWb1sm1R4l).

14.05.2020 · Tweet

@badz_nithin @LabonaChip But your idea of aqueous multiphase systems is interesting. The fluid density gradients would both separate the cells and also change the acoustic radiation force felt by the cells. If you set this up orthogonally, you could maybe get 2D separation, and resolve subpopulations?

14.05.2020 · Tweet

@badz_nithin @LabonaChip Thanks for sending this over! An advantage would be the avoidance of paramagnetic salts - acoustics would work in unmodified media. The separation would also be different - acoustics would separate based on the cell compressibility and size (rather than how diamagnetic they are).

14.05.2020 · Tweet

In today’s thread, I want to talk about some other fun things we do with sound! I've been lucky to work with a brilliant team (@NeleValeria @AcoustiCarolyn) on an exciting project using sound to trigger #enzyme #catalysis and #gelation! Read on for more details... https://t.co/91Yer3DLLX

14.05.2020 · Tweet

Our idea was based on using #liposomes - small droplets that can be filled up with different "cargo" (e.g., chemicals, drugs). Under the right conditions, you can use ultrasound to release this cargo into the surrounding liquid. This cargo can then be used for many things!

14.05.2020 · Tweet

For example, we used ultrasound to release a cargo of calcium ions - these ions could then stick to an enzyme (#transglutaminase) and activate it so that it could catalyze a chemical reaction. This was the first example of an ultrasound-triggered enzyme! But there is more...

14.05.2020 · Tweet

...once the enzyme is activated, it can then turn a liquid solution into a gel (#fibrinogen)! This was only the second example of an ultrasound-triggered hydrogelation (the other one used radicals - ours didn't).

14.05.2020 · Tweet

As usual, we should ask, why is this important? Well, enzymes are used all across industry and bio-sciences to catalyze chemical reactions, and hydrogels are commonly used as soft biomaterials for cell culture, tissue engineering, drug delivery, soft robotics and lots more...

14.05.2020 · Tweet

...and now we have a new way to activate enzymes and make gels! Unlike a lot of light sources, ultrasound can pass through opaque walls and through the human body, which means we can now start to trigger these processes in previously inaccessible locations!

14.05.2020 · Tweet

Another useful thing about this method is that it is "modular" - which means we are not limited to this exact system (calcium, transglutaminase, fibrinogen). We can switch out the cargo, the enzyme or the gels - something that we are exploring this now!

14.05.2020 · Tweet

We also showed that you can stick the cargo-loaded liposomes onto tiny gas bubbles. Ultrasound can be used to expand, contract and burst the bubbles- which helps to release the cargo even better! https://t.co/UyDuChEwOk

14.05.2020 · Tweet

I hope you enjoyed this thread! For more details, see our Advanced Materials @advscinews paper published earlier this year: https://t.co/h0n8CEeg7v Shout out also to @jono_woj (and others that aren't on Twitter) who helped make this happen!

14.05.2020 · Tweet

@1Gy_too_many @NeleValeria @AcoustiCarolyn Thanks for reading the paper and that's a really excellent question that has got me thinking about this in a way that I hadn't before. For this transglutaminase system, the cargo is not a crosslinker, rather it activates the crosslinking process...

14.05.2020 · Tweet

@1Gy_too_many @NeleValeria @AcoustiCarolyn ...which to me suggests that (in theory, under perfect conditions) the final crosslinking density should be the same regardless of calcium release - the only thing that will change is the gelation kinetics...@NeleValeria any thoughts?

15.05.2020 · Tweet

In my last "science" thread, I want to talk about other ways to build complex tissues - and why this is so important! If this interests you, check out our Advanced Functional Materials review on complex tissue engineering, written with @liliangouyang: https://t.co/Awt9ZcTzpn https://t.co/Ozcra59Lbb

15.05.2020 · Tweet

Why is complex tissue engineering important? Well, tissues are naturally complicated! They have layers, gradients, blood vessels, nerves, patterns of cells and lined-up fibres - all features that have evolved to keep the tissue healthy and play important functional roles!

15.05.2020 · Tweet

The take-home message is: If we can't replicate this structural complexity, then our lab-grown tissues will simply not work as they do in nature - and we won't be able to use them to effectively replace or study natural tissues.

15.05.2020 · Tweet

Luckily we have a lot of new methods for growing complex tissues. The review that I posted is about "bottom-up" methods. This means that we start with smaller "building blocks" - such as cells, organoids, fibres or sheets - and then assemble them into complex tissue structures.

15.05.2020 · Tweet

I've already spoken in previous threads about "remote assembly" methods using sound, light, magnets. There are also "self-assembly" methods that use a particular property of the building block (e.g., their shape or chemistry) to spontaneously and predictably assemble!

15.05.2020 · Tweet

However, you can do this in a far more controlled way by using a broad set of methods called "directed assembly". There are lots of examples of this - in fact, many methods used for tissue engineering (weaving, knitting, braiding) are borrowed from the textile industry! https://t.co/2NymcXDDNd

15.05.2020 · Tweet

Like many people, my favourite directed assembly method is 3D #bioprinting! Here, the "ink" contain cells and/or materials, and the printer deposits the ink into custom shapes. I've worked with many smart people on some exciting printing projects. Here, I will share 2 of these!

15.05.2020 · Tweet

The first of these was the development of a new type of ink with @perrimangroup @madelineburke3 and @BennyC. The problem we found was that some materials were "printable" and some materials were "cell-friendly" but rarely could materials do both jobs well!

15.05.2020 · Tweet

So we decided to make a "hybrid ink" - containing a printable material (#pluronic) and a cell-friendly material (#alginate). Pluronic is quite unusual - it turns from a liquid to a gel as it heats up! This meant we could print a cold ink that would set on a warm (37 deg) stage.

15.05.2020 · Tweet

We then washed our printed structure in a cool calcium bath, which did two things: - the calcium very quickly gelled the alginate. - the cooling washed away all the pluronic. This meant we could make large alginate structures (like the nose in this picture!). https://t.co/yvyKT00x7M

15.05.2020 · Tweet

We included stem cells in this ink and use it to grow cartilage and bone tissue. For more info, check out our Advanced Healthcare Materials paper: https://t.co/Jx0bMeVEqs

15.05.2020 · Tweet

I now want to talk about some awesome work, which was done with the amazing @liliangouyang! Here he addressed a big problem in tissue engineering: building tissues with blood vessels. Bioprinting is perfect for this as it allows you to build structures with open channels... https://t.co/7jbjdlvWgv

15.05.2020 · Tweet

...however, a problem with open channels is that you then need to put blood vessel cells in and let them stick to the channel walls. This is difficult and doesn't always work, particularly if you are trying to build small and complicated vessels...

15.05.2020 · Tweet

So what Liliang did was to use two materials - one filled with blood vessel cells to print tubes, and the other to print the surrounding tissue. The latter was then strongly gelled with UV light (it was GelMA for those interested).

15.05.2020 · Tweet

...the clever bit was that the tube material was gelatin - which turns into a liquid when warmed! As the gelatin turned to liquid, it released the blood vessel cells, which then stuck onto the walls of the channels. This worked even for thin and complex blood vessel networks!

15.05.2020 · Tweet

We call this method: "in situ endothelialization." If you are interested, check out our Advanced Functional Materials paper: https://t.co/tjH1SK5MQo

15.05.2020 · Tweet

@badz_nithin @liliangouyang Hi, thanks for a great question! Yes we are definitely looking at combining ultrasound patterning and gradient casting - the application here could be for osteochondral tissue where you have aligned deep zone chondrocytes plus a collagen / gag / mineral gradient!

16.05.2020 · Tweet

My last #RealSci_Nano thread! I want to talk about the important role of online seminars/conferences as free, open-access science during (and maybe after) this pandemic. I say this, as co-organizer (with @BrianAguado) of these #Virtual #Seminars in #Biomedical #Science 👇 https://t.co/u3R4PGdv3t

16.05.2020 · Tweet

I totally love the #TissueTalk series by @GVNlab, where you get to see incredible Professors such as @burdicklab and @kaplan_lorax. But I feel that it's just as important for graduate #students and #postdocs to have a platform to disseminate their results and build their network!

16.05.2020 · Tweet

This was the motivation behind the #Virtual #Seminars in #Biomedical #Science - and it is great to see so many similar initiatives focussing on early-career scientists. @gecedillo has compiled a great list of these events: https://t.co/6gYtjp8MWB

16.05.2020 · Tweet

I really strongly feel that this helps “democratize” science – free-to-access and open to anyone with the internet. I’ve been lucky to attend some great in-person conferences over the years - but these are expensive to attend and are therefore exclusive to those with funding!

16.05.2020 · Tweet

Another real issue with in-person conferences that needs to be discussed is that they can exclude those with care responsibilities or those with certain medical requirements. Providing talks online could make a major difference to these individuals.

16.05.2020 · Tweet

On this note, there are steps that organizers can take to make sure that their online events are really accessible to all. You can’t pick a timezone to suit everyone – I myself have had to miss some really great talks due to parenting duties...

16.05.2020 · Tweet

One option is to post talks online after the event so that they can be watched at a convenient time. With speaker permission - we are looking to do this with #virtual #seminars in #biomedical #science, and I know other organizers (such as @BEaTSResearch) have taken this approach.

16.05.2020 · Tweet

In summary - while nothing beats an in-person conference, I truly think that online science conferences & seminars (#free, #accessible and #ecofriendly) – can play a big role during the pandemic and also in complementing in-person conferences in a post-COVID world! 🤞

16.05.2020 · Tweet

To finish with a plug - I’m personally delighted to be giving an online seminar organized by @beatsresearch: https://t.co/2tWJPjkTFP and to be talking at this online symposium organized by @ClaudiaLoebel and @thewooj: https://t.co/X6yQd6zi4f Please join!

science and my doctoral research is in nanoscience and drug delivery. And now I'm working on bioinformatics of endometriosis.

When I decided to become a scientist at 7, I wanted to know how everything in the universe worked, from the tiniest atom to supermassive black holes, and how all the life forms function at the most basic level. It's impossible to know everything, but I've been fortunate enough

to explore so many fields of science, just as I always wanted to as a kid.

Meeting done! Does anyone have questions and anything they'd really like me to talk about this week? I'll be talking about my cancer research, endometriosis and the nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems I was developing

18.05.2020 · Tweet

It depends on which field of science you're in. Not all fields require a lot of advanced maths and programming. But the point of the training in science is to be good at learning and problem solving - so you can *learn* to be good at programming and maths https://t.co/1VWsspYA0Z

18.05.2020 · Tweet

So how does a molecular biologist end up researching nanotech and dabbling in materials science? The scales involved are pretty similar, I would say. And some of the concepts.

18.05.2020 · Tweet

Basically, it's all chemistry and crafting things from atoms. In biochemistry, it's molecules that have a biological function - tiny machines that are part of how the cell works

18.05.2020 · Tweet

In materials science and nanotech, it's the design of molecules and objects at the nanoscale that can act as tiny machines. It's basically mimicking the evolution of life through the evolution of inorganic structures. These structures, and machines - they are all

18.05.2020 · Tweet

designed to work the way biomolecules work; in a structured and ordered way. It fascinates me that we can do this with inorganic materials. It's also kind of fun to figure out what we can make and ways to make these devices

18.05.2020 · Tweet

So what is "inorganic" vs "organic?" Organic chemistry isn't pesticide free range chemistry 🤣 sorry basically, organic chemistry involves carbon chemistry; and inorganic chemistry covers everything else.

18.05.2020 · Tweet

Most of the huge biomolecules in our bodies and in all life are carbon based - carbon is an incredibly flexible atom. Most of the materials we use in nanotech are not carbon based, but can have some carbon components. But they can be made of metals - silver, gold, titanium -

18.05.2020 · Tweet

or made of silica - the atomic cousin of carbon - and so many other materials. Some of these devices are also made of organic molecules. What's so fascinating about it is that you can make use of the chemical properties of each of these substances to design particular devices

20.05.2020 · Tweet

21.05.2020 · Tweet

Sorry I've been quiet, tweeps! I've been unwell.

21.05.2020 · RT

RT @realscientists: [admin] Are you a materials and/or nano scientist? Do you like to talk about your research? Do you want to feature o…

22.05.2020 · Tweet

Hellloooo everyone! Sorry for the silence at my end, I've had a bit of a cold and felt exhausted for a few days. But I want to talk to you for a bit even though it's about 2.30am where I am

22.05.2020 · Tweet

So I spoke earlier about how we can use inorganic materials to mimic organic molecules. Think of it this way - instead of a biomolecules like a protein, an enzyme - you can try to make something that does the same thing, but it's made of a metal or silica - something inorganic

22.05.2020 · Tweet

and as a biologist, that is just amazing to me. For example, you can actually make tiny nanoparticles that can be used as catalysts - like enzymes . Or you can make gold nanoparticles of any shape or size you like - bipyramids, stars, spikes, spheres, rods - by just using

22.05.2020 · Tweet

chemical processes. It's *almost* like alchemy. So what does cancer research have to do with nanotech?

22.05.2020 · Tweet

We want to take what we know about cancer and its weaknesses and create treatments that target those weaknesses - you can think of it like looking for chinks in the dragon's armour

22.05.2020 · Tweet

We know what some of these chinks are. But with nanotech, you can be creative about how you deliver an attack - or an arrow to bring the dragon down.[ all i can think of right now is The Hobbit]

22.05.2020 · Tweet

So what are some of those ways we can beat the cancer dragon? We know that chemotherapies are really effective, but while they attack fast growing cells like cancer, they can also attack healthy tissue in the body - this is why chemo takes a lot out of patients

22.05.2020 · Tweet

So what would be ideal? We have chemotherapies - and other anti-cancer therapies - and we'd like to get them just to the cancer cells. Or even just most of it to just the cancer cells. Or we'd like to mark the cancer cells so we can find them without having to perform surgery

22.05.2020 · Tweet

We could also mark the cancer cells - and destroy them - without invasive surgery. And finally, we could try to deliver gene therapy to the cancer cells, so that we can modulate genes that can shut the cancer down.

22.05.2020 · Tweet

How would we do this? I have one word: nanotechnology. Tune in tomorrow to find out more.

23.05.2020 · Tweet

Before I talk about how we can attack the cancer dragon, does anyone have questions? Let me know if something was unclear, I will do my best to explain

23.05.2020 · Tweet

How can nanotech slay the cancer dragon? With gold.

23.05.2020 · Tweet

Of all the elements on earth, I never expected that the most venerated and valuable metal to be an almost magical substance with multiple properties that would make it ideal for attaching drugs, attacking cells, converting energy.

23.05.2020 · Tweet

Gold is actually quite non-reactive and can be turned into a range of nanoparticle shapes. It can be coated in antibodies and nucleic acids, modified so you can attach other drugs. It's surprisingly handy. Studies about its toxicity aren't extensive though

23.05.2020 · Tweet

It turns out that the shape of a gold nanoparticle matters; and each shape has unique properties. For starters, the colours of different particle shapes differ.

23.05.2020 · Tweet

Colloidal suspensions of gold nanoparticles don't look like gold. The particle size is so small, at the nanometer level, that they interact with light in a very specific way, producing what's called a surface plasmon resonance (SPR). We can use this to identify particles, to

23.05.2020 · Tweet

make barcodes made of gold; devices made of gold. We can use it to characterise gold particles with different coatings, and so on.

23.05.2020 · Tweet

So, the colours of gold particle suspensions: stars: green bipyramids: brown spheres: depending on the size, anything from brick red to maroon to purple 1-5 nm: brick red 10-25 nm: blood red 30-40 nm: dark red towards maroon 45-upwards: purple

23.05.2020 · Tweet

capsule-shaped nanorods of gold: green. Well, gold nanoparticles are colourful, and you can do some pretty great and specific surface modifications to them. But what's even more fascinating is that some particles can actually convert energy.

23.05.2020 · Tweet

Gold nanorods can be exposed to laser light at certain wavelengths, and they'll convert that energy down to heat. But not just a little heat, a lot of heat. Heat that can burn.

23.05.2020 · Tweet

One of the therapies developed by my colleague was gold nanorods that used an aptamer to target the rods to a specific kind of cancer cell. A low intensity laser was shone on the sample; the energy was converted by the nanorods into heat that destroyed the cancer cells

23.05.2020 · Tweet

Isn't that nifty? It's a very simple and elegant way to destroy the cells; and the aptamer made all the difference because it was selected specifically target that cancer cell. This is just one of the ways we can use gold nanoparticles to treat cancer.

23.05.2020 · Tweet

Another way to treat cancer cells is to blast them with gold nanoparticles with chemotherapies, gene therapies or antibodies attached to them. These therapies are aimed at killing the cancer cell; and the gold nanoparticle is used to attach the therapy and deliver it

23.05.2020 · Tweet

This is a basic principle - attaching an existing therapy to a nanoparticle - that's being developed for treating cancer and other diseases that need a little extra effort to treat. It's basically making teeny tiny nanocapsules - nanopills! - to treat disease.

23.05.2020 · Tweet

And you don't have to just use gold - you can use so many kinds of materials to make these tiny nanopills - polymers, chitin, silica, squishy heat reactive polymers, and other materials that you can use to make millions of regular particles and attach therapies to.

23.05.2020 · Tweet

This is the basic principle of using nanotech in drug delivery - and why a molecular biologist can end up working in this field (also, it turns out that engineers are not always keen to work with cells).

24.05.2020 · Tweet

Chris Bowen

@BowenNEMESIS · 24.05.2020 to 01.06.2020 · 54 posts

24.05.2020 · Tweet · Welcome [admin]

[admin] "Wonderful World of Smart Materials" Please welcome Materials Professor at @UniofBath - @BowenNEMESIS Listen to the podcast #57 to know what is coming your way this week https://t.co/A6X3SoKdxh

24.05.2020 · Tweet

Good morning everyone. I'll be hosting this week and will try my best to discuss materials, including ferroelectric and piezoelectric materials. It is a bit early, so I will try and wake up first.

24.05.2020 · Tweet

The direct piezoelectric effect relates to materials that develop a charge when subjected to a mechanical stress.

24.05.2020 · Tweet

Applications for the direct effect include sensors of force, pressure and acceleration. Microphones and hydrophones too. If you have used a gas lighter that generates as spark when you press it, that's also probably piezoelectric.

24.05.2020 · Tweet

I've been for a walk around Bath, which is where I live in the UK. Earlier I discussed the direct piezoelectric effect. My next posts will be on the indirect piezoelectric effect. https://t.co/vVrv4j1NQG

24.05.2020 · Tweet

The indirect (or converse) piezoelectric effect relates to the piezoelectric material developing a strain under the application of an electric field.

24.05.2020 · Tweet

Applications include actuators, nano-positioners, speakers, active SONAR (to send out the 'ping'), ultrasonic baths, nebulisers, & fuel injectors. If you ever received a card that played a tune when you opened it, it probably used a piezoelectric buzzer, like the one below. https://t.co/gZHIcTnVoj

25.05.2020 · Tweet

@palebluedot92 It will be a ferroelectric ceramic material based on lead zirconate titanate (PZT).

25.05.2020 · Tweet

So, why do certain materials exhibit piezoelectric properties? Well, it is usually a lack of symmetry in ionic materials.

25.05.2020 · Tweet

An example is lead zirconate titanate (PZT). At high temperatures (left image) the crystal structure is cubic/symmetric and non-piezoelectric. But on cooling is becomes tetragonal (right image) and you can see the black ion (Zr4+ or Ti4+) is displaced upwards, forming a dipole. https://t.co/yS8Gn8vhrd

25.05.2020 · Tweet

It is this dipole that provides the material with a direct or indirect piezoelectric response.

25.05.2020 · Tweet

In a material like quartz (SiO2) it is a little different, since in the stress free state the structure is symmetrical. It is the application of stress or field in a specific direction that leads to a loss of symmetry.

25.05.2020 · Tweet

For this tetragonal structure the black Zr4+ or Ti4+ ion can displace up, down, left, right and in and out of the image above. So, the dipole can be aligned in six possible directions.

25.05.2020 · Tweet

There are other crystal structures, but I find the tetragonal easier to visualise and it is important for materials such as PZT and barium titanate. For the rhombohedral phase the dipole can be along the eight possible diagonal directions.

25.05.2020 · Tweet

We can now imagine that a dipole is created from some asymmetry in the crystal structure. How do we ensure that all dipoles are aligned in the same direction in a piezoelectric device? For materials like quartz, AlN, GaN we must use in single crystal or highly aligned form.

26.05.2020 · Tweet

We have seen that one way to ensure dipoles are aligned across a material is to use single crystals cut in an appropriate direction (crystal 'cuts'). For polycrystalline materials, we can align the dipoles in materials called ferroelectrics (a sub-class of piezoelectrics).

26.05.2020 · Tweet

Ferroelectrics are special, as the dipole and polarisation direction can be switched by an applied electric field. For example, the black Zr4+ or T4+ in the right image can by moved up or down by changing the direction of the electric field applied across it. https://t.co/J1cccXj7vr

26.05.2020 · Tweet

A polycrystalline ferroelectric can be made piezoelectric by a 'poling' process. Initially, dipoles are randomly oriented (left image). We apply an electric field at elevated temperature to switch dipoles (middle), then cool and remove the field (right) to polarise the material. https://t.co/hbwGWKFDZY

26.05.2020 · Tweet

Lots of advantages. No need for crystals cut in specific directions, so you can create a variety of shaped ceramics and chose your polarisation direction later. Polycrystalline ceramics relatively low cost. The high degree of polarisation in ferroelectrics also makes them active.

26.05.2020 · Tweet

Examples of ferroelectric ceramics include lead zirconate titanate (PZT) and barium titanate. There are ferroelectric polymers too, like PVDF. All ferroelectrics can be made piezoelectric, if poled. Hence they are a sub-class of piezoelectrics.

26.05.2020 · Tweet

For example you can make tubular shapes and pole radially for nanopositioners, AFM etc. Not easy to do that with a non-ferroelectric single crystal. https://t.co/FLCmNNjpN4

26.05.2020 · RT

RT @RealSci_Nano: For example you can make tubular shapes and pole radially for nanopositioners, AFM etc. Not easy to do that with a non-f…

26.05.2020 · RT

RT @ProfRachelGaN: @RealSci_Nano Reckon that's sufficient excuse to share a hexapod video - cool example of nano positioners....https://t.c…

27.05.2020 · Tweet

[admin] "Wonderful World of Smart Materials" Listen to Chris (@BowenNEMESIS ) talk about his science on podcast #58 https://t.co/A6X3SoKdxh

27.05.2020 · Tweet

Once we have a poled ferroelectric we can apply an electric field for actuation. Apply the field in the poling direction for extension; imagine moving that black Ti4+ or Zr4+ further away from centre. Apply field in opposing direction for contraction, pushing ion to centre. https://t.co/AgX7MfOgCs

27.05.2020 · Tweet

@HelmanDaniel Good point, used the term 'usually' here with an eye on the ferroelectric ceramics. Any dipole / asymmetry will do, for example PVDF polymer due to H and F.

27.05.2020 · Tweet

What sort of strain levels can we achieve? For PZT, a rule of thumb is that the maximum strain at the maximum applied electric field of ~2-3 kV/mm is ~0.1%. That's 1μm displacement for every 1mm in length. The multi-layer actuator below is 9mm long and max displacement is 9μm. https://t.co/uOflmbA9M5

27.05.2020 · Tweet

The strain is small, but the force is large as the ceramic is stiff. For this small device the 'blocking force' is 3.5kN. Note: The 9μm displacement is a 'free displacement' at zero force, while the 3.5kN blocking force is at zero displacement. You can't have both at same time.

27.05.2020 · Tweet

As the field is mainly moving the ion, it has potential to operate at high frequencies. This 10x10x9mm device resonates at 152kHz. So high force, small strain over large frequency range.

28.05.2020 · Tweet

Yesterday we applied an electric field to our poled ferroelectric for actuation. Today we consider applying a mechanical load to develop a charge for sensing - the direct effect. If we apply a stress we now develop a charge and potential difference across the material.

28.05.2020 · Tweet

The amount of charge is proportional to applied stress and the sign of the potential difference changes with direction of stress. Great for sensing. It always seemed strange how charge and current could flow in a sensor circuit, as the ceramic is an excellent insulator. https://t.co/1gXpbrihTA

28.05.2020 · Tweet

Imagine the poled ferroectric with conductive electrodes at top/bottom. Screening charges collect at top/bottom to balance the polarised ceramic (left image). If we compress and reduce the level of ceramic polarisation, some screening charges are now free to flow (right image). https://t.co/tHBORkrluy

28.05.2020 · Tweet

Charge (Q) generated is proportional to stress. Since current is dQ/dt then short circuit current is proportional to rate of change of stress (dStress/dt). Potential (V) across ceramic at open circuit is proportional to stress (since Q=CV for capacitor).

28.05.2020 · Tweet

The ceramics are very good insulators, but do have a finite conductivity. Therefore they are typically used for dynamic forces - they are not used for static forces/pressures as the charge/potential across the ceramic will slowly decay and be lost.

28.05.2020 · Tweet

I guess a key point is that the change in polarisation with stress leads to the generation of piezoelectric charge for mechanical sensing. Tomorrow, we will see we can also have a change in polarisation with temperature. The pyroelectric charge can be used for thermal sensing.

28.05.2020 · Tweet

@JamieWHB In this case the high temperature phase is cubic and the polarised phase is tetragonal. So as you heat I guess it is getting closer to cubic and the dipole shrinks. https://t.co/GBJ5lW4ZjS

29.05.2020 · Tweet

We have seen all poled ferroelectrics are piezoelectric. These materials are also pyroelectric, where the change in polarisation with temperature leads to a current flow. The direction of current changes with heating (polarisation fall) or cooling (polarisation increase). https://t.co/biaRQklKRo

29.05.2020 · Tweet

Applications here include thermal/people detectors and thermal imaging. If a door has automatically opened as you walked towards it, a pyroelectric detector has probably been used to detect your body heat.

29.05.2020 · Tweet

Let's consider a PVDF element 10mm in diameter, 0.1mm thick subjected to a 1K temperature change. The pyroelectric coefficient provides the charge per unit temperature change and area (left equation). Knowing the capacitance (middle equation) we can also calculate the voltage. https://t.co/XMxkHFOlpY

29.05.2020 · Tweet

Notice the charge is proportional to area (and not thickness). This makes sense as it is the surface charge we discussed earlier. The voltage is proportional to thickness (and not area) , since the surface charge is more widely separated.

29.05.2020 · Tweet

Let's consider the 10mm diameter PVDF element, 0.1mm thick and subjected to a 1K temperature change. Using the equations, the open circuit voltage is ~33V.

29.05.2020 · Tweet

I can't go into the lab at moment, but here is a pyroelectric in my garden. The solar panel harvests sunlight and the LEDs are switched on at night when body heat changes the polarisation of the pyro-sensor (see central dome lens). Has worked for 3yrs with no battery replacement. https://t.co/d6jV49XQaT

29.05.2020 · RT

RT @JoFeanelwa: @RealSci_Nano That's why when I was too cold all the time, automatic doors couldn't see me 😫

29.05.2020 · RT

RT @BowenNEMESIS: Evening walk and look around the garden. Have a nice weekend. https://t.co/yj2kxOyOgB

30.05.2020 · Tweet

We have seen that the pyroelectric and piezoelectric signals originate from the change in polarisation of the material with temperature or stress. Therefore we need to take care to screen piezo-sensors from thermal signals and pyro-sensors from mechanical signals.

30.05.2020 · Tweet

So let's summarise, it is the weekend after all. 1. Ferroelectrics can have their polarisation direction switched by an applied electric field. All poled ferroelectrics are both piezoelectric and pyroelectric. Examples are PZT and BaTiO3. https://t.co/7i2dPCFZ44

30.05.2020 · Tweet

2. There are materials, like ZnO, AlN, and GaN, that are polarised but are non-ferroelectric. As you cannot switch the polarisation direction with a field we must use in single crystal like form. They are both piezoelectric and pyroelectric. https://t.co/F7eXv72Kpz

30.05.2020 · Tweet

3. There are materials, like quartz, which are only polarised after applying a mechanical load. As they are non-ferroelectric, they must be used in single crystal form. As they are not polarised in the stress free state, they do not exhibit significant pyroelectrict effects. https://t.co/vZ7KIpTgs5

30.05.2020 · Tweet

One advantage of quartz here then, less susceptible to thermal changes.

30.05.2020 · Tweet

I will try an experiment later tonight, when it is dark. I will see if I make the pyroelectric person sensor activate the LEDs by mechanical tapping to induce a piezoelectric signal. I need to sneak up to it first without my body heat setting it off. https://t.co/FiRA1jS5Zf

30.05.2020 · Tweet

Ah, seems to work. The pyroelectric detector is facing other way and I tap on back (with high tech spoon) to set it off. https://t.co/fVL5sOMaXz

09.06.2020 · Tweet

Hi everyone, I'm back to talk some more about #3DPrinting. First up take a look at the thread I made for @scottishscicomm's global science day back in March, to give you a quick whiz through what 3D Printing is and why it matters: https://t.co/W5hO8lujgH

09.06.2020 · Tweet

Then in a while I'd like to tell you about some of my favourite applications and processes, before we start getting into details about the science behind the processes and materials. As always let me know if you have questions or things you'd like me to talk about!

09.06.2020 · Tweet

So let's start talking about #3DPrinting processes. Almost all of them work from the same principle of building parts one layer at a time. (We're starting to see a few processes which have moved away from the layered approach, but I'll talk a little about that later.) https://t.co/TzJ7aIeamP

09.06.2020 · Tweet

Now for many years we couldn't all agree on how to categorise the processes. Should we focus on the type of material they use, the method used to join the layers, the properties of the parts, or something else entirely? After a lot of discussions (arguments?) a group of...

09.06.2020 · Tweet

process categories was defined, based on how we join our layers together. I'm not going to go through all of these now, but you can see a list in Section 2.2 of the ISO/ASTM standard here: https://t.co/5IxiDOPX2x

09.06.2020 · Tweet

I'll highlight a few example processes shortly, but what's quite interesting is the way in which processes have changed over time. The very first commercial processes had one thing in common, which is that they all used some form of single-point 'scanning' to produce the layers.

09.06.2020 · Tweet

You can think of this as being similar to colouring a picture - everywhere you want to colour, your pencil must touch the page. While this is an *effective* way of colouring, it's also pretty inefficient, and that's one reason why the early 3D Printing processes were a bit slow! https://t.co/b0Z3qXl2jP

09.06.2020 · Tweet

It became quite clear that having to scan, melt, or deposit each pixel of material in a layer individually wouldn't allow for the speed increases that were needed for many applications, and people started to look at ways to cover more area in a shorted time.

09.06.2020 · Tweet

Quite a few processes sprang up where a layer was covered in a single 'pass' of a print-head, array of nozzles, or similar. This allowed for quicker printing of each layer, but also in some cases had benefits in terms of processability and consistency. https://t.co/SNd9HHRIce

09.06.2020 · Tweet

From there it's a relatively quick stretch of the imagination to move towards producing the whole layer in a single 'flash', saving time per layer but with perhaps some added complexity to the overall process, or working to constantly 'grow' the parts without specific layers...

09.06.2020 · Tweet

I'll be back in a short while to give you an idea of just some of the range of processes we've seen since 3D Printing started, many of which are great and some of which might be better categorised as 'interesting'... I'll probably leave you to decide which are which!

09.06.2020 · Tweet

@John_Sevigny @KLeoPullin I agree! That's part of the fun of it for me, never knowing what will come up next!

09.06.2020 · Tweet

@KLeoPullin @John_Sevigny @RealSexyCyborg I didn't, but I do now! Thank you for the tip! :)

09.06.2020 · Tweet

Let's talk a little bit about #3DPrinting processes. The first to be commercialised was Stereolithography, which works by selectively curing cross-sections of a photo-curable resin using a laser. Laser Sintering (similar technique but using a powder rather than a resin) and...

09.06.2020 · Tweet

Fused Deposition Modelling (which effectively 'draws' the layer by extruding molten material from a nozzle) came relatively soon after, with variations of each method still being used a lot today. But what about some of the other processes which have been important along the way?

09.06.2020 · Tweet

One of my favourites when I first got into this was Z-corporation's 3D Printer range. They were the first people to enable full colour 3D Printing (OK, it was only surface colour but it was early days and quite exciting!). The process works by printing a binder onto a layer...

09.06.2020 · Tweet

of powder and bonding the particles together. The parts were quite fragile and needed some post-processing in order to get good colour vibrancy, but opened up a lot of potential especially for more realistic-looking prototypes.

09.06.2020 · Tweet

You can see some example parts in this video if you're interested in the sort of things these printers were making: https://t.co/7b4NHxiAo9

09.06.2020 · Tweet

On similar lines, the Connex systems from Objet Geometries were pretty ground-breaking, as they introduced systems than that could process more than one build material at the same time. Multi-material printing opens up a lot more design possibilities, so this was big news!

09.06.2020 · Tweet

These processes work by printing a UV-curable material, and following it with a UV lamp in order to cure it. Add more than one print-head, and you can print more than one build material. By 'grading' the amount of material you print across the build area, you can get a big...

09.06.2020 · Tweet

change in properties. After quite a few years they also launched full-colour systems taking advantage of the same build process. You can see a video of the process here, complete with enigmatic background music: https://t.co/Zyifi15deU

09.06.2020 · Tweet

One of the most exciting developments in recent years was Carbon 3D's Digital Light Synthesis technology (https://t.co/vQJrROLqob). Using UV light, a curable resin, and some clever chemistry, they 'grow' a part continuously, helping to eliminate some of the issues often found...

09.06.2020 · Tweet

at the boundaries between discrete layers. Although there are still downsides as with any process, lot of process developments have been quite small iterations from where we were so it was quite exciting to get something genuinely a bit different!

09.06.2020 · Tweet

To finish off today I thought I'd highlight a few processes you won't hear much about, but that always grabbed my attention for one reason or another! Early on I came across Rapid Freeze Prototyping. As you might guess, this involved... well... freezing stuff quickly!

09.06.2020 · Tweet

In this process you'd deposit droplets of water out of a nozzle onto a sub-zero plate or environment, where they would quickly freeze. Subsequent droplets will freeze on top of the previous layers, and you'd keep building up the part until it was complete.

09.06.2020 · Tweet

The most obvious application area was for making complex ice sculptures, but with potential for some casting or moulding applications. Of course the main disadvantage was that your part melting if you didn't use it quickly enough, but that was part of the charm for me!

09.06.2020 · Tweet

And a couple of others that aren't really around any more, but that I had a soft spot for!

09.06.2020 · Tweet

Araldite Digitalis (watch a video here - https://t.co/P7FDZPhLa7) used a system of micro-mechanical shutters to selective expose an entire cross-section of a photo-curable resin. This promised to be great for increasing process speed, with one other potentially big selling point

09.06.2020 · Tweet

The system was designed by Huntsman (a chemical company), based around their in-depth knowledge of their materials. There are a lot of potential benefits to designing processes around materials rather than the other way round, but sadly we've not seen much from this process :(

09.06.2020 · Tweet

And finally, a process I've always loved, despite it's flaws... Solid Ground Curing, from Israeli company Cubital, Inc. had more process steps than you could shake a stick at! The process worked by first creating a mask of toner on a glass plate, and applying a layer of resin...

09.06.2020 · Tweet

onto a flat build platform. The mask would be positioned above it, and flashed with a UV lamp to harden the un-masked areas of resin. Any un-cured resin was vacuumed away, and molten wax spread over the build area to fill in the gaps. Of course that layer of wax was...

09.06.2020 · Tweet

thicker than the intended layer thickness, and had to be milled back into a flat shape... Another quick cure of the resin layer, and the process started again. Far from the most efficient process ever created, but something about it always grabbed my attention!

09.06.2020 · Tweet

That's about it from me for today, but if there are processes you specifically hoped I'd talk about please let me know! I'll be back tomorrow to talk about some of the less-popular bits of the 3D Printing process chain (and why they're super important!)...

09.06.2020 · Tweet

which, almost as if I planned it that way, will lead nicely into how we go about research into materials and identifying the key things we need to consider! Talk to you all then :)
