[admin] "Cutting Through the Hype of 3D Printing" Extended conversation with @CandiceMajewski is out now - https://t.co/XtQRBdQSqu

11.06.2020 · Tweet

Hi everyone! As promised I'm back with more to say about #3DPrinting. I think we all know there are bits of any subject that are the 'cool' bits and others which are important but much less exciting, and 3D Printing is no different! Most often when we talk about these...

11.06.2020 · Tweet

processes, we focus on the manufacturing stage itself - the bit where we can watch the laser zipping around on the surface of the raw material, see the material being squeezed out of the nozzle, or various other visible aspects. https://t.co/bfjUKUlGjw

11.06.2020 · Tweet

I'm the first to admit that those bits are fun (I'm still just as excited to watch our machines do their thing!) but in reality what happens before and after the manufacturing stage can have just as much of an impact on the quality of our parts.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

My group is focused mostly on processes which use powdered polymers as feedstock, so I'll use that as an example. (I'll talk more about the processes in detail later on, but for now it's enough to know we're talking about polymer powders).

11.06.2020 · Tweet

Now our powders have a lot of history before we even put them into our machines. The powder has to be manufactured, transported and stored somewhere in our lab, and we often need to sieve the powder before we use it. https://t.co/jGtWYrUx4P

11.06.2020 · Tweet

We then pop it in the machine, deposit layers of powder onto the build platform and pre-heat the powder, all before we start the actual 3D Printing stage of the process!

11.06.2020 · Tweet

Afterwards we need to allow the parts to cool, remove them from the machine, clean off any excess powder, and post-process them (often by bead-blasting). We'll also capture any un-used powder for use later on.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

At every single one of those stages we can alter (sometimes deliberately but often unintentionally!) the properties of our material. This can also affect the final properties of our parts; that's not always a *bad* thing, but it's something we always need to be aware of.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

So, I thought I'd talk a bit more about a few of these aspects throughout the day, and how they tie in with some of the research we've been doing. First of all I have some project presentations to mark though, so I'll be back in a bit to tell you that stuff!

11.06.2020 · Tweet

I talked earlier about the different individual steps that make up an overall 3D Printing process chain. What's useful is that we can use those steps as a basis for defining where we need to focus our research, and where we think we can make the biggest improvements.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

If we focus on the Laser Sintering process, where we selectively laser scan and melt the required cross-sections of our polymer powder, we can split the process into a couple of main stages.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

First we need to deposit a nice smooth, well-packed, layer of powder onto a build platform, and then we need to make sure the powder melts and solidifies into a dense part. If we get either of these steps wrong, we can run into big issues!

11.06.2020 · Tweet

For the powder deposition step, there are a lot of things that can help/hinder us. The machine itself has a part to play - how does it deliver the powder to the build area and how does it ensure even spreading (for example using a roller or a blade). We don't want potholes! https://t.co/T7KjBNfEus

11.06.2020 · Tweet

The powder manufacturing method itself has a big effect too. Here's an image of one of the most 'standard' commercial materials, a Nylon-12, courtesy of one of our previous PhD students Alaa Almansoori. https://t.co/yZiqlR1tQg

11.06.2020 · Tweet

Note that the particles are relatively smooth, with a 'potato'- like shape, and a combination of small and large particles. Although not a guarantee of success, these things can help to allow the powder to flow and pack nicely within the powder layer.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

We can add small amounts of flow additives to help with this too, but we have to be careful - as with a lot of things in the world of 3D Printing, there's a compromise to be made - beyond a certain point the flow additives can start to have a negative effect on our properties..

11.06.2020 · Tweet

But quite often, and depending on the manufacturing process for the powder itself, we may not get such nice smooth, consistent particles, as you can see in this image of some Polypropylene powder from another of our previous PhD students, Luke Fox. https://t.co/4YfrKW1cV2

11.06.2020 · Tweet

When we end up with these more 'raggedy' (yes that's the technical term) powders we can still work with them but are less likely to end up with a nice dense layer of powder, putting a lot more pressure on the laser scanning part of the process to get the part quality we want.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

Other things we have to watch out for are moisture uptake in our powders, which is very dependent on the specific material we're using, 'settling' of any flow additives and/or different-sized particles from the transit or storage of the powder, and any contaminants in our powder.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

All of those considerations take place even before we start the build process itself, so what things do we have to look out for once we get started? I'll be back to give you an idea of the main things in a little while!

11.06.2020 · Tweet

Before I finish for the day, let's have a quick think about what happens when we start the 'making' part of the process. At its most simple, we're 'zapping the powder with a laser to melt it into the relevant cross-section', but in reality it's a lot more complicated...

11.06.2020 · Tweet

If we look at Nylon-12, the most common Laser Sintering polymer, there are a lot of things that make it really well-suited for the process. This chart from Mike Vasquez sums it up very nicely - x-axis is temperature, and y-axis is energy input/output. (https://t.co/dh8EIxx6ya) https://t.co/O03hqKllPG

11.06.2020 · Tweet

If we look at the graph carefully, we can see a number of key aspects that really help with the process. As we heat up the material, we come to a fairly sharp melt peak (evidenced by a relatively sudden intake of energy without an increase in temperature).

11.06.2020 · Tweet

This allows us to heat our powder quite close to its melt point before scanning with the laser, which as benefits in terms of processability. Heating further we can see a large 'Stable Sintering Region' - this is the temperature range in which we can keep heating the material...

11.06.2020 · Tweet

without causing it to degrade - if we push it further into that region we'll see a drop in mechanical properties of the resultant parts. Where it gets *really* interesting is when we start to cool the material... The temperature at which it starts to crystallise and solidify...

11.06.2020 · Tweet

is quite a bit below its melt temperature, which is probably the most exciting thing about it! This allows us to hold our un-sintered powder at a temperature *above* its crystallisation point, but below its melting point, meaning the areas which have been scanned and melted...

11.06.2020 · Tweet

are also held above their crystallisation temperature. Effectively this means the scanned areas remain in a molten state throughout the whole build process, which allows for much better bonding between consecutive layers. Pretty cool, right?

11.06.2020 · Tweet

It's probably no surprise to you that most polymers don't behave anywhere near this nicely! Many of them have much more complicated (annoying?) thermal profiles, and various other factors affect how well they can be processed.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

Melt viscosity determines how long it will take to fuse two particles together nicely, as well as the accuracy of the parts themselves - too 'runny' and we'll get poorly defined geometries!

11.06.2020 · Tweet

Surface tension also influences the way in which the particles will melt together, as does their physical size, and the rate (and consistency) with which we cool the parts will have a large effect on their final properties.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

And of course some materials we're asked to try (not mentioning any collaborator names, but you probably know who you are), behave completely the opposite of every material we're used to using, which leads to a whole lot of head-scratching while we try to figure it out! https://t.co/G8vjbE5Idq

11.06.2020 · Tweet

Really this means we've got plenty to keep us busy in terms of understanding how we can process more difficult materials. Sometimes it feels like the more we know, the more we realise we don't know, but I think that's all part of the fun of research!

11.06.2020 · Tweet

All of which neatly brings me to the end of the day, and a good point to pick up on tomorrow, when I'll talk a bit about what happens once we remove our parts from the machine, and the ways in which we can characterise and understand their properties.

11.06.2020 · Tweet

I'll also go into a little more detail on a few of the projects we're currently working on, so see you all then!

12.06.2020 · Tweet

It's Friday! Well done on making it through another week, or if you work different shifts In hope you're doing OK so far 👍 As promised, I'm going to talk a bit this morning about what happens after we've built our parts, and how that affects their properties.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

First up, let's think about the end of the Laser Sintering process. You can picture the end of the build as a bunch of parts (still molten), encased in a tub of relatively loose, warm, powder.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Polymers have pretty low thermal conductivity, meaning it takes a while for heat to dissipate through them - if left to cool naturally, parts at the centre of the build will take longer to cool that those at the surface or closer to the metal sides of the container.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Why do we care? Because the rate at which we let the parts cool will have an effect on how much they crystallise, which in turn has an effect on their mechanical properties.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

If we have variation in cooling rates that translates into variation in part properties, we're potentially losing some of the repeatability we're trying so hard to get!

12.06.2020 · Tweet

At this stage we also have to consider the effects of processing on the un-sintered powder surrounding the parts. We can quite easily recover most of this powder, but don't forget it's been held at a temperature close to its melt point for a long time by this point.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

This leads to changes in the molecular weight of the powder, and to how well it can be processed in future builds. It's standard to mix this 'used' powder with fresh powder to help keep things working well, but beyond a certain point we'll start to have a big effect on...

12.06.2020 · Tweet

'sinterability', part performance, and surface finish. Check out this work from the excellent folks in Louisville, who were the first to report on this: https://t.co/2WwXVM02kS and in particular this image of how these changes affect surface finish! https://t.co/2mf2VoyrB9

12.06.2020 · Tweet

So what can we do to check on the quality and consistency of our parts? We know that processing parameters (eg energy input, temperatures, speeds) have a big impact on part quality, and we're starting to understand a lot more about this and how we can use it to make improvements.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Within our EPSRC Future Manufacturing Hub we're doing a lot of work looking at how we can help powder-based manufacturing processes (not just 3D Printing ones) reach their full potential. You can see more at @mapphub or https://t.co/Va04rgYI4L

12.06.2020 · Tweet

One of our PDRAs, Zicheng Zhu, has been investigating the porosity of parts produced using High Speed Sintering. This process is similar to Laser Sintering but uses a combination of a printed ink and IR light to induce melting in the relevant areas of the powder layer.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

This image, taken from micro-CT data, shows what we get when we put in a lot of energy into our parts - the dark areas are solid areas of the part, and the light blue are pores within the solid structure. (There's about 7% porosity by volume in this part). https://t.co/OfSFfcypL2

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Now see what happens when we put a lot less energy into the parts - this part has about 32% porosity, and you can see how this porosity is aligned with the layers of the manufacturing process. (Excuse the picture quality, as I don't have the originals on this computer!) https://t.co/JR5kiqUN8T

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Using this sort of analysis we can start to see which individual processing parameters have the biggest effect on the size, shape and distribution of our pores, and what effect these have on our mechanical properties.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

By understanding these things better, we can start to work on making improvements to the systems themselves, with a view to gaining better control of the properties and repeatability of those properties, that we can achieve.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Keep an eye out for some upcoming publications on this as well as some super cool results from some in-situ testing, where Zicheng and out colleagues in Manchester scanned some parts while tensile testing them!

12.06.2020 · Tweet

I've mentioned the effect of our processing parameters, but as it's a rainy Friday (at least here in Sheffield), perhaps you'd enjoy a quick look at what happens when we don't quite get it right... https://t.co/KWkvgr3QPj

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Although we can take a good guess at some parameters (often through a combination of examining the material's thermal profile and comparing with parameter sets we already use for similar materials, sometimes it comes down to luck as to whether we get it on our first attempt!

12.06.2020 · Tweet

As well as understanding how things work in our processes, we're also keen to make our parts work harder! By introducing extra functionality into them, we can start to add a lot of extra value.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

I thought to end the week I'd talk you through how we go about this, using the example of some work we've done to investigate the inclusion of anti-bacterial functionality into Laser Sintered parts. You can read our recent paper on it here: https://t.co/xgiLyemo22 if you like.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

This EPSRC-funded project involved bringing together people from engineering and micro-biological backgrounds, so big thanks to @microshep, @Bobatron, Tom Paterson and James Wingham!

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Our aim was to introduce anti-bacterial properties into our parts, by incorporating a silver-based additive into one of our standard polymers. We chose nylon-12 because it's so easy to process, meaning we'd be reducing the likelihood of processing difficulties.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

A project like this necessarily starts by us seeing whether we can actually process the part in our machine, or whether including the additive would cause us problems. These images might not look that exciting, but they represent getting over a key milestone! https://t.co/Wkx53isFU6

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Next we want to see whether the additive has caused us any change in the mechanical properties of our parts compared with the base nylon-12 - thankfully we saw no difference between samples produced with and without the additive... https://t.co/qE4K6nTDuw

12.06.2020 · Tweet

During this time @microshep also ran some tests using human cells, in order to make sure we weren't going to hurt human cells in our attempt to get rid of bacteria! Looking good so far, so we started seeing what would happen when we expose bacteria to our treated parts... and...

12.06.2020 · Tweet

what we found was super interesting! Depending on the test conditions we used, our approach worked well, a bit, or not at all! From a research perspective that's given us lots more possible avenues to explore, which we'll hopefully get back to once our labs open up again.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Here's a nice (false colour) image from @bobatron, which I'm including because it's pretty awesome! https://t.co/SLhtye0r4P

12.06.2020 · Tweet

We also tried out some other interesting things along the way, including using micro-CT scanning to look at how well our anti-microbial additive was dispersed throughout the parts we produced.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Check out this lovely micro-CT image from one of my PhD students, James Wingham! The grey areas is our base nylon-12 material, which makes up most of the part. The black areas are pores within the part, and if you look closely you'll also see some little white 'dots'. https://t.co/wEP7yZlCTQ

12.06.2020 · Tweet

These are where our silver-based additive is found within the part! So from this one measurement we can get an idea of how porous our sample is, where that porosity is located, how big it is, what shape it is, *and* how well our additive is distributed throughout the part.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

Like all good researchers, we love when we can get plenty of information all at the same time! Hopefully that's given you a bit of a flavour of some of the #3DPrinting research we're doing at the moment, but please ask if you have questions or would like more info on anything.

12.06.2020 · Tweet

I'll finish off my week tomorrow by showing you a few of my favourite applications of 3D Printing, but for now I hope you all enjoy the rest of your Friday!

12.06.2020 · Tweet

@Bobatron Whoops, sorry! Thanks to TOM for the image, and Bob for giving him bacteria... You're right, that does sound a *tiny* bit bad...

Back for one last chat about #3DPrinting! To finish the week I thought it would be fun to talk about some of my favourite applications that I've seen! Let's start with the final frontier... https://t.co/V8PSzmybHu

13.06.2020 · Tweet

Space applications of AM have been talked about for quite a while; fixing things that are broken, creative solutions to things that go wrong up there, building space habitats, or even food for astronauts.

13.06.2020 · Tweet

When this was first talked about, the big question was 'can we get 3D Printing to work in low gravity situations'? One of my favourite ever images, which I can't find the reference for, is this one of a 3D Printer turned on its side as an initial test of whether it might work... https://t.co/IF8lAZXlfU

13.06.2020 · Tweet

Reader, it did! This was an extrusion-based machine, which was then tested on on the affectionately-named 'vomit comet', an aircraft following a specific profile to allow for a short time of weightlessness (see here for some more info - https://t.co/XUECyeaCGr)

13.06.2020 · Tweet

Again it worked, and (to cut a long story short) we now have 3D Printing capabilities on the International Space Station! If you're interested you can read some of my thoughts about 3DP in Space in this article I wrote a while ago here: https://t.co/XuCEmPnKyc

Something else we've seen recently is a lot more TV shows and movies using 3D Printing to create complicated and/or futuristic designs. One of my favourites recently was Queen Ramonda's crown in Black Panther: https://t.co/Y5lh0qrYBR

To digress slightly, fashion has shown quite a lot of interest in 3D Printing (see this *amazing* dress worn by Dita Von Teese - https://t.co/OKY1EW4I8z), and if you Google* '3D Printed high heels' you'll find a heap of cool shoe designs *other search engines exist

Iris van Herpen (https://t.co/UykvxQ40Tr) is definitely someone to check out if 3D Printer fashion is your thing!

Many of the big sports companies have been exploring the use of 3D Printing in their footwear, although this is yet to become really mainstream, and we can see a lot of cool jewellery and headwear designs coming through as processes have become better (and in some cases cheaper).

But back to TV/movies... As well as just making fancy props, some companies have been really leading the way in terms of how they apply 3D Printing to movies. Years ago I watched a presentation by someone from @LegacyEffects, and I was blown away by pretty much all of it!

I remember an advert they'd worked on for... I want to say one of the Halo games..? as well as how they'd used 3D Printing to make alien teeth for the movie Cowboys vs. Aliens!

13.06.2020 · Tweet

But what about people using 3D Printers in shows and movies themselves? I'll be honest, this one often leaves me conflicted! Once you know the ins and outs of how 3D Printing processes work, and what things they're suitable for, it's hard not to notice when shows get it wrong!

If you know me, it'll be no surprise that one of my favourite movie scenes is the one in Jurassic Park 3 when they've 3D Printed a raptor's voice box... They took a few liberties with some of the detail, but this scene gets replayed a *lot* in our house! https://t.co/DDEeHZYUXM

Small Soldiers is another favourite - who can forget watching those prototypes rise up out of a relatively realistic Stereolithography-type printer? 😃 https://t.co/JpizMvk8Ay

There are plenty of other movies featuring some 3D Printing, as well as bunch of TV shows - CSI, Batwoman, Westworld to name a few, and of course I'm always happy to argue about whether the Replicators in Star Trek count as 3D Printing!

Of course food is a big one that comes up - we've seen 3D Printed cheese, chocolate, plant-based steaks, sugar, and a (tenuous) 3D Printed pizza. Check out this example found by one of my students a few years ago! https://t.co/bLxMs93c13

I'll end today by saying how lucky I am to get to talk to you. Events of the last year lay bare how we must do better to protect each other. In industry, our safety slogan was: "Nothing we do is worth risking someone else's safety," and we must be aware of this every day.

16.06.2020 · Tweet

Hi all! @SoftMatterHackr here. As promised, a bit of background on my path to research. The people in my life were critical to my experiences and I do everything I can to pay that back to those who might not get a chance to connect to science and research. https://t.co/hYlKJHWmYG

16.06.2020 · Tweet

I was born in the US state of Delaware. It’s a tiny state but has a funny divide between its north and south. The north is urban, where the duPont chemical company and the University of Delaware were formed. https://t.co/gEDdYuNDMu

16.06.2020 · Tweet

Southern Delaware is fairly rural by comparison, with chicken and corn farms everywhere. It also has great beaches that attract huge numbers of out-of-state tourists every summer. I grew up very close to the beach and was hugely influenced by my parents. https://t.co/8Bm17rAJSU

16.06.2020 · Tweet

My father grew up quite poor but worked to become an accountant in the north, where he met my mom. He didn’t like working just for financial gain, so when Delaware created Community Colleges he left his corporate job to support education in the rural areas where we grew up.

16.06.2020 · Tweet

Dad worked as a COBOL, FORTRAN, and RPG programmer, reporting on demographic and internal data for the college and region, and taught a number of courses over time. He taught me to code and exposed me to early modems and online games in the late 70s and early 80s.

16.06.2020 · Tweet

My mom studied biology and was an amazing force, saving my life as a newborn. I had undiagnosed milk allergies that almost killed me. She was so angry at a doctor who dismissed her concerns she got more opinions and found someone who could supply infant formulas without milk. https://t.co/SXu6KzfeRd

16.06.2020 · Tweet

I had a number of jobs, and even apprenticed with an industrial glassblower. This is 15yo me working on a quartz “boat” that held silicon wafers for etching into integrated circuits. The quartz melted at very high temperatures and was my first really viscous fluid system! https://t.co/Oh3tOiPFs0

16.06.2020 · Tweet

I then got a summer job with the local plastics company run by a former duPont chemist who would employ anyone local who was college-bound. He talked me into studying chemical engineering at university. I was lucky to live in Delaware, where the state uni was a top ChE school.

16.06.2020 · Tweet

Once at UD, I worked as a lab assistant with Prof. Jon Sharp’s group in the Chemical Oceanography department near my home and the beach. I was there three summers, moving from simple tasks to an independent research project funded by the US NSF REU program.

16.06.2020 · Tweet

The group studied nutrient distributions in the Delaware Bay and River, using phytoplankton and other indicators of the health of the waterways. I worked on carbon levels in seawater, a measure of climate change. https://t.co/7gULKq4x3C

16.06.2020 · Tweet

The REU program's purpose is getting Americans to go to grad school. It worked! Being around the grad students, seeing research in pure and applied forms, and benefiting the health of a region and industry, won me over.

16.06.2020 · Tweet

My last college summer I wanted to do engineering, luckily Prof. Art Metzner referred me to an REU program at U. Cincinnati. There I met Prof. Sotiris Pratsinis, who assigned me to study sol-gel deposition of silica nanoparticles. At the end Sotiris offered me a PhD scholarship.

16.06.2020 · Tweet

My PhD was on flocculation, where small particles aggregate in mixed fluids, enhancing settling and filtration. This is used to treat waste and drinking water, and my project was sponsored by a company to improve recovery of valuable enzymes produced by engineered bacteria. https://t.co/6jJiDrMXnR

16.06.2020 · Tweet

I was the only student in my group working on colloids, everyone else studied aerosol nanoparticle production by high-temperature combustion, sponsored by the duPont Company, connecting me to industry and combined modelling and experiment used to understand material processes.

When I needed experimental equipment to quantify floc sizes and structure, my group infrastructure couldn't help with liquid studies. My supervisor didn’t have equipment funding but had travel money. He sent me to groups in Australia and the Netherlands to use their setups. https://t.co/x9o0aYdUgU

16.06.2020 · Tweet

These trips really opened my mind to other countries and cultures, and imprinted on me the importance and power of collaboration. I’ve worked from the same playbook ever since.

My time in Australia had broader long-term benefits. Returning to Cincinnati I went on a blind date with a woman who was also just back from Australia. Our mutual amazement at the coincidence broke the ice: we married the year after. https://t.co/aGbN7rqSt0

18 years later I moved my whole family to Sydney to take the job I’m in now, working with colleagues like Rose and Graeme who were PhD students when I first visited! https://t.co/MfQU9o4woD

Hi, @SoftMatterHackr here again. This time a thread about my experience working in industry as an engineering researcher for the Procter & Gamble Company. P&G is a company started in Cincinnati that originally made soap and candles and is now a huge consumer products company. https://t.co/X9Vf4k3Xxl

18.06.2020 · Tweet

I was hired into a group that acted as consultants for all of the product business units globally. Corporate Engineering was a scale-up consultancy, with strong knowledge about manufacturing products at a large scale (12 tons) but were developed on liter scales.

18.06.2020 · Tweet

P&G makes a lot of things, and my group focused on complex fluids, materials with non-Newtonian rheology. This simply means that their viscosity can change depending on how fast they flow, because they have properties of both solids and liquids.

18.06.2020 · Tweet

Cornstarch in water is a well-known non-Newtonian fluid, it thickens when deformed quickly. An opposite example is shampoo. If you measure the slow flow viscosity of shampoo it is nearly identical to honey. But if you make shampoo flow faster it gets thinner, or less viscous. https://t.co/SofKdQYQO9

18.06.2020 · Tweet

Shear-thinning occurs as microscopic particle structures temporarily break down in the shampoo. Honey, on the other hand, stays just as thick when you move it quickly, so don’t try to wash your hair with straight honey: your hair will not last!

18.06.2020 · Tweet

Complex fluids like shampoo are often water-based, but they can drastically change their flow properties when relatively small amounts of particles, surfactants, and/or polymers are added. Others: detergents, soaps, cosmetics, conditioners, shaving cream, mouthwash, toothpaste...

18.06.2020 · Tweet

A key economic point is consumer products can be made, using mostly water and small amounts of additives, to feel rich, creamy, and pleasant. These aesthetics distinguish such products from fine chemicals and petrochemicals.

18.06.2020 · Tweet

Petro- and fine chemicals are judged based on purity, while consumer products are judged on qualitative criteria like softness and qualitative criteria like the thickness of skin coatings. So knowledge of structures in complex fluids is very profitable.

18.06.2020 · Tweet

So a specialist organization is needed to make these materials at large scales. If the the fluid changes its properties while it is being mixed, for example, it is much more unpredictable as there is often not a reliable theory of how these products behave in processes.

18.06.2020 · Tweet

As a result, a lot of our work blended modeling and simulation with experimental studies of flow and structure of the products. One of my first projects with the company was studying how to make the wax crystals that are used to give shampoo a pearlescent appearance.

18.06.2020 · Tweet

The optical effect occurs when lots of flat, plate-shaped crystals line up in layers in the shampoo and light scatters from their edges and centers with interference effects similar to what is seen with real pearls. https://t.co/SO99hYBMaK

18.06.2020 · Tweet

After that I worked on a crystallization process forming nanoscale fibers to modify the rheology, or flow properties of beauty products. I noticed that melted droplets of these waxes could crystallize and repel their own solid phase, moving and producing "comet" particles. https://t.co/dfnZWhM4NT

18.06.2020 · Tweet

Next two things happened that really affected my career direction. P&G started to get interested in nanotechnology. The US had funded the National Nanotechnology Initiative and everyone was excited by the potential of nanoparticles and other nanoscale systems. https://t.co/qOiwyiL0ba

18.06.2020 · Tweet

P&G also realized they needed to look externally for some innovation. Big companies often can’t move fast enough to develop everything needed. Their new approach, called C&D or Connect & Develop, rather than R&D, meant partnering with others, say academics, to speed development. https://t.co/P34dYvDTNT

18.06.2020 · Tweet

In my next thread I’ll tell you about my biggest nanotechnology project for P&G and, really, in my research career. The best part of the story is that it made my employer the most money by far, but also got me in trouble for the first time there...

19.06.2020 · Tweet

Another post from @SoftMatterHackr here, this time about a nanoscience project we did while I worked at P&G. As with all of my projects, this was a collaboration, in this case with Dr. Matt Lynch and other colleagues at the company

19.06.2020 · Tweet

The project originally began as a conversation Matt and I had about self-assembled systems, where molecules like surfactants form larger structures on their own, without additional guidance or templating.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

We were originally interested in delivering anti-inflammatory drugs across the skin, and were considering liposomes as the delivery vehicle. Liposomes are simple lipid bilayers wrapped up into spheres, and were hoped to penetrate skin well enough to deliver the drug.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

But, commercially, you must avoid infringing on other patents. This was hard with liposomes. At the time there were thousands of relevant patents we had to avoid. Despite this, the excitement about nanoscience drove us to look at soft nanoparticles like liposomes as a solution.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

Fortunately, I’d just done a course on surfactant science with Prof. Stig Friberg at Clarkson U., and he’d talked about a new self-assembled particle: a cubosome. https://t.co/ZodlfZF1UE

19.06.2020 · Tweet

Where liposomes form from relatively simple curved bilayers, cubosomes are dispersed particles of cubic liquid crystalline phase, where the bilayers are contorted into space-filling minimal surfaces like this: https://t.co/bDGszRdegO

19.06.2020 · Tweet

When we checked, there were only four patents on cubosomes, so we felt there was a much better chance of creating something new with them. This is a nice example of patent maneuvering: we couldn’t patent cubosomes, but the key patent process could only make a few grams of them.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

The existing patent mixed a lipid and water in the right proportions, forming an extremely viscous cubic phase, and then used ultrasonic treatment to blast the material into nanoparticles. This meant only small volumes could be made, as power was aimed into a small container.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

Since we needed to make much larger quantities, we pursued a new approach. We treated the very viscous material as a solid, and reasoned that if we made a solution of it, then diluted it and precipitated the particles out, we could make nanoparticles with hardly any energy input.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

Because our new process allowed us to make cubosomes on a large scale, we were able to patent it. https://t.co/n2YxqxOsox

19.06.2020 · Tweet

Our team grew to include new employee Kristin Hayden and Janet Burns, who studied the phase behavior of the system and made critical cryo-TEM images of the particles to verify what we were making. https://t.co/DV4SxgjEDu

19.06.2020 · Tweet

The project followed a normal path for a while, and we started testing the materials for use in a skin treatment. One of the steps is to ensure that it doesn’t irritate skin. We did this with the Skin Science Institute at U. Cincinnati with Dr Marty Visscher and Dr. Steven Hoath.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

As part of the normal testing, Steve noticed something unique about cubic phase. Unlike occlusive treatments like petroleum jelly, that protect against drying but block exchange with the environment by skin, cubic phase kept the skin hydrated while still allowing skin transport.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

Steve hypothesized that this could be used for a different purpose than we originally intended. At the time there was no skin treatment for premature babies to protect them against infection.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

When we are born, we have a coating on our skin called a vernix, that is the remnant of the lipid template the body uses to form our stratum corneum layer. Premature babies can lack this because it hasn't finished forming and creating that skin barrier.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

So when born prematurely, we often lack a barrier against infection and are very vulnerable until our skin fully develops. They proposed we adapt the cubosome product to treat premature babies. We loved the idea, but commercially it was not viable for the company.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

Still, we persevered and worked with our internal tech transfer people to see about transferring the IP we’d created to Children’s Hospital in Cincinnati.This would allow them to develop a product, actually an artificial vernix, that could be applied to preemies as protection. https://t.co/AuK4T5dBND

19.06.2020 · Tweet

So, the company made money by donating our patents, the University Hospital got to help the babies, and the state government used our example to announce new tech collaboration program support. Here's the Governor of Ohio, Bob Taft, with Matt and me on the day of announcement. https://t.co/IOvgYaedko

19.06.2020 · Tweet

His photographer had a good sense of humor, as he carefully positioned me so that it looks like I am being immunized by a statue in the background. The statue is of Albert Sabin, developer of the live polio vaccine.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

And now the trouble I got into: I gave a lot of talks after this happened, both to share our work and to increase our collaborations with academics. At one of them I mentioned that these cubosomes were nanoparticles. There was a journalist in the audience...

19.06.2020 · Tweet

The journalist wrote that I said P&G products contained lots of nanoparticles. This is a big no-no for consumer product companies, as the public does not not like nano in their stuff. When I got back from the conference I got blasted by our PR people and had to help explain.

19.06.2020 · Tweet

It was a good lesson about nano, that is still valid in many ways: doing nano will get you credit in science but can cause trouble in the commercial food or consumer space. (Nanomedicine people get away with it because they are trying to save lives and fight cancer!)

19.06.2020 · Tweet

I'm almost done with my curation term. For my last thread I will bring you up to date and talk about what we're doing at UNSW in research and development!

20.06.2020 · Tweet

OK, @SoftMatterHackr back again. I had a lot of fun over 15 years at P&G, but was interested in making a change, both to pursue my interests a bit more and to move my family somewhere unique. I was fortunate that a job had opened at UNSW Sydney, and moved us to Australia in 2012.

20.06.2020 · Tweet

As you do, I recruited students for a while until I had built a core group of my first four PhD students: Dr. Haiqiao Wang, Dr. Jie Song, Dr. Prerna Dahiya, and Dr. Goldina Kwandou. https://t.co/GgJ12CENjP

20.06.2020 · Tweet

Dr. Dahiya studied droplet coalescence, understanding how rheology can offset interfacial tension and form non-spherical droplet shapes, but also how the process of arrest can be used to build larger-scale structures. https://t.co/qMczUHg82L

20.06.2020 · Tweet

Dr. Wang looked at cubosomes and similar particles, not as nanoparticles but as microparticles and she found a number of ways to produce particles with complex, controlled shapes as well as template them using polymerization processes. https://t.co/XYGiVvHmQR

20.06.2020 · Tweet

Dr. Song developed a new microrheology technique to study non-Newtonian fluids made from nanocellulose dispersions and measured complex yielding transitions of the fluids using tiny bubbles as probes of mechanical properties. https://t.co/ClHu0CkBgo

20.06.2020 · Tweet

Dr. Kwandou used a number of techniques to understand how biofilms form, and respond to novel treatments like cold plasma, showing that bacteria can be opportunistic and actually be preserved from thermal treatments because of structures formed by their dead brethren. https://t.co/Cc4jg3i9aO

20.06.2020 · Tweet

These days my research group focuses on the topics discussed above as well as some new areas. I discussed one of these when I spoke on the podcast: thunderstorm asthma. https://t.co/S2yIjetyGO

20.06.2020 · Tweet

Thunderstorm asthma is a unique but dangerous condition that is not fully understood. It is now thought to occur when storms draw grass pollens into thunderclouds, rupture the pollen, and disperse allergenic proteins, basically biological nanoparticles, into the population.

20.06.2020 · Tweet

The resulting effect on people inhaling these particles has been to cause difficulty breathing and dangerous symptoms of asthma. What’s even more remarkable about the phenomenon is that many of the people experiencing the effects had no previous history of asthma.

20.06.2020 · Tweet

We are collaborating with groups at U. Sydney, QUT, and UNSW to better map the mechanisms, using microfluidic channels to expose pollen to extreme conditions, simulate the experience in a thundercloud, and directly observe rupture and subsequent release of the allergens. https://t.co/D3r5EAOBb0

20.06.2020 · Tweet

Our collaborators are using these particles to quantify the level of inflammatory response the particles cause to differentiate between different starting conditions. We hope this work will lead to enhanced prediction and warning of thunderstorm asthma conditions.

20.06.2020 · Tweet

I hope this week has shown a bit of what we’ve done in the area of commercial and academic soft matter. I’m grateful to @MySci_PK for the chance to share it all and look forward to great future curators. Visit us at @SoftMatterHackr to discuss any of these topics. Bye for now! https://t.co/77kcHyp6PX

My first research project was on the topic of using optical fibres to remove wavefront aberrations induced by atmospheric turbulence to improve the performance of a stellar interferometer.- for imaging stars.

28.06.2020 · Tweet

That was in 1992 and was in the early days of optical fibre technology. I like to say that at the end of this project I saw the light and decided to shift from astronomy to optical fibre research. I started by PhD in the Optical Fibre Technology Centre at the University of Sydney

28.06.2020 · Tweet

My PhD was on Nonlinear fibre optics with a specific emphasis on solitons in optical fibres. I spent 6 months at Bell Labs in 1995 where I discovered a new class of soliton -the Bragg grating soliton. I graduated in 1997 and went back to Bell Labs as a postdoc.

28.06.2020 · Tweet

From 1997 to December 2002 I was at Bell Labs, Lucent Technologies (then OFS) as a Postdoc, Member of Staff, Technical Manager and then Director. I was there during the telecom bubble & burst and then 9-11 and decided to come back to Sydney at the end of 2002.

28.06.2020 · Tweet

In 2003 I started at @Sydney_Uni as a Professor in the School of Physics @sydney_physics as the founding Director of CUDOS, an ARC Centre of Excellene. Our mission was to create and develop a photonic chip - a cartoon schematic is shown here. https://t.co/0VFJpN77xS

28.06.2020 · Tweet

The photonic chip is an integrated circuit that is thumbnail sized, incorporating components for generating, manipulating and detecting photons, the building blocks of light. We use lithography to print circuits -leveraging the enormous investment that has gone into silicon https://t.co/k6pACFVH8H

28.06.2020 · Tweet

Photonic chips (photonic integrated circuits) can incorporate hundreds of components and can be used for advanced signal processing in telecommunicaitons, radar, sensing and quantum technologies. The feature sizes required to define the components is nanometre scale.

28.06.2020 · Tweet

I wrote an article in the conversation on the topic of nanophotonics - https://t.co/pcZajDI65z with a great link to a short cartoon on photonic chip: https://t.co/pcZajDI65z

In nanoscience, sonication is a powerful tool for dispersing nano materials. Sonochemistry is another area of research I have interests in, where the sonic energy can be used to perform chemical processes. This has been big for the environmental chemists and engineers.

10.07.2020 · Tweet

This is a probe sonicator, so high frequency (ultrasonic) pulses are sent through the liquid system via a vibrating probe tip. When this happens powerful bubbles collapse and recollapse inside the liquid system. This mechanical process can be used to separate materials

10.07.2020 · Tweet

Particles* i mean. Also, during ultrasonication, free radicals are created that can react with your system if you want. These radicals are short lived so the chemistry is very complex.

10.07.2020 · Tweet

Currently just sonicating nano particles in a solvent. I tend to use non reactive solvents to sonicate because you don’t always want to induce a chemical reaction when sonicating.

So I got my masters degree @SFSU in @LauraBurrusSFSU's lab! The lab works on WNT signaling, particularly during development. In my case I was looking at a protein called wntless, and what happens in the developing chicken neural tube when you 'knock it down' with siRNA.

12.07.2020 · Tweet

That's a lot of words. Basically, WNT is a protein (well, a family of proteins) that gets sent out as a signal from one cell to another nearby cell. It is important in a lot of different situations! One situation is helping pattern the future parts of your spinal cord!

12.07.2020 · Tweet

There is a protein that seems to be important for getting WNT properly shoved out of the first cell, so it can go signaling -- wntless (because if you get rid of it, you'll be wnt-less... Get it?) I won't belabor the point too much, except to say that dev bio is really amazing!

12.07.2020 · Tweet

It was an interesting experience studying something a little further away from my undergrad studies (and middle school ideas). But it was also an extremely useful experience. If I'm being honest, I was a pretty crummy scientist for the majority of my masters degree!

I think I learned and matured a lot during that MS though, which really prepped me to hit the ground running when I went to do my PhD. For folks outside the US, btw, an masters before a PhD in bio isn't all that common -- I think PhDs in the US take longer to compensate for that
