RT @PhD_Balance: @RealSci_Nano Thanks so much for the mention! And this actually is spot on for our #PhDStrongerTogether topic for this wee…

12.07.2020 · Tweet

Whew well that was a lot of autobiographical stuff! If you're hanging out on this Sunday and want something to do, drop in here and say hi! Are you interested in nanoscience? Cancer research? Immunology? Let me know! Have any questions? I mean, let's do this thing!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

I hope everyone is having the best possible Monday you can! I'm definitely someone that gets hit pretty hard by the start of the week... Anyway, today is going to actually take a couple steps away from nanoscience to lay some groundwork on biology things!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Specifically, I'd like to talk about cancer and the immune system! This is going to take a good amount of talking, because both cancer and the immune system are very complex *separately*, and mixing them together makes it all pretty confusing!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Okay so first of all, cancer is a pretty big term that covers things ranging from 'liquid' cancers in your blood to solid cancer in, say, your breast. Cancer can range in how aggressive their growth and metastasis is, can range in how many mutations they accumulate, etc etc!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

There are cancers that are intimately related to your immune system because they arise from the same (or related) progenitors -- cancers like lymphomas and leukemias. But most my knowledge is related to solid tumors and how the immune system interfaces with them.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

The immune system is around to do a lot of work, but one of the jobs we know it best for is keeping us safe from enemies. Those enemies aren't only 'foreign' things like bacteria and viruses, but 'domestic' enemies like misbehaving cells.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

There are a lot of things that can make a cell behave weirdly (including things like bacterial infections and viruses, but other stuff too, like mutations/genetic damage). Immune cells and neighboring cells are on the look out for cells being weird. They're on the lookout!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

So, for a cell to develop into cancer, there are a lot of hurdles to overcome, including avoiding this surveillance. A lot of cells get stopped in this process, so with cancer we are often seeing the 'ones that make it' or the 'ones that slip through the cracks'.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

When a cell is acting weird, there are a lot of ways that other cells can tell that something is going on. Cells stick stuff on their surface to help let other cells know what their inner workings are like!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Some proteins are signals other cells *expect* to see, like an "everything is OK" signal -- if it is missing, other cells can get suspicious Some proteins are signals that something is wrong -- so if you have that signal other cells get worried.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Our cells also have a protein called MHC I. MHC I is a protein that we stick little bits of other proteins on, almost like a 'sampler' dish of what proteins we're making inside our cell. Most of the time we're just making normal, everyday proteins encoded in our genome!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

But what about when we're infected with a VIRUS? When that happens, some (or a lot) of the proteins we're making are viral proteins because it is hijacking our machinery! Well if the MHC system is still working, we'll end up slipping a chunk of virus protein on our surface!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

This can help let your immune system know that something naughty is going down. So MHC I is something most of our cells keep updating, to show what they've been making lately! This is important for cancer!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Cancer cells often have accumulated some mutations (how many mutations can vary pretty widely!). Some of those mutations change the actual amino acid sequence of proteins the cancer cells are making (changing that sequence sometimes changes the protein function).

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Well, those parts of the changed proteins *might* be recognizable to your immune system as a 'foreign' protein if it is slapped on MHC I and put on the cancer cell surface!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

These are called *neoantigens* Neo because they're new! The cancer just made them through mutation! Antigens because that is what we call chunks of stuff (often protein chunks) that your immune system can recognize and mount a response to (typically adaptive).

13.07.2020 · Tweet

So cancer making these neoantigens is thought to be an important way that your body can mount an immune response against cancer -- they're little signals that your immune system can recognize that the cancer is something other than a regular cell in your body.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

But if it were that easy, we wouldn't be dealing with cancer in the clinic -- our immune systems would have this handled. Now, the immune system probably takes care of a lot of stuff before it ever makes it to cancer levels, but clearly we are still dealing with cancer today.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

That is because cancer is SO TRICKY. There are MANY ways that cancer is able to avoid the immune system. Different cancers have a tendency to rely on different methods of immune evasion, but they can probably use more than one! Gah!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Examples! Cytotoxic T cells are a kind of immune cell that are very good at killing cancer cells when they bump into them and recognize them. So cancer solution #1 -- don't let the T cells into the tumor. Seriously! Some cancers set up a "T cell exclusion zone!" https://t.co/SlW4ZV5GCG

13.07.2020 · Tweet

If someone is interested I can talk about some of the molecular mechanisms behind the set up of this zone (so tricky....), but for now I'm going to keep it relatively easy to digest and light on the details.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Anyway, I mentioned that cytotoxic T cells are dangerous for cancer cells. They are also important for fighting off viruses -- they kill infected cells so that the virus can't keep hijacking the cellular factory.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Cytotoxic T cells need to have an "off switch" though (all immune responses do) because you want to be able to wind things down when the infection is over! There are several different off switches that can tell cytotoxic T cells to calm down.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

One example is the kynurenine/IDO pathway. This is a situation where cells (often other immune cells) can toss out a signal into the extracellular environment that says "okay y'all, let's calm down this immune situation!". T cells respond to this signal by... calming down

13.07.2020 · Tweet

When you look inside a tumor. you typically see more than JUST cancer cells. You might see some of the 'normal' cells that were living in the neighborhood before the cancer cells started wrecking things. But in a lot of cases you'll actually see other immune cells

13.07.2020 · Tweet

...What the heck are those immune cells doing! Get to work killing that cancer! But unfortunately, these immune cells have been reprogrammed in the tumor microenvironment (neighborhood) to behave a certain way.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

These are pretty recognizable names in the immune cell world! Macrophages! Neutrophils! Dendritic Cells! Often these cells do a great job with things like launching off inflammatory signals and eating up bacteria. But in tumors, they often do the opposite!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

They often become kynurenine factories, pumping out that signal to turn off other immune cells. They can help in setting up that T cell exclusion zone I mentioned earlier! They can even put out growth signals to help egg on the cancer cells https://t.co/eIpScuhrHr

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Cancer cells can exploit another "off switch" that T cells have -- a kind of 'secret handshake' that tells the T cells that they bumped into a good cell and need to chill out. This GIF, except not cool ⬇️⬇️⬇️ https://t.co/ALljYWJeOi

13.07.2020 · Tweet

The handshake happens when certain proteins on the surface of T cells bump into and bind with proteins on the surface of other cells (sometimes cancer cells, but it can also be on those other pesky naughty immune cells that aren't doing their proper job!)

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Examples of this handshake can be: T cell | Other cell PD-1 PD-L1 CTLA-4 B7-1/2 LAG-3 MHC II TIM-3 Galectin-9 and more! https://t.co/aPd8WuOzfC

13.07.2020 · Tweet

When a T cell gets this handshake, it'll basically back off and cool down and won't kill the cancer cell. That is a significant bummer!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Tumors can also be 'immunologically cold' in that they haven't set off enough immune alarm bells to have their neoantigens recognized as foreign. Some cancers, by the way, hide their neoantigens by choosing to hide their MHC I! Man they are naughty.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

So the thing is, even if you have a tumor where: the cancer cells have neoantigens AND you got to see them AND T cells aren't excluded AND they aren't burned out from kynurenine some cancer cells can just shake the T cell's protein-hands and prevent them from doing their jobs! https://t.co/L87iisFlzZ

13.07.2020 · Tweet

A relatively recent trend in cancer treatments has been ~Immunotherapy~ Cancer immunotherapy is about giving treatments with the goal of helping the immune system overcome all these tricky hurdles that cancer can toss up!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

An example of cancer immunotherapy success has been the use of blocking antibodies to physically keep T cells and cancer cells from "shaking hands". So an antibody that targets PD-1, for example, binds to that PD-1 on the T cell and prevents it from hooking up with PD-L1

13.07.2020 · Tweet

This has been called immune checkpoint blockade -- the handshake is an 'immune checkpoint' because it can turn off your T cells, and these cool antibodies can *block(ade)* that processs! Nice!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Now, for what is likely to be a TON of different reasons, immune checkpoint blockade works very well in some people and some cancers, and like... not at all in others. This is truly a bummer. But that just means we need to keep working on it!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

In broad strokes, one very plausible reason why immune checkpoint blockade doesn't work in everyone is that it really only deals with *one* of the immune evasion tricks cancers have up their sleeves.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

For example: If the tumor is super T cell-excluded, does it matter if you block a handshake that couldn't happen in the first place? This reminds me of that thing about a tree falling in the woods with no one around.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Or another example: If a cancer isn't mutated all that much and doesn't have many neoantigens, T cells might never care enough about them to even notice them. So what could would immune checkpoint blockade do?

13.07.2020 · Tweet

There are other possibilities -- antibodies are smaller than cells and viruses, but are pretty big for proteins and *definitely* big compared to "small molecule drugs" like most chemotherapeutics. Do they have any issues getting into solid tumors?

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Antibodies are also pretty bioactive -- they are proteins our body produces itself and are recognized by a lot of our cells. When we use them as a treatment, do they sometimes get taken up or bound up before they get a chance to do their jobs?

13.07.2020 · Tweet

It is hard to make universal statements when it comes to cancer! But it certainly is the case that immune checkpoint blockade antibodies have helped many people fight their cancers -- these treatments are getting approved for more and more types of cancer each year.

13.07.2020 · Tweet

I think what is becoming clear (or at least, I'm advocating for this view) is that cancer immunotherapy is something that can work, but we probably need to combine multiple tactics so that cancer can't evade its way around our therapies!

13.07.2020 · Tweet

Some of this will boil down to a more 'personalized' look at the details of a patient's cancer. Does the cancer seem like it has a lot of neoantigens? Maybe immune checkpoint blockade will work without any help! If not, maybe we need to add something to the mix to help out...

13.07.2020 · Tweet

I'll get into this more (tomorrow? I think?) but this is one place I think nanoparticles can help out -- they can help deliver more than one treatment to the same spot (i.e. the tumor) Nano can help us make a combo punch to knock the cancer out!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

!!! Yeah! But some of the indicator lights work the way ours do, and other work the reverse — they’re always supposed to be on, and if they turn off, that means something is wrong. https://t.co/YjrnRLZaC4

14.07.2020 · Tweet

The "nano" part of RealSci_Nano is coming into play today! Mainly, I want to go over the multiple answers to the question "why use nanoparticles for drug delivery?" https://t.co/h37h6GKoZt

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Well what's the alternative, smarty-pants?! Just kidding. Many many of the drugs that are administered to you are "small molecules" and are typically under a nanometer in size.

14.07.2020 · Tweet

I have a little figure here that my friend and colleague Molly Frey made (from the Scott Lab, @NorthwesternU) at my request. These are 5 reasons I think nanoparticles are useful for drug delivery! The little yellow shape is a small molecule drug, the green ball is a nanoparticle https://t.co/kILolY3xG6

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Okay so let's do (a) first! Some small molecules don't really like floating around in water! If you put them in water, they tend to clump together and 'precipitate out'.

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Some small molecules get chemically modified to improve their water solubility, or get mixed with some stuff to try to help keep the drug from precipitating, like PEG400 (a polymer) or DMSO (an organic solvent).

14.07.2020 · Tweet

But another option is to put the small molecule into nanoparticles! Nanoparticles (here I'm thinking particularly about those that are amphiphilic, like lipid or polymer nanoparticles) have areas where they like water and areas where they don't.

14.07.2020 · Tweet

For example, you might make a nanoparticle out of some polymer. This polymer has two parts to it -- a 'green' part that likes water and a 'red' part that doesn't (this, by the way, would be called an amphiphilic diblock copolymer) https://t.co/T7HjsosKlk

14.07.2020 · Tweet

If you toss some of that polymer into water, the 'red' part that hates water will naturally try to hide from the water! This forces the polymer to 'self-assemble' with other polymer strands into little shapes where the 'red' is inside and the 'green' is outside, facing the water https://t.co/RQYcy6grDz

14.07.2020 · Tweet

That's a nanoparticle! I mean, depending on how big the polymer is (and other factors) it doesn't HAVE to be a nanoparticle -- it could be a microparticle instead. And it doesn't HAVE to form a ball with the red sitting in the center like that -- other shapes are possible! https://t.co/Rd7V9W5sKZ

14.07.2020 · Tweet

But the main point here is nanoparticles can have areas inside them that are 'red', that are *hydrophobic*. Those areas can be very accommodating and welcoming for hydrophobic small molecule drugs that reeaaally don't want to be hanging out in water.

14.07.2020 · Tweet

So, one big benefit of nanoparticles is you can make small molecule drug formulations with hydrophobic drugs that are otherwise really hard to make soluble! This improvement to solubility often also improves the *stability* of the drug in water -- it won't precipitate out easily

14.07.2020 · Tweet

@NotHF lol, I think they're nanoparticles so long as they're small enough 😉

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Whew, that was all for (a). What about (b)? https://t.co/1UtcZtL40p

14.07.2020 · Tweet

An important consideration when drugs are designed and tested is their pharmacokinetics -- covering criteria like their Absorption Distribution Metabolism Excretion Metabolism is chemical alteration of the drug in your body, which can change how well it works!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Sometimes that is a good change, but often it is a 'breaking down' process that makes the drug not work anymore. In some cases, putting your small molecule inside of a nanoparticle can help protect it from enzymes or other molecules that might damage your cargo

14.07.2020 · Tweet

@NotHF You fancy transition metal NP folks...

14.07.2020 · Tweet

@NotHF Luckily I never used a bath that hot, but making my polymer amphiphiles relied on plenty of "why does no one know why we do this reaction this way?"

14.07.2020 · Tweet

@NotHF I'm mostly making mesoporous silica nanoparticles right now and it is certainly... different, let's say... from self assembled polymer nanoparticles. Yeah. Different!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

So let's see... (a) Nanoparticles can help with solubility (b) Nanoparticles can protect small molecule cargo from degradation (c)? What's going on there? https://t.co/fWmYrnNQx6

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Okay so the idea behind (c) has to do with the distribution of your small molecule -- where does it go in your body and what cells end up getting treated? In most cases I can think of, when you take a drug it is intended to get to work on some subset of your cells

14.07.2020 · Tweet

But when you take a drug orally or by an IV injection or something, a lot of the time it ends up going to a LOT of places in your body, and can end up affecting MANY kinds of cells. Not all of those cells were really your 'target' cells.

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Sometimes that is fine, but sometimes that can cause damage and/or 'off-target' effects. Doxorubicin is a chemotherapy drug that can cause really serious heart toxicity (Why are you hitting the heart like that dox? Go fight the cancer!!)

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Well one *potential* benefit of nanoparticles is you can change where in the body the drug goes and what cells are more or less likely to take them up. There's probably a lot of reasons why this change happens.

14.07.2020 · Tweet

First of all, small molecules are... smaller than nanoparticles. So they can squeeze out of small holes in your body than nanoparticles and end up in different spots in different amounts than a nanoparticle would!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Small molecules can also *stick* to stuff and have that seriously impact where they go. For example, there are proteins in your blood like serum albumin -- some drugs LOVE sticking to serum albumin and can get dragged into different parts of the body.

14.07.2020 · Tweet

I don't, by the way, mean to say that nanoparticles themselves can't be sticky. Not only *can* nanoparticles be sticky, they almost ALWAYS are sticky. The 'stickiness' of nanoparticles is something scientists often try to modulate to change blood circulation time

14.07.2020 · Tweet

This is turning into a bit of a tangent, but in any case, the surface of your nanoparticle definitely impacts what organs it goes to and what cells gobble them up. And you can do some engineering to try to control that (some)!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Surface charge can impact where nanoparticles go! Surface hydrophobicity (and curvature, and other stuff) can impact 'protein adsorption', or basically proteins in your body glomming onto the nanoparticle. Nanoparticle SHAPE can impact cell uptake!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Yeah! Little nanostars can get taken up by different cells preferentially compared to little nanoworms, or nanodiscs, or nanofootballs, and so on! There's a lot of thoughts as to *why* this happens... maybe we can go into that tangent sometime...

14.07.2020 · Tweet

But anyway, you can also try to really specifically get your nanoparticle taken up by particular cells using *targeting stuff* attached to the surface of your nanoparticles. These could be antibodies, DNA aptamers, sugars, or seriously a ton of other things people have tried.

14.07.2020 · Tweet

I am *personally* a bit of a targeting skeptic -- I think it takes a lot of careful work and design to make a nanoparticle that *helped* by the addition of a targeting moiety more than it is *hurt* by the added complexity. But I love being proved wrong!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

So (c) is basically that you can engineer nanoparticles to change where your drug goes, compared to if it were floating around your body willy-nilly. In the example of doxorubicin, which I mentioned earlier, a nanoparticle-delivered version of dox reduced heart toxicity!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

It is broadly safe to use than 'free' dox, but has its own, *different* toxicities! lol Nanoparticles aren't always going to take something from 'dangerous' to 'completely safe'! Sometimes it'll be 'dangerous' to 'less dangerous' Or 'dangerous' to 'differently dangerous' 🤣

14.07.2020 · Tweet

(a) Improve solubility (b) Prevent degradation (c) Targeting/Distribution stuff (d) ? https://t.co/8EVdUkCTuh

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Sometimes one drug just isn't enough to do the trick! Maybe you want to be able to deliver 2-3 drugs all at once to The Same Spot or Cell If you just swallow 2 drugs, they might have very different pharmacokinetics! One could end up in the lungs while the other is in the liver!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Nanoparticles can act like a delivery vehicle, or like an Uber or Taxi, for your group of drugs. That one nanoparticle could be loaded up with all three drugs, in the ratio you want them delivered, and sent off!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

You can't guarantee it'll go EXACTLY where you want it to, but all the passengers will go there together! And they'll arrive at the same time -- in some situations that might be *biologically* a very important thing to accomplish!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

(a) Solubility (b) Protection (c) Distribution (d) Multiple Passengers! (e) ? https://t.co/giJVBOMMmW

14.07.2020 · Tweet

(e) Reflects a reality of drug discovery, which is that sometimes you find a molecule that can have the biological effect you want (like inhibiting some pesky enzyme), but the molecule itself isn't suitable for use in the body

14.07.2020 · Tweet

That can be for any of the ADME reasons -- maybe this molecule doesn't get distributed well in your body, or maybe it breaks down too fast or isn't soluble. So you probably want to tinker around with it! Add a chemical group here or there, maybe attach a PEG polymer on it

14.07.2020 · Tweet

OR... You can put it in a nanoparticle and get around the engineering issues on the nanoparticle level!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Basically, instead of finding a drug that works and then trying to further engineer it (at the risk of making it less functional or much more expensive), engineer that stuff on the nanoparticle level instead!

14.07.2020 · Tweet

Nanoparticles can add an extra layer of engineering on a drug formulation. That can mean more complexity and cost, but it can also mean more flexibility and can potentially open up more areas of the 'drug space' that were previously too challenging to use in vivo

15.07.2020 · Tweet

[admin] "Nanotaxies for Fighting Cancer" Extended conversation with @DishPodcast where Sean goes into the details of his scientific journey and more is out now https://t.co/HLGMvTdBy1

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Today I'm going to talk about nanoparticles that are *currently* approved for clinical use in the fight against cancer. That's right! There are nanoparticle treatments in the clinic right now and have been for years!

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Right off the bat let me say that there is a periodically updated review/survey of the clinical approval of nanoparticle treatments by @Aaron_Anselmo and @SMitragotri and I read it every time it comes out because it is *chef kiss* https://t.co/vQ7hMJWbrc

15.07.2020 · Tweet

I'm pretty sure the first nano-drug to get approved by the FDA was Doxil, which I actually mentioned yesterday. I say "pretty sure" because I'm a scientist and I've gotten really used to hedging any 'fact' I say, but I feel pretty good about this one.

15.07.2020 · Tweet

A pretty fun 2012 review of Doxil's history was written by Dr. Yechezkel Barenholz, one of the inventors. It is a pretty good mix of biographical insights, historical recollections, and experimental details. https://t.co/4ipRlDNMvV

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Doxil is a PEGylated liposomal formulation of doxorubicin -- I *definitely* talked about doxorubicin yesterday. It is a chemotherapeutic drug that can really kill the crap out of cancer cells (but can hurt other cells too if you aren't careful).

15.07.2020 · Tweet

The 'liposomal' part of a liposomal formulation means that the nanoparticle that was used was a little lipid bilayer sphere. It has a pretty similar bilayer to the one that cells do (with less lipid variety and fewer proteins and stuff shoved in there, typically).

15.07.2020 · Tweet

PEGylated means the liposome has some PEG polymer attached to its surface. PEG stands for poly(ethylene glycol), so it is a polymer made up of ethylene glycol units. PEG has a reputation for helping to extend the circulation time of stuff you toss into the bloodstream

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Part of the reason is thought to involve the prevention of protein adsorption onto nanoparticles (or drugs, you can PEGylate drugs). Proteins sometimes stick to stuff! PEG can just physically get in the way, like those noodle hats you can wear to enforce social distancing https://t.co/kZUJjjV1cU

15.07.2020 · Tweet

The size of the PEG and how much of it you attach to your nanoparticle is thought to affect its ability to do its job. Out of all the little lipids making up my liposomes, I typically have ~3% of them have PEG attached I use PEG that is ~45 ethylene glycols long

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Anyway the PEGylation is thought to help the nanoparticle float around longer in the blood without getting glommed onto by a bunch of proteins and cleared out really quick by your liver. PEGylation is not without some issues!

15.07.2020 · Tweet

First of all, some people have anti-PEG antibodies in their blood -- including people who have never been treated with a drug that has PEG in it. Some evidence suggests that having anti-PEG antibodies means you clear out PEGylated nanoparticles faster than someone without them

15.07.2020 · Tweet

That SUCKS. Stupid anti-PEG antibodies. Anyway. A second issue is that PEG might help some with protein adsorption and stuff, but it DEFINITELY does not STOP all protein adsorption. Proteins still adsorb onto PEGylated nanoparticles.

15.07.2020 · Tweet

So some people are working on other kinds of polymers that could someday replace PEG to try to get around these two issues. Best of luck, folks! Some of the contenders are zwitterionic polymers. PEG is cheap and works fairly well, so it'll be tough to replace.

15.07.2020 · Tweet

@Felgraf_Physics One of these upcoming days this week I'm going to go into the uses of nanoparticles to fight cancer that *aren't* drug delivery-based -- a lot of the approvals historically have been drug delivery focused, but nanoparticles can do a LOT of stuff...

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Wow wait, I was talking about Doxil and then I got side tracked by PEG. Sorry folks! Anyway, the PEGylation of Doxil was definitely important for its success, but so was the process for getting the doxorubicin INSIDE the liposome

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Liposomes are little bubbles with water inside and outside the bubble, and a thin bilayer of lipid in between. Some hydrophobic drugs occasionally get loaded into the lipid bilayer (this is not a trivial thing to do, you can potentially disrupt that bilayer).

15.07.2020 · Tweet

When you want to load hydrophilic stuff into a liposome, one way to do it is to simply form that lipid bubble AROUND the cargo you're trying to load! So now the drug is floating around inside the bubble!

15.07.2020 · Tweet

This is not typically a very high efficiency process. Generally, a lot of the 'space' when you're forming liposomes is *outside* the bubble, so a lot of your drug never gets encapsulated in the first place! Bummer!

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Small molecules can also potentially diffuse across the lipid bilayer of the liposome, meaning you can leak your drug out over time. Also a bummer!

15.07.2020 · Tweet

But that isn't to say it can't work! It is just that this kind of cargo loading has some difficulties associated with it.

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Anyway, 'regular old' loading wasn't working very well for doxorubicin. So they used a different kind of loading, one that is called 'remote loading'. In remote loading you make your liposomes, then add your cargo drug *to the outside* of those liposomes.

15.07.2020 · Tweet

"Wait Sean" you might say "If the drug is outside of the liposome, how do you load it in?" That's a great question, person on twitter! You let the drug diffuse into the liposome down its concentration gradient.

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Now, of course, if you reach an equilibrium then you really haven't done any better than 'regular old' loading. But with remote loading you have a cool trick -- your liposomes aren't empty, they're actually already loaded with a *trapping agent*

15.07.2020 · Tweet

The trapping agent is something that associates with your drug cargo and *traps it* inside the liposome, such that the drug cannot diffuse back out. Your liposome becomes a drug trap! Once the drug checks in, it can't check out (for a while, anyway). https://t.co/BUSXxaWbwy

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Remote loading can drive realllly high encapsulation efficiencies, like 90% -- which means out of all the drug you put into the mix with liposomes, nearly all of the drug ends up inside your little nanobubbles.

15.07.2020 · Tweet

The 'trapping' part can also help reduce the leakiness, so you don't prematurely lose your drug en route to the cancer! One downside of remote loading is that it does not work for all compounds.

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Based on the trapping agents currently used, you need a compound that is a weak acid or a weak base. The compound also needs to be able to diffuse through the lipid bilayer of the liposome!

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Ah also, it is nice if the compound is fairly water soluble, so you can mix a good amount of it with the liposomes. Not *too* water soluble because then it might not make it through the membrane! Given all the rules, it is maybe impressive that any drug qualifies.

15.07.2020 · Tweet

But several do! Including doxorubicin! Doxil was approved by the FDA in 1995, so it has been 25 years! Wow! Sometimes nanotech sounds very futuristic and there is an idea like "ah, the technology isn't here yet, but maybe someday". 25 years!

15.07.2020 · Tweet

A majority of the FDA-approved nanoparticles used for treating cancer are liposomal formulations. Liposomes have been around for a while and a lot of people have become pretty comfortable producing them at a large enough scale to be used clinically.

15.07.2020 · Tweet

That doesn't mean that liposomes are the *best* (or only) option! Personally, as a person who used polymersomes during my PhD, I sometimes feel the urge to list downsides of liposomes (replace all the lipids with polymer in a liposome and you get a polymersome)

15.07.2020 · Tweet

But liposomes have really paved the path to clinical acceptance for a lot of other nanodelivery vehicles that are currently in clinical trials, so I can't get TOO mad at liposomes!

15.07.2020 · Tweet

I want to highlight two FDA-approved formulations that AREN'T liposomes, though! They are: Abraxane and NBTXR3

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Abraxane was approved in 2005, 10 years after Doxil! To me, it is a particularly weird nano-formulation because it is the chemo drug (paclitaxel) attached to a protein (albumin) But hey, it is nano-sized and delivers a drug that helps fight lung , breast, and pancreatic cancer!

15.07.2020 · Tweet

Blah, I said NBTXR3 was FDA-approved a couple of tweets ago -- sorry everyone, it is NOT FDA approved. NBTXR3 has been CE approved in Europe (for marketing/commercialization), which is still a nice big step for them!

15.07.2020 · Tweet

But what is NBTXR3 anyway? It is a Hafnium oxide nanoparticle that you can zap with radiation and it will help kill tumors. Hafnium is an element on the periodic table that completely flew under my radar. There are many cool nanoparticles you can make out of metal oxides though!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

So personally, my work in based on using nanoparticles as little delivery vehicles to help drugs get into tumors. But that is not even close to the only way nanoparticles can be used to fight cancer! NOT EVEN CLOSE PPL

17.07.2020 · Tweet

Nanoparticles are currently being investigated (and some are FDA-approved) for help in *diagnosing and locating* cancer! "Definity" and "SonoVue" are examples of nanoparticles that are FDA or EMA approved for ultrasound enhancement of different cancers.

17.07.2020 · Tweet

But there are a lot of ways that nanoparticles can improve cancer diagnosis and the location of tumors! Nanoparticles could potentially help both within the bodies of patients and outside the body as crucial ingredients in diagnostic tests!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

One way nanoparticles can help is on the detection of biomarkers of cancer. For some types of cancer, we have found certain proteins elevated in the blood of people with that cancer, for example CA-125 for ovarian cancer and CEA for colorectal cancer.

17.07.2020 · Tweet

One fight, by the way, that I am wholly unsuitable for, is whether a particular blood protein biomarker is *actually* a good biomarker for a particular cancer. Some biomarkers are not without controversy -- the validity of biomarkers is an important thing to establish!!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

Anyway, there are several ways to try to tell if a specific peptide or protein you care about is floating around in your blood -- one way is a 'sandwich' assay using antibodies that are specific for that protein. Yum! https://t.co/8UPG0puIGu

17.07.2020 · Tweet

But in all these assays, there is a limit for how little of your protein there can be before you can't "see" it anymore. That limit of detection is something that nanoscience can help improve! There are a lot of ways to do this, tbh.

17.07.2020 · Tweet

One is to use quantum dots, which are nanoparticles that fluoresce when you shine a laser on them. And they fluoresce REALLY WELL. Being very bright has advantages, including really good detection ability at low protein amounts.

17.07.2020 · Tweet

This could potentially mean that really small amounts of your cancer biomarker could be found -- maybe making it possible to diagnose cancers at earlier stages than we currently do!* *Again, VERY dependent on biomarkers being valid and meaningful!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

But nanoparticles can also help in *collecting* those biomarker proteins in the first place! The other day I mentioned stuff about protein adsorption onto nanoparticles when those nanoparticles are floating around in your blood -- proteins love sticking to nanoparticles!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

In that way, nanoparticles can kind of act like little protein "vacuums" while they float around inside you. So the idea is, pop some nanoparticles into your blood, wait a bit for proteins to stick, then take them back out. Shake off those lil proteins and look for biomarkers!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

There are people researching how well this works as we speak! Here's some example papers on it! https://t.co/GXHfHr2Id1 https://t.co/qewrBVCJLk

17.07.2020 · Tweet

It is early days still, but you could imagine a situation where nanoparticles are used to collect cancer biomarkers from your blood AND used to help quantify those biomarkers in a sandwich assay! Double nanoparticles!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

Finding cancer using nanoparticles doesn't just need to be on the biomarker level. Nanoparticles can help image cancer within your body, including pesky metastases that can be hard to see otherwise!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

Nanoparticles can be detected using lasers, ultrasound, MRI, PET scans, and probably a bunch more -- nanoscience folks are very creative!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

So if you have a way to get nanoparticles to associate with cancer cells more than other cells, you can use them to help you locate tumors and metastases! There are several ways you can try to accomplish this, and there is a lot of preclinical work on figuring it out!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

Nanoparticles can also be used to fight cancer on the treatment side without bothering to deliver drugs! Nanoparticles can be used to heat up tumors until they die, enhance x-ray based damage to tumors, or generate damaging reactive oxygen species.

17.07.2020 · Tweet

Nanoparticles (and cells, for that matter) are so small that sometimes we don't think about them as 'real things'. We don't imagine them as having a physical body that physically bumps into cells and physically gets gobbled up. But they do! They're real!

17.07.2020 · Tweet

And what that means is that the *shape* of nanoparticles can change how they interact with their environment, especially within your body! Nanoparticles can be on the bigger side or smaller side, they can be squishy or hard, and they can be spheres or worms or other shapes! https://t.co/71Z1Q5fa48

17.07.2020 · Tweet

(Just look at the shapes in that figure, not all the other stuff about polymer design, blah blah). One of the ideas in that figure, by the way, is even with one type of polymer you can make different shaped and sized nanoparticles. But we aren't limited to just one polymer

17.07.2020 · Tweet

You can make nanostars! (From Liebig et al 2019 RSC Advances, https://t.co/0LDo9AsBTT) https://t.co/49aHsI3v0f

17.07.2020 · Tweet

Nanodiscs, nano deflated ball things (sometimes called stomatocytes), hard nanoballs, soft nanobubbles... https://t.co/oZ9F2ZzJpx

17.07.2020 · Tweet

In varying their shape and size, you change where those nanoparticles can go in your body! For example, your kidneys can directly filter stuff out of your blood, but only if the stuff is below a certain size! (6-8 ish nanometers, but also depends on the electric charge!)

18.07.2020 · Tweet

When you start to get pretty big in the nanoscale (like hundreds of nanometers in diameter), you start to have a hard time diffusing around in tissues. If you inject big nanoparticles under the skin, they'll have a hard time moving very far from where you injected them!

18.07.2020 · Tweet

Above a certain size, your nanoparticles get very attractive to cells in your liver that help clear stuff out from the blood. Sometimes this isn't what you want to have happen, but there are also situations where you WANT to deliver something to the liver!

18.07.2020 · Tweet

Stomatocytes by the way, in case anyone was curious. From Tu et al 2017 Angewandte Chemie ( https://t.co/7wOhXddIVI) https://t.co/lakwmM1N7G

18.07.2020 · Tweet

There is some evidence that 'worm like' nanoparticles circulate in your blood for longer, maybe because they don't slip out through gaps in your blood vessels as easily, or maybe because some cells don't know how to eat them... Karabin et al 2018 Nat Comm https://t.co/y4Rp3e453r https://t.co/MhV65b6ayb

18.07.2020 · Tweet

Look at those little wormy goobers! Some of those filomicelles may be 'nano' in their cross section, but end up being 'micro' in length!

18.07.2020 · Tweet

There is some evidence that suggests that how 'curved' your nanoparticle is influences what kinds of proteins like to stick to it and what sorts of cells like to eat them! Having 'flatter' areas (like a disc vs a sphere) might also provide more surface area for cell interaction

19.07.2020 · Tweet

I apologize for being AWOL today folks! Today, the last day for me, I just wanted to mention how well-suited nanoparticles are for affecting our immune systems (especially the innate)!

19.07.2020 · Tweet

Many nanoparticles are not so different in size and shape from viruses! And innate immune cells love trying to eat viruses and other nano-sized stuff: cells like macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells, and monocytes love eating nanoparticles.

19.07.2020 · Tweet

This is often, by the way, a detrimental thing. The immune system is so good at eating nanoparticles that it often prevents nanoparticles from getting to the cells you ACTUALLY wanted them to get to. ...unless the immune cells ARE the target! https://t.co/h2cN3Oio6c

19.07.2020 · Tweet

There are actually a lot of good reasons why you might want innate immune cells to be your target for nano delivery (or other nano hijinks)

19.07.2020 · Tweet

Maybe you want to deliver anti-inflammatory drugs to help reduce the perpetuation of pathological inflammation and to promote wound healing!

19.07.2020 · Tweet

Maybe you want to deliver antigen and adjuvant to immune cells as a *vaccine*! Several COVID vaccine candidates are delivered in your body by nanoparticles!

19.07.2020 · Tweet

Or on the flip side, maybe you want to deliver antigen and an immunosuppressant to try to build *tolerance*, like for diabetes or food allergies

04.08.2020 · Tweet

Welcome back everyone! Today we will be focusing on #terahertz radiation! What is it? Why is it awesome? How can it change society? So let's get started! #thzdoesitbetter

04.08.2020 · Tweet

So what is #terahertz radiation? Terahertz radiation falls in between #microwave (think microwave ovens) and #infrared radiation (heat) in the electromagnetic spectrum. One terahertz (1 THz) is equal to one million million hertz (1^12 Hz). https://t.co/Z61D2KL9QG

04.08.2020 · Tweet

The THz range encompasses light of frequencies from 100GHz up to 10THz and has wavelengths ranging from 30 microns to 3mm. It's energy range spans 0.4meV to 40meV ( heat energy from approx. -268 degrees Celsius to room temperature!) So what is exciting about this energy range?

04.08.2020 · Tweet

So why is the #terahertz energy range interesting? Well..... the energy of several quasiparticles (phonons, excitons, magnons) fall in this range. If we shine terahertz radiation at a material, we can look at how these quasiparticles behave and also promote collective excitations https://t.co/W2rApYniRo

04.08.2020 · Tweet

We can use terahertz radiation or #terahertz #spectroscopy to look at a material's optoelectronic properties. For example, we can look at its vibrational modes, how different carriers (electrons or electrons) move and scatter within the material and its magentisation dynamics.

04.08.2020 · Tweet

Here is a great video from Hannah Joyce and Chiara Ciccarelli groups @Cambridge_Uni showing how a typical #terahertz #spectroscopy system works! https://t.co/6rG9lHSFnJ It is a powerful tool for non-contact, non-destructive #optoelectronic #material characterisation

04.08.2020 · Tweet

So #terahertz radiation is useful for #material characterisation, but anything else? Of course! It has several uses from non-destructive medical imaging and security to revealing hidden secrets in art and looking at stellar dust in space! Let's look at a few of my favourite! https://t.co/PE6XGFXpiE

04.08.2020 · Tweet

Starting with THz body scanners! Unlike #xray radiation, #THz is non-ionizing and harmless to humans. The key signatures of several chemical molecules also fall within the THz range, making it ideal for security screening. Here's an example of a body image from @Terasense_Inc https://t.co/vILflhgAeg

04.08.2020 · Tweet

Not only can it identify hidden explosives, #THz imaging can also look at hidden layers in famous artwork. You can see lots of examples from Enrique Castro Camus' group at @CIOMexico https://t.co/VW6DNT50SG https://t.co/OcWUTkDl5b

04.08.2020 · Tweet

Another cool application is in the #Automotive automotive industry. One of the key challenges is non-destructive evaluation of coating thickness on new shiny cars. @TeraView have recently demonstrated a THz sensor (TeraCota) with comparable performance to current approaches! https://t.co/Q6RwmPBkZ1

04.08.2020 · Tweet

There is more! #THz also has applications in the #pharmaceutical industry. It can measure the porosity of tablets to improve quality inspection of new drugs. Check out the new tool from @THzCambridge and @TeraView for this inspection here: https://t.co/19Cke3Y43h

04.08.2020 · Tweet

THz can also be used for in-vivo skin imaging. This image is from work by Emma MacPherson group @WarwickTHz (https://t.co/NrIzobws7x) . There is lots of ongoing research looking at #THz imaging to identify depth of skin burns, onset of diabetes foot and skin cancer. https://t.co/YhzrsfhZ8d

04.08.2020 · Tweet

Finally, THz could provide ultrafast #wireless communication and carry up to 100 times more data! THz behaves differently though to #microwaves - so many groups are working on new components to make this possible. Check out recent from @opticsman et al: https://t.co/L4EQcf4rt7

04.08.2020 · Tweet

P.S. This is just a few limited examples, there are so many awesome #researchers out there working in the field of #terahertz #science and #technology! If you are one of those lovely people, please shout out about your work and any of your examples to this thread. :D

05.08.2020 · Tweet

[admin] "Non-destructive Electrical Characterization of Nanomaterials" ft. @DrJessBoland of @OfficialUoM on #70 Under the Microscope is out now This is an extended conversation with this week's curator- Jessica. https://t.co/mVgANDJ2fp

05.08.2020 · Tweet

So yesterday, we were looking at #terahertz radiation and I hope I've convinced you that THz is cool and will make a difference in your lives. Today, I want to look at another aspect of my #research -#nanomaterials! So stay tuned to find out about #semiconductor nanowires

05.08.2020 · Tweet

So why do we need #nanomaterials? You've heard about them in the news, but are they really revolutionary? Let's first think about how technology has changed during our lifetimes - the technology powering our devices has got smaller, faster and smarter, but is reaching a limit.. https://t.co/3gPjG0B8tL

05.08.2020 · Tweet

This change is known as #MooresLaw, which predicts the number of #transistors on a chip doubles roughly every 2 years. At present, we have computing power equal to a mouse brain and are close to a human brain, but this trend is slowing down! Current Si transistors are only 7nm! https://t.co/HWNWjXluSD

05.08.2020 · Tweet

We are already at the #nanometre length scale. At this length scale, #quantum effects start to come into play and we need to investigate #nanomaterials to work out how we can harness them @IBM have recently demonstrated 5nm #transistors using nanosheets https://t.co/KxvQk4mhW7

05.08.2020 · Tweet

There is a lot of research into use of #nanomaterials for #device applications and there are already some examples. Below you can see some examples with a #solar cell, a #laser, and #transistor all made out of #nanowires and #nanoparticles for drug delivery! https://t.co/w1UnB2Dy1j

05.08.2020 · Tweet

There are several advantages that #nanomaterials can offer. For the past few years, I've been looking at #semiconductor #nanowires as building blocks for devices. Nanowires have diameters on the order of 100nm and lengths of up to a few microns. https://t.co/sAM5OxPSil

05.08.2020 · Tweet

There are several groups working on nanowire growth and their application in devices. I've had the pleasure of working with @i_morral group @EPFL_en, who can answer any tricky questions! But one of the main advantages of nanowires is the chance to build heterostructures https://t.co/8dSpwU6RDA

05.08.2020 · Tweet

We can theoretically take any two materials (even if they are lattice mismatched) and grow an axial or radial heterostructure. Axial heterostructures can build p-n junctions for transistors and solar cells, whereas radial heterostructures are crucial for building nanowire lasers

05.08.2020 · Tweet

We can effectively build this structures from the atom up! We can add dopants to build customised heterostructures for specific device applications, allowing us to design their optoelectronic properties from the start. https://t.co/s8eo4X6Xf1

05.08.2020 · Tweet

But the best advantage of #nanowires, is that they have comparable optoelectronic performance to bulk materials! They maintain high electron mobilities (high device speeds) while reducing material composition. So expect to see nanowires in your devices soon!

06.08.2020 · Tweet

So yesterday, we looked at the use of #nanomaterials as building blocks for nanodevices. But are there any other exciting materials that could influence society? I'm currently interested in some new exotic materials called topological insulators. #research #STEM https://t.co/FJqb7OJ9Vt

06.08.2020 · Tweet

These materials are really weird! They are insulating in the bulk but highly conductive at the surface. So the middle of the material can't support any electrical currents but the surface hosts fast electrical currents (~100 times faster than silicon) - great for #electronics https://t.co/OCphBij1PT

06.08.2020 · Tweet

These surface currents are spin polarised. There are two channels - one for electrons with spin up and one for electrons with spin down. This allows us to carry twice as much information - we can use both the charge of an electron and its spin to give us an on/off signal.

06.08.2020 · Tweet

But the coolest thing about these materials, is that they are topologically protected! Surface electrons cannot be backscattered from defects or impurities (they just carry on through). They travel as if on a tramline or ice rink - in one direction with less heat and resistance. https://t.co/0crpOTjdY9

06.08.2020 · Tweet

Topological materials are great candidates for #electronic #spintronic and #photonic devices and could provide a step change in performance and energy efficiency! Recent research has also shown that they could push devices into the #terahertz range! https://t.co/9ZchOktUMv

07.08.2020 · Tweet

Good morning everyone! I hope you enjoyed seeing a small snapshot of my #research. Today is my last day of tweeting for @RealSci_Nano and I would like to share my experiences as a #deaf/hard of hearing #researcher and discuss topic close to my heart...…#accessibility in #STEM https://t.co/Y685zb3Yjy

07.08.2020 · Tweet

I've been hard of hearing since birth and rely on #lipreading for everyday communication. I got #hearingaids when I was around 14 and have had a love/hate relationship with them ever since. I recently started learning #BritishSignLanguage again and am using it more and more

07.08.2020 · Tweet

Lot's of people have asked what it's like being #disabled in #STEM and it is always an interesting question for me.. First, I don't feel or identify as #disabled - it is a term I use to access support and reasonable adjustments, but I am #scientist, #engineer and Jessie foremost!

07.08.2020 · Tweet

My #disability is a hidden disability, so some of my colleagues out there may not even be aware that I am #deaf (surprise!). Up until studying for my PhD, I tried to hide my deafness and fit into a #hearing world. Now, I much more proud and open about it.

07.08.2020 · Tweet

Looking back, I was afraid to talk about my deafness and ask for support because I didn't want to be 'different' or a 'hassle'. I felt like a problem. I didn't want to miss out on opportunities because of #unconsciousbias or the fact that I needed subtitles, microphones, etc.

07.08.2020 · Tweet

The lack of these adjustments made events (such as conferences) inaccessible for me. If we everyone to participate in #STEM equally, we need to remove these barriers and make STEM #accessible. And we need to start by asking is STEM #equal #diverse and #inclusive and #accessible? https://t.co/BxQwqIwbRt

07.08.2020 · Tweet

#accessibility benefits everyone not just #disabled #researchers. For example, small changes, such as using microphones at conferences, will make a huge difference to researchers who are hard of hearing, but will also make life easier for everyone!

07.08.2020 · Tweet

So I would like to start a discussion around #accessibility . Please feel free to ask any questions you may have about my experience and barriers facing #disabled #researchers.

07.08.2020 · Tweet

@jemimatabeart Hi Jemima. Thanks for the question! Moving to online webinars has been one of the most difficult parts of lockdown for me. I've found that a lot of conferencing tools don't have good subtitles so have had to rely on remote captioning and occasional #BSL interpretation.

07.08.2020 · Tweet

@jemimatabeart Zoom is the most popular tool at work but doesn't have automatic captioning. Microsoft teams does but only if you have a subscription, so it's been a lot of extra work organising my support. However, one positive is that there is more research and push for AI for captioning

07.08.2020 · Tweet

@jemimatabeart I've started using https://t.co/9hOEeS92Ru from @aimediaUK, which has been a useful backup for when there isn't subtitling or no palantypists have been available. It is free and helps, but doesn't cope well with #STEM vocab. One of the simplest things that helps is turn-taking:

07.08.2020 · Tweet

@jemimatabeart @aimediaUK Keeping the pace slow in meetings, leaving your video on for #lipreading and turntaking really help with video conferencing. There are some tips in this blog I co-wrote with @BMatB @EstOdek Odek @webmz_ @jesswade : https://t.co/uPLBSaU8XX

07.08.2020 · Tweet

@luke_phys Hey Luke! Hope you're doing well. Great question! For digital events, there are guidelines from @w3c to make content accessible. https://t.co/QtYbYkmx6N @DisabilitySmart have also realised an inclusive toolkit for communication and have great resources https://t.co/j7ncJ1VX2b

07.08.2020 · Tweet

@luke_phys @w3c @DisabilitySmart @nadsn_uk have loads of resources on their website: https://t.co/B2DteTClPl and the FDA also have some nice guidelines https://t.co/01bejGhmXU https://t.co/DMh3yKfbhs

07.08.2020 · Tweet

Want to know more about the barriers facing #disabled researchers and what can be done to address them? Check out this interview with @katesang @DisabilityIncl1 https://t.co/U9PtuVwtKG

07.08.2020 · Tweet

There is also a great article from @ncjbrown on #Ableism in #academia - it presents #research in this area to 'provide food for thought, stimulate a debate and #raiseawareness'. Please check it out! https://t.co/MVV7VPrP7S

07.08.2020 · Tweet

@jemimatabeart I know! I use the auto-transcription a lot for recording lectures so its heartbreaking it doesn't work live :( Fingers crossed Zoom will add this soon!

07.08.2020 · Tweet

So how can you be an #ally to #disabled researchers? First, when considering #accessibility in your events and institutions, engage us! We have a whole wealth of knowledge from lived experience to contribute. Ask us what we need and how you can support. #nothingaboutuswithoutus

07.08.2020 · Tweet

Put #accessibility first at the very start of any design process or discussion. This ensures #inclusivity and #accessibility is embedded at all stages (It also saves time and cost later on!) Consulting with your local #disabled staff network is a great way to do this. @nadsn_uk

07.08.2020 · Tweet

There are also little changes that all of us can make. For example, why not make sure you use and ask others to use a microphone at conferences? If you are making a new lecture course, could you make sure all your resources use sans serif font with minimum font size 12?

07.08.2020 · Tweet

#accessibility is about #raisingawareness and making small changes that will make a huge difference to others in #STEM, so I would like to ask all of you today to identify one small change you can make and to think about #accessibility in your #research #allypledge

Starting off with colours and magic: Did you know most blue colours you see in nature are not due to a pigment but to structural colours? This means the colour in 🦋 is due to light interacting with very small features on the wings which are about the wavelength of light. https://t.co/cgcALBojnZ

17.08.2020 · Tweet

The same happens in sea shells for example. The awesome iridescence you see on them is due to the very small hexagonal platelets of Calcium Carbonate which are in the range of 400-600nm thick, again, the wavelength of light! On Nature, you awesome thing! https://t.co/YTWm2H1hcz

17.08.2020 · Tweet

Can us scientists make this happen in the lab? Yes, if we use a technique called "micropatterning", where essentially we can take a surface and transform it to create small features that would reflect light like a prism does. we do this for example in Diffraction Grating Film.👇 https://t.co/VTYuyXBMaj

17.08.2020 · Tweet

@nadiahhusseini ask away questions on my profile or on my tweet if you want. I'd be happy to explain in more detail :)

17.08.2020 · Tweet

@nadiahhusseini Great question! There are many different techniques and they mostly depend on the type of material you are working on. Diffraction films are often obtained by photolitography, which works by exposing a substrate to light through a "mask" that determines the pattern on the surface

17.08.2020 · Tweet

@nadiahhusseini Then once this "mask" has been imprinted on the surface, you have chemical treatments that allow the erosion of only those selected areas on the film. You can also use photosensitive gels (but they don't create micropatterns,they use the change in refractive index within the gel)

17.08.2020 · Tweet

@nadiahhusseini Together with those techniques, you can create synthetic opals for example by depositing microsphere of polystyrene on a substrate. this has the same effect. Look at this video for example. The results are incredible (second link). https://t.co/pgR5zZhuE5 https://t.co/MwWWFpUuek

17.08.2020 · Tweet

@MinoritySTEM @NatalieGCheung Relatability - talk about subjects students have some knowledge of (e.g. smartphones, who doesn't have one?) Language - Keep the jargon to a minimum and explain everything you say. Context - Provide a story/background, something to keep them wanting to know "how it ends" ...1/2

18.08.2020 · Tweet

@MinoritySTEM @NatalieGCheung Excitement - Show enthusiasm for the subject, whatever it is! Discovery - Now introduce new ideas they might not have heard of, but in a fascinating new light! Future - Provide context for what could be done next/where this discovery could lead to.

18.08.2020 · Tweet

@MinoritySTEM @NatalieGCheung There is also the issue of age, different audiences will need different methods of communication. 14-18 YO respond better to challenges 9-14 to group work and exploring things in detail 4-9 to "amazing" fun new subjects!

So, we know now how liquid crystals work, what happens in LCD Displays? White light passes through a polariser, gets "twisted" by a layer of liquid crystals and is then filtered through a second polariser. If we apply a voltage to the LC, there is no twisting, so we see black. https://t.co/8yVxUK6Juh

18.08.2020 · Tweet

This happens because the voltage "breaks" the order of the molecules in LCs. What is a polariser? A thin patterned film that functions as a light filter. Only light with a particular "direction" (ie polarisation) will pass. So, 2 ⊥ polarisers will not let any light through.👇GIF https://t.co/g40wlS3Z9x

18.08.2020 · Tweet

And the coolest thing happened today as I was trying to make GIFs for you on linear polarisers, look what happens if I place a linear polarising filter in front of a Thermochromic Liquid Crystal sheet 😍🌈 https://t.co/jZINlDzbCq

Today is World Self-Healing Day. Joking, just made it up, but we are talking about self-healing materials today. So here is me 10 years ago, synthesising my first self-healing polymer: Silly Putty! (I know, I made a portrait video, I'm sorry 🥺) I was so proud of myself! https://t.co/FZAvguVtZ0

20.08.2020 · Tweet

Silly putty is probably one of the first examples of man-made self-healing materials. As usual, Nature does it first, take skin, bones🦴...But did you know also inanimate objects could repair on their own? It's only a handful of them tbf, and it is due to their chemical structure https://t.co/47uo9QHqnm

20.08.2020 · Tweet

The Self-Healing skills of this material are due to Dynamic or reversible bonds. In the case of Silly putty there are hydrogen bonds (same ones you have in water, quite weak) and some Si–O : B bonds. These links can be broken fairly easily however they also reform very easily!

20.08.2020 · Tweet

Now you might think: well, silly putty is quite weak though, how can you possibly use it in anything? Here is were composites open up an incredible world of possibilities! You could have a self-healing mortar within a brick structure: once the crack closes, the material heals. https://t.co/GRUmOHNj7v

The amazing world of Shape Memory doesn't end at Nickel Titanium Alloys "remembering" their original shape when heated up in hot water. Some Brass Alloys have a 2-way memory! Now things get interesting: If we combine a shape-memory polymer with a superlight 🪶 graphene foam, what we get is an amazing composite that can change shape just having a small voltage applied to it, and still be strong enough to lift a load 100X its own weight!💪 https://t.co/QmKZBiICAE

25.08.2020 · Tweet

Today I will talk a bit about Brownian Motion (BM), as it is key to understanding how my nanoclusters are observed. BM is the random movement of particles in a fluid (liquid or gas) medium. #brownianmotion

25.08.2020 · Tweet

The fluid medium is made of many small molecules that collide with particles being observed. Collisions cause the particle to move in various directions, hence the randomness in the particles’ movements.

25.08.2020 · Tweet

Think of it this way: notice how dust particles move in a ray of light. They are all over the place! They are moving within a fluid medium (air). The dust particles (bigger, observable) collide with the molecules of the air (smaller, undetected) & as such appear to move randomly. https://t.co/BBbAqWZV0N

25.08.2020 · Tweet

It was named after Scottish Botanist Robert Brown, who first studied such fluctuations (1827). He observed, under a microscope, that parts of pollen were jittering on the surface of water. At first he thought it meant the pollen was alive. https://t.co/u5gZo1CtkG

25.08.2020 · Tweet

But that was not the case. Brown, like the proper scientist he was, decided to test his hypothesis. He tried the same thing with sand, which is obviously not alive. The sand produced the same movement! What was going on? His work was forgotten for a while... https://t.co/HxY3p4jADF

25.08.2020 · Tweet

In 1905 some young lad was doing his PhD in diffusion of colloidal suspensions in liquids. He combining Newtonian mechanics to thermodynamics. He observed random forces and speculated they might be Brownian Motion, which was later proved to be correct. He was Albert Einstein. https://t.co/H1sjd83jIa

25.08.2020 · Tweet

So why all this talk about BM and Diffusion? Because of their size, my nano bits and pieces cannot be observed using optical microscopes. Lasers are used, but not to observe the nanoclusters directly. They are used to detect the Brownian Motion of the clusters! #lasers, #nano https://t.co/BEFaGBnH6F

25.08.2020 · Tweet

Of course, there are other methods to "see" nano-sized objects, and I will refer to some throughout the week. Tomorrow, though, I will talk a bit about my current main project, my uncanny nanoclusters! See you then! https://t.co/YJhBP95kx4

26.08.2020 · Tweet

[admin] "Nanobits in Water" Extended conversation with the amazing @zimbitas on #76 Under the Microscope podcast is here https://t.co/kaFW8VDdAz

26.08.2020 · Tweet

So for today, a bit about the research. Recent studies have seen small molecules associate to form sub-micron clusters in some solutions. They often occur in solutions of highly soluble small molecules, e.g. concentrated protein solutions and aqueous glycine solutions. https://t.co/thW8fzCbB5

26.08.2020 · Tweet

These clusters are not your ordinary clusters; they present liquid-like properties and can be fairly “large”. They are unusual, as they appear as discrete domains in the solution that contain higher solute density than the rest of the solution....

26.08.2020 · Tweet

Here is the interesting bit: these domains are dispersed throughout the bulk of the solution, but are not considered a separate phase! #nano #clusters #assembly #homogeneous https://t.co/c6JcJYDW0O

26.08.2020 · Tweet

So my nanoclusters are there, but the solution is homogeneous! I mentioned before that crystallisation has featured heavily throughout my research. The crystallisation process is extremely important to understand, as it is widely used in many industries...

26.08.2020 · Tweet

When phase separating a solute from a supersaturated solution to form a crystalline phase, 2 main steps are involved: 1) nucleation (formation of a stable crystal nucleus), & 2) crystal growth (material added to existing crystal lattice). https://t.co/VqNOeD2Oqr

26.08.2020 · Tweet

Many significant efforts have been made in the last 30 years to better understand the process. So why are these nanoclusters important? Their existence has rendered interest due their possibility of being metastable intermediates for crystallisation! https://t.co/puCjZstyRD

26.08.2020 · Tweet

Experimental and theoretical computational results have led to alternate two-step processes of crystallization being proposed. One proposal suggests disordered metastable molecular assemblies are produced before nucleation of more ordered nascent crystals. https://t.co/qBARB5v0h7

26.08.2020 · Tweet

Another alternative proposal sees nanoparticles form a crystal-like lattice that ultimately transforms into a molecular crystal. Recent studies focus on identifying if there is indeed a direct link between the presence of the solute molecular clusters and a crystal formation. https://t.co/mTbgfZRv4b

26.08.2020 · Tweet

Whatever the case, the presence of these nanoclusters needs investigation!!! For example, the kinetics and thermodynamics of the formation of these liquid-like species is yet to be understood. #crystallisation #molecular #nano #kinetics #thermodynamics https://t.co/INIl9wQ8ik

26.08.2020 · Tweet

My work involves looking at various aspects of such liquid-like clusters for nanoparticle production. Collaboration with the Uni of Edinburgh (Dr. M Sweatman, Dr. C.A. Ferreiro-Rangel) using experimental and computational data aims to answer questions regarding their stability.

26.08.2020 · Tweet

Collaboration with the Uni of Sheffield sees us investigating how the presence of these clusters can influence nanoparticle formation, mainly silica (with Prof. S. Patwardhan @GreenNanoRes, and @amber_keegan) and magnetite (with Dr S. Staniland & L. Norflok).

26.08.2020 · Tweet

All of this is part of the @SynBIM project which works on creating transformative knowledge and toolsets for larger-scale "green" manufacture of tunable and sustainable, synbio nanomaterials. Check it out! https://t.co/pRN20TErkb #sustainability #nanomaterials https://t.co/4QTNCOwaTA

27.08.2020 · Tweet

Today I will talk about one of the main techniques I use to detect the presence of my nanoclusters: Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS).

27.08.2020 · Tweet

A laser light hits the sample, whereby the light is scattered by my liquid-like clusters. A detector placed at a known angle to the incident beam picks up part of the scattered light. #laserscatter #nano https://t.co/Plt1HbZRpl

27.08.2020 · Tweet

What the detector is picking up is referred to as the “speckle pattern”. This pattern fluctuates with time due to the Brownian Motion of the particles in the solution. This fluctuation is recorded by the detector, ultimately giving us the intensity (count rate) plot. https://t.co/88MSOQz3yF

27.08.2020 · Tweet

@RoyDhimanSci Hello Dhiman, regarding the shape, an upcoming tweet will respond to that (short answer, it doesn't tell us much about shape!).

27.08.2020 · Tweet

@RoyDhimanSci As for dimension, I will not go in depth in the tweets but yes, a lot can be determined by measuring the nanoparticles at different scatter angles (changing the detector angle). The particles' dimensions are proportionate to how quickly they diffuse (move in the sample).

27.08.2020 · Tweet

@RoyDhimanSci Finally, there is no excitation wavelength measured; only the scattered laser light is detected! In fact, any excitation wavelength detected near the DLS can actually interfere with the results! Thank you for your questions Dhiman!

27.08.2020 · Tweet

The time-dependent part of the speckle pattern fluctuation (intensity decaying over time) gives us the autocorrelation function. The intensity decay correlates to how fast the nanocluster is moving, i.e. diffusing in the solution. #diffusion #lightscatter https://t.co/flsOUEvKqe

27.08.2020 · Tweet

Using this Stokes-Einstein equation for diffusion, and having some known parameters, the hydrodynamic radius of the detected species can be determined. https://t.co/2pbL3LHVer

27.08.2020 · Tweet

But what happens if there are more than one scattering species with different sizes present in the solution? Well, things get a bit more complicated. For example, when 2 species of very different sizes are present, the autocorrelation function has two distinct decays. https://t.co/2UXiouLhw7

27.08.2020 · Tweet

Generally, the DLS comes with special software that can give the user lots of info regarding the hydrodynamic radii of the species detected, as well as an indication of the degree of polydispersity of sizes scattering the light.

27.08.2020 · Tweet

My systems are simple and as such I was able to write my own little Matlab script used to analyse the raw data away from the DLS computer. In light of the last few month, that script came in very handy! https://t.co/HLR7GF1eCw

27.08.2020 · Tweet

I mentioned before that the DLS measures hydrodynamic radius. The hydrodynamic size (radius or diameter) is that of an equivalent hard sphere diffusing at the same rate as the species under observation. It does not tell us a lot about the shape, because it assumes it is spherical https://t.co/GYtiHDA5aM

27.08.2020 · Tweet

@EmmRankinWilson Trade secrets - they don't want us to know! 😅

27.08.2020 · Tweet

DLS is quick – a scan can be done anywhere between 5s up to a few minutes! Multiple scans are necessary for accuracy. Most often, it’s also non-intrusive. You can measure the same sample again on a later date, or you can measure it to check for changes occurring over time.

27.08.2020 · Tweet

I use my 2 trusty DLS machines for more than detecting my snazzy nanoclusters.

27.08.2020 · Tweet

For example, I recently used DLS to verify the presence of nanoassemblies of peptoids, which was part of the brilliant work in mediating activity and nano-assembly of antimicrobial peptoids led by Dr H.K. Aaron Lau (@LauResearch) here at Strathclyde. https://t.co/9ST2AnAIFc

27.08.2020 · Tweet

Dr @ManlioTassieri of the Uni of Glasgow first combined novel theoretical models & DLS to determine the persistence length (Lp) of semiflexible polymers within solutions. We recently teamed up to get even more data for a more detailed model.

27.08.2020 · Tweet

I even created a user-friendly Matlab script (based on his Labview script) that uses DLS data to give various properties of the polymers, including Lp. Hopefully this publication will also be out in 2020! https://t.co/OTks23Q1Xw

27.08.2020 · Tweet

Tomorrow I will be back to talk about another laser scattering technique I have used, Brownian Microscopy. See you then!

28.08.2020 · Tweet

Today I am going to talk a bit about Brownian Microscopy. It shares many similarities with the DLS technique such as the fact that it too uses laser light to detect entities in the nanoscale. The sample here is placed in the sample holder, and the laser light passes through it. https://t.co/CCDkWp7kyk

28.08.2020 · Tweet

The light that is scattered from the nanoentities present in the sample can actually be visualised by a 20x magnification microscope that is mounted onto a camera, an example of which is seen below #nano #microscopy https://t.co/x1HlX9Vrky

28.08.2020 · Tweet

The above shows a sample of Ludox in water. Each of the light points seen are due to a Ludox particle present in the water medium. Powerful software is used to track the movement of each light point. I am using NTA (nanoparticle tracking analysis) software. https://t.co/9X2m26XQfu

28.08.2020 · Tweet

The NTA software follows the centre of the light point and determines the mean-square displacement, in the x and y axis, as a function of time. From there, it estimates the diffusion coefficient and, as we saw before with the DLS, the hydrodynamic size of the particles is found. https://t.co/N2om21uQud

28.08.2020 · Tweet

Using NTA software allows for the determination of a size distribution profile of small particles. NTA is used for particles with a diameter of app. 10-1000 nm, whereas DLS can be used for particles as small as 1nm diameter up to even larger than a micron (in some cases). https://t.co/LF01w2kPfB

28.08.2020 · Tweet

So both DLS and Brownian Microscopy rely on scattered light & Brownian Motion, but there are also differences between the two techniques.... https://t.co/6IJ2Am0gsH

28.08.2020 · Tweet

A major difference is that DLS does not visualise each particle separately, but rather relies on a digital correlator to analyse the time dependent scattering intensity fluctuations. This difference is important when determining the size. #nano #nanotechnology https://t.co/YeDVAu1vhF

28.08.2020 · Tweet

DLS: size is based on the intensity of fluctuations of the scattered light. NTA: size is dependent on the number of scattered light points. Both give hydrodynamic sizes, but one is intensity weighted and the other number weighted!

28.08.2020 · Tweet

That is why the same sample measured with the two techniques can give similar trends, but different size results! https://t.co/F3llvwRIS5

28.08.2020 · Tweet

In general, using NTA software is preferred when you are interested in determining the concentration of nanoparticles in the sample, when you have polydisperse samples and you want better resolution of size peaks, or when you have extremely dilute solutions.

28.08.2020 · Tweet

That’s it for today! Join me tomorrow when I talk about other techniques used to help with detection of my nanoclusters, such as SAXS and NMR. See you then!

29.08.2020 · Tweet

There are many more techniques for measuring nano-sized bits and pieces. Today I’ll be mentioning two of them, without going into too much detail - they were used as additional techniques in my research regarding my lovely nanoclusters!

29.08.2020 · Tweet

First up, NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) It is another spectroscopic technique that can be utilised to help get data on nano-sized entities, mainly of organic molecules. It is often used in advanced medical imaging techniques, such as in MRI (magnetic resonance imaging). https://t.co/08AbJahGgG

29.08.2020 · Tweet

(Very!) simply put, NMR utilises a magnetic field to see at what energy ranges (in radio waves) specific nuclei of interest (e.g. protons, 1H) flip from being aligned to the field (low energy) from no longer being aligned (high energy), giving us info on the species examined. https://t.co/vAOPDJaVY8

29.08.2020 · Tweet

For my nanoclusters, NMR whiz Dr John Parkinson (Strathclyde) used what is known as proton NMR Diffusion-ordered spectroscopy (1H-NMR DOSY). This type of NMR is used to obtain diffusion coefficient values. And what happens once we have the diffusion coefficient?

29.08.2020 · Tweet

Yep, you guessed it – we can use the Stokes-Einstein equation to determine the hydrodynamic radius! #NMR #Diffusion https://t.co/ch1u7VwFwV

29.08.2020 · Tweet

Small angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS) uses a monochromatic X-ray beam in a somewhat similar manner as DLS uses a laser....

29.08.2020 · Tweet

The X-ray beam hits the sample whereby some of the X-rays are scattered by the species present in the sample. The scattered X-rays are picked up by a detector, with the scattering pattern providing info on said species. #SAXS #nano https://t.co/UA1DJErVAp

29.08.2020 · Tweet

The measurements provide us with angle dependent scattered intensities I(Q), with the angular dependence being presented in terms of the scattering vector Q, as seen in the previous plots.

29.08.2020 · Tweet

By recording the scattering of X-rays at various angles, SAXS allows for the acquisition of information about the size of species within a sample. From the slope of what is known as a Guinier fit (log[I(Q)] vs Q) we can obtain the radius of gyration (Rg) of the species present. https://t.co/c1BiWpnJv3

29.08.2020 · Tweet

An (over)simplified definition for Rg is that it is the mass weighted average distance from the core of the species examined to each mass element in that species - it's not the same as the hydrodynamic radius (Rh)! Rg and Rh often have different values! https://t.co/UPM3EgmxeV

29.08.2020 · Tweet

SAXS gives info not only about size, but also about the structure of species! The Form Factor (FF) of the sample is the scattering that occurs due to the shape of species present. By fitting the data with appropriate theoretical FF we can get an estimate of the shape! https://t.co/344X8d9mYN

29.08.2020 · Tweet

That’s it for today! Tomorrow will be a small recap of the week – see you then!

We live in an age of unprecedented stress, yet few of us would consider taking time out to promote good mental health. We’re lead to believe that only hard work is productive. But I always say work smart not hard!

12.09.2020 · Tweet

We stay so busy that we don’t have much time to think deeply (or broadly) about our work. While it might sound counterintuitive, taking breaks is an essential component of optimal thinking.

I am a final year PhD candidate in chemical engineering at UCL. I work on nature-inspired solutions to engineering problems, more specifically the "dirtying" (aka) of membrane filters in water purification

15.09.2020 · Tweet

The natural(no pun intended) thing to explain first is what fouling is & why you should care. Fouling is essentially the accumulation of unwanted material on a surface (i.e. Plaque build-up on your teeth is a type of fouling & we all know how important it is to brush your teeth!) https://t.co/k2f8Hhu4Vt

15.09.2020 · Tweet

Fouling is a huge problem in many industries ranging from medical implants to ships. Marine growth on ship hulls costs the US Navy $180-260M per year alone (Schultz, 2011). Fouling can be caused by organic(proteins, oils, bacteria etc) and inorganic substances. https://t.co/dYSfWBLojP

15.09.2020 · Tweet

So my research aim is to make new materials with improved anti-fouling performance by fine-tuning their nanoscale properties

15.09.2020 · Tweet

Welcome to my membrane 101 class: Membranes are essentially a semipermeable barrier used to separate things. They use different driving forces to achieve separation i.e. pressure, temperature etc. I work on pressure-driven membranes for use in water treatment https://t.co/shSRUO4qpm

15.09.2020 · Tweet

Polymers are usually the material of choice for membranes. They can be formed in a number of ways including phase inversion, electrospinning and track etchting. The membrane here was formed using phase inversion https://t.co/pjoKY3cKUS
