Shark skin is the very clear winner here! Stay tuned for this thread 😊 https://t.co/VYm52Q1GMY

17.09.2020 · Tweet

There are two mechanisms for filtration depending on pore size. For larger pore size membranes (micro and ultrafiltration) rejection is size selective. Unlike cats, if it doesn't fit it doesn't sit https://t.co/us8tX9dEKw

17.09.2020 · Tweet

Nanofiltration and reverse osmosis membranes reject based on the solution diffusion model. This just means that the solutes dissolve into the membrane and diffuse down a concentration gradient

17.09.2020 · Tweet

As I mentioned earlier in the week, my research is inspired by nature, more specifically by the kidney. Why the kidney? Because it's capable of producing 180L of primary urine everyday whilst still remaining intact and fouling free. Warning: there's a lot of bio in this thread!

17.09.2020 · Tweet

A quick refresher on kidney filtration: Filtration is carried out by nephrons, each kidney has roughly 1million of these units. Within the nephron there are two stages of filtration 1) Glomerular filtration 2) Tubular reabsorption (Labelled below, img: Wellcome trust) https://t.co/jytZs8Blvx

17.09.2020 · Tweet

The first stage removes urea, ions (salts etc) and water from the blood stream to produce primary urine. The second stage selectively reabsorbs water and other small molecules that you need back into your blood stream

17.09.2020 · Tweet

My work is inspired by the 1st stage which is a bundle of specialised blood vessels. The wall is made up of multiple layers (see left). The really cool thing about this structure is that albumin (protein ~4nm) can be rejected by the 1st layer even though the gaps are 100nm https://t.co/jxTCzCPkDP

17.09.2020 · Tweet

Why is this so cool? With a pore size of 100nm separation should be based on size (see quoted tweet). This layer shouldn't be able to reject such a small protein but somehow it does? Amazing! https://t.co/DnGY6vTfcv https://t.co/Vwz0rxWlHJ

17.09.2020 · Tweet

While there is no agreed filtration mechanism, my work looks mostly at how this system avoids the accumulation of plasma proteins and how I can adapt this for the application of water filtration. The most striking part is the hairy structure on top (see right) https://t.co/EsrtS00qc6

17.09.2020 · Tweet

This structure is known as the endothelial surface layer. This layer is negatively charged and hydrophilic. This means that it can repel the plasma proteins (usually also negatively charged) and prevent adsorption by binding water within its structure.

17.09.2020 · Tweet

The way that I've been applying this inspiration is by grafting polymer brushes which I'll delve into in another thread https://t.co/oZ6GUr57fO

Leading on from my nature inspiration in this previous thread, most of my current work revolves around the synthesis of polymer brushes. Polymer brushes are very aptly named, they're basically polymer chains that are tethered to a surface by one end like this 👇🏾 https://t.co/iXttYtYiPD

18.09.2020 · Tweet

The two most popular methods of attaching these chains to a surface are: 1) Grafting to: premade polymer chains which bind to an anchoring site 2) Grating from: polymerisation of the chain from an initiating species on the surface https://t.co/gkFLkutvTT

18.09.2020 · Tweet

Grafting from a surface is the most commonly used method. Different surface initiated controlled radical polymerisation (SI-CRP) techniques are used to graft these polymer brushes to create different (and all beautiful) polymer architectures https://t.co/YdW6jxsZIz

18.09.2020 · Tweet

In a later thread I'll get into the different applications that polymer brushes are used in! Hopefully I'm starting to win you over about how cool polymer brushes are?

18.09.2020 · Tweet

Polymer brushes have a very versatile portfolio. Flexibility over which polymer you graft can give you control over a material to make it: stimuli responsive (pH, temperature etc), compatible with different solvents, or further functionalised with desired compounds. https://t.co/h62W4Z4Xw7

18.09.2020 · Tweet

Catalysis: Polymer brushes can be used as a way to immobilise catalysts. One example is the grafting of PHEMA-PEG brushes on the interior of microreactor channels to immobilise gold and palladium nanoparticles. Paper doi: 10.1002/chem.201000948 https://t.co/tM59cm6POJ

18.09.2020 · Tweet

Energy storage: Polymer brushes can provide an elegant solution to incompatibilities between ceramic and polymer matrixes in energy storage devices (e.g. batteries, capacitors). When used as a bridge between components, the energy density can increase. https://t.co/moeFOvTuKU

18.09.2020 · Tweet

Fuel cells: Polymer brushes can provide a platform to improve humidifying additives in proton conducting membranes. Silica nanoparticles modified with a polymer brush integrated into Nafion increased proton conductivity by 4x https://t.co/EoZbvPZPdK

18.09.2020 · Tweet

Biosensors: Polymer brushes can be end functionalised with groups to aid specific adsorption of the biomolecule in question while preventing non-specific adsorption by others (aka fouling 😉) https://t.co/DMs6tDeIXS

18.09.2020 · Tweet

These are just a few applications of polymer brushes. I'll post another thread on polymer brushes as anti-fouling strategies soon! So, polymer brushes, cool or not?

So I'd like to talk about the most common anti-fouling techniques 1) Fouling resistance 2) Fouling release 3) Biofouling control The first two are passive methods to reduce the interactions between the surface and foulants whereas the third is an active method to prevent biofilms https://t.co/UoqPeUN2sG

19.09.2020 · Tweet

1) Fouling resistance This scheme is the most common anti-fouling technique which aims to prevent attachment through the hydrophilic nature of the surface. The bound hydration layer makes adsorption thermodynamically unfavourable for adsorption https://t.co/iMwvIwH5eN

19.09.2020 · Tweet

2) Fouling release In this method, adsorption is not being prevented, instead the surface is modified so that the strength of the interaction between the foulant and the surface is low. That way they can be easily removed. Low surface energy is usually the aim of the modification https://t.co/zvwwtzEJs6

19.09.2020 · Tweet

3) Biofouling control The overarching aim here is control/prevent biofilm growth. This can be done in many ways i.e. using bacterial behaviour against them (quorum quenching), integrating biocidal elements into a matrix (antibiotic reagents, heavy metals) etc. https://t.co/QPY5d2mSyc

19.09.2020 · RT

RT @realscientists: Growing up I didn't see anyone who looked like me that was involved with marine mammals (or any wildlife, really). I ha…

19.09.2020 · RT

RT @MySci_PK: Representation matters!!

20.09.2020 · Tweet

Polymer brushes as an antifouling technique! 🔊 So from my previous tweet you'll know the common antifouling strategies. Polymer brushes can be used to integrate one or more of these techniques to withstand adsorption of unwanted material. More examples below 👇🏾

20.09.2020 · Tweet

1) Bactericidal brushes Quaternary ammonium salts (QAS) show antibacterial activity. By grafting with QAS the brush is capable of killing the bacteria that settle onto its surface. https://t.co/YR88j39miu

20.09.2020 · Tweet

2) Biomedical devices The formation of biofilms on biomedical devices(i.e. catheters) can lead to bacterial infection. By grafting polymer brushes, initial adhesion of bacteria (up to 90%) can be avoided. https://t.co/Q856DDv88e

20.09.2020 · Tweet

3) Contact lenses If, like me, you wear contact lenses you'll know that protein buildup makes them very uncomfortable. By grafting polymer brushes to improve the hydrophilicity of the lens (fouling resistance), protein adsorption can be reduced https://t.co/B6IMlrF5UU

20.09.2020 · Tweet

DOIs for papers on these topics 1) 10.1021/ACS.langmuir.8b04187 2) 10.1088/1748-3190/aadcc2 3) 10.1016/j.surcoat.2018.08.078

20.09.2020 · Tweet

By popular demand, this thread is on shark skin! https://t.co/MgbOaODQO1

20.09.2020 · Tweet

Shark skin has a very interesting microstructure which has both anti-fouling and drag reducing properties. The features of this structure is in the micrometer range with 30-100um spacing and 200-500um in length https://t.co/Zm7Miqc9tB

20.09.2020 · Tweet

How does it resist the settlement of bacteria? This relates back to my previous thread on anti-fouling techniques and fouling release strategies. The micro-pattern can reduce the available surface area for colonisation due to roughness, reduce the time for settlement due to... https://t.co/n6awKgwQPI

20.09.2020 · Tweet

...the accelerated flow at the surface and the movement of the scales due to changes in pressure internally or externally.

20.09.2020 · Tweet

Sharklet technology has provided a way to harness this property for applications such as wound dressing. This pattern has been tested with staphylococcus aureus, MRSA , Escherichia coli etc to show it's effectiveness across multiple microbes. https://t.co/RYfBREUVTf

20.09.2020 · Tweet

Others have also built on this by not only utilising inspiration from shark skin but also building upon it to also kill bacteria. Through the use of photocatalytic titanium dioxide and nanoimprint lithography, surfaces which prevent settlement AND also inactivate bacteria. https://t.co/klewgNL43I

Today I want to discuss my nanomaterial, Nanodiamonds, they're not as expensive as you might think https://t.co/H5vW4TTsd3

22.09.2020 · Tweet

When we think diamond we usually think of big shiny 'rocks' set in engagement rings or tiaras, and we typically think clear or colourless diamonds are the best. https://t.co/sCM4qkpRwN

22.09.2020 · Tweet

But what is diamond really and is a nanodiamond the same as a the gemstone we like to adorn ourselves with? At the very basis of it, yes gems and nanodiaomnds are made of the same stuff...

22.09.2020 · Tweet

That is to be called a diamond (whether regular or nanosized) it must be Carbon (C) atoms arranged in a crystal lattice structure. This structure is a face-centred cubic, each C bonds to 4-neighbour C's forming a regular tetrahedral structure. https://t.co/YHFTy3E2q7

22.09.2020 · Tweet

Naturally formed diamond is the result of C atoms being pressed together under High-pressures and high-temperature (HPHT) within the earth. This process can be replicated in the lab to make the synthetic material I study, which is sometimes called HPHT Diamond. https://t.co/OFj8o04ZnI

22.09.2020 · Tweet

Note: there are several different ways to synthesis diamond in the lab, including the HPHT method, CVD (chemical vapour deposition) & Detonation methods there are tone of great reviews on the diamond synthesis, I like this one focusing on nanodiamonds, https://t.co/p2Xheef5Qj

22.09.2020 · Tweet

But any way you make it, the structure of the natural (mined) & synthetic (lab-grown) diamond are identical. But how do we make them nano? Stay tuned for the next part where I'll discuss the top-down and bottom-up approaches to creating nanodiamonds https://t.co/D9nQf1BoqG

22.09.2020 · Tweet

@IreneSuaMar No pressure then 🤣😊, oh wait, 💎 needs pressure 🤔

22.09.2020 · Tweet

Top-down synthesis refers to the process where we start with larger pieces of nanodiamond (ND) & make them smaller. E.g. we start with a micron-sized HPHT diamond &, crush it & then mill it to nanoparticles of diamond (NDs), similar to making flour from grains of wheat. https://t.co/BflF7mjQQo

22.09.2020 · Tweet

Bottom-up methods include the so-called detonation nanodiamonds (DNDs) (yep what it sounds like). Carbon precursor is loaded into a chamber w/ an explosive (TNT). The nanodiamonds I study are HPHT fluorescent nanodiamonds (FNDs), I’ve briefly covered the HPHT part & how we get nanosized diamond particles yesterday, but where do diamonds get the fluorescence properties? Gee, I’m glad you asked ;)

23.09.2020 · Tweet

First Let take a look at a couple of my samples under room light…

23.09.2020 · Tweet

My FNDs can be dispersed in water (handy for bio-applications). They aren't very pretty to look at under room light. The 140 nm particles look very milky. This is due to the highly scattering nature of the particles. As we go smaller the solution becomes translucent & darker. https://t.co/p29sw8WbB6

23.09.2020 · Tweet

So what about this fluorescence I keep promising… https://t.co/bS8egnss7u

23.09.2020 · Tweet

Well, Diamond, its self isn’t fluorescent, so I’ve not been exactly accurate when I say fluorescent diamonds. To get them to glow we need to create defects in the diamond lattice. https://t.co/8O9N3q83Ty

23.09.2020 · Tweet

These defects occur in natural diamonds which gives then colour, e.g. if a carbon atom is replaced by nitrogen then the diamond will look orange, the most expensive nitrogen coloured gem is “The Orange” diamonds (a whopping $35 M). https://t.co/ApVO4eEOj4

23.09.2020 · Tweet

Nitrogen-substitution is the most common colour defect in diamonds & in my nanodiamonds also. So we have the N which helps to give the diamond the orange colour, but to get the funky fluorescence we need one more thing… https://t.co/UFiHhlW7y4

23.09.2020 · Tweet

Or instead, we need to remove something. We remove a carbon atom from the diamond, creating a vacancy in the lattice structure! The removal of an atom is done by firing high energy electrons & the material, (there are other methods, but my NDs use electrons)… https://t.co/FP2CWN84v3

23.09.2020 · Tweet

The Carbon atom is “knocked out” leaving the vacancy. Then we need the nitrogen & the vacancy to be next to each other. Luckily heating atoms makes them want to dance & its energetically favourable for the vacancy & the nitrogen to want to be together. This is called annealing! https://t.co/i1Zyd8duX8

23.09.2020 · Tweet

So by replacing a carbon with nitrogen then removing some carbons and heating the sample we finally get the fluorescent centre called the nitrogen-vacancy centre or NV centre for short. (Image from https://t.co/tuchTj1YJc) https://t.co/ryATZsjqQY

23.09.2020 · Tweet

Now we need to excite the NV centre, this means we need to give the electrons of the atoms some extra pep to make them jump out of their ground state to the excited state & as they relax back down they give off some excess energy as a Photons https://t.co/Sd0HcR1e4d

23.09.2020 · Tweet

That is a very rough quick explanation of Fluorescence… There are tons of great videos and books on fluorescence but here is an intro video that I like (they do lots of cool sci stuff) https://t.co/FDPweKhiM3

23.09.2020 · Tweet

To excite the NV centre we use “green light”, we shine the green light (commonly 532 nm wavelength) and the NV centre will glow (Fluoresce) in the red & if we measure the emission spectra it will look like this (image https://t.co/u9qem55Kxc) https://t.co/ZfEUkzg2Pj

23.09.2020 · Tweet

Notice in the spectrum, the two peaks labelled ZPL? This stands for Zero phono line. The NV centre has 2 ZPL because it can have 2-charge states, it can either have an extra Electron (NV minus [NV–] ) & No extra electron (NV neutral [NV0]).

23.09.2020 · Tweet

So the NV spectrum is actually made up of two separate spectra, These charge states are part of what makes these types of fluorescent nanodiamonds (FNDS) so cool with a huge array of potential applications. (image https://t.co/u9qem55Kxc) https://t.co/AIr2FWAomL

23.09.2020 · Tweet

The NV centre is sensitive to its environment so it can be used to sense things, like magnetic fields, temperature changes, & chemical changes. https://t.co/tFmW2RGEsE

23.09.2020 · Tweet

Here are a couple of papers (see next tweet) if you're interested. If you have work in this field please add your papers here too. There is so much good work and I don’t want anyone to feel left out 😊. I’m all for shameless self-promotion

Now let’s look at some fluorescence (Optical) based applications of Fluorescent nanodiamonds (FNDs), I discussed how the fluorescence of FNDs is actually from the Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre. & that the NV centre has 2-charge states, negative (NV-) & neutral (NVo)… https://t.co/M4dVOHze5F

25.09.2020 · Tweet

The NV centre charge states are sensitive to change in their environment, so whether it is NV- or NVo can change, and this can alter the optical properties. Let look at an example of this… https://t.co/JIkQ8gXAzk

25.09.2020 · Tweet

This research from Petrakova et al. (2015) combines DNA and FNDs (two of my things) & the following is from this work https://t.co/Jk4O3bZxkB

25.09.2020 · Tweet

Inserting exogenous DNA into a cell is called transfection, think Gene therapy. And FNDs can be loaded with DNA and carry it into the cell & this paper shows a way to measure the delivery of the DNA using the NV fluorescence. Neat no?... https://t.co/ZQWt9URFgA

25.09.2020 · Tweet

The negatively charged surface of the FND is coated in a polymer (PEI, commonly used in cell transfection) this makes the surface positive so now the DNA will attach to the surface & the FND@PEI@DNA NP are taken up into the cell where the DNA is released. https://t.co/D4UJIEc9ok

25.09.2020 · Tweet

Changing the chemical charge on the Surface of the FNDs, first from neg to pos by adding the PEI, then back to neg with the addition of the DNA changes the electronic charge density … https://t.co/mvaLplqRXr

25.09.2020 · Tweet

This is observed by imaging the NV fluorescence & looking at the change in the ration of NV-: NVo by a change in intensity of the ZPL peaks associated with the 2 charge states. As the DNA releases from the FND@PEI the intensity of the NV- peak decreases relative to the NVo peak👇 https://t.co/092xFoKNIX

26.09.2020 · Tweet

Due to COVID-19 the public is being exposed to more scientific terminology and concepts than ever before. This language can often be very jargony & difficult to penetrate. Even for those of us that work and study medical science, it can be a lot to get ones head around. https://t.co/MEfutpCZfn

26.09.2020 · Tweet

things I see in the media a lot are the terms PCR test, antigen v antibody test, diagnostic V screening, Rapid versus gold standard test. But what does all this mean in practice & what are the key distinctions?

26.09.2020 · Tweet

Firstly, Diagnostic V screening: a diagnostic test is one that confirms someone's disease status, either that they are positive (have the disease) or are negative (do not currently have the disease. https://t.co/vzmIEfFFYb

26.09.2020 · Tweet

A screening test is less certain, it indicates that someone may have the disease. typically screening is used when the risk is low or if their status is already confirmed positive & we want to know how they are responding to treatment.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

Whether the test is classed as diagnostic or screening will typically depend on its sensitivity and specificity. Sensitivity = how much of the test target (e.g. infection) needs to be present to show up in the test Specificity = do the tests only detect the test target https://t.co/wT8NHSoU0Y

26.09.2020 · Tweet

how sensitive or specific the test must be will depend on the disease it is testing. One disease may need the diagnostic to 100% sensitive & 99.5 % specific, while another could be 95% sensitive and 98% specific.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

PCR – Polymerase Chain reaction detects nucleic acids (think DNA) here is a great vid explainer 👇 https://t.co/1NG0VPZ3iU

26.09.2020 · Tweet

An antigen (Ag) is a foreign or toxic substance that triggers an immune response they can be specific to a single species or common amongst a class of organisms. So an Ag test detects the presence of the infecting organism or its antigenic proteins.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

An antibody is a blood protein that your cells produce in response to an antigen. They bind the antigen to help the immune system to clear the antigen from the body.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

This video from https://t.co/KAClIKJQZm is a quick explainer of the difference between these tests. Note: there are now available Antigen tests of COVID-19. this vivid is 4 mths old, but it shows how quickly the technology is moving to help combat the current global pandemic

26.09.2020 · Tweet

The "gold standard" test typically refers to the legally approved method for diagnosing a disease. e.g. In Australia, there are 3 approved methods PCR - nucleic acid detection Rapid Antigen test Serological test

26.09.2020 · Tweet

Note: although the newly approved Antigen Rapid test is classed as diagnostic all positive tests must be confirmed by the PCR test before being added to our COVID numbers. This practice is pretty standard in Australia for infectious disease rapid diagnostics.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

All these terms, concepts and practices are strictly defined in documents called “Standards”, in Australia we used both Australia Standards (AS) & International standards (IOS). A Standard is a legal document that defines & outlines “best practice”.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

By using Standards, we help to ensure practices, like diagnostic tests are comparable from lab to lab. this is all highly regulated in countries like Australia and is partly why we have good reliable health care. https://t.co/rXOPdnOnW1

26.09.2020 · Tweet

Approval of medical devices (e.g. test) is governed by an official agency, in Australia, it's the TGA (Therapeutic Goods Administration), in the USA the FDA (Food and drugs Administration) & in Europe the EMA (European Medicines Agency).

26.09.2020 · Tweet

For Australians, the TGA website is a great source of COVID testing information so if you want a deeper understanding please go there https://t.co/cVsWRdrHLF for other countries & regions see your own governing bodies for relevant information

26.09.2020 · Tweet

A rapid diagnostic test (RDT), simply is a test that is faster than the existing gold standard. E.g. for bacterial infection PCR is classed as an RDT, the gold standard for diagnosing bacterial infections are biochemical tests that can take up to 10 days for the diagnosis.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

In cases were PCR is now the “gold standard” an RDT could include an antigen test such as the one recently approved in Australia. Also in Australia Diagnosis of a disease can only be done by an approved lab using one of the approved methods.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

Next, I’ll give a general walkthrough of what we do in a medical device evaluation @NRLScience without going into specifics because we deal with IP and confidential material. I just want to give you an overview of this challenging but rewarding line of scientific work

26.09.2020 · Tweet

Evaluation of a proposed Rapid diagnostic test (RDT): This evaluation can only be done by an approved lab with trained & qualified staff. For example, I recently joined a project to validate some RDTs, I have undergone intensive training, down to my competency to use a pipette. https://t.co/xNopR5fvfv

26.09.2020 · Tweet

The process of making sure an RDT works as the manufacture says is heavily regulated. Each step & protocol is controlled, in fact, @NRLScince has 700+ controlled documents that we used to ensure we are compliant with the different entities we work with. https://t.co/F1TleNLD7s

26.09.2020 · Tweet

They tell us how we are to conduct each task, although we don't need to know all of them. Some will be for tasks that I don't do. And I can look up the documents I need any time I need to refer to them.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

Let look a one way we might run an evaluation for an RDT. Say a company wants to get their new RDT out to market – they have tested it and are confident in the test, but they need to have it validated by an authorised & independent lab, such as @NRLScience.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

Once the contract is agreed and the goals and parameters outlined we get to the practical task of testing the test. the example I'm giving here is for subjective tests, think pregnancy strip. Do I see a line or no line, Do I give it a 1 or a 3 etc.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

We receive the RDT & assemble the test samples, these include controls & reference samples – a ref sample is a sample that has been tested using the gold standard & its status is known. All samples are randomised & the work is done blind (testers don’t know the sample status)

26.09.2020 · Tweet

In my current role 3 of us work together so we can triple check our work. We then run the test according to the manufacture's protocol. The aim is for us to follow the test as it would be done by someone in the real world. We check the quality of the kit... https://t.co/U62nXrFmcn

26.09.2020 · Tweet

We may also make notes on the ease of use, e.g. if the manufacture says the test could be done by someone with no scientific or medical training do we agree, are the instructions clear & easy to follow. These points are subjective that's why we have multiple people. https://t.co/A1BdwiKxhF

26.09.2020 · Tweet

We run the test, this involves 100’s of samples over multiple manufactures Lots (different batches) of the RDT, this way we can see if the manufacturing quality is consistent from lot to lot... https://t.co/vmtHWV21fA

26.09.2020 · Tweet

It’s no good if one Lot is 100% sensitive & 99.9% specific if the next lot is only 90 % sensitive. The RDT must perform the same (within a very narrow range) test-to-test and lot-to-lot. https://t.co/Sb2Lel9CEg

26.09.2020 · Tweet

We then interpret the result, and check if all 3 of us are in agreement (again this is for a subjective test). 2 out of 3 of us must agree in our interpretation of the result, i.e. is the sample positive or negative?. If we don’t reach consensus the test is redone. https://t.co/ymmjbNnsqy

26.09.2020 · Tweet

you need to be confident in your evaluation, it's really important once we start that my grading scale is consistent from our first run to our last. And that I don't let my colleagues change my opinion on what looks like a positive V a negative to me. https://t.co/AkvGyPHFSG

26.09.2020 · Tweet

We take detailed notes on each run and even take photos, we need to be scientific as possible and evidence must be given at the end of the evaluation. There are even regulation on how we write our notes 😳 https://t.co/Ztw1obh1ZP

26.09.2020 · Tweet

This work is highly repetitive and we must do it methodically so breaks are important so we don’t get fatigued & make errors. We follow a work instruction, it's a little like doing a pre-flight checklist & excellent verbal communication is vital. https://t.co/jolrhRU9cc

26.09.2020 · Tweet

This work is not for everyone, it requires focus & an eye for detail and an ability to follow a check-list and do a repetitive task the same again and again. It costs the manufacture a lot of money & lives might depend on us doing our job right. This is a lot of pressure. https://t.co/YEuPFBdprd

26.09.2020 · Tweet

But, it is very rewarding knowing that you are contributing to work that can help improve health outcomes. https://t.co/cO9iZIRBCZ

26.09.2020 · Tweet

If this sounds like something you might find interesting & you are coming to the end of your science degree wondering what to do next. Jobs in evaluation come up often. Even if they don't have jobs listed it can be worth reaching out. Some labs will have studentships too.

26.09.2020 · Tweet

So that was a general overview of RDT evaluations prior to approval to go to market. let me know if you want more detail about anything I've covered and I'll do my best to answer your questions 😊

Time for some information about #nanozymes. The word NanoZyme comes from two words - NANOparticles and enZYME. A nanoparticle is called a nanozyme when it can mimic the catalytic activity of a natural enzyme. https://t.co/QyHGYJJ2VG

29.09.2020 · Tweet

This is quite fascinating! To think of it - an inorganic particle which does not show structural similarity or the complex folding patterns of a natural enzyme can still drive the same catalytic reaction to completion as seen in a natural enzyme.

29.09.2020 · Tweet

As a biologist, the first curious question that comes to mind - if the complex folding plays an important role in the activity of natural enzymes what is the driving force in nanozymes?

29.09.2020 · Tweet

It is the surface atoms in nanoparticles that play an important role in the catalytic activity

29.09.2020 · Tweet

Next obvious question is why do I need nanozymes? Natural enzymes are temperamental and difficult to work with. Let's be honest no one likes that :) NanoZymes are easier to work with, we can fine-tune the activity, and are robust.

29.09.2020 · Tweet

It's not all positive for nanozymes - believe me. As amazing nanozymes are - we have not been able to achieve the high level of specificity and complexity we see in natural enzymatic systems. I talk about this in my biochemistry lectures https://t.co/ngeSx8oB0E

29.09.2020 · Tweet

For anyone who knows the concepts of Km and Vmax - you can ignore this post

29.09.2020 · Tweet

Compared to natural enzymes, nanozymes are sometimes better for their catalytic activity. How can we compare this?

29.09.2020 · Tweet

There are two factors we consider to compare enzyme and nanozyme - how much the enzyme loves its substrate (Km) and how fast can the enzyme convert the substrate to product (Vmax). https://t.co/xBOSVX8AfK

29.09.2020 · Tweet

A simple analogy for this concept is your car (body), engine (enzyme) and fuel (substrate). Km is like your measure of fuel efficiency. The less fuel you need the more efficient your car is. Vmax is the fastest speed that you can drive at. So you need low Km and high Vmax.

29.09.2020 · Tweet

Many of us have heard of an enzyme horseradish peroxidase (HRP). If I was to compare the peroxidase activity of this enzyme with nanozymes with respect to Km and Vmax, let us see what we get

29.09.2020 · Tweet

Woah! We can see some of the nanozymes are a lot better than HRP. Isn't this amazing. Although it took a lot of time to get to this point, it is great to see the performance of nanozymes keeps getting better. https://t.co/K8wun8Uj6v

29.09.2020 · Tweet

@avpoltral Lol. I still remember reading about enzyme kinetics as an undergrad student. Never thought I will ever use this in my career and here I am sitting and analysing kinetics data.

29.09.2020 · Tweet

An interesting fact about nanozymes # 1 - I heard that the first report on nanoparticles showing enzyme-mimic activity was a serendipitous discovery. This is something that we see a lot in research. Opens up exciting possibilities.

29.09.2020 · Tweet

An interesting fact about nanozymes # 2 - We have been able to mimic the catalytic activity of peroxidase, oxidase, catalase, haloperoxidase, glutathione peroxidase, uricase, methane monooxygenase, hydrolase, superoxide dismutase and pan-enzymatic activity. That is a lot.

29.09.2020 · Tweet

An interesting fact about nanozymes # 3 - We have a new field today called Nanozymology

29.09.2020 · Tweet

An interesting fact about nanozymes # 4 - The word nanozyme was only coined in 2004.

29.09.2020 · Tweet

30.09.2020 · Tweet

Yesterday we got to see how fascinating #nanozymes are. We even saw that we can apply biochemical principles we use to understand natural enzymes can be applied to understand nanozymes as well. Today we look at how we can use nanozymes for sensing.

30.09.2020 · Tweet

Yesterday we ran a poll trying to guess how many papers have been published in the area of nanozymes. The answer is...

30.09.2020 · Tweet

wait for it

30.09.2020 · Tweet

wait for it

30.09.2020 · Tweet

Over 400 papers have been published just this year. So congrats to everyone who selected that option. https://t.co/U2vCbS4GQR

30.09.2020 · Tweet

Before we dive into how we can use nanozymes in sensor development, there is something we need to know. For a sensor to be able to do its job, we need something that will recognise our analyte of interest in a complex sample matrix

30.09.2020 · Tweet

Sample matrix - this will contain a mixture of substances. For e.g., if I want to detect a pesticide, it may be present in the soil or on the surface of a fruit, which will contain a lot of unwanted molecules including other pesticides.

30.09.2020 · Tweet

You need something that will specifically identify your analyte of interest. It is like finding a needle in a haystack.

30.09.2020 · Tweet

We can use antibodies, enzymes, proteins, lectins, carbohydrates or aptamers. Traditionally, we have focussed a lot of work on antibodies. In our work, we use aptamers to specifically bind to our target.

30.09.2020 · Tweet

Lets first look at what is an aptamer. Aptamers are oligonucleotides or peptides and bind to their target analyte with high affinity. For instance, a DNA aptamer contains single-stranded DNA containing anywhere between 20-60 nucleotides.

30.09.2020 · Tweet

This single-stranded DNA will fold and create a unique 3D structure that will then recognise its target. A very effective molecule to recognise its target. https://t.co/BiatWSWjyu

30.09.2020 · Tweet

But why not just use an antibody? Aptamers offer better target discrimination, have lower batch-to-batch variability and in many instances have higher specificity towards its target. They are also easier to store. I say if it's better why not use this instead of an antibody

30.09.2020 · Tweet

Yesterday we saw that a nanozyme can catalyze a reaction similar to natural enzymes. Now we will see how we can combine aptamers and nanozymes.

30.09.2020 · Tweet

When we expose aptamers to a nanozyme, the aptamers bind to the surface of the nanozyme. In this process, they block the surface atoms. This results in the nanozyme to lose its catalytic activity.

30.09.2020 · Tweet

Remember how we said that aptamers have a very high affinity to their target?

30.09.2020 · Tweet

If we now expose the aptamer-nanozyme complex to a solution containing a target that the aptamer recognises, they will dissociate from the surface of the nanozyme and bind to their target.

30.09.2020 · Tweet

When aptamers dissociate, they expose the surface atoms of the nanozyme. This means, the nanozyme now regains its catalytic activity.

30.09.2020 · Tweet

If I expose the aptamer-nanozyme to a solution containing a target that the aptamer does not recognise, they will not dissociate from the surface of the nanozyme. This means the nanozyme will still be inactive. The figure here is quite useful to understand the concept https://t.co/E9w92k6Xjd

30.09.2020 · Tweet

This simple yet effective strategy has helped us develop sensors to detect pesticides, an antibiotic, and even a whole virus.

30.09.2020 · Tweet

Here is the links for virus detection (https://t.co/KImIVxjIXw)

30.09.2020 · Tweet

Here is the link for pesticide detection (https://t.co/9KYDFWDcwL)

30.09.2020 · Tweet

01.10.2020 · Tweet

Ooooo looks like a lot of people voted for gold nanoparticles in yesterday’s poll. But the first report of nanoparticles showing enzyme like behaviour was - iron oxide nanoparticles. :)

01.10.2020 · Tweet

So yesterday we saw how we can combine the strength of nanozymes and aptamers to create aptasensor platform. A simple yet effective tool to create a sensor.

01.10.2020 · Tweet

Today we look at how we look at combining natural enzymes and a nanozyme as well as a protein and nanozyme. Let's look at combining natural enzyme and a nanozyme

01.10.2020 · Tweet

In this example, we will look at the detection of urine glucose. We all have heard of diabetes. It is a disease that causes high blood sugar. If you have suffered from diabetes for a long time, it can lead to renal complications.

01.10.2020 · Tweet

Interestingly, we have blood glucose monitors that are portable and easy to use. However, they do not give you any information about renal complications. We decided to address this.

01.10.2020 · Tweet

We had a particularly challenging problem. The concentration of glucose in the urine is quite high - generally in the millimolar range. You see - we always had sensors to look at low concentrations. So the challenge was now to develop a sensor to look at high concentrations

01.10.2020 · Tweet

Instead of using nanoparticles directly, we embedded them in a piece of cotton fabric. WHY? Two reasons - (i) we can load a lot of nanoparticles and (ii) cotton being an absorbent material, it will bring the glucose in close proximity.

01.10.2020 · Tweet

What was the recognition element in this case - easy - we used the enzyme glucose oxidase. This will specifically convert glucose to form hydrogen peroxide. This is the key. The hydrogen peroxide is one of the substrates for the nanozyme.

01.10.2020 · Tweet

Before we go away, one last concept about how we can combine proteins and nanozymes. Yesterday if you recall, aptamers and nanozymes interact in a dynamic manner. That means, the aptamers can move from the nanozyme to bind to its target.

01.10.2020 · Tweet

We found that this approach did not work in some cases. Don't you hate it when that happens! But we came up with an alternative approach. This is an example where the nanozyme activity is always ON.

01.10.2020 · Tweet

Let's see - we now have a protein called transferrin. This protein will specifically go bind to cells that have a transferrin receptor. The probe in this case is the nanozyme-protein conjugate. However, unlike yesterday, the nanozyme activity here is still on. https://t.co/SICHk0WmXL

01.10.2020 · Tweet

If I mix some cells with this probe - say some specific type of cancer cells that have transferrin receptors. The transferrin protein-bound nanozyme will now go bind to these cells. If the probe does not find transferrin receptors they will be free.

01.10.2020 · Tweet

If we isolate the cells and wash them now - the free probe is gone. What we are left with is just the transferrin protein-bound nanozyme tightly stuck to the transferrin receptors. If we now do the assay, we get colour. Isn't this cool :)

01.10.2020 · Tweet

We actually didn't just stop there. We also showed that this strategy can be used for receptor profiling - Oh sciency words. What I mean is I can look at how much transferrin receptors are produced by different cells using this :) https://t.co/gnjqC8p4a9

01.10.2020 · Tweet

For anyone who is interested in this - have a look at https://t.co/TqauIIfVyJ For anyone who is interested in the glucose-sensing - have a look at https://t.co/cFmuz7GyIy (and a new one to be published very very very soon!)

01.10.2020 · Tweet

Tomorrow we look at how to kill some bugs using nanozyme!

01.10.2020 · Tweet

@NotHF So true! Fenton reaction at its best :)

02.10.2020 · Tweet

Today we look at how we can kill bugs using nanozymes. We also look at how we can use light to enhance this process. https://t.co/8Tg1vSgKTb

02.10.2020 · Tweet

The first one we will look at it just using a nanozyme without light. We already know how we can use a nanozyme to convert a colorless substrate to a colored product. One of these substrates is H2O2. Nanozymes convert H2O2 to form a very reactive species called OH radicals https://t.co/ScYR5hvPXL

02.10.2020 · Tweet

This radical targets the integrity of the bacterial cell - if the bacterial cell membrane is destroyed then the poor bacteria does not survive. Well the process is something like the one in the gif https://t.co/oiPwuroTFF

02.10.2020 · Tweet

What does light have to do with the concept of nanozymes? Well, we know that nanoparticles interact with light. This leads to some interesting properties. Look at the GIF of the Lycurgus cup made in the 4th-century made by the Romans. https://t.co/YqTyMpE96Q

02.10.2020 · Tweet

It changes color as it has gold and silver nanoparticles embedded in the glass. This results in the change of color depending on where the light source is. We use the ability of nanoparticles to interact with light.

02.10.2020 · Tweet

We saw that nanozymes can convert H2O2 to OH radicals (post in the morning). In that case, if the nanozyme is given 4 H2O2, it only converts one to OH radical. If we shine light on the same nanozyme, it will convert all 4 to OH radicals. https://t.co/ugGB6Q05O6

02.10.2020 · Tweet

This means more killing of bacteria. :) It is important to remember that the light source to be used will be determined by the nanozyme composition and nanozyme morphology.

02.10.2020 · Tweet

Here is the work from the group where we have used visible light to improve the killing of bacteria. https://t.co/Sligcvxf4h

02.10.2020 · Tweet

What we show here is that light not only improves the affinity of the nanozyme to H2O2, it also improves the catalysis by 20 times. This is just an example of how we can use nanozymes to kill bacteria.

02.10.2020 · Tweet

04.10.2020 · Tweet

What a week it has been - we looked at how nanoparticles mimic the catalytic activity of natural enzymes - we call them nanozymes; how we can use nanozymes to develop sensors to detect small molecules to cells and also how we can use them to kill bacteria.

04.10.2020 · Tweet

Yesterday we had the opportunity to meet the amazing young researchers who are part of the @RMIT_NBRL group

04.10.2020 · Tweet

Today I want to deal with something we are all going through - COVID. I was just having a chat with my wife about how things are different now - we don't go to conferences anymore, we don't get to see each other, networking is down to people we know.

04.10.2020 · Tweet

This led me to think - When I was a PhD student and an early career researcher - what was the thing that helped me the most? I could only think of one thing - networking, networking and networking.

04.10.2020 · Tweet

Networking helped me to know researchers working in the area, made some amazing friends, ideas were exchanged, developed new projects, even submitted grants with some of them, got to understand how research works in different countries - I can keep going with this.

04.10.2020 · Tweet

With COVID how can we help students and ECRs to get the same level of exposure? In my mind, I think organising conferences within the department across the university or even have conferences with just two universities. It helps them with confidence and introduces new people.

04.10.2020 · Tweet

Encourage students to attend virtual conferences - I know it is not the same but none-the-less useful.

04.10.2020 · Tweet

Have departmental seminars where someone external to the university presents. This way students are exposed to work outside their university.

04.10.2020 · Tweet

Encourage students to join Chemical / Engineering professional organisations - attend their events - generally, they are cheap or free for students - helps with networking (you never know - you may find your potential employer)

04.10.2020 · Tweet

Introduce your collaborators to the group or have their students present their work once a fortnight. Helps them with interacting with researchers not directly associated with their work and will improve their perspective

04.10.2020 · Tweet

I would like to know what has helped everyone else during their PhD and post-doctoral career that they think the younger generation is missing out on due to COVID and how we can address this. Comment on the post and share your ideas. Would love to learn!

04.10.2020 · Tweet

Today's topic will be 2D materials, starting with #graphene, and electronic structure. 😎🥳😱 https://t.co/qDupUuj6Uo

14.10.2020 · Tweet

Graphene is a single layer of graphite, material commonly found in pencils. Main reason why pencils are so good for writing is that all of these graphene layers inside of #graphite are very weakly bound and separate easily, while leaving trail on the paper ✏️

14.10.2020 · Tweet

Graphene is 1 atomic layer thick, and is basically only a surface, so 2D. Really crazy thing, since our world is 3D! All atoms in graphene are carbon atoms, and they are arranged in a honeycomb structure. Something like on this picture https://t.co/uajJIpC78i

14.10.2020 · Tweet

#Graphene was first isolated using a sticky tape, a really cool method. You first use sticky tape to peel off a bit of #graphite, and then you use another piece of sticky tape to thin it down. You keep doing this until you get only a single layer of graphite, #graphene https://t.co/5CdLXJ0Vt1

14.10.2020 · Tweet

Once you are happy with the #graphene you got, you can either place it on a substrate you want to use, or on another 2D material. Sort of like arranging atomic Legos!! If you are interested in how to make atomic Legos, check out the talk by @semontis #LEGO https://t.co/iRlaiYVN33

14.10.2020 · Tweet

#Graphene has many really interesting properties. Despite being just a single layer of atoms thick, it is one of the strongest and most elastic materials we know! It also has a very special electronic properties, such as really fast electrons that have no (effective) mass.

14.10.2020 · Tweet

#Graphene discovery was so important that a Nobel prize was given to a A. Geim and K. Novoselov in 2010 for graphene discovery!🥇🎖️ @NobelPrize You can even watch the Nobel lecture on the research that led to graphene discovery https://t.co/K42kB2lREo

14.10.2020 · Tweet

#Graphene discovery paper was published in 2004 @ScienceMagazine and you can say that the era of 2D materials started with it https://t.co/JSQKWmnS2h https://t.co/0EPx1BxoVA

14.10.2020 · Tweet

[admin] "Supercool Electrons in 2D Materials" Extended podcast with Antonija (@CaboAntonija ) is out now - https://t.co/qd0RUSC1Rn

14.10.2020 · Tweet

#Electronic band structure describes the range of energy levels that electrons can occupy or not. States that electrons can occupy are called bands, and ones that they cannot occupy are called gaps. 2 most important bands are called the valence and #conduction band https://t.co/uS2LOVn7l4

14.10.2020 · Tweet

These 2 bands are closest to the Fermi level. Fermi level is the highest energy #electron in the material can have. Valence band is under the Fermi level and is occupied, conduction band is above the Fermi level and is not occupied, but is important for the #conduction of current https://t.co/IjjC6CLB29

14.10.2020 · Tweet

#Graphene is a special kind of material, it is not just a simple metal or a semiconductor, but is something called a semimetal (or a zero band gap semiconductor), and it has bands in a shape of cones. These cones are called Dirac cones, and are the reason for very fast #electrons https://t.co/s2kVZsfLDF

14.10.2020 · Tweet

A really cool video was made by my summer student, Sean Solari @Monash_Science @FLEETCentre , showing #graphene #electronic structure and cones, called Dirac cones https://t.co/wq4caRXYfk Do you have any questions about this (for me) super exciting topic? 😄 https://t.co/Ek5UR868wz

14.10.2020 · Tweet

Morning! ☕ The winner of yesterday's poll about #graphene growth was molecular selfassembly, so we'll spend some time today talking about it 🎉 https://t.co/Adel8XVg1n

15.10.2020 · Tweet

I should have probably called it molecular assembly, instead of "self-assembly", as that is more correct, but anyway, molecules!

15.10.2020 · Tweet

Molecular assembly is a type of #chemistry driven bottom-up approach to grow #graphene. Bottom up meaning that we go from small nano-blocks to build a larger thing, graphene. This approach allows for an amazing control over how, for example, graphene edges are defined.

15.10.2020 · Tweet

A small molecular blocks, monomers, are combined on the surface and bound into larger units, polymers. Molecular assembly is most often used to grow a very specific kind of graphene, #graphene nanoribbons! Different molecular precursors can be used to grow different nanoribbons. https://t.co/ozFGP3Z0Lx

15.10.2020 · Tweet

As molecules are used to grow #graphene (nanoribbons), the edges of the structure are always well defined on the #atomic level, which is really cool! Usual molecular precursors are various molecules that already have carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal rings.

15.10.2020 · Tweet

This is a good starting point to grow a larger sheet that is supposed to consist of infinitely repeating carbon hexagons! #graphene 💍 https://t.co/OFTziOqmG5

15.10.2020 · Tweet

@Lions_and_Bees So we can have a monomer misnomer? 😁🤔🤔

15.10.2020 · Tweet

There are a lot of molecules to choose from, and a very popular monomer to use is 10,10′-dibromo-9,9′-bianthryl. Depending on the type of monomer you use, #graphene nanoribbons can have different edges, width and even doping!

15.10.2020 · Tweet

As we mentioned yesterday, #graphene is a semimetal. A semimetal will always conduct electricity and therefore will not be a very good to use in transistors. Graphene nanoribbons on the other hand, can be semiconducting or metallic depending on their edge type!

15.10.2020 · Tweet

If you choose a right precursor molecule, and a right substrate, you can grow an armchair-edge #graphene nanoribbon and it will be semiconducting. This is really cool if you want to use them for some kind of transistors, for example. https://t.co/zQmJ3vQzGH @acsnano

15.10.2020 · Tweet

#graphene nanoribbons with zig-zag-edges, on the other hand, tend to always be metallic. https://t.co/ncGnmHSCSV

15.10.2020 · Tweet

Great thing with the molecular bottom-up approach is the amoutn of control you have when you grow things. You can control the edge type, doping, and with a bit of assistance from your substrate, width and #topology of your #graphene nanoribbon! https://t.co/15ERsbyPxE @nature

15.10.2020 · Tweet

You can also make heterojunctions between different #nanoribbons https://t.co/5iG580KMat @NatureNano

15.10.2020 · Tweet

All of the previous examples were for #graphene nanoribons grown and measured on #metals. If you would prefer to have them in a different form, you can even disperse them in a solvent! https://t.co/OULLKXZT8w https://t.co/J9Ohphon1b @J_A_C_S

15.10.2020 · Tweet

If you would like to learn more about assembling molecules on surfaces, you can follow the work of @DrJenMacLeod @QUT and @DrJayEllDee https://t.co/WsgwiEp0l8 @IOPPublishing

15.10.2020 · Tweet

Before concluding the part of molecular assembly I would just like to mention that not only you can grow #graphene (nanoribbons) in this fashion, but you can also use graphene as a pattern to assemble molecules! https://t.co/FVQSv6mEvI @DrJenMacLeod

15.10.2020 · Tweet

You can even transfer the self assembled molecules (and atoms) from #graphene to other substrates! https://t.co/Hbdv1AgCn0 @acsnano

15.10.2020 · Tweet

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, or as I will call it ARPES, is a technique used to measure electronic band structure of materials. It is based on the photoelectric effect, a discovery for which #Einstein won the Noble prize in 1921! https://t.co/lXIsU5mJZH

15.10.2020 · Tweet

Beam of light (blue) falls on the sample and photoexcites electrons (red). Electrons are captured by electrostatic an #Lens and pass through the analyser. Everything is designed in a way to preserve the information about the kinetic energy and angles that electrons have https://t.co/10hWYaHyBq

15.10.2020 · Tweet

Electrons that pass through the analyser hit the array of electron multipliers (MCP) that boosts the signal which is then mapped on the phosphorous screen. Finally the photoemission intensity is captured by a CCD camera and you get an image like this (bilayer #graphene). https://t.co/DZ6ItDsNB5

15.10.2020 · Tweet

ARPES only measures up to the Fermi level (highest energy state electron can occupy), which is seen as a sharp decrease in the intensity. Also, ARPES has to be done in vacuum. https://t.co/GrGAZUiueK

15.10.2020 · Tweet

ARPES can be done with different setups and different sources of light. As a light source you can use a helium lamp, a #laser or a synchrotron! all of these systems have different advantages and disadvantages.

15.10.2020 · Tweet

@TobiasAdeJong Hmmm I'm not sure! We recently received our new detector, so once that's up and running, I can tell you if it is the MCP-phosphor-CCD based or the direct CMOS 😀

@Guybrush42 I'm doing something similar to XPS. Principle is the same, but we are scanning across different angles around normal emission to be able to measure band dispersion. Synchrotrons have tuneable energy range and lower photon energy gives better resolution close to the Fermi level

16.10.2020 · Tweet

Poll results came in, and it seems that majority would love to get a tour and hear about how to become a user. Luckily for us, many synchrotrons are doing virtual tours #virtualtour ! So after brief introduction to synchrotrons I will be sharing link to some of these tours 💫 https://t.co/WNdG07K1MM

16.10.2020 · Tweet

Synchrotrons are circular particle accelerators that accelerate electrons to speeds close to the speed of light and produce synchrotron light that is very intense. Synchrotron light is much more intense than if you produced X-rays with a lab source @lightsources https://t.co/oG9y9DSx4b

16.10.2020 · Tweet

Synchrotrons are also able to provide light of different energies (wavelengths), which can affect your energy resolution, but also whether you probe deep into your sample or just the surface. It can produce light in VUV, sorf and hard X-ray range.

16.10.2020 · Tweet

Different beamlines, places where light comes out of synchrotron and experiments are performed, will receive light in different energy range. 🌈 Beamline you use (and energy range) will depend on type of experiments and science you are doing.

16.10.2020 · Tweet

Hard X-rays are more often used for #biology experiments, while material science and #physics is more often done on the soft X-ray end of the spectrum. Of course, that is not always the case. ARPES experiments, though, are mostly done in the UV and sometimes soft X-ray range

16.10.2020 · Tweet

I did my PhD on a small synchrotron in the basement of Aarhus University in Denmark @AarhusUni called ASTRID2, so you could say that ASTRID is my favourite synchrotron! Here is a photo from one of exciting ASTRID beamtimes done with help of a cool dragon, Sissy 🐉 https://t.co/kTs0nbtwOW

16.10.2020 · Tweet

I've done a lot of fun and cool experiments on 2D materials on ASTRID, including one where we used hydrogen to turn #graphene from a semimetal to a #semiconductor! https://t.co/wf0Wra6hUP @acsnano

16.10.2020 · Tweet

We've also looked into how a 2D semiconductor MoS2 looks when grown on gold. https://t.co/cYY0aD6fMT @PhysRevLett

Besides ASTRID, I did some really cool experiments at @MAXIVLaboratory located in Lund, Sweden, and @elettrasincro near Trieste, Italy.

You can also get a #virtualtour of @DiamondLightSou https://t.co/A6lxBAbIRX

16.10.2020 · Tweet

And now briefly about how to become a synchrotron user! Most synchrotrons have calls for proposals a few times a year, where you send them a short proposal on experiment that you would like to do. Good start is to check website of the synchrotron and see the format & check dates

16.10.2020 · Tweet

Most of beamlines have both technical data, that will make it easier for you to figure out whether your experiment can be done there or not, and also most recent publications. Is there anything from your field there, does it look like suitable for your project? https://t.co/HMpjowpAPv

16.10.2020 · Tweet

You can also contact a beamline scientist working on the beamline you would like to apply for. They are very knowledgeable and experienced and can help you decide whether to apply or not.

16.10.2020 · Tweet

More practically, when applying, it is always good to have some initial data, to show that the project can actually be done. Also, you should have a plan B and come with several samples (of the same kind). Time is short, and maybe your 1st sample won't work, but 2nd will 🙂🙃

@smileyATI Measurements are always done in vacuum, so your sample needs to be able to survive that. Also, surface needs to be very clean. So we are talking either growing sample in the ARPES system, cleaning it by heating to 100+ degrees Celsius or cleaving/using sticky tape to clean it.2/2

17.10.2020 · Tweet

@smileyATI Actually, samples can also be grown somewhere else and transported with a #vacuum suitcase. You just need a surface that's clean of adsorbates. Measurements are typically room temperature or at cryogenic temperature (to improve resolution). You can also heat samples a bit.

Even though I'm mostly working on 2D #materials , they are not the only type of materials ARPES can measure! "Regular" 3D crystals, and even quasicrystals and heterostructures can be measured with ARPES.

17.10.2020 · Tweet

One popular group of materials that are studied with ARPES are topological insulators such as Bi2Se3. They also have linear dispersion similar to graphene, but their Dirac cones are 3D. https://t.co/tnmQEICbDM @ScienceMagazine

17.10.2020 · Tweet

You can also use ARPES to studi 2D electron (or hole!) gas on the surface https://t.co/dXe1j8TKiT @PhysRevB @DiamondLightSou @AarhusUni

Or even a combination of the two, topological states and 2D electron gas states! https://t.co/y8Nia8CosF @NatureComms

17.10.2020 · Tweet

17.10.2020 · Tweet

Sometimes materials are 3D, but they are layered and the layers don't interact strongly with one another, at least not strong enough to matter for the electronic structure. To determine whether the electronic structure is 2D or 3D, you do ARPES at many photon energies https://t.co/mXzw50YlnK

There are many materials you can measure, including "regular" metals, such as gold https://t.co/JPf5NSBM9g @PhysRevB

Hello everyone! ☕ Today is my last day curating and I just wanted to say that I really enjoyed it and had a lot of fun. If you are working in #nano, consider applying to become a curator for a week!

18.10.2020 · Tweet

As the last topic, I'd like to briefly discuss collaborations and open access publishing, as those are some of the things I think are important in science today.

18.10.2020 · Tweet

There is a lot of push to move to more open access publishing, for example Plan S in Europe, in order to make science more accessibly. This is something I think is really important, as it will make science more accessible to our colleagues and general public.

18.10.2020 · Tweet

Unfortunately, it often costs a lot of money to get your paper published open access. Luckily there are some alternatives that can still make research more accessible. One of these alternatives is a use of preprint servers and self archiving.

18.10.2020 · Tweet

In #physics it is quite common to place preprints on @arxiv and majority of journals allow for this, which I think it is great! Of course, these are not peer-reviewed articles, but it still increases accessibility and you get access to new research much faster! https://t.co/RDMVis3Wm6

18.10.2020 · Tweet

Are preprint servers common in your field and what are they?🧐🤔❓❔

18.10.2020 · Tweet

Second thing I would like to talk about today are collaborations. 😃 Majority of work I do is highly collaborative, and if you look at my publication list, you will see that most of my articles have very long list of authors. https://t.co/7bHzBAzJy4

18.10.2020 · Tweet

In part, this is because I am doing a lot of work on synchrotrons and ARPES experiments usually require a lot of input from beamline scientists. We also often get new materials from our #chemistry and material science colleagues and get support from #theory group for models.

18.10.2020 · Tweet

All of this means that there are a lot of people involved. Of course, there are also projects where you can do everything "in-house", prepare a sample, do measurements and make simple model. 😄

18.10.2020 · Tweet

I enjoy collaborative projects, as you get to learn a lot. One of my favourite projects was done in a collaboration with an electrochemistry group during my PhD @iNANO_AarhusUni. I was preparing #graphene on iridium which my #chemistry colleagues would then transfer on silicon.

18.10.2020 · Tweet

I got to learn a lot from them and the project was a lot of fun! We successfully transferred #graphene from iridium https://t.co/LC3YGHvUvq @IOPPublishing and I also got a publication in a #chemistry journal https://t.co/CLOvDLsvom @ChemEurope 😎

18.10.2020 · Tweet

@carlosromvil @arxiv No, unfortunately those are usually not allowed so preprints don't fully replace an open access publications. Different journals have different rules, though, so it is a good idea to check them when posting preprints. Sometimes they allow for different versions to be uploaded.

18.10.2020 · Tweet

Doing ARPES also means that I frequently publish in collaboration with beamline scientists. Those projects are always exciting because often it means that you are doing something very new on the beamline. https://t.co/Xld1vO8dkT

18.10.2020 · Tweet

#CarbonNanotubes (CNTs) are super cool materials – they’re basically a sheet of graphite (graphene) ✏️rolled up tightly into a tube. In the same way as rolling a sheet of paper makes it harder to bend, rolling up graphite makes it much stronger too 💪💪. https://t.co/CRELWloCsa

26.10.2020 · Tweet

Unlike rolling a piece of paper, which is still a piece of paper that isn’t conductive🤦 CNTs are much more conductive that graphene – up to ‘ballistic conductance’ ⏩⏩which sounds super cool but just means conductivity is independent of length (ok – that’s still super cool). https://t.co/tqs8gr71IQ

26.10.2020 · Tweet

This happens because the electron orbitals on each atom are deformed by the CNT being rolled up – so they overlap a bit more. This concept is pretty simple, but really defines what I try to do in my research – control the form of a material to manipulate its function! 🗞️⚡️☑️ https://t.co/3JoVG0UF4P

26.10.2020 · Tweet

As CNTs are strong and electrically conductive (and chemically stable) – as well as made from one of the most abundant and well understood elements on earth (carbon) 💎 – they are great for energy storage 🔋devices! #Supercapacitors #FuelCells More on this tomorrow!

26.10.2020 · Tweet

This was a bit of a boon and a curse A boon: it extender the start of my ‘ECR’ period – the time given to you to establish yourself (or not) as a researcher ☑️ A curse: it was a massive detriment to my mental health.🙊

During this time I was working in the @MatteviC research group, Dr Mattevi is an expert in 2D materials - especially #TransitionMetalDichalcogenides. So I pivoted my research focus into these 2D materials - which are amazingly versatile

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Unlike Graphene which is: ☑️1 element ☑️1 atomic layer thick ☑️flexible ☑️1 material Transition Metal Dichalcogenides are: ✔️2 elements (a metal, and a chalcogen) ✔️3 atomic layers (one metal layer between 2 chalcogen layers) ✔️rigid (ish) ✔️a family of materials

27.10.2020 · Tweet

The fact it's a family of materials is super powerful, you suddenly have a huge range of chemistries 🧪 you can play with (beyond carbon) - electronic properties. The beauty here is you can stack different TMD chemistries together almost as though they were one material! https://t.co/mxouVtOt9G

27.10.2020 · Tweet

This week I'll talk about 1. My journey - done! ✔️ 2. Making Nanomaterials! - Coming right up! 👇👇 3. The art of science - 🗓️ 4. Assembling Nanomaterials - 🗓️ 5. Wearable Energy Harvesters - 🗓️

27.10.2020 · Tweet

So lets get starting making nanomaterials! First – there are two main approaches: 1.Bottom up – starting from building blocks and making nanosized materials 📈 https://t.co/ECPZO1jb1a down – starting from a larger material and etching/milling it to make nanosized features 📉

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Pretty much everything I do is bottom up – so I’ll be talking about the ways we do this today! https://t.co/Dn3paG51mX

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Nanomaterials are tricky to make – you need to give them energy to grow 📈– but stop the process before they get too big! This means most processes use heat and/or pressure 🥵to provide energy to start the reaction – and cooling/quenching 🥶to stop it Lets get into it!

27.10.2020 · Tweet

We can do nanomaterials synthesis from gases, liquids or even solid starting material. Gases ⛽️ (not that gas!) are my favourite – so I’ll start talking about my long acquaintance, Chemical Vapour deposition or CVD 🔥🔥. https://t.co/Wz0MdG0dU6

27.10.2020 · Tweet

CVD is a quite simple process to talk about – everything is in the name – you take some ‘chemical vapours’ (gases) and ‘deposit’ them on a substrate to form a new material. https://t.co/pgyZ02nNeH

27.10.2020 · Tweet

In practice CVD is most commonly done with a tube furnace – effectively a long tube of quartz or alumina that runs through one or multiple furnaces. We hook this up to a vacuum pump so we can lower the pressure as needed. 👇 Thanks @stephen_beirne for the schematic! https://t.co/ZVvnFPW93R

27.10.2020 · Tweet

High temperatures ♨️ means we can vapourise our precursors and provide energy for them to react Low pressures 🌩️ makes it easier for our starting material to get into the gas phase or stay in the gas phase.

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Choosing the substrate for the gases to ‘deposit’ on is crucial as the crystal structure 💎💠♦️(or lack thereof) 🪟 of the substrate affects how the nanomaterial assembles!

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Lets talk about simple systems – carbons. Specifically carbon nanotubes. To grow carbon nanotubes we only need a single furnace, some hydrocarbon gas – typically methane, ethane, ethylene, or acetylene – and a metallic catalyst for the gases to deposit on. https://t.co/8P8wu2BBjl

27.10.2020 · Tweet

We heat the gas up to around 1000C 🔥 which causes it to break down into its atomic carbon and hydrogen components 💥🌬️. At the same time, the metallic 🪙 catalyst is changed by the high temperature as well.

27.10.2020 · Tweet

When carbon radicals at this high temperature interact with certain metals (Iron, Cobalt, or Nickel most notably) they dissolve in it (like in iron to make steel). You can picture this as a sponge absorbing water - although the carbon is chemically bound to the metal!🧽🌊

27.10.2020 · Tweet

These metal particles can only take so much carbon at once though, what happens when they’re full of carbon but we keep supplying hot gas? ⁉️🔎👇

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Well what happens is carbon keeps going into the metal particle, but because it’s full it pushes new solid carbon out of the other side, potentially forming carbon nanotubes! This is called the Vapour-Liquid-Solid mechanism (VLS) 👇 https://t.co/J1OgjjrqtL

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Depending on how fast you push carbon in (temperature/pressure/concentration), and what type of metal used, we can tune the length, diameter, and wall number of CNTs. This method is great for making large areas of nanotubes in defined geometries! You can even line them up! https://t.co/f4dKDAQWHN

27.10.2020 · Tweet

One of the things I like about science is your ability to take something simple, and change it and make something new. Carbon nanotubes are just hexagons all next to each other. 6⃣ What happens if you put a pentagon 5⃣ or heptagon 7⃣ in a CNT ⁉️

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Answer: They twist! https://t.co/teA2N8ldXY

27.10.2020 · Tweet

The advantage of making twisted carbon nanotube is they open-up a lot of space between adjacent carbon nanotubes – meaning we can fill this space with interesting things like electrolytes for batteries 🔋or chemical functionality of sensors📤! All that space 👇 https://t.co/zfcDMpLGBc

27.10.2020 · Tweet

We did this in our research by adding Sulfur to our CVD system, giving us exceptionally conductive, porous structures! We also cheated a bit by using acetylene to bind individual CNTs into a single film – because it reacts with itself! https://t.co/7S8Fa6Ufqy

27.10.2020 · Tweet

If you’re interested in this type of thing: We could use these devices for: Sensing: https://t.co/9szbTDUor7 Capacitors: https://t.co/dlFW6WDX2U Batteries: https://t.co/teVM1b8VyW Fuel Cells: https://t.co/2LQMaqV9d1 📰📰📰

27.10.2020 · Tweet

I'll move onto graphene, and transition metal dichalcogenides synthesis via CVD in a new thread a little later today! https://t.co/99WxmYU0sg

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Lets move away from Nanotubes 🗞️🗞️ now - into the wonderful world of 2D materials, Graphene and Transition Metal Dichalcogenides! 📜📃📄 https://t.co/dwhOhSoCDa

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Lets start with graphene – it’s the same chemistry as CNTs – but a different growth process 💥🌬️⁉️ First of all, rather than use metallic catalysts and metal particles – we use metal sheets (normally Nickel or Copper).

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Why the difference? – and I’ll focus on copper here because the nickel mechanism is a bit harder to explain. Well, graphene grows by templating on the crystal lattice of the metal and the copper surface – normally (111) – is ideal for this. https://t.co/r6KxhQrxcD

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Secondly, because the ‘solubility’ of carbon in copper is so low the reactive carbon species from our gas phase doesn’t dissolve in and then precipitate out of copper during cooling breaking the up the newly formed carbon layer! (from: https://t.co/EXozD0exzJ) https://t.co/ThQpvUMjev

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Since this method is effectively chemical self-assembly 🧪you can start to do 3D structures 👇📰– provided your starting architecture is smooth and pure enough! Getting graphene off 3D foams in one piece is a whole other problem - but that's not for today! 🤦‍♀️🤦‍♂️🤦 https://t.co/Z1x81Pohfz

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Transition metal dichalcogenide CVD growth is a bit more complicated! ⁉️ They template on a substrate just like graphene ✅ – but now you need to have a chemical reaction between two different elements as well🧞🧙‍♀️! Don't worry - it's not magic - still chemistry!

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Due to this difference you start to use a lot more gases! Rather than just a hydrocarbon and hydrogen as active gases, for TMDs you either use solid precursors, or inorganic vapours containing each element itself! https://t.co/o4pd8sPA7W

27.10.2020 · Tweet

My work has focused on using solid precursors for synthesis – so I’ll focus on that here. Because we are using different starting materials we now need different temperature at different points in the furnace 🔥 to get each one in the gas phase 💨 at the right time ⏲️!

27.10.2020 · Tweet

To give you an idea of the spread of temperatures – for one of the most common TMDS – tungsten sulphide (WS2) – we used 150C for sulfur and 850C for tungsten! This is a huge temperature gradient 🏔️.

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Also because the ‘weight’ of the element being carried in the gas phase is a lot heavier – these will deposit on a substrate at different positions along the tube furnace. Finding the right place where the right amount of S and W deposit is crucial! See below 👇 https://t.co/iuRRZkcTC2

27.10.2020 · Tweet

If you do it right though, you can get beautiful triangles. https://t.co/JvCkSXWtWl

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Or beautiful films (the blue is MoS2, the purple is the silicon substrate!) https://t.co/NCsDrza2Oj

27.10.2020 · Tweet

And if you change how the TMDs bind to the surface, you can even make the 3D structures I’m so fond of! https://t.co/fmzIikVZHF

27.10.2020 · Tweet

TMDs are great for catalysis! Have a look how we used these systems to break down salt water here: https://t.co/TUeOjJh1pC And how we describe the fundamental growth processes here: https://t.co/jfcVYaT40E

27.10.2020 · Tweet

I’ve tried to keep this pretty simple – please comment below if you have any questions or want any concepts expanded on!

27.10.2020 · Tweet

I'll be back a bit later to talk about our solution phase synthesis of metal nanoparticles and some more TMDs! https://t.co/jmr7WhTM5x

27.10.2020 · Tweet

@MySci_PK Lets see if I can dig them up - these ones are pretty old! https://t.co/m3rV76mlM0

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Moving on from gas 💨 phase synthesis - lets have a talk about how to make some selected nanomaterials in solution 🥤! I'll talk about: 1. Transition metal dichalcogenides 📜📜; and 2. Metal nanoparticles 🪙 https://t.co/PzfqMQHLwk

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Lets start with TMDs! Growing TMDs in solution is quite tricky - you need to: A) find two starting materials of the metal, and the chalcogen that can dissolve in the same solvent; ✅and B) Make them come together in the right way to grow a 2D material ✖️

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Luckily there are a lot of different precursors out there. But making them come together in the right way is not so simple! https://t.co/YxAvwcsxlK

27.10.2020 · Tweet

There are a lot of different variables that you can try in solution phase synthesis: 1. Temperature ♨️ 2. Pressure 🌩️ 3. Solvent 🥤 4. Precursor ⁉️ 5. Concentration 📈 6. Rate of precursor addition 💉 7. Time ⏲️ 8. Additives 💊 and many more https://t.co/kvtM9a9yxh

27.10.2020 · Tweet

For 2D materials - (like TMDs) - the key things to control that give you an advantage are the solvent and the additives. It is crucial to select an additive (or ligand) that binds strongly to one 'face' of your material - this can stop your crystal growing in that direction!

27.10.2020 · Tweet

The problem then becomes controlling nucleation - growing pure 2D sheets is hard - all start from the same point and grow outwards into beautiful flowers! 🌻🌹💮 Below is some of our work growing WSe2 and Bi2Te3 (ok tha'ts not a TMD but still 2D!) Scale bar = 5 nm @MySci_PK https://t.co/aK8GkcB7pH

27.10.2020 · Tweet

If you're interested in reading on these type of things in more detail - including a great review on how to make TMDs in any way - check out these 👀👀: WSe2: https://t.co/ynt1AK8H9L Bi2Te3: https://t.co/N744tZXPJy Review: https://t.co/wgsueaIwyX

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Now we've got the complexity of growing 2D materials in solution out of the way - lets talk about how to do metal nanoparticles. These are a lot simpler to control because you don't have worry about restricting their growth in any direction! 😅

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Instead, the key challenge in growing metal nanoparticles 🔹is to stop them growing into being - well - just particles 🔷!

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Similar to the selective ligands we used for 2D materials, for metal nanoparticles a 'capping agent' to stop them continually growing or 'agglomerating' is normally used. The most common of these is sodium citrate - something that comes from citric acid!

27.10.2020 · Tweet

There are a multitude of chemistries that you can use to make metal nanoparticles. I'm going to talk about my favourite way because it's: 1. Quick ⏲️ 2. Easy ✅ 3. Cheap 🪙

27.10.2020 · Tweet

If you take a metal salt, something like Gold Chloride, and put it in Ethylene Glycol - heat it up and stir it overnight you'll notice you get a beautiful colour change 👇👇 - it's basic - but if you add NaOH it'll go even faster. https://t.co/f80UbWt5A8

27.10.2020 · Tweet

This still takes a few hours - and if you're particularly impatient (like me) you'll want to harvest your gold dust even quicker. We're already heating ♨️, we're already adjusting pH 🧪 - so how do we speed it up even further?

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Well, you really just need to find a way to provide more energy ⚡️ to your reaction! The easiest way in this case was to place it in an old microwave! (yes the type you reheat food in) 🧑‍🍳

27.10.2020 · Tweet

If you put the same solution in a microwave and turn it on for just 120s you get beautiful reduction (to give you an idea below here is the 'absorption spectra' of both normal, and microwave reduction) https://t.co/dvd7t4MjWd

27.10.2020 · Tweet

I'm talking about gold here, but the same thing holds true for platinum, palladium, nickel, silver, copper, and cobalt nanoparticles - just with different starting precursors.

27.10.2020 · Tweet

120s is great, 2 minutes. But can we make this even faster?? The answer is yes✅! If you add a tiny amount of carbon nanotubes - you take this time from 120s to 10s for reduction⌛️. Why? - what's going on here? https://t.co/BjuJukYdyG

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Well, the structure of CNTs has lots of C=C double bonds - and one thing C=C double bonds are good at is absorbing microwave energy. This means at the wall of the CNTs two things are happening: 1. Localised heating; and 2. They become highly reactive (forming a carbon radical) https://t.co/xWwuzGiNIF

27.10.2020 · Tweet

This carbon radical is highly highly reactive - and will donate it's electron to 'reduce' the metal salt in solution to a metal nanoparticle. The CNTs become a little less conductive - but we can live with that! Proposed mechanism below 👇 (from: https://t.co/dlFW6WDX2U) https://t.co/ZbJHLyPZaW

27.10.2020 · Tweet

So what does this look like? Beautiful assemblies of CNTs and metal nanoparticles - just the start of our assembling of the nano(avenger) materials! All in just 10s! https://t.co/j0LUjttQPS

27.10.2020 · Tweet

Again - I've tried to talk about concepts rather than specific details, but any questions leave a comment below! 👇 I'll be back later to talk a bit about the art of science! https://t.co/WjrRFiSt1e

28.10.2020 · Tweet

@Lolchu These are called 5,7-ring defects. The bonding of the sidewall of CNTs is really a delocalised sp2 network. When you interrupt the aromaticity of an area (i.e. a 5,7-ring defect) you are change one (or more) carbons in those rings to sp3 - and cause the CNT to bend or twist 👇 https://t.co/3zFWZ1fris

28.10.2020 · Tweet

@Lolchu Something I didn't detail too much in the thread above is there is a lot of H during CNT synthesis from: 1. H2 gas 2. decomposition of hydrocarbons In our case, either H or S - can react with these defect sites to form either sulphate functionality or hydrogen termination.

28.10.2020 · Tweet

@Lolchu The modelling CNT growth is in nanoseconds! It's a hot system (around 1000C) so it's really unclear exactly what the bonding state is during the actual reaction. Or at least it's beyond my understanding. We characterise the produced materials and infer understanding from that

28.10.2020 · Tweet

@thushrocks It is related to the size of the particle - but not wholly dependent on it. Due to the temperature of the reaction the metal itself can get deformed quite dramatically 👇 The image shows a Ni particle in a CNT - this happens when you have weak substrate-metal interactions https://t.co/EuD8bUp6dk

28.10.2020 · Tweet

@thushrocks Have a look at 'fluidized bed' CVD , where particle size is even more loosely defined. You can even grown aligned CNTs on metal foils - where there is no clearly defined particle at all. It's all about carbon solubility and catalyst-substrate interactions!
