@barrygoldman1 These actually came from a failed experiment - their a mix of copper, tungsten and sulfur. We were looking at trying to grow WS2 via chemical vapour deposition on 3D substrates - and of course - we just made W-doped copper sulfide!

29.10.2020 · Tweet

@MySci_PK This one was Tungsten Disulfide - interesting thing about this sample was the open pore structure on top actually changed the colour of the film - these were a deep teal/green colour 🟩. A nice change when everything you're used to working with was black ⚫️😅

29.10.2020 · Tweet

@barrygoldman1 We didn't have a look at it too specifically for these samples but in general: 1. They grow like this (sort of like fractals) because you start from a (very hot) solid metal foam and are flowing hot gases over it. The metal absorbs/reacts with the elements in the gas and expands

29.10.2020 · Tweet

@barrygoldman1 because the sample is expanding and absorbing new elements it tries to expand in directions where there is more space to move (hence a spiral/fractal sort of pattern). 2. The rounded edges come from the symmetry of the crystal structures unit cell (the smallest crystal possible)

29.10.2020 · Tweet

@barrygoldman1 in this case, its lower energy for the crystal to grow along certain 'facets' of the crystal structure, so they form rounded edges. That's oversimplifying it a bit - these are grown at 1000C at low pressure - so there's quite a lot going on!

29.10.2020 · Tweet

@barrygoldman1 Sorry! I still need to work on my communication 😉 The field I work in is Nanotechnology - although it's super broad. This is a (high T) crystallisation reaction, so falls under physical chemistry - wiki has a decent summary - but it's quite technical: https://t.co/xiUOzOpQYe

29.10.2020 · Tweet

@barrygoldman1 Geodes are from solution. These are grown from vapour at around 1000C, I'm not confident enough to ascribe it to a simple rate (i.e. fast = fractal or slow = fractal)

29.10.2020 · Tweet

@barrygoldman1 There area lot of competing factors - these are also not homogenous pure crystals - they're a solid solution of Cu and W with some S thrown in - so their stoichiometry varies wildly. These were also cooled quite rapidly, from 1000C to 25C in about 15min - which has a huge impact

We're getting towards the end of the week and ticking off topics ☑️✅✔️ Today I'll be talking about my favourite - assembling or 'structuring' nanomaterials 🗼

29.10.2020 · Tweet

Before we start - let's talk about why nanomaterials are so impactful for research 👩‍🔬and society👨‍👨‍👧‍👧 Then we can start talk about how and why we put them back together!

29.10.2020 · Tweet

When you take a large material and shrink it down to have nanoscale dimensions - quite a few things change - even if it maintains it's same shape. One of the biggest things is a dramatic increase in surface area 👇 https://t.co/N902sybB0V

29.10.2020 · Tweet

This increase is hugely important because surfaces are: How the material interacts with its surrounding environment 🏝️ Where chemical reactions can occur ⚗️ High energy ⚡️- they want to merge together to form a lower energy system ❌!

29.10.2020 · Tweet

This means as we make a material smaller, we can use less of the material but still have the same amount of chemical/electrical or device performance! https://t.co/Ps3JlUeFM3

29.10.2020 · Tweet

As you enter the nanosize domain, your nanomaterials typically have a dimension that is close to the wavelength of light (~400-700 nm). This means you also start to get some really cool optical effects! https://t.co/nPqKpI3HnC

29.10.2020 · Tweet

Stopping to think about it - having all this surface area, and ability to interact with light is super cool. ❄️ I already mentioned the high surface area means things want to combine together to form a larger material again. So how do we keep our amazing properties? Assembly! https://t.co/hiElxbJNCU

29.10.2020 · Tweet

Starting with my old favourite! Carbon Nanotubes. I've already spoken about growing aligned carbon nanotubes via chemical vapour deposition 👇 https://t.co/SJUWTbWcwH

29.10.2020 · Tweet

The aligned carbon nanotubes are amazing materials - but you'll notice that if you look at the top surface - there is zero space between adjacent CNTs. ❌ This is because of the strong 'van der Waals' interactions between adjacent CNTs leading to a tightly packed structure! 💪💪

29.10.2020 · Tweet

This means all that beautiful advantageous surface area I introduced above - we simply can't access! Nothing can get between the CNTs to interact with them. ☹️ (these find great applications in membranes). ✔️

29.10.2020 · Tweet

However, by changing the growth process just slightly (adding in some Sulphur) - we can stop these materials stacking together - and suddenly we have a lot of free space and can access all the surface area of the carbon nanotubes! I've added a photo to give size context as well https://t.co/94Tc0rXFjV

29.10.2020 · Tweet

This free space induced by our growth method is really important if you're looking at electrochemical energy storage devices. For those not familiar, supercapacitors, fuel cells, and batteries all rely on the interface between an electrolyte (containing ions) and an electrode.

29.10.2020 · Tweet

The ions in the electrolyte need to be able to move freely in the device in response to either a load (discharging) or energy input (charging). Diffusion is a physical process - so having this open pore structure lets ions move much more quickly! So we can charge much faster! https://t.co/aNfLGVH8AF

29.10.2020 · Tweet

CNTs are great by themselves, they're electrically conductive, strong, and chemically stable. ☑️✅ However, if you're looking at something catalytic - like a fuel cell or water splitting - you typically need an active material. You can probably guess - metal nanoparticles! https://t.co/hR1h2MVjF3

29.10.2020 · Tweet

Getting metal nanoparticles into this free space between carbon nanotubes without clogging all the pores is tricky! This is why I put all that effort into producing them super quickly using microwaves.

29.10.2020 · Tweet

Since microwaves interact strongly with CNTs - we get metal nanoparticle reduction *only* at the interface between the CNTs and the solution. Meaning our pores stay open!! 👇 https://t.co/cXGTZwzowB

29.10.2020 · Tweet

So our overall process ends up looking something like this 👇 And the furnace was pretty hot! https://t.co/Fpj1rNVqFZ

29.10.2020 · Tweet

So why do we care about all of this at the end of the day? Well the catalyst for fuel cells is platinum - platinum is expensive and scarce. Using our method we reduced the amount of platinum needed to run a fuel cell by a factor of 10!! https://t.co/T9jhaoNZqs

29.10.2020 · Tweet

This is super cool - but it's still a flat film? What if we want to do this on complex structures. Well we can - by a complex substrate with precursor we can grow these same structures over nearly anything! Steel substrates 👇 https://t.co/XHxPcPrpXR

29.10.2020 · Tweet

Carbon foams 👇 (https://t.co/FCsgLYUdlF) https://t.co/hnhcoGh7qr

29.10.2020 · Tweet

or even (carbonised) paper! (https://t.co/en8vRZb7xm) https://t.co/V1ZUGgJU3q

29.10.2020 · Tweet

I'll be back in a little bit to talk about assembling different types of nanomaterials and what we can do with them!

30.10.2020 · Tweet

Lets get back into it! I've spoken a bit about electrochemical energy storage - what about the optical side of assembling materials? 👁️ https://t.co/h9KtGiNWo6 https://t.co/JLxUOmRjH4

30.10.2020 · Tweet

One of the interesting things about the hydrogen economy - is the huge abundance of water 🌊. Of course, lots of that water is salty which makes splitting water into oxygen and hydrogen quite difficult.

30.10.2020 · Tweet

There are a few ways you can split water: electricity ⚡️ (electrolysis) electricity ⚡️+ a catalyst 🐈(electrocatalysis) light 🌞+ electricity ⚡️+ catalyst 🐈(photoelectrocatalysis) light 🌞 + a catalyst 🐈 (photocatalysis) My assembly work is around photoelectrocatalysis

30.10.2020 · Tweet

The catalysts role is to lower the energy needed to split water. Adding light or electricity can provide any energy still needed to either allow the reaction, or make it happen faster.

30.10.2020 · Tweet

All of this will still happen in solution - so everything I talked about before - diffusion to and from a nanomaterial - is still crucial! You also need lots of material to make enough hydrogen to be worthwhile!

30.10.2020 · Tweet

So 2D materials for water splitting, how do we structure these. The first work we did was driven by the brilliant @Budinelli - making thin films of two different transition metal dichalcogenides (MoS2/WS2) 👇 https://t.co/EXb8XI64sZ

30.10.2020 · Tweet

This work (that we published here: https://t.co/WBf5bGAxAu) - showed the first use of TMDs as photoelectrocatalysts for water oxidation✅☑️✔️! But it had problems Low efficiency ❌ Low overall current ❌

30.10.2020 · Tweet

So what happens when we take a 2D film of these materials, and take it into 3D structures? Our efficiency goes 👆 Our total current goes up 👆 Why? https://t.co/sJMQ0Krojb

30.10.2020 · Tweet

Well basically for 2 reasons; 1. having a rough surface causes light to bounce around more, so a photon that's not absorbed intially can be absorbed by another part of the electrode 2. a much better contact between MoS2 and WS2 - meaning charge can move in the system easier! https://t.co/TCGhQ8wezR

30.10.2020 · Tweet

I'm running a bit late today but I'll be back to finish this thread soon! If you're interested in reading more: https://t.co/TUeOjJh1pC

31.10.2020 · Tweet

Running out of time for what I wanted to talk about this week ⌛️ Lets get back into assembling nanomaterials and how we can use these to harvest energy from motion! 🏃‍♀️

31.10.2020 · Tweet

One of the really cool things about nanomaterials - is because of their high surface area ratio - you can put a tiny amount of them in a different material, and dramatically change that materials properties 📈! Stronger ✔️ More conductive ✅ Change the crystal structure ☑️

31.10.2020 · Tweet

The crucial thing to understand when adding a nanomaterial into a different material - is how they interact both chemically ⚗️and electrically ⚡️ If you can control these interactions, you can make your new composite material have amazing properties!

31.10.2020 · Tweet

The easiest nanomaterial to talk about this sense is either carbon nanotubes 🗞️or graphenes 📰 These are typically pure carbon when they're made, but can be easily functionalised with oxygen, nitrogen, or even sulfur groups - making them more water loving or 'hydrophillic'

31.10.2020 · Tweet

This is really important for electrochemical storage devices - because you want the electrolyte (which can be either water based or an organic chemical) to want to touch the surface of the nanomaterial. 👇 is a drop of water on pure, or oxygen functionalised carbon nanotubes! https://t.co/f6HILnQ69f

31.10.2020 · Tweet

A similiar effect happens when you mix nanomaterials with polymers, how the polymer 'wets' the nanotube is crucial for a good transfer of properties. https://t.co/Ob1e47yZv8

31.10.2020 · Tweet

The polymers we're particularly interested in mixing nanomaterials with are 'piezoelectric' polymers. These polymers can change mechanical force (like running 🏃, vibrations 🔊, cars driving 🚗) and make electricity from it!

31.10.2020 · Tweet

To reason these polymers can convert mechanical to electrical energy is they have an asymmetric structure. The most common type of piezoelectric polymer is polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF). 👇 https://t.co/bEQlJB4A7A

31.10.2020 · Tweet

But just being asymmetric isn't enough, they also need to be arranged in a certain way (the Beta/Gamma structures above) 👆 And then these arrangements need to be aligned within the whole film! 👇 That's a lot of control needed from the nanoscopic up to the macroscale order! https://t.co/1SAm64E2OZ

31.10.2020 · Tweet

I'm not going to go into detail here, there are some great papers out there if you really want to dive into the science of this including from our own groups @ShepelinN https://t.co/xp87pNfjZ8

31.10.2020 · Tweet

What we try to do with our nanomaterials is control how these domains of polymers are aligned. So we can save loads of time ⏳, energy ⚡️, and money 💰 in making these materials.

31.10.2020 · Tweet

We used a modelling tool called molecular dynamics - done by the amazing Dr Eirini Goudeli (https://t.co/veTjua0L8F) - to show that if we add just a tiny amount of carbon nanotubes into our polymer we could control how the polymer assembled on a macroscale!

31.10.2020 · Tweet

Check out our beautiful dancing polymers along a carbon nanotube 👇👇 (from another of superstar @ShepelinN papers: https://t.co/yiD23OISPl) https://t.co/T0oI9iQZxt

31.10.2020 · Tweet

If we do this we can make polymer patches in 30s for around 0.4AUD each that can make voltage from a finger tap over 100s of cycles - even able to charge a capacitor! https://t.co/DFOE5tHqBH

31.10.2020 · Tweet

We showed that this effect wasn't because of a change in crystallisation of the polymer, we didn't have more beta/gamma than without nanotubes - rather it was the way the nanotubes and polymer aligned together made all the domains point the same way! https://t.co/JIf3CmKses

31.10.2020 · Tweet

The next steps for us are to figure out how we can do this better - improve the assembly of nanomaterials, by changing the chemistry, geometry, and type of material! But - I'm not ready to talk about that bit yet 😉

31.10.2020 · Tweet

I'll be back for my last curation day tomorrow to talk about my perspective on research in a COVID world, and try to give some tips for aspiring researchers! https://t.co/bzXDSbOksG

04.11.2020 · Tweet

I've been a bit slack finishing up 📰📜🧑‍💼- so this will be my last thread from this account. I hope you've enjoyed the topics I've covered and please ask me questions @NanoIn3D about anything! Lets get into: 1) Research in a COVID world; and 2) Advice for new scientists! 👇

04.11.2020 · Tweet

This year has been like no other. (Obviously). It has disrupted every industry to some degree Academic research is no different, my perspective is tinged from 🇦🇺Australia but there are common threads globally that tie it all together. 🌏

04.11.2020 · Tweet

Lets talk about immediate impacts ⏲️ 1. Researchers unable to access lab facilities This is the most obvious problem - the pipeline of experiments that flows is disrupted. People can keep generating outputs from previous data, but in 2021 and 2022 scientific reporting will drop.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

2. Significant delays in shipping ordering chemicals Even when we get into the lab - getting anything is super slow, this makes planning - already ridiculously difficult at the moment - even harder

04.11.2020 · Tweet

3. Increased teaching load giving remote lectures. Each hour of lecturing takes 2 to 3 times longer to do remotely than to do face to face, this increase further takes away from researchers time doing, well, you know, research! 🧪

04.11.2020 · Tweet

Those are immediate, not including the huge mental health and anxiety challenges that are exasperated by the pandemic. Academia already has a disproportionally high rate of mental health issues. This needs to be addressed separately from the pandemic.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

Slightly longer term: 1. Decreased enrollment numbers - means less student fees and less institutional funding for research AND less for research support - administration that is just as important.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

2. Decreased access to undergraduate students - means it's challenging to recruit new Masters and PhD students into a lab. Couple this to:

04.11.2020 · Tweet

3. Closed Borders - means getting international students in is nearly impossible right now. Again there will be a flow on effect in a couple of years from this. Students are finishing, there are very few to replace them.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

4. University job losses - in the Australian sector these have been massive. We can't quantify them because of the casualisation of the workforce (another problem that needs a separate thread) - but even the fixed term/continuing staff that have been let go is a huge number.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

This has all been negative so far, well unfortunately the pandemic has been pretty damn disruptive to scientific research, and government funding cuts/exclusion of universities from government pandemic support has made this worse.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

There are positives through. (Australian) Universities have been brilliantly positive in allowing people to work from home, we are able to keep getting paid, and work remotely - this is likely to continue into the new year.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

There has been a boom in virtual conferences, allowing those who would otherwise be unable to travel able to access a much bigger pool of events. Anything that helps inclusivity in science is important to preserve.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

The constant 'Zooming' means there is very little difference if a collaborator is next door or halfway around the world - so it's easier to work with people globally.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

There are lower expectations. Science glorifies overworking, sacrificing everything for your 'passion', and a false belief that 'if there is a will there is a way' (there just isn't in the competitive nature of research funding sometimes - rejection isn't a reflection on you).

04.11.2020 · Tweet

The pandemic has helped shift this (in Australia), people understand the challenges (like in my case daycare being closed so having a 2 year old climb over me constantly). Whether Institutions recognize this career interruption long term is a different story. https://t.co/ArZspoUR5c

04.11.2020 · Tweet

The pandemic has brought massive challenges to academic research, those changes will be felt for the next 10 years at least. You quite simply can't turn it on and off like a tap. It's a pipeline of skilled people who leak out of the system when the tap is off.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

Right - away from that gloom! Advice for up-and-coming researchers 👇 https://t.co/Sf62szT47n

04.11.2020 · Tweet

My biggest advice is always two things: 1. Find research you really enjoy, a topic you're interested in, or tasks you like doing - pursue that. There are benefits to academic life - but the pitfalls are so much worse if you're doing something you dont enjoy.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

2. Find out what the group leader is like to work for, a good group leader makes your work enjoyable. A negative group leader will crush you - if you're applying for a Ph.D. this is particularly important, have a chat to previous Ph.D. students.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

Apart from that it's about being proactive from the first day you step into research, apply for grants you're eligible for, be selective about (but definitely get involved in) relevant societies.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

and finally, put your face out there - talk to everyone. Network, network, network. Academia has a lot of nepotism (it's getting better but...) - getting to know people will give you an advantage in the job/PhD hunt.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

Don't make assumptions about who someone is, take the time to meet and talk to everyone you can at conferences/events/meetings - you never know when that person next to you might be your best collaborator, or a future employer/industry rep interested in investing.

04.11.2020 · Tweet

Hi, Cornelia Hofmann (@coenneli) at the helm for this week 😃 No, I didn’t start on the #VendeeGlobe2020, I am a theoretical physicist in strong-field attosecond science, aka shooting atoms apart with very short laser pulses. But I don’t have cool lab shots, so here we are 😉 https://t.co/9d05tQj9pE

09.11.2020 · Tweet

and then had a postdoc position at @maxplanckpress Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems in Dresden. And yes, most of the time my “complex system” consisted of a helium atom and a laser field. #womeninSTEM https://t.co/XYxFmGIGO5

So, what am I going to talk about during my takeover? Here’s my current plan (I might adapt it, depending on your feedback and responses): Later today I will give you an introduction to my field of research, scale you down from the world of nano down to atoms and electrons. ⚛️

09.11.2020 · Tweet

Right, now, on to attoscience (which combines #quantum #physics with #ultrashort #lasers). First, I dusted off an overview slide of my thesis presentation. Attoscience studies electron motion in bound states, ionization processes, charge transfer, and similar. https://t.co/IDKAncL5Ir

09.11.2020 · Tweet

All of this happens on the time scale of attoseconds, 10⁻¹⁸ seconds (and sometimes femtoseconds = 10⁻¹⁵ s), which is almost unimaginably fast. In the short intro podcast with @the_ScienceTalk, I explained the comparison with the age of our universe. https://t.co/LRsB1gNSff

09.11.2020 · Tweet

To measure such fast dynamics we need an equally as fast tool, which is laser pulses of a few femtosecond duration or shorter. Because a lot of energy is compressed in a very short time, the peak power of these pulses can reach terawatts (similar to nuclear power plants). 😲☢️ https://t.co/dkE1aAaLW2

09.11.2020 · Tweet

These high intensities of the electric field can then compete with the binding Coulomb force in atoms (and molecules, larger structures, ...) and not only mess with the energy levels, but also cause ionisations. https://t.co/AHhoOphqBD

09.11.2020 · Tweet

Now you might wonder, what on earth does that have to do with nanoscience? Well, in my personal research, I have exploited the interaction of nanostructures with the laser field to create various spatial structures in the electric field. But more on that later in the week.

09.11.2020 · Tweet

Besides that, attoscience is concerned with understanding the dynamics of electrons in various materials, the field has started from studying atoms, to include molecules, surfaces, semiconductor structures, liquids…

09.11.2020 · Tweet

You see where this is going? I talked a bit more about that in the @the_ScienceTalk podcast which will be released on Wednesday 🤗

09.11.2020 · Tweet

@MySci_PK I did once help out in a science fair where our booth was titled "faster than what the police allows" 😂👮 (in German) https://t.co/S8C9MAMBf3

Hello everyone! To talk about my research, I decided to theme it by "studying the ionisation process itself" (today) and "possible things that can happen afterwards" (tomorrow). https://t.co/ABoN1AJ5yO

10.11.2020 · Tweet

I'm going to keep the explanations in the threads fairly colloquial. But I will link the corresponding publications (open access whenever possible) so you can dig into the details there if you wish. Or of course, just ask me any questions you might have and I'll expand on that 😉

10.11.2020 · Tweet

Yesterday I have already introduced the idea that the strong electric field of the laser pulse modifies the Coulomb potential which keeps electrons in bound states. The video shows a classical picture of this: https://t.co/VhfiL03IlZ

10.11.2020 · Tweet

However, we are actually dealing with a quantum system, and for typical strong-field parameters, most of the ionisation processes happen by quantum-tunnelling through the potential barrier https://t.co/gzh0A961nb

10.11.2020 · Tweet

One of the key questions which is still being investigated in detail is then, what the electron wavefunction looks like at the end of this tunnelling process. Does it have some momentum? How wide is its spread? https://t.co/UINPh87MuJ

10.11.2020 · Tweet

These characteristics are important because they determine where the electron (probability distribution) will go subsequently, and this is precisely what is measured at the end on a detector. (video not mine) https://t.co/BjnG6vdTkg

10.11.2020 · Tweet

By comparing simulations with different momentum distributions along the tunnel-ionisation direction against a set of experimental measurements, we found that the (previously common) assumption of (almost) 0 momentum along that direction is not a good approximation.

10.11.2020 · Tweet

publisher version: https://t.co/OmJqLly5lY open access (OA): https://t.co/5YrHVTZ84l

10.11.2020 · Tweet

And this finding is independent of whether we are in an adiabatic regime (i.e. the wavefunction can always instantaneously adapt to any situation) or non-adiabatic (i.e. the temporal evolution matters) https://t.co/Wha2Ir9xua OA: https://t.co/hBQfCBSIZC

10.11.2020 · Tweet

Another key question is: "how long does this process take?" ⏲️. At first glance, this might sound like a straightforward question, but since the phenomenon of quantum tunnelling has been discovered almost 100 years ago, there has been a debate about this. https://t.co/ahfToRizYk

10.11.2020 · Tweet

So, #attoscience tries to time-resolve electron dynamics, where one of the dominant processes is quantum tunnelling 😉 Of course, our field developed both additional theories and several experiments to try and measure the/a tunnelling time https://t.co/krsPPMHHWD

10.11.2020 · Tweet

Most commonly, the laser field is elliptically polarised, so that the electric field rotates around like a clock, but still has clearly defined moments of strongest field leading to highest probability of ionisation https://t.co/VR1hG4PPxl

10.11.2020 · Tweet

The interaction with the laser field after ionisation imprints the moment when an electron exits from the potential barrier onto the final momentum direction. This moment appears to be later than the maximum ionisation probability moment. (first image: https://t.co/FKP8c2Pw9I) https://t.co/XYgCwLL1Lb

10.11.2020 · Tweet

Unfortunately, this "exit time↔️final momentum" mapping is disturbed by many factors, such as the Coulomb attraction of the parent ion, momenta/energy at the tunnel exit, and more. This debate still continues... https://t.co/PGuFaqnNMR

10.11.2020 · Tweet

about me: https://t.co/kxln6Un7GI

10.11.2020 · Tweet

Quick Crash Course to the research field: https://t.co/FYxsuHWMEk

10.11.2020 · Tweet

Investigating strong-field ionisation itself: https://t.co/D3JuyrYTRC

Good evening! While my fan heater is doing its job, why don't we catch some electrons? https://t.co/yDtMYkK43p

11.11.2020 · Tweet

In yesterday's thread, the electrons which have been freed from their bound state by the laser mostly just oscillated around (steered by the electric field) and eventually flew off and away (until they hit a detector). https://t.co/h7dlDy6I3e

11.11.2020 · Tweet

However, not all electrons are so lucky. For some of them, their trajectory ends up looking almost like that lasso up there. This is if their kinetic energy at the end of the laser pulse is not quite enough to escape from the Coulomb potential of the atom/ion. https://t.co/FAfAJGaFIc

11.11.2020 · Tweet

The nucleus is marked by the "x" at position (0,0,0). The electron exits from the quantum tunnel (beginning of the red dotted path) and starts oscillating in the laser field until it ends up on an elliptical, bound trajectory (blue dotted) once the pulse has passed. https://t.co/GQOBX6kbYJ

11.11.2020 · Tweet

The blue bound trajectory looks like a Kepler orbit, because the maths is (almost) the same: Planets are kept on their elliptical orbits by gravity, while electrons are bound by the Coulomb attraction with the ion (except, one is a quantum particle and one clearly isn't 😉). https://t.co/HAvUyyEGiY

11.11.2020 · Tweet

Therefore, the final fate of these types of electrons is a highly excited bound state aka Rydberg state. And if we look at the entire process as one, there is no actual ionisation happening, in the end, we are left with a neutral, but highly excited, atom again. https://t.co/L4c6O4SiSV

11.11.2020 · Tweet

I should probably also mention the units on the plots: a.u. = atomic units. Our preferred units because all the important reference quantities of an electron are set to unity. 1 a.u. in length equals the Bohr radius, approximately ½ Å.

11.11.2020 · Tweet

If the laser is polarised linearly (or only has low ellipticity), a significant part of all tunnelled electrons ends up in Rydberg states. We can then use them for different purposes in our investigations, for example:

11.11.2020 · Tweet

taking them as a reference point to study shifts in the photoelectron momentum distribution https://t.co/1recHd4UrH (OA: https://t.co/BNvcGloutm)

11.11.2020 · Tweet

or searching for (and finding) non-adiabatic effects, meaning that the dynamics of the process is relatively fast and the wavefunction reacts to the entire temporal history rather than only a given instantaneous situation https://t.co/ZrVAVVjINZ (OA: https://t.co/D5fN8oHVIB)

11.11.2020 · Tweet

Tunnelled electrons which don't manage to escape from their parent ion: https://t.co/dcxifHkzFK

I have this itch to swing back to talking about physics after yesterdays more meta thread, much like a pendulum always striving towards the middle position, but constantly overshooting. BTW, pendulums are an excellent representation of how short laser pulses are created! https://t.co/oDO2eRyvYq

13.11.2020 · Tweet

You have probably heard (or learned) that laser light has a very defined colour (one specific wavelength/frequency), and all photons are in phase with each other, all their waves are perfectly synchronised (coherent). (Image source: https://t.co/ad2csUMm1u) https://t.co/hg0vR934iE

13.11.2020 · Tweet

However, if we only allow one single wavelength, then the laser light is continuous. Only when we add up several slightly different wavelengths (or frequencies) do we get a short and intense pulse, right at the moment when all those different waves happen to align with each other https://t.co/9iDFGM7JGG

13.11.2020 · Tweet

Before and after, when all the different contributions are not perfectly aligned, their individual troths and peaks partially (or completely) compensate each other. https://t.co/X4Nn0k1TWS

13.11.2020 · Tweet

Obeying the laws of the Fourier Transforms, shorter pulses require a broader spectrum. And ultrashort pulses consequently require a very broad spectrum, which means only very few lasing materials can be used to create these. [https://t.co/7lC7vUJ2uH]

13.11.2020 · Tweet

With Ti:sapphire lasers, the pulse duration can be around 5 - 30 femtoseconds (fs). For the attoclock method, this is fine because one rotation of the field is around 2.7 fs, giving attosecond resolution in the angle. https://t.co/ioQWdW4Gdu

13.11.2020 · Tweet

But for most other methods, we need pulses which are themselves shorter than one femtosecond. We are exploiting an effect which is part of strong-field physics: High Harmonic Generation (HHG), which converts infrared photons of a fs pulse into extreme ultraviolet (XUV) photons. https://t.co/16JwRTPZmo

13.11.2020 · Tweet

The key components of HHG are beautifully demonstrated in this video by the Photonics and Laser Applications Group of University of Salamanca, and JILA, University of Colorado https://t.co/dJmHms6MGr

13.11.2020 · Tweet

In my own research, I have 1⃣ looked into phase-matching: How coherent are the different XUV photons which are being emitted by all the recombining electrons distributed in the gas cloud? https://t.co/ugryUi8XzC

13.11.2020 · Tweet

and 2⃣ also played around with: what happens if the laser field is a mix of two very different frequencies creating a fancy pattern? And if additionally, you have nano-particles nearby, creating a spatial dependence in the laser field? (second image: https://t.co/WYcVpxYaHc) https://t.co/D4AwqyBHwY

13.11.2020 · Tweet

(yes, this is me actually talking about something nano finally 😉)

13.11.2020 · Tweet

The three-fold symmetry is imprinted onto the typical paths that electrons are taking (first image). But with the spatial dependence on top, that symmetry is completely broken (second image), and the energies with which these electrons are recombining are vastly different. https://t.co/HZd5JlHs8m

13.11.2020 · Tweet

Preliminary results of this investigation are on arXiV: https://t.co/WwFYp4SKQ5

13.11.2020 · Tweet

Hi everyone :-D We have reached the weekend already. Over the last few days, I hope I managed to give you a small glimpse into my research field. But one promise I have not yet delivered on: Where will all of this lead? What's the point? https://t.co/42NTKJZwa7

14.11.2020 · Tweet

First of all, I don't think I have to convince you that the quantum tunnelling phenomenon is found in all kinds of fields. Recently I came across a paper discussing tunnelling times during a photosynthesis cycle in an organic molecule. https://t.co/3TYV78sUPV

14.11.2020 · Tweet

Many might be familiar with Scanning Tunnelling Microscope (STM) technique to investigate surface structures with (sub-)atomic spatial resolution (or make an atomic stop-motion movie 😄) https://t.co/kMEaFwxdFm

14.11.2020 · Tweet

And an example of future innovation development is in transistors for electronics, where quantum tunnel leaking is currently presenting a limit on the miniaturization, and dedicated quantum transistors could present a new breakthrough. https://t.co/LwVO0AIF1p

14.11.2020 · Tweet

There are of course many more fields and technologies. For any of them, new insights gained from #attoscience about the quantum tunnelling process itself can deliver new puzzle pieces.

14.11.2020 · Tweet

Another aspect: we study electron motion. And understanding charge transport (usually electrons moving from one place to another) at the microscopic level for example in heterojunctions of photovoltaic cells allow a possible new pathway of trying to improve their efficiency. https://t.co/ULzYm6M3yy

14.11.2020 · Tweet

More and more aims move from "observing" to "controlling" electron dynamics with tailored fields. This invites dreams and hopes of controlling electron dynamics for example during chemical reactions, taking femtochemistry (dynamics of nuclei) to the next level. https://t.co/qIEHb83LBS

14.11.2020 · Tweet

Obviously, there are also more applications within #attoscience itself, where we're using the photoelectrons or emitted radiation as a secondary tool to investigate for example dynamics in molecular orbitals, and more. Some of the applications I have listed above are ongoing

14.11.2020 · Tweet

already, others are still hopes, dreams and ideas. A lot of work still remains to be done, both by the attoscience community and also all related fields. After all, we're still a very young, exciting and growing field 😉 https://t.co/4cBH7CX5zr

Born in the North of England, moved to the South when young - retained a love of gravy and football, and a hatred of ballet (poor satirical joke for the UK followers, #jakeberry). Enjoyed chemistry, biology, and maths at school, but had no idea what I wanted to study at uni. https://t.co/XSlxxTrkzt

So I ended up studying Natural Sciences, a real mish-mash of anything and everything science-related for the undecided! I loved the freedom I had to study evolution one day, thermodynamics the next (that's a lie, I hated thermodynamics and still do, but I did enjoy evolution).

There aren't that many universities in the UK that offer Natural Sciences courses still, but for young people who aren't sure what they want to do and don't want to be pinned to a decision yet, they're a great option. 16.11.2020 · Tweet

16.11.2020 · Tweet

making certain parts of a cell light up so we can study how these amazing building blocks of our bodies really work, or to allow us to make tests that can diagnose diseases really fast like a pregnancy test.... the list is endless

Morning everyone, I realised that two days in to curating this account and I still haven't really told you all about what we actually do! So today I'll be tweeting mainly about our research - why we do it, how we do it, and also some shameless plugs of some of our papers

18.11.2020 · Tweet

[admin] "A Chemist's guide to the Nanoscale" Extended podcast with @spicerlab is here 🥳 https://t.co/ZztOxHcPDe

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Let's start with a very broad overview - our goal is to design materials that we can use to treat disease, specifically those where one of the tissues in the body has been damaged in some way. This encompasses things like heart disease, arthritis, nerve damage, and loads others

18.11.2020 · Tweet

To do this the material should help us repair the damage, or replace the original function of the tissue somehow. This field is called 'tissue engineering', and the technologies it encompasses are really broad, from 3D printed organs, through to new tissues grown in petri dishes https://t.co/yWUJkJhteL

18.11.2020 · Tweet

This is a super interdisciplinary field, populated by engineers, materials scientists, tissue and cell biologists, surgeons, polymer chemists, imaging physicists....... I discovered yesterday that it's even been used in Grey's Anatomy (though have to admit I've never watched it) https://t.co/4mAtglKblt

18.11.2020 · Tweet

One technology is to use material 'scaffolds' that can be used by cells as a framework to grow new tissue. Just like the scaffolding on a new house. Except ideally this scaffold should not only be structural, it should also tell cells what to do so that they form a new tissue

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Giving cells the right signals at the right times is REALLY hard. Nature is complex. We need to get way better at designing materials that recreate this complexity, but it's like having an IKEA manual for a Boeing 747. https://t.co/mtr4kcebPb

18.11.2020 · Tweet

A lot of the 'tissues' we engineer therefore just can't function well enough to treat diseases in real patients. Tissue engineering has huge potential, but not that many technologies have actually benefited people suffering from these awful diseases yet

18.11.2020 · Tweet

That's where we come in - we look at tissue engineering from a slightly different perspective, and look to use our skills as organic chemists and chemical biologists to see how manipulations at the molecular level can affect how cells behave at the scale of a tissue

18.11.2020 · Tweet

If we can really control what's going on at the level of single molecules and how these interact at the nano scale, then we have far more chance of controlling what's happening at the level of something you can see and hold.

18.11.2020 · Tweet

The grand vision is that we can then come up with better design principles, that then allow us to make better materials, that grow better tissues, that allow us to better overcome the symptoms of disease, and ultimately improve the lives of millions of peoples across the world. https://t.co/j9mXrYBxQQ

18.11.2020 · Tweet

For the rest of the day I'll be tweeting some examples of how we do this, as well as highlighting some of the challenges we face both as a group and a community moving forwards.

18.11.2020 · Tweet

@ahugumrah I couldn't agree more! Experiments fail all the time, rather than hide failure we should own it, and learn from it! There's nothing worse than the phrase 'my experiment didn't work' - what about it didn't work? What happened instead? What could we do differently?

18.11.2020 · Tweet

@ahugumrah In this instance, we ran some tests yesterday afternoon and turns out the gels we made were just too weak. Not as 'gel-like' as we hoped, and therefore they just fell apart overnight in the fridge and dried out. Lesson learnt, now we now what we have to do to improve the system

18.11.2020 · Tweet

This is the most recent example of this chemistry-led approach to biomaterial design, from my postdoc. We showed that we could design electroactive materials that could be used to stimulate neuronal cells and change their behaviour https://t.co/IGLxYrVjzL

18.11.2020 · Tweet

This was work that was mainly led by an amazing PhD student called Kaja who did a fantastic job bringing together a really interdisciplinary study. We're joint first authors on the paper but she needs to take most of the credit

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Key to this was some synthetic chemistry that I developed way back in 2017 for making a series of molecules known as oligoEDOTs. PEDOTS (the polymer equivalent of the molecules I made) are a bit like molecular wires, acting to conduct electricity https://t.co/ZXCI6YaMfn

18.11.2020 · Tweet

You could do similar things with metals, that conduct electricity better, but metals are stiff and inflexible - the complete opposite of what we want a material to look like to grow nerve tissue. Conductive polymers partly get around this problem.

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Our oligoEDOTs are basically very short polymers, and are even better at overcoming the rubbish mechanical properties of metals. This is with a trade-off of much worse conductivity, but our recent work shows that they are electrically-active ENOUGH to be able to influence cells

18.11.2020 · Tweet

The benefit of our system was that we could create really cool architectures at the nanoscale using a technique called melt electrospinning, that basically draws lines of polymers like a printer would. This was a big advance in this work and something we were really proud of

18.11.2020 · Tweet

It's not a big jump to imagine using these materials to control the growth of nerve cells in particular orientations, allowing us to start to mimic the bundles of cells that form in your nerves.

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Here's another from earlier this year. We got involved in this collaboration when I was in Stockholm with a group who were interested in making cements that could be used to glue biomaterials to tissues, particularly bone https://t.co/mNyFzozUmM

18.11.2020 · Tweet

This is a really big problem - we are actually quite good at making materials that help to repair bone, but they can't be used in any part of the body that is subject to mechanical force because the interface between the bone and the material is really weak.

18.11.2020 · Tweet

A couple of years back @alinavkirillova reported that adding a modified amino acid, phosphoserine, to a class of materials known as cements helped overcome this problem. Our collaborators (who aren't on twitter) had found the same thing but they didn't really understand why

18.11.2020 · Tweet

We realised that we'd need to understand what was happening at the nanoscale interface between the material and tissue, and also at the molecular level. If we could build a load of phosphoserine mimics with subtly different structures we might get some important insight

18.11.2020 · Tweet

What started off sounding easy led us down a rabbit hole that resulted in a new synthetic method to make phospho-amino acids, that we then used to make a library of mimics. Using this we could really pinpoint what chemical features were essential for adhesion and which weren't

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Turns out having a phosphate group and a carboxylic acid is essential, but the amine is pretty much dispensable. This opens up lots of possibilities to make new additives for bone cements that might improve their mechanical and biological applications

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Huge potential for these kinds of materials in treating bone breaks and defects. At the moment one of the most popular treatments is to cut out a chunk of bone from somewhere else in the body and implant it at the site of damage, the use of cements would be a big step up on this!

18.11.2020 · Tweet

During my PhD my research focussed on developing new chemistries that could be used to modify proteins with high precision, at just a single amino acid. This is really difficult to do, proteins can be huge molecules composed of hundreds or even thousands of amino acids (1/12)

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Modified proteins are hugely important for loads of applications, such as therapeutics (biologics were worth $240 billion last year), for visualising and understanding what is happening inside a cell, or for creating diagnostic devices for detecting disease (2/12)

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Single amino acid precision is really important - if you don't have control, when you try and attach something to a protein you will often completely kill its activity and it becomes useless. Specificity and selectivity are key! But they're hard to achieve (3/12)

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Making it even more complicated is the fact that these proteins are made up of just 20 amino acids, with an even smaller number of chemical functionalities. How can we selectively modify just one? One common approach is to use unnatural amino acids that are unique (4/12)

18.11.2020 · Tweet

These can be installed via a process called codon reassignment - very complicated, but very powerful. We wrote a review on it way back in 2015 that shows some of the diverse structures you can insert into a specific position in a protein (5/12) https://t.co/ytNOGlduYd

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Building on work by @ChalkerChem when he was in the group, I got working on trying to target one such unnatural amino acid using palladium catalysed reactions. These reactions have revolutionised chemistry over the last 50 years, but applying them to proteins was new (6/12)

18.11.2020 · Tweet

My very first paper back in 2011 showed that we could do one specific palladium-catalysed reaction, a Suzuki reaction, on a protein with high efficiency. This was a big breakthrough for us, as well as a special moment for me personally (7/12) https://t.co/Rox5hyJseJ

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Apparently, Suzuki means sea bass in Japanese! Or so I've been told, happy to be corrected by any Japanese speakers out there. Had to talk my boss down from making a sea bass-based journal cover on more than one occasion (8/12) https://t.co/9q5Galh9Cf

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Anyway, we then went one step further and showed we could even do Suzuki reactions on the surfaces of living bacteria. This work really set the groundwork for lots of advances in recent years doing metal catalysis inside cells. (9/12) https://t.co/0qN1IMVMDD

18.11.2020 · Tweet

An emerging strategy is even using these reactions in animals as a way to 'uncage' drugs, potentially minimising side effects and giving far more potent treatments for diseases like cancer. (10/12)

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Another PhD student, Matt, went on to show why these Suzuki reactions were so powerful - he did an amazing job showing that they could be used to really probe the mechanism of a human protein called glycogenin went about storing glucose in the body (11/12) https://t.co/o7SOJqptUa

18.11.2020 · Tweet

This enzyme is key to energy storage in humans, and importantly no other chemical strategy was able to probe this mechanism in the same way. A really powerful example of how chemical biology can give us new understanding (12/12)

18.11.2020 · Tweet

A final one for today is a review article we published last month and are really pleased with. In it we provide an overview of how we can use light to make cyclic peptides. This important class of molecules have emerged as really promising drug candidates https://t.co/i5dbh4njTa

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Cyclic peptides can disrupt the interactions between two proteins in the body - interactions that are implicated in loads of diseases such as cancer, yet were previously thought to be 'undruggable'. By cyclising the peptides they become more more potent and more stable

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Making cyclic peptides can be tricky though. Using light to trigger reactions (photochemistry) has emerged over the last decade as a really useful way to achieve cyclisation. With ever increasing numbers of photochemical reactions out there, their use is only going to increase

18.11.2020 · Tweet

I'm particularly proud of this paper because it was the first written by members of my group since I started at York. PhD students Laetitia and Nick did a fantastic job writing it, all brilliantly overseen by our then-postdoc James. My input really was minimal

18.11.2020 · Tweet

It was written in the depths of lockdown when I was doing a terrible job of balancing child care and work. I was very lucky to have such a great team around me who managed to pull us through a really difficult period with something productive to show for it.

18.11.2020 · Tweet

Hopefully it will be the first of many but this review will always have a place in my heart - the memories of trying to have a virtual meeting about figures while also trying to stop my daughter from eating a ladybird are embedded in my brain forever.

Reviewing a paper today I was really impressed by the results it presented, until I got to the SI which was really poor - it didn't necessarily affect the results or conclusions of the paper, but it really affected the way I judged the paper and made me overly critical

20.11.2020 · Tweet

Made me think about how important this part of a paper is. In some ways the most important, in many journals it's the whole experimental - what the authors actually did and the data that supports their discussion. Yet so often it's left till last and done in a mad rush

20.11.2020 · Tweet

I'm always shocked by papers that have 2-3 page SI for a 10 page paper - how can the details that support that work be so scant? And so often it's just a couple of hastily thrown together graphs and no explanations, its pretty much meaningless.

20.11.2020 · Tweet

My other major pet peeve is experimentals that just say 'we did it like these other people did'. I don't want to have to follow a literature trail (that can often go back 6 or 7 papers) just to find out how you did a simple experimental.

20.11.2020 · Tweet

It would take the authors 5 minutes to just write it down, or me an hour to go searching for it. Why would you not want to make a reader of your papers experience as pleasant and easy as possible, so that people could reproduce your work and cite you?

20.11.2020 · Tweet

Maybe I'm missing something and would be interested to hear people's thoughts. For me a robust, long, and detailed SI is always a good thing. If it's well organised and easier to follow, all the better. It will certainly make me feel a lot more positive when I review your paper!

20.11.2020 · Tweet

While I always try hard to not let my instincts affect my opinion/review, no matter how much you try to be objective we're all human and it is inevitable that it will cloud judgement. I don't get why you wouldn't put in that extra days effort to stop that affecting your paper!

I had an AS level in maths. Everybody else had at least an A level, mostly one in Further Maths (exactly what it says on the tin) and some, mostly private school students, also had STEP qualifications (Yet More Maths I guess). So I had a lot of catching up to do.

23.11.2020 · Tweet

Next up: how did I get a postdoc? Because it's hard. I kept applying and applying. Every unsuccessful application is a practice run at writing statements and doing interviews if you get that far.

23.11.2020 · Tweet

To write an application statement for a postdoc: go through the job specification/person specification thingo they link to in the ad. Copy & paste the points into a Word or whatever document. Then write underneath each point, how you meet it - or, how you would learn it.

23.11.2020 · Tweet

I found it easiest to write completely overhyped hubris in the very first draft, then go through and edit it to sound reasonable. "Electron microscopy skills" "I am the best microscopist in the world EVARRRR" - once you set the bar "too high" it's easier to edit down than edit up

23.11.2020 · Tweet

Sort of like haggling a price with your own embarrassment - start by stating a ridiculous amount and then you will end up somewhere reasonable in the middle. (Incidentally I suck at actual market haggling.)

23.11.2020 · Tweet

You don't have to then turn it into prose - bullet points is quite possibly how the recruiting prof wants to think about it in their head anyway, so you may as well leave it like that as long as it's coherent.

23.11.2020 · Tweet

Interview tips: if you don't know something, don't lie or bullshit (pardon my language). Say you don't know. Say how you would find out. It's easy to spot a bullshitter. And a prof usually wants somebody who will be honest about progress, not lie and then mess up the plan.

23.11.2020 · Tweet

Have a lot of tea/coffee/cake/whatever makes you awake and happy in the morning. DO NOT go to an interview without breakfast. I did this once and looked like a total plonker until 10am when I woke up.

23.11.2020 · Tweet

Most importantly: show your enthusiasm, about their project, about your previous projects, about your PhD, about science in general. Interviewing is boring. Running a project is often depressing. Be somebody who wakes them up and makes them feel happy and optimistic again.

23.11.2020 · Tweet

This advice isn't a foolproof guide for how to get a job, it's just little bits I picked up.

23.11.2020 · Tweet

Good morning HU-MANS. Time for more science. Today I'm going to nerd about electron microscopes. Many introductions to electron microscopy say that an electron microscope is like a light microscope but with a shorter wavelength to get better resolution. Well, sorta.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Electrons can act as waves and their wavelength is very short. Look up wavelength limit if interested. BUT. This is like using a Red Arrow performance jet to carry passengers to Germany faster. Like, you CAN. But it can do so much more.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

A crystal is like a ceilidh for electrons, all dancing around in arrays that match where the atoms are. When another electron from the microscope comes in REALLY fast, Usain Bolt there has to get through a room of dancers, and join in the dance to get to the other side. https://t.co/phty9Mcokv

24.11.2020 · Tweet

It's the outcome of all that dancing that makes it really interesting. The electron comes out of that a changed person. It's a different shaped wave. And some of the electrons hit things in the material and lose energy and you can measure all sorts of things from that.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Walking into the electron microscope room is like putting on 5 different sets of night vision goggles. You can see so many more things. This is why Geordie LaForge is my favourite Star Trek character (narrow margins). He walks around and sees all this with his actual face. https://t.co/l5NQxzXnam

24.11.2020 · Tweet

So. Some of the electrons get poinged back out the top of the sample. Some hit the electron clouds of the atoms near the top, and knock out some of those electrons which go flying out the top. Byeeee

24.11.2020 · Tweet

How they fly out depends on where there are hills and valleys in the surface so if you count how many come out at each bit of surface, you can map the hills and valleys. That's a secondary electron image.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Some of the electrons get unlucky and manage to almost crash into an actual atomic nucleus. They get sort of slingshotted backout, and from a lot deeper in the sample. Those are called backscattered electrons.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

A nucleus with more protons in it has a lot more flinging power. So if there's a blob of something heavy like tungsten hiding in your sample it will glow like a little fairy light. This is VERY useful for a first figure out of what's going on.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

These kinds of images are all formed by scanning the electron beam over the top of the sample and recording the intensity of what comes back out the top and sorting it by beam position. So we do these in a machine called a scanning electron microscope.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

I just had a look and all my SEM images are of super secret Rolls Royce things 😭if anybody has any awesome non-secret SEM images they would like to share, drop them here! (If nobody wants to, that's ok too)

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Wait that's not quite true...here is a (I think) secondary electron image of a cube on a stick that's being sliced and diced by kickass Jack Donoghue in Manchester (more on slicing and dicing later). https://t.co/RCOGmjhEYX

24.11.2020 · Tweet

@DrStuartR Beautiful!

24.11.2020 · Tweet

We can get even more cool stuff to happen if we - and bear with me here - chop off the bottom of the sample, leaving only 100 nm or even thinner, and make the electrons go a leeetle bit faster, so they can dance all the way through the sample and out the other side.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Then you can stick some more microscope on the bottom to deal with the electrons that have gone all the way through - it's called a transmission electron microscope.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

At this point I need to introduce my glamourous assistant Colm O'Regan, experimental officer and champion eater of biscuits, who has been taking photos of microscopes for me, because I'm not allowed in the lab unless I have an actual experiment to do. https://t.co/LANdUczrXe

24.11.2020 · Tweet

THIS is a transmission electron microscope. That door in the background is a normal sized door for people to walk through. The sample goes in behind that round blob on the front left. https://t.co/FckSoxAFU5

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Front right. Not front left. I have always had problems between left and right.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

The sample needs to be riiiight in the middle of that column, so it sits in the right place in the middle of the lenses to make the beam do the right thing. So we make this tiny thin disc 3mm across (more on that later and then we attach it to the end of a stick. https://t.co/jvbLKWmLp2

24.11.2020 · Tweet

One such stick is in that clear box near the back of the table. The little cradle at the front is to hold another stick (sample holder) that is in the microscope with a sample attached. Also in the pic: tiny screwdriver for attaching. Loads of tweezers for sample handling!

24.11.2020 · Tweet

So what cool stuff comes out the other side of the sample? First up: DIFFRACTION. The electron wave comes out arranged according to the crystal structure in a pattern of spots. The pattern tells us things about the crystal. See also: lots of maths. Here is a diffraction pattern. https://t.co/BvzIAXcB2G

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Things like crystal defects, that I was talking about yesterday, also put their imprint in the diffraction pattern. You see those streaks in between the dots? Yeah I have no idea what that is yet. Still got to analyse that data. But it'll be something like that.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

When you have a glass lens for light, if you stand sort of halfway between the lens and where the image is in focus and put a screen up, you get a pattern equivalent for this one. (Lasers best. Don't go blind though.)

24.11.2020 · Tweet

But for a TEM, you don't put a screen in halfway up the column. Electron lenses are special - you can change their strength. So you can tell the microscope to do some wacky projectory stuff and make the diffraction pattern end up on the screen at the bottom where you look.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Or - this is quite cool - if you blank off all the spots except one of those side spots and then tell the microscope to show you an image from JUST THAT SPOT, you can see crystal defects as little bright lines. Look, here they are! https://t.co/qXi6KEYn5A

24.11.2020 · Tweet

This is what it looks like when you sit at the bottom of the microscope and look at the screen. The screen is inside that round hole but in this picture there is a detector for another instrument looking inside so we can't see into the microscope. https://t.co/raMgZwBLy6

24.11.2020 · Tweet

The buttons and screens at the side are where you control all the lenses and widgets to make the beam move about and everything. It's like flying a plane except if you mess it up, nobody dies (unless you screw up so badly the centre manager loses it and kills you).

24.11.2020 · Tweet

This microscope is my new best buddy the JEOL F200 at Sheffield by the way. https://t.co/YWaaymGwpn not pictured: room full of computers, cupboards, sample holders, boxes and chairs. And it being dark so you can see the screen when you're getting all the widgets set up right.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

I'm going to have a little break now, but I will be back at 2ish to talk about how you make something 100 nm thin anyhow, and then some of the other things you can find out in a magic electron microscope.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

@beamsontoast Aw man, I never even thought of that. And if you try and stand round the other side to use your left hand you'd be standing in the table. How annoying!

24.11.2020 · Tweet

SO as promised, this is how you make a thing less than 100 nm thick. There are two ways, really, and they all involve ending up with a thing 100nm thick stuck to another thing that is 100 microns thick so you can see it and handle it with tweezers.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

The first way is by making a little disc and grinding it to 100 microns thick all the way across, then you erode the middle of it somehow until you get a hole, and the bit around the hole is thin enough to let the electrons through.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

If it's a nice helpful metal you can squirt it with acid in cold gloopy solvents with an electric potential across it and if you get it right, your sample comes out lovely and smooth with a nice wide thin part. Here is the machine in a fume cupboard. (Thanks Colm) https://t.co/2sOooPmBjE

24.11.2020 · Tweet

If it's not a nice helpful metal you can carefully polish the middle down with a tiny little grinding wheel, then you fire a broad beam of ions at it in this machine which works kind of the same. This is good for ceramics and semiconductors and stuff. https://t.co/mXfYoHy3Zb

24.11.2020 · Tweet

The other way (and this is my favourite way because it's SO COOL) you can put it in an SEM with an extra bit attached to fire fast ions at things, and you can carve out a little bit, pick it up with a tiny stick, and glue it to a support with a tiny glue nozzle.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

This way is also quite cool because you can look for a specific thing on the surface or just below the surface and dig just that bit out and look at that in the TEM. Let me see if I have some pictures of that somewhere...

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Aha here is a picture of a little slice of material that's been dug around ready to lift out. The slug thing on top is platinum that you deposit on top to protect the top surface of the actual specimen when you're slicing and dicing round it. https://t.co/1LKeUYa5Xr

24.11.2020 · Tweet

The slicey dicey machine is called a FIB - focused ion beam. You can go even faster if you use Xe ions and let them make a bit of plasma (like the sun but less hot) around the surface while you're digging - then you can pull out a massive cube like this (Jack's!) https://t.co/VSDbOCTEbq

24.11.2020 · Tweet

That picture is Jack picking up a 100 micron cube with the little pick-up stick, ready to stick it on the support in the picture I showed you yesterday to get cross-sectioned. The big tube is where the Pt comes out to deposit as that protective layer and as glue.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

@LunchBobs 👏🏼👏🏼👏🏼👏🏼👏🏼🤦🏼‍♀️

24.11.2020 · Tweet

The last bit of electron microscopy that I haven't talked about yet is spectroscopy. That means you hit things with electrons and electrons or X-rays come out again whose energy depends on what element the electrons hit. It's very helpful for finding stuff...

24.11.2020 · Tweet

The electrons in the beam can push an electron from a lower shell into a higher one, like from 1s into 2p or something. That means if you catch the original electron coming out the other side, it's missing that amount of energy.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Well you know how much energy it had to start with because you gave it the energy. So you can do a graph: electrons that came through vs how much energy they lost. And you get a spectrum that's like an autograph book for all the elements in that bit of the specimen.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

That's called electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS). You can also see clever stuff to do with chemical bonds. When atoms form bonds their electron levels move about, and the gaps between them change. And this information is in the EELS spectrum too, if you speak eel.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

But there's another half to this story. Your beam electron pushed another electron from a 1s to a 2p orbital or whatever they were. But that electron doesn't want to stay where it fetched up now the bully has gone. So it hops down.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

But one cannot simply HOP into another energy level. It has to shed some energy to do that. And that comes out as an X-ray. And just like the EELS electron, that has an energy that is a signature of the element. But this time not the bonding, just the atom. https://t.co/K2gtnnTIrp

24.11.2020 · Tweet

That's called Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy, EDS or EDX depending on how it feels (EDX is what its mum calls it when it's in trouble, EDS is for its mates). EDS and EELS are kind of like those friends that are a bit different but always get each other.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

EDS isn't that good with light elements, because their transitions are only little amounts of energy, and the EDS detector can't see them very well. EELS isn't that good with heavy elements, because the EELS signal gets weaker toward the big energies.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

So if you use them both, you can find out loads of stuff. EELS on the left, EDS on the right. https://t.co/txUW9PIsX0

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Back to the TEM picture: the bit at the top liberates electrons from a little bit of tungsten and flings them down the column through all the lenses and stuff. (This is the R005, an older TEM than the F200, which has extra glasses but is also harder to use.) https://t.co/8BZVyUEIm4

24.11.2020 · Tweet

The EDS detector is that big thing on the right (yes the actual right this time) which is a tiny detector and a big tank of liquid nitrogen to keep it cold. That's an old design, new ones don't need the tank, and they are hidden away inside on the F200.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

Electrons are not actually green - but when they fall on the screen at the bottom (behind the round hatch there) they hit a screen of phosphor which emits green light to show you where the electrons are, so you can line things up before you record your images and data.

24.11.2020 · Tweet

24.11.2020 · Tweet

@NotHF Aw, thanks! 😊
