[admin] "Electrons can take you Anywhere" Extended conversation with the amazing @JoFeanelwa is out now - https://t.co/uFZiAjpecg

25.11.2020 · Tweet

Good morning Twitter people! Today I'm going to talk about alloys and why some of them are super. An alloy is a metal, with a mixture of elements in it. A normal alloy is mostly one metallic element with bits of other elements in.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

A recent development is a thing called a "high entropy alloy" - which it turns out was not that high entropy, and has many other names now too - where you have about the same amount of multiple elements.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

High entropy alloys haven't proved awesome for anything yet, but people said that about electricity and the telephone, so...it's good to have them around and known about to see what happens. Anyway. That's not my area, I'm rambling.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

I'll cover a couple of alloy families that are put in the burny whooshy bit of aeroplane engines - nickel superalloys (they are rather super) and titanium alloys.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

I'm going to unashamedly link to Wikipedia here, so that I know I'm not accidentally putting up something confidential from my own pile of diagrams. So. This is a jet engine. https://t.co/w57maRIuov

25.11.2020 · Tweet

I'm going to talk first about the spinning blades just after the bit where the burning happens - the last purple ones in that diagram. Those have one very important role that they have to not screw up. They have to spin round really fast in very hot gas and NOT GET LONGER.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

If they get longer they scrape the outside of the combustion/hot gas chamber too hard and engine go kablooey. There is a very special class of materials made specially for this, called nickel superalloys. They are very super indeed. https://t.co/auiaMbLqw1

25.11.2020 · Tweet

When an alloy is sort of more than halfway to its melting temperature, it wants to get longer if you hang a weight on it, or spin it around very fast. Atoms diffuse along defects in the structure where it's quite loose - grain boundaries and dislocations, mostly.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

This is called creep. (It creeps up on you and then crunch.) To make it not creep, we want to not have pathways of dislocations and grain boundaries going from the inside to the outside of the turbine blade, so the atoms can't sneak along them.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

We do this with dislocations by tying them up in knots. If you make a certain composition range of Ni alloy, with a lot of Ti and Al, it forms these squarey precipitates called gamma prime γ'. Loads of them. Rafts and rafts of them. More than half the alloy can be precipitate.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

A prof called Dierk Raabe made an AMAZING video showing this - it's at the top of this page. The thing at the start is a turbine blade. The blocky things when it's most of the way zoomed in are some of those precipitates. https://t.co/1BlrQ7vb8H

25.11.2020 · Tweet

This γ' precipitate is very clever because its structure is ALMOST the same as the Ni around it except some of the atom sites in the crystal structure are systematically occupied by Ti or Al not Ni.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

If a dislocation goes through, it unzips the ordering and leaves a bit of really very unhappy material behind where the wrong atoms are next to each other. You can re-zip it by having a second dislocation follow the first one close behind.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

So dislocations have to wait for a friend to join them to go through. But the dislocations in the Ni are in those narrow channels between the γ' blocks. It's like trying to find your mum again in the supermarket. So by and large, they are stuck and tangled up in the forest of γ'.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

So, there isn't a nice easy dislocation path for atoms to diffuse towards the outside of the turbine blade and make it grow. WIN. But there are still grain boundaries. We can deal with this in two ways: block them up with rubbish, or take them away altogether.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

By rubbish I mean carbides of heavy things like maybe Hf, Ta, W, what else...all sorts. There can be like 10 elements in one of these superduperalloys. These make the grain boundaries also not want to move about and line up along the blade, so they're not useful roads for atoms.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

They're kind of like if you wanted to run raindrops along string to the ground, but the string is stuck to a board with drawing pins.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

That's good enough for the really-quite-hot bits of the engine. For the very-hot-indeed bits, you take the grain boundaries out altogether and grow a turbine blade that is just one big crystal, by growing it with a squiggly bit at the bottom. What?!

25.11.2020 · Tweet

Like in this video from the Prof Hongbiao Dong via Prof Sir Harry Bhadeshia https://t.co/aUtLfmkWWa The squiggle goes at the bottom of the blade; you can just see the bottom of the blade on the left. The bit on the right is sort of a supply vat.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

Ooh this video is awesome too, look! https://t.co/xzWNQifmhu I've been in that brick building to visit my colleagues in materials research. They have cabinets of old turbine blades and pictures and the way to the toilet was "left by the blades, right after the helicopter".

25.11.2020 · Tweet

I have to host a seminar soon, so I will be back this afternoon to ramble on about titanium.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

I'm back! So, titanium. (I like it.) Titanium is light and strong at the same time. This is used for the slightly less hot bits of engine, because nickel is heavy. If you made all the turbine blades out of Ni you would use loads of fuel and put unnecessary stress on bits.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

A lot of other bits are made of Ti alloys too - landing gear, engine casing, etc. plus all sorts of bits in other industries. So it is a very important and very cool metal.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

Titanium on its own, not alloyed, likes to be hexagonal close packed at ordinary sort of temperatures (including in that bit of engine). Once you get to sort of 1200C it changes its mind and wants to be body centred cubic instead. https://t.co/1fgPyhdziD

25.11.2020 · Tweet

Hexagonal (hcp, α) is comparatively squishy, it can absorb some stress and move dislocations about and cope - it is tough. BCC (β) is comparatively stiff and strong. If you get both of them together, you get the toughness from α and the strength of β. TEAMWORK

25.11.2020 · Tweet

You get this by putting other stuff in the Ti to make an alloy. For example something like Mo will make β happily stick around down to room temperature, and other elements will also make α be there too, so you get this nice strong tough both-together structure.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

If you get the heat treatments right you can also grow some big lumps of α to absorb energy & make it tough, then some middle sized ones, then some little ones with a good network of β between them for strength. Here is the sort of thing I mean https://t.co/wIQwDa3Hh6

25.11.2020 · Tweet

That's a backscattered image from an SEM - the β shows up bright because it has nice heavy Mo in it like I said before. That image is where I accidentally analysed the handle of a different thing (oops).

25.11.2020 · Tweet

Because the microstructure is so so clever and particular and depends on heat treatments, it can be quite challenging to additive manufacture things out of Ti - I will talk more about this tomorrow!

25.11.2020 · Tweet

So as a last bit for Wednesday - what do I do with these alloys? I get given bits that have been additive manufactured or processed by some other cool new method, and I find out what's inside.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

I might be looking for particular features, or I might be finding out what the microstructure is like (and how it changes across the sample, sometimes). I will usually do some optical microscopy and make a plan first, because electron microscopes are expensive to use.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

Then I will decide what length scale I need to look on and what analysis techniques I need to use, and make a Cunning Plan, usually involving FIB slicing and dicing somehow, to get the information we need. Then...I do it!

25.11.2020 · Tweet

(There's usually an intermediate step of figuring out how much ££ it will cost, in microscope time and Jo time, and squeezing that through the Finance machine so I'm allowed to do the work...)

25.11.2020 · Tweet

Once I have data, I have to sit and process it to find out what it says, and most importantly put it in a way that the sample's owner will undertand - especially important when it's a company and you might be talking to people who are not materials scientists by background.

25.11.2020 · Tweet

Soooo that's me done for Wednesday. Tomorrow I will be writing about additive manufacturing, in between madly writing a thingo to try and get some ££ for a project about additive manufacturing, in some kind of supreme irony. Have a nice evening everybody!

26.11.2020 · Tweet

Wowww I overslept. Today my plan is to tweet about additive manufacturing. Morning everybody.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

Ok so what's additive manufacturing? Making things bit by bit instead of all in one blob. Kind of like lego or knitting. You can do this with loads of different materials but in very different ways. It's called "3D printing" but that's only one bit of it.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

3D printers that you can buy, use polymer in strings that is heated up to sort of melty temperature so it will stick together and you can build little plastic thingos from a hot print head that moves about in layers. That's nice and easy except when it gets lost and prints a mess

26.11.2020 · Tweet

That's a very specific set of polymers - you can also do things with UV curing and all sorts. Polymers aren't really my field - @CandiceMajewski knows looooads about this.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

You can also print ceramics in an organic sort of gloop, then burn away the gloop and you are left with a nice ceramic structure. There are all sorts of possibilities along the way. Look for...Iuliia Elizarovna and friends at Imperial College London, for example.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

Metals are the bit of additive manufacturing that I'm involved with. They usually involve metal powder, a great big laser and a lot of pew pew pew, and I will talk more about that after lunch.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

Most of my additive manufacturing work is with the MAPP consortium (Manufacturing by Advanced Powder Processing) @mapphub which involves Sheffield, Leeds, Manchester, Oxford, Diamond X-ray source, Imperial, UCL and...have I missed anybody? I hope not.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

We work together on all sorts of additive manufacturing and general powder-related stuff, and do some exciting stuff. I will link to some stuff on MAPP's youtube account later when I talk about metals and pew pew lasers!

26.11.2020 · Tweet

Ok metals! When you additive manufacture metals you need two things: 1) Metal 2) Energy 3) In many cases an inert gas atmosphere 4) A LOT of PPE for dealing with all that crazy ass metal powder.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

The energy can be in the form of a laser (pew pew pew) or an electron beam (in which case everything happens in a vacuum). The metal can be in the form of powder or a wire like welding.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

The powder can be introduced to the pew pew pew in two ways: you lay down a bed of powder and trace the laser/e- across it in the outline of the thing you're building, or you attach hoses to the laser and fire powder into the focus of the laser beam and hope it sticks.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

When you've done one layer, you go back to the other end of the thing you're building, move up a bit and add another layer on the top. It sounds like a ridiculous idea but it happens like magic, suddenly there's this thing emerging.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

The first one is called Selective Laser Melting or Powder Bed, the second one is Directed Energy Deposition or Blown Powder. Here is an animation from the MAPP Youtube channel about DED! https://t.co/QAdvmt1ICN

26.11.2020 · Tweet

And here is a video from a company that make the machines for DED, called BeAM. PEW PEW PEW https://t.co/TKf3cequgK

26.11.2020 · Tweet

You see there's a glowy bit at the top? That's mostly metal that's just solidified and is still glowing hot, but right under the beam is a bead of molten metal that's catching the melty bits of powder that have been through the laser, which we call the melt pool.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

All sorts of cool stuff goes on in the melt pool. Because most liquid metals have a surface tension that depends strongly on temperature, and there's a massive laser at the top and a big lump of metal underneath, there is crazy fast stirring going on in that melt pool.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

Which way the stirring goes and how fast it goes, and the shape and size of the melt pool, and how hot the layer underneath gets when you build the layer on top, and loads more things decide the microstructure of the metal you get.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

The size and shape of the grains and which way round the crystal structure is compared to the shape of the part (orientation), and the shape & size of precipitates and little bits of phases in the metal (like α and β in Ti) are all affected by all those things.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

The end result is that additive manufacturing of metal (and everything else) is really, REALLY complicated. But it's also really awesome. You can make stuff that you'd never be able to make any other way.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

For example (and this isn't secret) many jet engine companies are starting to make bits of engine that have the discs and blades all forged into one lump, not separate blades that come off, so they can extract more power more efficiently from the engine.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

When one of the turbine blades gets damaged, for example a bit of grit goes through the engine or a fatigue crack is found in regular inspection, it's silly to replace the entire massive part. It's better to cut off the broken bit and just...regrow a new bit on top.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

So GE, Rolls Royce and a few more companies are doing a lot of work into being able to grow back a bit of engine with a little bit of powder, some PEW PEW PEW and some very clever machines.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

So how do we untangle all this mess? A lot of approaches. Peter Lee & his group at UCL have a magic setup at the Diamond X-ray source where they can do the PEW PEW PEW in the middle of an X-ray imaging machine and make videos of what happens in the middle of hte melt pool!

26.11.2020 · Tweet

You can also systematically vary different parameters and see what the outcome looks like in the final builds, which we do a LOT of at Sheffield. This goes in parallel with a lot of computer modelling, including machine learning, from other partners in MAPP.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

Pores turn out to be a pain in the neck for additive manufacturing. Because of all this stirring, bits of gas can get stuck in the melt pool, both from the chamber and from any powder particles that were hollow. And some of them get stuck.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

That leaves a pore in the finished build which is not helpful; it concentrates stress and makes it vulnerable for fatigue failure. I, Jack who I mentioned on Tuesday, and a team of other awesome people did a study on pores recently.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

You can squish pores away under high-ish temperature, but if you then heat treat the material (like Ti alloys need to be the right microstructure) the pores grow back. We found that they grow back a really funny shape. (My little potatoes!) Paper out soon...

26.11.2020 · Tweet

Oh! Talking of fatigue failure - a woman called Constance Tipper founded a lot of that entire field in the 1920s. Just look how awesome she was! https://t.co/z3CiVpcCDQ It is my absolute mission to put this woman in lecture notes one day. She was just great.

26.11.2020 · Tweet

And with that, I will declare this the END of Thursday because I have to do some project planning. Tomorrow I will be tweeting about dyspraxia because I've got it like a slightly painful free gift. Right now though I have to calculate things with money. Wah. Byeeeee

26.11.2020 · Tweet

@mapphub Awww thanks! 😊

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Ok good morning! And quite a late morning because I had a lot of things to clear out of my brain before it had space to think. Today I am tweeting about dyspraxia!

27.11.2020 · Tweet

What is dyspraxia? It's a thing where your brain deals with information strangely. This is most obvious in the way it deals with information about where your body is in relation to everything else - inaccurately. It is sometimes called "clumsy child syndrome".

27.11.2020 · Tweet

My brother has it worse than me and he literally walks into every new door frame he meets. I got a new bigger fridge what...2 months ago? Yeah, still crashing into that thing.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

It's also most obvious in handwriting - fine motor control is difficult so our handwriting is terrible. My brother's is very large and angular and child-like. Mine is more...it's a line with lumps in. Nobody else can read it. Problem is nor can I most of the time.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

As an undergrad this was PROBLEMATIC in lectures - doubly so because I didn't know that I had dyspraxia. I came on a fix where I would concentrate ONLY on writing the gist of what I heard, legibly, and go to the library in the afternoon to actually *understand* and rewrite.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

This also means that we have to concentrate super hard on tasks like writing and walking. I do canoe slalom. I'm rubbish, I rarely come in the top half of my division. But my brain is working so hard. That's why I had to pick a sport that was great fun, to compensate.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

And yes - I was terrible at PE at school - both because of this and because of the other features that I will talk about later today.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Finding small movements difficult makes TEM an...interesting career choice. I can only use one kind of tweezers, the kind that hold themselves closed, so I only need to think about moving and not gripping too. If I lose them, I can do nothing.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

I lost my tweezers last year for a few days and I had to ask somebody else to mount my samples for me because I couldn't use tweezers anymore. I actually cried in the lab with frustration.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

The physical part makes other things hard. Walking on an uneven surface - this is where I work https://t.co/K1Nel1711N you see the surface in front is all bibbly-bobbly and then goes down a hill? That is SO HARD to co-ordinate my feet on. Luckily there's a side door.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Building sites drive me crazy - suddenly a bit of pavement I at least knew is different and needs ALL my concentration to walk on - usually with cars going past so I need 2 brains, one for the cars, one for the ground.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

And buses oh my GOD - walking to a seat, sitting on the seat, getting up from the seat, walking to the front. There are potholes right before my bus stop. Those b****ds have made me hit the bus floor several times. And I look drunk, and people frown. But I'm just different.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Maintaining posture is also tricky - my back bends a bit too much unless I concentrate really hard on it. And the ground. And the cars. And the person talking to me. And and and. It is all hard.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

This is why during lockdown I had an *easier* time than normal, and why only now do I have the brain space to career plan and apply for funding and things. Because I'm not always exhausted to the point of collapse from just getting to work and back every day anymore.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

I have to go get a flu jab today (woohoo) but after that I will talk about how dyspraxia is different in different people, and the bits people miss until it causes a disaster - verbal processing and sensory processing.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

I have been flu jabbed. My arm hurts. Ok back to dyspraxia. Dyspraxia in my case strongly affects verbal processing. When I had the ability tests at Occ'l Health & got diagnosed I did pretty good on everything then when we did the verbal processing test she just...stared.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Apparently I am in the bottom 10th percentile of the population for verbal processing ability and the rest of my brain has been carrying that bit for my whole life. What does this mean in practice?

27.11.2020 · Tweet

When I'm talking, it's hard to put the words in the sentence properly. Like, the right words in the right places to say the thing I want to say. The native language in my head is mostly pictures. This makes me quite good at languages, ironically, because I don't go via English.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

So when I try to say something, sometimes the other person/people don't understand the sentence, it doesn't make sense. It's easier in text because I can read it back before I press enter. But in person I sometimes have to have a few goes.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

It made me very VERY bad at essays at school. Talking on the phone is hard too - I have to write a script to get it right. It's not just output that is affected - verbal input has problems too.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

When I read scientific papers, I usually have to use 90% of concentration to understand the syntax of the sentence, and not enough is left to understand the actual meaning. So I have reading journals where I translate the paper into diagrams/brain language and then understand.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Here is some journal - there are words but they're more like...names of things and ideas with symbols for how they relate to each other, than sentences. https://t.co/fozmmYFKCk

27.11.2020 · Tweet

(Also this is my bestest writing so that I can read it) Writing is also a problem but...not as much, because I tend to write in very simple constructions, so I more get told it's too informal. Writing papers is like filling in a form where you know what to put where.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Because of the co-ordination thing, I also find food time at conferences difficult. I can stand and eat as long as nobody's watching. I can stand and talk but I tend to get nonsensical fast. Stand + eat + talk is usually a recipe for disaster, if I've been listening all day.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

This does mean I get to meet some interesting people though because I started carrying a blanket to sit on the floor when there aren't enough chairs for everybody and it turns out I'm not the only one and often gain some lunch buddies.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Verbal processing's evil twin is: auditory processing disorder. This means I hear EVERYTHING equally. Listening to a seminar and a lorry drives past outside? Bye bye speaker's sentence. And when there are lot of people talking, I hear all of them and understand none.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

(People who bring rustly food into seminars and eat it there have a special place in hell and that place is LOUD and ANNOYING)

27.11.2020 · Tweet

In person, lip reading helps enormously. It's like a verification dataset for the stream of noise and its 50% accurate brain interpretation. On recorded media, captions are excellent. I rely on subtitles for Midsomer Murders exactly as much as for Wallander.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Remote meetings have been...interesting, for this. Ideally you can listen to the person talk and watch their lips and it's almost the same.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

But in a big meeting people turn their cameras off to save bandwidth so they can hear. That means my brain is suddenly using all its effort to interpret the audio input because the lipreading has gone.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

If I do that for an hour, I'm knackered until the next day. If I do that for four hours, the rest of the week is gone. And by knackered I mean, can't operate a bottle top or a teaspoon without 3 goes. It's ALL connected.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Not every conferencing platform is created equal. U. of Sheffield use Blackboard, which is adequate for a small number of people but for a big number something weird happens to the sound. Like some of the Fourier components get fluffy somehow. And parsing is even harder.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

I'm told Zoom captions are usually adequate. But Blackboard captions are jellyfish cushion procrastination knife fork spoon brushing. I mean, so inaccurate as to be basically useless.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

I found out last time I did a long Blackboard meeting that it's easier if I lie on the floor in a ball on a yoga mat with my eyes closed. Something to do with not needing to concentrate on posture or vision, I guess. Mmm, professional.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

So the Year of the Plague has been...interesting. Also a thing, coupling with auditory processing: sensory overload. I am usually operating at 90% brain load just to not get run down by a car or talk semi-coherently. So it doesn't take much to make by brain struggle.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Loud room full of jostling people? Loud noises? Fireworks? A really strong smell? Bright fluorescent lights? Bye bye ability to do things. (People who wear loads of cologne to microscope sessions can Just Stop It.) I turn out the lights in the FIB room to do a hard lift-out.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

Now a thread about late diagnosis. I didn't find out I have dyspraxia until a few years ago...34 maybe? 35? I had just gone through school accepting that PE teachers and English teachers thought I was lazy, stupid and/or and a bad person.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

It didn't occur to me that there was some problem in the disparity of their opinion compared to science and maths. As a child you just...assimilate it into your idea of how the world goes. Some teachers hate me. Ok then. Maybe I suck.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

In the 80s and 90s, my brother was diagnosed with dyspraxia because he really, really had problems writing. Mine is less severe and I think it was easier then to write off a little girl as messy, a bit dozy, not really with it.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

As a teenager I think I got sorted into "the technical type" so I was expected to be bad at English, History, home ec, art, etc. and it was seen as evidence that the model of the world as having two types of people is correct, rather than symptoms of a possible problem.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

As an undergrad, I struggled enormously, with getting to practicals, doing practicals, HEARING in practicals, understanding lectures, almost everything. I thought, ok, finally the world is seeing that I do in fact suck, this is what I expected really.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

But in the second and third years I started noticing what was easier and having the...confidence? No. Cheek? Maybe. To decide to do things a different way to how I was told to. Like scribbling the lecture notes in the morning then going to the library in the afternoon.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

I found out, when there was practical work that involved figuring out how a material worked rather than following instructions from a long way away in a bright room, I was getting really good marks. So I worked my ass off on those, knowing my exams would suck.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

My PhD was... honestly I liked it. I still didn't twig that things weren't this mismatched for other people. And my supervisor saying that reading wasn't work, didn't help at all. But I figured out ways through and somehow did it.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

I only thought about a SpLD a few years ago when I went to a session on how to support students with SpLDs and they got to dyspraxia and I thought...waaaait...that's me. Then they said it runs in families and I went awwww shit, will you look at that.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

So I got in touch with the Disability & Dyslexia Support Service and had some tests done of various dimensions of cognitive ability and it came out, yes, I have dyspraxia. And suddenly a lot of things made sense - and most things in my life were not in face because I suck.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

So for anybody else out there who is really good at some things but every now and again you wonder why you are so stupid in very specific ways the "spiky profile" description - if you can, investigate. You never know.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

So - last proper thread of the week. There may be some snaps of the weekend if I do anything fun. What has dyspraxia taught me as a scientist?

27.11.2020 · Tweet

It has made me be resourceful and courageous. If one way to do something isn't working, I know now to stop doing it that way and find another way that does work. Energy is precious. Other people's whining about appropriateness is infinite. Find a way that works.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

It has made me need to be patient - especially talking to people, when they don't understand and I don't understand and I need to have a few tries.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

It has made me STUBBORN. To be fair I think some of that might be genetic. I will. Not. Quit. Nope. If I have to crawl in a blizzard I will get that thing done. Because usually, I do end up doing the equivalent.

27.11.2020 · Tweet

So, what's DFT anyway? It's a smart idea to reduce the complexity of quantum mechanics. Quantum mechanics can be super complex, even for a single atom. DFT can let you do quantum mechanics for hundreds, or even thousands of atoms. DFT is so smart it got a Nobel prize. 1/n

02.12.2020 · Tweet

What's meant by "do quantum mechanics"? I mean learn the properties of something. Formally speaking, it means solving the Schrodinger equation, one of the toughest equations in physics 2/n

02.12.2020 · Tweet

and when you solve the Schrodinger equation, you learn the properties of your atom via the properties of its electrons. When there are so many electrons in the atom, it becomes pretty hard to solve its Schrodinger equation 3/n

02.12.2020 · Tweet

And that's where the coolness of DFT emerges: just don't bother about the electrons individually. Instead, deal with electrons as a "sea of charges". This reduced the complexity of quantum mechanics tremendously but at the expense of accuracy 4/n

02.12.2020 · Tweet

And here's why different papers would get different results for the same material using DFT: DFT is an approximation, and there are many flavors of DFT, each claiming to be a better approximation. So either the two papers used different flavors, or one/both papers suck(s). 5/n

02.12.2020 · Tweet

New DFT student wonders: which flavor to start with? Crystal systems? PBE is a good starting point, and then u can add sub-flavors to it. Molecules? There's a war going on now on this - if I suggest #B3LYP (traditional choice) I'll hear shots being fired 😱 but its not bad. 6/n

02.12.2020 · Tweet

Bacteria cells, in this case MRSA, contain efflux pumps that are able to resist treatment due to their ability to efflux multiple drugs outside of the cell

09.12.2020 · Tweet

Because of this, this allows cytotoxic escape in both bacterial infections and cancers. Studying the kinetics of these efflux pumps allows us to provide more efficient treatment

09.12.2020 · Tweet

We studied the kinetics of these efflux pumps by using Silver (Ag) Nanoparticles as optical probes in MRSA cells and observed them in real-time under Dark-Field Optical Microscopy, or DFOM https://t.co/cBqVYBSYVd

09.12.2020 · Tweet

I called AgNPs “biological glitter” because there are 3 colors that are exhibited under the DFOM. Red, Blue, and Green! The same as primary colors 🥺

09.12.2020 · Tweet

However, these 3 colors are indicative of different sizes of the AgNPs and the smallest of the 3 are blue, while red seemed to be the largest https://t.co/rilkJKiHD7

09.12.2020 · Tweet

This is how the AgNPs loaded into the MRSA cells appear under the DFOM. See if you can spot all 3 colors!! 👀 *Side note: Dust is also really pretty under a DFOM 😂 https://t.co/1OtRnfNlrH

09.12.2020 · Tweet

When the AgNPs are on the outside of the MRSA cells, they appear bright (pictured above), but when they are inside the cell, the intensity is very dim. This is how we are able to know if the AgNPs are inside of the cells

09.12.2020 · Tweet

We used the DFOM to record real-time of this constant in and out of the cells in 20 minute intervals. From the recordings, we are able to obtain snapshots at different time points as well so we can count the cells

09.12.2020 · Tweet

After counting, we were able to create this graph to visualize the AgNPs that were most prominent. In Trials 1 & 2, Blue was the most successful spending about an hour in the MRSA cells. Green and red AgNPs did not last as long. https://t.co/LZUcFEynyQ

09.12.2020 · Tweet

From these results, we can conclude that smaller, blue AgNPs were the most effective at staying inside of the MRSA cells. Thus, these results are promising to the future of drug delivery. Here’s why!!

09.12.2020 · Tweet

If we are one day, able to combine these AgNPs with a drug to treat these bacterial infections, we are on our way to more efficient treatment! Also, we decrease the risk of these efflux pumps eliminating drugs before they get a chance to work.

09.12.2020 · Tweet

So it turns out ✨biological glitter✨ is actually pretty useful! Let me know if you all have any questions!! https://t.co/yaujP1YXKr

So my Master’s thesis was based upon improving drug delivery to the posterior segment of the eye to better treat Age-Related Macular Degeneration https://t.co/Yh2aoc8qsH

09.12.2020 · Tweet

In order to achieve this, I decided to use a MPEG-PCL micelles to encapsulate my drug. These polymeric nanoparticles are favorable due to their minuscule size and their proven biocompatibility

09.12.2020 · Tweet

The preparation of these nanoparticles include the sonification of MPEG-PCL polymer (A) and the anti-VEGF drug Sunitinib malate (B) into one mixture seen in the figure below https://t.co/ChLN86joP7

09.12.2020 · Tweet

After prep, we confirmed the efficacy of our SM-MPEG-PCL formulation by using DSC Analysis. Chaotic, I know, but I can explain! https://t.co/azm3gKcI01

09.12.2020 · Tweet

Peaks represent a melting point for each of the 4 samples (Formulation, Drug, Polymer, and Physical mixture of drug & polymer)

09.12.2020 · Tweet

DSC Analysis confirmed that the nanoparticle formulation is stable and the drug was properly loaded into the polymer

09.12.2020 · Tweet

Further analysis included particle size, zeta potential, entrapment efficiency (~64.3%) for this particular formulation. The first picture is an TEM image of the size range of the nanoparticles seen here https://t.co/MSsS4owAN8

09.12.2020 · Tweet

MTT Assay of our formulation reported a cell viability of >88% for all concentrations at both 24 and 48h. 100% viability at 10 & 20 μM. Meaning that our formulation is nontoxic to ARPE-19 cells

09.12.2020 · Tweet

We also performed an anti-VEGF ELISA with the formulation and the analysis showed that the drug solution and formulation reduced VEGF expression up to 72h

09.12.2020 · Tweet

Morning all! Today I'll be sharing my tips and tricks for how we can use storytelling to communicate science better, not just communicating it to the public, but to each other too. 🧵 https://t.co/UzKJpfgEmO

15.01.2021 · Tweet

First up: STRUCTURE. I often teach researchers about the Hero's Journey story structure. It's how many of us will intuitively tell stories anyway, but it's a helpful double-check of whether all the compelling details are in there... https://t.co/nfElEVAocx

15.01.2021 · Tweet

For example, in the Results sections of many papers, experiments are often presented in a seemingly random order. The HJ says that all actions should be causal, and occur because of what came before. That's how we do science! But that's not often well-communicated in papers...

15.01.2021 · Tweet

Second is CHARACTERISATION. We're trained as scientists to write/speak in the passive voice; "the experiment was done". Science is done by flawed humans, and I believe it's important to give scientists agency by including them in the stories we tell as we communicate the science.

15.01.2021 · Tweet

@nlidgi Ooh that's a really interesting distinction. I've definitely seen 'we' used increasingly in English, but it's definitely not mainstream.

So, How does someone end up working on microscopes with a physics degree? Well, physics includes the study of electromagnetism, one of the fundamental forces of nature. (Image courtesy of Wikipedia) https://t.co/g9I71calIB

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Optics, the bit of physics that studies the interaction of light and matter, is kinda a subset of electromagnetism, and it is an important part of how we build everything from glasses to the lenses on your cellphone cameras to how we build microscopes

27.01.2021 · Tweet

So among the *many* strange corners of physics, there are labs that basically spend all their time applying these principles to trying to build fancier and fancier microscopes

27.01.2021 · Tweet

this is not the only weird corner of physics involving optics btw, there are people out there levitating tiny bits of matter with lasers or using them to observe physical phenomena that happen on the pico-femtosecond time scale (under a trillionth of a second)

27.01.2021 · Tweet

That said, the study of optics actually predates the existence of physics as a formal field of study. My favorite ancient optical physicist was Ibn al-Haytham, a Muslim scientist born what is now Iraq in the late 900s

27.01.2021 · Tweet

He was a mathematician, an astronomer, a translator of ancient works and an actually foundational thinker in the field which I now work over a thousand years later (picture also courtesy of Wikipedia) https://t.co/3sX95opXxW

27.01.2021 · Tweet

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Now we can move on to talking about microscopes proper. For people who don't work with them for a living, you probably haven't seen once since school and you remember them looking like this https://t.co/Y3DF2OIXw5

27.01.2021 · Tweet

The strange thing is, that's not hugely different from what microscopes looked like for a long time. Original microscope design in the 1600s looked like this. A single ball of glass in a metal holder https://t.co/ZnDOb6qvR4

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Within a century though, they looked like this. And that fundamental design did't change hugely for a long time. Lens building got better, people figured out how to use bright lamps for light sources and focus them in samples, but the basic design didn't change too much https://t.co/xP08yKbOUZ

27.01.2021 · Tweet

So... What do they look like now? Here are some examples of systems I have worked on/with https://t.co/FzBvzXBecv

27.01.2021 · Tweet

If those don't look like you expect, it is because the last 3 decades or so have massively changed what microscopes look like and the ways they are used, and that change is accelerating

27.01.2021 · Tweet

The cause of those changes? Also Physics (I may be a tad biased) Basically optics got a little better, but what has really driven innovation has been three kinda connected things. Computing power, lasers and image sensors

27.01.2021 · Tweet

I say connected, because all three things exist because we discovered quantum physics in the mid 20th century and then applied it to understanding how materials behave. Hence solid state physics, hence lasers and transistors, hence the field that makes me a living

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Why lasers? Because most modern microscopy methods use a principle called fluorescence. Basically, you shine light of a specific wavelength/colour on a material, it absorbs that light and it emits light back at a different colour (purple laser, blue fluorescence on the right) https://t.co/rfVbDhTaj7

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Lasers allow us to deliver very bright light to a specific point in space, which is great for lighting up samples to be imaged. We use some fancy biochemistry to stick fluorescent molecules to the things we want to, we hit them with bright light, and we take a picture

27.01.2021 · RT

RT @ShroukELA: My company is hiring! Lots of roles, including for bold and creative engineers looking for Electronic Engineering roles in M…

27.01.2021 · Tweet

To go one level down, why fluorescence? Because a cell is basically a sack made of fatty acids in which a whole bunch of chemistry happens. Most of the stuff biologists care about is transparent, so we have to label it to look at it

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Next, Image sensors, also known as the piece of silicon in your digital camera that actually collects the light and converts it to a digital signal.

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Quick bit of history: Early microscopists looked through the glass and drew what they saw by hand. Then film cameras came along and people started mounting film cameras on microscopes, taking pictures of they samples, and developing them

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Then we got point detectors, which were sort of like reverse CRT screens. they could convert a spot of light focused on them into an electrical signal, so you could scan a point of light across a sample and record the light coming back one point at a time

27.01.2021 · Tweet

These existed in parallel with film for a while, because for some kinds of microscopy, point detectors didn't make much practical sense

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Then came image sensors, and all of a sudden biological images could be pushed directly from a microscope to a PC without a few hours of messing around with chemicals

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Also image sensor technology kept advancing and got so sensitive that they could detect single photons of light, so microscopes could "see" things that had previously been invisible

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Nowadays the kind of image sensors that end up in scientific cameras are almost as sensitive as the most sensitive point detectors, and almost as fast, but they can take a singe image at once instead of one point at a time, so they are more useful for most kinds of microscopy

27.01.2021 · Tweet

And the thing that ties them all together, faster computers. To get why computers matter so much here it helps to realize that a digital image is a picture represented as a series of numbers, and you can therefore use maths to 'see' things in the image...

27.01.2021 · Tweet

Since computers are good at maths, and since cameras can pump out images as fast as computers can see them, you can now create computerized tools for looking at pictures and extracting interesting data out of them

27.01.2021 · Tweet

So basically the kind of maths that can be used to recognise faces in photos can also be used to do things like count cells, measure their sizes and shapes, track their movements etc. etc.

27.01.2021 · Tweet

You tie all of this together and all of a sudden microscopes become big data tools that can take incredibly large numbers of pictures of impossibly small amounts of light inside cells and turn that into numbers that tell us what is going on

27.01.2021 · Tweet

@danguyf That is *very* much a thing. And probably going to be for years to come

Hi All, apologies for disappearing yesterday. This has been a busier week than originally planned. Thankfully it is now the weekend and I have done my customary Saturday chores and long walk, so I can settle in for the next couple of hours

30.01.2021 · Tweet

So... who wants to talk about diversity issues in science! Or rather, who wants to listen to me rant and occasionally interject?

30.01.2021 · Tweet

So where are we starting today? With a story about the microscope I already showed in this tweet https://t.co/TmA8cxgfSE

30.01.2021 · Tweet

that microscope is based on the one that would have been used by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch businessman and scientist who lived in the mid 1600-early 1700s and is widely regarded as one of the foundational figures in the history of microscopy and microbiology

30.01.2021 · Tweet

Sidenote: The businessman part is important because it is worth noting that a lot of the structures of modern science was created by wealthy European men working in their spare time. I'll talk a bit more later about why this matters

30.01.2021 · Tweet

For now, the important thing is that van Leeuwenhoek made what were at the time incredibly sensitive microscopes, then applied them to looking discovering microscopic life. Including his own semen

30.01.2021 · Tweet

(and yes, I have made all the jokes that I could think of about how he acquired his samples)

30.01.2021 · Tweet

When van Leeuwenhoek and his assistants described what they saw while looking at semen, they all claimed to be able to see little people inside of the sperm cells they saw wriggling around

30.01.2021 · Tweet

Now: (a) those microscopes probably weren't powerful enough to allow them to see tiny people inside of cells but more importantly (b) We know now that there are no tiny people inside sperm cells So why make the claim?

30.01.2021 · RT

RT @Hayley_Barlow: TONIGHT: shocking Channel 4 News report reveals how hundreds of overseas students have become destitute in the UK during…

30.01.2021 · Tweet

To understand that, you have to understand that there was a long history in western philosophy of the idea that men provided the "seeds" of what makes a person and women purely provided the "soil" for the new person to grow

30.01.2021 · Tweet

... and those ideas had grown into a legitimate scientific theory by the time van Leeuwenhoek looked through his microscope at those sperm cells. He was aware of these ideas, probably took them seriously.....

30.01.2021 · Tweet

...and so when he saw his own "seeds" it wasn't a huge step to conclude that there were actually people in them

30.01.2021 · Tweet

the lesson here isn't that he set out to mislead people or that he was a bad scientist, it is that he was a man who grew up in a world that fed him certain ideas about how the world worked, and those ideas leaked into his observations of the world

30.01.2021 · Tweet

(It is also worth noticing that science and philosophy in his era were both the domains of rich European men, and that had to have an effect on which ideas were considered legitimate and which weren't)

30.01.2021 · Tweet

The lessons of this story: Science as a discipline is meant to be a completely objective context-free search for the truth, and sometimes scientists assume this means *we* are also magically objective creatures who exist only to search for the truth

30.01.2021 · Tweet

In reality though, scientists are people, and like all people, we absorb the biases and prejudices of the societies we are surrounded are. And if we go on to build institutions, we embed those biases in them

30.01.2021 · Tweet

we are surrounded *by* I desperately need a proof reader

30.01.2021 · Tweet

Anyway, this observation becomes really important when you consider that, like I said earlier, the foundation of modern science were mostly erected over the last 500 years ago by a group almost exclusively made up of well-off European men

30.01.2021 · Tweet

and baked into the institutions they created are a series of prejudices they inherited and formalised around race, gender, class, sexuality, disability etc.

30.01.2021 · Tweet

And that process is as much a part of the history of science as the invention of the microscope or the discovery of DNA

30.01.2021 · Tweet

Also, the consequences of that process live with us now, in terms of who is allowed to take part in the creation of new science and what kinds of questions are considered worthy of study

Hi all, Today is my last day curating this account, and I figured I'd spend today giving some advice about careers in science, but also answering any questions people might have

31.01.2021 · Tweet

so if you have any questions, feel free to tweet at me and I'll see if I have something that looks like a sensible response

31.01.2021 · Tweet

On science careers, I'm probably going to do something slightly unusual in that I'm going to recommend people *not* do most of the things I have done

31.01.2021 · RT

RT @IgualdadLGBT: ¡Última Hora! Angola despenaliza la homosexualidad 🇦🇴🏳️‍🌈 https://t.co/17NbqAWR3y

31.01.2021 · Tweet

Things I would recommend that I did: (a) Try really hard to work for decent people and avoid terrible ones (b) Follow what you find interesting/exciting

31.01.2021 · Tweet

(c) Try to be a decent person yourself. Be the person who people in your circles know they can come to if they have a problem

31.01.2021 · Tweet

Things I recommend that I am terrible at: (a) Invest *heavily* in time management skills. Make the best use you can of your work hours, be as productive as possible (b) Have long term plans. Have a feel for what you want your future to look like and plan for it

31.01.2021 · Tweet

(c) Prioritize academic output. Don't put your name on terrible papers, but if you do anything actually interesting, get it published (d) Be tactical. Chase collaborations, chase speaking engagements, make sure important people know who you are

31.01.2021 · Tweet

Also, be realistic about job prospects. Academic science in the 2020s is not a viable career path for the majority of the people who are skilled enough and motivated enough to do the work

31.01.2021 · Tweet

...So keep an eye out on all of the possible career paths that exist outside of academia. And recognise that you aren't planning this because you are incapable of doing the work, but because you may not get a chance regardless

Hi everyone! My name is Otto Mustonen and it's my pleasure to curate Real Scientists Nano this week. I'm going to tweet about quantum materials and doing experiments at neutron and muon facilities. @OHJMustonen @isisneutronmuon @ILLGrenoble @msesheffield

Quantum materials is a research area in the intersection of physics, chemistry and materials science. The peculiarities of quantum mechanics give rise to exotic properties and states in these materials. This often involves the collective behavior of electrons. It's like magic. https://t.co/wBtMiAA4XN

08.02.2021 · Tweet

Quantum materials include superconductors, multiferroics, quantum magnetism, topological insulators and Weyl semimetals etc. The unusual properties can be the total loss of electrical resistivity, massive quantum entangled states and even magnetic monopoles.

08.02.2021 · Tweet

The applications of quantum materials are often related to quantum technologies in general such as quantum computing, but we all use these materials when we get an MRI or when we read data off a HDD.

08.02.2021 · Tweet

The 2021 quantum materials roadmap gives an excellent overview of the different types of quantum materials and the main challenges in the field. It is also open access! https://t.co/y2TrhTnULn @IOPscience @IOPmaterials #quantummaterials #openaccess

In 1911, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes was investigating the properties of metals at very low temperatures. When he cooled mercury to below 4.2 K, its resistivity suddenly dropped to zero. He had discovered superconductivity. #superconductors #NobelPrize https://t.co/TFiPsYXo4P

09.02.2021 · Tweet

This experiment was possible due to Kamerlingh Onnes' other great gift to science: liquid helium. Helium has the lowest boiling point of any gas at 4.2 K. It is used for cooling in almost all low-temperature physics. A good helium cryostat will get you down to 1.5 K. @OxInst https://t.co/V2mexWscGS

09.02.2021 · Tweet

The superconducting state has two important properties: the absence of any resistivity and the expulsion of magnetic fields. The latter is called the Meissner effect (perfect diamagnetism), and is the reason why a magnet will levitate on top of a superconductor. #levitation https://t.co/qF5DKDGuR8

09.02.2021 · Tweet

Coincidentally this is my absolutely favorite demo to show to students. I wish I had taken video to show you, it's awesome! And freaky! Safety note: liquid nitrogen is still very cold and bad for you, and make sure you're in a well-ventilated space.

09.02.2021 · RT

RT @ZJAyres: Honestly, one of the best bits of advice for navigating academia (and life) is to find genuine joy in other peoples' success.…

09.02.2021 · Tweet

Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer developed a microscopic theory of superconductivity. An electron moving in a crystal will feel resistance, but two electrons can pair up to move without resistance. At low temperatures these Cooper pairs condensate to form the superconducting state.

09.02.2021 · Tweet

The pairs are bound by a weak interaction with the lattice, and can be easily broken up as temperature increases. Here's the weird part: the electrons in the Cooper pair are hundreds of nanometers apart and moving in opposite directions! https://t.co/ul2jqMKGGX

09.02.2021 · Tweet

John Bardeen won the Nobel Prize in physics for both the BCS theory of superconductivity and for inventing the transistor. That is quite the legacy!

09.02.2021 · Tweet

@JoFeanelwa Hi Jo! New Cooper pairs are formed spontaneously, because they have a lower energy than individual free electrons in a superconductor. The interaction between the pair is something that is just not strong. In the BCS theory it occurs via a lattice vibration (phonon).

09.02.2021 · Tweet

@JoFeanelwa A negatively charged electron moving in the lattice of positively charged ions causes a small movement of the ions toward the electron. This displacement of the ions then attracts an electron moving in the opposite direction. This interaction binds the electrons into a pair. https://t.co/LmvuR1meh6

09.02.2021 · Tweet

@JoFeanelwa The interaction via this displacement is surprisingly long range, so the electrons can get pretty far away form each other before separating (>100 nm). But yes!

09.02.2021 · Tweet

@JoFeanelwa To be honest I don't know, but I don't think it can be done on the level of measuring the individual displacements of ions. The lattice vibrations (phonons) can be measured with techniques such as inelastic neutron scattering and it is possible to measure electron-phonon coupling

09.02.2021 · Tweet

Conventional superconductors are metals or intermetallic compounds. In 1986, Bednorz and Müller discovered superconductivity in a ceramic copper oxide at 30 K, a temperature on the edge of what was thought possible by BCS theory. https://t.co/UkIFbU8SLn

09.02.2021 · Tweet

The next year Chu and coworkers discovered YBCO (YBa2Cu3O7-d), a superconductor with a previously unthinkable critical temperature of over 90 K. This allowed the use of liquid nitrogen (77 K) instead of liquid helium (4.2 K) for cooling the material to the superconducting state. https://t.co/BFqKTSbdkq

09.02.2021 · Tweet

Anderson proposed this high-Tc superconductivity might be related to a novel quantum state known as the resonating valence bond state (a type of quantum spin liquid). I'll talk more about this in relation to my own research later.

09.02.2021 · Tweet

The high-Tc superconductors are very different from the materials before. They are ceramic instead of metallic, their parent phases are magnetic whereas magnetism usually destroys superconductivity, and they have layered structures with a superconducting CuO2 layer.

09.02.2021 · Tweet

The high-Tc cuprate superconductors are part of quantum materials known as strongly correlated electron systems. These materials cannot be described using conventional band theory, which assumes individual electrons do not interact with each other.

09.02.2021 · Tweet

This often involves materials with partially filled d or f shells, which are more localized on the ion compared to s and p orbitals and therefore interact more strongly. In the cuprates, the superconductivity arises from the interactions of the strongly correlated Cu2+ 3d9 states

Magnetism in solids is a bit tricky to explain. We all learn in school that an electric current going round and round in a loop will induce a magnetic moment. This is how electromagnets work. We can use this analogy for electrons and cations in solids. #magnetism #miracles https://t.co/ZioUxIEFPM

10.02.2021 · Tweet

Electrons have a negative charge, and so they also have a magnetic moment when they go round and round. Electrons have an inherent magnetic moment called spin, which is due them spinning around their axis (kind of). They also have a moment related to their orbital in an ion. https://t.co/sDjTq19gES

10.02.2021 · Tweet

Magnetism of filled orbitals and electron shells cancels out. Magnetism in solids requires unpaired electrons! These are found in transition metals such as iron and lanthanides such as neodymium. Magnetic moment of a cation is related to the number of unpaired electrons it has.

10.02.2021 · Tweet

We can treat magnetic cations as tiny magnets inside a solid. Magnetic properties of a material are defined by what the cation is, how they are arranged and how they interact with each other. The interactions cannot be described without quantum mechanics, but that's ok.

10.02.2021 · Tweet

Quantum magnetism occurs, when this "oh they're just tiny magnets" analogy breaks down. This occurs when the cation only has one unpaired electron, which can then start to misbehave due to quantum mechanics and do all sorts of weird things. https://t.co/bB9tk7YPrY

10.02.2021 · Tweet

@goldclusters Excellent question! The idea here is that if you have a localized electron on a d orbital and you put another electron on the same orbital, the presence of the first electron will strongly affect the second one and you have to take this electron correlation into account.

10.02.2021 · Tweet

@goldclusters This correlation is a really complex many-body problem. When the electrons are delocalized, they are far away from each other and can be modeled like a non-interacting free electron gas. The electrons don't spend much time close to each other, and this approximation is alright.

10.02.2021 · Tweet

Magnetic interactions try to align spins (moments) in a material either parallel (ferro-) or antiparallel (antiferromagnetic) to each other. When all the interactions between spins cannot be satisfied at the same time, the material is frustrated. https://t.co/MHhVoNJemz

10.02.2021 · Tweet

Frustration occurs when the spins are arranged in certain shapes such as triangles, tetrahedrons or squares. It can stop materials from magnetically ordering (all spins have a fixed direction). Instead, the spins can form collective quantum entangled states with weird properties.

10.02.2021 · Tweet

Anderson proposed a quantum spin liquid state on a triangular lattice of spins (moments). In this state, the spins do not freeze even at absolute zero. Instead, they pair up to form valence bonds. The QSL is a superposition of all the different ways to cover the lattice in bonds. https://t.co/d0psDda6UU

10.02.2021 · Tweet

QSLs are quantum states with a massive number of entangled spins. They're very weird. If given some energy, the QSL state can have excitations that carry only spin instead of both spin and charge like electrons. QSLs could have applications in a new type of quantum computer.

10.02.2021 · Tweet

A number of excellent QSL candidate materials are known. Herbertsmithite ZnCu3(OH)6Cl2 is a QSL candidate with a Kagome lattice of Cu2+ spins (see the Kagome basket below). There is no single "smoking gun" experiment for identifying a QSL, which makes it all quite difficult. https://t.co/k1UvR8BUbS

10.02.2021 · Tweet

This review by Leon Balents is an excellent introduction to the field of quantum spin liquids. https://t.co/6Mq3rVEQtf

10.02.2021 · Tweet

[admin] "Strange World of Quantum Materials" Extended podcast conversation with the amazing @OHJMustonen is out now! https://t.co/RKBdCQCqLR

10.02.2021 · Tweet

Anderson proposed a quantum spin liquid state also on the square lattice, which is found in high-Tc superconductors. For over 30 years there were no QSL candidates on the square, until me and coworkers discovered one. https://t.co/dDA1GMCrmu

10.02.2021 · Tweet

This was a collaboration between my PhD supervisor Maarit Karppinen's group at @AaltoUniversity, physicists in Brazil, Germany and Japan and muon and neutron scientists at @psich_en and @isisneutronmuon. Thank you so much everyone!

10.02.2021 · Tweet

Two different antiferromagnetic arrangements of spins are possible on the square. The one observed depends on the interactions in a material. However, if the interactions are just right between these states, a QSL might be found. https://t.co/zWLltQG1ex

10.02.2021 · Tweet

We found that two almost identical copper compounds have these different magnetic states, with the only difference being a Te6+ (d10) instead of a W6+ (d0) cation. I had the simple idea of let's just mix the two and see what happens. And it worked!

10.02.2021 · Tweet

This mixed compound Sr2CuTe0.5W0.5O6 has many of the properties expected of a QSL. Most importantly it does not magnetically order down to 19 mK despite antiferromagnetic interactions. This material could be a QSL or a QSL-like random singlet state.

10.02.2021 · Tweet

Measuring this compound at @psich_en was probably the coolest moment in my (brief) scientific career. We had no idea what would happen going in, and I was just so excited to find out it might be a QSL. And then we walked to a nearby village for a lovely dinner. https://t.co/T3vhEvlZes

Neutrons are subatomic particles that help keep the cores of atoms together. But they are also waves! This means we can do science with neutron beams like we would with beams of light. Neutron scattering is a powerful technique for investigating materials. #waveparticleduality https://t.co/utFxkYWgdg

11.02.2021 · Tweet

Neutrons can be used to measure the structure of solids at the atomic level and dynamics like lattice vibrations. Neutrons penetrate deep into materials. This means we can use neutrons to study the strains and stresses in large objects like turbine blades.

11.02.2021 · Tweet

Most importantly for me: neutrons have a magnetic moment. This makes them very useful for studying magnetic materials, since they are scattered by the spins (magnetic moments) in materials unlike X-rays. #magnetism #neutrons

11.02.2021 · Tweet

There are two ways to make neutrons. In nuclear fission, the nucleus of a heavy element splits into lighter ones while releasing energy and neutrons. The other is spallation: a proton travelling almost at the speed of light hits a nucleus shooting neutrons all over. #neutrons https://t.co/NfaO2GH7t8

11.02.2021 · Tweet

The need for a nuclear reactor or a particle accelerator means neutron science can only be done at large central facilities. Reactor sources include @ILLGrenoble and @ANSTO while spallation sources include @isisneutronmuon, @ORNLNeutrons, @psich_en and @essneutron. #neutrons

12.02.2021 · Tweet

I went on a trip to a nuclear power plant when I was a kid. I was so disappointed we only got to see the visitor center! I finally got to go inside the actual reactor building at @ILLGrenoble , which was really cool. #neutrons https://t.co/rEcZseQVNo

12.02.2021 · Tweet

Understanding how the atomic level structure of materials affects their properties is one of the cornerstones of materials science. Neutron diffraction is an excellent method to determine that atomic and crystal structure. #neutrons #diffraction https://t.co/4d1grBNqdo

12.02.2021 · Tweet

Most solids are made of tiny crystals with all the atoms arranged in a repeating pattern. Neutrons (or X-rays, or electrons) only scatter from crystals at certain allowed angles depending on their crystal structure. This is called diffraction. #braggslaw https://t.co/FzFpYkX9Hh

12.02.2021 · Tweet

Neutron diffraction makes it possible to accurately determine the positions of light atoms like lithium and oxygen, which is difficult with X-rays. Hydrogen is still problematic as it increases the background, and it is often replaced with deuterium for neutron experiments.

12.02.2021 · Tweet

In magnetic materials, the directions of the spins (magnetic moments) of all the magnetic ions can be determined with neutrons. This is possible, because neutrons have their own spin and are scattered by the magnetic ions. #neutrons #magnetism https://t.co/gGNmpNl42z

12.02.2021 · Tweet

Inelastic neutron scattering is a technique, where the neutrons lose energy as they scatter from the material. This makes it possible to study excitations such as lattice vibrations (phonons) and spin waves, which are tiny distortions of the ordered magnetic structure. #neutrons https://t.co/vCC3Re5rfD

12.02.2021 · Tweet

Lattice vibrations play an important role in heat conduction, electric transport and superconductivity. Investigating the spin waves of a magnetic material make it possible to determine its magnetic interactions.

12.02.2021 · Tweet

Our recent paper on magnetic double perovskites highlights some neutron scattering techniques. We used neutron diffraction to solve the magnetic structure and inelastic neutron scattering to investigate magnetic interactions. @isisneutronmuon @msesheffield https://t.co/SteTJ0TcCJ

12.02.2021 · Tweet

Inelastic neutron scattering data just looks cool. Each yellow or light blue point corresponds to a neutron exciting a spin wave. Measured data on the left, simulation on the right. https://t.co/NUZedpcrUS

12.02.2021 · Tweet

These experiments allowed us to formulate simple rules for magnetism in double perovskites that have a nonmagnetic d10 or d0 cation on one of the B-sites. d10 cations will lead to Type 1 magnetic order and d0 cations will lead to Type 2 order. #perovskites https://t.co/mBtGqmcVoF

12.02.2021 · Tweet

This week I'm running an experiment at the D7 polarized neutron diffractometer at @ILLGrenoble . Polarization analysis allows the separation of the structural and magnetic scattering from each other. This can be used to study dynamic magnetic states like spin liquids. #neutrons https://t.co/eBtUxS1fRT

12.02.2021 · Tweet

I'm very sad this is a remote experiment as I love Grenoble. Beamtime is my favorite part of the job, and it's just not the same when you're sitting at home. That said, many thanks to all the dedicated instrument scientists who make these experiments possible at all! #beamtime

12.02.2021 · Tweet

The real cost of beamtime at a neutron facility is of the order of £20 000 a day. This means we always need to apply for beamtime even though we don't directly pay for it. The proposals are ranked by a scientific panel, and the best ones get beamtime. #neutrons #beamtime https://t.co/Bh6zKw5EXp

12.02.2021 · Tweet

A beamtime proposal will include the scientific background including what you already know about your sample, an overview of the proposed experiment and what it will tell you, and the reason why neutrons are the only/best way to find out.

12.02.2021 · Tweet

If you're interested in doing an experiment at a neutron facility, instrument scientists are the best people to contact. They will be able to tell you if your proposed experiment is sensible and the best instrument for it. Instrument scientists are awesome! https://t.co/OYytsnMfes

Muons are short-lived elementary particles that are a bit like heavy electrons. They are produced when cosmic rays hit the atmosphere and in particle accelerators. Muons are a highly sensitive local probe of magnetism. Muon sources: @isisneutronmuon @psich_en @TRIUMFLab @J_PARC https://t.co/78OF7dY6Ia

13.02.2021 · Tweet

Muons have a fun property: their magnetic moment points in the opposite direction of where they're going. We can use this spin polarization in muon spectroscopy to study magnetic materials, superconductors and ionic conductivity in batteries. #muons #musr https://t.co/dRsu5VkW2j

13.02.2021 · Tweet

In muon spectroscopy, positive muons are implanted in the sample. The muon spin will start to rotate in the internal magnetic field. The muon quickly decays into a positron, which flys mainly in the direction of the muon spin at time of decay. The positrons then are measured. https://t.co/IXIGOGsBDQ

13.02.2021 · Tweet

Where the positrons are going tells us what the muon spin is doing as function of time, which in turn gives us information on the properties of the material. Muon spectroscopy is related to NMR, but it works even in zero magnetic field.

13.02.2021 · Tweet

Muon spectroscopy can be used to study both both static and dynamic magnetism. It's great for quantum spin liquids, which have no "smoking gun" experimental signature. But muons allow us to rule out more common states such as magnetic order or a spin! #muons #spinliquids https://t.co/dQFKIZ6Qx8

13.02.2021 · Tweet

Oops, rule out a spin glass state I mean.

What is computational chemistry? We can say that is the use of computer simulations (in silico experiments) to solve chemical problems. But this actually covers a lot of different fields and applications, from drug design to astrochemistry. 1/5 https://t.co/LsGEIijr6N

23.02.2021 · Tweet

Nowadays it is mainly used to give guidelines to scientists performing experiments, speeding up the research process. And, with the development of software and hardware, computational sciences are becoming more important. 2/5

23.02.2021 · Tweet

The efficiency and low cost of computer simulations makes them the perfect tool to predict properties and behaviour of different substances and then proceed to test non-virtually just the ones with a specific profile. 3/5

23.02.2021 · Tweet

I apply these concepts to understand how different 2D-materials can be exploited for analysis, electronics or catalysis. I still rely on good experimental data to check the accuracy of my simulations and to reproduce, as much as possible, the real-world conditions. 4/5

23.02.2021 · Tweet

Of course still a lot of progress is needed in computational chemistry. We work with approximations and it is impossible to reproduce everything that happens. We can just try to find better models and methods, and improve the efficiency of the algorithms used. 5/5

Graphene: what is it and how was it discovered? #graphene is a 2D material composed only by carbon atoms. These atoms are disposed in a hexagonal lattice, like a honeycomb. It is an extremely robust, conductive material, with a lot of possible applications (see next tweets). 1/3 https://t.co/76yyHICc4J

24.02.2021 · Tweet

Graphene is obtained by graphite (the main ingredient of pencils leads). Graphite is composed by a lot of super-thin (one atom thin) layers of carbon sheets. Each one of these is a graphene sheet. 2/3 https://t.co/kXmJLRDu9m

24.02.2021 · Tweet

The first report of graphene was just in 2004, by professors Geim and Novoselov. They discovered the secret amazing material hidden in the underestimated graphite. If you want to know more about the discovery and the discoverers: https://t.co/ohhr06nsZS 3/3

24.02.2021 · Tweet

Pristine graphene, as the perfect infinite hexagonal lattice we are used to see, is an ideal material. What it is obtained in a reality is a material containing defect, holes and impurities. The ideal graphene does not exist but there are bright sides. 1/4 https://t.co/GhxYv0ZbA0

24.02.2021 · Tweet

The possibility of changing the structure and the composition of graphene during the synthesis allows us to obtain a whole family of compounds: graphene-based materials (GBMs). 2/4

24.02.2021 · Tweet

We have then a big pool of 2D materials to exploit and study! While some defects or functionalities are randomly introduced during the production of graphene, some of them can be introduced voluntarily, using different synthetic conditions. 3/4

24.02.2021 · Tweet

Some of these "defects" are quite useful. For example, it was discovered that, while pristine graphene is almost useless in catalysis (not very reactive), a simple oxidation of it allows to unlock good catalytic performances. 4/4

24.02.2021 · Tweet

@goldclusters Partially yes but also the ways to obtain graphene are responsible for it. The conditions used introduce new defects.. like if you form it on a metal surface some metal atoms "enter" in the lattice or if you exfoliate graphite holes or deformations can be produced

25.02.2021 · Tweet

Using computational chemistry is it possible to study the properties of molecules, understanding the mechanism of reactions and design drugs or catalysts. But it also possible to design a material. How can we do it? 1/5

25.02.2021 · Tweet

1)think about which kind of material we want, both composition (graphene derivative? inorganic material?..) and function (adsorbant? sensor? ..). At that point it is necessary to check the literature to see how different material perform for the desired task. 2/5

25.02.2021 · Tweet

At that point it starts the difficult part: we need to find some property we can calculate or simulate and try to see if there is a relationship between the performance shown by the material and the computed property. 3/5

25.02.2021 · Tweet

If you find that the relationship exist then we can "design" a material, compute the property and from that predict how well it will perform. If we don't find a relationship probably the chosen property has no effect on the performance and we should try others. 4/5

25.02.2021 · Tweet

There are some challenges: use accurate methods to simulate the material and compute the property, the need to consider the different experimental conditions in which our data were measured, the performance probably depends on more than a single property.. 5/5

26.02.2021 · Tweet

Graphene and its derivatives are the most famous between 2D materials. These materials are very interesting because: - high surface/volume ratio - usually high mechanical robustness - particular optical and electrical properties - tunability of structure and properties.

26.02.2021 · Tweet

2D materials can be used, exploiting their particular properties for a lot of different applications, from nanoelectronics to water depuration. 1/4 https://t.co/aBCLEK6ydu

26.02.2021 · Tweet

My interest in mainly in environmental applications. As I said 2D materials have an high surface/volume ratio, so if they interact with contaminants they can be used as filters for water or air. 2/4

26.02.2021 · Tweet

Many 2D materials (like graphene derivatives) are semiconductors and they can be used as sensors, to determine the quantity of contaminants in a sample. The molecules will get adsorbed and this will cause a measurable change in the properties of the sensing material. 3/4

26.02.2021 · Tweet

There are a lot of other amazing applications for 2D materials. They have been used to obtain highly efficient solar cells, they have been used in photothermal therapy and to enhance the mechanical properties of hydrogels. 4/4

28.02.2021 · Tweet

Today is my last day of take-over and I want to talk about the future of my field. The future for computational chemistry looks exciting and full of challenges and possibilities. New developments in computer science are giving scientists amazing tools! 1/4 #compchem https://t.co/ocsepZS0sz

28.02.2021 · Tweet

Machine learning is one of the most hyped and promising tools. The possibility for a machine to find trend and properties in large datasets of molecules, with the aim to predict and design new systems is incredible and almost scary. (https://t.co/P2NWFom1Ix) 2/4 #machinelearning

28.02.2021 · Tweet

The development of super efficient computational algorithms has also offered the possibility of analysis large numbers of systems, causing the building of large databases, so the choice of the studied set is becoming less difficult, because it is possible to not be selective. 3/4

28.02.2021 · Tweet

The role of the computational chemist is clearly changing and developing. It is still important for chemist to invest time and research into developing computational methods, to couple the performance of machines with the experience and instinct of chemists. 4/4

28.02.2021 · Tweet

This is the end of my take-over. I'm really glad for this opportunity to share my research and my ideas! If you are interested in computational chemistry and 2D materials follow me at @AnnaPiras19

Computational research goes better with experimental results. As a purely computational group, we rely on experimentalists to provide their data for comparison. https://t.co/hj8QzsC6Bm

07.03.2021 · Tweet

A common way is comparing vibrational spectra. But my clusters are metallic and the metal-metal interaction falls in the Far infrared spectrum, which is not easy to observe experimentally.

07.03.2021 · Tweet

You need a laser that has: ✅tunable wavelength ✅wavelenght at the Far IR ✅powerful enough A Free-electron laser ticks all the boxes

07.03.2021 · Tweet

Like the one in Nijmegen (The Netherlands) at Radboud University. Its name is FELIX. https://t.co/8um9uXg5qO

07.03.2021 · Tweet

Obtaining the IR spectrum computationally is relatively easy, all you need is a Frequency calculation. https://t.co/5VSNxlAkLS

07.03.2021 · Tweet

Another way to compare experimental data with theoretical results is using mass spectrometry.

07.03.2021 · Tweet

After photofragmentation experiments, we can obtain a mass spectrum informing us about the relative stability of our clusters. A high intensity in the spectra indicates a high relative stability of these clusters.

07.03.2021 · Tweet

Then we calculate dissociation energies using Density Functional Theory. A higher dissociation energy will indicate that the cluster is more stable.

07.03.2021 · Tweet

This way we can find which clusters are more stable, what we call: magic numbers and magic clusters. https://t.co/DyV6AWdZ6H

07.03.2021 · Tweet

I did this for this paper, in collaboration with @KU_Leuven https://t.co/b870H0WY1t

07.03.2021 · Tweet

and I discussed the paper in this thread https://t.co/BtDnwWSBUF
