Today, I'll use this platform to share some #science w/ u. Maybe it inspires some of u 2 come up w/ new ideas or 2 collaborate. Since I heard a lecture by Prof. Wuttig @RWTH, I've been fascinated by phase-change materials & studying them for ∼10 yrs now. #AcademicTwitter 1/n https://t.co/vUVPG04gVZ

10.03.2021 · Tweet

Phase-change materials exist in at least 2 structural states - 1 amorphous & 1 or more crystalline. The reversible transition can be triggered by heat, e.g., by an optical or electrical pulse. After, the material will remain in its state w/o any heat supply needed. 2/n https://t.co/eNmLGDMWWc

10.03.2021 · Tweet

The structural transition is accompanied by a significant property contrast. The electrical resistivity can change by up to 5 orders of magn & the refractive index contrast can be up to 3.6 (huge!). Additionally, the density can change up to 10%. 3/n

10.03.2021 · Tweet

This property contrast has been used for different applications, ranging from optical data #storage (DVD RW, Blu-Ray discs), to #memristive elements, & active #photonics. For the most part of my research, I've been focussing on the latter. 4/n

10.03.2021 · Tweet

For my first #PhD project I worked on #antenna resonance tuning by using phase-change material thin films (x0 nm). Therefore, I fabricated aluminum (evap.) nanorods via e-beam #lithography & covered them with a sputtered phase-change material (e.g., Ge3Sb2Te6). 5/n https://t.co/HnifvOnboG

10.03.2021 · Tweet

Changing the structural state of the phase-change material allowed for a resonance shift of the nanorod arrays. Due to the large optical contrast, the shift is quite large. However, increasing absorption in the cryst state leads to resonance damping. 6/n https://t.co/LYLRevKPk4

10.03.2021 · Tweet

The aforementioned resonance tuning principle is not restricted to nanorods but can be extended to #plasmonic #absorbers, #chiral structures, etc.. 7/n https://t.co/DeBz1NHPaV

10.03.2021 · Tweet

During my PhD, I also worked on the reversible switching of nanorod #metasurfaces. By collaborating with a group @Stanford, we could show that #femtosecond laser pulses allow for switching of the nanoantenna arrays shown above. 8/n https://t.co/Hx27aQ96S7

10.03.2021 · Tweet

By comparing different phase-change materials, we could show that thorough knowledge of the material properties is crucial for successful sample design. Unfortunately, in many studies, prominent compounds instead of "the best 1s" are still favored. 9/n https://t.co/5d4NPVu7sG

10.03.2021 · Tweet

A tricky part of revers. (optical) switching of phase-change materials is the volume extent of the structural transition. A detailed 3D analysis of our #metasurfaces showed the extent of the switched spots & the max resolution possible. 10/n https://t.co/bS5UtjFAdj

10.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ So what IS a semiconductor? There exists a loose definition saying that semiconductors are materials with an electrical conductivity somewhere between that of metals (very conductive) and insulators (not conductive at all). Of course that is very difficult to quantify.

22.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ What threshold value of the conductivity does the material have to exceed to qualify? This is not a good definition. We'll come back to one later. In terms of conductivity, solid state physics only knows two types of solids: conductors (metals) and non-conductors (insulators)

22.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ The distinction is made by looking at where electrons in the solid "live". More specifically, which energies can electrons in the solid have? Atoms have fixed energies for each electron orbital. In solid matter, which is built up from atoms, this scheme is partially preserved. https://t.co/LKB9W6teJc

22.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ Singe-energy levels from atoms will combine to broad regions with "allowed energies", called bands. Sometimes, these bands are being pushed into each other, and they merge into one broader band. In other cases, there will be a gap between some states -- the so called band gap.

22.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ When we now "fill" these states (figuratively) with electrons, they will occupy the available states. When all electrons a material ahs have been "poured" into the solid, we get to an energy that separates occupied from unoccupied states. https://t.co/YTdMip8iOu

22.03.2021 · Tweet

6/ In the example above, one band has been completely filled, and one is completely empty. There is no possibility for carrier movement in any of the two bands -- one has no room to move, the other one has no electrons. This material is an insulator.

22.03.2021 · Tweet

7/ Let's assume our original simplified atom has one electron more. Building up a solid with it, this situation will result. Now we have free electrons in the band. This is probably a good conductor, i.e. a metal. https://t.co/2CbfzQhPO4

22.03.2021 · Tweet

8/ This picture has no room for something "in-between". A material is either a metal or an insulator, and that seems to be the end of it. We will have to find a better definition. I can at this point already tell you that a semiconductor can only be obtained in cases with a gap.

22.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ To approach a better definition of a semiconductor, we'll have to look at defects. What are they? Most solids form crystals. Crystals are pieces of matter in which atoms are arranged in a fixed pattern, the so-called lattice. Each kind of atom (or rather: ion) has its place.

22.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ (I'll not talk about amorphous substances here; in these, "defects" are much more difficult to define.) If something in the crystal is not where it should be, this is called a defect. Atoms can be missing, replaced by another atom, or sit on sites not part of the lattice. https://t.co/xvJk47BFdc

22.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ The first one is called a vacancy, the second an impurity, and the third an interstitial. These three are the simplest 0-dimensional (or point) defects there are, and probably also the most important ones.

22.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ Because a defect disturbs the perfect lattice, it will introduce new electron energies into the energy scheme we have drawn that weren't there before. In some cases, these energies will end up in the band gap. Those are the most interesting ones! https://t.co/8lbEyhGuHc

22.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ The one to the left there is really close to the lowest empty band (also called "conduction band"). If it comes with an additional electron, for example because the defect is an impurity atom with 1 electron more than the host material, this electron can easily leave...

22.03.2021 · Tweet

6/ the defect and freely move in the conduction band -- we have made the material slightly more conductive. Adding impurities in a controlled way to manipulate the electrical conductivity is called doping.

22.03.2021 · Tweet

7/ By choosing the amount of dopants, the conductivity can be changed by orders of magnitude, which translates into the property of semiconductors to have such a variable conductivity. This principle only works when there is a band gap.

22.03.2021 · Tweet

8/ It also only works when defects with small energy separation from a nearby band (so-called "shallow defects") exist or can be found. This can be tricky, which I'll come back to later. So, how about this definition: semiconductors are insulators that can be doped.

22.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ This definition is still "fuzzy", because it depends on the knowledge of appropriate dopants, which may change as science progresses. For example, until a while ago, a material like gallium oxide was considered an insulator. Today, we know.... https://t.co/PU5JeydTdH

22.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ that by adding silicon to it, we can obtain semiconducting gallium oxide. Silicon was long considered to be a metal because the samples people studied contained so much "dirt" that they always were conductive. Today we know silicon as THE prototypical semiconductor, because

22.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ we have figured out how to make clean samples. This brings me to the next point: abundance of defects. Theoretically, we can prepare any sample in such a way that it doesn't contain any impurities. Defects like vacancies or interstitials, on the other hand, also occur...

22.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ in the clean lattice. In fact, the laws of thermodynamics demand that any sample HAS TO contain a certain concentration of these so called intrinsic defects (= defects that come from only displacing atoms of the host crystal).

22.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ This means that we have to live with them being there! And that can make our lives as researchers quite difficult. The energy levels of intrinsic defects are often buried deep inside the semiconductor's band gap. For example, a free electron can get caught in it. That means...

22.03.2021 · Tweet

6/ that it cannot contribute to conductivity anymore. For many devices, such as solar cells or LEDs, "deep" defects like that are detrimental to the performance. Control and engineering of defect formation is key!

22.03.2021 · Tweet

We will see in the further course of this week that defects are not always unwanted. Gemstones actually get their beautiful color because of impurities! This picture contains a large variety of sapphire crystals. Adding small traces of titanium, chromium, or iron to... https://t.co/fKQsYawTUc

22.03.2021 · Tweet

clean aluminum oxide Al2O3 (or corundum) produces electronic states in the band gap. Electrons in these states absorb and emit light of a particular wavelength. (image source: https://t.co/2zlRfrFSVa, author Wisebwoy, license CC BY-SA 4.0, https://t.co/JzqGWpdz3Q)

22.03.2021 · Tweet

I think that is enough facts for today! If you have any questions, shoot :) I'll now have a cup of coffee, and then prepare a presentation I'll be giving on Friday.

Time to call it a day! Tomorrow will be all about methods for detecting and studying defects, and I'll show you the instruments we use for that. I hope you had a good start into the new week!

23.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ Good morning! Before we dive into how we can detect defects, I want to say a bit more about the importance of defect research -- not sure if that came across enough yesterday! More or less all of our modern-day electronics needs semiconductors to function.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ Microprocessors consist of incredibly large numbers of nano-sized electrical switches called transistors. The same type of devices is behind the electronics controlling the screens on our mobile devices. Solar cells are nothing else but a "block" of semiconductor absorbing...

23.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ light and converting its energy to usable electrical power. LEDs are in a way a "reversed solar cell", converting charge carriers into photons. High-power electronics are part of our power grid systems, converting the electricity coming from power plants to "usable" values.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ For all these devices, it is extremely important that charge carriers can move as freely as possible. Defects can mess with that by capturing charge carriers. In some cases, already one defect per 10 billion atoms (!) can make the difference between a good and a bad device.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ This means that we need VERY sensitive equipment to find out if defects are present in this concentration range, and to study how they interact with charge carriers.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ There are many ways to detect defects in semiconductors. One of the "simplest" ones is related to the picture of the colorful crystals I showed yesterday. Electrons caught in defects can absorb and emit light. If we use a laser... https://t.co/DfJSSb8NQY

23.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ to illuminate a sample, the electrons go into a short period of being "excited" (i.e. having a bit larger energy than in their ground state) and then fall back to where they were before, re-emitting light of a specific wavelength that we can detect.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ Each defect has characteristic emission lines, similar to what atoms do when you "excite" them. By identifying these lines, we can learn which defects are present in the sample. This method is called photoluminescence (PL for short).

23.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ This is what a PL spectrum looks like. The material we are looking at here is silicon carbide (SiC), an important material for high-power electronics and quantum technologies. Here, we are only seeing a narrow wavelength window where the lines of the silicon vacancy "live". https://t.co/kH7B3aDX4x

23.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ You can see two datasets here: one from a sample with only a few vacancies, and one with a lot. The signal intensity is related to the concentration of the defect -- more signal = higher concentrations. PL is not a quantitative method, it only gives relative information.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

6/ Here are some impressions from our PL lab! The grey box with the yellow stickers is one of the lasers we use. The light is sent through a sometimes really complicated arrangement of optical components to the sample, which sits in a cryostat -- the blue cylinder to the left. https://t.co/JgTfL7foed

23.03.2021 · Tweet

7/ Cryostats are chambers that keep the sample at very low temperatures (down to 4K). That can be important because thermal energy also interacts with the charge carriers inside the defects uncontrollably, which worsens signal quality.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

8/ The silicon vacancy in SiC (more specifically the modification 4H-SiC) has become interesting defect for quantum technologies! The light that it emits is different from what we know from everyday light sources -- it only comes in packages of exactly 1 photon per defect...

23.03.2021 · Tweet

9/ making the defect a so-called "single-photon source". Really valuable for secure quantum communication. Also, electrons captured in the defect show very long spin coherence times (I'll talk about that on Thursday!), so it can serve as a qubit in quantum computers.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

@BarnabyWalters It's a class 3B He-Cd laser, so powerful enough to damage eyes if you look directly into the beam. We wear laser goggles when operating it, and of course the alignment is done very carefully to avoid light bouncing around. The optical table is also waist-high to reduce risk.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

@BarnabyWalters Beefiness does also not necessarily translate to higher power. He-Cd lasers are more voluminous than diode lasers, but do not necessarily have higher optical power (but not a laser expert here tbh!)

23.03.2021 · Tweet

We don't have to use laser light to excite the defects. The same can also be done using high-energy electrons. Electrons are charged particles, so they can be accelerated to high speeds with electrical fields & then shaped into a beam with magnetic fields https://t.co/nIkvyIe8B5

23.03.2021 · Tweet

The electron beam is directed at the sample, where they excite all sorts of things, one of them being other electrons trapped at defects. This technique is called cathodoluminescence (CL) and can be done using a scanning electron microscope. This is our microscope. https://t.co/lZMdDGkGJI

23.03.2021 · Tweet

The advantage of CL over PL is that the excited region is much smaller (PL: ~10 micrometers, CL ~100nanometers), giving it much better spatial resolution, while the spectral resolution is typically not as good. Upside is that you get some really nice micrographs of your sample!

23.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ PL and CL are powerful methods, and we use them a lot, but the methods I specialize in use the ELECTRICAL response of defects instead of the optical one. For that, the sample structure becomes a little more complicated, which can be quite challenging. https://t.co/dLRFBs49qA

23.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ The property used in these methods is the charge state of defects. Defects with electrons in them are more negatively charged than ones without electrons, and the process by which defects change their charge state (capture or emission of charge carriers) gives away details...

23.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ of the defect, like where their energy levels are in the band gap of the semiconductor. Knowing that value is a central part of learning the identity of a defect. The problem is that normally all defects of a certain type have the same charge state in the entire sample.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ To make them change charge states, we have to apply a trick. We have to remove a part of the free charge carriers (those that move in a band). This new charge balance forces some of the defects to change their state. This carrier removal is done by bringing our sample...

23.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ into contact with another material that has less or more electrons than the sample itself. Imagine you connect two glasses filled with water to different heights by a tube. Water will flow from one glass to the other, until the water level is the same in both glasses.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

6/ This is the same principle: find a material with a different "sea level" of electrons than you sample, and bring them in contact. That creates a region close to the interface with almost no free charge carriers where the defects become "visible".

23.03.2021 · Tweet

7/ This region is called space charge region, and the methods that make use of it are called space charge spectroscopies. These are what I mainly use in my research!

23.03.2021 · Tweet

Our lab for these electrical measurements does not look fancy, but it is! It has five of these high-sensitivity setups, with cooling and heating capabilities and hardware that makes it possible to find tiny defect concentrations down to 1 in 1 trillion! https://t.co/0z0riuQSUY https://t.co/kJLegRaPqT

You see the small circles on the sample? Those are the contacts I talked about. Below them, inside the actual sample (the square), is now a thin layer without free electrons. That makes the defects in it detectable.

1/ Finding a suitable material for space charge spectroscopy on a new material can be super challenging. There are a few rules of thumb that one can use to at least identify candidates, but sometimes life is more complicated. Searching for contact materials is a science in itself

23.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ This brings me to the material I'm mostly studying: nickel oxide. Super versatile stuff, has applications in all sorts of devices: solar cells, LEDs, smart windows, batteries, and detectors for UV light. As I explained yesterday, doping of a semiconductor is key to making...

23.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ full use of its potential. People realized quite early on that nickel oxide (NiO) can either be doped by putting some lithium in, or by making samples that have more oxygen than nickel. In the latter case, nickel vacancies will be quite abundant, and they are a decent dopant.

23.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ Although it has been very clear that these two methods work, people so far had no idea where the energy levels of these defects actually were in the band gap. That can be very important information when designing and making devices. This is where our most recent work comes in

23.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ More or less by coincidence, we found a material -- fluorine-doped tin dioxide, FTO -- that does the trick. That allowed us to detect the two most important energy levels belonging to the two dopants in NiO, and closed, as they say, a "knowledge gap"! https://t.co/tA9NwciEEF

23.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ Today is experiment day! I told you yesterday that doing the electrical characterization of defects we would like to do requires a device that removes a part of the free carriers in the semiconductor. We will make such devices today. Our studied semiconductor is nickel oxide.

24.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ We will make thin (~200nm) NiO layers on top of materials that induce this depletion of free carriers. I have already told you that we have identified FTO (fluorine-doped tin dioxide) as appropriate for that, but in theory, aluminium should also do the trick.

24.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ Now, when I tried to make Al contacts on NiO before, it never worked. I don't really know why, but one big difference to the FTO samples was that in these, the NiO layer is deposited on top of the contacting material. Sometimes, the order of making layers makes a difference.

24.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ So for today's experiments, we'll be depositing NiO ON TOP of aluminium, to see if that's true here too. For comparison, I will also make devices on FTO like before. To have even more to compare, I'll be using two methods for NiO deposition: evaporation and sputtering.

24.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ In the first case, we heat up a bit of Ni metal in a vacuum chamber, using an electron beam until it starts boiling. We will also fill the chamber with a little bit of oxygen, which will give the evaporating metal a chance to oxidize, i.e. form NiO. This will then condense...

24.03.2021 · Tweet

6/ on our substrates which are placed in the chamber. Sputtering is also a vacuum technique. A piece of the material we want to deposit (called target, see picture) is exposed to ionized gas that slowly ablates material from the target's surface. These parties then end up on... https://t.co/nOvEPgHnvq

24.03.2021 · Tweet

7/ our substrates. This is what the sputtering system looks like in operation. The purple color comes from the gas we use (pure argon here). Sputtering is a bit more flexible than evaporation. We can also add oxygen to the gas, which makes the film more oxygen-rich. For NiO... https://t.co/OTRxrYfT3i

24.03.2021 · Tweet

8/ that means we have control over the amount of nickel vacancies (remember, a really important defect in NiO!). This is not the case for evaporation, here we just have to live with the stoichiometry we get.

24.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ The fabrication of these samples takes a lot of steps and can't be done in just one day, so I had to prepare a little. First of all, I cut the substrates (2 FTO ones, and 2 glass pieces that I coated with aluminium) into pieces. The picture shows the 2 Al ones (the foil is.. https://t.co/RKNZij0mam

24.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ just for wrapping them). Unfortunately I forgot to take a photo of the FTO-coated pieces. They are completely transparent (as glass and FTO is), and are roughly the same size (some mm x some mm).

24.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ The easiest step to proceed is now simply to deposit the NiO layer on top of these, such that it covers the entire area of the sample. That is, however, usually a bad idea. These heterostructures are sensitive to small non-idealities, and only one "bad spot" (that can be a...

24.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ piece of conductive "dirt", like a larger metal particle for example) then ruins the entire sample. So what we want is to pattern the NiO layer into smaller structures, which then decouples them from one another. That increases the chance of finding a device that works.

24.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ In side view, this is what we want. The thickness of the layers is not to scale here, the layers will be much thinner (few 100nm) compared to their diameter (few 100µm). The easiest way to achieve this is to put a "shadow mask" (=sheet of metal with holes in it) on top... https://t.co/VXbBtfpDRX

24.03.2021 · Tweet

6/ of the sample while we deposit the NiO. The shaded regions then don't get any NiO deposited on them. There are several problems with this, one of them being that shadow masks can get really dirty over time, and it's near to impossible to align them when you want to make...

24.03.2021 · Tweet

7/ more than one layer in different machines (which we will be needing). So no shadow masks! The alternative is something called photolithography, a technique that is also widely used for nano-fabrication in industrial processes. It uses a material called photoresist...

24.03.2021 · Tweet

8/ a polymer that changes it's properties when exposed to UV light. You coat your sample with it, and then illuminate the regions that you want to be exposed. Then we put that into a chemical called developer which dissolves the illuminated parts again. This was, you get...

24.03.2021 · Tweet

9/ something similar to a shadow mask, but it's fixed on your sample so you can move it around. Now you deposit your material on top of this structure, and afterwards remove the remaining photoresist again (this is called lift-off). Here is the work flow. https://t.co/Mf53antg6t

24.03.2021 · Tweet

10/ This way, we get our NiO only in defined areas, while others remain uncoated. We're almost there, there is just one tiny problem: photoresists typically don't withstand temperatures higher than 150°C. I want to deposit the NiO at 300°C, so that won't work. We have to...

24.03.2021 · Tweet

11/ make use of a trick: We'll replace the PR by a more resilient material that can also be easily dissolved later. We will call this a "sacrificial layer". It works this way: instead of depositing NiO directly, we first deposit zinc oxide (ZnO), a thermally stable but...

24.03.2021 · Tweet

12/ chemically unstable material. It can be dissolved in very weak acids (here: phosphoric acid) which, at the same time, won't hurt the rest of our sample. We will need to use the negative of the original illumination pattern for the photoresist, but that is not a problem. https://t.co/XssaGlW4pk

24.03.2021 · Tweet

13/ Now we have the recipe for making patterned NiO on our substrates! In the end, we will also make another thin layer of metal on top of the NiO -- this will serve as front electrode since NiO is not really conductive.

One thing I really like about our photolithography is that it has a so-called maskless aligner. In many systems, you need a version of the mask you want to pattern into your sample. There are suppliers that make them for you, you only have to design them and send them the layout.

24.03.2021 · Tweet

The downside is that this is not very flexible. If you want to make small changes to the layout, you have to order a new mask, which can take a few weeks to get delivered. Maskless aligners use a write head with an LED in it to directly write your pattern into the photoresist.

24.03.2021 · Tweet

You design you layout on the computer, upload it to the aligner, load your sample and then it writes the pattern like in the video. The whole process takes only 20mins! The resolution is very good, you can get features down to a few micrometer in size with this. https://t.co/7f4ms5mLIU

24.03.2021 · Tweet

@inaquantumdot The one that we use here is simply called LayoutEditor. There is a free version that comes with some limits on how complex your designs can be, but it's enough for most things we do here!

polarity will fill the semiconductor with free carriers. For that polarity, the device becomes conductive, and there should be quite a large current flowing. A device with such an asymmetric current flow is called a diode, and observing it on the sample is a prerequisite for...

Today I had planned to talk about a little about the things defects can actually be good for. So far, I only mentioned the downsides of having them in semiconductors, but there is actually many ways of turning their presence into something useful: the functionalization of defects

25.03.2021 · Tweet

The live experiment took longer than I had expected, so I'll make a shorter thread now about one of the ideas people have for defect functionalization, and maybe another one tomorrow, if you're interested!

25.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ How defects can be useful for neuromorphic computing: a 🧵! A defect of any species is tied to a certain site in the crystal lattice. For example, a Ni vacancy in nickel oxide can, by definition, only "live" where Ni atoms belong. But this doesn't mean defects don't move!

25.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ Quite the contrary. High temperatures, electric fields or other driving forces can lead to atoms redistributing in the lattice. By moving a Ni atom into the Ni vacancy, the defect and the atom "swap sites", which can happen again with the next Ni neighbor and so on.

25.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ This diffusive movement of Ni vacancies at higher temperatures is something we have directly observed recently, by doing electrical measurements with an extremely high-precision method, called broadband dielectric spectroscopy (BDS). Here's the paper: https://t.co/sAiP9jQq9H

25.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ Because the Ni vacancy is also responsible for the electrical conductivity in these samples, that means that by targetedly moving Ni atoms (or vacancies) around, we can in principle create and destroy conductive paths through a NiO layer.

25.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ This is related to a phenomenon that occurs in a lot of metal oxides: resistive switching. Simply by applying a voltage across a piece of them, they change between a conductive and a resistive state. The transition between these can be incredibly fast -- below 1 nanosecond!

25.03.2021 · Tweet

6/ There are two general mechanisms that cause this switching: the filament and the interface mechanism. Here is a schematics of what happens in these two. In the filament process, defects migrate to form a conductive chain that connects the two electrodes. In the interface... https://t.co/VmWtOsdqWJ

25.03.2021 · Tweet

7/ process, the cell's resistance is increased because defects accumulate below one of the electrodes. Both of these processes are reversible, i.e. they can be repeated many times. This is similar to what conventional transistors in modern microelectronics do, just A LOT faster

25.03.2021 · Tweet

8/ They are also much simpler from a device design perspective: they only have two electrodes. Transistors typically have three, separating current conduction and control over conductivity. The simpler principle of resistive switching cells and their high speed makes them...

25.03.2021 · Tweet

9/ good candidates for artificial neurons! Here is a relatively recent paper with a tutorial on how one could use resistive switching cells to emulate biological brains: https://t.co/BSTP6gvNre

25.03.2021 · Tweet

10/ So far, nothing of that magnitude has been achieved yet. There are many problems around these resistive switching cells, many of which relate to the fact that we don't really understand the physics behind the switching. Since it is ultimately because of defect movement...

25.03.2021 · Tweet

11/ this means we need to understand better how (and which!) defects move in these materials, how they form larger structures in electric fields and temperature gradients, how they break down again, and what can be done to make the process more robust and predictable.

25.03.2021 · Tweet

12/ I think I'll leave it at that for now! Let me know if you have questions :) By the way, this topic is also the focus of a grant proposal I recently submitted. Finger-crossing is highly appreciated!!

25.03.2021 · Tweet

@goldclusters 1/ That is a difficult question! If the defects you have in your quantum dots are shallow (=dopant), i.e. they produce free carriers, that can mean the particles form diodes with other materials. If they are deep levels, less so! Doping beyond a certain levels can also kill...

25.03.2021 · Tweet

@goldclusters 2/ the diode behavior, because the space charge layer becomes super thin, so the electrons can tunnel through.

26.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ What is transparent photovoltaics? The sunlight that reaches Earth's surface contains up to ~1 kilowatts per square meter of optical power. That's quite a lot: every m² receives enough power to supply a vacuum cleaner! This immense potential is the reason why photovoltaics...

26.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ have become so important in the past two decades. To harvest all that energy, we use solar cells that we put up in areas that we don't use otherwise, like on our roofs or as huge solar power plants in the uninhabited countryside. But there are many surfaces around us that..

26.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ are also illuminated by the sun, but that cannot actually be equipped with conventional solar cells. Large glazed facades of buildings, or their roofs. Or cars, or even the displays of our mobile devices. You don't want to have normal cells on them, because they change...

26.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ the way these surfaces look, or even function (a window would become completely opaque). And here is where transparent photovoltaics comes in! Half of the power contained in the sunlight is in wavelength regions we cannot see. Most of that (93%) is in the infrared (IR)...

26.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ and about 7% in the ultraviolet (UV) spectral ranges. Solar cells that use this light, but let the visible parts pass through, would be almost invisible to the human eye, while providing us with electrical energy. And because they're invisible, we could put them wherever!

26.03.2021 · Tweet

6/ There is an incredibly large amount of research around this. See this review: https://t.co/6U8u1m4a2Y

26.03.2021 · Tweet

7/ The tricky part is to get the visible light (medium photon energy) through while at the same time absorbing the lower-energy photons from the IR. From the perspective of a semiconductor physicist, making a UV solar cell, however, is the obvious first step. All we need is...

26.03.2021 · Tweet

8/ a semiconductor that starts absorbing light in the UV. It is then naturally transparent for all the lower-energy light. It won't convert IR light though, so it is going to be less efficient. But this may be compensated by the simplicity of the device, of its fabrication, and..

26.03.2021 · Tweet

9/ the low cost of the materials we use. In my PhD thesis, I studied (among other devices) transparent solar cells made from the inexpensive and easy-to-process materials zinc oxide and nickel oxide.

26.03.2021 · Tweet

1/ The transparent solar cell project became quite a success very soon after we started. We found that a simple device, that basically only consisted of a layer of ZnO in contact with a layer of NiO, plus a front and back electrode, did the trick. The cells we made immediately...

26.03.2021 · Tweet

2/ beat the previous world record of the conversion efficiency for UV solar cells by a factor of 20! It was still quite low though: only 3.1% of the power in the UV spectral range were converted into electricity. Here is the publication we wrote: https://t.co/Y5NGp3daK5

26.03.2021 · Tweet

2*/ The paper was also selected for the journal cover that month! I learned a lot of things about graphics design (mostly how not to do it...), and in the end, this came out: https://t.co/yK7t7UpkHv

26.03.2021 · Tweet

3/ After that, I started looking more into what still went wrong. And it turned out defects were behind most of it! If you put two crystalline materials together, the interface between them is, in principle, nothing but one extended defect. And this defect can do all...

26.03.2021 · Tweet

4/ the things 0-dimensional defects also do. In particular, they also capture electrons if they have the chance. The ironic thing was that some parts of the sunlight messed with the way the interface defects interact with the charge carriers in the two semiconductors...

26.03.2021 · Tweet

5/ mainly in the ZnO, because that is the component that does the light absorption and provides charge carriers loaded with the energy of the sunlight. The NiO is "only" responsible for making them move in a particular direction, so we get a current.

26.03.2021 · Tweet

6/ When the light was on, the defects at the interface suddenly started eating away much more charge carriers from both sides of the contact. So illumination made the cell perform much worse than one could expect from how it behaved in dark. https://t.co/NdhZrh1H2l

26.03.2021 · Tweet

7/ Interfaces between two different materials are often a problem in photovoltaics. It takes some challenging engineering of the interface to make the cell perform well, and in the end, this often has to do with controlling where defects live.

26.03.2021 · Tweet

8/ To make things more ironic, I then found a second loss mechanism that further decreased our efficiencies that ALSO had to do with light! Ni atoms from the NiO diffuse into the topmost regions of the ZnO where they replace some of the Zn atoms, producing...

26.03.2021 · Tweet

9/ the nickel-on-zinc substitutional defect! That's a bad one because it sits deep inside the ZnO band gap, so that it can kill charge carriers coming by and trying to cross the interface to the NiO. Here's the paper: https://t.co/B9aLpL5zW6

26.03.2021 · Tweet

10/ In spite of our defect-related troubles, the device was still at 3.1% efficiency. With the two above loss mechanisms suppressed, that could be 15%! And even with 3.1%, you can do a few things. Some applications don't really need a lot of currents -- they mostly want...

26.03.2021 · Tweet

12/ voltages. And our cells were quite good at providing that! We developed this mini-module (1x1cm) with 49 cells connected in parallel and in series, that gave an output voltage of 3.5V, and maximum power of 12µW. Low-power electronics could live off of that! https://t.co/RyjjKtruKZ

So why the big fuss? The story is about how electronic devices were the size of a room and ever year or so the device would get smaller and smaller and smaller to the point that we are capable of making a device using a DNA type of molecule and stick to gold, silver or such...

30.03.2021 · Tweet

With silicon-based technology almost reaching the limit and us living in the Internet era which has almost infinite amount of information and data to be processed, we need alternatives not only cheaper but also capable of handling such larger amount of data..

30.03.2021 · Tweet

But to make even smaller devices or what is known as miniaturization of electronic devices is always very challenging, which can be explained from either the issues with such technique or even simply not understanding enough how the electrons moving around such devices works...

30.03.2021 · Tweet

So for example to be able to use almost 1nm molecules, within a device to perform like a switch or increasing the flow of current or as a memory allows us to say that molecular devices have the potential to maybe replace traditional solid-state device in the near future.

Quick recap: The electronic transport properties of molecules when subtended between gold electrodes showed the reduction(oxidation) of 15Q(17HQ) led to a significant current enhancement compared to the respective oxidation(reduction)of 15HQ(17Q). Thus, ‘‘switching on’’. SO: https://t.co/1yexewjutP

06.04.2021 · Tweet

To explore the underlying reason for conductivity change, we first plot the transmission function on a logarithmic scale versus electron energy (given with respect to the Fermi energy) for the four systems at zero bias voltage. Something only shown in zero transmission can do so:

06.04.2021 · Tweet

That reason is destructive quantum interference (DQI). Quantum interference is a purely quantum mechanical concept explored in different transport device studies. Exploring it at molecular level provides new insights towards manipulating electronic transport at the wavefunction https://t.co/VkC4FZajlH

06.04.2021 · Tweet

level through chemical design and electrical control. The DQI mechanism in molecular transport disrupts the conduction of electrons through the molecule resulting in current suppression. DQI prediction in molecular electronic structures has been suggested through several models. https://t.co/w5B1XoqoJk

06.04.2021 · Tweet

However, although there are some contradicting conclusions, in particular, for the case of azulene, there is controversy as to whether DQI exists in certain azulene derivatives. To find DQI, look at T(E) at 0 V and find an anti-resonance dip around the Fermi level. Lets see! https://t.co/Nf0mX8r2OJ

06.04.2021 · Tweet

Figure below shows T(E) plotted on a logarithmic scale at zero bias for the 4 molecules. We use logarithmic scale to highlight possible anti-resonance. We see no such dips in the region of the Fermi level. Thus DFT + NEGF does not identify the presence of DQI in these systems. https://t.co/ZEBKInZmB7

06.04.2021 · Tweet

We were stuck and we needed something to at least give more insight to our story. That's when I read this beautiful review paper called Quantum Interference, Graphs, Walks, and Polynomials By Y. Tsuji, E. Estrada, R. Movassagh and R. Hoffmann, Chem. Rev., 2018, 118, 4887–4911. https://t.co/G0l5kNV5HP

06.04.2021 · Tweet

Graph theory gave more insight: the ‘‘graph’’ characterizes the molecule as being made of vertices and edges which signify the atoms and their bonds respectively. This is much more straightforward than utilizing purely mathematical Green functions needed in DFT+NEGF. So: https://t.co/yY4d9dA2gg

06.04.2021 · Tweet

This molecular graph is represented by the vertex adjacency matrix, A, which is an N by N matrix, with N being the number of atoms and holds the information on how the vertices inside the molecule are connected. The inverse of A as shown below will allow us to search for DQI. https://t.co/XcRFD53if7

06.04.2021 · Tweet

That is, 0 in the elements of the Green’s function matrix, will signal the presence of DQI. To get A we consider all bonds like: between atom 1 and 2, so element in A is 1. If we look at 1 and 3, that element is 0. If we consider 5 and 13, different atoms would mean not 1 https://t.co/kNAweO0E0n

06.04.2021 · Tweet

From A, we determine the inverse and consequently the Green Function. We are mostly interested in the path from atom 14 to atom12 (A14,12 or A12,14) (from one sulfur atom to other sulfur atom).The value of the matrix element for 15Q is not zero https://t.co/VbB6TINens

06.04.2021 · Tweet

Hence predicting no DQI, in disagreement with the DQI graphical scheme14,15 but in agreement with the DFT–NEGF result. Therefore, the present results highlight, in particular, that there are still questions concerning the DQI graphical scheme agreement in an azulene derivative https://t.co/Izp7ZpHQpu

However, I was never offered a workshop on grant proposal writing. I have now managed to write one by looking at other people's proposals, and by getting feedback from. But I was lucky, many people do not have good mentors, for example.

12.04.2021 · Tweet

Also, grant proposal writing is very different from paper writing. Yes, the science must be there, but it is more of a sales pitch, think of a Dragon's den or a Shark's tank. You need to sell your idea, that you're the right person, and have a coherent plan for the research.

12.04.2021 · Tweet

This is just my first grant proposal, so I am sure it has many 'areas of opportunity', but it has deeply made me ponder on why I do what I do, which path I might want to take, and how being a researcher is never what you though it would be.

12.04.2021 · Tweet

Which is why, I think that people coming from certain areas of industry or working at the interface might have a better chance at getting grants. As they have had to hone their communication skills. But this is just a thought.

12.04.2021 · Tweet

What becomes to me ever more clear is that scientists, at their core, are communicators. We pass our lives writing about what we have done, presenting our work to our peers, or if one is into #scicomm to non-academics, or to scientists outside our area. #communication

12.04.2021 · Tweet

We need to be versatile as we need to communicate these ideas to a variety of audiences, with different purposes, we need to be able to find the thread connecting it all to bring a coherent story.

12.04.2021 · Tweet

I was once said that the science should speak by itself, in the context of getting prestige perhaps or grants. But I think it is up to us which voice we want to give to it. If it is secretive, mysterious, or if it is open. #scicomm #academicWriting

I had now learned about lab-based X-rays, the kinds you can fit indoors (think of when you get an X-ray of your teeth, or a broken bone). But there are also these considerably larger X-ray facilities called synchrotrons! I knew about the linear accelerator in Mexico, and CERN...

13.04.2021 · Tweet

But these were more to understand particle physics, little did I know that synchrotrons are large facilities where electrons are accelerated close to the speed of light, and then their path is bent by very powerful magnets. The electron loses energy and emits light.

13.04.2021 · Tweet

So yes, we basically make the electrons work hard to get our lovely X-rays. #synchrotron #xrays

13.04.2021 · Tweet

@JohannesBaller Thanks a lot!

13.04.2021 · Tweet

These facilities have the electrons running 24 h a day, and there are many researchers wanting to use these X-rays, so we need to make a case, write a proposal, asking for time to use the X-rays, the beam. If successfull, you get allocated a specific number of hours.

13.04.2021 · Tweet

I have now mentioned that they invited me to join them to an XFEL, but what is this? Is this just some other version of a synchrotron?

13.04.2021 · Tweet

So the first thing that is different between the XFEL and a synchrotron is their shape. In a synchtrotron, you first accelerate electrons (in a linear accelerator) and then you put them in the storange ring. Ring being the key thing. Whilst an XFEL is "just" a linear accelerator.

13.04.2021 · Tweet

The XFELs can be from a bit more one km one, like the one in Korea, or over 3 km long, like that in Germany (@EuropeanXFEL ) or the one in Standford (@SLAClab).

13.04.2021 · Tweet

In XFELs you accelerate the electrons to high energies, then they go and wiggle around through magnets (called undulators), where they emit X-ray radiation. Importantly, the radiation keeps getting amplified here, and the electrons organise themselves into thin disks, leading to

13.04.2021 · Tweet

X-ray flashes!

13.04.2021 · Tweet

So here you do not really get a continuous stream of radiation, but rather pulses. These pulses are then controlled in spacing and duration, allowing us to access molecular processes and structures never seen before. I will actually tell you later how we have used them.

And mind you, cocoa butter is the fat naturally found in the cacao beans, from which chocolate is made. Now, whether you think that white chocolate is chocolate or not, that is a different story. But for sure, to call it chocolate, it needs that amazing cocoa butter.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

@realscientists This links with what I was talking about yesterday ! :D

14.04.2021 · Tweet

Thing is, cocoa butter, fats, when solid, they form crystals! Yes, crystals are not only minerals, like the ones you see for healing, meditating and stuff...

14.04.2021 · Tweet

And since it is not straightforward for molecules to arrange themselves into a nice periodic structure that has local and long-range order, we have different types of crystalline forms of cocoa butter. We call this property "polymorphism" so multiple forms.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

Some people call them with roman numerals from I up to VI, and then, we have the greek letters sub-alpha or gamma, alpha, beta prime (III and IV) and beta (V and VI) in order of increasing stability (melting temperature!).

14.04.2021 · Tweet

So yeah, even scientists can't agree on how to name things...

14.04.2021 · Tweet

But anyways, of all of these crystals we want, not crystal VI, but crystal V! Why? Crystal VI is too hard, has a higher melting point, but Crystal V is the best for a good sensory experience, it is the one that melts at body temperature.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

So how do we get the right crystal? By using a process called tempering, which people in metallurgy might be familiar with! Although also, foodies, chocolate aficionados and the like.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

I left off saying that to get the right crystal we need to temper the chocolate. But how does this process look? Well basically it is a temperature game.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

You first melt your chocolate (depending on the type, the temperature, being the highest for dark and the lowest for white), and you keep it there for enough time that all, or most of the crystals disappear and become liquid.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

Then, you cool it down carefully to roughly 27 °C (again, lower for milk and white), so that the beta prime and beta crystals form. If you go lower, lots of alpha, unstable crystals will form.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

And finally, you want to get rid of the beta prime crystals, and only leave the beautiful beta V. For this, you can take advantage of their different thermal stability. So you heat your chocolate to 30/32 °C, thus melting the beta prime, and leaving only the beta V.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

You can then pour your chocolate into moulds and let it set! If it has been well tempered, the chocolate will contract, making extraction of the moulds very simple. Otherwise, you will have a hard time taking out, unless you heat your mold and melt it all again. #chocolate https://t.co/wzfcgYV3AN

14.04.2021 · Tweet

Now, if you have done tempering at home or in a cooking class, this might not be the method you have followed, but rather, you might have added some shavings of chocolate, to your molten mass. This method is called seeding.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

Basically those chocolate shavings serve as "seeds" from which beta V crystals can grow. https://t.co/ejP7VJHCnf

14.04.2021 · Tweet

It is really convenient for very small batches, but not so much in industry because cocoa butter really likes being in the most stable forms (The betas! For once beta means better than the alpha...), so crystallisation tends to happen so fast, and grows like a monster...

14.04.2021 · Tweet

You can imagine it gets then really hard to pump the chocolate into the moulds for bon bons and bars...

14.04.2021 · Tweet

@gcouprie Exactly! It is essentially the same :) Each type of crystal has a different melting point starting from the sub-alpha to the beta VI (16 to a bit over 36). So you first melt to a high enough temperature than even the most stubborn beta VI will melt. Like a clean slate.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

@gcouprie The first cooling will lead to the crystallisation of cocoa butter, but you cool it to a temperature above the melting point of the sub-alpha and alpha. And you heat again to melt any beta prime, but keep the beta.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

@gcouprie Do you mean in chocolate? Or elsewhere?

14.04.2021 · Tweet

@gcouprie Usually you are always looking for the beta five. So this is the one temperature treatment you use. You really do not want any other form as they melt too fast, or feel waxy in the mouth.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

@gcouprie I believe tempering is not so important when you are doing chocolate sculptures. Then you are not looking for a glossy fragile structure, but rather something that you can shape.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

So one of the things that I was interested in was if the most frequently used temperature (60 °C) was ideal or if you need to heat it more (above 80 °C). Note, that a higher temperature in chocolate itself is not advisable due to the interactions with other ingredients.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

What I observed and reported in my thesis was that the temperature at which you melted cocoa butter, before you cooled it down, did affect the order in which the different crystal forms would appear. So by heating it to a higher temperature, it would take longer to crystallise...

14.04.2021 · Tweet

But the transformations were not affected, actually there was a hint that transformation to the beta-V might be accelerated. But this was pure cocoa butter. And you always have something else in chocolate...

14.04.2021 · Tweet

Here is an image from @compoundchem on the different crystal forms of cocoa butter. https://t.co/26Q6kEs3iY

14.04.2021 · Tweet

As to why it would crystallise faster if I first melted at 60 rather than 100 °C? It is hard to tell, I did check for oxidation, but my cocoa butter was stable for a few solid hours before degrading...

14.04.2021 · Tweet

The trouble with working with natural fats is that they are not only made of one component, but rather by a multitude of them!

14.04.2021 · Tweet

Cocoa butter, as well as most other fasts and oils, is composed by molecules called triglycerides, which are three (hence the tri) fatty acids (heard of omega 3, or palmitic acid?) that are joined together by a molecule called glycerol (you guessed it, glyceride comes from it)

14.04.2021 · Tweet

Now these triglycerides, or more correctly triacylglycerols can have different fatty acids, attached in different order. And these fatty acids can be all straight, or have kinks because of two atoms sharing a double bond.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

Cocoa butter has many different triglycerides (let's call them TAGs). OK, not as many as milk fat... but amongst these, it's main ones are the ones I, and others, like calling SOS, POP, and POS. So easy to remember...

14.04.2021 · Tweet

The S (Stearic) and the P (palmitic) fatty acids are the straight chains, and the only difference between them is that one is shorter than the other, so they get along together pretty well when they are closely packed in the crystals.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

Whereas, the O (oleic acid) has an insaturation, a kink. So that kink, unless it is next to another kink that gives it space (kinda like two spoons), it is unhappy, because then it is sitting too close to another atom...

14.04.2021 · Tweet

@mkolsek Perhaps you are tempted now to have some chocolate? Would be a nice pick-me-up for a Wednesday...

14.04.2021 · Tweet

So yeah, those oleic acids like spooning. https://t.co/NtHix5YnuU

14.04.2021 · Tweet

This is what drives the different stabilities in the different crystal forms. In the less stable phases, they arrange in what we call a 2 L phase, so the length of the layer of the crystal is that of two fatty acid chains. This means that some kinks will be unhappy.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

You could in very broad terms say this is because they are in a hurry to get into a packed solid structure, so they do not get into the most perfect packing.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

After some time though, or if you crystallise at a higher temperature and have the patience to wait a bit more, like in tempering, the packing changes into a 3L structure. And yes, this means that the length of the crystal layer is of 3 fatty acid chains.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

To achieve this, all, or most, of the oleic acid chains get on a single line, separating themselves from the rest.

14.04.2021 · Tweet

A sneak peak to today's topic. #ice #popcorn #amorphous #phase transition #polyamorphism https://t.co/3KWmcCMpnb

15.04.2021 · Tweet

You might have guessed from my tweets yesterday, and from the hashtags I used that the thing you are seeing is ice, as it transform in yet another type of ice!

15.04.2021 · Tweet

Even though you might thing ice very well, especially since freezers came into existence it became more common place even in warmer countries, ice is not as simple as the ice cubes that you put in your preferred summer beverage. https://t.co/YYoVmgSUy4

15.04.2021 · Tweet

There are may different types of ice! In fact, in terms of "crystalline ice" so yes, the one with short and long-distance structure and order, there were 18 forms known, and recently the structure of ice XIX was elucidated! https://t.co/U4kmC2tQws

15.04.2021 · Tweet

For those of you wanting to read the paper: https://t.co/xsc4haRwvb

15.04.2021 · Tweet

So for those of you who had heard about ice-nine from "Cat's cradle" let me tell you that it actually exists! It just does not turn all liquid water into ice, it is actually only stable at 140 K and at higher pressures... So don't panic! https://t.co/WTTDmr2IbX

15.04.2021 · Tweet

What you see in the GIF above is not the terrrible ice-nine, but your usual ice (ice I) coming into contact with supercooled water. Supercooled means that it has been chilled to a temperature below it's melting point (0 °C), this is achieved by having ultrapure water.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

But, even if you manage to cool it down so much, it does prefer to be in the most stable phase under those conditions: ice, which is why the moment it gets into contact with the ice cube, it crystallises. It's as if it had just been waiting for the instructions to arrange itself.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

More to come after lunch! And given how sunny it is, perhaps I can treat myself to some icecream... https://t.co/q4dM1oiTQL

15.04.2021 · Tweet

But why should we care about supercooled water? Besides the obvious (supercool remember? * sorry not sorry *).

15.04.2021 · Tweet

It turns out that water is a pretty unusual liquid, yes, it is ubiquitous on our planet, but it does not behave as normal liquids should! #strangewater #water #anomalous. For example, your usual water cubes float in liquid water, whereas a normal liquid sinks, such as methanol! https://t.co/MCOUJ2WQFI

15.04.2021 · Tweet

If one fits a power law to the thermodynamic properties (density, compressibility, heat capacity...) of water, they all seem to diverge at a temperature of 228 K. (https://t.co/ZwdvFhCWVI)

15.04.2021 · Tweet

But what is happening here? There has been several hypothesis, supported by theory and molecular simulations, but one of these is that water is in fact two liquids, a high-density one, and a low-density one. At very low temperatures you would be able to see the transition.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

*hypotheses

15.04.2021 · Tweet

Not only this but as one approaches the temperature mentioned before, at positive pressures, one reaches a critical point (LLCP) where the two liquids coexist but are fluctuating constantly. These density fluctuations are thought to then be the origin of the anomalous properties.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

So far, it had not been possible to study this region experimentally, as crystallisation (ice formation) happens incredibly fast, which is why this region has been called "no man's land", it has been unchartered territory for a long time.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

But I have been lucky enough to have been part of the team that has managed to go past the icy wall, to tread where no one had (am I being too proud of the achievement of the team?). And all thanks to the amazing XFELs!

15.04.2021 · Tweet

We managed to observe how the high-density liquid transformed into the low density one BEFORE ice formation started! And this is indeed very cool! https://t.co/hcloL1WFZc

15.04.2021 · Tweet

Here is the link to the paper: https://t.co/3NiyPMwWpB

15.04.2021 · Tweet

@CandiSpillard LOL, there is an ice IX! But it was not discovered after Cat's Cradle ;)

15.04.2021 · Tweet

@CandiSpillard Unless you literally meant time-wise, in which case, I think the novel came out in 1963 and the ice was discovered in 1968, but I cannot swear by it.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

Now I have talked about supercooled water, next stop: the popcorn ice! https://t.co/bGxAT41non

15.04.2021 · Tweet

@CandiSpillard All they say, I am afraid is: "...the designation "ice IX" is proposed. This designation has already been used by Vonnegut for a phase of ice, but since it was a fictional phase, the name is not pre-empted." https://t.co/L9R01lniln

15.04.2021 · Tweet

@yolicomoelrio Awww gracias! https://t.co/UoSxDpwvtk

15.04.2021 · Tweet

Sorry I went very quiet, but my meeting became longer than anticipated! I hope you still want to know a tid-bit about amorphous ices! https://t.co/Zr0e1TLfOD

15.04.2021 · Tweet

In the cropped image you can see above, you will see that it says "amorphous ices" and you might wonder why, as I have been talking about supercooled water so far.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

To get to the supercooled regime, you can come from the top (higher temp) or the bottom (lower temp). If you come from the top, at least in our group, we tend to use droplets under vacuum, which will then cool down by evaporative cooling, kinda like how sweat cools you down.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

But we have "only" managed to go down to 227 K... https://t.co/ZuWmENK3sO

15.04.2021 · Tweet

That is relatively straightforward to understand, you come from liquid water and you cool it, but what lurks in the depths of the phase diagram of water, at really low temperatures and higher pressures? Yup, amorphous ices.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

They were first discovered in the 80s by Mishima, and they can be formed in the lab by crushing crystalline ice, and then by annealing (like maturing) at specific temperatures and pressure you can get different types.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

We primarily have two: low-density amorphous ice (LDA) and high-density amorphous ice (HDA), I know, not super original, but very descriptive, which is what we need.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

It is easy then to suspect that they might relate to the high- and low-density liquids (HDL and LDL). This is indeed then how we approach things from the bottom up, and is what we did in the Science paper.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

We basically had our grid with HDA and then fired a lase to increase its temperature really fast, and then we shot the ice with X-rays to probe it and take a "picture" of it. We took X-rays at different times after we "pumped" the ice with the laser. This is known as "pump-probe"

15.04.2021 · Tweet

Between our previous knowledge (both from within the group and literature), and through simulations, we could ascertain that the HDA had transformed into HDL, and then to LDL, and finally crystalline ice.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

Now you might wonder why all this is ultrafast! As I said before, crystallisation happens crazy fast, with this experiment we saw it begins at around 1 to 3 microseconds at 205 K, so we if take our sweet time to heat and measure, we miss this transition.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

You might think that this is really nice and pretty, but it is all "in the lab" and that you might only care about "real" ice (so ice I). The thing is, the most common ice in our Universe is not ice I, but it seems that it would be something more like our LDA.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

You heard that right, amorphous ice is prevalent in our Universe, it is present in interstellar dust. If you want to get closer to our planet, it seems that before ice I forms in clouds, we first have amorphous ice.

15.04.2021 · Tweet

That is all from me for today, but I will leave you once more with a poll. Now that you learned about amorphous ices: HDA and LDA, what do you think you are seeing in the small video I posted this morning?

I thought I would talk to you a little bit about how COVID 19 has affected my research. At least in terms of the practicalities of it. I do not want to focus on the "doom and gloom", not take seriousness out of it, but because there is a lot of bad stuff to read in the news.

16.04.2021 · Tweet

Of course, it has affected me mentally, yes even if I have been in "lockdown-free" Sweden. I am not one to be able to carry on when the whole planet is in pain, and especially when far away from my family and friends.

16.04.2021 · Tweet

But focusing only on this, only makes things harder, plus, I am sure that lots of you know how hard it has been, and still is.

16.04.2021 · Tweet

The main way in which COVID 19 has affected my research are beamtimes! Yes, they have been limited now because of the type of work I do. I know people have not been able to access their labs in many places, but here, sometimes I wish I would do more lab-based stuff...

16.04.2021 · Tweet

Some of the X-ray facilities have closed for different periods of time. And when reopening, they have several restrictions, on top of the traveling restrictions from that country. This makes it hard for us....

16.04.2021 · Tweet

There are some groups and teams that have been able to pursue their experiments, sometimes because they are within the same country so things like quarantine are not needed, or their experiments can and have been adapted for "online" or "distance" beamtimes.

16.04.2021 · Tweet

Some experiments might be more routine-like and are already customarily done remotely, by sending the samples in, but others have required a vast effort from both the facilities and the user's to perform the experiment!

16.04.2021 · Tweet

But some of us have setups and samples that cannot be adapted to this kind of beamtimes. Our setups are custom-made, our samples need to be AT ALL TIMES under liquid nitrogen, and are awfully fragile! So, unfortunately, we are only able to have beamtimes if travelling is possible

16.04.2021 · Tweet

Of course, flying to Germany is indeed feasible, but how affordable is it to stay in isolation for two full weeks, plus the week of the experiment? Not that much, especially if we are talking of a team of at least 4 people.

16.04.2021 · Tweet

We still managed to have a beamtime last year @desynews !!! :D This was end of August, when cases had dropped across Europe. Part of the team drove up there, and we were limited to four people total, max two at a time, and mask-wearing was, of course, a must.

16.04.2021 · Tweet

All of these facilities, just like everything else, has had to adapt. First delaying beamtimes, in the hopes of a soon resolution, but now a complete rescheduling of beamtimes as we do not know for how long COVID-19 is here to stay.

18.04.2021 · Tweet

And this pain makes sense, bad posture, non-ergonomic chairs, at my place I've no desk, and then there's the lack of movement. Of course having made a short exercise program would've made sense, but my mind was elsewhere engaged. Which means that better planning is due next time!

18.04.2021 · Tweet

This (and ofc the covid scare) has actually made me reflect on, of course, health, how precious it is... Last year, as COVID started, COVID was not my only health concern, the previous November I had tripped on the stairs and hit my knee. Not broken, just damaged the nerves.

18.04.2021 · Tweet

I was given anti-inflammatories, asked to not walk (yay for a month in bed...) things got better, but then I flew from Mexico to Sweden and all my efforts went down the drain... In the end, after some physiotherapy, I can walk more than 10 min now without pain or my knee swelling

18.04.2021 · Tweet

But it's still incredibly weak. I'm trying to strengthen it, but it's not easy. Also, there's stuff that still isn't right, if I sit or stand for long periods of time, it still gets funny. So yeah, seems the damage is here to stay. #kneeproblems

18.04.2021 · Tweet

But as aware as I was always tried to be for other people's predicaments, it's never the same as actually living through them. The fact that I could not dance, run, or even walk for long periods of time as I used, to took a big tall on my mental health. I lost motivation.

18.04.2021 · Tweet

Then, why not, came COVID and everything it has brought to us. I can honestly say I was struggling a lot, I was especially worried about my family. Also, after only a year in Stockholm, I didn't quite have a strong support network, my close friends are scattered across the globe.

18.04.2021 · Tweet

But somehow, I ploughed through it, and it's brought me closer to the few friends that I had managed to make in that year. Also, one eventually learns how to live in this madness, although it's not smooth sailing all the time ofc.

18.04.2021 · Tweet

Once at the airport, I also met a lovely man who pushed me in my chair around the airport. He told me he used to have a shop, but he felt he was fooling people by selling for a higher price than to what he bought the goods for.

So he closed it down and got the job he now had @Schiphol Airport. And he said he loved it, because he was helping others, and he also got to meet people from around the world. And that for him was more important. Sadly, I did not get his name. But he was inspiring.

Here in Zurich with @NorrisOMEL I work on semiconductor nanocrystals. Because they're so small, these nanometer-sized crystals have properties that are dependent on their size and shape.

21.04.2021 · Tweet

The most well known manifestation of this is that larger particles absorb/emit longer wavelength light. In this picture by Stefan Meyer, all these vials are filled with the same material, CdSe nanocrystals, but with different shapes sizes giving them different colors. https://t.co/qljtx7HNx5

21.04.2021 · Tweet

Working with my PI David is a great because he's knows so much about nanocrystals. In fact, he's literally been studying them since before I was born! For example this project he worked on in the 90s really made controlled nanocrystal synthesis possible: https://t.co/V2ghUTIHgc

21.04.2021 · Tweet

Specifically I work on magic-sized nanocrystals. These grow via discrete jumps in size, rather than the continuous growth seen in conventional nanocrystals https://t.co/juKKrqqDZn

21.04.2021 · Tweet

I actually first heard about these magic-sized nanocrystals when I was a grad student in Columbia. @brandicossairt and @theowenlab did a lot of great work in this field some years back. https://t.co/DZSoP3R74m

21.04.2021 · Tweet

One of the big issues with nanocrystal synthesis is a distribution of particle sizes. The stepwise growth of magic-sized nanocrystals could help us get around this, giving us batches of nanocrystals with more uniform sizes and properties

21.04.2021 · Tweet

Sergio and @AniketMule93 recently showed that magic-sized nanocrystals are tetrahedra that grow layer-by-layer. Only perfect tetrahedra exist since they're local energy minima. And this is the reason for the stepwise growth we see. https://t.co/PhXuUl3ehL

21.04.2021 · Tweet

Even though they have all these potential benefits over traditional nanocrystals, magic-sized nanocrystals have a lot of drawbacks. For example they're usually not very ambiently stable, and they're fluorescence isn't as controlled as we'd hope

21.04.2021 · Tweet

And this is what I work on, trying to figure out how we can make these magic-sized nanocrystals compete with other state of the art semiconductor nanocrystals

22.04.2021 · Tweet

So, I hope you all had a good day, and are still up for some tweet sized bits of information about #neutron scattering and why neutrons are such a unique probe: https://t.co/zjRJYT7G6L

26.04.2021 · Tweet

Neutrons are NOT charged, but they possess a magnetic spin. This allows them to penetrate deep into matter, and they are sensitive to magnetic phenomena within a sample. https://t.co/qzG4QoMnsN

26.04.2021 · Tweet

On the downside the lack of electric charge makes them very hard to transport, since they can’t be accelerated with an electric field like charged particles...

26.04.2021 · Tweet

For a long time neutrons were just flying through the air to pass from the source to instrument. Many neutrons were lost this way. Since the 70ies neutron guides have been in use...

26.04.2021 · Tweet

They consist of nanostructured multilayers and transport neutrons of a certain wavelength range. Mostly they are made of Fe/Si or Ni/Ti. And this is what it looks like if you look through one: (Foto: @MCQST_cluster, Jan Greune) https://t.co/f7rMNgtrPX

26.04.2021 · Tweet

One big advantage of neutrons is that in contrast to X-rays, the scattering cross-section of neutrons with the different elements does NOT scale with atomic number: https://t.co/c8NTN3iKam

26.04.2021 · Tweet

Therefore, neutrons are much better at distinguishing elements that are next to each other in the periodic table. It is even possible to distinguish different isotopes (Image: https://t.co/8nOAqdyTMq)

27.04.2021 · Tweet

@gns6w3 Indeed! It is crazy how well you can distinguish those with #neutrons and what possibilities this offers for soft matter research. Although for me personally as a hard condensed matter gal (and having had a pretty bad experience with a wrongly labelled target box)....

27.04.2021 · Tweet

@gns6w3 ... the most amazing part is that you can distinguish Fe and Co so well :D

Let’s dive a bit further into #neutron scattering. First a disclaimer: I am by far not an expert in all neutron scattering techniques, but I for sure can point you towards at least one for each of them if you want more information 😉

27.04.2021 · Tweet

So, I will give you a brief overview of the different techniques, before diving into my field of expertise, the MIEZE technique, pretty fascinating a #neutron spin-echo technique (fun fact: MIEZE is basically German for kitty, which is why I got these nice ears in our hutch) https://t.co/jU4th4KahE

27.04.2021 · Tweet

Let’s start with #neutron diffraction: Many of the (#nano) scientists here will be familiar with X-ray diffraction. Neutron diffraction is based on the same principles. A particle hits our sample, and we can observe a diffraction pattern. https://t.co/6d39vQ9MgA

27.04.2021 · Tweet

For this we need to remember that the neutron can not just be described as a particle, but also as a wave. https://t.co/WhFLGWOWEr

27.04.2021 · Tweet

From the diffraction pattern we can discern the crystal structure of our sample. #neutron vs. #Xray scattering? Due to their magnetic spin, neutrons can see underlying magnetic structures, so the diffraction pattern shows structural AND magnetic peaks. HOWEVER…

27.04.2021 · Tweet

(since my background is nano science I am always a bit sad about the fact that the possibilities for #neutron scattering on nano structures is limited. There are of course neutron techniques for thin films, but we will get to that later)

27.04.2021 · Tweet

I went to the FRM2 today, because a colleague told me he could show me a very special view of the triple axes spectrometer @PandaMlz. I am gonna share this with you: You can see here one of the monochromators of PANDA where #neutrons of a very specific energy are selected. https://t.co/DrmCUh8cO6

27.04.2021 · Tweet

From this point, the neutrons fly towards the sample, which is where I am looking from. The 3 axes spectrometer gets its name from its 3 axes that can be moved completely independent from each other.

27.04.2021 · Tweet

(In comparison, a #neutron diffraction instrument could also be called a 2 axes instrument). With a 3 axes spectrometer it is possible to measure excitations in a material with extreme accuracy .For example the energy dispersion of phonons, spin waves or any other excitation

28.04.2021 · Tweet

The order in which I wanted to go through the different #neutron scattering instruments got a bit jumbled up yesterday when I got to see all the way inside @PandaMlz. But, I still think that was pretty cool, and I had to share it :)

28.04.2021 · Tweet

And I just remembered that I did a crazy detailed sketch of @PandaMlz for the colleague who showed me this awesomeness, so, I am gonna share that now: https://t.co/0x3y0jtkf2

28.04.2021 · Tweet

Next up is a spectroscopic method that is nicely complementary to 3 axis spectroscopy, #neutron Time-of-Flight (mostly referred to as ToF) spectroscopy. While for 3 axis spectroscopy the incoming neutron energy gets selected and scanned carefully to map out an excitation…

28.04.2021 · Tweet

in ToF #neutrons of many different energies hit the sample. To gain information about the energy of the incoming and detected #neutron, their flight times are measured. ToF instruments usually have HUGE detector tanks to catch #neutrons in as large a solid angle as possible.

28.04.2021 · Tweet

So, simplifying a lot, one could say that with a ToF instrument, you can cover excitations in a very large range of phase space, so it is amazing to get an overview of what is happening in your material…

28.04.2021 · Tweet

With a 3 axes instrument on the other hand you can map out specific excitations in amazing detail. (Yes this is simplifying it a lot, but to really do these techniques justice would require a lecture of several hours for each of them, as you might guess from the sketch 😉)
