29.04.2021 · Tweet

So, are you ready to learn more about spin-echo (SE) techniques and eventually @RESEDA_MLZ? Firstly, SE techniques use the fact that a spin in a magnetic field starts to precess like a spinning top… https://t.co/iyl3768J62

29.04.2021 · Tweet

Now, if we have a very well defined magnetic field region (we know the length and field strength very well), and we know the speed/wavelength of our neutron (which we can ;) ) we can calculate how often the spin precesses. https://t.co/5hS18YtqNh

29.04.2021 · Tweet

In a magnetic field that has the same length, and field strength but opposite sign, the spin would precess all the way back, like winding and then unwinding a watch.

29.04.2021 · Tweet

So if we take two such magnetic fields, put a sample in between and a detector at the end, we can actually measure the dynamic properties of materials (yes I am simplifying here a bit as well 😉) https://t.co/TAq6DsZuGc

29.04.2021 · Tweet

This technique is excellent to measure the dynamics of soft matter samples. However, it gets tricky if you want to measure anything magnetic. Because a magnetic field at the sample position would depolarize our neutron beam (mess with the “precession pattern”)

29.04.2021 · Tweet

There is a SE technique that is optimized for anything magnetic, which is called MIEZE, and is the technique we used the most @RESEDA_MLZ. As you can see in the figure, RESEDA has two “arms”, so we can do spin-echo AND MIEZE. (Foto: Jan Greune @MCQST_cluster) https://t.co/NgosbiBCDw

29.04.2021 · Tweet

More about MIEZE and RESEDA after lunch 😉 Stay tuned!

29.04.2021 · Tweet

@gns6w3 Thank you! 🙂 For me the trickiest thing is always to know which explanation to go with, since there are so many ways of explaining SE... Classical, Semi-classical, Quantum Mechanical... Their suitability completely depends on the audience 😅

29.04.2021 · Tweet

@gns6w3 Unfortunately, for MIEZE the classical explanation doesn't quite work anymore, and I am still trying to find the most intuitive way to explain it... I guess my audience here will serve as somewhat of a test audience 😅

29.04.2021 · Tweet

@RESEDA_MLZ isn’t a classical SE setup. It is actually a #neutron RESONANT SEsetup. But what’s the difference? SE measures the (normalized intermediate) Scattering Function as a function of TIME rather than energy, which is what most other spectroscopic neutron instruments do…

29.04.2021 · Tweet

The maximum time that can be reached depends on the length and strength of the magnetic field in the main coils. The larger they are the larger the time. Achieving a homogeneous magnetic field with larger and larger coils becomes exceedingly difficult...

29.04.2021 · Tweet

So, Golub and Gähler came up with the idea to replace the big coils with resonant spin flippers, which are placed at the position where the edges of the big coil would be, the neutron resonant spin echo (NRSE) And you know what? The neutron doesn’t really notice the difference… https://t.co/jvf66aGhwD

29.04.2021 · Tweet

The downside of this approach is, that the beam size usually has to be a bit smaller and some intensity is lost, which is why there are still more classical #neutron SE instruments, some of which are now using #superconducting coils! (e.g.: J-NSE @mlz_garching, Foto: O. Holderer) https://t.co/QWTmMykXOp

29.04.2021 · Tweet

Let’s go to another advantage of NRSE: Imagine the neutron precessing in the magnetic field. To actually have it precess nicely (so the beam doesn’t depolarize) you need a minimum field, otherwise all sorts of magnetic field, even the earth magnetic field will disturb the neutron

29.04.2021 · Tweet

NRSE offers a solution for this: Since there is now more space, since spin flippers are more compact than big solenoids, you can add another coil in between the flippers which can help you access shorter spin-echo times.

29.04.2021 · Tweet

Now, it will become a bit tricky, since to explain MIEZE I will need a dash of quantum mechanics, but I hope you will bear with me… Let’s quickly remember, that while we can describe a neutron as a particle, we can also describe it as a wave! https://t.co/FztpdxUK0z

29.04.2021 · Tweet

So instead of imagining a beam of neutrons flying through @RESEDA_MLZ, we can imagine neutron wave packets (yes we are going a bit #quantum here now). Much like #Schrödinger’s cat can quantum mechanically alive and dead… https://t.co/uFv0L6VmZH

29.04.2021 · Tweet

(I know simplifying and trying to make quantum mechanics more intuitive is dangerous I hope all hard core quantum physicists forgive me for this)

29.04.2021 · Tweet

The neutron wave packet we are looking at now has up and down spin. The spin flipper however treats up and down differently. The up-spin “part” gets faster while the down-spin “part” gets slower with respect to each other.

29.04.2021 · Tweet

This is compensated at the second spin flipper. The trick is now however, to OVERCOMPENSATE. So the two parts of the wave package still need some time to catch up to each other, and at the point in space where they do, we put our detector.

29.04.2021 · Tweet

Between the 2nd flipper and the detector we have an analyzer and our sample. The 2 wave packet parts will not arrive at the sample at the same time. So if in the time between their arrival something changes in the sample, we will notice this by a loss of contrast at the detector.

29.04.2021 · Tweet

Since this is all a bit difficult to understand (believe me it took me months and many, MANY discussions with my colleagues before I finally understood this), I tried to nicely sum this all up in a #sketchnote https://t.co/cMOX93dudw

29.04.2021 · Tweet

Since this was a bit intense, I will stop for now 😉 But later (or tomorrow, let’s see 😄) I will show you what cool science we can do using the MIEZE technique @RESEDA_MLZ

PROTEIN CAGES are everywhere and have important jobs to do! This is because PROTEIN CAGES have hollow internal cavities that serve as: reaction chambers for enzymes; storage containers for inorganic materials; and protective carriers for genetic material.... and more

18.05.2021 · Tweet

There's sooooooo many PROTEIN CAGES!🤩 Protein cages can be categorized into: (1) Non-viral cages e.g., ferritins, vaults, lumazine synthase & encapsulins (2) Empty viral capsids (or virus-like particles) e.g., cowpea chlorotic mottle virus (CCMV), & Bacteriophages MS2 & P22. 👇 https://t.co/rCyocAMY2U

18.05.2021 · Tweet

Great! Nature has provided us with a diverse toolbox of Protein Cages. Excitingly, Protein Cages can be modified by both genetic & chemical strategies. Also, they have 3 key engineerable components: (1) internal cavity; (2) external surface; (3) interfaces between the subunits. https://t.co/J0LQTCeENj

Hi everyone, here's some of our PROTEIN CAGE research. Here, we show how to re-program #encapsulin protein nanocages into photosensitizing nanoreactors for photodynamic therapy! I'll share the highlights below... https://t.co/se1aoDwyC6

19.05.2021 · Tweet

Encapsulins are unique protein cages that self-assemble around #proteins tagged with an encapsulation signal peptide (ESig). We adapted this system to load the photosensitizing protein mini-SOG into the nanocages. Mini-SOG produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) under a blue-light

19.05.2021 · Tweet

Excitingly, we found that these mini-SOG loaded encapsulins were capable of generating significant amounts of ROS when we fired a blue laser beam at them. ...We had made a light-activatable encapsulin nanoreactor that generates ROS "on-demand" https://t.co/XTI5nPAoH5

19.05.2021 · Tweet

As a proof-of-concept, we explored the application of this nanoreactor in photodynamic therapy (PDT). In PDT, photosensitizing agents are activated by light to convert the oxygen inside tumor cells into lethal ROS, killing the cell.

19.05.2021 · Tweet

We visualised the delivery of the encapsulin nanoreactor into tumour cells. Once inside, the nanoreactor was excited by blue-light and generated ROS, which induced intracellular oxidative stress and lowered tumor cell viability! This suggests our nanoreactor has potential in PDT! https://t.co/JdwXpjhr9X

19.05.2021 · Tweet

Overall, our study showed that encapsulin protein cages can be readily bioengineered and are heaps of fun to play around with! We hope our work will encourage everyone to exploit the unique properties of these protein nanocages to create cool innovative #nanotechnologies https://t.co/P5sJuofJFf

Good morning everybody! ☀️ Today it's time to discuss a bit about perovskites and how they behave under pressure 🗜️🤯

26.05.2021 · Tweet

What is #perovskite? It's a class of compounds which have the same type of crystal structure as CaTiO3, known as the perovskite structure. Although the mineral was discovered in the Ural Mountains in 1839, its use in the field of PV, LEDs, scintillators (...) is quite recent

26.05.2021 · Tweet

In particular, the type of perovskite used in these fields is the metal-halide perovskite with formula ABX3 where B is a divalent cation (mainly Pb2+ or Sn2+), X is the halide (I-, Br- or Cl-), and A+ is a monovalent cation that can be either organic or inorganic https://t.co/g69taq5ZHy

26.05.2021 · Tweet

The structure I showed before is related to the 3D perovskite but there are also 2D ones used for the same applications. This class is even younger! In simple words, the idea here is that an A+ cation with a long chain (or an aromatic ring) is used as spacer inducing confinement https://t.co/RWqIAcVcs4

26.05.2021 · Tweet

Now perovskites are very popular and you can also find lead-free perovskite and double perovskites where the Pb2+ is replaced by two cations of different oxidation state (a B+ and a B3+ for example) https://t.co/xBJFJ9oUz6

26.05.2021 · Tweet

@ElAbdleb https://t.co/BP5GiqbeLb

26.05.2021 · Tweet

As this material is so popular, it is easy to get confused about what is a perovskite from a crystallographic point of view. We tend to call everything derived from the ABX3 structure "perovskite" but it is not always correct: https://t.co/9ZWwJXAzZg

26.05.2021 · Tweet

But why are these #perovskites so popular? Their easy fabrication in solution is one of the reason. You just need to mix the precursors in the solvents with no special expensive treatment to obtain your precursor solution. The most common solvents are DMF, DMSO, NMP

26.05.2021 · Tweet

What is really amazing of this fabrication is that by changing the ratio of the precursor materials you can also tune the bandgap of your perovskite! For example, if you start to replace part of iodide with a bromide precursors you will obtain higher energy bandgap! https://t.co/pCOUMvzGKa

26.05.2021 · Tweet

For the people not in the field, you should know that we like to use A LOT abbreviations. MA is the methylammonium cation and MAPI stands for MAPbI3, the most common perovskite we use

26.05.2021 · Tweet

Speaking of the easy fabrication and easy bandgap tunability, these are very interesting for application where you want to be able to tune the bandgap of the material for example LEDs or tandem solar cells. But not all that glitters is gold...

26.05.2021 · Tweet

If you have a mixed-halide perovskite in thin films and you apply an external bias or you illuminate the material, you loose the bandgap due to a process called "phase segregation". Ions in the perovskite are very mobile, and when illuminated they form I- and Br-rich domains https://t.co/hhRq0Qyfci

26.05.2021 · Tweet

This is the paper: Hoke et al., Chem. Sci., 2015, 6, 613-617

26.05.2021 · Tweet

Two questions raise now (or maybe more, so please ask in the comments!) : how do we investigate this process? What is the origin of this process? https://t.co/Ovus5x1WQG

26.05.2021 · Tweet

[admin] "Who Performs Better Under High Pressure - Humans or Perovskites?" Extended conversation with @la_muscarella is out now, give it a listen 👇🎙️🎧 https://t.co/c865Wr6g6f

26.05.2021 · Tweet

One technique for probing the phase segregation could be a photoluminescence-based technique, very common in many labs but... all the charges funnel into the low-energy iodide-rich domain so we cannot really probe the PL of all the domains https://t.co/h01tA9HwN0

26.05.2021 · Tweet

We decided to use a pump-probe technique based on absorption, transient absorption spectroscopy setup. Clearly you can probe the mixed-phase but also the bromide and iodide-rich phase if you repeat the experiment after illuminating the film. https://t.co/zKE0Vwpny5 https://t.co/Xxtv9RkcRz

26.05.2021 · Tweet

Now that we know what technique to use, let's do a step back to understand what possibly is the origin and how we can validate some theory...

26.05.2021 · Tweet

One hypothesis for explaining why after illumination the series of mixed-halide shows a PL at 1.7 eV (= composition of 20% Br- incorporation) was a phase transition from tetragonal to cubic when the %Br is > than 20%. #Inotherwords the cubic structure is unstable...

26.05.2021 · Tweet

I worked together with @emhutter1 on this project, it was a great time and fun together! There were also some very frustrating days but we know... it is how science works! We combined a transient absorption setup with a pressure cell to induce external compression in our films https://t.co/hg7hKJnAF1

26.05.2021 · Tweet

Challenging? We had to perfectly align 3 beams inside this pressure cell. It looks big but the windows are very small... 3 beams for excitation, probing and inducing the phase segregation via light-soaking. It took a while but I am proud to share the results of all these efforts! https://t.co/GPxPxqxkGT

26.05.2021 · Tweet

But okay, you might wonder, why pressure? In the range of pressure we use (0 to 0.3 GPa) there is no phase transition from cubic to tetragonal. So, if phase segregation stops cannot be due to the phase transition to the tetragonal phase

26.05.2021 · Tweet

In addition, bromide and iodide-based perovskites have different compressibility (different bulk modulus) and the Gibbs free energy contains a PDV term we could use to see if pressure has a significant impact on the thermodynamic stability of our material...

26.05.2021 · Tweet

This is what you get with a 50%Br sample when you illuminate at 0 and 0.3 GPa. At 0 GPa, immediately there is the formation of iodide- and bromide-rich phase (high and low energy), but very different behavior under pressure! More here: https://t.co/uv06kTk44i https://t.co/RmjxOXZxBj

26.05.2021 · Tweet

This is true also when 70% of bromide is incorporated in the composition. Seems to be a very general effect. Btw, this is what each datapoint in the 2D plot I showed look like. These are the ground state bleach of the mixed, iodide- and bromide-rich domain https://t.co/dyHxPvooIG

26.05.2021 · Tweet

If we fit all these peaks, this is what we get: the peak energy as a function of real time and pressure. https://t.co/QXereFEVcp https://t.co/HTyLR9db9S

26.05.2021 · Tweet

First result: the final composition after light-soaking is different as a function of pressure (unit cell volume). The higher the pressure, the closer to the original mixed composition. Terminal x-value determined by volume instead of phase transition! https://t.co/0hmoG2tJpd https://t.co/V253au4irA

26.05.2021 · Tweet

Under pressure, phase segregation becomes slower. If we derive the relation between the migration rate and the activation energy for the halides using the diffusion coefficient formula, we see that pressure seems to increase the activation energy for these halides to migrate https://t.co/PzBHUzktmf

26.05.2021 · Tweet

Before to leave you for today, I have to tell you what we think is going on with pressure and these mixed-halide perovskites 🤔

26.05.2021 · Tweet

When we compress the mixed-halide perovskite we are changing the PDV term in the Gibbs free energy of mixing. This term is usually overlooked for other semiconductors as much more stiff than perovskites. We also change the enthalpic term (due to strain in the material)

26.05.2021 · Tweet

The enthalpic term is positive at ambient pressure and quite high because there is a lattice mismatch between the iodide- and the bromide- lattice. Under P, the iodide lattice compresses more (smaller bulk moduli than the bromide one) and the lattice mismatch reduces

26.05.2021 · Tweet

#inotherwords: enthalpy dominates at ambient pressure, entropy dominates at high pressure where the enthalpic term reduces. Read more here: https://t.co/uv06kTk44i https://t.co/ICE2hvLWNb

26.05.2021 · Tweet

You might say "Yeah, nice but we cannot put solar cells/LEDs under pressure". True, but we can induce strain to simulate the effect of the external pressure! We reduced the unit cell volume by using Cs+ instead of MA+. Similar results! https://t.co/QXereFEVcp https://t.co/VhVlZAwOIo

26.05.2021 · Tweet

These works are just two examples on how fundamental studies can be useful for further optimization of devices. If you are doing fundamental science, it doesn't mean that is not important for applications! Actually, I think the opposite 🔥

26.05.2021 · Tweet

Perovskite solar cells or LEDs cannot be put under pressure in real life, but they behave extremely good when a stress is applied. Next step? Let's transform this external pressure into internal pressure to obtain the same result 🧐

26.05.2021 · Tweet

It's time to sleep here, but tomorrow I will talk a bit about another interesting effect of pressure on perovskites and my experience during the #ErasmusPlus project. Good night 🌙

27.05.2021 · Tweet

Goodmorning world! ☀️ Yesterday I promised a bit more of perovskites under pressure and here it is..

27.05.2021 · Tweet

Another interesting property of these halide perovskites is the extremely slow hot-carrier cooling in comparison with other semiconductors

27.05.2021 · Tweet

When you excite a semiconductor with energy higher than the bandgap of the material you have excess of energy. When carriers move to the band edge to be collected (e.g. in solar cells), this excess of energy is lost... and also almost 35% of the efficiency...

27.05.2021 · Tweet

This schematic from T. Gong et al., J. of Photonics for Energy, 6(4), 042510 (2016) can be very useful to visualize the process https://t.co/jzncewbj98

27.05.2021 · Tweet

The timescale of this hot-carrier cooling (HCC) is still quite fast: picoseconds. Carriers cool down through scattering and being able to manipulate the scattering of electrons with phonons can have an impact on the HCC especially for polar semiconductors as perovskites

27.05.2021 · Tweet

We need a technique fast enough to capture the evolution of these hot-carriers. It is high-speed photography. We need to make a ton of picture of our electrons/holes to look at this fast process in detail https://t.co/txirZYR3xC

27.05.2021 · Tweet

And once again, I combined this with hydrostatic pressure. Why? Perovskites are polar semiconductors and electronic properties are expected to be strongly coupled with the lattice vibrations. Pressure can have an effect on phonons and therefore on the cooling https://t.co/acO9fd2LeG

27.05.2021 · Tweet

The perovskite I studied here is the MAPI - the simplest perovskite with the A+ cation organic

27.05.2021 · Tweet

We follow the tail of the ground state bleach as a function of time and pressure. The broad tail represents the presence of hot-electrons (with high energy). As a function of pressure the decay of the tail becomes faster and so the cooling. More here: https://t.co/He6X1kj1kx https://t.co/IDtvfz75bj

27.05.2021 · Tweet

You see here that this effect is present only at a certain excitation density. We chose these two because these represent excitation density below and above the Mott transition (where polarons overlap). Below this threshold, pressure has no effect

27.05.2021 · Tweet

Our collaborator @JarvistFrost calculated the electron-phonon coupling for each phonon mode as a function of pressure. The mode mostly affected by pressure is the one around 1 Thz, the octahedral twist. https://t.co/si1DyjbNhm

27.05.2021 · Tweet

We think that when above the Mott transition, polarons overlap and form hotspot where heat is difficult to dissipate. Pressure increases the electron-phonon coupling and therefore offers new pathways to dissipate the excess of energy https://t.co/k5yOtEYHIQ

27.05.2021 · Tweet

This is a fundamental study, how can this be used in real life? HCC is important for many applications. For example, thermoelectric devices require slow HCC, lasers and single-photon sources a fast one. Tuning the HCC allows to optimize the material depending on the application!

27.05.2021 · Tweet

At @_amolf we also have a very special system for Electron Backscatter Diffraction (#EBSD). Maybe some of you working in material science know already this technique. It is combined with the SEM and we can construct spatially-resolved maps with structural data. Credits: Ivar Pel https://t.co/g6WCihg5Dl

27.05.2021 · Tweet

Why is this special? It is a direct-electron detector meaning that there is no phosphor screen to enhance the signal. By using this, we can work with very low current and exposure time. Perovskites are also very sensitive (really to everything!)

27.05.2021 · Tweet

This is my first work as PhD. I looked at MAPI perovskite and EBSD maps show that "grains" we see in the SEM most of the time are not a real grain but made of many crystallographic grains. Watch out for misleading SEM! More here: https://t.co/6gq2FDDgCn https://t.co/jDv0wR2nhb

27.05.2021 · Tweet

I promised to talk about my experience as student in the context of the #Erasmus project. I definitely recommend all the students to apply for this opportunity. It’s not all rainbows and unicorns but it's a great experience everyone should do once in a lifetime

27.05.2021 · Tweet

I found out about this Erasmus opportunity thanks to my Bachelor's thesis advisor (Prof. Ilaria Fratoddi, La Sapienza). She was coordinator of the Erasmus office. Every year she was trying to convince students to apply to do an experience abroad, either for exams or thesis

27.05.2021 · Tweet

I was skeptical, i didn't want to do exams abroad (the ones at my uni were quite tough but the level was very high) but i wanted to see how people were working in Europe. On the other hand, i was just a student and my finances were not that great to live abroad for too long

27.05.2021 · Tweet

My parents were ready to help me (as they were already doing since I decided to live in Rome for my studies) but let's be honest... Some countries in Europe are definitely much more expensive than living in Italy

27.05.2021 · Tweet

Positive sides of the Erasmus scholarship is 1) you have a lot of choices. That depends a bit on your university but usually you have quite a lot of options. There are two version of this scholarship, in Europe or in the World

27.05.2021 · Tweet

2) Part of your expenses are covered by the scholarship. Usually, depending on how "rich" is the destination country, you will receive more or less money. For example, Amsterdam is quite expensive and therefore I received more money than who went for example in Spain

27.05.2021 · Tweet

3) you have to prove that you are actually doing what you were supposed to do. #inotherwords you cannot be paid by Erasmus to watch Netflix all day long but you have to show you attended classes, did exams or the internship

27.05.2021 · Tweet

4) you meet a lot of people from different countries, with a different language, cousine culture and so on. You have no idea how much will enrich your soul! Diversity is what makes us better!

27.05.2021 · Tweet

5) You go out from your "comfort zone". We are all good in doing what we always do, but there is no better way of learning new things by travelling, meeting people and experiencing a new environment

27.05.2021 · Tweet

6) Professionally, you create a NETWORK. As scientists, we cannot work alone. We need collaboration to develop new concepts. Interdisciplinarity is the key of the future. Having a network of different scientists will bring a great benefit to your science and career!

27.05.2021 · Tweet

Today I will try to show some of the basics of Scanning Probe Microscopy #SPM, and in particular, Atomic Force Microscopy #AFM. An easy way to understand how it works is to think on how the blind use their canes to follow the height changes in the floor. https://t.co/mBV25M3HJ0

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Scanning Probe Microscopy #SPM is the general name of the family of microscopes that use a very sharp tip to detect an interaction with the surface. If this interaction decays very fast with tip-sample distance, then it will allow very small height changes to be detected.

15.06.2021 · Tweet

The first #SPM was the Scanning Tunneling Microscope #STM. It takes advantage of the quantum tunneling effect. If a metal tip is at atomic distances(!!) of a metallic or semiconducting surface, a tunneling current that depends exponentially with the tip-sample distance can appear https://t.co/lXv0bEQHoo

15.06.2021 · Tweet

The first #STM out of the IBM labs in Zurich @IBM was brought to the Autonoums University of Madrid @UAM_Madrid, being the origin of the #SPM tradition at UAM in particular, and in Spain in general. https://t.co/xIZNW44jQg

15.06.2021 · Tweet

After the #STM, the #AFM (or SFM, from Scanning Force Microscopy) was developed. In this case, forces between tip and sample are detected. This allows to study any kind of sample, not only conductors or semiconductors, giving it a lot of versatility. https://t.co/ngQWGOByny

15.06.2021 · Tweet

There are other #SPMs that can also detect light, and thanks to having the tip so close to the sample, they can overcome the diffraction limit. https://t.co/yEWZpRQQVd

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Some of main components of an #AFM are the tip, the scanner, the control unit and the software. https://t.co/FL9ZrEya0R

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Most of the #AFM tips come at the end of a cantilever beam integrated into a carrier chip. They are consumables and depending of the shape, size and material of the cantilever, we will have access to different ranges of forces and properties. https://t.co/Lp69dfpPD6

15.06.2021 · Tweet

To detect the force between tip and sample, the deflection of the cantilever is detected. The most usual method for this is known as beam deflection: a laser is focused at the end of the cantilever and its reflection is monitored in a photodiode (gif from the University of Basel) https://t.co/P49VKl0WJR

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Using a 4-cuadrant photodiode allows obtaining both the vertical deflection: Normal force, and the torsion of the cantilever: Lateral force, which is related to the friction. https://t.co/bv3uqXZEx3

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Typical scanners in #AFMs are made of piezoelectric materials. These expand/contract when a voltage is applied to them, allowing atomic displacements in a very controlled way. They are used to scan the tip or sample and to move it up/down following the surface topography. https://t.co/HTiiDbKcYK

15.06.2021 · Tweet

The control unit and the software drive the signals from/to the #AFM head, allowing the implementation of different measuring modes and custom experiments.

15.06.2021 · Tweet

#AFMs spatial range typically is 0.1 nm-100 microns, and can detect forces between 10 pN and 10 microN, making #AFMs ideal tools for the nanoscale. https://t.co/0tyKe7vLFp

15.06.2021 · Tweet

In #AFM, there are different interactions between the tip and the sample. This allows getting a lot of extra information apart from just topography. https://t.co/dI8upDS67J

15.06.2021 · Tweet

This also enables multiple #AFM modes depending on the information you get. Sometimes the nomenclature can be overwhelming 🥴, but in the end all are #AFM 😅. But almost all of them are based on 3 basic modes: Contact, Dynamic (sometimes known as Tapping) and Force-distance based https://t.co/aKBoypTlOZ

15.06.2021 · Tweet

In Contact mode the tip is touching the surface. This allows for example to obtain friction information. https://t.co/eEM7Z2TxuS

15.06.2021 · Tweet

In Dynamic modes, the cantilever oscillates at or near its resonant frequency, either without touching the sample (non-contact) or with intermittent contact (depending on the oscillation settings). The Phase shift of the oscillation can map variations in surface properties. https://t.co/myviZ2jP2p

15.06.2021 · Tweet

In Force-distance based modes, at each pixel of the image the tip is approaching/withdrawing from the surface (literally "jumping" from one point to another). This allows very precise control of the applied load and allows for adhesion and stiffness mapping. https://t.co/isNy1uHhye

15.06.2021 · Tweet

#AFM also allows spectroscopic modes. The most basic spectroscopy is Force vs. distance plots, recording the force change with the tip-sample distance. From these plots a lot of information of the tip-sample interaction and properties of the surface can be gained. https://t.co/a6iy18VH2j

15.06.2021 · Tweet

A clear utility of these curves is, for example, the study of protein folding, by pulling the bound proteins between an #AFM tip and a surface to understand their mechanical properties and interactions. https://t.co/07g8mRkVv5

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Other #AFM modes allow for different characterization of samples. For example, in Conductive AFM #CAFM a conductive tip is used as a second mobile electrode to study transport properties on the nanoscale. https://t.co/eMgIOCuZWl

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Or in Magnetic Force Microscopy #MFM, where a magnetic tip is used to probe nanoscale magnetic domains. As the magnetic interaction has a relative long range, by lifting the tip a few nm over the surface it can detect the magnetic interactions. https://t.co/R5AuyTAC6a

15.06.2021 · Tweet

As I told you, there are plenty of different modes, so I will not go through all of them. Then, we also have the lithographic modes, where the tip is used to draw/modifiy/manipulate the samples. There are plenty of modes as well, I will mention now some of the most popular:

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Among the most widespread we can find local oxidation, where the tip is used to carry out a local chemical reaction on the surface. https://t.co/jGcTh3wHMQ

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Dip-pen nanolithography, where the tip is used as a "pen" to draw with a controlled release of molecules as "ink". https://t.co/6JPE6aATVR

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Thermal scanning probe lithography t-SPL, where a special tip that can be heated is used for nano-patterning. https://t.co/Rgkvn0Ev6p

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Nanomanipulation, to move nanoparticles, nanotubes, nanowires... In this case we can see the tip as a "finger" that can manipulate nano-objects at will. https://t.co/tOePviIuHq

15.06.2021 · Tweet

@carlosromvil In principle yes. You can find more details on Phase imaging if you are interested here 👉🏽 https://t.co/XM6JylvEFP

15.06.2021 · Tweet

@carlosromvil Here is an own example. This is a few-layer graphene flake on a diamond substrate. The phase contrast between both of them is clear, but for instance the triangular terrace in the diamond substrate presents no phase contrast. https://t.co/IWPAix9us5

15.06.2021 · Tweet

All the capablities already mentioned together with the possibility of working under different environments make #AFM an extremely versatile tool. https://t.co/2cGMxwBVtw

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Being able to work in liquids, its application for biological research is gaining more and more importance. Even more so with the latest generation of AFMs, which can work at high speed, allowing the visualisation of biological processes. See for example https://t.co/QvP0bF8XiK

15.06.2021 · Tweet

It can also operate in ultra-high vacuum #UHV conditions at cryogenic temperatures. Under these conditions, a CO molecule can be attached to the tip end, allowing experiments with unprecedented resolution. https://t.co/FMACqYnA0S

15.06.2021 · Tweet

Despite celebrating its 35th anniversary this year, #AFM is still an evolving technique in which a new breakthrough is made every few years. What will be the next...? https://t.co/kaonLH6fnK

16.06.2021 · Tweet

Today I will continue to talk about some of my work, focusing on 0D and 1D materials studied with #AFM. https://t.co/qEj9bq3R7M

16.06.2021 · Tweet

I'll start with the development of Magnetic Force Microscopy #MFM in liquids, together with @JrcMiriam and @aasenjobar, allowing #MFM to study nano-bio-magnetic samples in their natural environment, hampered by how an #AFM works in liquid. Details here 👉🏼 https://t.co/giUz3oPlW1

16.06.2021 · Tweet

First of all, just an idea on how the magnetic contrast appears in #MFM images. Depending on the orientation of the magnetic domains (out of plane, in plane or combinations), we will detect bright and dark contrast regions, as depicted here 👇🏼 https://t.co/k2NEu3FYsJ

16.06.2021 · Tweet

The #MFM contrast is typically obtained in a Dynamic mode, in the Phase shift (or the Frequency shift) signal at a given lift distance. But a cantilever oscillating in liquid is subjected to much more drag than in air (or vacuum), worsening the signal. https://t.co/4FvVhM8fBX

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We optimized the measuring mode and acquisition conditions to be able to detect similar #MFM constrasts in air and in liquid. We first used a calibration sample, such as a piece of a hard disk drive, visualizing its magnetic bits. https://t.co/dieffYyVlg

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We observed that in liquids we could get the #MFM contrast oscillating the tip closer to the sample, allowing similar contrasts but noisier data, due to intrinsic limitations on the characteristics of the commercial #MFM probes, which are designed for measurements in air. https://t.co/Qqhj8HFDIz

16.06.2021 · Tweet

Then we studied the magnetic contrast of 0D magnetic nanoparticles, such as those studied for hyperthermia cancer treatments, in buffer conditions somehow similar as to when injected into a human body. https://t.co/Y7M7eYJnNn

16.06.2021 · Tweet

With such a demanding sample we were able to again obtain similar #MFM contrasts as in air, although not so good due to these intrinsic limitations on the probes. https://t.co/QODVuHY867

16.06.2021 · Tweet

That is why, in collaboration with @deteresa5 group, we developed a method to fabricate magnetic tips on cantilevers designed for liquid measurements. Here all the details 👉🏼 https://t.co/pKYyrhU93i https://t.co/aagUUFbQ4m

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We again tested these tips with a calibration hard disk drive, obtaining now results in liquid as good as in air. And moreover these tips are less invasive for the samples. In conclusion, the #MFM in liquids is now ready for the most demanding samples. https://t.co/UIGDJx00LV

16.06.2021 · Tweet

[admin] "Nano Fun with AFM (Atomic Force Microscopy)" Extended conversation with the amazing @pablerasares ir out now 🎙️✨🎧 https://t.co/SygDKyF1z3

16.06.2021 · Tweet

I will go on with another development, a setup for simultaneous high resolution #AFM and Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence #TIRF microscopy, really useful for studies at the single molecule level of viruses. This work was carried out in collaboration with Dr. P.J. de Pablo. https://t.co/tkkszncGiJ

16.06.2021 · Tweet

In a #TIRF microscope the light is driven at the total internal reflection angle, and therefore only an evanescent wave reaches the sample, observing fluorescence mostly just from the nano-objects attached to the coverslip. https://t.co/8bRe1Sq0TU

16.06.2021 · Tweet

The development of a simultaneous #AFM - #TIRF suitable for high resolution studies presents some challenges. Luckily, @alvrooe, who got his PhD with P.J. de Pablo and also worked with Dr. I. Schaap, had experience on it. https://t.co/93IQrIarp6

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We designed a setup minimizing the mechanical loop of the system to reduce as much as possible instabilities, and used @WSXM_official to control our microscope, taking advantage of all its capabilities. We first tested it in ambient conditions, ensuring its high stability. https://t.co/RoJ9g7V2sx

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We then tested it in buffer conditions, studying P22 viral particles, being able to visualize them and resolve different adsorption geometries and the capsomers forming the capsid. https://t.co/uXZvwfp8ZO

16.06.2021 · Tweet

To test the combination of #AFM and #TIRF, we used commercial fluorescent polymer beads. We first simultaneously visualized them both with #AFM and #TIRF https://t.co/jVdvRVJpFW

16.06.2021 · Tweet

And then we carried out a nanomanipulation experiment, removing on of the beads with the #AFM tip while we monitored it with the #TIRF https://t.co/ePeeehnDsA

16.06.2021 · Tweet

This system is now operative at the @fmcatuam and @ifimacuam for a hot topic such as the study of viruses. A setup based on this one is also under construction at @UoMPhysics, as a multiplatform for simultaneous #AFM and optical studies.

16.06.2021 · Tweet

16.06.2021 · Tweet

@ScienceByDRE @fmcatuam @ifimacuam @UoMPhysics @ourANU Sure, nice! We also had some experience with a MFP3D coupled to a TIRF, but we were not able to resolve viral capsids as well as with our system. But I'm sure this has improved as well now.

16.06.2021 · Tweet

I'll move forward now to some examples of 1D nanostructures studied with #AFM. The first case is the high resolution visualization of double standed RNA #dsRNA in buffer conditions using different #AFM acquisition modes. Work in collaboration with @FMorenoHerrero. https://t.co/agtZdm7FHy

16.06.2021 · Tweet

The details can be found in these two publications: https://t.co/lvZKIf4LfY https://t.co/8wO6vKx5Vf

16.06.2021 · Tweet

#dsRNA plays an increasing list of roles: genetic material of a number of viruses, a key activator of the immune response against viral infections, and mediates the suppression of specific gene expression. All this raised interest to study its mechanical properties and structure.

16.06.2021 · Tweet

#dsDNA had been extensively observed at high resolution with #AFM, but similar studies were lacking in #dsRNA. This was very likely because of the higher complexity of imaging the #dsRNA structure. https://t.co/D8CD2ew1RE

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We first used #dsDNA as a molecular standard to adjust the conditions for high resolution imaging of nucleic acids in liquid. Then we imaged for the first time #dsRNA with a lateral resolution sufficient to resolve its helical periodicity with different #AFM acquisition modes. https://t.co/bbHf8aGZ8e

16.06.2021 · Tweet

Finally, we simulated how the molecules would look like from their crystal structures with different tip radii R, finding that R<~2.5 nm allowed for both major and minor grooves visualization, while ~2.5 nm<R<~5.5 nm led to images where only a single periodicity was detected. https://t.co/LKeJF0oFeG

16.06.2021 · Tweet

This work pointed out two critical aspects for high resolution of nucleic acids in liquid: 1- The interacting force, minimized fine-tuning each imaging mode parameter. 2- The sharpness of the tip, likely arising from a protrusion or a small feature at the apex of the tip.

16.06.2021 · Tweet

I will now leave liquids aside and move on to another 1D system. In this case I will show you our results on the conductive properties of metal-organic fibres at the single-molecule level. This was the first of multiple fruitful collaborations with @fzamora0 https://t.co/cKWEoCcdl7

16.06.2021 · Tweet

The details of the work can be found here 👉🏼 https://t.co/5PFvaksVpa

16.06.2021 · Tweet

MMX metal-organic polymers are quasi-1D sequences of single halide atoms X bridging subunits with two metal ions MM connected by organic ligands. They are excellent conductors in bulk and as nanoribbons, but theoretical calculations predict even higher conductances than reported. https://t.co/CMtITMUoZ5

16.06.2021 · Tweet

In this work we were able to produce individual chains of the above MMX polymer by a simple drop-casting procedure. By optical inspection we located the thicker fibres, and then with #AFM we could locate chains down to 1-2 nm height, compatible with just 1-2 MMX molecules. https://t.co/wBcioqwrzW

16.06.2021 · Tweet

Next, we evaporated a sharp-edged electrode and observed it for molecules protruding. On these, with a metal-coated tip, we performed conductive #AFM, with the tip as a second mobile electrode. We were able to obtain resistance vs. lentgh plots down to the single-molecule level. https://t.co/DS8cs9bBV5

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We found significative currents for a single-molecule experiment, even at distances beyond 250 nm, surpassing that of all other molecular wires reported so far!

16.06.2021 · Tweet

However, the resistance was still much higher than predicted by calculations. Its exponential dependence with the distance pointed to Anderson localization caused by the interaction of electrons with structural defects.

16.06.2021 · Tweet

To verify this, we did theoretical simulations at different levels, mimicking possible defects. We observed that iodine vacancies are the ones that reduce electron transmission the most, and that only 6-8% of vacancies would be responsible for the observed exponential behaviour. https://t.co/R9aEZog7Ht

16.06.2021 · Tweet

This work puts into perspective the role of defects in electrical transport at the single-molecule level. And that, despite the influence of defects on electrical conductance, coordination polymers are one of the best choices for long-distance molecular wires.

16.06.2021 · Tweet

@inaquantumdot These were done by our colleagues J.J Palacios and J. Soler. They basically first simulate the defects with Density Functional Theory (DFT), obtaining the electron transmission for each type.

16.06.2021 · Tweet

@inaquantumdot Then, for the vacancy, they carried out quantum transport calculations using a single-orbital tight-binding model, with parameters fitted to reproduce the single-defect transmission.

16.06.2021 · Tweet

To finish with 1D systems, I will show our work on the fabrication of nanoelectrodes by #AFM nanomanipulation and cold welding of gold nanowires, one of the funniest works I have done, also in collaboration with @fzamora. You can find the details here 👉🏼 https://t.co/bKv7XzNOXu

16.06.2021 · Tweet

In our experiments studying electrical transport on the nanoscale, we found that conventional micro- and nanoelectrode fabrication presents some limitations: high temperatures while metal depositions, use of resins, chemical agents or static electrodes (non-reconfigurable)

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We needed to overcome those limitations. We got to know about the work by Lu et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 5, 218-224, 2010, where they used Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to visualize the cold welding of gold nanowires #AuNWs, just by mechanical contact! https://t.co/89ol8m4Mtm

16.06.2021 · Tweet

This is due to their high surface-to-volume ratio, similar to two water droplets merging into one when they touch. https://t.co/IWUNTowdPA

16.06.2021 · Tweet

So we deposited #AuNWs on a substrate and using an #AFM tip successfully manipulated and cold welded them. https://t.co/weUuxG2PrG

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We then fabricated devices following this procedure 👇🏼 https://t.co/oLD5s0dSlG

16.06.2021 · Tweet

This way we obtained clean and reconfigurable nanoelectrodes, without the need of high temperatures, resins or chemical agents, that we could assembly into different configurations. https://t.co/fWbBlr0wP6

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We first tested few-layer graphene, as it is a very well-studied material, with a single #AuNWs electrode + a metal #AFM tip as a second mobile electrode. We found electrical characteristics similar as using standard fabrication, but overcoming their abovementioned limitations. https://t.co/2VslGRGoqt

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We wanted to check the quality of our #AuNWs electrodes, so we fabricated one close to 150 microns long, with almost 100 NWs. We found that its conductivity was almost that of bulk gold, with just a single grain boundary in each NW junction (BTW we contacted several 2D flakes 😅) https://t.co/hsxURwlDri

16.06.2021 · Tweet

To test our nanoelectrodes we carried out multiple experiments in different configurations. Here my colleague M. Moreno-Moreno did an awesome job. For example, we fabricated another device on a few-laer graphene flake, but in this case in a more standard 4-terminal configuration. https://t.co/2DvJFjRuzO

16.06.2021 · Tweet

We also wanted to push the limits of the technique, so we proceeded to make a device connecting a ~10 nm gold nanoparticle, something quite difficult without very expensive dedicated nanofabrication setups. https://t.co/tQ2mxyMLn8

16.06.2021 · Tweet

Finally, we also explored its potential for molecular electronics. To this end, we approached two #AuNWs avoiding contact, and then coated them with 1,4-benzenedithiol molecules, measuring stable currents through the molecules for hours at room temperature, with great stability. https://t.co/7yfpWGrkHY

16.06.2021 · Tweet

I think this is only the tip of the iceberg. #AFM is a very common tool, present in many labs and easily available, so this technique has the potential to provide a new and accessible platform for nanocircuitry fabrication, opening the door to a plethora of new experiments. https://t.co/800X3on7LZ

16.06.2021 · Tweet

@muellerwHH Indeed!! The TEM movies from Lu et al. are totally amazing! They were really inspiring to develop our nanoelectrode fabrication technique.

16.06.2021 · Tweet

Really impressive! Congrats! https://t.co/jfbRXRj4jQ

17.06.2021 · Tweet

Today and tomorrow I will continue to tweet about some of my work, focusing now on AFM studies of 2D materials. https://t.co/xVM8ZujUez

17.06.2021 · Tweet

I will start with a work on #graphene, where we tune its properties by applying ultrahigh pressures with a diamond 💎 #AFM tip. Details on this work can be found here 👉🏼 https://t.co/LXizWFTdBg https://t.co/UGZH2Wpdx6

17.06.2021 · Tweet

An #AFM with a diamond tip can be seen as a nanotechnology version of a diamond anvil cell, the standard instrument for ultrahigh pressure experiments. https://t.co/ncDlIRMWcy

17.06.2021 · Tweet

Since the Pressure is Force/Area, and the #AFM tips have nm-sized radii, with moderate forces we can apply ultrahigh pressures in a simple way. https://t.co/5mQSa6fB3K

17.06.2021 · Tweet

When we were thinking about which material to try to squeeze hard with the tip of the #AFM, immediatly #graphene came to our minds. https://t.co/SO0SOYPppC

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We used mechanically exfoliated high quality monolayer #graphene crystals. https://t.co/hECHKnv75w

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We first imaged the flake in a Dynamic mode. Then we brought the tip into contact with a Pressure setpoint value and scanned under these conditions in a given area. After this, we brought the tip back to Dyanmic mode to visualize the modifications. https://t.co/M07dFyIRrJ

17.06.2021 · Tweet

By controlling the Pressure setpoint we observed that we could control #graphene coupling with the underlying SiO2 substrate. https://t.co/UPO0uQcRXA

17.06.2021 · Tweet

As the doping level is known to depend on this degree of coupling, we were expecting to control the doping level locally on these areas, which we confirmed by Raman spectrosocopy https://t.co/G9l9Hnzigm

17.06.2021 · Tweet

And also by Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy, #KPFM, an advanced electrical #AFM mode that allows to measure surface potential differences. https://t.co/iqlIeusEPu

17.06.2021 · Tweet

Therefore, with this ultrahigh pressure modifications, we were able to tune locally the electronic properties of #graphene. https://t.co/MHsAQJODQw

17.06.2021 · Tweet

To understand the origin of this doping, we carried out some theoretical simulations, that pointed out that some of the carbon atoms of #graphene could be bonding to the substrate, even if very few, being responsible for the observed charge transfer. https://t.co/hl0Tp88LEV

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We took some samples to the Elettra Synchrotron in Trieste, to a beamline allowing imaging spectromicroscopy and microspot spectroscopic modes. The spectra showed an extra component in the carbon peak, compatible with some carbon atoms of #graphene bonding to the substrate. https://t.co/UQrZxJMJL8

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We studied the electrical resistance of ultrahigh pressure modifed areas using conductive #AFM. These doped areas presented lower resistance, therefore this appraoch could be used to improve metal contacts in #graphene devices, leading for example to less power comsuption. https://t.co/sgxbONUbfX

17.06.2021 · Tweet

I will continue with ultrahigh pressure experiments on #graphene. Since we could improve the coupling to the substrate, we decided to apply it to better seal blisters consisting on #graphene over microcavities, a standard setup for nanomechanical devices and membrane applications https://t.co/mIl5kjRUGm

17.06.2021 · Tweet

Some of the people involved in this work include @yolicomoelrio, @JrcMiriam, and the details are here: https://t.co/kxLwg6IBoN

17.06.2021 · Tweet

In the group there was a lot of experience studying #graphene mechanical properties upon #AFM nanoindentations with these blisters, also at different pressures, having an #AFM in a variable pressure chamber from high vacuum to several bar. So we could inflate/deflate the blisters https://t.co/M94LhXk2Sm

17.06.2021 · Tweet

Studying the height evolution with time, we saw the gas inside our blisters typically leaked in a few hours. https://t.co/400J9yshfZ

17.06.2021 · Tweet

The leakage was faster in a given flake for blisters closer to the flake's edge. With a simple toy model (tha gas leaking through a cilindrical pipe), we could estimate an effective leakage radius, and this was independent of the distance to the edge for a given flake. https://t.co/RAT3iB5XcL

17.06.2021 · Tweet

Since the leaks of the blisters can be a drawback for technological applications, we tried to improve them by sealing the blisters applying ultrahigh pressures with the shape of a nanometric wide square rim. https://t.co/kzoTJychqj

17.06.2021 · Tweet

In this way, we effectively sealed the blisters, significantly increasing leakage times. Importantly, this demonstrated that most of the gas leakage takes place at the interface between #graphene and the substrate and not by diffusion through the microcavity walls. https://t.co/rOTWhdxn5u

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We observed an improvement of the leakage times and a reduction of the effective leakage radius in all the cases, proving this methodology as a simple way for easy improvement of devices and membrane applications based on #graphene on SiO2 substrates. https://t.co/LuZEpcXFLw

17.06.2021 · Tweet

Next I will tweet about a novel 2D material isolated for the first time in my PhD, #antimonene, a single layer of antimony atoms. We published several works that have attracted the interest of the scientific community, opening the path for the experimental research on this field. https://t.co/q13V0zegTS

17.06.2021 · Tweet

Many people involved, including @Fernandastico, @alonsoxK93, @SDiazTendero, @fzamora0, @carlosgp92, @__mariavarela, @Gonzalo_Abellan, together with other #notinTweeter authors. Here the links for the two main publications: https://t.co/aU53SRdBGy https://t.co/h3r1tR4SmE

17.06.2021 · Tweet

Back in 2015, there was a great interest (and there is still) in finding 2D materials with electronic gaps between 0.5 and 1.5 eV, suitable for some optoelectronic applications. Thin layers of Black Phosphorus (BP) were isolated, presenting gaps on this range. https://t.co/4CuanfW1c9

17.06.2021 · Tweet

But BP is highly hygroscopic, this is, it absorbs water from ambient humidity, degrading and changing completely its properties, needing to work under control environments or to encapsulate it to take advantage of all its potential. https://t.co/ZPGKOt8grD

17.06.2021 · Tweet

In the same column of the periodic table as phosphorus is antimony, which is also a layered material, although with stronger interactions between the layers. https://t.co/6G25p38Wcj

17.06.2021 · Tweet

At that time, there were a lot of theoretical papers predicting very interesting properties for #antimonene and few-layer antimonene, but nobody had isolated it yet. https://t.co/AHVyfZBscg

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We were able to isolate it, first using a micromechanical exfoliation approach and later using a liquid phase exfoliation procedure. https://t.co/nWIt6vHlzi

17.06.2021 · Tweet

After exfoliation and deposition on a substrate, we inspect it with optical microscopy, finding large thick flakes. But when scanning with the #AFM around these flakes, we usually found smaller thinner ones, with terraces down to ~2 nm, compatible with 2-3 layers. https://t.co/YaYP9FRvjy

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We used a battery of techniques to confirm the antimony nature of these flakes, including high resolution #AFM visualizing their atomic lattice. https://t.co/KyEfSn1ZET

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We sometimes found terraces below 1 nm, compatible with single layers (the presence of trapped molecules between flakes and the substrate can induce to observe these heights when scanning single layers of 2D materials). How to check if these terraces where indeed single layers?

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We used again #AFM, in this case to manipulate a terrace, folding it over the rest of the flake. By measuring the height of a sinlge fold we found ~0.4 nm, in good agreement with a single layer of #antimonene. https://t.co/bixEblMl2U

17.06.2021 · Tweet

Finally, we tested their stability, imaging some flakes with #AFM. After 2 months in a box at ambient conditions, we imaged them again and they looked exactly the same. We immersed them in water, and they still looked the same (even seeing the atomic lattice in these conditions) https://t.co/7PwQe316jP

17.06.2021 · Tweet

These experiments demonstrated the possibility of isolating #antimonene and proved its stability, opening the door to its use for different purposes. https://t.co/VK0oNXTpba

17.06.2021 · Tweet

I'll finish today by delving a little deeper into #antimonene. We also did some studies on its optical properties and noncovalent functionalization. The details for these two works in these links: https://t.co/zlmhMS8j7T https://t.co/N9DsT8a7Br

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We combined optical microscopy characterization at different wavelengths with #AFM heights to obtain few-layer #antimonene refraction index, following a similar prodecure used with #graphene and other 2D materials, based on a Fresnel law model. https://t.co/xIEAkqporY

17.06.2021 · Tweet

In this way, we were able to obtain the refraction index in the visible region and also to study the optical contrast as a function of the thickness of the SiO2 substrate, finding the optimal ones to work with #antimonene. https://t.co/2GvlzZcDzK

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We also explored chemical properties of #antimonene, carrying out the noncovalent functionalization of few-layer flakes. We functionalized the flakes by drop-casting a THF solution of a tailormade EDTA-PDI (EDTA=ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) derivative on the flakes.

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We characterized them using different techniques, including #AFM, which for example allowed us to quantify the increment in thickness from the molecules attached to the flakes. https://t.co/ZhiNpy7JCl

17.06.2021 · Tweet

We carried out synchrotron measurements, showing that the functionalizing molecule acts as an electron acceptor, in good agreement with our theoterical calculations. https://t.co/uBRwYbCYwf

17.06.2021 · Tweet

These experiments indicate that the noncovalent functionalization of #antimonene gives rise to a charge-transfer band gap of ~ 1 eV, being a promising route for tailoring its electronic properties.

18.06.2021 · Tweet

Today I will continue to tweet about some of my AFM studies on 2D materials. Let's try to debunk the myth that sequels are never any good! 😅 https://t.co/XxbH3QV0Y0

18.06.2021 · Tweet

I will start with our work using 2D materials to fabricate nanochannels to confine water with atomic-thickness precision and then study its dielectric properties once confined. https://t.co/RjxjYhQ7aP

18.06.2021 · Tweet

Here I want to shout-out to @lfumagalli28: she led the project and is one of the world's experts in scanning dielectric microscopy. The details of the work here 👉🏼 https://t.co/1bCrAqrj0F

18.06.2021 · Tweet

Taking advantage of the experience and facilities at @UoMPhysics @UoMGraphene, we fabricated nanochannel devices where the height of the channels is given by the thickness of layers of 2D materials, enabling to control it at the atomic level. https://t.co/zkbY6E2ve0

18.06.2021 · Tweet

Here are some optical images from our devices, where the thicker channels are clearly visible, and even where we could see when water filled them. https://t.co/pw9AkzYrIm

18.06.2021 · Tweet

But for the thinner channels it was not possible to detect optically if the water was in. To this end, we used #AFM to image the devices before and after water filling. https://t.co/N76hc3UGeD

18.06.2021 · Tweet

When the channels are empty, the top cover sags into them, but when water is present, the water pushes it upwards and the sagging disappears. https://t.co/cbwR4dE2HC

18.06.2021 · Tweet

Then, by using scanning dielectric microscopy, we were able to probe the out-of-plane dielectric properties of the water confined in the nanochannels. https://t.co/xUfS3lMLJZ

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We found a strong contrast that reversed with decreasing thickness, indicating that the polarizability of confined water strongly depended on its thickness and reaches values less than that of hBN, with an already low dielectric constant of ~3.5 https://t.co/6YxqF83emV

18.06.2021 · Tweet

By carefully determining the tip geometry and its radius, using finite-element analysis we could quantify the value of the out-of-plane dielectric constant of water for the different thicknesses. Recognition here to @reneif07 as well. https://t.co/KFJxaRhmFv

18.06.2021 · Tweet

By doing so, we could plot the out-of-plane dielectric constant of water as a function of thickness down to less than 1 nm, finding an anomalously low value of ~2 when extremely confined!! https://t.co/KC7WiBcu8l

18.06.2021 · Tweet

Our results revealed the presence of an interfacial "dead" layer two to three molecules thick, and are important for better understanding interactions in biological systems, in areas such as electrochemistry and energy storage, or to fine-tune future simulations of confined water

18.06.2021 · Tweet

The gif above was incomplete 😅, here is the right one https://t.co/qrLA31g9KI

18.06.2021 · Tweet

I will go on with our work on studying the piezoelectric properties of single layer #hBN using #AFM electrostatic measurements #EFM. People in this work also include @lfumagalli28, and the details can be found here: https://t.co/TPaPrA5z2J https://t.co/iFdqyH5zXs

18.06.2021 · Tweet

The piezoelectric effect is an important property consisting in the internal generation of electrical charge resulting from an applied mechanical force. https://t.co/t4FcLhFNcH

18.06.2021 · Tweet

For piezoelectricity to appear, it is needed a broken symmetry in the material structure. Centrosymetric crystals, such as graphene for instance, where all are carbon atoms, are not piezoelectric. https://t.co/0ro2lBXspi

18.06.2021 · Tweet

When symmetry is broken, as in non-centrosymmetric crystals, piezoelectricity arises. This is the case of single layers of 2D materials such as #MoS2 or #hBN, for example. But when symmetry is recovered, as in bilayers (in general, even number of layers), piezoelectricity is lost https://t.co/XNS6ubYoNK

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We used a variant of electrostatic force microscopy #EFM in such a way that we got an electric image, coming from the electric fields from the sample, and a simultaneous dielectric map, that we used as a control image to rule out artefacts and crosstalks. https://t.co/MZcvK5FNEa

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We deposited single layers of #hBN on other 2D (starting with bottom #hBN), favouring bubbles and creases. We then obtained #EFM images of these areas, as bubbles and creases are features inducing high strain, observing high contrast within and especially around the bubbles. https://t.co/SPL0KDKo2C

18.06.2021 · Tweet

The contrast inside the bubbles was also visible in the dielectric maps, and could also come from the substances trapped inside or be a topographical crosstalk. But around the bubbles the areas are perfectly clean and flat, so the contrast could be due to piezoelectricity.

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We took images of bubbles with well-defined shapes and made theoretical simulations mimicking those shapes, finding a fairly good agreement, confirming the piezoelectric origin of the observed contrast. https://t.co/ikdwh6u96q

18.06.2021 · Tweet

In the case of depositing single layer #hBN on bottom #graphene, we also observed contrast around bubbles. https://t.co/j8PTxIUdU1

18.06.2021 · Tweet

A closer look at this areas indicated the presence of ultrathin creases, which we also mimicked theoretically, showing a good agreeement with the measurements. https://t.co/kM4tT998uR

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We confirmed the piezoelectric origin carrying out a battery of control experiments where no piezoelectricity was expected, such as areas without strain, bilayer #hBN or graphene bubbles and ultrathin creases. None of them showed the contrast observed in single layer #hBN. https://t.co/ftGQ2VrTvN

18.06.2021 · Tweet

Our work gave evidence of the generation of piezoelectric fields in highly strained single layer #hBN, important if monolayer #hBN is used to encapsulate other 2Ds, and we also showed how electrostatic #AFM (#EFM, #KPFM) can be used to detect piezoelectricity on the nanoscale.

18.06.2021 · Tweet

I will continue with more experiments related to bubbles in 2D materials. In particular, the effects of van der Waals (vdW) interactions in the formation of wrinkles around bubbles. Again with @lfumagalli28 among other #notinTwitter authors. Details here 👉🏼https://t.co/z2Cb0WK5G8 https://t.co/eakCj6LjnQ

18.06.2021 · Tweet

While studying the piezoelectricity in single layer #hBN, we noticed the occasional appearance of wrinkles around bubbles. For example, their formation was favoured by exposure of the samples to high humidity. https://t.co/pMTCXNRiqL

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We prepared high-quality vdW heterostructures with atomically flat monocrystals of #hBN and #MoS2 presenting different thicknesses, promoting the formation of wrinkles around bubbles. We imaged them using #AFM and measured the wavelentgh of the undulations. https://t.co/IdjRmgNFmI

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We started with incommensurate samples (atomic lattices between the botom and the top 2D materials were not aligned) and we observed radial wrinkles whose wavelength ℓ depended on the thickness of the membranes. https://t.co/akrq5d6Qfl

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We developed a theoretical framework based on the "local wavelength law". The bending rigidity favors undulations with large ℓ, and the restoring forces small ℓ. At long ℓ, the mutual slippage between the layers is suppressed while at short ℓ, intralayer slippage is prominent https://t.co/qzJjMPitEB

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We also produced commensurate samples (atomic lattices aligned between bottom and top 2Ds) of monolayer #hBN. A moiré pattern appeared and the behavior was different: the wrinkles exhibited a substantial deviation from radial orientation and became constrained to the moiré. https://t.co/eDqCch4kNB

18.06.2021 · Tweet

Our #AFM measurements of the various features of the deformed membranes can be harnessed to provide a very convenient, indirect metrological probe for the dependence of the bending rigidity on the number of atomic layers and for the magnitude and steepness of the vdW potential. https://t.co/RXB5ZyFrsl

18.06.2021 · Tweet

The last work I'll tweet about is our study of #hBN crystals stacked at small twist angle. We used #AFM to see ferroelectric-like domains arranged in triangular superlattices. People in this work include again @lfumagalli28 and @reneif07, details here 👉🏼 https://t.co/bWqnKv7nRF

18.06.2021 · Tweet

One of the most promising avenues for controlling the properties of vdW heterostructures is to adjust the angle between the stacked 2D crystals. https://t.co/pMj44bO8bP

18.06.2021 · Tweet

In this work, we produced #hBN crystals placed at an intentionally small twist angle, so they create a superlattice of charge-polarized macroscopic domains confined to the interface. https://t.co/UqXnKUVuEa

18.06.2021 · Tweet

The #hBN unit cell has two non-identical sublattices, resulting in two cases of perfect alignment, parallel and antiparallel, giving rise to six highly symmetric stacking configurations for an hBN-hBN interface that differ in the position of the interfacial N and B atoms. https://t.co/EWJbPVX9YI

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We used #AFM electrostatic modes #EFM and #KPFM to visualize the ferroelectric-like electrostatic supperlattices caused by the different stacking domains in vdW structures of several thicknesses. https://t.co/4xAtF4L6do

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We detected no superlattice patterns in the topography images, but we detected clear triangular domains periodically arranged in many regions in the electrostatic images. https://t.co/V2noDOnqqG

18.06.2021 · Tweet

Twisted heterostructures with monolayer steps on the surface of the bottom #hBN crystal showed clear triangular pattern only on one side of the terrace, suggesting that periodic domains are possible only for one orientation type, either parallel or antiparallel. https://t.co/eticI4TIZc

18.06.2021 · Tweet

We calculated superlattice reconstructions at the twisted hBN interface, that when compared with the #EFM and #KPFM results strongly suggest that the observed superlattices represent the parallel alignment with alternating AB and BA domains. https://t.co/QSc6mgdgzd

18.06.2021 · Tweet

This worked showed a simple and non-destructive #AFM technique able to visualize moiré-superlattice electrostatic potentials. The demonstrated charge-polarized superlattices provide a fascinating platform to study superlattice phenomena and engineer vdW heterostructures.

Ok so I have now talked about the how and why of my research path, but now I think it is time to introduce the "what". What exactly am I doing?? This will be a brief overview as I will dig into the details during the week. https://t.co/pDjVdXieXT

21.06.2021 · Tweet

As mentioned, I like to study crystalline materials as they are changing. This change could be during synthesis, when the materials are being utilised in a battery or when the materials have been accidentally left out on a bench and slowly degrading

21.06.2021 · Tweet

To study these changes I use diffraction. In this experiment, X-rays (or neutrons) are directed at a crystalline sample. The X-rays scatter from the array of atoms in the sample forming an interference pattern. From the pattern we can determine atom identities and their locations

21.06.2021 · Tweet

For example, below I have a series of diffraction patterns collected during lithium insertion and extraction from a material. You can see the peak shift corresponding to a volume expansion and contraction. Copper is present as an inert current collector so it doesn't change https://t.co/7onRjawAOV

21.06.2021 · Tweet

That is my main methodology, the materials which I investigate are known as rock-salt derived oxides and Prussian blue analogues. Rock-salt derived oxides are a class of structure that most commercialised cathode materials for Li-ion batteries adopt. https://t.co/k4hIlGo6yG

21.06.2021 · Tweet

Finally, Prussian blue analogues are a class of porous framework materials based around transition metals bridged by cyanide ligands. They have an open structure making them ideal for the larger cations utilised in sodium and potassium ion batteries https://t.co/J9YYmOzj6B

21.06.2021 · Tweet

Over the next few days I will describe how we study the material changes during synthesis, storage and battery operation using advanced in-situ and operando diffraction techniques. The end goal being to design greener materials which lead to better performing batteries!

But first, I think it is good to generally introduce what a Li or Na-ion #battery is built up from. While I am not an electrochemist by any stretch, I do work a lot with batteries and will mention them often.

22.06.2021 · Tweet

A battery is comprised of four key components. Two electrodes connected to an external circuit: a positive (high potential) and a negative (lower potential) electrode. These are electrically isolated from each other by a separator soaked in electrolyte allowing ions to pass. https://t.co/suyzENp5Mq

22.06.2021 · Tweet

The electrons pass via an external circuit where they perform work during battery use. Both the positive and negative electrode materials need to accept both electrons and ions (such as Li+) reversibly. Designing materials which can do this is quite challenging.

22.06.2021 · Tweet

In modern lithium-ion batteries the negative electrode (often called the anode) is graphite and the positive electrode (cathode) is either a metal oxide with a rock salt type structure or a polyanionic structure, namely LiFePO4 (LFP)

22.06.2021 · Tweet

It is interesting to reflect on the fact that the first commercially successful positive electrode material was developed in 1980 (LiCoO2), and most commercial materials today are based on this same structure. https://t.co/eLJuN4hWFY

22.06.2021 · Tweet

Aside from LiFePO4 which is quite different, are there no other viable positive electrode material classes for lithium-ion batteries? There are many being investigated but not so many that make the cut for commercialisation.

22.06.2021 · Tweet

We just got back from a group lunch/farewell to @ashok_menon12. I will use this opportunity to talk a little bit about what Ashok has done during his PhD. Ashok has worked with what is known as Li and Mn-rich layered oxides.

22.06.2021 · Tweet

The Li and Mn rich oxide materials are interesting as they have the potential to store a lot more energy compared to regular battery cathodes. https://t.co/QlHZIRrgz5

22.06.2021 · Tweet

The reason is due to the excess lithium which sits in the transition metal layer. The presence of Li in this layer creates local Li-O-Li bonding environments allowing of anionic redox due to unhybridised O orbitals. Below I show the regular LiCoO2 (yellow) and Li2MnO3 (purple). https://t.co/BsbGu4Fh6U

22.06.2021 · Tweet

However, this excess lithium has other structural consequences. Namely, the formation of a hexagonal arrangement of cations in the transition metal layer. https://t.co/kD8tTwxknR

22.06.2021 · Tweet

However, how these layers in the structure arrange can shift. Leading to a kind of disorder known as stacking faults. In the clip I represent Li and Mn environments as hexagons. The shifts show how two adjacent layers can be placed relative to each other. https://t.co/zcNvFrysnf

22.06.2021 · Tweet

The question that Ashok aimed to answer was how the synthesis route impacted the degree of faulting and properties in the relatively simple compound Li2MnO3. https://t.co/wNeSyuxIa6

22.06.2021 · Tweet

It turns out that the synthesis route did have a significant impact with a solid state "shake and bake" route producing a mix of faulted and unfaulted structures and the solgel route forming a more homogeneous structure.

22.06.2021 · Tweet
