23.06.2021 · Tweet

[admin] "Embracing Change - Materials for Greener Tomorrow" Extended conversation with the amazing @willrbrant1 is out now. 🥳🎙️👇 https://t.co/oY7fa0pkdq

23.06.2021 · Tweet

After our initial work on Li2MnO3, we discovered that there was a debate in the literature for a related compound. The more promising Li1.2Mn0.54Ni0.13Co0.13O2. It is the Li and Mn rich analogue to the Li[NiMnCo]O2 oxides used in commercial batteries.

23.06.2021 · Tweet

What was this debate? It was whether the material existed as a solid solution or if it was an intergrowth or mix of Li2MnO3 and Li[NiMnCo]O2. Ie, if the composition crystallised as one or two phases. Here is an excerpt highlighting the debate https://t.co/rNJ2ihG8uY https://t.co/aTr4I7Sr8J

23.06.2021 · Tweet

And here is what the two proposed models are. In the multi-phase model the hexagonal ordering occurs exclusively for Li and Mn whereas in the single phase Li in the transition metal layer can also have Ni and Co as nearest neighbours. https://t.co/X1ch7X4gcN

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Why does this matter? It has been argued that the additional capacity, specifically the anionic redox capacity, originated from the Li2MnO3 phase. Thus, its presence is necessary for that additional capacity.

23.06.2021 · Tweet

So why is this so difficult? Surely a diffraction experiment can tell you whether multiple phases are present. Lets play a game of spot the difference🙂. Below are diffraction patterns (X-rays and neutrons) from a confirmed "single" and "multi" phase samples https://t.co/wDCj3VYNSu

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Aside from intensity differences in the neutron diffraction pattern, they look pretty similar. Figuring out this puzzle is further complicated since the compound has disorder over several length scales. Short to long: Atomic site mixing, stacking faults and phase segregation https://t.co/3mKL1M8idR

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Disorder over multiple length scales means to answer this question multiple characterisation tools are needed. This is what we did, looking at both local and long range information. The methods were diffraction, raman spectroscopy, magnetic susceptibility, and STEM measurements https://t.co/Ly1atHr4tA

23.06.2021 · Tweet

What did we learn? Is the material one or two phases?? The answer is: both and it depends on how you synthesise the material. Similar to the first paper, solid state gives an inhomogeneous distribution of elements whereas the sol gel method is more homogeneous https://t.co/tSuRtdUUEI

23.06.2021 · Tweet

It is not too surprising that this has led to conflicting results over the years. It does raise some interesting ideas about tailoring phase intergrowth via different synthetic pathways however.

23.06.2021 · Tweet

The full story can be found here: https://t.co/GSJts7b2AJ

23.06.2021 · Tweet

@realscientists This is actually a great idea, I might have to borrow that one🙂

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Now to talk about Prussian blue analogues! To begin I have to tell the story behind them because it is one of my favourite pieces of chemical history. It is a tale of alchemists, theologians, famous paintings and about 200 years of wondering what Prussian blue was. https://t.co/rbeaQIJeEd

23.06.2021 · Tweet

It all began in Berlin in 1704 with an enterprising dye maker by the name of Heinrich Diesbach. He was most interested in producing a red dye by the name of Cochineal red lake. The ingredients were iron sulphate, potash and crushed up beetles #alchemy https://t.co/0GxjR9T9AY

23.06.2021 · Tweet

But Diesbach was running low on potash. Enter the scene one Johann Conrad Dippel. Master theologian, physician, alchemist. Dippel was captured by the allure of alchemy and like any good alchemist began his attempts at transmuting gold. https://t.co/flKvNWZRGk

23.06.2021 · Tweet

This failed, but it did not deter him from making a miraculous "animal oil" and releasing it upon an unsuspecting public. The concoction, distilled from the ground up remains of animals, was so foul it was believed it must be good for you (like any good medicine right?)

23.06.2021 · Tweet

What does this have to do with a dye maker? Diesbach is said to have been preparing his dyes in Dippels laboratories. His potash shortage was solved by buying from Dippel. Now, Dippel was not a great alchemist and a terrible chemist so of course the potash was contaminated

23.06.2021 · Tweet

And so, unsuspectingly using the potash contaminated with animal remains Diesbach tried to produce his red dye. He did not get a red dye. He produced a very blue powder instead. https://t.co/4Tva0GXC1k

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Keep in mind that obtaining vibrant blue colours for paint or clothing in these times was not easy, and not cheap. Diesbach knew this and quickly attempted to recreate the recipe and sell his new blue pigment to the world leading to several famous paintings. https://t.co/Iads1W6V3i

23.06.2021 · Tweet

The original recipe called for dried ox blood as a key ingredient. Of course, they can't have known what was really going on at the time because the discovery of several key elements had not yet happened (like nitrogen in 1772). So what did they really make?

23.06.2021 · Tweet

The key ingredients are iron and cyanide. The cyanide, which originated from various alkyl cyanides in the animal remains, dramatically changed the reaction leading to what is now known as Prussian blue. But it took a few hundred years to figure this out https://t.co/5zkyzWKRSY https://t.co/rOnZ9EqqKJ

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Finally, using X-ray diffraction, it was determined that Prussian blue was a coordination framework compound consisting of iron centers bridged together by cyanide ligands. Each iron can be coordinated by six cyanides giving the porous cubic structure. https://t.co/kL6P23luoa

23.06.2021 · Tweet

This was just the beginning. Prussian blue is one member of a family of compounds known as Prussian blue analogues. They share the same coordination environment of CN bridges, but the transition metal can change and the pores in the structure can host many different species.

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Many different compositions leads to a variety of properties and applications. Prussian blue analogues are more than just pretty colours. They can be used for treating Cesium and thallium poisoning, CO2 capture, in electrochromic windows and of course, in batteries! (and more) https://t.co/AtYlncEnq8

23.06.2021 · Tweet

For more detail on the history of Prussian blue, I recommend the work by Alexander Kraft, who has written a few times on the history of the pigment (https://t.co/is3OMqFpuQ) and also a nice perspective by Andreas Ludi: https://t.co/ogjXNcAWFp

23.06.2021 · Tweet

So how about Prussian blue analogues (PBAs) in batteries? In addition to @Altris_ab there are a number of other companies developing this class of compounds for energy storage applications. What makes them so attractive?

23.06.2021 · Tweet

PBAs are commonly used as the positive electrode in beyond Li-ion batteries (sodium, potassium). They have an open structure leading to fast cation insertion. Additionally, due to the strong bonding of the cyanide ligand transition metals like iron have a decent voltage output. https://t.co/vjzNrlIjVD

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Indeed, the performance metrics of PBAs, in particular the iron-based Na2Fe[Fe(CN)6], are quite similar to those of LiFePO4 (LFP). However, PBAs have the additional advantage of a simple and low cost synthesis making them very interesting to develop cheap sustainable batteries https://t.co/4KDjKd01L3

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Also the electrodes cast using PBAs look really nice :) https://t.co/kbwR71naE7

23.06.2021 · Tweet

It was the simplicity of synthesis and performance reliability which first attracted @RezaYounesi and his PhD student Ronnie Mogensen to Prussian blue analogues. The full story on this is coming up next🙂

23.06.2021 · Tweet

The story of how @Altris_ab came to be and my involvement in PBA research is also a nice one. It was really a combination of the right people meeting at the right time and at the right place.

23.06.2021 · Tweet

It began with Ronnie Mogensen, who was working on polymer electrolytes at the time and just needed a reliable positive electrode that was easy to make. He tried NaFePO4 which didn't always function. Then he turned to NaxFe[Fe(CN)6]. This always worked to a reasonable degree

23.06.2021 · Tweet

He then stumbled upon a paper where the group of John Goodenough (Nobel laureate in chemistry for Li-ion #batteries) made rhombohedral Prussian white. https://t.co/xdiIwbj6Mj

23.06.2021 · Tweet

What is Prussian white? Specifically, when the sodium content in NaxFe[Fe(CN)6] reaches a maximum with few structural defects, the material adopts a white colour rather than its famous blue. https://t.co/n5S7Xv9P02

23.06.2021 · Tweet

It also has very impressive electrochemical performance with a capacity around 160 mAhg-1 and an average voltage of 3.4 V. Needless to say, @RezaYounesi was intrigued and wanted to produce the material for his #sodium #battery research.

23.06.2021 · Tweet

The problem was the synthesis, which required the use of a hydrothermal reactor with a built in stirrer. We did not have such an autoclave available so he needed an alternative approach.

23.06.2021 · Tweet

It should be mentioned that until this stage, most synthesis routes to prepare PBAs for electrodes resulted in low capacities and low reversibility due to the presence of [Fe(CN)6]3- vacancies and water in the structure. So this needed to be addressed

23.06.2021 · Tweet

This was around the time that I got involved in the project, purely because I happened to be in the department and eager to collaborate. However, I had some light experience working with PBAs and methods of chemically intercalating materials. So together we devised a new approach

23.06.2021 · Tweet

The original idea of the synthesis was to optimise for low vacancies, high sodium content and low water in separate steps with sodium and water contents reliant on a low vacancy content. We split up the process and recreated the result from Goodenough but with simple equipment. https://t.co/Y1jB41yZR5

23.06.2021 · Tweet

And here is a picture of the compound before (right) and after (left) the sodium enrichment step. https://t.co/TqIhOWUmn2

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Given our success Reza suggested we should patent this, why not? Afterall, in Sweden the researchers own the idea, not the university. Of course we needed to pay for this ourselves but thanks to the generousity of @KristinaEdstrm2 we had available funding to do just that.

23.06.2021 · Tweet

So we were pretty happy with managing to patent our idea. However, it was not the end as another chance encounter with Adam Dahlquist from @InnoEnergyEU pushed us in a new direction: Creating @Altris_ab

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Adam introduced us to Paul Larsson to take care of the business side of things and we set to work on first creating the company and then taking on the hard work to get into the EIT InnoEnergy Highway® program, which in 2017 we succeeded in doing

23.06.2021 · Tweet

This was quite unusual because when we started the application, Altris didn't even exist. But the four of us really believed in the idea. Plus, the willingness to bring in Paul and share the company was positively recieved. Afterall 1% of 1 million is better than 100% of nothing https://t.co/qrPy2cHnkU

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Now the real work began. Scaling up production. Here we hired Dr Tim Nordh as our first ever employee and began to scale up the synthesis within the @StructuralChem1 labs. https://t.co/KLGd9tcVV3

23.06.2021 · Tweet

We also started collaborating with a local company LiFeSiZE to produce prototype #batteries. https://t.co/WlnLghzmcn

23.06.2021 · Tweet

These were extremely challenging years as we were finding our feet as a company, looking for financing, trying to get things right with scaling up the synthesis AND building prototype cells for the first time. Many road blocks were encountered. https://t.co/c7zTutF68i

23.06.2021 · Tweet

But we persevered! And very soon out grew the university as we were ready for the next step. Adam Dahlquist joined the company in 2019 and began pushing expansion. We obtained a site for a small pilot factory and then built the place ourselves (or Tim and Ronnie did).

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Here is a photo of the team as it was at this stage. It is one of my favourites :) https://t.co/lRomVqPHVC

23.06.2021 · Tweet

We had a new challenge to achieve now. Cell producer partners wanted our Prussian white (which we trademarked as "Fennac" and they wanted a lot (or a lot by our standards). 50 kg by 2020 which was 50 times more than we had ever produced before. https://t.co/WRa5ZJzZXj

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Of course, then Corona hit. But this didn't slow us down. Altris had won funding from @vinnovase and @Energi_mynd and came out over subscribed in the seed round of investments.

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Since then, things have been ever accelerating and now @Altris_ab is working with cell producers in China, India and Europe to bring Fennac based batteries to market.

23.06.2021 · Tweet

Phew, so the story of Altris is quite a long one. Looking back its always amazing how far we have come despite the challenges. But we just never gave up. Now that big cell producers are looking to #sodiumion #batteries Altris will be entering a new chapter in its story.

Good morning! Today will be a busy day. In addition to wrapping up teaching preparation for the summer, I will be buying ingredients for #Midsummer celebrations tomorrow and getting #vaccinated! In between all this I will talk a little on the PBA activities I have been up to

For now I am heading into a meeting with a summer worker who will be spending the next few weeks building 100s of #batteries https://t.co/QbKCYUrGjH

24.06.2021 · Tweet

Back onto the science before I head out for vaccination. How have I contributed to the PBA work? One of the earliest questions we were asked by funding agencies was about the thermal stability of Prussian white. So we dug into this question: https://t.co/7iLq5UUBFU

24.06.2021 · Tweet

One of the main concerns was that Prussian white would exhibit thermal stability similar to that other PBAs which have been shown to release CN compounds at around 200C https://t.co/KlwAMyxqVH

24.06.2021 · Tweet

What we determined was that if you already have a low vacancy structure like Prussian white, the thermal stability is determined by the sodium content. The more sodium the more thermally stable it is. A bonus result was that the water uptake is also increased for increased sodium https://t.co/MBPRf02PCF

24.06.2021 · Tweet

The latter result is important to consider since Prussian white should be used in non aqueous batteries. So removing all the water prior to implementation in a battery is essential. Understanding the material drying parameters has improved our sample processing @Altris_ab

24.06.2021 · Tweet

Of course, the thermal stability is highly dependent on the environment and the conditions tested here aren't the same as in a battery. Regardless, relative to other PBAs it seems that Prussian white is more thermally stable under the same conditions. https://t.co/tSDYLlLKB5

24.06.2021 · Tweet

Here I made a nice table of contents figure summarising the key take home messages. https://t.co/CoQYz7MS70

24.06.2021 · Tweet

Lunch time question to you all! How important do you think understanding visual #design is for scientists? I spend a lot of time making TOC images but am not the best designer :p. Feel free to write your opinion too!

24.06.2021 · Tweet

@ChirpDontTweet Yeah, I would tend to agree. You don't have to do much for good data visualisation to raise the quality over what is generally out there. Less is more as they say.

24.06.2021 · Tweet

Nice to see that many think its important. Of course when I say visual design I mean data visualisation #dataviz. Presenting data in a way which is clear and conveys the correct message without ambiguity I think is really important

24.06.2021 · Tweet

The other aspect related to PBAs in #batteries are their moisture sensitivity. PBAs, like many porous compounds, are hygroscopic and adsorb moisture from the air. For Prussian white this comes with a colour change. Left is sample exposed to oxygen, right is to air. https://t.co/5sYkcA4IQp

24.06.2021 · Tweet

This is a little bit of a problem since you don't want water in a battery, this leads to all kinds of nasty side reactions. So how do we solve this? Well, my mantra is if you want to solve a problem you must first understand it. https://t.co/0gnG5FcTTx

24.06.2021 · Tweet

The question I wanted to answer, jokingly, was what happens if I accidentally leave my Prussian white on the bench for a month? The actual question was, how does moisture exposure during storage impact capacity fade? https://t.co/m951WWdsIi

24.06.2021 · Tweet

It is useful to point out at this stage that Prussian white exists in two forms. The hydrated, monoclinic phase with water inside the pores and a dehydrated rhombohedral phase, which is a slightly collapsed structure. What comes out of a reactor is the monoclinic phase. https://t.co/9XPyzfmqge

24.06.2021 · Tweet

When you dry the material you transform to the rhombohedral phase. We exposed both forms of Prussian white to different humidity levels for 7 days. The monoclinic was unchanged up to 75% relative humidity. The rhombohedral degraded heavily. Left: pristine. Right: exposed https://t.co/ElJ5QPnuIv

24.06.2021 · Tweet

Not only were the particles visibly damaged, when held at 55% relative humidity for up to 90 days the capacity was found to rapidly decay before stabilising. It also seemed to occur from one plateau only. So we began to dig into the mechanism for this fade. https://t.co/9KazJwMLkj

24.06.2021 · Tweet

To cut a long story and complex puzzle short. Using X-ray diffraction, XPS, mössbauer spectroscopy, IR and Raman we determined that the material degraded in two steps. First the reversible extraction of sodium to form NaOH, then the irreversible basic degradation of the framework https://t.co/4SYWRZM5jA

24.06.2021 · Tweet

Such degradation is not unknown for PBAs, however, the impact on electrochemical performance had not been quantified before. Follow on studies from this have significantly impacted how we handle and treat PBA material at Altris.

Since coming to Uppsala I have focused more on battery cells for X-ray #diffraction, and mostly using our in house diffractometer. This has been work I have done for others in the group. Its amazing how much you can achieve without going to a #synchrotron (though I do miss going)

We have studied materials like LiFeSO4F in pouch cells. This was a particularly good success as it is an Fe containing material on a Cu source diffractomerer. Before we start diving into science, allow me to introduce the team first: I started my research group 1 year ago with this amazing bunch of talented students (Marie, Leona, Max). Since then we are working towards #THz & #MIR control of structural dynamics. Why that? Stay tuned! https://t.co/28Ka3nfFNt

28.06.2021 · Tweet

So why *structural dynamics*? Material properties are fundamentally determined by the spatial arrangement of atoms, ions or molecules. If we can modulate this spatial structure on ultrafast time scales, we might control properties on demand or even discover new material features. https://t.co/5jIruHWDsv

28.06.2021 · Tweet

@_AFox_ Thanks, very solid question: In the field of laser spectroscopy people loosely refer every faster than a couple of hundred picoseconds (ps) as "ultrafast". What is important here are the natural oscillation periods of elementary vibrations, usually a couple of ps.

28.06.2021 · Tweet

And why *THz* or *MIR*? Intense and phase stable laser pulses in the THz to MIR spectral range enable us to directly drive specific resonances on their fundamental time and energy scales. With these, we can control IR-active modes resonantly and Raman-active ones nonlinearly. https://t.co/HaaYTptiQ6

28.06.2021 · Tweet

Where to get these high-field THz / MIR pulses from? Unfortunately there's no out-of-the-box laser pointer for that. So one of the main tasks in our group is to keep our big baby happy and running. #Laserlife More lab impressions to come on #LaserLabThursday. @sfmaehrlein Labs https://t.co/QVEPNTm8jl

Can we access novel spin states via specific lattice vibrations? Yes! In the ferrimagnetic insulator Yttrium Iron Garnet, we showed that resonant lattice excitation leads to a transient spin-state of elevated temperature, but yet unchanged magnetization https://t.co/iz61Z7SNmd

30.06.2021 · Tweet

Let's kick off day 3⃣ digit three with a few fundamental scientific questions.

30.06.2021 · Tweet

How fast is the angular momentum transfer between spins and the lattice? In magnetic insulators, when angular momentum transfer has to rely on spin-orbit coupling, it is slow ~ns compared to the lattice excitation. Thus the intermediate state is determined by constraint heating. https://t.co/CLJTWPm4hg

30.06.2021 · Tweet

Thermodynamic picture: A) Lattice heating under the constraint of conserved total spin angular momentum (pot+lid) ➡️built up of "spin pressure" ➡️ B) new state: internal spin redistribution ➡️C) demagnetization via angular momentum release to lattice 🧲 https://t.co/YJjB91BgYb

30.06.2021 · Tweet

Okay, #phonon #control seems useful, but what if there's a desired target mode without electric dipole moment for coupling to the #THz field? We found the sum-frequency counterpart of stimulated #RamanScattering to access these previously IR-silent modes. https://t.co/0x6FrEWAIB

30.06.2021 · Tweet

The same sum-frequency excitation can be driven by phoNons instead of phoTons via #NonlinearPhonincs: Anharmonic coupling can lead to sum-frequency ionic Raman scattering. Great theory collaboration with D.M. Jurascheck (@NarangLab, prev. @NicolaSpaldin) https://t.co/dk5fqx6JYq https://t.co/OJrsLfzFRS

1/ as promised, today a lab tour @PhoND_UAM! In bits and pieces, I´ll give you the ins and outs of our work on visualising energy transport in nanomaterials... First a general tour of our laser lab! 🔬 https://t.co/kgPCNgANaC

13.07.2021 · Tweet

2/ Our labs are located at the @UAM_Madrid Cantoblanco campus on the north side of Madrid. We are in the basement, which is really quite convenient when trying to keep sunlight out of the lab (cause sun we have in Madrid 😄🌞) https://t.co/AZH5wvdJqW

13.07.2021 · Tweet

3/ The most important piece of optics we have is the 18 m2 L-shaped floating table. This is where we perform all our most sensitive microscopy and spectroscopy measurements. https://t.co/yE5f1LCZOd

13.07.2021 · Tweet

4/ we love inverted optical microscopes, cause the exit ports at the bottom allow you to easily couple the light out of your microscope and send it free-space to your favourite detector. https://t.co/m47C25jdUU

13.07.2021 · Tweet

5/ many of our ports are equipped with @Thorlabs adapters to directly mount cages, making for easy alignment in and out of the microscope. Here for example, you see the in-coupling of our single-mode excitation laser for diffraction limited illumination. https://t.co/9OIfuih0ZF

13.07.2021 · Tweet

6/ we use diffraction limited excitation of our samples to generate the fluorescent signals that give us a ton of info about the material. we analyse these signals using different space, time, and energy resolved techniques. https://t.co/HpbmrKE8HJ

13.07.2021 · Tweet

7/ our favorite layout uses relay lenses to project the image onto the slit of an imaging spectrograph. The slit is motorized such that we can either propagate the spectrum to the camera (slit closed, grating in place) or the full image (slit open, mirror instead of grating) https://t.co/KgmNYG12MS

13.07.2021 · Tweet

8/ The best part of this layout is that you have plenty of space to introduce for example polarisers, additional filters, or a so-called Bertrand lens that allows you to do angle resolved spectroscopy(more about that tomorrow!)

13.07.2021 · Tweet

9/ for spectroscopy, we really like our imaging spectrographs with double exit ports. The standard layout gives you the spectral dispersion directly on your camera (EMCCD in our case). But alternatively, you can send the light out to the side to an avalanche photodiode. https://t.co/NWSxJZVgeV

13.07.2021 · Tweet

10/ this gives you the option to do spectrally resolved lifetime measurements... basically it´s very a simple streak camera with a timing of some 100 ps and spectral resolution depending on your grating.

13.07.2021 · Tweet

11/ Finally, on the other side of the microscope, we have our scanning avalanche photodiode, which has a ridiculously simple layout, but is the key to all our energy transport measurements. I will tell you all about transient microscopy in a dedicated thread! https://t.co/VWi0CvFUwY

13.07.2021 · Tweet

1/ A thread on transient microscopy techniques! This simple technique allows you to visualise carrier transport in a variety of materials, giving direct information about how fast and how far carriers move. (this is going to be a long thread, bear with me!) https://t.co/EZ8vIl8vFi

13.07.2021 · Tweet

2/ Understanding carrier transport is crucial for optoelectronics. In a solar cell, for example, carriers need to travel as far as possible to reach charge collecting interfaces. https://t.co/3jnWU1z2Vp

13.07.2021 · Tweet

3/ traditional techniques are time-averaged methods that only measure the average speed of the carriers during its lifetime. This works well for perfect lattices of a single crystalline semiconductor where speeds are constant... but not for more complex nanomaterials!

13.07.2021 · Tweet

4/ we started working on this problem around 2013 at MIT, with a team of people from the Bulovic and Tisdale labs. The idea was to create exciations in one spot, and detect how long it would take for that excitation to reach a different position. https://t.co/BxShPvKr2s

13.07.2021 · Tweet

5/ Gleb Akselrod, a senior grad student at the Bulovic lab, built the first version of the transient microscope, and it was remarkably simple: a fixed diffraction limited excitation, and a motorized APD in the image plane for raster scanning. https://t.co/BMOTPoTeUQ

13.07.2021 · Tweet

6/ the excitation spot is kept tiny using a high NA objective (>250 nm), and by scanning the APD across the fixed exciation spot, you obtain a beautiful visualization of the broadening of the carrier population! https://t.co/vspwzIpb5q

13.07.2021 · Tweet

7/ if your material is isotropic, a single line scan gives you all the info you need. But as Gleb showed beautifully in the first publication on transport in tetracene organic crystals, different axis can give anisotropic transport. https://t.co/O7liprXJl3

13.07.2021 · Tweet

8/ In the tetracene paper, things were relatively easy cause carriers are triplet excitons that live very long and travel far (100s of nm)... but what about single excitons with short lifetimes?

13.07.2021 · Tweet

9/ we tested this with thin films of colloidal quantum dots, where singlet excitons hop from one particle to the next through energy transfer. This process is slow, and excitons only live about 20 ns in these materials. The transport was therefore not expected to go very far.

13.07.2021 · Tweet

10/ but transient microscopy can measure tiny displacements far below the diffraction limit! This is because you only need to determine the difference between the population width at different times and to determine the width, it´s all signal-to-noise! https://t.co/euf1S93g3q

13.07.2021 · Tweet

11/ the precise determination of the width at different times is what allows us to determine the mean-square-displacement (MSD) of the population, and the slope of the MSD tells us how fast the carriers move.

13.07.2021 · Tweet

12/ back to the QD thin films: because they are so bright, signal to noise is awesome! So we showed that even the tiniest displacements could be resolved using transient microscopy... travelling just 10s of nm during their lifetimes! https://t.co/paVtwvs0eh

13.07.2021 · Tweet

13/ this is a bit short of course for a solar cell, but turns out well for an LED for example. More important was all the info we got from these measurements... cause it turned out the transport was really not your conventional random walk.

13.07.2021 · Tweet

14/ As I mentioned, the slope of the MSD tells us how fast the carriers move. If the slope is constant, the speed is constant and we have a normal random walk. But for QDs the slope is never constant and transport is always slowing down (subdiffusion)! https://t.co/zSO0B95eii

13.07.2021 · Tweet

15/ Carriers slowing down is a clear indication of a bumpy energy landscape. Carriers start at the top of the hills, move down relatively fast, but slow down as they reach the valleys.

13.07.2021 · Tweet

16/ We could relate this directly back to the tiny variations in size of the different QDs, which give tiny variations in the optical bandgap of the particles.

13.07.2021 · Tweet

17/ The study on QDs really showed the strength of transient microscopy, cause it turns out that in nanostructured semiconductors, transport almost never undergoes a standard random walk. This technique is what allows you to visualize that.

13.07.2021 · Tweet

18/ okay, going to try to wrap up this thread by showing some of the newer developments in transient microscopy. The early days used fluorescence as the probe of the carriers, but that only works for bright materials. What if your cariers dont like to emit light?

13.07.2021 · Tweet

19/ the @HuangLabPurdue for example haev pioneered transient absorption microscopy. Rather than looking at emission as the probe, they look at the change in absorption when a carrier is present. An extremely versatile technique! https://t.co/gGOrjJn4BK

13.07.2021 · Tweet

20/ and more recently, an interferometric scattering based technique has been developed by the Ginsberg group at Berkeley - an extremely powerful demonstration that really boosts the signal from any carrier! https://t.co/RPVNSfDA7n

13.07.2021 · Tweet

21/ sorry for rambling on 😉... I´ll try to find some time later to tell you about more recent work from my own lab, where we use transient microscopy to visualize transport in perovskite materials! https://t.co/CY3RvrAirM

13.07.2021 · Tweet

ps: really nice review on the topic is this one by Ginsberg and Tisdale: https://t.co/EiXmyFf1Ll

13.07.2021 · Tweet

1/ ok, final thread of the day... let´s see if I can keep it shorter than the previous one 😉... we continue with transient microscopy, but now on the family of 2D perovskites! Specifically, how tiny changes in the perovskite composition have a huge impact on energy transport! https://t.co/v43h5DyQoN

13.07.2021 · Tweet

2/ so perovskites are all the hype right now of course, showing really promising efficiencies for solar cells. Main issues that remain are related to the stability and this is where lower dimensional perovskites (such as 2Ds) can help.

13.07.2021 · Tweet

3/ using long organic cations, you can cut up the conventional 3D perovskite lattice into layers, forming the 2D perovskite lattice. The long cations protect the soft inorganic lattice from exposure to air and humidity, improving the stability of the material. https://t.co/nTTocmLGGq

13.07.2021 · Tweet

4/ but, cutting up your lattice changes everything in terms of carrier transport! Not only do you place these organic barriers there, the confinement of the carriers to a thin plane changes their interaction: free charges become bound electron-hole pairs (or excitons). https://t.co/oydM2yTzfI

13.07.2021 · Tweet

5/ so how do excitons move through these layers? Can they move between layers? And how do changes in the composition change the transport characteristics? Due to their tunability, layered perovskites are a perfect platform to study structure-property relations 👌

13.07.2021 · Tweet

6/ so first, if we want to study structure-property relations... we need to make different perovskite variations. Luckily, 2D perovskites are extremely forgiving and crystallise very easily from concentrated solutions... you literally see them grow! https://t.co/HDZnyhYvf3

13.07.2021 · Tweet

7/ we grow the crystals on glass slides and use good old scotch tape exfoliation to isolate single crystalline flakes large enough for transient microscopy measurements. https://t.co/SrYjJKrNXo

13.07.2021 · Tweet

8/ then we run our favorite experiment again, first on one of the typical 2D perovskites, with a phenethylammonium (PEA) organic spacer between the layers. The population of excitons broadens fast, so transport in the 2D plane is efficient! https://t.co/AevUVWdd0G

13.07.2021 · Tweet

9/ but what if we change the spacer to another commonly used example: butylammonium (BA)... to our surprise it behaved completely different! https://t.co/MLcgNj8vGl

13.07.2021 · Tweet

10/ if we translate it to a diffusion length L_D, it´s a massive difference! Why? Especially considering that the carrier live in the inorganic lattice, and the spacers should have little influence on the electronic properties. https://t.co/KNUK5mvYmu

13.07.2021 · Tweet

11/ by exploring more spacer cations, we found that exciton transport scales beautifully with the stiffness of the lattice, showing that exciton-phonon interactions are the dominant parameter determining transport. https://t.co/YYwAT2vwmw

13.07.2021 · Tweet

12/ knowing this relation between transport and lattice stiffness, we can now start thinking of designing even better 2D perovskites for energy transport. These results were summarized in the first big publication coming out of our madrid lab. https://t.co/k1laNQIDWs

13.07.2021 · Tweet

13/ beyond the clear differences, transient microscopy can also give very subtle info on the details of transport, for example about the types of traps you have in your material. https://t.co/rvscrtX7fm

13.07.2021 · Tweet

14/ and how about interlayer transport? Turns out it is really quite efficient in 2D perovskites! https://t.co/FIumX55Jkn

13.07.2021 · Tweet

15/ more stories are coming up soon, as we are still exploring the large parameter space of these materials... and other systems are lying on the shelve... measurements take time though, and careful data analysis is crucial in this field!

13.07.2021 · Tweet

16/ last week we celebrated the PhD defence of @M1chaelSeitz, who has been the driving force of setting up this work. While it is sad to see talented people go, we can be very proud of the result! Luckily we have a very talented @Alvaro_Mgd who has taken over 🙂 https://t.co/bbGSndN3Et

13.07.2021 · Tweet

17/ with that I close for the day! tomorrow I´ll be back her @RealSci_Nano with some nanofabrication of nanomaterials!

14.07.2021 · Tweet

[admin] "Nanoscale Energy Transport: The Motion Picture" Longer conversation with @FerryPrins is out now 👇🎧 https://t.co/EseHse1jwg

14.07.2021 · Tweet

1/ Today I want to talk a bit about nanofabrication with nanomaterials! We are used to do nanofabrication on metals and crystalline semiconductors, but how to create structures out of softer nanostructured materials? for example, a pyramid from (roughly) 250.000 nanoparticles? https://t.co/JZkHMbsn4D

14.07.2021 · Tweet

2/ during my time @NorrisOMEL, we were always looking for new tricks to structure optical materials and improve their photonic properties. The specialty of the group was (and still is) a technique called template-stripping, but till then was mostly used on plasmonic metal films.

14.07.2021 · Tweet

3/ template-stripping of metallic films was developed by David Norris together with Sang-Hyun Oh (@OhLabUMN) during their time together at Minnesota. It´s an amazingly powerful and simple technique to create extremely high quality structures! https://t.co/b39WZLdmkL https://t.co/pFt5S6CPij

14.07.2021 · Tweet

4/ You start with a simple Si wafer, and do your favorite patterning (litho&etch) to create what we call the template. You then evaporate your material onto the template and glue a glass slide (UV epoxy). Final step: you separate the glass slide with the metal from the template. https://t.co/e0ZL9NfrSc

14.07.2021 · Tweet

5/ the beauty is that now you have exposed an ultrasmooth, patterned surface! While the evaporated metal film has nm-scale roughness, your stripped surface is as smooth as your silicon template. For plasmonics this is essential: any roughness can scatter your propagating plasmon.

14.07.2021 · Tweet

6/ ok, back to the patterning of nanoparticle films... can we use template stripping to structure thin films of colloidal quantum dots for example? The problem is that when your materials sticks too much to the silicon, the stripping gets ugly.

14.07.2021 · Tweet

7/ then we remembered this really nice paper by Lee et al., in which they make a silicon wafer super non-sticky (extremely hydrophobic) to QDs using a dense self assembled monolayer (SAM). https://t.co/Bif2XsbOXC

14.07.2021 · Tweet

8/ so, template stripping of QD thin films using a template with a SAM? Works beautifully! drop cast your solution onto the template and just clip it of... https://t.co/ABkhznOg5k

14.07.2021 · Tweet

9/ here are thin films of different colors of QDs, stripped from their templates shown on the left. https://t.co/ofnZxwJzlN

14.07.2021 · Tweet

10/ First structures we tried were simple gratings out of QDs, which would allow you to couple light out of the film more easily. This SEM image shows nicely the arrangement of particles for a 400 nm periodicity of a grating. https://t.co/3DURqt4tql

14.07.2021 · Tweet

11/ so why the grating? Cause it can help the outcoupling of emission from the film. For a flat film of QDs, a lot of light get´s trapped into waveguide modes due to total internal reflection (a problem of momentum mismatch). This can be as much as 80% loss! https://t.co/Nzu3aQzw3C

14.07.2021 · Tweet

12/ the grating creates Bragg scattering at the interface, giving the waveguided light a bit of extra momentum that helps it to couple to free space. by changing the periodicity of the grating, we can control which wavelength couples out under which angle. https://t.co/qDI5CLi1gR

14.07.2021 · Tweet

13/ here you can see circular gratings of different periodicities (pitches), where the red emission couples out under a straight 90 degrees angle for a periodicity of 400 nm. So, patterning is a great way of improving the brightness of your QD film! https://t.co/gt1VQeALm3

14.07.2021 · Tweet

14/ we did a bunch of other demonstrations, mixing different colors, and making the patterned films on flexible substrates. https://t.co/BhDkolaDqf https://t.co/KSrIgN06LD

14.07.2021 · Tweet

15/ beyond gratings, you can also make waveguides out of QDs, and this turns out to be a great way to make a ring laser! here you can see the transition from just waveguiding to the lasing action at higher pump fluence. https://t.co/F4z24qtBaF https://t.co/WGmY627O1L

14.07.2021 · Tweet

16/ the nice thing is that the template stripping can also be applied to other solution processable materials. Here an example of patterning of a perovskite thin film with feature sizes below a micron! 👇 https://t.co/060vf8pLEd https://t.co/8QqQPioxHq

14.07.2021 · Tweet

1/ so as I mentioned earlier, when we pattern the surface of a thin film of quantum dots with a periodic grating, we can control the angle of outcoupling of the emission. So how do we measure angles? A small thread on angle-resolved microscopy! https://t.co/HhXVfPgkz9

14.07.2021 · Tweet

2/ let´s think for a second about how an objective works: it collimates a cone of angles. This means that the so-called back-focal-plane (BFP) of the objective is a map of all the angles of the light! This is the basis for BFP imaging (aka fourier or k-space imaging) https://t.co/JXsz6n33IB

14.07.2021 · Tweet

3/ the size of the BFP is given by the NA of the objective, and translates directly to the k-vectors (or angles) of the collected light. The larger the NA, the wider your angular map you can obtain.

14.07.2021 · Tweet

4/ but how do you get this map? For this you need to introduce a Bertrand lens into your optical path. This sounds like a magical piece, but is just an ordinary lens placed at the focal length from the fourier plane of your collimating lens. https://t.co/FXikaEBJrf

14.07.2021 · Tweet

5/ flipping the Bertrand lens in and out in this configuration allows you to switch immediately from a real-space image to the fourier image. there are many guides online, particularly good is this one by the group of Rashid Zia: https://t.co/EoR8DhoLhT

14.07.2021 · Tweet

6/ you get beautiful images of the angular emission patterns of your samples. In our case with the patterned circular gratings of quantum dot thin films, the right pitch gives a beam of light at perpendicular angle, while other pitches couple at higher angles giving donuts. https://t.co/no84Y0dHDl

14.07.2021 · Tweet

7/ it gets even better if you project your fourier image on the entrance slit of your imaging spectrograph... by dispersing the angular pattern you get direct access to the photonic band diagram of your structure! (shown here for a linear grating) https://t.co/hIHpWqPeUF https://t.co/k5Nip6beFT

14.07.2021 · Tweet

8/ so check it out, cause angle-resolved microscopy and spectroscopy are really not as difficult as it sometimes sounds (I was surprised how easy it was when I first set it up). You can get a ton of extra info about your samples!

14.07.2021 · Tweet

9/ further reading: another really nice reference on this is from the group of Femius Koenderink @_amolf, where they set up angle-resolved microscopy with polarimetry. This paper contains a ton of nice technical details to help you. https://t.co/uqXFtBEIkp

14.07.2021 · Tweet

10/ another favorite of mine is this paper by Schuller et al on the measurement of the dipole orientations in 2D materials using angle-resolved microscopy: https://t.co/PoAXH25Gae

14.07.2021 · Tweet

Tomorrow @RealSci_Nano: Things I learned starting a new lab! (or basically, the stuff you wished they told you before accepting that faculty job 😱😄) https://t.co/rAVAAZZwpJ

15.07.2021 · Tweet

1/ Today: things I learned building up a new lab! Things I was told by helpful seniors beforehand 🙏 and things I wish I´d known 😬 parts of a long thread along the day: 1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 2⃣-all things purchasing 💸 3⃣-staying sane ❤️ Part1⃣coming up! https://t.co/v9yrelQGMa

15.07.2021 · Tweet

2/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 When you finally get that precious offer the temptation is high to just accept and jump right in... but no need to rush🙂 In many cases there is a ton of things to negotiate. Some examples of things I´ve come across👇

15.07.2021 · Tweet

3/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 👉 Most importantly, you can often negotiate your starting date. If you still have a year left on your PD, just wait! It´s precious time to wrap up things and start preparing construction of your lab and team. https://t.co/gPTjhi0qr3

15.07.2021 · Tweet

4/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 👉 now, salaries and startup packages can often not be negotiated, but some places do give a relocation package if you (and your family) are coming in from abroad. Worth checking.

15.07.2021 · Tweet

5/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 👉 absolutely critical is to get as much lab space as you can at the beginning. It´s the only time you can get space without going having to fight a massive department battle! Be generous on your estimates!

15.07.2021 · Tweet

6/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 👉 if they are constructing a new lab for you, dont rush it! Of course you want the key as soon as possible, but an incomplete lab costs you time later on. Ask for all the connections and gas lines you may need!

15.07.2021 · Tweet

7/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 👉 similarly, check what can be included in the construction budget. Getting fumehoods, exhausts, safety measures included saves money on your startup package (I´ve heard some people getting even laser tables included 😉)

15.07.2021 · Tweet

8/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 👉 important: if you already owned some equipment at your old institution, negotiate that your new employer pays for the shipping and possible amortised cost.

15.07.2021 · Tweet

9/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 👉 If you are planning to use a specific facility at your new institution a lot, you can sometimes negotiate a discount or even waiver of the user costs for your group. This can save you a lot of money in the long run!

15.07.2021 · Tweet

9/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 👉 Negotiate your teaching load! Especially in the first year. You´re going to be overwhelmed just with building up everything and getting settles. Less teaching hours or even a complete exempt year can help a lot. https://t.co/19VsjIYc7k

15.07.2021 · Tweet

10/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 👉 If you are on a tenure track, get as clear as possible what are the conditions for your tenure evaluation! It may seem far away, but surprises halfway can cause huge amounts of stress toward the end.

15.07.2021 · Tweet

11/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 👉 Finally, if you are moving to a new location with a family, try to get support for the job/school search through your new employer. In some cases, the university can even find direct employment for your spouse!

15.07.2021 · Tweet

12/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝 OK, these where the things I could think of. if anyone has more tips (or questions), please share them in the comments! I´ll be back later with the next thread... navigating the madness of purchasing an entire lab from scratch!

15.07.2021 · Tweet

13/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 This 2nd part is all on purchasing, which can be one of the most overwhelming things in the beginning. So now you have this start-up package - how to spend it without going crazy (and how to save some money along the way) https://t.co/R8rrsimO7q

15.07.2021 · Tweet

14/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 vendors are your friends! Explain them your plans and let them think along. They can come up with surprising or innovative solutions! A state-of-the-art solution can give you advantage over the competition.

15.07.2021 · Tweet

15/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 Vendors are your friends, but please negotiate prices for everything, big or small! You´d be surprised how much margin there is... I´ve seen discounts up to 50% on big items. Play hard-to-get! https://t.co/ImkxjAFm9P

15.07.2021 · Tweet

16/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 know what equipment more of less should cost before negotiating. Prices are never listed, so talk to colleagues to get ballpark figures. "What´s your budget?" is the first thing a vendor will ask, and you better give a smallish number😉 https://t.co/uK4go6JpAx

15.07.2021 · Tweet

17/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 as with all bargaining, discounts get bigger when you buy in big quantities, so if you can combine different pieces of equipment into one big order from the same vendor, you may save money.

15.07.2021 · Tweet

18/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 I personally dont like to micromanage, but for big purchases it´s critical! I´ve lost months on some purchases because the paperwork of the public tender got messed up. Admin can be complicated, ask for help to seniors with experience! https://t.co/ar1ERnAxnK

15.07.2021 · Tweet

19/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 for capital equipment, local service beats the lowest price. For example, dont buy a glove-box if the vendor cannot guarantee a local service engineer. Flying in the engineer for repairs can cost a lot in the long run!

15.07.2021 · Tweet

19/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 same thing with the delivery... ask for details before buying! You´ll regret the moment they drop a massive crate on your doorstep and run off... (though it gives you awesome stories to tell when you´re older 😉) https://t.co/oUkQQS8ViW

15.07.2021 · Tweet

20/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 same thing with the installation... I had one vendor deliver me complex optical equipment and tell me I probably knew better than him how to align it... he was not my friend anymore after that 🤨. Make sure things are clear before buying.

15.07.2021 · Tweet

20/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 new lab discounts!!! yes, this is a thing. If you´re planning to spend a lot of small items with one vendor, they sometimes offer a new lab discount (usually 5-10% for a year). This is awesome!

15.07.2021 · Tweet

21/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 academic discounts!!! yes, this is also a thing. Some places offer you academic discounts, cause compared to industry, we are relatively poor. Just ask!

15.07.2021 · Tweet

22/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 check out the local workshop and make friends there! here @UAM_Madrid we have a great glass blower that only charges the raw materials... your Schlenck line is suddenly a 10th of the cost! Same for electronics and vacuum pieces. https://t.co/kuv8ou0lR2

15.07.2021 · Tweet

22/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸 👉 finally, talk to your admins to set up a good work flow of invoices and payments... it´s the only way to stay sane through the purchasing storm at the beginning... more on staying sane in the 3rd and final part of this loooong thread 🙂

15.07.2021 · Tweet

this story comes with more ancient pictures that I´m sure @TisdaleWA can also appreciate 😂 👇🧵 https://t.co/DPDqKbIqzK

15.07.2021 · Tweet

so we had a massive four-glove glovebox, dropped on the other end of the infinite corridor @MIT... and while we managed to drive it on its casters all the way to building 66 (2 hour scenic tour)... https://t.co/i6mlG7mrtC

it didnt make the final turn because the cooling unit stuck out too far... lessons learned: clarify the delivery conditions 🪚😌 https://t.co/IUOf1DqQaz

23/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️ Perhaps the most important part of this thread: how to manage stress and not underestimate the risk of a burn-out when starting your faculty job... https://t.co/8xKoMHnhxp

15.07.2021 · Tweet

24/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️ 👉put priorities, perhaps first get settled yourself. Many of us move to a new place/country for the faculty job... first arrange your housing, school, immigration, make sure you and your family are comfortable... juggling all at once can be too much.

15.07.2021 · Tweet

25/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️ 👉think on how fast you want to grow your team... getting many people started right away costs a ton of time. It may be good to start small in the first year.

15.07.2021 · Tweet

26/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️ 👉once you start having a team, dont be afraid to delegate some of the tasks. Dont overwhelm your students of course, but establishing group responsibilities is a great way to involve everyone in the lab.

15.07.2021 · Tweet

27/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️ 👉a very pratical tool to protect your time a bit: Slack workspaces. You can automatically turn off notifications out of office hours and it clearly separates work messaging from your personal life. https://t.co/qA2ew1xnCD

15.07.2021 · Tweet

28/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️ 👉similarly, dont be afraid to put out-of-office replies when you take some days off. You´d be surprised how many things already got resolved while you were away 😉 https://t.co/nepJHO86p1

15.07.2021 · Tweet

29/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️ 👉think of the projects you want to tackle... maybe mix big ambitious ones with some lower hanging fruit. Biggest stress comes often from a lack of output in the beginning. A small methods paper after two years can help a lot 🙂

15.07.2021 · Tweet

30/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️ 👉finally, and most importantly, surround yourself with people that can support you... faculty colleagues that can mentor you and people outside of academia that you can blow off some steam with. Dont try to do it all by yourself!

15.07.2021 · Tweet

31/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️ ok, so much for all the unsolicited advice from my side. Starting your own group is a lot of fun, but there can be a lot of stress coming along with the new responsibilities. tldr: Pace yourself 🙂

1/ a change of scenery today, with a thread on single-molecule electronics! My favorite topic during my younger years as a grad student... 👉 take an individual molecule and hook it up to an electronic circuit using two electrodes with about a nm separation👌 https://t.co/LXRiXO7pLy

16.07.2021 · Tweet

2/ it´s kind of your ultimate pleny-of-room-at-the-bottom experiment... it´s also pretty much a nightmare of failed device after failed device... 😉 https://t.co/Ex2A3gH840

16.07.2021 · Tweet

3/ now, of course you could just use an STM to measure the current through a molecule on a substrate, but for some people that´s not complicated enough: what if you want to make a transistor out of it? - meaning you need a gate electrode as well...

16.07.2021 · Tweet

4/ in 2000, in a paper that is one of the true classics of nanoscience, this impressive list of nanoscience pioneers reported on a the measurement of a single C60 molecule in a three-terminal device. https://t.co/gcscd39hGB

16.07.2021 · Tweet

5/ the key in this paper was the use of so-called electromigration to break a gold wire into nm-separated electrodes. Like this, you have a planar device that can be gated using a back electrode.

16.07.2021 · Tweet

6/ electromigration can be a pretty dramatic though: at very high current density in a metallic wire, the electrons start hitting the atoms so hard that atoms get displaced. It´s well known in integrated circuits as a source of breakdown.

16.07.2021 · Tweet

7/ to make nm-separated electrodes more reproducible, feedback control of electromigration was introduced by Strachan et al. This gave gaps that were way cleaner. https://t.co/f5XK0XsDvB a number of such advances allowed us to do the final breaking way more gradual. https://t.co/0T0fHMY4F1

16.07.2021 · Tweet

8/ biggest issue was though that gold is not very stable at room temperature - it behaves almost like a liquid at the nanoscale! So unless you did all your measurements at cryogenic measurements, your gap would continue to grow and your molecule would not be able to bridge!

16.07.2021 · Tweet

9/ in comes my PhD project @tudelft: can we make a single molecule transistor that is stable a room temperature? So this meant stepping away from Au electrodes... it was not until my final year in 2011 that a completely failed experiment brought the solution.

16.07.2021 · Tweet

10/ I was helping a colleague cleaning graphene transistors using the feedback control I mentioned earlier. The surface of graphene can be cleaned at high current densities due to Joule heating. The feedback was to prevent it from blowing up, but this failed at some point.

16.07.2021 · Tweet

11/ Just for fun we checked the result under the AFM and to our surprise we saw that a beautiful nanogap had formed, exactly like an electromigrated gold nanogap! But of course, the covalent bond structure of graphene is fully stable at room temperature. https://t.co/QdNIWDGkge

16.07.2021 · Tweet

12/ we optimized the feedback, and realized that this was more like "electroburning", making graphene react with oxygen at high temperatures. Still at the height of the graphene hype, the joke quickly became that even burned graphene serves a purpose.

16.07.2021 · Tweet

13/ so, long story short, we placed some molecules on our graphene nanogaps and managed to measure some gate modulation at room temperature! All well that ends well, but the four years of blowing up devices that led up to this were not easy 🙂 https://t.co/8bm6Vmp3uj https://t.co/NgCF3lilPH

17.07.2021 · Tweet

Scanning Probe Lithography (SPL) is a family of lithographic techniques, where the chemical or/and physical interactions between an atomic force microscope tip and a sample in intimate contact are exploited to create the nanostructures https://t.co/tMXRtUvxH0

Like Electron Beam Lithography and Focused Ion Beam, SPL is a maskless, direct lithography technique with high resolution capability (sub-10 nm), which can be used in a wide range of applications...Some examples if you follow the thread! https://t.co/vX8xJBrCDC

Once upon a time, a Spanish Korean-born Physics student at Universidad Complutense de Madrid earned a FPI fellowship in 2010 to do a PhD under the supervision of Prof. Ricardo Garcia at Instituto de Ciencia de Materiales de Madrid (CSIC) https://t.co/wdchPacmkg

20.07.2021 · Tweet

For her was a huge surprise to discover that an atomic force microscope not only could be used to make images and characterize properties of a material, but also as a lithographic tool Image: slide of PhD defense presentation in 2015 (the surprise lasted until then, still lasts) https://t.co/ADEISOQ3W6

20.07.2021 · Tweet

During my PhD, I developed my work using the oxidation SPL modality to fabricate nanostructures and electronic devices. In oxidation SPL, the AFM tip approaches to the surface. A voltage is applied between them, within a water meniscus.

20.07.2021 · Tweet

The water meniscus acts like an electrochemical cell at the nanoscale. The high electric field formed inside the cell induces the hydrolysis of water. The oxygen species are directed to the sample oxidizing it.

20.07.2021 · Tweet

The main parameters to control the width and height of the oxides are the relative humidity, the oxidation voltage and the oxidation time. Source: https://t.co/97MqafyfNp https://t.co/6OV0onUN1A

20.07.2021 · Tweet

2013. "Single Nanometer Manufacturing for beyond CMOS devices" European project started. I worked in this project and I could learn a lot of lithographic techniques and be in contact with state-of-the art centres such as IMEC, IBM Zurich and beyond https://t.co/RvfvEEB0mF https://t.co/uNmMcAEwXw

20.07.2021 · Tweet

I used o-SPL to fabricate silicon oxide masks on an ultrathin silicon on insulator substrates to achieve silicon nanowires by dry etching transfer (Reactive Ion Etching).

20.07.2021 · Tweet

The control of the mask size by o-SPL parameters and the control of the RIE conditions were key to achieve the SiNWs with the highest resolution possible and fully transferred onto the 12 nm thick silicon top layer Source: https://t.co/6OaDR4agsp https://t.co/Ko7wO1VXV2

20.07.2021 · Tweet

Different lithographic techniques: photolithography, electron beam lithography, focused ion beam, SPL...can be used to fabricate the same nanostructures o devices. Therefore, they must be compared and position each other in terms of resolution, cost-effectiveness and throughput

20.07.2021 · Tweet

I fabricated SiNW-based field-effect transistors by SPL and EBL using the same starting substrate (silicon on insulator) and the most similar geometry possible in order to check if the performance of the SiNW FETs fabricated by o-SPL were comparable to the ones fabricated by EBL

20.07.2021 · Tweet

And indeed! After rapid thermal annealing to improve the metal/SiNW contact, the devices fabricated by the two methods behave similarly! Source: https://t.co/Fg6w7bSomx https://t.co/9x5Jj7rTKY

20.07.2021 · Tweet

I started to discover also the 2D materials! We performed o-SPL on WSe2 thin layers. We controlled the size of the structures by controlling the relative humidity, the oxidation voltage and the oxidation time https://t.co/07g5WAmXlt

20.07.2021 · Tweet

We also discovered that the oxides generated by o-SPL were soluble in water, so after wet etching in deionized H2O the oxides left a groove, since the oxides by o-SPL grow above and below the surface.

20.07.2021 · Tweet

We could controlled the thickness of the oxides below the substrate surface as a function of the thikness of the oxides grown above the surface. We exploited this to define isolated high-resolution constrictions in WSe2 thin layers Source: https://t.co/37sdZeoeCe https://t.co/TIISgugyc8

21.07.2021 · Tweet

After I finished my PhD, I wanted to continue learning and working on SPL. I had the opportunity to do a postdoctoral stay in the group of Dr. Armin Knoll, the group where the thermal SPL was developed, at IBM Zurich where...

21.07.2021 · Tweet

...the Scanning Tunneling Microscope (Nobel Prize in Physics 1986) and the Atomic Force Microscope (Kavli Prize in Nanoscience 2016) were invented!!! https://t.co/Fra3K8Q6Fq

21.07.2021 · Tweet

In thermal SPL, a devoted cantilever with three silicon legs that have different doping levels to heat the tip was developed. The technique has a close-loop system that allows the in-situ inspection of the written line and

21.07.2021 · Tweet

the correction of the writing parameters for the next line. By this way, the user can monitor the writing process while happening and interrupt it if the patterning will not be successful. Sources: https://t.co/3KjQdkcwd4 https://t.co/D8icGlgb5s https://t.co/cyhB6NGGVA

21.07.2021 · Tweet

t-SPL can be performed at ambient conditions, no cleanroom requirements are needed. The main parameters that control the size of the nanostructures are the tip temperature and the tip-sample contact force. Also, t-SPL can be used to do 3D lithography with nanometric precision.

21.07.2021 · Tweet

The hot tip can be used to indent resist layers or modify a material directly with the contact. The tip, when is "cold" can be used to image the topography of the written patterns like an AFM. If you want to read more: https://t.co/v0rz7MOfMO

21.07.2021 · Tweet

Moreover, in t-SPL there is no need to fabricate localization markers because the topography of the buried nanostructures can be taken with the tool and then, design the patterns on the topo image and then, write the patterns: Source: https://t.co/D3lQCePYWE https://t.co/fVOrT5l8CC

21.07.2021 · Tweet

During my stay at IBM Zurich, I studied the writing conditions, the thickness of the imaging resist layer (PPA) and the RIE conditions, achieving the record of resolution in t-SPL up to now: 7 nm wide SiNWs array at 14 nm half-pitch!!! Source: https://t.co/NKifC0TwvY https://t.co/fBqULYZay2

21.07.2021 · Tweet

I also participated in the fabrication of the first devices using a mix-and-match or hybrid lithography prototype that the lab at IBM Zurich had developed. Sequential lithographic techniques such as Electron Beam Lithography or Scanning Probe Lithography have a main drawback:

21.07.2021 · Tweet

a low-throughput. One of the strategies to overcome this issue is called: mix-and-match lithography. It consists in the combination of two or more lithographies in a cost-effective way, where the smallest nanostructures are defined by the high-resolution lithography and

21.07.2021 · Tweet

the microstructures in large areas are defined by the high-throughput lithography.

21.07.2021 · Tweet

In my group, a laser writing setup had been developed coupling it with the t-SPL writing setup. By this way, the high-resolution parts were fabricated by t-SPL and the large areas by optical lithography, within a single step, using a single tool. https://t.co/3oapg6sRUn

21.07.2021 · Tweet

We demonstrated the fabrication of a set of two silicon single electron transistors in an area of 30x30 microns square in less than 5 minutes. Source: https://t.co/u92t1c4cjA https://t.co/Afmy9or9ZG

21.07.2021 · Tweet

Finally, I participated in a nice collaboration with the group of Prof. @MuranoPerez (@imb_cnm). We applied t-SPL in order to create guiding patterns to order blockcopolymer(BCP) domains at high-resolution. Sources: https://t.co/CLAD5FgNvj https://t.co/LfAbmwBAA5 https://t.co/ZX7GohBpaw

21.07.2021 · Tweet

Finally...You must know! t-SPL has reached a high technological maturity (it keeps under continuous development), so much that the awesome tool is at the commercial level by @HeidelbergInstr @SwissLitho https://t.co/SyElLYuPSl https://t.co/MdK6TXPQdO

22.07.2021 · Tweet

In the story of my academic life, today: "CHAPTER III. POSTDOCs AT ICMM (CSIC): OXIDATION SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY AND STRAINTRONICS If you want to read the chapter, follow the #thread! https://t.co/37eaiSz70o

22.07.2021 · Tweet

After IBM Zurich I came back to Spain and I did first a postdoc stay in the group of my PhD supervisor, Ricardo Garcia, at ICMM (CSIC), to continue working in the systematization of o-SPL on 2D materials, concretely transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs)

22.07.2021 · Tweet

We discovered that o-SPL on pristine MoS2, MoSe2 and WSe2 thin layers did not produce nanopatterns with controllable sizes and geometry (height, depth, width, array of periodic nanowires...) because of the influence of the 2D materials crystal lattice symmetry...

22.07.2021 · Tweet

Therefore, we had to grow a thin oxide layer on top of the MoS2, MoSe2 and WSe2 surface by a short oxygen plasma. This thin, uniform oxide layer screens the crystal lattice and allows to control the size of the structures by the oxidation parameters, as expected. https://t.co/7j3VG8Ybex

22.07.2021 · Tweet

Since we could now control the patterning of these 2D materials by o-SPL, for example, in the case of MoS2 thin layers, we were able to achieve a sub-10 nm constriction and we developed a process to fabricate nanoribbons based FETs (applicable for all the studied materials). https://t.co/8fiGz796aB

22.07.2021 · Tweet

Sources: https://t.co/6RKLYhnw1U https://t.co/ncn98fiWkM

22.07.2021 · Tweet

Then, I had the opportunity to do a postdoc in the group of Dr. Andres Castellanos-Gomez, also in the same institute (ICMM, CSIC)

22.07.2021 · Tweet

I participated in a review with @Andres_2DMat and @RiccardoFrisen2 about how to fabricate van der Waals superlattices using 2D materials. There are so many ways to modulate the properties of 2D materials😮 Look at this table! Source: https://t.co/7d39tBi9kF https://t.co/69XMvUuI6t

22.07.2021 · Tweet

The review also earned a front cover, made by the fantastic scientist-artist @Scixel https://t.co/AH66ki0QC3

22.07.2021 · Tweet

I also participated in a work inside the field of straintronics. We modulated the bandgap of MoS2 few layers by biaxial strain. This biaxial strain was induced transferring the MoS2 flakes by dry deterministic transfer (https://t.co/jhvHJT5fqN)

22.07.2021 · Tweet

into the middle of a metallic microheater fabricated by photolithography on polypropylene, a polymeric substrate. Under different applied voltages, the current through the microheaters heated the polymer causing the biaxial strain on the 2D material.

22.07.2021 · Tweet

The different applicable temperatures induced different levels of strain, which were monitorized as shifts of the excitonic peaks by differential reflectance spectroscopy (https://t.co/4mOLVO6ank). Source: https://t.co/j7J8jYcJm8 https://t.co/lN2KaobxVd

Finally today I am going to explain the current chapter in my academic life. https://t.co/b6oWqen4Y0

Hi again, its my Day 2 on the @RealSci_Nano account today as @ServetOzdemiro. Today I will give a brief history of the field of 2D materials from a physicists perspective, how it all began in 2004 and where it is now! 🙂

27.07.2021 · Tweet

The story begins with the paper 'Electric field effect in atomically thin carbon films' published in the journal @ScienceMagazine. The incredible Sir Kostya Novoselov was able to find extremely thin pieces of graphite crystals down to 1 atom thickness. https://t.co/F7CrZla1Hr

27.07.2021 · Tweet

Remarkably, the 1 atom thick graphite pieces, which was dubbed as graphene long before 2004 was isolated using a very simplistic method namely by using the adhesive properties of a scotch tape to detach graphene layers attached to each other by van der Waals forces. https://t.co/TFZzxppuzT

27.07.2021 · Tweet

Only a year after the publication of the first paper in 2004, two papers have appeared back to back in @Nature in 2005. The papers reported relativistic nature of the electrons in graphene, with Berry phase manifesting itself in the observed quantum Hall effect.

27.07.2021 · Tweet

Here are the links to two papers, first one by Novoselov and Geim from Manchester group: https://t.co/810B1INxjX And the second one by the group of Philip Kim which was at the time at Columbia https://t.co/FQsMfRym27

27.07.2021 · Tweet

Geim and Novoselov also in 2005 showed that scotch tape method was applicable to other crystals, reporting isolation of atomically thin layers of Boron Nitride, and Transition Metal Dichalcogenides in a paper titled 'Two dimensional atomic crystals' https://t.co/xX3TRCzkTh

27.07.2021 · Tweet

In the coming years, en explosion of research occurred in the field of nanoscience on graphene, which is touched upon on this early review article https://t.co/5KDVS1BpCL

27.07.2021 · Tweet

In 2010, just as some were believing that things were saturing in the field, Hone and Dean et al. from Columbia have shown superior electronic properties of graphene when it is on top of an atomically smooth hBN substrate. https://t.co/LFZbPeY8hR

27.07.2021 · Tweet

At this point, the field has moved from studying isolated 2D crystals to studies of van der Waals heterostructures of them, showing that by combining crystals with different properties in a specific way, unique physics can be unleashed. https://t.co/yadvmzTajl

27.07.2021 · Tweet

In 2013, three groups have demonstrated a fractal phenomenon in the altered electronic structure of graphene (when it's aligned with hBN substrate crystal) known as Hofstadher Butterfly, for which the observation previously required gigantic magnetic fields which wasn't possible. https://t.co/xbMXclr33G

27.07.2021 · Tweet

Links to the 3 papers are: https://t.co/X7gtjfKSy4 https://t.co/h7wLFAzl1y https://t.co/71jahZYQiL

27.07.2021 · Tweet

Things have also become very stimulating in the field from an #optical perspective when 4 groups in 2015 have demonstrated single photon emission from localized sites in 2D semiconductor WSe2 flakes.

27.07.2021 · Tweet

Below are the links to 4 papers: https://t.co/JMyEY4jeHY https://t.co/eEid0miRfb https://t.co/ANAGmay62Z https://t.co/Jc2rzkbA4Q

27.07.2021 · Tweet

Despite the observation of many exotic phenomena including Ising superconductivity in MoS2 and NbSe2, no intrinsic magnetism was observed in any 2D crystal ubtil 2017, when a layer dependent ferromagnetism was shown on air sensitive CrI3 crystals. https://t.co/pPeRDiAOGM

27.07.2021 · Tweet

The moire superlattice work initially kickstarted on hBN/graphene heterostructures took a completely different spin in 2018 when Herero group from MIT showed superconductivity on the predicted moire flat bands of two 1.1° aligned graphene crystals. https://t.co/r60vhOfFiF

27.07.2021 · Tweet

Twistronics, 2D Magnetism and Excitonics remain to be current hottest topics in the field of 2D Materials 🙂.

Hello, today my Day 3 as the @RealSci_Nano content curator as @ServetOzdemiro. Today I will talk about the fascinating physics I discovered during my PhD on rhombohedral graphite crystals 🙂

28.07.2021 · Tweet

Natural #graphite occurs in two forms, which are namely, the Bernal hexagonal stacking and the #rhombohedral stacking which are both illustrated on the picture below. https://t.co/VqlssA2LH2

28.07.2021 · Tweet

Due to the Bernal graphite being more energetically abundant, experimental investigations into Rhombohedral graphite were limited to a few layers, until Henni et al. showed rhombohedral stacking on exfoliated graphite crystals up to 16 layers in 2016 https://t.co/942Xz4Dqpt

28.07.2021 · Tweet

This was very exciting from an electronics point of view, as rhombohedral graphite thin films are a 3D generalisation of simplest 1D topological insulator system Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain https://t.co/rkyvC2UHH9

28.07.2021 · Tweet

Therefore, being a nodal line semimetal in bulk limit, rhombohedral graphite in thin film limit had flat bands with simplest tight binding calculations suggesting a p^N dispersion, where N is the number of layers, being susceptible to magnetic and superconducting interactions.

28.07.2021 · Tweet

https://t.co/ZmcA7f3he8 https://t.co/ArszJbLGT1 https://t.co/jTV7lZSV5r

28.07.2021 · Tweet

Plenty of electronic interactions being predicted at the low energy limit, the challenge was to study scotch tape exfoliated rhombohedral domains in high quality electronic devices after encapsulating them with hBN crystals https://t.co/Pv1WB67ZtS

28.07.2021 · Tweet

Following finding of rhombohedral domains in hBN encapsulated graphite flakes, electronic devices in form of Hall bars were formed, enabling Landau level spectroscopy in presence of magnetic fields https://t.co/RchEwwaB7C

28.07.2021 · Tweet

Following magnetic field characterisation of the samples, aftwr reaching to temperatures down to 10mK, we have found that the electronic structure of rhombohedral graphite films is an N-layer generilisation of graphene, with flat bands being quadratically dispersing https://t.co/9ZOG8FaZPo

28.07.2021 · Tweet

Being accompanied by a Berry phase of NPi, the flat bands display a spontenous metal-insulator transition for the case of 9-12 layers of graphene thick samples with magnetic field characterisation suggesting a magnetic nature of the gap responsible for the transition https://t.co/eFlUYV2jX0

28.07.2021 · Tweet

Being an alternative to twisted graphene systems, the predicted superconductivity in rhombohedral graphite is yet to be seen. For more details on rhombohedral graphite please look at our paper published last year @Nature https://t.co/8KSlI4GTLt

30.07.2021 · Tweet

Broadly, the goal of my PhD was to find new ways in which nanophotonics could improve the performance of solid-state light-emitting devices. We focused on arrays of resonant metallic nanostructures (nano-antennas), which enhance the light emission from a top layer👇 https://t.co/fUfDiJHF8H

04.08.2021 · Tweet

My first PhD paper was in PRX 👇 We studied metallic nanoparticle arrays supporting collective optical resonances. These emerge from coupling localized surface plasmons to diffraction. We coined the term SURFACE LATTICE RESONANCE, now used by many https://t.co/uUgsDQX4gm

04.08.2021 · Tweet

These resonances were actually first studied inthe 80s, by KT Carron et al: https://t.co/gu2SR9F73f ~20 years later, GC Schatz et al. revived interest in them when they found extremely sharp (for plasmonic standards), <1 meV, resonances. J. Chem. Phys. 121, 12606 (2004); https://t.co/7vj4nyCVKi

04.08.2021 · Tweet

Few years later came this 👇 important/beautiful paper from the group of Prof. Bill Barnes at Exeter. They reported collective resonances in Au (no data supporting collectiveness) BTW: I highly admire Bill Barnes: Brilliant, playful, & humble scientist https://t.co/BEs6bJ7JnX

04.08.2021 · Tweet

So we followed up on that, and published another nice result in my PhD. 👇 We showed (exp+theory) that surface lattice resonances are indeed collective, i.e. their quality factor depends on the number of particles (see legend below) in the array. https://t.co/DAUrQELJHT https://t.co/GWK0ACIkBZ

04.08.2021 · Tweet

You may now wonder: Who cares about these collective resonances in metallic nanoparticle arrays? Why was it so important that these resonances )in contrast to localized surface plasmon resonances) are sharp? What are the implications? https://t.co/kgIklvHuAj

04.08.2021 · Tweet

Around that time we put a thin luminescent layer on top of metallic nanoparticle arrays supporting SURFACE LATTICE RESONANCES. Lo and behold, the light emission from the layer got A LOT brigher! White spot below is blue laser + yellow luminescence. Diffraction -> small spots. https://t.co/aY0CfsjJo2

04.08.2021 · Tweet

When I showed the above effect to my advisor, he got extremely excited. He called the BIG BOSS at Philips, so he could, with the naked eye, see the light emission enhancement from metallic nano-antennas. When the big boss saw this, a LOT (!) of money came in from our research https://t.co/EKKZh9QLAB

With that money, the group massively expanded and deepened on "Plasmonics for Solid State Lighting". The idea was simple: Replace lossy and bulky secondary optics in modern LEDS (see 👇) with metallic nanoatennas! The antennas enhance & redirect light emitted from the layer. https://t.co/6TTLKEGBvj

04.08.2021 · Tweet

We published LOTs of nice papers on how metallic nanoatennas can enhance light emission from thin layers. We probed configurations similar to those in modern white LEDs, where a blue LED pumps a yellow phosphor to create white light (blue+ yellow=white). Brief highlights below.

04.08.2021 · Tweet

Here we showed how to get direction emission from surface lattice resonances (SLRs) in nanoatenna arrays: https://t.co/7vU1bftP66

First paper from my postdoc: We showed how to control the phase that photons pick, when hopping from one cavity to another, via the incident optical power (effective photon-photon interactions). Check out the phase measurements in there 😉 https://t.co/IqSdXN1LrN

04.08.2021 · Tweet

Then came the most extensive & important work from my postdoc: We probed a Dissipative Phase Transition (DPT) of light by measuring the dynamic optical hysteresis of a micro cavity. 👇 https://t.co/AvBuWovAvB https://t.co/70BhmxmONL

04.08.2021 · Tweet

A DPT is to dissipative systems what a 'normal' phase transition is to Hamiltonian systems. Instead of the Hamiltonian gap closing at the transition, the Liouvillian gap closes. Its really fascinating physics! A new way to understand phase transitions of open quantum systems.

04.08.2021 · Tweet

The physics of DPT and dynamic optical hysteresis has strong connections to the beautiful & universal physics of the famous Kibble-Zurek Mechanism, relevant to many areas of condensed matter physics 👇 Check out our PRL mentioned above for details. https://t.co/IduGaUhkeX

04.08.2021 · Tweet

In the experiments mentioned above, noise (fluctuations in light) played a prominent role. This made me want to learn more about noise. Then, I realized that many biological systems USE NOISE TO THEIR ADVANTAGE! 🤯 That powerful realization would re-orient my career, again. https://t.co/MsXoLUTNMo
