Hello friends! Today I share about my group at @_amolf 😀 I hope many of you remember AMOLF. Some weeks ago, the fantastic @la_muscarella (who sits down the hall) shared a lot about AMOLF. Next week I'll share some too.😉 Lets start this 🧵with a pic from my group pre-covid! https://t.co/BzIgMXqMQ4

05.08.2021 · Tweet

The name of my group is 'Interacting Photons'. Hopefully that tickles some of you. It's "common wisdom" that photons do NOT interact. IF free-space photons would interact, we would see them scatter off each other, like 👇 But we dont see that! Image: Christine Daniloff/MIT https://t.co/2175qOciKn

05.08.2021 · Tweet

The trick is that IN NONLINEAR MATERIALS photons effectively interact. To make interactions stronger, we confine the photons to a small volume where the nonlinear material is. We achieve that with a pair of mirrors facing each other, which make a cavity. Our typical system 👇 https://t.co/WTh02CueYT

05.08.2021 · Tweet

Yoy may now wonder: Why go through all that trouble *just* to make photons interact? https://t.co/fIwoF2ZEq0

05.08.2021 · Tweet

Well, there's really a LOT you can do IFF photons interact. To give you a flavor: Some of the things we look at are novel optical sensors, computing systems, signal transmission schemes , funky nonlinear dynamics, memories, energy harvesters, and more. Ill share that later 😉

05.08.2021 · Tweet

But if the above doesnt resonate with you, then this is the killer argument to make photons interact: You can make lightsabers, a la Star Wars! Two of my group members (Falco & Giel) showed how to control one light beam with another in the @amolf open day 2 of years ago 👇 https://t.co/wACM4bjX8k

05.08.2021 · Tweet

There are several nonlinear optical materials where photons can effective interact. In my group we use two materials. 1. A drop of oil (like olive, castor, or macadamia oil) 2. Semiconductors (like perovskite, the beloved one of our solar cells friends) Pros & cons below figs👇 https://t.co/Zi1jwJsQMg

I still recall the first time I told my colleagues (and student): Let's put olive oil in the cavity! Everyone laughed 👇 Honestly, I felt uncofortable.🙄 But then it worked !!!!! https://t.co/sd3GGY9Nms

Hello Friends! In this 🧵I will tell you about my favorite topic: NOISE 😁 Richard Feyman once said: "There's plenty of room at the bottom". So here we are, nano-enthusiasts 😀 Now that the room is shrinking, I hope to convince you that "There's plenty of Energy in Noise" 😉 https://t.co/dxJLEM2npu

06.08.2021 · Tweet

Remember: We have an energy crisis, not a size crisis. So KUDOS to all those who make increasingly smaller technologies. We love them! But the REAL challenge is to make all those nano-technologies ENERGY efficient. And for that, we need to take into account NOISE! https://t.co/fCeFw8Q5FE

06.08.2021 · Tweet

Let me first tell you how I got into this topic. As a postdoc, I was studying a new type of dissipative phase transition of open quantum systems. 👇 Noise played a prominent role in those experiments, so I started to dig more into 'stochastic systems' https://t.co/AvBuWovAvB

06.08.2021 · Tweet

During my literature search, and also hearing 1 colleague (who is now retired) in the field of polaritons, I came across the term "STOCHASTIC RESONANCE". This is a phenomenon wherein a certain amount of noise (in a nonlinear system) AMPLIFIES a periodic signal. I was 👇 https://t.co/06dVOdt5Qu

06.08.2021 · Tweet

STOCHASTIC RESONANCE was introduced as a plausible explanation for the recurrence of ice ages in our planet. https://t.co/45H3RADhEm Did you know our planet goes into an ice age every 10^5 years or so? It was really difficult to explain this time scale. But SR *could* do it. https://t.co/KfSKFYXAgQ

06.08.2021 · Tweet

There are actually much 'faster' variations in our planet's temperature too. See e.g. the figure👇, taken from https://t.co/u1TZToDCYX Every time I see this plot, I realize: a)We're so lucky to live in a warm (unstable) RARE EVENT b)Our planet's T is so fragile to perturbations! https://t.co/hzsjMQ8EDE

06.08.2021 · Tweet

We literally owe life in this planet, as we know it, to noise. So how does that work? I'll try to explain the mechanism of Stochastic Resonance in the next few tweets👇 https://t.co/08daYYuSCv

06.08.2021 · Tweet

First: Huge Thanks to @KJH_Peters for the GIFs! Imagine you have a Brownian particle in a double well potential (DWP), like this 👇 The particle's position fluctuates, due to (thermal) noise. Meanwhile, the DWP is modulated at period T. For weak noise, the part stays in 1 well. https://t.co/xJWV1eIqQl

06.08.2021 · Tweet

If the noise strength increases a little, the particle can now make *random* jumps between the potential wells, like this👇 https://t.co/SkRW0ZSjEl

06.08.2021 · Tweet

If the noise is VERY strong, the particle now makes LOTS of random jumps between the potential wells. Notice there are many (>>2) jumps per modulation period. https://t.co/rlXN8u58C9

06.08.2021 · Tweet

But if the noise strength is right --- not too weak, not too strong ---, the random jumps of the Brownian particle can synchronize with the modulation. 👇 This occurs when the mod. period T is ~twice the avg escape time of the particle from a well. THIS IS STOCHASTIC RESONANCE. https://t.co/AgFvJCapNN

06.08.2021 · Tweet

This simple model - Brownian particle in a double well potential - allows us to understand SO much. You'd be surprise to discover how many different systems, dead & alive, can be understood in this way. And so many display STOCHASTIC RESONANCE! Some examples below👇

06.08.2021 · Tweet

Stochastic Resonance, i.e. noise-assisted amplification of a periodic signal in a nonlinear system, has been observed in: electronics: https://t.co/Dvs1qWvNR7 lasers: https://t.co/PnAjDUhZ3j superconductors: https://t.co/iZ9C5K3y7w Carbon nanotubes: https://t.co/bOq77HmtNH

06.08.2021 · Tweet

Stochastic resonance has also been observed in a: polariton gas: https://t.co/kRVDwKr0WM cantilever: https://t.co/x8rb0oL0tt optomechans: https://t.co/QiIWv9mSVI levitated nanoparticle: https://t.co/VymsMxs0CO

06.08.2021 · Tweet

Further, Stochastic Resonance has been observed in a: nano electromechanical membrane: https://t.co/V8d7VK1PQU in #quantum systems: https://t.co/OiewwH8Rrq and in chemical reactions: https://t.co/tAiLnkTYZr

06.08.2021 · Tweet

But all those systems are 'constructed' by people. To me, the most amazing examples of Stochastic Resonance are found in living organisms. There are really MANY noise-loving organisms (like me 😊). I'll share a few examples 👇

06.08.2021 · Tweet

This guy👇 uses noise to enhance information transfer to his mechanireceptors 😮 https://t.co/fgnuKcz6Lr https://t.co/wgmFYKmUIH

06.08.2021 · Tweet

This paddlefish👇 (fig from wikipedia) lives in muddy watters & eats plankton. He can't see very well (tiny eyes). He uses electrical detectors in his big 'nose' (paddle) to detect plankton, and that detection range is enhanced by noise !😮 https://t.co/PVATlIgbns https://t.co/IIfzCLCzT6

06.08.2021 · Tweet

There's also been a lot of work on stochastic resonance in the human brain. See for example: https://t.co/DllfqbkUVd Apparently, noise enhances our brain/perception 😮 https://t.co/5acdynwNlG

06.08.2021 · Tweet

Even your tactile perception can be enhanced by noise: https://t.co/JsXWd3Vhp7 https://t.co/3w3YmyfhlJ

06.08.2021 · Tweet

Also your visual perception can be enhanced by some noise 🤯 https://t.co/tEhI6zccOK https://t.co/U55tYPnTBH

06.08.2021 · Tweet

And if you want to get rich in the market (or try to avoid loosing your money when it crashes), maybe its good to read a bit about stochastic resonance? https://t.co/4vDsUz3xA2 https://t.co/kl8lxIht4i

06.08.2021 · Tweet

There are also many applications of stochastic resonance, like this one to imaging https://t.co/lOekcOvsVq

06.08.2021 · Tweet

Seeing all this made me curious. How can stochastic resonance manifest in so many systems, when the phenomenon itself is so fragile? Remember we have to match the escape time to the modulation period, and the escape time depends EXPONENTIALLY on barrier heigth / noise strength

06.08.2021 · Tweet

So we took a step back, and went to the beginning. Really, the beginning👇 Remember Newton's laws? Well, fundamentally, they're wrong. He argued that there are instantaneous forces. But NOTHING responds instantaneously! https://t.co/8ABnuWIHrH

06.08.2021 · Tweet

Examples: When you pull a rope, someone at the other side doesnt feel your force instantaneously. The 'pull' has to travel via rope, and that takes time. Or if you dial up the heating (or cooling), that also takes time. https://t.co/wbMocTSs03

06.08.2021 · Tweet

So we took at look at what happens to stochastic resonance when you let the NONLINEAR part of the force be non-instantaneous. We start from a so-called overdamped Langevin equation (x=position, F=force, \Xi =noise), and then we introduce a memory kernel for the nonlinearity. https://t.co/dDDJwm9kQk

06.08.2021 · Tweet

The oil-filled optical cavity I mentioned yesterday is nicely explained by such a model. However, instead of position, we describe the light field in the cavity. The non-instataneous nonlinearity arises because the oil takes some time to warm up after the laser hits it 😉 https://t.co/UfXJsB0NCB

06.08.2021 · Tweet

We then imprint a signal on the incident (continuous wave) laser by modulating the cavity length. Further, we add noise to the laser's amplitude and phase using modulators. So our experiment looked liked this 👇 https://t.co/ZH2JnMoJdR

06.08.2021 · Tweet

We then measured the transmitted signal to noise ratio (SNR) as a function of the *input* noise. And found the peak characteristic of stochastic resonance. So our optical signal is amplified by a finite amoutn of noise. https://t.co/hCswN47Zcn

06.08.2021 · Tweet

The cool part of the experiment (details here: https://t.co/uzVKP3VQHJ ) is that the frequency range over which we could observe stochastic resonance is enhanced, BY ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE, thanks to the non-instantaneous nonlinear response 😁

06.08.2021 · Tweet

In that paper we also consider, theoretically, applications to energy harvesting. We find that the non-instantaneous nonlinearity can enhance the efficiency of those devices by a factor of 10 or more! 😮

06.08.2021 · Tweet

Based on the success of our press release for the cavity with olive oil, we didnt want to let macadamia oil stay behind. So we wrote another one. And it got a lot of coverage by the media. We were very happy 😁 Below I'll share a few links to those 'reader's digest' articles 😉

Hello friends! Today I share about the fascinating physics of fluids of light! 🧵 Did you know that light in a cavity behaves like a fluid? Top image is a boat cruising through a lake. Bottom image is our laser cruising through the cavity mirrors and scattering off a defect.😮 https://t.co/1iuEmNmVEH

10.08.2021 · Tweet

Normally, when light encounters an obstacle it scatters. Then, incident & scatttered light interfere, resulting in fringes. See image above 👆 However, in 1999 Chiao et al. predicted that light may transition to a SUPERFLUID and flow without scattering! https://t.co/IfCKUNY4V5

10.08.2021 · Tweet

However, to realize superfluid light, photons need to interact. And they normally dont. So, Iacopo Carusotto & @CristianoCiuti proposed leveraging the strong interactions of polaritons (1/2 light, 1/2 exciton quasiparticles) to realize superfluidity! https://t.co/5dAswzs3Xd

10.08.2021 · Tweet

This is a figure copied from their article, cited 👆 On the left you see a polariton fluid scattering off a defect in the center. On the right you see a polariton superfluid, which doesnt scatter. To get there, they increased the laser power (fluid density). Amazing effect!😉 https://t.co/2VMig92Si8

10.08.2021 · Tweet

Then, in 2009 came these beautiful experiments by Alberto Amo (one of my postdoc advisors) et al verifying the predictions of Ciuti & Carusotto. https://t.co/wveXhNNlU8 Left: 'Normal' polariton fluid, scattering off a defect. Right: Polariton SUPERfluid, flowing past the defect https://t.co/YvT6Q6BGLa

10.08.2021 · Tweet

The results above gave birth to a new research field called "Quantum fluids of light". Results up to 2013 were reviewed in this nice & didactic Review of Modern Physics by Carusotto & Ciuti. Check it out if you're curious about the physics 😉 https://t.co/ro1Fi8nWan

10.08.2021 · Tweet

The experiments of Amo et al used a sample at ~5K. It needed to be so cold for polaritons to exist and strongly interact. So several researchers began working on new platforms where superfluids of light can exist at room temperature. Major result 👇 https://t.co/vtWuCbMFJU

10.08.2021 · Tweet

The above result (group of Daniele Sanvitto) is VERY nice. They showed, for the first time, a polariton superfluid at room temperature. However, since interactions in organics are so weak, they pumped the sample with a powerful amplified laser. And the fluid died within 0.1 ps😖

10.08.2021 · Tweet

Inspired by all results above (+others), my group started an experiment aimed at observing superfluidity of light (photons, not polaritons) at room temperature AND in steady state. Imagine: A photon superfluid that lives forever😮 Our sample👇: A cavity filled with olive oil 😋 https://t.co/2q0el5692c

10.08.2021 · Tweet

Together with Giel Keijsers (formerly MSc, now PhD student ) we got some nice results: https://t.co/ppmnaWyVeB Check out our preprint if you're curious about how a drop of olive oil between 2 mirror can suppress scattering of a light 😉

10.08.2021 · Tweet

Here an movie of our data. Left: Real space, laser flows left-to-right to defect. Right: Momentum space. As time progresses, the photon fluid velocity increases. We start in the superfluid state, which later breaks down at high velocities -- fringes & backscattering appear. https://t.co/V2qpRRRXC8

10.08.2021 · Tweet

Our manuscript shows many nice measurements. But, I admit, results are not as strong & conclusive as we would like. The referees, while most supporting publication, picked on that. So we've been doing new experiments for past months. We have amazing result in store for them😁

10.08.2021 · Tweet

Unfortunately I cannot share them yet --- I dont want to compromise a future publication. But, if you like to know more later, follow me on my account, @srk_rodriguez , and I'll post the new results and movies when they ready😉

Hello friends! Before leaving this account, I'd like to share valuable insights & experiences I gained as PhD #student, #postdoc, and #newPI. These are on various aspects of science. My insights are obviously not universal. Please take them with a 'big grain of salt'. Open 🧵

13.08.2021 · Tweet

#1. NEVER EVER write an email when overwhelmed by emotion. This is especially relevant when the emotion is anger, regardless of whether it is justified or not. When receiving bad / unpleasant news, it's best to let it rest AT LEAST 1-2 days before responding.

13.08.2021 · Tweet

#2. In myself and in my scientific team members, I welcome every feeling/state (expressed with respect) EXCEPT BOREDOM. A person that is bored has lost curiousity, and awareness of how little she/he knows of this AMAZING universe. There is always something great to learn!

13.08.2021 · Tweet

#3 A. When searching for PhD/PD position, many these days recommend setting "emotional support" as no. 1 in search criteria. I never did that. For em. supp. I have my wife, my parents, close friends, and coach. Of course, em. support from PI is very important, but not enough.

13.08.2021 · Tweet

In a #PI, I searched for someone with: 1. Inspiration & Creativity 2. Scientific & Personal Qualities which I lack, and ability to teach them 3. Resources 4. Ability to guide with enthusiasm 5. Local environment where I can thrive 6. Strong Internatl Network 7 Easy to talk with

13.08.2021 · Tweet

#4. You can learn what you need along the way. Ex: As young student, I thought I should the be able to solve all (or nearly all) problems in Jackson (hard book!) before doing any research in E&M / Optics. I was wrong. Solid foundation is good, but adaptability also. .

13.08.2021 · Tweet

#5. A highly DANGEROUS time (physically) for an academic is during PhD thesis writing. I foolishly thought "I will not stand until I finish writing this section". So I spent too many hours sitting. I injured my back badly (sciattica) and suffered for years after. Health FIRST!

13.08.2021 · Tweet

#6. Between my PhD and PD, I published my 1st single-author paper. I highly recommend that. It's a good way to demonstrate independence, as well as ability to conceive, implement, and finalize a scientific project. It can also prove good writing skills --- essential in academia.

13.08.2021 · Tweet

#7. Every paper that I wrote eventually got published. Sometimes many things had to change, and once the revision process took 3 years. But eventually it was published. So I've learned not to sweat paper rejections. I know the outcome 😉 (Grants are different 😖).

13.08.2021 · Tweet

#8. As #newPI in experimental group, I've learned to ask my students if they would like me to join them in their experiment. Some students feel pressured by my presence. Others feel supported. So I just ask , and I'm happy to join when my presence helps. And not sad otherwise.

13.08.2021 · Tweet

#9. When responding to referees, remember: their (our) only reward is the satisfaction of helping a good paper become better (rejected papers appear elsewhere later). So I listen to referees & follow their advice as much as possible. It's better than to fight them all the time😉

13.08.2021 · Tweet

#10. When a Referee is unreasonable/absurd (rare, but can happen), remember: we do NOT have to convince Referees. The Editor decides. That's why I rather publish in journals where Editorial decisions can be assessed by members of the science community via appeals, if necessary.

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#11. Time is our most valuable resource. Many people ask: Is this an idea worth researching, or a paper worth writing? That's a bad question - can lead to time waste. I rather ask: Is this the *best* idea worth researching, or best paper worth writing, given our possibilities?

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#12. More experiments/data alone rarely lead to deeper understanding. Actually, they often strengthen the confusion. Understanding emerges from our ability to reproduce and predict partial observations using a "simple" model/abstraction of reality.

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#13. For me, the best experiments (worth doing) are those for which I don't know the result in advance, can surprise me, or are beyond theoretical reach. Otherwise, if the theory has been tested to death, and we know it faithfully models our system, why do the experiment?

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#14. I've seen many students choose to work on a topic because of its *potential* relevance to an issue they care about, e.g. health, sustainability. But many soon realize that they do not enjoy their daily activities so much. Daily inspiration is AS IMPORTANT as purpose.

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#15. A great challenge as a PI: When someone systematically doesn't honor IMPORTANT agreements (they may think it's not important), how to express that behavior is unacceptable WITHOUT diminishing their motivation? Nobody likes to be reminded of agreements they didnt fulfill.

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#16. In personal relations with fellow scientists, I appreciate modesty and detest self-adulation (e.g. bombastic claims that their research will save the world). Unfortunately, that doesnt work well in proposals. Non-specialists easily fall for nicely-written bombastic claims.

14.08.2021 · Tweet

@n_maccaferri Thank you Nicolo!

14.08.2021 · Tweet

@nur_ayukaryana Important decision! Did you see my point #3 (2 tweets)? Other factors I considered: 1. Quality of life (for me: salary, living, transport, access to nature) 2. Before accepting PhD offer, I asked my adivsor for support to visit theory group for few months. 3. Technical support!

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#17 In France, I learned that a scientific group's leader is called "animateur". Funny, I thought. But there is so much wisdom in that name. Truly, the greatest aspiration of a group leader is to amplify the motivation of her/his group members.

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#18. The most important & difficult decision of a #newPI is in hiring. Unfortunately, this is likely also the decision we are least prepared to make. IMO, character is the most important quality to look for. Its easier to teach exp skills than to change character.

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#19 As PhD & young PD, I thought that increasing my skill set was the best way to land in a tenure-track position. I was wrong. Hiring committees rarely look at skills. Most look for innovative ideas (of the type that can bring millions), ability to lead, & a friendly colleague.

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#20. In my PD, when starting to search for tt position, I didnt have a research statement ready. I thought I would make one when I apply. Then, a senior colleague I admire said: "If you dont have your proposal always ready, you'll never get a position." He was right.

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#21. As PhD student, I improved my presentation skills thanks to detailed (written) feedback I got right after each talk. This is standard practice at nanophotonics at AMOLF. For years, I've seen the big difference that giving this feedback makes in the quality of student talks.

14.08.2021 · Tweet

#22. The classic mistake of an enthusiastic PhD student (I was one) is to start more research projects than s/he can finish, i.e. lead to publication. IMO, there's no point in starting projects one cant finish. In long run, only the projects one finishes (publishes) matter.

15.08.2021 · Tweet

@nur_ayukaryana Sure. I like doing experiment & theory. My MSc supervisor (offered me PhD) was very strong experimentally, but not so much theoretically. So, when I expressed my concern (wanted to also do theory), he offered me a few-month paid visit to top theory group in Spain, which I did🙂

Todayyy a short thread about our favorite issue in the lab! Exfoliation!!! 😍

17.08.2021 · Tweet

As you probably know, exfoliation is a technique to obtain very thin samples of layered materials. And it's very extended! So, if you are familiar with the technique, do not hesitate and tell us your experience :) (luckily I'll complete the thread with some pics tomorrow)

17.08.2021 · Tweet

First of all, you need a small (but macroscopic) piece of the material that you want to use. And put some of it in a scotch tape. Then, you peel it with the tape, and if you are lucky, there will be some very thin and large layers of whatever you are exfoliating...

17.08.2021 · Tweet

Directly pressing the substrate where you want to build the sample against the tape. Then, look in the optical microscope and search if there is any layer adhered to your substrate.

17.08.2021 · Tweet

There may be many, but if you are interested in a specific thickness and area, finding a good one usually takes many tries and a lot of time...

17.08.2021 · Tweet

I think that the second most common technique is, first, pressing a layer of a viscoelastic material (such as PDMS) and then transferring it to the exact place where you want your flake to be.

17.08.2021 · Tweet

If you put everything in contact, and then tear the viscoelastic very slow and gently, the flake will remain where you put it in the substrate. Some groups use commercial PDMS, others make their own... what do you think is better?

17.08.2021 · Tweet

Also this transferring technique allows making heterostructures of many layers, as you know exactly where the new flake will be in the substrate. You can even create rotated samples!!!

17.08.2021 · Tweet

But I forgot to talk about the most important thing when preparing samples 😱 which material do you want? 😱

17.08.2021 · Tweet

The only thing you need to know before starting to exfoliate, is if your material can be layered. The difficulty will vary depending on the interaction between the layers, so you need a lot of patience. Also optical contrast will change depending on the material and thickness.

17.08.2021 · Tweet

This is something that a lot of people do, specially at the beginning of our journey in 2D materials, and can be a bit boring and/or stressful, so I'd recommend that you exercise your eyes and let them rest while listening some good song! Can you recommend any?

Good morning! Today's and tomorrow's thead(s) will be about AFM and its possibilities. Today: I'll tell you the two basic modes to take topography images, and some other techniques I've used so far. Tomorrow: techniques I haven't used but are super interesting and useful.

18.08.2021 · Tweet

In simple words, an AFM consists of a very thin tip at the end of a cantilever that you can move around a sample with very high precision. Depending on your system, is the tip or the sample what moves! You measure the deflection of the cantilever by reflecting a laser on it.

18.08.2021 · Tweet

By doing this, you can measure the force between the sample and the tip, as the cantilever will bend depending on it. If you put the tip in contact with a surface and sweep it keeping the force constant, you can actually have an image of its shape!

18.08.2021 · Tweet

https://t.co/rf8K8zQdVV

18.08.2021 · Tweet

https://t.co/3ZpZekeM6H

18.08.2021 · Tweet

https://t.co/ddCfNRepyO

18.08.2021 · Tweet

https://t.co/836AYW2aMx

18.08.2021 · Tweet

https://t.co/IqDhDy8AkK

18.08.2021 · Tweet

Something you can do when mapping the topography of the sample is applying a constant voltage. If the tip is conductive, it allows mapping electrical properties of your sample 😏 (current maps)

18.08.2021 · Tweet

If the applied voltage oscillates, then you can even map the piezorresponse of the material 😱 (piezorresponse force microscopy)

18.08.2021 · Tweet

It is also possible to follow the topography in dynamic mode. In this case, the tip is in constant oscillation, and what remains constant is the amplitude and phase of the oscillation when it interacts with the sample at short distances (5-20 nm)

18.08.2021 · Tweet

This other method is less invasive as you are never applying force in the sample, so it is useful for soft materials, for example.

19.08.2021 · Tweet

Going one step further, you can also apply an oscillating voltage to the tip 😱 two oscillations at the same time 😱 that's Kelvin Probe Microscopy (KPM). Following the phase of this second oscillation it is possible to map the electrostatic potential of metallic samples ❤

19.08.2021 · Tweet

Other uses of AFM are possible when combining dynamic and contact modes 😀

19.08.2021 · Tweet

Indentations: with the dynamic mode you can locate the tip in a specific point of the surface. Then, in this point, you can apply a force and/or a voltage leaving the rest of the sample untouched.

19.08.2021 · Tweet

SPANC! Scanning probe assisted nano-circuitry. Several nanowires and particles on a surface can become a circuit with some help of an AFM tip. If they are not very attached to the surface, the tip can move them with a touch, and map the resulting circuit without touching :)

Ready for Day 2? Today I'm going to be introducing you all to thin films and plasma polymerisation! So, to start with, what is a thin film?

23.08.2021 · Tweet

To explain thin films, we first need to define what a surface is. This might seem obvious to some, but when we talk about a surface in science, we mean the outside layer of an object, usually the 'top' as a lot of the objects we work with are 2D, like silicon wafers! https://t.co/rtcybo5j49

23.08.2021 · Tweet

A 'thin film' is a coating that we typically deposit onto a surface, usually nanometers (0.000000001 m) to micrometers (0.000001 m) thick! Typically we refer to these materials that we coat as substrates. https://t.co/uVS37ioIVK

23.08.2021 · Tweet

@ChrisMillsRD @realscientists I'm #FirsGen too. I don't know what it's like in other countries, but my lecturers regularly told us all about summer job/project opportunities. I got my cement QC job through my own initiative, but I'm pretty sure the research project would have been widely advertised.

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Now that we know what a thin film is? What type of thin films are there out there? And how do we deposit them?

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Thin films can be organic (only containing O, C, N, H, S, P) or inorganic (Like Al2O3, ZnO, SiO2 etc.) Whether you need an organic or inorganic film depends on what you want your film to do! And type of film you want dictates what deposition methods you need!

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Thin film deposition can range from quite crude, such as using a doctors blade, where you're simply spreading a paste onto your surface that then dries and forms the thin film! https://t.co/kg6YOM11qc

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Or you can have very precise deposition, like atomic layer deposition (ALD) where you're actually growing ultra thin layers atomically on a surface! https://t.co/Wrdlm5edI4

24.08.2021 · Tweet

I'm going to be focus on the more precise lab scale thin film deposition technqiues, which we typically separate into physical vapour deposition (PVD) or chemical vapour deposition (CVD).

24.08.2021 · Tweet

So what's the difference between PVD and CVD?

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Physical vapour deposition (PVD) typically has the substrate mounted opposite the source material which then physically deposit the source material on the substrate by heating/ablating/sputter of the source material https://t.co/8cZuDfmQRB

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Some example of PVD are sputter coating, thermal evaporation, electron beam evaporation etc. https://t.co/VEoxrnFVHS

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Now that I've covered PVD, it's time for CVD! In Chemical vapour deposition (CVD) the wafer surface is exposed to one or more precursors, which react and/or decompose onto the substrate surface to produce the desired thin film https://t.co/S38RmxASrH

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Examples of CVD techniques aerosol assisted CVD, plasma enhanced CVD, hot/cold wall CVD, metal organic CVD etc. Plasma polymerisation is a type of CVD, that I'll be discussing in more detail later today! https://t.co/0ACpFgdf7Y

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is a special type of CVD, where the film grows atomically. By keeping the deposition in the ALD rather than CVD regime, specific film properties, such retarding moisture/oxygen permeation, can be produced! https://t.co/lxsRiJFDzb

24.08.2021 · Tweet

So what's the advantages and disadvantages of PVD and CVD? PVD: Typically deposits single single/simple materials but harder coatings, wide variety of film types available across a variety of techniques, but also require 'line of sight', so difficult to coat complex geometries

24.08.2021 · Tweet

CVD: Typically produces more uniform coatings and onto more complex geometires, can be used to deposit coatings that do not have suitable PVD sources but often requires higher temperatures for the reactions to occur

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Here's some useful figures that compare PVD, CVD and ALD! https://t.co/dOcRD5hn5v

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Now that we've covered PVD and CVD broadly, now its time to introduce my thin film deposition technique of choice.....PLASMA POLYMERISATION!

24.08.2021 · Tweet

But before we explain plasma polymerisation, lets familiarize everyone with plasma itself! Plasma is the 4th state of matter, and results from the excitation of a gas, which fragments the vapour molecules. This fragmentation is what produces the characteristic plasma glow! https://t.co/wqE72FaGGi

24.08.2021 · Tweet

99.9 % of the universe is plasma, because most of space is comprised of plasma! Some examples of plasma here on Earth you might have seen are neon signs, lightning or the Aurora Borealis/Australis! https://t.co/5vIz9MkWeZ

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Now that we're familiar with plasma, how do we use it to deposit thin films? Plasma polymerisation is actually the same as plasma enhanced CVD (PE-CVD), but is typically used to refer to the deposition of specifically organic thin films.

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Our plasma polymerisation takes place in a vacuum reactor, where we suck out the air to reduce the pressure. A medium vacuum (10-3 to 10-2 mbar) is required for plasma polymerisation. We won't be able to ignite the plasma if the pressure is too high or too low! https://t.co/MMUW1mNX9z

24.08.2021 · Tweet

We place our sample onto the sample stage.... https://t.co/fgiwTDSAex

24.08.2021 · Tweet

And once the pressure is suitable, we can introduce our liquid monomer. This monomer either has the chemistry we want to add to our surface, or makes a film that has the properties that we're after! Introducing the monomer to the vacuum evaporates it into a vapour. https://t.co/VnuTqEDRTi

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Once we have our vacuum chamber filled with the vapour, we can ignite our plasma! The monomer is fragmented, and produces the plasma glow! These fragments deposits on everything inside our chamber, including our sample! https://t.co/97Y5M1nvMZ

24.08.2021 · Tweet

We call the films we deposit 'plasma polymers', although that's not true in a traditional sense, as they don't have the repeating sub-units of conventional polymers such as PET or PVC! https://t.co/GVIrmzoqmd

24.08.2021 · Tweet

@SvenAskes No, but typically unsaturated molecules fragment to form more stable films due to their double bonds. Saturated monomers tend to fragment too much and deposit deposit as stable films, especially if you want to put them in solution!

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Last tweets for today.....so what type of films can we deposit with plasma polymerisation? The films that we most commonly do are: -Allylamine: forms +ve amine terminated films -Acrylic acid: forms -ve carboxyl terminated films -Octadiene: forms carbon rich hydrophobic films

24.08.2021 · Tweet

But, there's a whole lot of other monomers out there -Cineole: deposits films with antibacterial properties -NIPAM: deposits temperature responsive films -Allyl alcohol: deposits hydroxyl terminated films -Glyme (glycol ethers): deposit low fouling/protein adsorbing films

24.08.2021 · Tweet

Signing off here for today! If you're interested in what sort of applications we use plasma polymers for, come back on Friday when I'll be exploring how we encounter thin films in our everyday lives!

25.08.2021 · Tweet

Good morning everyone! Today I'm going to be tweeting about the organisation that I work for (@ANFFHQ - The Australian National Fabrication Facility) and discuss the benefits of open access user facilities!

25.08.2021 · Tweet

The Australian National Fabrication Facility (ANFF) provides open access to micro and nanofabrication facilites for Australian researchers. The ANFF network is made up of over 500 instruments spread across 20 sites.

25.08.2021 · Tweet

ANFF also has over 100 staff that can train users to independently use the ANFF instruments after training or have their work performed by ANFF staff under a fee-for-service agreement.

25.08.2021 · Tweet

Since forming in 2007, ANFF has grown from 360 users and 38,000 user hours to 3000 users and 245,000 user hours in 2019/2020.

25.08.2021 · Tweet

The instruments at ANFF are separated into the broad categories below, with some examples: - Deposition (ALD, CVD) - Etching (RIE/DRIE) - Lithography (EBL) - Packaging (Bonding and wafer dicing) - Testing and validation (XPS, profilometry, ellipsometry)

25.08.2021 · Tweet

The ANFF @ANFFHQ network is composed of eight nodes, with their locations and specialties below! If you're interested in learning more about ANFF, check out their website: https://t.co/RfhlrODshS https://t.co/hBOW6s6aFb

25.08.2021 · Tweet

ANFF is funded by the Australian federal government's National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS) and supported by both State Governments and member institutions.

25.08.2021 · Tweet

NCRIS provides a national network of world class infrastructure that facilitates research excellence and collaboration between 35,000 users from academia, government, and industry to drive greater innovation in the Australian research sector.

25.08.2021 · Tweet

Apart from ANFF, there are a number of awesome Australian NCRIS facilites, such as: -@AuScope (Earth and Geospatial Science) -@micro_au (Microscopy Australia) -@NIFAus (National Imaging Facility) -@ARDC_AU (Australian Research Data Commons)

25.08.2021 · Tweet

-@NCInews (National Computational Infrastructure) -@TERN_Aus (Terrestrial Ecosystem Research Network) -@phenomics (Phenomics Australia) - National Deuteration Facility (NDF) To name but a few!

25.08.2021 · Tweet

Now lets talk about open access user facilities in general. I've listed some of the ones available in Australia, what about in your country? Have you used any of them?

25.08.2021 · Tweet

Open access user facilities, for research typically mean you can use the facilities of another institution, usually for a fee. You can either get them to 'do' the work for you, or they can train you to do the work using their equipment.

25.08.2021 · Tweet

So what are the advantages? I'm going to focus on those relevant for physical sciences, but there will be some overlap with other areas of research!

25.08.2021 · Tweet

1. Expertise - You can utilize the knowledge and skill of staff to help you with an idea/process that you don't possess and may not have the time (i.e. during a PhD or an industry project) to develop 2. Access - You can access a tool quickly without purchasing or setting it up

25.08.2021 · Tweet

3. Cost- Being able to access multi-million dollar equipment and processes that your organisation can't afford 4. Maintenance - Someone else's job to pay for and maintain costly equipment

25.08.2021 · Tweet

5. Niche - Being able to access equipment that you might only need short term access to, so isn't worthwhile your group/university buying. Also may only be required by a small user base, so no point multiple institutions having one if its only used occasionally.

25.08.2021 · Tweet

6. Optimisation - Accessing equipment to see if it works for a particular process before purchasing. Especially useful for industry! So, can you think of any other advantages of open access user facilities for research?

25.08.2021 · Tweet

Day 4 people! Today I'm going to be tweeting about our facilities at the ANFF-VIC Biointerface Engineering hub at @Swinburne! Unfortunately, Melbourne is in lockdown so I won't actually be in the lab, but luckily I've got a good set of photos filed away for things like this!

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Our @ANFFHQ lab at @Swinburne is a pretty standard looking wet chemistry lab but it houses a number of our thin film deposition and surface characterisation tools! https://t.co/AE4x3HrJAT

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Lets start off with my favourite instruments, our plasma polymer reactors. I explained all about plasma polymerisation on Tuesday, but for a recap....

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Plasma polymerisation is a plasma enhanced CVD technique that is used to deposit organic thin films. We have 6 reactors. 1 each for air plasma treatment (makes polymer surfaces more hydrophilic), allylamine (+ve amine), acrylic acid (-ve carboxyl) and octadience (hydrophobic) https://t.co/oxyh6GELRx

26.08.2021 · Tweet

We also have two specality reactors: 1 heated, for the deposition of low volitile monomers such as NIPAM or Glyme and 1 for in-situ film deposition measurements with ellipsometry and IR. https://t.co/ehaiKoC03g

26.08.2021 · Tweet

We usually do our deposition onto pieces of silicon wafer, but if it fits in the reactor, we can coat it, like these carbon fibers below! https://t.co/Ht2RZ9UJsh

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Our reactors look like pretty standard vacuum reactors https://t.co/476qqsgYFn

26.08.2021 · Tweet

But we do get to do some cool things with them... https://t.co/xkg44m8Hwt

26.08.2021 · Tweet

And take some cool pictures of plasma! https://t.co/cfhHLd9wX5

26.08.2021 · Tweet

What else have we got in our lab? My next favourite.....it's full name is a variable angle spectroscopic ellipsometer (VASE), but we just call it an ellipsometer! I've recently written an online learning module about ellipsometry, so I'll be stealing some of that info!

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Ellipsometry is a quick, highly sensitive and non-destructive technique that is used to determine the thickness and optical properties of thin films from a few microns down to sub-nanometre. Here's our ellipsometer! https://t.co/rMZiIEULV8

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Ellipsometry theory is complex, but put simply, a light at variable wavelength (200 - 1600 nm typically) is shone our sample, some is absorbed, some is reflected. The changes in the light that are reflected back to the detector, can be used to determine properties of the film. https://t.co/LhdNBy6l3o

26.08.2021 · Tweet

In ellipsometry, the thickness and other properties of the film aren't measured directly. You need to create a model that generates a data set, and that data set is compared to the experimental data and is then used to calculate the various film properties

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Here's an example of the data collected during ellipsometry. The red and the green lines are the parameters collected by ellipsometery (Psi and Delta) at the different wavelengths. https://t.co/4yHTRFZ8I3

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Here's the process you go through to measure and fit ellipsometry data! https://t.co/UqGrOHADmc

26.08.2021 · Tweet

To start the ellipsometry fitting process, you'll have your data (red and green lines) and model (black dotted line), and you'll need to change the parameters of your model for it to fit the data! Compare these unfit and fit data sets! https://t.co/RcY2HBaI3q

26.08.2021 · Tweet

We typically use ellipsometry to measure film thickness, but it can also be used to investigate film: ▪Thickness ▪Surface roughness ▪Interfacial mixing ▪Composition ▪Crystallinity ▪Anisotropy ▪Uniformity

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Apart from taking simple measurements, we can do a whole lot of cool things with ellipsometry!

26.08.2021 · Tweet

By compiling single measurements across a silicon wafer, we can building mapping scans to tell us how uniform our coating is https://t.co/muXm2pJceg

26.08.2021 · Tweet

We also have a variety of accessories that go on our ellipsometer: 1. Liquid cell - Investigate how film change upon exposure to different liquids i.e. vary pH or salt concentration 2.Temperature stage - Investigate how films change at elevated temperatures https://t.co/jiTycsvZzG

26.08.2021 · Tweet

3. QCM module - Ellipsometry can be performed on a QCM crystal to do simultaneous QCM and ellipsometry measurements 4. Focus probes - Reduces spot size to look at very small features or films that are non-uniform over large size scales. https://t.co/JJAvivuSMO

26.08.2021 · Tweet

5. In-situ - Components of the ellipsometer can be detached from the arms and attached to an appropriately outfitted deposition chamber to collect ellipsometry data during film deposition https://t.co/zfD7O5yogE

26.08.2021 · Tweet

These are plasma polymer reactors, essentially PE-CVD. These are for our allylamine, acrylic acid and octadiene.

Alas, got a few more instruments to talk about! A quick one is our multivessel dip coater! A dip coater is basically a robotic arm that holds a sample, and can then be program to dip into various solutions to build up a coating! https://t.co/Pcq9zRZGWk

Here's a great diagram from one of our previous users Daniela, on how she used our dip coater to deposit graphene oxide-gold nanorods https://t.co/5QsG3dawGO

Okay, last instrument! Now we're up to our Quartz Crystal Microbalance with Dissipation (QCM-D). QCMs have been used for a long time in thin film deposition equipment.

26.08.2021 · Tweet

In QCM-D, we start with a quartz crystal that vibrates at a particular frequency. If there's any addition or subtraction of mass, that changes the frequency, which the instrument can use to determine the change in mass.

26.08.2021 · Tweet

The dissipation part comes in as if there are conformational changes in the mass adsorbed, then that alters how long the crystal vibration takes to stop. This can be summarised in the below diagram. https://t.co/YhsvZrAqts

26.08.2021 · Tweet

This is our QCM-D instrument. Off to the left, we'll have the solution we're exposing our crystal to. This solution travels through the tubing, and into the four grey cells which contain the crystals, also shown. The pump to the right pulls the solution through. https://t.co/DvyYET2eTG

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Here's an example of QCM data. The frequency of the crystal decreases as mass is adsorbed. This work shows how negatively charged lipids are attracted to our positively charged plasma polymerized allylamine surface! If you're interested, https://t.co/wlGyuSCy3k https://t.co/bIUPiajdED

26.08.2021 · Tweet

@ServicesVacuum @ANFFHQ @Swinburne Yes, we have cold traps between our chambers and the pump to try and condense as much of the monomer as we can. But we do get oil contamination, and have to change the pump oil more frequently, depending on how much the instruments are used.

@BreakingTaps Excellent question! A competitive ablation and polymerization (CAP) process occurs during plasma polymerization. So if the power is too high, a film won't be deposited as ablation will be dominant. So we have to keep it in the polymerization regime to deposit a film!

Today, I'm going to be tweet about what surface properties we can modify withthin film coatings and then what applications thin films are used for. I'm going to be talking in general about thin films, so hard/soft, organic/inorganic, so not all films will do all of these things!

26.08.2021 · Tweet

What surface properties can we modify with thin films? This list is not exhaustive. I'll discuss each one in more detail later. -Charge -Wettability -Reflectivity -Biocompatibility/Cell growth -Conductivity -Bacterial growth -Biofouling -Hardness -Colour Any others?

26.08.2021 · Tweet

Lets start with colour, because its a fun one. No real scientific use here, but there's a lot of thin films that are used just for decorative purposes. You may have seen these cool rainbow coloured objects! https://t.co/scLcsj8KCN

26.08.2021 · Tweet

In the lab, these rainbow coatings mean we have a non-uniform film, because colour gives us information about film thickness. But what is the relationship between colour and film thickness? https://t.co/c9bvQ47eSU

26.08.2021 · Tweet

To start with, we need to actually explain what 'colour' is. If you have a red shirt, it appears red because it's reflecting the 'red' wavelength, back to you. All light has a wavelength, which determines if we can see it or not and if we can, what colour is it? https://t.co/Hnah7GvUlA

26.08.2021 · Tweet

So, the colour of a thin film is determined by what colour/wavelength light it is reflecting. This changes depending on how thick the film is, as shown in these images! https://t.co/I5XaYiAnEA

27.08.2021 · Tweet

Next up is wettability. If a surface is hydrophilic (water loving) then a water droplet will spread. If a surface is hydrophobic (water hating) then a water droplet will bead! Below are some examples of how wettability influences surfaces! https://t.co/uBWvpW6lP7

27.08.2021 · Tweet

Generally, you can make a surface more wettable by adding oxygen groups to the surface or make it less wettable by adding F or C groups. https://t.co/AwwTG9FUsG

27.08.2021 · Tweet

Both hydrophilic and hydrophobic coatings are required for different applications! 'Self cleaning' windows can be made using a hydrophilic coating, where the water runs off the surface. Hydrophobic particles can be used to remove oil contaminants from water! https://t.co/dGeQ8jI0cY

27.08.2021 · Tweet

Surfaces can also be made 'super hydrophobic' by making the surface rough, but this usually needs another technique to roughen up the surface in addition to just thin films! https://t.co/Uzf5sSkgL4

27.08.2021 · Tweet

Next up is reflectivity. Anyone who's got glasses might have been sold 'anti-reflective coatings' when they bought their glasses. Often this appears as a green tinge on the surface. That's the thin film!

27.08.2021 · Tweet

Anti-reflective coatings work by increasing the transmission of light and decreasing the reflection of light through the glass, so that they appear clearer! https://t.co/if6zPR7sYk

27.08.2021 · Tweet

https://t.co/LMdVifu1ws

27.08.2021 · Tweet

We might want a certain surface charge so we can build up a film, layer by layer! https://t.co/Gg3DPHLC4q

27.08.2021 · Tweet

Or we might want to attract something out of solution, to remove it! In this photo below, I removed humic acid (-ve charged water contaminant) using a positively charge plasma polymer to produce clear water! https://t.co/YAHI6bCdmn

27.08.2021 · Tweet

Making surface conductive is super important these days, given all the devices we have in our bags/pockets/houses! We also need conductive films for solar cells! There are a number of thin films that can be used to create conductive surfaces! https://t.co/nemKgJ1c2w

27.08.2021 · Tweet

Creating hard surfaces is also really important, especially for a number of engineering applications. These are typically metal/metal oxide films. No body wants a drill bit that keeps breaking! https://t.co/5RNMOF0k5h

27.08.2021 · Tweet

Now we've just got biological surfaces to talk about. When we're talking about surfaces for biofouling, biocompatiblity, cell or bacteria growth, it's really the sample principle. What is it that we want to attract and/or repel!

27.08.2021 · Tweet

In marine biofouling, you want to put a thin film down that repels the ocean critter than gum up the bottom of a boat! https://t.co/3hp7JQvD8M

27.08.2021 · Tweet

If we've got an implant we want to put in the body, like for a tooth or a hip, we want it integrate into the bone, so it doesn't become loose. In this case, we'd put a thin film on that promotes bone integration! https://t.co/ds9WpUsdNy

27.08.2021 · Tweet

We might also want to put an implant into the body that repels bacteria growth, or something like a door handle that can also prevent bacterial growth! There's thin films that can do that too! https://t.co/vc3PiumdW8

27.08.2021 · Tweet

29.08.2021 · Tweet

#1 - I mentioned this during the week. Take advantage of summer projects, internships, work experience etc. Science is so broad, so you it's really important to find out where your interests lie!

29.08.2021 · Tweet

#2 - Work life balance. It's really hard to maintain work life balance when you see those around you working really long hours in the lab and writing papers and grants. Especially when it looks like they're getting ahead. Find out what work life balance looks like for you!

29.08.2021 · Tweet

#3 - Success. There are so many ways to be a 'successful scientist' and being an academic is only one tiny fragment of that. Those working in industry, government, comms, are all still 'scientists'. Just because you're not at the bench, doesn't mean you're not still a scientist!

29.08.2021 · Tweet

#4 - Personality. This kind of links in with #1, but find what type of job suits your personality. If you want to work in a basement lab and not talk to anyone all day, that's cool! I like working with people, so I love that my job involves working with others!

29.08.2021 · Tweet

INTERFACE will be the highlight of my tweet thread later today. The basic tool to explore interfaces & surfaces is: Photoelectron Spectroscopy (PES). This can be done in-house or at synchrotrons. Here is how an PES system looks like (my 2021 front cover). Stay tuned! #SciArt. https://t.co/OUrXMwHorb

26.09.2021 · Tweet

Hope you all are having a great weekend! Here are some facts on Photoemission Spectroscopy (PES) - a great tool to have in the toolkit of a materials scientist. /1 https://t.co/WAeNKIofRC

26.09.2021 · Tweet

PES is based on the photoelectron effect. The sample to be studied (film, powder, crystal) is excited with photons of a certain energy. The electrons emitted from the sample upon absorption of these incident photons are collected and parsed for crucial info about the sample. /2

26.09.2021 · Tweet

There are 2 modes of PES. One uses high-energy X-ray photons (>1000 eV) and studies the chemical composition. Chemical environment, oxidation states, etc can be clearly explained. This is called XPS (X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy).

26.09.2021 · Tweet

When low-energy photons (usually UV) with energies in the range of 10s-100s eV are used, electrons that form the valence band structure of the sample are detected. This is UPS (Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy).

26.09.2021 · Tweet

UPS reveals information about energy levels, work function and defect states. Great tool to study optoelectronic devices!

26.09.2021 · Tweet

Great thing about PES is that it's highly surface sensitive, and a usual in-house system gives information about the top 1-5 nm of the sample surface! Thin crusts and interfaces can be studied in detail - Interfaces that define optoelectronic devices!

26.09.2021 · Tweet

I have used PES extensively – both in-house and @CanLightSource – to characterize interfaces in solar cells. https://t.co/WAeNKI6Et2

26.09.2021 · Tweet

These studies revealed a wealth of insights into nanocrystal and perovskite surfaces, specially on how the environment interacts with these materials, and what strategies need to be in place to make more stable optoelectronics.

Or in small nanoflakes an imbalance between the two different sublattices. Check the publications of @Springfetopen for details and refs

18.10.2021 · Tweet

What can we do with it? We can look at single #atoms or #molecules like these: Thanks to Stefano for the image of the atoms https://t.co/l2EXgvckii

18.10.2021 · Tweet

How does it work? Imagine being an #electron in a metal, you are free to surf around your wavefunction anywhere in the metal, actually, even outside the metal! Physically speaking you can “penetrate into the energy barrier” #Donttrythisathome https://t.co/fgiKIcLqm1

18.10.2021 · Tweet

If you find another piece of metal in that tiny distance you can jump there. This is called #tunneling. If there is a bias voltage applied between the first and the second metal piece, we can measure the current flowing, even if the two metal pieces don’t touch

18.10.2021 · Tweet

In the experiment we move a sharp needle, the tip, very close to the surface that we want to look at. Changing the distance between tip and surface by about one atom changes the current by a factor of ten!

18.10.2021 · Tweet

Ever used an electric lighter? You press it, this creates a bias voltage and a current flows. We use it the other way round. We apply a bias voltage and the piezocrystal squeezes together some fraction of a #nano|meter. That’s how we move the tip so precise.

18.10.2021 · Tweet

Now we only need a tip that ends in one single #atom and we can get beautiful images… okay, and a sample to look at… https://t.co/kzswMURldU

18.10.2021 · Tweet

Our project partners in @springfetopen at @IBMResearch in the group of Leo Gross are experts in #AtomicForceMicroscopy. It works almost the same as an STM, but with forces instead of current, that way they can work on insulating samples

18.10.2021 · Tweet

Can we go smaller? Of course! Placing a single CO-molecule on the tip apex of your microscope will give you #atomicresolution inside a single #molecule (sadly though, it is hidden from the public by a big paywall since 12 years) doi:10.1126/science.1176210 https://t.co/liLb0g42YQ

18.10.2021 · Tweet

During my master I worked on another exciting #research project: #ScanningQuantumDotMicroscopy or #SQDM in the group of Stefan Tautz at @fz_juelich This is a very underrated technique, a powerful tool to image #electronic #surface properties.

18.10.2021 · Tweet

I worked with #PTCDA, but it works also with other #molecules. It is an incredible technique where you use a single #molecule hanging from the tip of an #AFM to measure electric #dipoles on the surface with atomic precision. https://t.co/85ETaNMAfF

18.10.2021 · Tweet

You can even stand up PTCDA on the surface and it does not topple over. So far, it is not fully understood, how this is possible, but I assure you, it works. #discovery #science #howdoesitevenwork https://t.co/y9BrcP9IEr

Today, I will reflect on the #working conditions in #resarch. Spoiler alert: They are not very good for most #scientists, and I think they are not even good for #science.

21.10.2021 · Tweet

#WorkLifeBalance for #scientist... Wait, there is a life that is not related to work?! https://t.co/KTO42g1rEX

21.10.2021 · Tweet

Reading my tweets about #science and #work|ing in science? Would you like to work in science or #academia? Tell me why!

21.10.2021 · Tweet

You are essentially a #selfemployed #scientist, although you work for a university or institute. It will always be your name on the #publications that counts. If you want to keep doing what you do, better invest a 👉lot👈 of time

21.10.2021 · Tweet

If you want to #stayinresearch, you are competing over #money (salary or to spend) against everyone in #science, many times even against people from very different fields. The metric you compete on: #paper|s and #citations

21.10.2021 · Tweet

As #science is a #creative process it is difficult to judge what is good science and what isn’t. To come up with “objective” criteria, #scientists are judged mostly by their written, hopefully #peerreview|ed publications, mostly in expensive journals

21.10.2021 · Tweet

You are forced to focus on publishing as many #paper|s as possible, because #citations, number of #publications and #hindex are very important factors when you apply for a scholarship, a grant or a position at an institute or university.

21.10.2021 · Tweet

I guess you get an idea, why there are #scientists publishing #junkscience in #predatorjournals, a practice that is obviously bad and hurts #science. Still, I understand the structural dynamics leading to these decisions.

21.10.2021 · Tweet

The #publishorperish mentality is clearly not in the interest of the individual, as it incentives to push yourself beyond the limit. #Depression and #Anxiety are very high under #PhDs. #mentalhealth is only slowly leaving the tabu-status @Nature https://t.co/C8YwAh9DFo

21.10.2021 · Tweet

Bad for #scientists, good for #science? No. #Science is a creative process that connects ideas, you need time to play around, to try, most importantly to #fail! Focusing on publishing many #papers forces you to take tiny steps forward. #IncrementalScience

21.10.2021 · Tweet

Me, taking over a twitter-account and telling you about my #science likely won’t be valued, neither organizing this a twitter account, which takes a lot of work from people like @MySci_PK, Sanket Dash and @svenja_lohmann. Work, that isn’t spend on writing the next paper.

Hello! I’m Giulia Pacchioni, @Giulia_Pacc, tweeting for the week from London! I’m a Senior Editor at @NatRevMater, where I handle content on a broad range of topics in materials science. This week I'll share some tips on writing, publishing & on life as an editor. https://t.co/IcErSb0ryN

26.10.2021 · Tweet

Today I will put the spotlight on editorial jobs, telling you about how my own path led me to this fun career and what an editor actually does.

26.10.2021 · Tweet

I'm a physicist by training: I did my master and bachelor degrees at @LaStatale in Milan, then moved to @EPFL_en in Lausanne for my PhD. I worked with scanning tunnelling microscopy, something you have learned about last week from @cienciaparaelf2! Here's me with my STM in 2014 https://t.co/azlAnsfwGc

26.10.2021 · Tweet

My PhD project, in Harald Brune's group, involved studying how (and why) small molecules self-organize on surfaces & how the patterns they form can be used to template the organization of atoms & clusters with cool catalytic/magnetic properties. STM pictures in silly colours ⬇️ https://t.co/xV7aewaV2D

26.10.2021 · Tweet

As I was nearing the end of my PhD, a friend pointed out that an editorial job would bring together all the things I was passionate about: physics, writing, and science communication. He was right!

26.10.2021 · Tweet

I started collaborating with blogs discussing science and co-organized a summer school to tailor my CV to this type of job, and landed a position on the launch team of @NatRevMater, which was, and still is, my dream journal 🙃 https://t.co/CYukVsMMM1

26.10.2021 · Tweet

Over the years I have also worked with @NatRevPhys to prepare their launch in 2019, and for a few months with Nature Materials. I will tell you more about how to find editorial jobs and what an editor does in my next threads! https://t.co/lwd9Spi5yd

26.10.2021 · Tweet

Let me tell you more about my job as an editor at @NatRevMater. We are a team of 3 (with @ChristineHorejs & @arianevartanian) and publish Reviews and Perspectives on all topics materials science, + Comments on topics such as mentoring & inclusivity in academia. Lots of variety! https://t.co/TmtcxQJev6

26.10.2021 · Tweet

Editors also write content such as Research Highlights & Editorials -- the latter require a lot of reading and thinking and are a stimulating team effort, such as this recent one led by our brilliant team member Ariane: https://t.co/gUVSol0jcS https://t.co/taZin0y0zp

26.10.2021 · Tweet

As editors we need to know what’s new in the fields we cover; we keep up to date reading the literature and going to conferences & talks (now virtually!) to identify both timely topics and interesting authors. We also encourage unsolicited submissions. https://t.co/LLvSEGGddW

26.10.2021 · Tweet

We ask authors to prepare an outline of their Review planning how much content to cover, how to structure it, and ideas for figures & tables; we give feedback on the outline trying to ensure the angle of the article is clear and the amount of content appropriate https://t.co/JJfCGOksNm

26.10.2021 · Tweet

We then keep in mind the submission timelines of each manuscript and check on authors regularly. We publish a fixed number of articles per month, so it’s important to ensure we have a steady number of submissions through the year, but we also need to plan for unexpected delays

26.10.2021 · Tweet

Once submitted, if a manuscript is not in top shape we suggest ways to improve the structure, clarity & accessibility of the text and to make the figures easier to understand and more useful for readers. https://t.co/Cct4ieWNF1

26.10.2021 · Tweet

As you have guessed, the next step is to find expert reviewers to comment on the manuscript and, when the reports are back, guide the authors through the revision process https://t.co/6WsKGtW7GS

26.10.2021 · Tweet

The most involved step of the process is the in-depth editing of the text to ensure every paragraph is clear & precise and the writing concise. Our art editor applies our colour palette and fonts to all figures & redraws schematic so they are all consistent across the manuscript https://t.co/47Q3TSIDMk

26.10.2021 · Tweet

The final step is checking the proof to ensure everything is in good order before publication, and enjoying the article in its final, highly polished form. Publication is always a proud moment, sometimes the culmination of a process of over 2 years since inviting the author! https://t.co/2rULyvZI1e

Let’s now look at some simple writing tips. The main thing to keep in mind when writing scientific articles is that the point is not to write beautiful prose, but to be understood clearly. We are not Shakespeare! In our case, clarity is better than beauty. https://t.co/48FAZYsbtZ

27.10.2021 · Tweet

You want your paper to tell a story. Start with your scientific question & how it fits in the context of previous results. Then state what you did & how (in logical, not chronological order) and what you found. Finish with *reasonable* implications and next steps. https://t.co/OQFhxDHma9

27.10.2021 · Tweet

Use a clear structure to guide the reader. One paragraph, one idea. Use short sentences linked by appropriate connectors (therefore, however) Use simple but precise words, always using the same word to describe the same thing. Avoid empty words (very, quite) Define all acronyms!

27.10.2021 · Tweet

Metaphors can be confusing, and we often don’t realize how strongly related to our own culture they are. We don’t all grow up with the same myths and stories, hence, if you don’t want your metaphors to become your Achilles’ heel, avoid them. https://t.co/DA9KnMRQMW

28.10.2021 · Tweet

As a reviews editor I get often asked ⭐What makes a good Review?⭐ Here is a summary of my answer in 8 points: 1- Timely: cover an emerging topic or address a need for clarity in a specific area. Make sure you can answer the question ‘why now?’ before you start writing. https://t.co/2tc41jk3PP

28.10.2021 · Tweet

2- Original: ensure you have a new angle/message such that the new review is a useful contribution to the literature. Writing a good review is a lot of work, so make sure the final product will be valuable for readers. Make it count! https://t.co/rxHxrztMXw

28.10.2021 · Tweet

3- Insightful: you don’t want your review to be a laundry list of results in the field. Use your experience to select the most important results, assess them critically and show readers how they fit together in a bigger story https://t.co/qKe0kZnMQD

28.10.2021 · Tweet

4- Balanced: cover fairly the contribution of the various groups active in the field. If there are different points of view, acknowledge them. It’s not always possible to be fully comprehensive, but make sure you clarify what is your focus and how you selected the works to cover https://t.co/ViDxGHqY8Y

28.10.2021 · Tweet

5- Accessible: explain non-obvious concepts, use clear definitions and briefly introduce the important ideas in the field so newbies can delve into the topic. Reference tutorial reviews where the can learn the basics. https://t.co/qzeFnSrSLY

28.10.2021 · Tweet

6- Well illustrated: mix published figures that exemplify important results in the field and new figures such as schematics of processes & graphs comparing results or showing trends to illustrate your main points clearly and effectively https://t.co/x8r4YOe0xS

28.10.2021 · Tweet

7- Forward looking: think carefully about your conclusions and perspectives: What are the open problems in the field? What are the promising directions? Here is the place where you can be a bit more opinionated and discuss your own insights on the future of the field https://t.co/Q6HXTf3li0

28.10.2021 · Tweet

8- Well-planned: once you choose a journal for your review, discuss with editors to see if they have suggestions on the focus or specific guidelines for length and format. Do this before writing the whole thing! This step can save you a lot of work revising.

29.10.2021 · Tweet

The topics I want to cover today are ⚡️cover letters⚡️ & ✨appeals✨. What's the point of a COVER LETTER? It is your opportunity to briefly highlight the main point & significance of your work. Don’t copy and paste the abstract! Editors read both. Keep it brief & to the point. https://t.co/9Nkk3ziErY

29.10.2021 · Tweet

A common question is how to address the letter. With ‘Dear Editor’ you never go wrong. Avoid ‘Dear Sir/Madam’: it’s outdated, and the editor is likely a Dr anyway! Check out this blog post by @stuartcantrill for detailed cover letter tips: https://t.co/mQnBLxAQyT

29.10.2021 · Tweet

APPEALS: Not happy with the editor’s decision? You can always appeal. Make sure you clarify any misunderstandings & explain why you think your paper should be reconsidered. Don’t just ask the editor to rethink their decision: add new data/information to help change their minds.

29.10.2021 · Tweet

Avoid just stating how much your previous articles are cited, or insulting the editor & reviewers. Be polite and use constructive arguments to make your point. Appeals take time, so avoid just ‘trying’. Read more in this @NaturePhysics editorial: https://t.co/pSIfABhAn6

29.10.2021 · Tweet

I was forgetting to share a useful resource: a great @NatRevChem editorial discussing how to pitch review ideas to journals: https://t.co/QZYPZrjNe6 https://t.co/5uNXlquDYu

30.10.2021 · Tweet

Let me tell you what I love about being an editor, and why it’s a great career option for those who don’t wish to go down the academic career path, but want to keep having fun with science

30.10.2021 · Tweet

As an editor, you work on a variety of tasks, including reading, making decisions, editing & writing, and you're exposed to a broad variety of topics. You get to interact with a lot of passionate scientists at all career levels. It’s rarely boring!

30.10.2021 · Tweet

Editors travel quite a lot: in non-pandemic times I used to attend a couple of big conferences a year (such as APS & MRS meetings), plus several more focused conferences. We also organize lab visits & give publishing talks. I have visited a lot of amazing places through my job!

30.10.2021 · Tweet

A big advantage of editorial jobs is that they're secure and flexible. Meeting publication deadlines can be stressful, but generally the pressure is much lower than in academia. Note that things can be different at different journals, this thread just reflects my own experience🙂

30.10.2021 · Tweet

So, how to find editorial jobs? A good place to start is the Nature Careers website, https://t.co/RT9n5PMbPO, where you can find listings for editorial jobs both at Springer Nature and other publishers. Don’t be shy to reach out to editors on Twitter if you have questions!

30.10.2021 · Tweet

A good way to add to your CV something valuable when applying for editorial positions is to co-organize a conference: it showcases organizational skills, enthusiasm & the ability to select good topics. For example MRS Spring 2023 is looking for organizers: https://t.co/dtKaU467lN
