Hello! I’m Dr Tiffany Harte (aka @UltracoldTiff), a postdoc in the many-body quantum dynamics group @CaMBQD in @DeptOfPhysics @Cambridge_Uni. Join me this week to read about Ultracold Atoms and their applications, and get a glimpse into my week as a scientist! #ColdAtoms

01.11.2021 · Tweet

How cold is Ultracold? https://t.co/T3Q24FmTOI

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Absolute zero is at 0 Kelvin, or -273°C - this is the lower limit on absolute temperature and it becomes increasingly difficult to reach the colder you get (negative absolute temperatures are an interesting but separate discussion!).

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Water freezes at 273 K, and the Antarctic can get as low as 190 K. Cryogenic systems can use e.g. liquid nitrogen (77 K) or liquid helium (4 K), but are limited to a few mK. Even outer space is around 2.7 K from the cosmic microwave background. We need to go much colder!

01.11.2021 · Tweet

A cloud of atoms can be cooled down to temperatures approaching absolute zero - commonly a few hundred nano Kelvin (nK - a billionth of a °C) but sometimes as low as tens of pico Kelvin (pK - a trillionth of a °C) - more on how to do this later!

01.11.2021 · Tweet

I’m referring to a ‘cloud’ of atoms because we work with a dilute gas of atoms held inside a vacuum chamber. Each cold atom (or molecule) experiment will be carefully designed around a small number of atomic species depending on the application.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

The temperature of the atom cloud is related to the velocity distribution of the atoms. To cool the cloud, we want to narrow this distribution and reduce the atom velocity. Tune in at lunchtime to find out how!

01.11.2021 · Tweet

How do we cool atoms down? (Part 1 of 3) https://t.co/9mjaTNtioG

01.11.2021 · Tweet

There are lots of ways to cool an atom cloud, and the methods used will vary between experiments and different atomic species - but there are a few methods that many experiments have in common.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Here’s a photo of a potassium source: we buy the source in a sealed ampoule and place it inside our vacuum. We break the ampoule and the source gradually vaporises (sometimes helped by heating). These ampoules should produce enough atoms for several years of operation! https://t.co/O8g4qspD2B

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Once we have enough atomic vapour we use lasers to slow the atoms down and reduce their temperature - lasers don’t just heat things up!

01.11.2021 · Tweet

If the laser beam is at a wavelength that matches an atomic transition, an atom can absorb photons, transferring the photon momentum to the atom. When the atom returns to its ground state and releases a photon, this gives another kick, but in a random direction.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

So if we want to slow down an atom then we need to make sure that it can be cooled from all directions, but preferentially absorbs photons from a direction that opposes its motion. We use the Doppler shift to achieve this!

01.11.2021 · Tweet

If we set the laser to a slightly longer wavelength than the transition, an atom moving towards that laser beam will see the light Doppler shifted to a shorter wavelength - back into resonance with the transition and more likely to be absorbed.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

To make sure that we can slow an atom moving in any direction we overlap three orthogonal pairs of beams propagating in opposite directions. This is called optical molasses because it makes a ‘sticky’ region that slows down (but doesn’t trap) the atoms. https://t.co/GfVJQMrPJm

01.11.2021 · Tweet

To turn this into a trap we add a weak magnetic field that creates a force imbalance and a restoring force to the centre of the beams - a ‘magneto-optical trap’.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Here’s a photo of some of the lasers we use to cool potassium and rubidium - the optics on the table are used to distribute the light, precisely shift the frequencies of different beams, and shutter the light at different times in the experiment sequence. https://t.co/Qv0v7zvoPD

01.11.2021 · Tweet

How do we cool atoms down? (Part 2 of 3)

01.11.2021 · Tweet

There are a few laser cooling temperature limits. The Doppler limit is proportional to the linewidth of the atomic transition, and is related to to the random direction of photon emission when the atom de-excites (after absorbing the initial photon from the laser beam).

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Fluctuations cause a random walk in the atom velocity and so limit the temperature. This limit varies a lot with atomic species - e.g. 146 μK for rubidium, but just 180 nK for strontium which has a very narrow linewidth transition.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

The Doppler limit is an exciting chapter in cold atom history! In 1988 experiments showed temperatures much lower than those predicted by theory: https://t.co/GagJyLyoyQ. This turned out to be due to a more complex atomic energy level structure than was originally accounted for.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Work on laser cooling won the 1997 Nobel Physics prize: https://t.co/qsgexg1TeL.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Another temperature limit is the recoil limit, from the energy associated with the momentum kick of a single photon. This is determined by the mass of the atom and wavelength of the transition - e.g. 360 nK for rubidium-87.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

This still isn’t the final limit though - various sub-recoil methods have also been developed, for example by preventing atoms from absorbing photons if their velocity falls below the recoil velocity.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

How far the atoms are cooled with laser cooling methods depends on the atomic species, the goals of an experiment, and the choices and interests of the research group. Generally speaking, these methods get harder to implement the colder you want to go!

01.11.2021 · Tweet

How do we cool atoms down? (Part 3 of 3)

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Laser cooling is often followed by evaporative cooling. Evaporative cooling is pretty much the same process as the evaporation of your afternoon coffee! The highest-energy atoms leave the trap, and the remaining atoms rethermalise at a lower temperature.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

The atoms are trapped using laser beams or magnetic fields (sometimes both!), and the higher-energy atoms are pushed out of the trap by lowering the trap walls or applying a field that drives them into an untrapped state. A lot of atoms are lost during this stage of cooling!

01.11.2021 · Tweet

There are of course a lot of other methods, tricks, and details I haven’t mentioned! But this outlines the basic atom-cooling toolkit. If this all seems like a lot of effort, join me this evening to find out why we care about making our atoms ultracold!

01.11.2021 · Tweet

The next few hours will be quiet from me because I’m teaching tutorials this afternoon (called ‘supervisions’ in Cambridge). Today we’re looking at magnetostatics! After atomic physics, I think electromagnetism is my favourite part of an undergrad physics course - what’s yours?

01.11.2021 · Tweet

A lot of interesting things happen when you cool atoms to ultracold temperatures https://t.co/BacR3fSqcJ

01.11.2021 · Tweet

The Heisenberg uncertainty principle tells us the position of an atom is spread out in space - the position uncertainty increases as you decrease kinetic energy. This is described by the de Broglie wavelength, which is inversely proportional to the square root of temperature.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

At room temperature, the de Broglie wavelength is much smaller than the spacing between atoms, but as you cool the cloud this approaches the atom spacing. Atoms might now try to occupy the same quantum states - this is where atoms will behave in a way that depends on their spin.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Bosons (particles with integer spin) are able to occupy the same state - at some phase-space density (the number density multiplied by de Broglie wavelength cubed) the particles will fall into the ground state, acting like a single wavefunction - a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC).

01.11.2021 · Tweet

The BEC transition can be seen by looking at the atom momentum. We release the cloud from the trap and allow atoms to move freely for several ms, which maps their initial momentum into position.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

A thermal cloud has a Gaussian distribution, but a BEC looks like an inverted parabola - you can see the BEC peak emerge as you go further in the evaporation process! Here's a gif of the BEC signal appearing as we evaporate (decreasing the power of an optical trap). https://t.co/4dhDCBLJkm

01.11.2021 · Tweet

In contrast, fermions (particles with half-integer spin) are forbidden from occupying the same state by the Pauli exclusion principle. The atoms will instead fill the available energy levels sequentially, and become a degenerate Fermi gas.

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Starting tomorrow we’re going to look at some applications of cold atom systems, starting with the example of building experimental simulations of complex quantum materials!

01.11.2021 · Tweet

Unfortunately the gif I pasted into my last thread didn't work - here it is in the original post! https://t.co/v2feEx98k4

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Every Tuesday morning the @CaMBQD group gets together for #JournalClub where we read a paper in advance and then discuss it. This week we’re looking at a paper by our PI @UlrichCamPhy so we’ll have the expert on hand! Why not read along with us? https://t.co/C9z75kOf1D

02.11.2021 · Tweet

We can use #ColdAtoms to create experimental simulations of complicated systems. Today I’ll show you the first experiment that I worked on in Cambridge, building a quantum simulator for the physics of flat energy bands and frustrated magnetism!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

The first step in building a cold atom quantum simulator is encoding the problem so that the behaviour of the cold atoms captures all the important characteristics.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

For example, a lot of interesting materials have a periodic structure with a lattice of positively charged ions surrounded by a sea of negatively charged electrons. These lattices and the associated electron behaviour can produce some incredibly complex material properties!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

This complex quantum behaviour can be difficult to directly measure or numerically simulate, so we construct an experimental simulation on a larger scale, using patterns of laser light to represent the lattice of the real material and ultracold atoms to represent the electrons.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

This creates a very clean system that has the same or similar geometry to the real material, so that it captures the same physics. We can tune details like how tightly the atoms are held to a lattice site, the interactions between atoms, and can introduce noise or other features.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Because the cold atom system is on a larger scale than the real material (atoms representing electrons, and lattice sites separated by hundreds of nm instead of hundreds of pm) we can measure dynamics of the system at a single-site level using atom fluorescence and a good camera.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

These experimental models are therefore tuneable, easy* to measure, and capture the quantum properties of the real material. This means we can use them to get additional insight into the properties and behaviour of the systems we're modelling *relatively easy

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Tune back in over lunchtime to see just how we use laser light to create the structure of the quantum simulator! https://t.co/W4gUqh2nB5

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Yesterday we saw that laser light can be used to cool atoms. Because a light field affects the atom's energy levels, lasers can also be used to trap them!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

If the wavelength of the light is longer than the atomic energy transition (“red detuned”) the atom is attracted to high intensities. If it is shorter (“blue detuned”) the atom is repelled.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

So if we can make patterns of light with a geometry that captures the physics we’re interested in simulating, we can use this to trap the atoms and create our simulator!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

A popular method of creating patterned light is to use the interference between overlapping waves. You’ve seen this effect before - think of the patterns that form when two ripples overlap on a lake or pond!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

The same thing happens with light - when the waves overlap they add together, creating variations in intensity with a length scale smaller than the laser wavelength (hundreds of nm). By shining laser beams with a certain geometry we can create a huge range of patterns!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Here’s an illustration from my research group @CaMBQD - laser beams (blue) are reflected from mirrors (circles). Where each beam overlaps with its reflection, interference creates a pancake-like structure. Where beam pairs overlap we get a 3D cube of high/low intensity. https://t.co/alcGiNOJ66

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Here’s another example from my research group (I don’t work on this experiment) - four laser beams (blue arrows) are reflected from mirrors (grey circles). This particular symmetry creates a quasicrystal instead of a periodic structure. ￼ Image credit: Dr Ed Carter (PhD thesis) https://t.co/7ACSAAzeUI

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Learn more about quasicrystals here: https://t.co/Nzet1hUCA1

02.11.2021 · Tweet

We also have an experiment studying the kagome lattice (this is the experiment I started building when I first moved to Cambridge). The kagome lattice is the pattern of triangles pictured below. https://t.co/aeaU7YiQya

02.11.2021 · Tweet

We need two laser wavelengths to create the kagome lattice! A blue detuned interference pattern (short wavelength, atoms repelled from high intensity) is overlapped with a red detuned pattern (long wavelength, atoms attracted to high intensity).

02.11.2021 · Tweet

This is shown here - arrows represent the laser beams (no reflection this time!) and where these arrows overlap I’ve shown the spatial variation in atomic energy levels - atoms are trapped by purple and pushed away from yellow. Adding the lattices creates the kagome structure. https://t.co/AoglB1N4eP

02.11.2021 · Tweet

More about the interesting physics of the kagome lattice later today!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

One interesting property of the kagome lattice is geometric frustration where particles that want to align with their spins (arrows) opposite the spin of their neighbours find that they can’t - quantum simulation is one approach to working out how these systems behave. https://t.co/ARM3sB69zK

02.11.2021 · Tweet

The (calculated) energy structure of the kagome lattice is pictured here (energy on the y axis) - one feature here is a flat energy band, where particles should behave as though strongly correlated and infinitely heavy. We want to study this flat band physics! https://t.co/F9EdT0bxI3

02.11.2021 · Tweet

The kagome lattice exists in solid state systems too - see e.g. https://t.co/CtENOj8rqH and https://t.co/HbSewzXVRM

02.11.2021 · Tweet

A quantum simulator can give tremendous insight into the physics of a complicated system - however I think it's important that we acknowledge both the power and limitations of the technique, and keep talking to scientists tackling similar problems using different methods!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Join me later for a virtual lab tour to see how these different ideas come together to create a real quantum simulator!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Time for a lab tour!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

The kagome lab uses rubidium (bosons) and potassium (bosons and fermions). We prepare all the light for laser cooling, optical trapping and optical lattices on two big optical tables, and our vacuum system sits on a third. Here are our laser tables: https://t.co/OnolDfz0zX

02.11.2021 · Tweet

This is a CAD model of our vacuum system - atoms are cooled from left to right in the system following the methods described yesterday (see posts below) https://t.co/7M0WSVPsMz

02.11.2021 · Tweet

The ampoules of potassium and rubidium sit in the bellows labelled ’source’ and atoms diffuse into the rectangular chambers above. These are our 2D magneto-optical traps (MOTs) - the first stage of laser cooling.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

A beam of laser cooled atoms is pushed into the 3D MOT, where we continue laser cooling. The atoms fluoresce - here’s a photograph of a brightly-glowing cloud of laser-cooled rubidium (a few tens of million atoms, at around 200 μK). In reality this is a beautiful red colour! https://t.co/nMQEaTICIV

02.11.2021 · Tweet

We turn up a strong magnetic field and a laser beam (together making a ‘hybrid’ trap) to trap our atoms for evaporative cooling. We load atoms at a few μK into a focussed laser beam and use lenses with a tuneable focal length to transport the atoms 50 cm into our science chamber.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

In the science chamber we can evaporate the atoms further, by lowering the depth of an optical trap made of crossed laser beams, and then load into our optical lattice. Our lattice lasers only arrived a few weeks ago so this is still a work in progress!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

We also have the label for ‘DMD’ potential - this is a plan for the future, where we will project additional laser patterns onto the lattice using a programmable micromirror array.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

The ‘quantum gas microscope’ is for single lattice site imaging. We will make the lattice very deep (to hold the atoms in place) and then simultaneously laser cool the atoms and gather their fluorescence using an objective lens inside the vacuum chamber.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Putting the objective in the vacuum system was daunting - the objective had to be perfectly aligned to the lower viewport. Fortunately we measured this carefully before pumping out our vacuum - the first time we put it in there was a slight tilt! Second time worked perfectly😅

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Here’s a photo of PhD student Dan carefully placing the objective lens inside our vacuum system - and the same chamber once sealed and surrounded by coils and optics! https://t.co/T94E3mSxW4

02.11.2021 · Tweet

We can get complementary information about the cold atom system by dropping the atoms as I described yesterday - releasing them from the trap and letting them fall freely will give us useful information about their momentum.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

A cold atom quantum simulator takes a long time to build! Over the last four years we've turned an empty lab into a working cold atom apparatus and are currently making the last refinements to turn this into a fully operational quantum simulator.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

We have plenty of experiments planned out, so the next few years will be filled with data analysis and exciting results!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

One of my favourite things about being an experimentalist is that you get to think and learn about both the practical aspects of building an apparatus and the exciting physics that the experiment is used to study!

02.11.2021 · Tweet

All experiments are a team effort! The current kagome team is PI Ulrich Schneider @UlrichCamPhy, postdocs Tiffany Harte (me!) and Mehedi Hasan @mhasan137, and students Dan Reed @danreedphysics, Max Melchner, Luca Donini @lucad_96, Sompob Shanokprasith and Dan Braun.

02.11.2021 · Tweet

Today I've been getting things ready for us to start assembling the vacuum chambers for our new experiment where we'll use #ColdAtoms to detect #DarkMatter and #GravitationalWaves! More details about that coming tomorrow!

03.11.2021 · Tweet

[admin] "Creating New Quantum Materials Atom by Atom" Extended conversation with the amazing @UltracoldTiff is out now 👇🎙️🎧 #UnderTheMicroscope #SciencePodcast https://t.co/xc14oBS5ma

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Yesterday I talked about using #ColdAtoms trapped in laser light patterns to build experimental simulations of quantum materials. Today let’s look at a different application of similar techniques: atom interferometry to detect #DarkMatter and #GravitationalWaves.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Interferometry is commonly seen using light. Here is a sketch of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, where a laser beam is split in two then recombined, and the signal detected by photodiodes (grey semicircles) reveals any difference in phase between the two branches. https://t.co/jUmPOpmsaO

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Atom interferometry is exactly the same idea, but using clouds of cold atoms instead of light! Lasers (yes, lasers again!) can drive transitions between atomic states. This can either create a superposition of states (a ‘beamsplitter’) or completely switch states (a ‘mirror’).

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Here’s a Mach-Zehnder interferometer for atoms (straight lines): blue is the ground state, and dashed purple the excited state. Grey wavy lines are the laser pulses that act as mirror and beamsplitters. https://t.co/Rss13zu89d

03.11.2021 · Tweet

The ground and excited states have different momenta, so travel along different trajectories. Any difference in phase that these clouds accumulate can be inferred from the interference pattern obtained after the final ‘beamsplitter’ laser pulse recombines the clouds.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

The atom interferometer is therefore sensitive to anything that might change the phase evolution between the two branches - tune back in at lunchtime to see how this relates to dark matter and gravitational waves!

03.11.2021 · Tweet

I’m currently working in a new consortium called AION (Atom Interferometry Observatory and Network) which plans to build cold atom detectors to test ideas about fundamental physics and complement traditional technologies such as LIGO.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

We will operate two interferometers in parallel, separated by a very long distance - 1 km separation is planned for the final terrestrial detector, and then we plan to put the interferometers into space! The detector will look like this: (Image https://t.co/KAFNOhmgzI ) https://t.co/lsLAWpRky3

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Each 'atom source' is a cold atom cloud that we launch in an interferometry sequence. The red shading represents the laser beams used to create the beamsplitter and mirror interactions.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

We will make a differential measurement between the two separate cold atom interferometers, and will be sensitive to any differences between them.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

For example, a gravitational wave will stretch and compress space-time. This will change the amount of time that it takes laser light to travel between the two interferometers - we will detect this as a time-varying difference in the interferometer phase.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

We will be sensitive to mid-frequency gravitational waves (tens of mHz to a few Hz) which will complement the sensitivity of LIGO (tens of Hz to kHz) and the planned LISA detector (below Hz) - this means we can get information about different stages in e.g. black hole mergers.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Dark matter is a very different detection problem because it’s still such a mystery! An atom interferometer will be sensitive to the predicted couplings of dark matter models to standard model fields, and so can be used to either detect or exclude certain interactions.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

e.g. ultra-light scalar dark matter is predicted to be an oscillating field that will change the electron mass and fine structure constant. This will change the atomic transition frequency and so the phase evolution that we can detect in the differential measurement.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

A longer separation between interferometers will give a greater sensitivity but will also have technical challenges - space missions and even a 1 km terrestrial detector are still decades in the future! This afternoon I’ll describe the work we’re doing now towards this goal.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

I got caught up in work this afternoon so forgot to post! A very long thread is incoming…

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Over the next 2-3 years, we'll develop technologies that will make the large-scale AION detectors possible. There are 5 cold atom research groups, each with our own apparatus so that we can research in parallel and then combine all the techniques in a single prototype.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

This project is a new way of working for me! In cold atoms we typically work in small groups to build and operate an experiment. Here we’re working extremely closely with the other experimental teams - it’s more like being in one big research group spread across multiple sites!

03.11.2021 · Tweet

This level of collaboration means a lot of meetings, and disagreements about the best way to build an experiment! But it’s also a great way to spread the workload and have access to expertise in different areas. It’s also a great chance to work with and learn from more people!

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Right now we’re working on preparing a suitably cold cloud to use in the interferometer - our final target is less than 1 nK! There are also teams looking at improving sensitivity, such as by increasing the separation between the interferometer arms with repeated laser pulses.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

The colder the cloud, the less it will spread out and so the longer the possible duration of the interferometry sequence - this increases the detector sensitivity.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

A compact cloud also means the atoms should all see a more uniform laser intensity, improving the fidelity of the interactions between atoms and light.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

We’re going to start assembling our vacuum system in the next few weeks, and this is what it will look like: (description below) https://t.co/3fdhCPbklI

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Like the apparatus I showed you yesterday we start with laser cooling in a 2D magneto-optical trap (MOT) (see Monday’s thread on laser cooling) to create a pre-cooled beam for laser cooling in a 3D MOT.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

We will then trap in a laser beam to evaporatively cool the atoms and transport them by moving the laser beam focus into a test chamber for interferometry.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

This final chamber isn’t the long tower that we’ll be working with in future years! We’ll develop the technologies on an apparatus that fits nicely on an optical table, then transfer the upgraded cold atom source (everything up to and including transport) onto the final detector.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

We’re using ultracold strontium atoms - I’ve previously only worked with rubidium and potassium (group 1) so it’s exciting to be working with a group 2 element!

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Strontium has an energy transition with an extremely narrow linewidth (mHz) and a correspondingly long-lived state - this is called a clock transition because it's very useful for keeping time! https://t.co/oNJAyJfUoz

03.11.2021 · Tweet

This narrow clock transition allows us to use a single-photon instead of two-photon process for our mirrors and beamsplitters, eliminating laser noise in the differential measurement and allowing us to use a large separation between the interferometers (increasing sensitivity).

03.11.2021 · Tweet

The Cambridge team is working on the techniques to cool and transport the atom cloud, to provide the best possible starting point for interferometry. Our goal is to provide atom clouds with as many atoms as possible, as cold as possible, and produced as fast as possible!

03.11.2021 · Tweet

This includes the methods I’ve discussed previously, as well as tricks like using carefully controlled laser pulses to act like lenses to collimate or focus the cloud as it travels (https://t.co/OGM3SZxfu0).

03.11.2021 · Tweet

The project started in May, and we've spent the last few months designing the apparatus, working on calculations, and setting up the lab. We’ve also been testing some optical transport techniques so that we can transport the atoms with as little heating or atom loss as possible.

03.11.2021 · Tweet

We’re at an exciting time for the experiment, getting the vacuum chambers assembled and filling our tables with laser cooling optics! We’ll be spending some time tomorrow tidying the lab and making space for deliveries - an experimentalist’s job isn’t always glamorous!

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Once again this is of course a team effort! The current (Cambridge) AION team is PI Ulrich Schneider, postdocs Tiffany Harte (me!) and Kimberly Tkalčec, and students Xintong Su, Michael Hsu, Brian Bostwick and Zach Eyler. The full AION collaboration list is very long!

03.11.2021 · Tweet

Tomorrow I’m going to change direction and talk more about myself, and how and why I became a physicist. Since we're approaching the end of my week here, let me know if there are any other aspects of my experiments you'd like to hear about!

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I became interested in #Physics as a teenager because I loved reading fantasy books 📚 The one that influenced me the most was Philip Pullman's #HisDarkMaterials which has lots of science ideas woven through it, including atoms and dark matter, parallel universes and more!

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I started reading about the science behind all this and knew I had to keep learning more! Chemistry was my favourite subject at school but I knew early on that I wanted to study physics at university, and that I wanted to be a scientist working on 'magic' in real life!

04.11.2021 · Tweet

Are there any books or authors that changed the way you see the world, or that you think influenced your life choices?

04.11.2021 · Tweet

@Felgraf_Physics Yes! His books are incredible, I wish I'd started reading them earlier. Although at least that means that there are still plenty that I can still enjoy for the first time now!

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I studied undergraduate physics at the University of St Andrews in Scotland and loved the physics department @PhysAstroStAnd. The department clearly cared about teaching, and the academics were always so supportive and welcoming of questions.

04.11.2021 · Tweet

Students were encouraged to do (paid!) research projects over the summer, and this was a fantastic way of integrating undergraduates with the research activities in the department. As a student it was great to get experience of research before committing to a PhD.

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I had two amazing summer projects - one in cold atoms @UltracoldStAnd and one on scanning tunnelling microscopy in the predecessor of @Kinggroup_ARPES. The research groups were incredibly welcoming and supportive of students making mistakes and finding their feet in the lab!

04.11.2021 · Tweet

It was then that I fell in love with cold atoms 😍 The experimental techniques are fun and varied, and the underlying physics and experiment goals seemed incredible. When I first stepped into the cold atom lab it felt like I'd finally found the magic I'd been looking for!

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I was lucky enough to be working on a really fun project - designing holograms to use as traps for ultracold atoms, supervised by then-PhD student @grahamdbruce.

04.11.2021 · Tweet

This used a spatial light modulator, a programmable liquid crystal array that imprints a phase pattern on a laser beam (by slowing down different parts of the beam). After some simple optics this phase pattern creates intensity variations, making an interesting optical trap!

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I continued working on this for my MPhys research (the final year project for an integrated undergraduate masters), and developed a flexible approach to calculating the phase patterns based on cost function minimisation (https://t.co/aU5azvl1LJ)

04.11.2021 · Tweet

The research (and team) was so much fun that I continued some work with them after I'd left - extending the holographic trapping work and applying the methods to a completely different (theory) problem with @PhysicsSteve (https://t.co/fnMqyPLstd, https://t.co/sgE9gfo4XY)

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I feel so lucky to have had such an amazing undergraduate experience! I'm incredibly grateful to all my lecturers and tutors, especially those who patiently answered my long lists of questions - I now have a better appreciation for how busy they must have been!

04.11.2021 · Tweet

During one of my summer projects I read a paper about creating vortices by rotating a cold atom cloud, a branch of quantum simulation that uses parallels between the forces on rotating neutral atoms and charged particles in a magnetic field. https://t.co/IHPYdYQIrF

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I knew at that stage that I wanted to do a PhD, and was pretty certain I wanted to continue with cold atoms, so I applied to (and was accepted by) the cold atom group at the University of Oxford who had written that paper.

04.11.2021 · Tweet

(This is a compressed version of that story! I applied to several research groups, who all do incredibly exciting work. I definitely recommend students explore their options and apply to (and visit) several groups to work out what research and group dynamic works for them.)

04.11.2021 · Tweet

My PhD research was on radiofrequency-dressed magnetic traps for ultracold atoms. These are magnetic traps with a radiofrequency field applied to create a trapping surface where the atomic energy level splitting due to the magnetic field is resonant with this frequency.

04.11.2021 · Tweet

For us this created tuneable ellipsoidal trapping surfaces, and my main PhD result was the first experimental demonstration of using several radiofrequency fields to create concentric trapping surfaces for quantum simulation or atom interferometry. https://t.co/Hmrz9fKemQ

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I also continued working on shaped optical traps - this time using the deflection of a laser beam by acousto-optic devices (where an acoustic wave in a crystal creates a diffraction grating) to rapidly ‘paint’ and also create precisely-controllable arrays of individual beams.

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I quickly felt overwhelmed when I started my PhD. I had expected a steep learning curve, but I wasn’t prepared for such a ‘sink or swim’ environment.

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I’m sure this works well for some people, and there can be a lot of value in being given the independence to try things out for yourself and make mistakes - but I think this should be balanced with enough guidance and support for each student to thrive.

04.11.2021 · Tweet

However, this PhD experience gave me the confidence of knowing that I could learn to understand, build and fix a complicated system. I also learnt a lot of interesting physics, and good science practice along the way!

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I was also fortunate to share most of my PhD years with the best possible lab-mate, @drbentine, and other fantastic students. I learnt the value of teamwork in facing challenges that would be much more difficult alone!

04.11.2021 · Tweet

I finished my PhD knowing that I wanted new challenges, but also that I wanted to continue working in cold atoms. That's why I was so excited to start a postdoc building a new experiment and working on optical lattices!

05.11.2021 · Tweet

I started my postdoc at @Cambridge_Uni @DeptofPhysics four years ago, and have grown a lot as a researcher both inside and outside the lab. I’ve talked a lot about my research over the last couple of days, so this will be a short thread about some of the other things I do.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

I’ve been lucky enough to belong to a college while here - first @JesusCollegeCam and now @Kings_College. College membership is a nice way to stay connected with the broader life of the university. There’s a great community and opportunities to learn about interesting research!

05.11.2021 · Tweet

Through college I was able to start running some of my own public outreach and engagement events. I love running workshops for primary school children and seeing their enthusiasm for science! I’m also really excited about an upcoming game exploring quasicrystals and 4d space!

05.11.2021 · Tweet

I’m co-chair (with the amazing @beth_tennyson) of the department Research Staff Committee, where we represent postdocs in the wider department, and build a community for research staff.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

We’ve been organising discussions and social events exploring ethics in physics research. I think that researchers should be aware of the impact of their work, and some study of ethics could be a useful part of researcher training.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

It’s very easy to become single-minded about your research but I think I’m a much better scientist (and a happier human) when I make time to pursue other projects and interests!

05.11.2021 · Tweet

I’m not sure what my career holds next. I'm enjoying my current research and am trying to learn more about funding processes. I have a few applications currently in progress so hopefully the next few months will bring good news!

05.11.2021 · Tweet

This will be my last day on this account - I’m following my own advice and taking the weekend off from anything remotely adjacent to work! Today I will talk about some of the practical side of working with cold atoms, and offer some advice for people interested in the field.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

One of the things I love about our experiments is that we tend to work in small teams building our own apparatus, so you have to be familiar with every part of the experiment.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

(This is less true of my new interferometry research, where a huge team will be involved in building the full-size detector. Being less directly involved in various aspects of the experiment and apparatus is something I’ll have to get used to!)

05.11.2021 · Tweet

This means understanding an experiment timing system that will control laser powers and frequencies, shutter light, and control magnetic field sweeps - all at μs precision or better. This includes both hardware and the software that controls it.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

You will spend a lot of your time working with optics and lasers - optics alignment can get competitive! You will work on ultra-high vacuum systems if you’re building or extending an apparatus. There are always small (or large) electronics tasks so you’ll be good at soldering!

05.11.2021 · Tweet

You will also do a lot of computational simulation and modelling to explore ideas for new experiments and help inform design choices. Once an experiment is running you'll need to be able to analyse and understand the results.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

Disclaimer - this is a list based on my own experiences! Different research groups operate differently, and there will be an emphasis on certain tasks more than others at various stages of an experiment’s lifetime.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

This means there are always opportunities to develop new skills! Absolutely no-one enters the field with all those skills already, and joining a new research group is a learning curve even if you’ve already worked on similar experiments before.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

You’re unlikely to enjoy every part of the work - e.g. I really don’t enjoy machining parts so am glad now that I can delegate those jobs! Everyone has natural strengths and interests that they will gravitate towards in finding their niche in the team.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

And let’s not forget the other important research skills - teamwork, communication, problem-solving, planning, and time-management. As you progress in your career, leadership and management. These are so often overlooked but research would fall apart without them!

05.11.2021 · Tweet

I think that the most important skills I’ve developed during my career have been general problem solving: being able to take a complicated problem or system and work out how to methodically break it down into solvable parts.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

Thread on my advice if you’re a student interested in a cold atom PhD, or a PhD or postdoc looking for a change in direction - bear in mind that this is based just on my own experiences and opinions!

05.11.2021 · Tweet

It’s worth thinking about what skills you want to develop and where your interests are. e.g. are you more interested in thinking about physics goals and analysing data from an experiment that’s already running, or would you like to be part of the design and engineering process?

05.11.2021 · Tweet

Try to align this with your long-term goals (with the understanding that these might change!) - e.g. if you want to run your own group one day it’s a good idea to get some experience of building an experiment.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

But also consider that this will affect your publications - unfortunately these matter! A brand new apparatus might take 3 or more years before you start seeing high-impact papers, so weigh this against the skills you’ll develop during the building stage.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

That is something I should have considered more seriously! If you are at the start of the building process make sure that your funding covers long enough to have a reasonable chance of publications, and discuss the option of publishable side-projects with the PI.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

Think about how your previous experience and existing skills fit in with the type of work you’d be doing. A lack of direct experience shouldn’t prevent you from joining an experiment (in my opinion) but think about how your existing skills and interests can be expanded.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

Personally I’m always happy to be contacted by prospective students by email, but we can have a much more constructive conversation if you show that you’ve looked into our research and have a general idea about the kinds of work this would involve.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

Try to visit a research group and speak with the current students and postdocs. Don’t be afraid to ask awkward questions to check it would be a good fit for your specific needs and goals. If you want to spend time on e.g. outreach or teaching, make sure the PI would be on board.

05.11.2021 · Tweet

I mentioned this yesterday, but invest time in developing other skills and interests - this makes you a happier person, increases your skills, exposes you to different career options, and can end up increasing your motivation for your research!

05.11.2021 · Tweet

Finally: the experiment will always be there. Don’t be afraid to go on holiday, spend time with friends or family, or take weekends off - sometimes an emergency or set of measurement will require long hours but this shouldn’t become your standard way of working!

05.11.2021 · Tweet

That’s all from me - I hope you’ve enjoyed hearing about my work and the world of the ultracold this week. Thanks so much to the RealSci_Nano team for having me, and follow me @UltracoldTiff for more updates! https://t.co/54mKV3xNsA

So, time to get the answer.... the electron images shown earlier come from the shell of two snails species. Why are they interesting? because if you at it carefully, you can see some structure in it. This structure comes from microparticles oriented in specific directions...

08.11.2021 · Tweet

Yes: the shells of snails are microstructured composites: particles in a matrix with a specific orientation. Now, why are they so? probably because this makes the shell strong, and protective, while remaining lightweight. Microstructured composites have unusual properties!

08.11.2021 · Tweet

Also, these 2 shells comes from very funny snails, provided by my colleague Yuta Morii from Kyoto University https://t.co/UDrgjwDY1w. Yuta is a zoologist studying species. Those 2 snails come from Hokkaido, and have different defense mechanisms...

08.11.2021 · Tweet

The first one retracts in its shell... while the other snail swings its shell like a club to scare predators!! Check out the paper and the supplemental material for the video: https://t.co/cxG7JDev3W https://t.co/VxwDYDqrLs

08.11.2021 · Tweet

One striking particularity here, from a biologist point of view, is that both snails live at the same place and have almost the same genome, yet they have very different pheonotypes. So, looking closely at the microstructure-properties of the shells was interesting. ...

08.11.2021 · Tweet

interesting to understand the constraints of the environment and how it leads to this 2 evolutionary paths. The conclusions are that there might be an evolution driven by predator-prey interactions... and that it can bring some bioinspired ideas.

Thank you for waiting! So, the morphing from carnivorous plants is complex, but can be simplified by the principle of bistability. Each leaf of the trap can be schematized as a bilayer composite with perpendicular fibers. https://t.co/aEoT0WaS7L

10.11.2021 · Tweet

Due to the perpendicular orientation of the fibers, stresses are stored in the structure, leading to 2 stable states of the bilayers, and a fast snapping from one state to the other, exactly like snap bracelets. https://t.co/lVyIlntYdH https://t.co/J1Qv285JKh

10.11.2021 · Tweet

With this principle, artificial flytraps have been made using carbon reinforced composites: https://t.co/NnUcR1wEC5 https://t.co/j0osnPRxfd

Finally, what is also pretty cool for the Shrimp is that it is has a chitin, like beetles or cockroaches. Chitin is a hydrophobic, tightly crosslinked hydrogel that can be used for sustainable materials like packaging and many others applications! https://t.co/fKBzt4ZQGI

11.11.2021 · Tweet

Recently, one of my colleague @NTUsg used derivatives of chitin for green hydrogen generation! Instead of chitin, the material used was chitosan, basically a hydrophobic version of chitin that is more easily processable. https://t.co/8OwEheQW6H

Mantis shrimp is a source of many bioinspired materials. Material researchers are exploiting similar helicoidal microstructure to increase the mechanical properties... using cellulose nanocrystals or even cement!

[admin] "Dancing Atoms and the Stories they Tell" Please welcome @BGuzelturk for an amazing week of materials/nano science! ✨ Listen to the podcast to know what is coming your way this week 🎧🎙️👇 - https://t.co/SP5xq9sAYf #UnderTheMicroscope #SciencePodcast

15.11.2021 · Tweet

Hello Materials/NanoScience Enthusiasts! My name is Burak Guzelturk. I’m excited to share my journey in science this week. Before kicking in with exciting ultrafast X-ray science - big applause to organizers of this account for bringing wider voice to scientists around the world!

15.11.2021 · Tweet

A little intro about me: I am a beamline scientist at Advanced Photon Source, a synchrotron part of Argonne National Laboratory. In our beamline, we are doing time-resolved X-ray scattering and spectroscopy experiments on a wide range of material systems.

15.11.2021 · Tweet

We are shooting lasers and X-rays onto the samples at the same time and watching how atoms jiggle and wiggle due to excitation, how they interact and relax over time. https://t.co/bQ6sw8po0W

15.11.2021 · Tweet

You will hear some of the recent exciting stuff using such ultrafast structural measurement techniques throughout this week, how useful they are... Also tips and tricks on how to get beamtimes at large user facilities, prepare for beamtimes and hopefully get successful results! https://t.co/5t5p1TBoPi

16.11.2021 · Tweet

Alright, let's get into business of ultrafast X-rays!

16.11.2021 · Tweet

Synchrotrons (and XFELs) are basically giant machines acting as X-ray lasers! https://t.co/4TbCYgS5fg

16.11.2021 · Tweet

These places provide pulsed X-rays with well defined repetition rate, which enables time-resolved X-ray experiments. APS has 24 bunch mode, giving 24 X-ray bunches separated by 153 ns within a period of the storage ring, so simply an X-ray laser with 6.5 MHz repetition rate.

16.11.2021 · Tweet

We synchronize our ultrafast lasers that can produce visible/IR light with the repetition rate of the X-rays. Therefore, we can adjust the arrival time of a laser pulse with respect to that of the X-ray pulse quite precisely, the technique known as pump-probe in optical domain

16.11.2021 · Tweet

This has similarities to a stop-motion photography or slow-mo which helps to to resolve fast motion happening Image ref:https://t.co/YVERqBkpso https://t.co/FLdx2VqIWj

16.11.2021 · Tweet

But, different than macro-scale, we are interested in visualizing dynamics happening at the atomic scale following a laser excitation. Non-equilibrium induced by the excited state and its relaxation.

16.11.2021 · Tweet

As compared to complimentary techniques such as optical transient absorption, time-resolved photoluminescence, TR-ARPES etc etc. probes like X-rays and electrons provide the point of view of the atomic structure different than electronic structure and provides new aspects https://t.co/oqxyKEqk1Z

17.11.2021 · Tweet

Let’s talk about how optical pump / X-ray diffraction/absorption probe experiments. Why are they useful? And how? https://t.co/0EJpsGzpCP

17.11.2021 · Tweet

Two directions: (1) Visualization of energy conversion processes in photoactive materials (Ex/ photocatalysts and photovoltaic materials) by probing how light energy and hot-carriers are turned into into lattice heating or carrier trapping causing local lattice deformations... https://t.co/ROEmte0K13

17.11.2021 · Tweet

(2) Manipulating matter with laser pulses and creating dynamic new states. Optical pump/X-ray probe allows probing these states: Ex/ transient phase transformations, light-induced bond-breaking-forming etc.

17.11.2021 · Tweet

Before we dive into some cool examples, let’s check out what are key observables in these experiments

17.11.2021 · Tweet

In optical pump/X-ray diffraction probe, we basically do XRD transiently. Therefore, observables are Bragg peaks, their positions, intensities and widths.

17.11.2021 · Tweet

Bragg peaks may shift to low Q for example. It means the material expands. It typically happens when hot-carrier relax via electron - phonon coupling. There could be other ways that cause shift of Bragg peaks due to induced and relaxed strain in the material. https://t.co/WpNGaES1tK

17.11.2021 · Tweet

Specific phonon modes may be launched due to photoexcitation. This can lead to periodic modulation of the structure factor, hence up and down periodic changes of the Bragg peak intensities https://t.co/yx86vVRbZI

17.11.2021 · Tweet

Or, some of the Bragg peaks may disappear while other may appear. The number of peaks may go down if the material converts from a lower symmetry structure to a higher symmetry structure. All these changes indicate the unit cell representing the material is now different. https://t.co/SciSMGRp82

17.11.2021 · Tweet

Last example of observables in optical pump/XRD probe experiments is the changes in the Bragg peak intensity and width. Peak intensities can go down if the material is becoming more disoredered. This happens, for example, when you heat up a material https://t.co/3kOwe9t8cX

17.11.2021 · Tweet

We can also talk about different set of observables associated with optical pump/X-ray absorption experiments. I am showing here a Co K-edge X-ray absorption spectrum. The spectral region around the absorption edge is called XANES - X-ray absorption near edge structure. https://t.co/xZHkz29VuS

17.11.2021 · Tweet

XANES region is sensitive to electronic perturbations. Localization of an electron or hole around the element gives rise to shifts to either low or higher energy. As well as pre-edge structures can change due to this.

17.11.2021 · Tweet

EXAFS is the absorption that extends many 100 eV away from the absorption edge itself which is mainly sensitive to the local structure, i.e., bonding, around the element withing the material. Changes in this region indicates changes in the bond lengths.

17.11.2021 · Tweet

These regions are overall summarized here https://t.co/PlecozD8VY

17.11.2021 · Tweet

These hopefully give more concerete sense on what these measurements show and why we do them... Next up: some of the literature examples! https://t.co/WiKbm2W4Uz

17.11.2021 · Tweet

[admin] "Dancing Atoms and the Stories they Tell" Extended conversations with the amazing @BGuzelturk is out now. 🎙️👇 #UnderTheMicroscope #SciencePodcast https://t.co/jK6EXYbTu3

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Let’s check out some classical work that utilized ultrafast structural measurements and also more recent ones. This is definitely not an exhaustive list of papers but some that I personally find useful (and also a little bit of shameless self-promotion of our work)! https://t.co/2wAbt7KHq6

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Early work was focused on using optical pump / X-ray (or electron) diffraction probe experiments to investigate how fast bonds break and how fast materials transform. Questions like how fast can you melt a material or how fast can you break a bond? https://t.co/GmbVIVxrGq

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Tribute to late Ahmed Zewail who pioneered a lot in ultrafast comunity. His group’s paper back in 1997 is one of the first to resolve chemical bond breaking in a molecule after photoexcitation. https://t.co/YVXipbSQkw

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Another early paper is from Bradley Siwick and Dwayne Miller in 2003. They visualized transient melting of aluminum after laser excitation. Aluminum film can melt as fast as 3.5 ps after laser excitation. https://t.co/AUaZjjeCEl

18.11.2021 · Tweet

More recent work attempted to use such measurements to characterize how atomic structure deforms due to an electronic excited state, the so-called polarons which play important roles in optoelectronic properties of materials using for photocatalysis and photovoltaics

18.11.2021 · Tweet

An example is using transient X-ray absorption experiments resolving carrier localization and small polaron formation in iron oxide nanoparticles commonly used as catalysts in various applications. They utilized iron edge transient XANES measurements. https://t.co/6WSLRUqqob

18.11.2021 · Tweet

More recent example is from our work, where we used transient diffuse X-ray scattering to visualize dynamic growth of point-defect like structural deformations after photoexcitation in lead halide perovskites indicating the presence of large polarons https://t.co/j3iCT4QnGF https://t.co/gVaMLaoXQ1

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Also, it turns out ultrafast structural measurements are excellent ways to make transient thermometry of materials at picosecond timescales which is otherwise quite challenging task via optical methods. This allows one to characterize how fast hot carrier cool and lattice heat up https://t.co/zSZzAgEc1R

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Therefore, one may call “hot carrier cooling” == “cold lattice heating” https://t.co/AwK5sK9Meo

18.11.2021 · Tweet

An example of this is from our work where we looked into hot carrier cooling and electron phonon coupling in gold nanocrystals and showed strong size and surface chemistry dependence. Larger particles have weaker electron – phonon coupling, hence longer lived hot carriers.

18.11.2021 · Tweet

However, ligands such as thiols that strongly bound to the gold surface can slow down hot-carrier cooling via transient surface energy transfer across metal – ligand interaface. https://t.co/e2IEpunPM5 https://t.co/uA1ZnkaBvM

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Other recent work have attempted to resolving transient strain in materials and especially in nano-objects under non-equilibrium conditions

18.11.2021 · Tweet

This paper by Ian Robinson has beautifully resolved transient strain evolution in large gold nanoparticles (>300 nm) by applying a coherent Bragg diffraction imaging technique combined with a pump/probe scheme. https://t.co/IyxohHCHZN

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Another example is a recent work of ours where we looked at smaller CdSe/CdS nanocrystals that are used in QLED TVs. Under UV light, highly localized lattice deformations arise due to trapping of carriers on surfaces that dynamically distorts the surface https://t.co/KYzVVgCC9U

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Other examples include novl ways to utilize lasers or external excitation means to create useful states of matter for potential applications such as computing, information storage etc...

18.11.2021 · Tweet

One such example is electrical pump / X-ray diffraction probe experiment on ferroelectric samples. They looking into speed limits of ferroelectric polarization switching and showed sub-nanosecond regime is possible https://t.co/svChDHJroP

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Another cool example using laser pulses to make a transient superconductor. https://t.co/DrgWV5zW9D

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Creation of supercrytals upon photoexcitation is also another quite interesting finding in complex oxides. This state of matter could not be created by just heating up or cooling down the material but just through intense laser excitation. https://t.co/XHtqIm1ZNB

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Final example is a switch, "crystal symmetry switch". Light excitation generates a shear mode in a two dimensional material and modulates the crystal structure from a high symmetry one to a non-centrosymmetric, a new way to store info with >500 GHz. https://t.co/dF2Sntkrj0

18.11.2021 · Tweet

Huh, a long chain of tweets! If you reached this point, congrats!!! Tomorrow I will talk more on the fun aspects of being a beamline scientist and will start talking more on how to get beamtimes, how to prepare and tips!

19.11.2021 · Tweet

Synchrotrons are very dynamic places to work at. At APS there are 60+ beamlines, meaning 60+ different experiments going on simultaneously on the experimental floor on a typical day.

19.11.2021 · Tweet

There are always new experiments and new challenges. That I find quite exciting. Also, working with people from all around the world is quite fun and a continuous learning experience.

19.11.2021 · Tweet

Technique development and improvements at the beamlines is significant part of the job of a beamline scientist in addition to supporting experiments and attracting researchers and forming flourishing user base at the beamline.

19.11.2021 · Tweet

If you are new to synchrotron based experiments, but do not know where to start. Check out the technique you are interested in, locate the relevant beamtime and then email beamline scientists working.

19.11.2021 · Tweet

Beamline staff will be happy to chat, provide information about the capabilities, if needed set up a meeting and discuss about needs of your potential experiments.

19.11.2021 · Tweet

The next step is to get a beamtime is to submitting a proposal. The next step is to get a beamtime is to submitting a proposal which is generally 3-5 pages of document answering questions like scientific purpose, why need for synchrotron, what is the need for specific beamline...

19.11.2021 · Tweet

Key aspect is to convince the external reviewers about the feasibility of the experiment in addition to the novelty/importance of the scientific question. Getting feedback from beamline scientists is quite useful before the submission and it definitely does not hurt!

19.11.2021 · Tweet

Let’s say that you got a beamtime awarded. Now what? https://t.co/hlhkUXbCqD

19.11.2021 · Tweet

Preparation is everything! All the way from sample preparation to logistics, team work and data analysis. Beamtimes are generally for few days to whole week that continue for 24 hr. Therefore, it is not a one person’s job but requires multiple people, an experiment team.

19.11.2021 · Tweet

Sample prep and making contingency plans is needed as some samples can turn out to be low quality or degraded. Or, they might degrade under X-rays... Therefore, having a set of samples and various backups is critical.

19.11.2021 · Tweet

Another important aspect is the on-line data analysis. Most beamlines have some sort of analysis environments for typical experiments. However, for specific experiments, new data analysis scripts may be needed and users should take initiative to prepare this before the beamtime.

19.11.2021 · Tweet

Having data but not knowing what it tells you can be really bad especially when you need to make decisions during the beamtime like what parameters to choose next or scan. Asking beamline staff for exemplary data beforehand to familiarize your self ahead of time is a great idea.

21.11.2021 · Tweet

The week is about to end and I have a a short story about a recent paper of mine before my curation ends here @RealSci_Nano

21.11.2021 · Tweet

This week one of my paper got accepted in ACS Photonics that will be online soon. This paper has an interesting story with it that I thought I would share it with you all.

21.11.2021 · Tweet

During my postdoc, I was studying terahertz emission spectroscopy on various solar energy materials. One of the samples that I studied was PbTe. THz emission showed quite interesting dynamics and spectral responses from PbTe.

21.11.2021 · Tweet

We thought THz emission from PbTe may help to explain some of the mistery on optical phonon modes in this material. It has a simple cubic crystal structure but neutron measurements showed multiple transverse-like phonons at zone center that are not expected

21.11.2021 · Tweet

Some of these paper reporting phonon anomalies in PbTe: https://t.co/uDKAqq5CbC and potential Pb off-centering https://t.co/nmJzFoi4yc

21.11.2021 · Tweet

I did a time-frequency domain analysis (moving window FFT) analysis on my data, and we were seeing delayed responses associated with a transverse optical mode with respect to others and we thought we might be seeing the anharmonic phonon-phonon renormalization in real-time.

21.11.2021 · Tweet

If this was true, then it would mean that we could solve some of the mistery in this material...

21.11.2021 · Tweet

We got some theory support doing some MD simulations and overall things were looking consistent. I wrote the paper and got it polished it. We were about to submit it. All this was back in summer of 2018.

21.11.2021 · Tweet

There was a little point about the moving window FFT analysis that was bugging me. I was worried whether the result can be uniquely explained by different onset times of two modes, so whether there was a real time delay between spectral features.

21.11.2021 · Tweet

Before we submitted the paper, I decided to play around more and simulated some signals mimicking the experiment and THz emission. I realized that this type of analysis cannot differentiate phase difference or time (on-set) delay. Therefore, our results were not conclusive!

21.11.2021 · Tweet

This was frustrating at first. I had spent many months on the data, experiments and paper... Anyway, I decided to hold off the manuscript.

21.11.2021 · Tweet

After three years, last summer I decided to go back and look at the data now with a fresh eye. I realized there was already quite interesting response in the Thz emission that I did not pay attention much as got so focused on phonon anharmonicity aspect.

21.11.2021 · Tweet

THz emission from PbTe could be significantly tuned spectrally under varying photoexcitation density. Tunability was quite significant from 3.2 to 2.4 THz and such large tunability was not observed in other THz emitter before. I thought this is something to tell to the community

21.11.2021 · Tweet

Therefore, I decided to re-write the paper and still disseminate these results. The reviewers really appreciated the results and the paper got quickly accepted.

21.11.2021 · Tweet

I think if we have kept forward back in 2018, that paper could got published... but potentially would create more conflict in the community than solution. I think one of the take-home message behind this story is that scientific rigor is essential no matter what!

21.11.2021 · Tweet

24.11.2021 · Tweet

Time for fun facts! Today's topic is anisotropy. Anisotropy is the property of a material showing the difference of the physical or mechanical properties when measured under different directions, as opposed to isotropy. This is a concept across many fields https://t.co/9Nz3S5O3K4

24.11.2021 · Tweet

For example, wood is stronger along the grain than perpendicular to the grain. Strength is a property of the wood and this property depends on the direction, which is wood's anisotropy. For more details, check out the wiki page above☝️ Picture courtesy of AhsanAronno https://t.co/TwM6bVljHo

24.11.2021 · Tweet

Here I want to focus on the optical anisotropy of crystals. The crystals are anisotropic to light. Many of you may hear of birefringence or double reflection, which is commonly seen in polarization optics. It is interesting to learn about how optical anisotropy develops.

24.11.2021 · Tweet

The discovery of birefringence in a crystalline material can be traced back to 1669. Erasmus Bartholinus, a Danish physicist and mathematician, discovered the phenomenon of double refraction of calc-spar (a type of calcite). Pictures from Science Photo Library and Wikipedia https://t.co/C6fBS0O4Zm

24.11.2021 · Tweet

In 1690, Christian Huygens, a Dutch physicist (yep who proposed Huygens principle), interpreted the double refraction by assuming that in the crystal there is a secondary ellipsoidal wave in addition to a primary spherical wave, which is the fundamental discovery of polarization.

24.11.2021 · Tweet

Isaac Newton explained this phenomenon by assuming that light particles have "sides", and used it as an argument against Hooke's wave optics. At that time, only longitudinal (acoustic) waves were known, and they could not explain transverse polarization.

24.11.2021 · Tweet

In 1808 Étienne Malus observed the reflection of direct sunlight from a window through calcite and found the two images obtained by double refraction varied in relative intensities as rotating the crystal.He formulated Malus law and applied first the term "polarization" to light

24.11.2021 · Tweet

In 1809 Arago discovered the polarization of light from the clear blue sky. In 1811 Arago observed the optical activity of quartz, and Biot discovered the high polarization of the rainbow. In 1812 Arago constructed a filter from a pile of glass sheets.

24.11.2021 · Tweet

In 1815 Biot established the optical activity of certain liquids and discovered the strong dichroism of tourmaline crystals. In the same year, Brewster discovered the law of Brewster's angle, also known as the polarization angle.

24.11.2021 · Tweet

In 1828 Nicol invented a prism, which was the first easily usable polarizing filter. After that, the theory and experiment of optical anisotropy and polarization optics were being improved and developed. The story never ends. Next I will introduce what we discovered on this topic

24.11.2021 · Tweet

Source and reference: 1. Historical notes on anisotropy https://t.co/Ed4xVmUzaw 2. Gabor Horvath’s thesis https://t.co/UdanJMIt2G 3. Conifold's answer from @StackExchange https://t.co/iUBV1VPcPx 4. https://t.co/WCZZnzJDBJ 5. https://t.co/jCqsslR4YF

25.11.2021 · Tweet

Why do we care about optical anisotropy? In the sense of polarization optics, there are devices that we commonly use, such as wire grid polarizers, polarizing beam splitters, waveplates... All of them rely on some kind of optical anisotropy to manipulate the polarization of light https://t.co/qd4g1l52tB

25.11.2021 · Tweet

For wire grid polarizers, structural anisotropy in terms of patterned wires can absorb/reflect light at a certain polarization. But for PBS and waveplates, the anisotropy comes from the crystal structure itself of the material. For these systems, large anisotropy is the key. https://t.co/VLGUJEjt6P

25.11.2021 · Tweet

For uniaxial materials, birefringence is to quantify the anisotropy of a material, which is the difference between extraordinary (along the optical axis) and ordinary (perpendicular to the optical axis) refractive index (delta_n). https://t.co/fLLe7lskOx

25.11.2021 · Tweet

The most commonly-used birefringent materials are calcite, rutile, and cadmium selenide. Calcite has a large birefringence span UV through near-infrared. And rutile extending more towards mid-infrared. Cadmium selenide is another birefringent material working in mid-infrared.

25.11.2021 · Tweet

But you can see their delta_n are actually very small. So this leads to a question, can we find, or create a material that is highly birefringent across the infrared ranges? And this leads us to this concept of engineering the polarizability of a crystal structure.

25.11.2021 · Tweet

Given the idea of polarizability engineering, we looked at a perovskite-type crystal structure. Its crystal structure is anisotropic and intrinsically has in-plane anisotropy. https://t.co/BGvvLLTIe3

25.11.2021 · Tweet

Besides the fact that the crystal is anisotropic, we also need to think about what kind of chemicals can we use to maximize the polarizability difference between the planes. So we want to pick chemicals that give us lower polarizability in one direction versus the other. https://t.co/Zb6Iw9m8pM

25.11.2021 · Tweet

In this case, barium, titanium, and sulfur provide good candidates. And this is our first attempt at engineering polarizability. In 2018, our group, together with Prof. Ravichandran's group and Prof. Han Wang's group from @USCViterbi reported giant birefringence of BaTiS3 (BTS)

25.11.2021 · Tweet

https://t.co/TzzTYX3vZQ In this paper, we reported a difference between the ordinary and extraordinary refractive index up to 0.76 in a mid-infrared region of transparency, which is the largest of any bulk material with the in-plane optical axis that we know at that time. https://t.co/v02McOop6j

25.11.2021 · Tweet

But after that, during an experiment we found that the refractive indices of extraordinary and ordinary of BTS were mixed up. Actually it has positive birefringence instead of negative in the infrared range, and its giant anisotropy still works. This mistake was surprising to us.

25.11.2021 · Tweet

After that, we submitted the author correction and right now it's up online. https://t.co/jCWg2WLV05

25.11.2021 · Tweet

So I'd love to walk you through how we characterize this anisotropic material and how these mistakes occurred. As a super early-stage researcher, it's worth learning and thinking about "science is always self-correcting"

25.11.2021 · Tweet

For this work, we came up with a comprehensive optical characterization method by combining polarized infrared spectroscopy with generalized spectroscopic ellipsometry. This allows us to extract optical properties spanning UV to mid/far infrared range. https://t.co/8022uWr5G0

25.11.2021 · Tweet

We used VASE from @JAWoollamCo to collect ellipsometry data across UV to near IR range. The idea of ellipsometry is to build up an optical model that can fit the values. here we created a generalized oscillator model that is a summation of Kramers-Kronig- consistent oscillators. https://t.co/wFUi1MdoXx

25.11.2021 · Tweet

To further expand to mid/far infrared range, we can include the polarized reflection spectroscopy data in our fitting data set. By manipulating the oscillators, reflection data can also be fitted. https://t.co/5uzQGSriLz

25.11.2021 · Tweet

From that, we're now able to extract the optical properties of BTS from UV to mid/far IR. As I mentioned above, we ended up mixing the ordinary and extraordinary refractive index. This is due to two mistakes we made during the fitting.

25.11.2021 · Tweet

The first error, we found that wrong Euler angles were defined in the model. The ellipsometer we used defines the c-axis into the substrate (out-of-plane), but we set the c-axis along the substrate (in-plane), which rendered a 90° offset. https://t.co/5KLD6z0lkq

25.11.2021 · Tweet

Second, the direction of our IR polarizer was mixed up. Wire grid polarizer is vertically polarized when the value is set to be 0° but we did it wrong previously. So the sets of the polarized reflection data are flipped for perpendicular and parallel directions during fitting. https://t.co/N1NstHXCNv

25.11.2021 · Tweet

The lucky thing is they both got 90° offsets and the two errors actually cancelled out, so the fitting is still valid, but the definition of the axes was wrong. To make it more clear, I put the original figure in the paper and our corrected figure here. https://t.co/SeqLuVSl2e

25.11.2021 · Tweet

By now, it seems we are done with BTS but this group of perovskite material really has a lot of interesting things to explore. So besides BaTiS3, we also looked at other combinations of elements to get a better understanding. Further interesting works are in progress.😉

25.11.2021 · Tweet

Happy weekend! Today I am gonna talk about FIB (focused ion beam) technology and what we did with a FIB!!! https://t.co/pCKPMUQUlQ https://t.co/Q0iKfcCacJ

27.11.2021 · Tweet

Focused ion beam (FIB) is a technique frequently used in semiconductor industry, materials science, and biological field. A FIB instrument is almost identical to an SEM, but uses a beam of ions rather than electrons. Pictures from: https://t.co/l96Un7Vpyy https://t.co/X2dhK5Hp6v https://t.co/Axhr3xeBcL

27.11.2021 · Tweet

FIB is a well-established technique for high-resolution area-selective milling and deposition. We can use a FIB to directly mill the specimen surface, which can be controlled with nanometer precision. FIB-assisted deposition has also been broadly used in micro-/nano-modification. https://t.co/DR6xbxeqOF

27.11.2021 · Tweet

Our new effort is to use a FIB to realize direct writing, mask-free, any number of doping levels in a single step. We demonstrate the spatial modification of the optical properties of metal oxides (zinc oxide ZnO and vanadium dioxide VO2) using a commercial FIB system.

27.11.2021 · Tweet

First, we demonstrate ion implantation using FIB, where we used zin oxide (ZnO) as a host material. Using a 30keV Ga+ FIB and thermal annealing, we demonstrated variable doping of ZnO, achieving plasma wavelengths from the mid-infrared to the near-infrared range. https://t.co/ABj1e4yTiQ

27.11.2021 · Tweet

Then we demonstrate defect engineering of VO2 using FIB. FIB implantation (without annealing) can also be used to introduce structural defects into a material, and the induced defect density can be continuously controlled by varying the ion fluence. https://t.co/AXafqfGciO

27.11.2021 · Tweet

Such defect-engineering techniques can be useful for locally modulating the insulator-to-metal transition (IMT) temperature of thin-film VO2. We achieved a reduction of the IMT temperature by ~15 °C in VO2. https://t.co/fSsJLd3RXe

27.11.2021 · Tweet

The FIB process doesn't require lithography or masking process. Due to the versatility of commercial FIBs, this technique can be used to modify and engineer materials with high resolution even for irregularly shaped materials where conventional lithography is challenging.

28.11.2021 · Tweet

Quantum Dots are a perfect example of how a name change resulted in history being lost. Originally called quantum heterostructures, then quantum boxes, the name “dots” is a semi-recent term. Today, we're going to explore this evolution! #sciencetwitter #nanomaterials #phdchat 🪡 https://t.co/kT3bvuId0b

14.12.2021 · Tweet

They began as a way to study quantum mechanics. First proposed in 1963, one of the first demonstrations was in 1974 by Dingle and Wiegmann from Bell Labs using a AlGaAs-GaAs-AlGaAs quantum well structure to study energy states of GaAs. https://t.co/c5O7qk1Zn8  @APSphysics

14.12.2021 · Tweet

This work led to several landmark papers, including the first demonstration of a quantum well laser in 1978: https://t.co/2KMa29Ra7w @APSphysics But, both of these papers involved epitaxy-based growth methods.

14.12.2021 · Tweet

To transition to largescale production (& enable apps like bio-imaging), it was neccesary to develop a wet-chemistry method. In comes the Chemists, & a pair of articles by L Brus from the 1980’s in J of Chemical Physics @AIP_Publishing https://t.co/EZn6JfhdbT (Pic is wrong)

14.12.2021 · Tweet

Article 2: https://t.co/4qRESg9l18 To differentiate these from the planar "quantum well" system, they were called "dots". #chemtwitter (Note: the picture is wrong)

14.12.2021 · Tweet

With both planar and liquid synthesis approaches in hand, researchers began exploring applications as well as new material systems to reach new wavelengths. And thus, the entire field of Quantum Dots/Wells was launched! #AcademicTwitter #technology https://t.co/w18fjJ9PM0

Hi again everyone: today I'll talk a bit about how electrons are organised in materials, and venture into the lab! While I prepare some material, let's see how everyone's doing: How do you like Tuesdays?

08.02.2022 · Tweet

So as we saw yesterday, there are LOADS of electrons in your average material. How can we organize them? We do this with the "band structure", for which a quick image search gives us lots of funky stuff! https://t.co/iS1vRZu7Tz

08.02.2022 · Tweet

These busy figures are sometimes affectionately called "spaghetti" plots 😅. https://t.co/Jn70Ets4XJ

08.02.2022 · Tweet

@bkpipr I'm not an expert on calculations myself, but there are lots of good online resources. I'll try to look something out.

08.02.2022 · Tweet

So where do these "bands" come from?

08.02.2022 · Tweet

Ok let's start from the top with a very simple "material": two hydrogen atoms "A" and "B". https://t.co/bFMRWCEI6U

08.02.2022 · Tweet

Each atom has a single electron that is found somewhere near the nucleus. Exactly where, we don't know, but the possible locations are shown by the little peak above each atom, representing the wavefunction.

08.02.2022 · Tweet

Both electrons will have the same energy level (shown on the right) when the atoms are far enough apart that they don't see each other.

08.02.2022 · Tweet

And if we bring them close together so they can see each other? What happens then to the energies of the two electrons? https://t.co/kWZXncg9Hd

08.02.2022 · Tweet

The region in red is key. That's where the atoms can interact: where their wavefunctions overlap.

08.02.2022 · Tweet

Now instead of two separate atoms we have one combined system, and it's the combinations of the wavefunctions that give us our new energies.

08.02.2022 · Tweet

Turns out we have two ways to combine these two electrons, as sketched here. Remember, it's that interaction region in red that's key! https://t.co/fnWKp1wArm

08.02.2022 · Tweet

We can either have a combination that adds togther in the interaction region (which we call "bonding") or subtracts and gives a zero crossing ("anti-bonding").

08.02.2022 · Tweet

These two possibilities have different energies, with the bonding state lower in energy than the anti-bonding one.

08.02.2022 · Tweet

As we add more atoms to our little system, there are more and more ways to combine all the electrons, so there are more energy levels! Here's a nice way of seeing that that I've taken from Hoffmann's paper: https://t.co/Q8uwVfTZK5 https://t.co/Z9q1I5xXLJ

08.02.2022 · Tweet

The dark and light balls represent the bonding and anti-bonding type pictures I drew before.

08.02.2022 · Tweet

So now we have a whole lot of energy levels. But it would still be useful to organise them a bit better.

08.02.2022 · Tweet

To do that we use not the real-space positions of the electrons but their MOMENTUM (k) in the crystal as an index along the x-axis. In this case we still have the bonding states at lowest energy, and the anti-bonding states at higher. Hoffmann: https://t.co/mhkoi8kpvd https://t.co/HcRVUhtBjQ

08.02.2022 · Tweet

And that is our "band" in energy and momentum space. All the complex spaghetti from before comes from this, just with more and different atoms! https://t.co/1g84DhYDBN

08.02.2022 · Tweet

Phew, we made it! And as a reward, this afternoon we can go and take a peak in the lab 😉. https://t.co/DYvnD0Zjjh

08.02.2022 · Tweet
