So what about those movies? https://t.co/1KLygJvwBh

09.02.2022 · Tweet

As I mentioned in the podcast chat, I'm interested in the DYNAMICS of electronic strucures (see also yesterday: spaghetti 😉)

09.02.2022 · Tweet

What that means for me is looking at how electrons behave on really short timescales: 10^-15 s or "femtoseconds". https://t.co/4hDJH2s1Gm

09.02.2022 · Tweet

We need to look at those very short times since that's where electrons do stuff like transfer energy. They are ultra fast! https://t.co/9KvGSbzkT9

09.02.2022 · Tweet

So our experiments use pulsed lasers to measure at such short times. Basically it goes like this: Excitation pulse (red) Wait... Probing pulse (blue) Electrons are detected https://t.co/Le4M3ODlHn https://t.co/vYYuYvfiX5

09.02.2022 · Tweet

So the excitation pulse gives energy to the system, and then the probe pulse takes a snapshot of what the electrons are doing depending on how long we wait between them.

09.02.2022 · Tweet

If we change the delay we can see how the electrons behave at all time points after the excitation pulse, and putting all those snapshots together we get a moving view on the electrons!

09.02.2022 · Tweet

It's kind of like making a slow motion movie: we take quick snapshots at lots of times and then put it all together. https://t.co/fT5PR39UYU

09.02.2022 · Tweet

And just like the video of the bursting water balloon helps us see how that process occurs, our electronic movies help us see the details of what exactly is going on inside materials! https://t.co/WgjNXnv5os

09.02.2022 · Tweet

Stay tuned for some real life examples!

09.02.2022 · Tweet

Like I said before, in our lab we use pulsed lasers to follow electronic behaviour down at the femtosecond timescale. The kinds of materials we're interested in can often dramatically change their physical properties. https://t.co/kiwfhDaqnh

09.02.2022 · Tweet

Here's one of our electronic structure movies. https://t.co/FftlR8qGhW You can see really clear differences before and after we excite the material (check out the timer on the right). https://t.co/BdEu5S3d2R

09.02.2022 · Tweet

From this data we can extract a lot of information about about the way this material behaves, both from the electronic and crystal point of view. Pretty neat, huh?

09.02.2022 · Tweet

Using different types of analysers gives us the opportunity to measure different aspects of the dynamics too, for example with a "momentum micrscope" we can look at scattering all throughout the Brillouin zone at once! https://t.co/I6wVbsWRyQ

09.02.2022 · Tweet

And we can also freeze the movie and take a more detailed look at the full electronic distribution. So beautiful! https://t.co/4rEnOxftFi

28.02.2022 · Tweet

I'll start with a current challenge, in the last field I entered: magnetic materials. Recent magnetic force microscopy (MFM) of sputtered Ni layer are slightly strange: it was magnetized in-plane, however still shows stirpes of out of plane magnetization!! https://t.co/Qnbe8Zg3BK

28.02.2022 · Tweet

This is a signature of materials showing "transcritical" magnetization loops, and we are trying to see how this is related to the structure (mechanical stresses?) of the underlying substrate. However, apart from the science>>

28.02.2022 · Tweet

A lesson I've learned, going into a new field, is how much good peer-review can contribute. Even in rejected work, good and thorough PR can go a long way. In this case, we really didn't know what to make of the "strange" loops we measured, until the right term came up. https://t.co/bSuc9Emdq7

28.02.2022 · Tweet

1/ Onwards and upwards! Or perhaps backwards (in time). I'd like to share parts of my journey from an BSc in EE to multifunctional nanomaterials and to pin-point the moment I was hooked on doing science - I hope you'll share yours (Refs. welcomed)

28.02.2022 · Tweet

2/ I joined a nanoelectronics lab for MSc (Yaish lab) when the nanoworld was gaining much attention. My project which was about single Si nanowire FETs. Naturally, it evolved to something completely different within a few months - mechanical properties of suspended SiNWs>> https://t.co/6nR3c4dCl6

28.02.2022 · Tweet

3/ It was pretty cool: the bottom-up NWs on the growth substrate looked like a spaghetti bowl, but you could still disperse individual ones, make them out in an optical mic. (despite ~ 30-60 nm in diameter) and use e-beam lithography and make suspended devices (Fig from paper) https://t.co/fJcUj7ndMW

28.02.2022 · Tweet

4/ at that time, using an AFM to bend/deform such NWs was quite common and the scientific community was in turmoil: what happens to the elastic properties of nanomaterials? Experimental reports were showing different trends...

28.02.2022 · Tweet

5/ It's a good time to remember a fundamental truth about nanomaterials: surface is much more important in nanomaterials. Think about the ratio between the surface area and volume of a sphere, it follows ~ 1/r. https://t.co/iYqJ5eJElc

28.02.2022 · Tweet

6/ So people said that the SiO2 surrounding the NW plays an important role in the mechanical properties as it is actually a core/shell composite. That's true - but not the whole story and does not account for the results

28.02.2022 · Tweet

7/ There is another interesting property of nanomaterials: they are much more flexible. As you recall, the NWs look like spaghetti, although they're made of brittle Si. That's because of their aspect ratio, which is very different than that of the Si wafer you use in the lab https://t.co/XF6kzGJoAh

28.02.2022 · Tweet

8/ So these tiny beams, although made of a relatively rigid material, exhibited quite the deformation under an AFM tip - in fact, the elastic regime went from bending to tension - as evident from the recorded force curves that displayed stiffening (Fig from paper) https://t.co/BHEDqs7CD3

28.02.2022 · Tweet

9/ So now we had basic beam theory (Euler–Bernoulli) and the addition of tension (great paper by Heidelberg et al) however, fitting the tension model to our measurements did not yield reasonable results (huge Youngs modulus for Si). that's when I got hooked on science https://t.co/4tJ6ikTbq9

28.02.2022 · Tweet

10/ We realized that people disregard the residual stress in the beams, and that it can be detrimental, especially if you use the linear model. So we added a residual stress term to the model, and kaboom - model yields very reasonable results

28.02.2022 · Tweet

11/ we found our wires belonged to two populations of Young's moduli - which was in agreement with their known crystalline orientations. and I know I have to keep on doing this thing :) find this paper here (it came a few years after the work was done) https://t.co/jZUoyIysLO

28.02.2022 · Tweet

12/ So that's how I started really loving science, which naturally led me to venture into a new topic epitaxial NW growth (tomorrow) and that's also how I got my name next to Euler's in review papers 😆 (Fig from doi:10.1039/C6NR00863A) https://t.co/sddFahb6cp

I also had good times in @ProfRachelGaN group, studying piezoelectricity in GaN. They have A LOT of porous GaN activity going on there - and we became interested in studying nanoporosity effects on GaN piezoelectricity It's actually quite interesting:

03.03.2022 · Tweet

porosity makes mater compliant - so in a piezoelectric this means you get a stronger response. Porous ferroelectric materials suffer a penalty due to pores interfering with poling process, however GaN is not ferroelectric, so this can actually be useful https://t.co/C9j64H2Bp7

Hello everyone! My name is Rebecca and I'll be taking over RealSci Nano this week. I'm a PhD student at @UofG_MCMP in the University of Glasgow and I can't wait to tell you about my research this week!

07.03.2022 · Tweet

I'm going to start off by introducing myself a bit more, and talk about how I ended up doing my PhD! I always loved physics, and knew from pretty young that I wanted to study it at uni and ended up doing an integrated masters in physics at the University of Kent

07.03.2022 · Tweet

It was there that I got into materials physics... kind of by accident. I was doing study abroad and missed the deadline for picking my masters project! I got assigned a materials project and very luckily, I loved it!

07.03.2022 · Tweet

My project was looking for a new phase in bismuth ferrite using x-ray absorption spectroscopy, specifically extended x-ray absorption fine structure, or EXAFS. As part of my project I got to go to Diamond Light Source, which felt like finally taking part in “proper” science!

07.03.2022 · Tweet

After that I decided to apply for PhDs because I knew I wanted to carry on studying, and because I’d really enjoyed my masters I decided to apply for materials projects. I accepted an offer from Glasgow, and that’s how I ended up where I am now!

07.03.2022 · Tweet

Finishing up the day by talking a little bit about my PhD! My project uses electron energy loss spectroscopy (or EELS - remember this term! We'll be coming back to it later in the week) to look at the mirror coatings of gravitational wave detectors

07.03.2022 · Tweet

I'll be going more into the specifics of my PhD later in the week, but suffice to say, knowing the structure of the mirror coatings can be really important to gravitational wave detectors, even though they're such a small component!

07.03.2022 · Tweet

So although I'm a materials scientist, my samples are used for gravitational wave astronomy. That's probably my favourite part of materials, and spectroscopy in particular; how cross discipline its applications are!

07.03.2022 · Tweet

I'll be talking about my research in more depth tomorrow but that's it for today, I'll leave you with a picture of the sun catching the buildings opposite my newly-returned-to office: https://t.co/EHBKbJEb6L

08.03.2022 · Tweet

Today I’m going to be talking about my PhD project (and definitely not procrastinating writing my thesis…). So like I said yesterday, my project uses electron energy loss spectroscopy to investigate the mirror coatings of gravitational wave detectors

08.03.2022 · Tweet

Starting with some context: why are the mirror coatings of GW detectors important? GWD are huge interferometers and they have have a bunch of mirrors inside them, not just at the end of the arms. The mirrors are made of silica...

08.03.2022 · Tweet

and it’s crucial they absorb as few of the laser photons as possible, as this would lead to heating of the mirrors, and cause warping, and affect the sensitivity of the detector.

08.03.2022 · Tweet

One of the things done to mitigate this is to coat the mirrors in multi-layer coatings, of high-refractive index and low-refractive index layers, but the coatings also contribute to the noise in the detector, particularly through thermal noise.

08.03.2022 · Tweet

Fully understanding the structure of the coatings is the first step in characterising that noise so it can be subtracted from the GW signal, or eliminating it entirely!

08.03.2022 · Tweet

So that’s the background for why coatings characterisation is important, I’ll be back after lunch to talk about HOW we do it!

08.03.2022 · Tweet

While coatings characterisation can take many forms, I use EELS. Very simple, for any unfamiliar with it, use an ARM, shoot electrons through sample, how much energy they’ve lost will tell you what elements are in your sample.

08.03.2022 · Tweet

The intensity of edge at the characteristic energy-loss is proportional to the amount of the element in the sample. We can also use high-angle annular dark field imaging to spatially resolve microscope images the heavy atoms will deflect the electron beam more strongly...

08.03.2022 · Tweet

providing images with Z-contrast. Combining these two (with some clever maths) gives you spatially resolved images with absolute quantification, i.e. you can count the number of atoms of a specific element in any given pixel.

08.03.2022 · Tweet

Going back to the coatings, it was known that there was argon in the coatings that wasn’t supposed to be there, and that there were little holes in the coatings. Using our technique we found they weren’t holes at all, but rather bubbles of argon.

08.03.2022 · Tweet

Because we could count the number of argon atoms in the pixels we could work out the pressures and densities of the argon bubbles! And this research has applications outside GW detectors -- bubbles of noble gas form in the cladding of nuclear reactors in a similar process!

10.03.2022 · Tweet

Took an unexpected break yesterday because it ended up being busier than expected! Thought I'd talk a bit about what my days have looked like this week as a final year PhD student!

10.03.2022 · Tweet

10.03.2022 · Tweet

10.03.2022 · Tweet

Pre-pandemic I was part of a wind band but that obviously fell by the wayside, and I haven't managed to go back yet. I'll do some Italian prep in the morning around cake and then after see what odds and ends need doing before wrapping up for the weekend!

11.03.2022 · Tweet

Thought I'd round up the week by talking a bit about spectroscopy itself! While the GW part of my research is very cool, it's the spectroscopy that I really love, so lets do a quick rundown!

11.03.2022 · Tweet

EELS, my speciality and therefore obviosuly the best kind, is done in a microscope. Advantages: if you have a microscope it can be done in house, high spatial resolution, other characterisation can be done with the microscope's other capabilities

11.03.2022 · Tweet

But it also has disadvantages, most notably that microscope samples are easily damaged by the beam and signal to noise is often a problem

11.03.2022 · Tweet

X-ray absorption spectroscopy is the other spectroscopy type that I have some hands-on experience with. Work very similarly to EELS, except you're using an x-ray beam at a synchtrotron.

11.03.2022 · Tweet

Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy is a type I don't have any experience with but works by exposing a sample to light and seeing what characteristic frequencies are absorbed

11.03.2022 · Tweet

X-ray fluorescence is the last type I'm going to talk about, and it works a little differently, rather than looking at what is absorbed, you expose your sample to X-rays and then see what is fluoresced by your sample

11.03.2022 · Tweet

All these spectroscopy types rely on the fact that the energy levels of different elements are different and unique, so you can figure out what elements are in your sample by looking for information at characteristic energies (543eV is the oxygen k-edge for example)

11.03.2022 · Tweet

If you have a spike at 543eV, there's oxygen in your sample!

11.03.2022 · Tweet

But why did I pick those two types of spectroscopy, when there's dozens to go around? Quite simple really, they're used a lot for one of my favourite applications of spectroscopy: conservation

11.03.2022 · Tweet

No, not the ecological kind but rather conservation of artworks and cultural artificacts! For these types of samples, understanding their structure and how they've changed since they were created can give important information on how to preserve them

11.03.2022 · Tweet

For really old samples, they can even tell us what they used to look like! For example, we know that old frescoes and the like used to be painted in vibrant colours thanks to trace amounts of these elements left behind

11.03.2022 · Tweet

This is part of why I really love spectroscopy; although there are lots of varieties the principles are the same throughout, and they can be used for such a variety of things from helping observe the universe to preserving our history!

A lot has happened since then on X-ray scattering, some of which I discuss in detail in my presentation here ( https://t.co/dtSvgNlXEh). But the field remains small. At the triannual scattering conferences, there are maybe ~300 participants. 2/10 https://t.co/bHjE3eid8S

14.03.2022 · Tweet

In theory, X-ray scattering’s simple. A narrow beam of X-rays goes through a sample, and we look at the “splash” (scattering pattern) that emerges. In practice, it’s easy to get such a pattern on your detector when you stick a sample in, but that’s where it stops being easy. 3/10

14.03.2022 · Tweet

The first problem is isolating the real scattering effects from your sample, from all the other – for lack of a better word - “shit”, that you get on your detector from the imperfections imposed by practicalities of reality. Part of this is the data correction step. 4/10 https://t.co/P1Jg1DCCaD

14.03.2022 · Tweet

Together with many colleagues, I’ve been working on perfecting this data correction problem for years, as summarized in this talk: https://t.co/0ricmoEmxc . We’re still working on fine-tuning the last few corrections, but most are available as part of @dawnscience 5/10

14.03.2022 · Tweet

@DAWNScience The other part is to take practical steps to clean up your scattering pattern before you collect it. That’s what we did when we bought and adapted an already heavily customized @xenocs_news instrument four years ago. 6/10

14.03.2022 · Tweet

@DAWNScience In trying to improve this already custom machine, we started changing hardware components and the control software. The data processing software that came with it was unused from day 1. More on our reasoning for that in a later thread. 7/10 https://t.co/9Xp9VZZGe1

14.03.2022 · Tweet

@DAWNScience So now we can get a pretty clean signal to begin with, and then extract only the scattering from the sample using the extensive data corrections. Now comes the analysis, the most painful part of the whole process. This almost invariably needs to be customized to the sample. 8/10 https://t.co/9uMr4FgNGG

@RKarsthof @svenja_lohmann @becky_rbc Good question. That much depends on the energy of the X-ray photons, but “X-ray” covers a whole range of energies. The ones we use have photons of 8 and 17 keV (emitted by copper and molybdenum targets, respectively). For copper, 1m of air would halve your flux. 1/n

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@RKarsthof @svenja_lohmann @becky_rbc So by evacuating, we lose fewer photons through absorption by air. A second phenomenon is scattering by air, when a beam of X-rays passes through air, interaction with the suspended molecules scatters a fraction, which muddies our sample signal. 2/n

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@RKarsthof @svenja_lohmann @becky_rbc We can subtract such parasitic background again from our measurement, but the counting noise (uncertainties) adds if you subtract the signal. So having any background decreases your signal-to-noise ratio rapidly. That means minimizing windows and air paths.. 3/n

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@RKarsthof @svenja_lohmann @becky_rbc This is investigated in detail in appendix F of our last monster paper: https://t.co/QS7G2trUPj . You’ll still see many instruments with air paths or windows, but we chose to minimize our background for the sake of improved statistics with a continuous vacuum path. 4/4

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@RKarsthof @svenja_lohmann @becky_rbc 5/4 Another option would be increasing the energy of our X-rays, higher energy interacts less with air (or any matter). There we have other problems: the efficiency of both monochromatic X-ray generation, focusing, collimation and detection all drop off. Additionally, to

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@RKarsthof @svenja_lohmann @becky_rbc 6/4 measure the same size nanostructure in your samples, you need to measure to much smaller angles. That requires even better beam parameters and exponentially longer instruments (as both collimation and flight path need to extend greatly).

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@RKarsthof @svenja_lohmann @becky_rbc 7/4 You then end up with high-energy X-ray scattering instruments of hundreds of meters long, exclusively found at synchrotrons (better beam parameters). These machines have a niche purpose, but given the difficulties, it’s easier to stay with lower-energy photons (fin].

15.03.2022 · Tweet

Trying to wrap my head around the effect of inter particle interactions to SAS patterns is doing my head in, so let me take a break by showing you how SAS analysis usually pans out (after many weeks of careful deliberation and trying (and failing) several approaches):

15.03.2022 · Tweet

Let’s start with one of the easier examples that @s9glen and I contributed to: a study by researchers of the @v_saggiomo group of @WUR on special optical properties of gold- and silver nanoparticles in 3D-printable composites. https://t.co/htQL7fyrFs

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR This was relatively easy from the X-ray scattering viewpoint, but still threw up a few interesting questions. So here, the researchers put gold and silver nanoparticles inside a polymer. Then, they would print that polymer in a filament-fed 3D printer into funny shapes. https://t.co/sTIAgrqfmj

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR We measured the scattering patterns of the silver nanoparticles suspended in their initial liquid, the silver nanoparticles in the PVA polymer, and the silver nanoparticles in the PVA polymer after printing. After correction, we get nice wide-range X-ray scattering data. https://t.co/N1Avn3li9q

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR So now we can get to the tea-leaf reading aspect of X-ray scattering: for those familiar with the method, we can already read off some information off of these scattering patterns: The shoulder at low Q tells us of one population of particles, https://t.co/Py2Cfa7qlJ

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR the lack of oscillations tells us they are polydisperse in shape or size, and the absolute scattering level tells us it’s a realistic amount of scattering assuming silver in liquid (so we didn’t fuck up on the data correction step or the phase assumptions). https://t.co/QKDxl9AmOj

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR So far so good, but wait! There’s a second hump in one of the samples, is that a second, independent population of smaller particles? It looks to be the case, so let’s dig deeper and actually analyze these patterns using my McSAS software (https://t.co/NTj6NMWEJ0). https://t.co/h5xP0QHFLj

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR This software needs an overall shape assumption (here spheres), and then spits out the size distribution required under that shape assumption to get this scattering pattern. Here, there’s no need to assume a gaussian or lognormal, monomodal or multimodal distribution. https://t.co/NOPs4XxBuB

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR So for these three measurements, we see: 1) a monomodal population of (silver) particles, 2) a bimodal population, silver particles and something else, and 3) a monomodal population of silver particles again. What’s going on here? https://t.co/HcyRJQv8nZ

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR Well, we first double-checked to make sure we didn’t make a mistake in measuring or correcting our data. Then we thought and discussed with the other scientists, and after some time, found out there’s a stabilizer added to the particles… https://t.co/IoTYPRBlzS

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR Stabilizers are typically organic molecules added to nanoparticle suspensions to make sure the particles don’t stick together immediately. In this case, the authors had added a large excess of PVP https://t.co/Nb7Sl3wTtb .

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR In the liquid sample, this PVP is swimming freely around, and has a low contrast compared to the liquid. When mixed into the PVA polymer matrix, however, it looks like this PVP is phase separating out into small globules alongside the particles → there’s our small population. https://t.co/5i51YN2asr

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR Then, when melting the entire composite at much higher temperatures during printing, these PVP particles dissociate and mix with the PVA polymer. At least that’s our working hypothesis, not contradicted by the data (best we can do without deeper study). https://t.co/tuLuTG9IKh

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR (An alternative is that at higher temperature, the PVP globules meld together to form a few large globules, I did not test for this explicitly)

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR During all this, the silver nanoparticles are mostly stable, although they do start clumping together a bit leading to an upward shift of our population. Apart from dimensions, we can also get volume(or mass) fractions out of this data, thanks to our absolute-scaled intensity.

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR In this case, there were no surprises, the silver was in there at the expected concentration, and the fraction of PVP also did not contradict our assumptions. But abs-scaled data is essential for double-checking assumptions and interpretations! https://t.co/dftVgraFko

15.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @V_Saggiomo @WUR So now you know what we can do with X-ray scattering data (for easy cases), but is it really true or did we just get lucky here? Why does it sometimes not work? Big questions worthy of upcoming threads… https://t.co/aK0gInqXAy

USAXS stands for ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering; measuring smaller angles, we can measure larger structures. I’ve been building machines for this for a while, here’s one we tested at @i22_DLS: https://t.co/RG7J4ggz3J

16.03.2022 · Tweet

@I22_DLS We also recently tested this in the MOUSE 🐭, and it seems to be working just fine! I’m not happy with the cable salad though, so that led to me starting on v.2 of the motor controller to help clean that up. The USAXS then allows us to measure structures up to 2-3 micrometer!

16.03.2022 · Tweet

@I22_DLS With our normal SAXS/WAXS operation in the MOUSE, we quantify structures with dimensions from ~0.5 Å to 300 nm, so the USAXS adds a nice decade on top of that. It’s a much more tedious scan to measure these ultra-small angles, but it’s more information and that’s always good.

Since the beginning of the technique, there has been a lot of skepticism, and rightfully so. I remember many papers stating that “SAXS dimensions are always bigger than TEM dimensions”, or papers explaining away differences with handwavy arguments. 1/7 https://t.co/EsdwqwfQAa

17.03.2022 · Tweet

This could be part of what gives X-ray scattering an occasional bad rep: even when it ostensibly works, the results aren’t comparable to other techniques, in particular to TEM, so why bother? However, when tested against standards, it matches! What’s going on here? 2/7

17.03.2022 · Tweet

Part of this was due to the (continuing!) poor data correction standards, more on this later. Another problem is the inherent complexities in accurate TEM size distribution determinations, which an electron microscopist can explain far better than I. 3/7 https://t.co/f6Hl0d1wBU

17.03.2022 · Tweet

But a main problem is that X-ray scattering gives a signal that closely matches a volume-weighted representation of the size distribution. (typically monodisperse) standards don’t have this, and voila, the size match between TEM and X-ray scattering is near perfect. 4/7

17.03.2022 · Tweet

But add a bit of polydispersity, and all intercomparisons must be corrected either one way or the other before comparing. One example of not enough effort in SAXS analysis, coupled with handwavy dismissals of discrepancies can be found in this paper ( https://t.co/V01owZTQIM) 5/8 https://t.co/RbXl7X4IoE

17.03.2022 · Tweet

This work has 1) no indication of data correction being done 2) fits that don’t fit (lacks dispersity) 3) hand-wavy excuses about volume weighting skewing their results. This is unfortunate, because a little bit of effort would’ve brought these results in line. 6/8 https://t.co/6W4DAXQGqB

17.03.2022 · Tweet

But as it is now, it looks like another piece of evidence that SAXS sucks. There are unfortunately many papers like this, I suspect the main issue is that not enough care is given to the experiment, probably due to juggling too many tasks and papers, or being overloaded. 7/9

17.03.2022 · Tweet

With microscopic techniques, if you don’t put enough effort into them, you still have a reasonably correct resulting projection (image). With X-ray scattering experiments, however, if it’s not done with sufficient care, the answer is plain wrong in unpredictable ways. 8/9 https://t.co/uV8F1B4Rjb

17.03.2022 · Tweet

And that segue’s nicely into my next topic: what has to go right for an X-ray scattering experiment to work?

🧵 How can you organize an X-ray experiment to avoid most of the mistakes? That’s something @s9glen and I recently wrote an absolute monster of a paper about (still a good read though!). That paper is here: https://t.co/hKYM8ordZg 1/

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen (apropos, that paper comes with a 20+ GB repository of data and jupyter notebooks used to calibrate, analyze and visualize: https://t.co/uZmFRAtWEI)

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen This paper takes an unconventional “holistic” approach: for an X-ray scattering experiment to go right, you must do good 1) sample prep, 2) data collection 3) data correction, 4) data analysis and 5) combining X-ray scattering results with those of other techniques 3/

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen Any imperfection in any of these, and your X-ray scattering experiment is unreliable. Do all these right though, and the results can be very gratifying. And that’s what we’re aiming for, absolute perfection.. (cc. @I22_DLS and @timmy864 for their help towards this) 4/ https://t.co/eZlTmPgV45

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 Step one is the sample preparation. Frustratingly for our materials science colleagues, it’s not easy to say what samples will and won’t work. I made a video that discusses a few details of sample selection for scattering: https://t.co/wxHCvWexHv 5/

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 Secondly, we have the data collection. We now collect an enormous amount of data in an automated way, measuring multiple repeats of 600s exposures of every sample in multiple instrument configurations. For a normal sample we typically do 600s * 33 repetitions per sample 6/ https://t.co/8M0PXLTb52

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 … this can rapidly increase though if we do special measurements or use multiple X-ray sources. These 33 measurements come with 33 flux, beam and transmission measurements to monitor instrument and sample stability, which are stored as part of the measurement metadata. 7/

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 And we do all this for up to 48 samples per two- to three-week “run”, so that’s easily 1000 measurements. We’ve adopted the NeXus format for storing all this data in an archival, easily understood and very comprehensive format in an HDF5 container. 8/ https://t.co/XUbpY1rzrq

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 Note, by the way, that this is far from the “standard” in the field (if there is such a thing). Many instruments and places still use clicky interfaces to start single measurements, doing things right on those machines is a royal pain in the ass. 9/ https://t.co/mc7p3KkyIV

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 In step 3, we take these NeXus files (containing the repeated datasets) and process them using the corrections implemented in the @dawnscience software by @jacobfilik together with @timmy864 over the course of several years. Here too, things are more extensive than normal. 10/

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik For example, nearly all the datacorrection steps are done on the 2D scattering images, before in the end they may be converted to a 1D scattering curve. We do this so that if there is alignment in the sample, we can get precisely corrected data for that in 2D. 11/

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik I am very proud of the data corrections, it has been a long journey, but now we have a universally applicable data correction sequence. Works for every sample we throw at it, both on the MOUSE, but also at the @i22_DLS beamline and lab instrument too! https://t.co/7Wa1HGdH2s

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik Given the success of that, I wish we could convince other X-ray scattering instruments to use these methods, but a combination of (perhaps) pragmatism and “not invented here”-syndrome seems to be blocking its adoption. Scientists can be surprisingly conservative! 13/

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik Also the “argumentam ad antiquitam” is one I hear often: “we’ve always done it like this…”, to which my response in most cases is “yes, and it’s always been shit”. But I digress.. This data correction is now automatic with us, no human input needed, no knobs to twiddle. https://t.co/8CVVGkkCel

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik So given our “as good as it could get”-data now, we move on to step 4: analysis. This is not automated by far, and it is our bread and butter. This is where we spend 80% of our time if not more, trying to find a model to fit the data with. That model needs to do two things: 15/

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik 1) the model needs to be able to describe the data precisely. That’s not always easy and sometimes requires quite a few components, and 2) the model needs to be physically realistic for that sample: the model components need to be justified with e.g. TEM images. https://t.co/UHRWSk2H6N

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik coming back to that last point, it’s no use having a fractal model to describe your data, if there are no fractals in your sample. Don’t use cylinders if there is no evidence for them, etc., etc. Your model must be in accordance with the physical structure of the sample. 17/ https://t.co/bhRliYE0Af

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik one problem with X-ray scattering analysis is that I can get many models to fit the same data. However, just because it fits your data doesn’t mean it’s the right model. X-ray scattering data doesn’t have a lot of information, so a lot hinges on using the correct model. 18/

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik And that trips people up. Here’s a paper that argues that since a disk model fits the data better than spheres or cylinders, it must be the right model: ( https://t.co/KjQsiiIevW ). McSAS tells me that the shape and size distribution are inherently linked. 19/ https://t.co/79vNsHJObz

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik That means that I can get a perfect fit with e.g. spheres, but also with cylinders (see images). The difference then lies in the size distributions. Both fits are equally valid, so you’ll need to supply extra evidence (for example TEM) to validate the shape assumption 20/ https://t.co/r5ui4ZgcBH

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik So in the end, for SAXS to be any good at all, all these aspects need to be flawless, from sample prep to interpretation of the analyses. And there’s no magic solution that fits them all.. That’s the challenge of the X-ray scattering field, and it’s what’s keeping us very busy! https://t.co/QZkS67peC0

17.03.2022 · Tweet

@S9Glen @I22_DLS @timmy864 @DAWNScience @JacobFilik And with these ridiculous machine efficiencies we’re reaching now, we’re trying to solve many dozens of independent analytical challenges every year. It’s honestly exhausting, and we really need more people in the team to help analyze and interpret these masses of data. 22/EOF

17.03.2022 · Tweet

I happen to reside in a pretty section of Berlin, and walking through it offers a nice glimpse into the older architecture styles of the early 1900s. What brings it down for me, though, is the eyesore created by the rows of parked cars. Seeing pictures of the same streets from 1/

19.03.2022 · Tweet

… from the past, it is amazing what space there is available on these streets, plenty for trams (since demolished) to drive around and still offer oodles of space for pedestrians and cyclists. That space has all been taken now by private oversized cars. 2/

19.03.2022 · Tweet

I understand the need for cars in areas with low population densities, and little in terms of public transport, but Berlin’s neither of those. Like Amsterdam in the 80s, this place needs a rethink of how people move around. This has become painfully obvious in the last two 3/

19.03.2022 · Tweet

In the last two years with rapid acceleration of bike use, something that was already increasing steadily year over year. We’re getting to the point (that I call the carpocalypse), where something needs to give. Until then, neither side will be happy and stress levels rise.

19.03.2022 · Tweet

It’s an interesting transition to experience, but also a very dangerous one. I see and experience aggression on the street on a weekly basis, I’ve been pushed off the road, shouted, honked and spat at, and overtaken with no space to spare more times than I can count.

19.03.2022 · Tweet

There’s no doubt in my mind that an accident will happen sooner or later, which will result in scratches on someone’s car, and possibly hospitalization on my side, it’s a very uneven damage balance. Oh yes, I’ve also been deliberately run into, but at that point I was on skates.

19.03.2022 · Tweet

I’ve received “lectures” from car drivers on that I need to show them “gegenseitige rücksichtname” when there was no space for them to overtake me. But I keep cycling, it’s free fitness for me, and a way to relax. In Japan, I did own a (nice RX-8) car which was fun…

19.03.2022 · Tweet

But I also noticed there that if I would commute to work by car, I would get very unhappy and stressed. Once I discovered that, I could remedy it and go by bike which alleviated things dramatically. It’s not a solution for everyone, I know, but for me it works.

20.03.2022 · Tweet

There was a thing in the Netherlands salary scheme called "superannuation", which if I remember right, was a yearly salary increase to compensate for inflation. No such things seems to exist here. So every year we're a little worse off it seems (there's no career plan here)

20.03.2022 · Tweet

We do have salary increases in the governmental "TVöD"-scheme, but the longer you stay in the scheme, the further apart they are - and the increases don't seem to cover the inflation we've had here for the last years. I often hear "but you like what you do, right?"

20.03.2022 · Tweet

However, my partner also likes what they do, and they get regular salary increases. Those who earn enormous salaries also probably like their jobs, so the argument doesn't hold. (in fact, those with tiny salaries aren't necessarily ecstatic about theirs..).

20.03.2022 · Tweet

Now I may just be another whiny millennial, but I suspect I'm not. I'm not an expert on wage disparity and inflation, though, so I'll leave this discussion there. However, if we want to encourage people to go into science, the least we can do is offer them a competitive salary.

20.03.2022 · Tweet

I'd also like to say a few words about argumentation and argumentative fallacies, a topic I believe should be part of any decent high-school curriculum. This forms the basis of - and essential tools for - critical thought processes.

20.03.2022 · Tweet

There are many ways in which we can be fooled - or how we can even fool ourselves. Some of these have been codified as argumentative fallacies. Learning about these has opened my eyes to them, I can recognize them in scientific papers too!

20.03.2022 · Tweet

I learned about many of these by reading Madsen Pirie's "How to win every argument". I believe this is out of print, but if you search, you can find a PDF on google: https://t.co/T77DmaUOKe It's a seemingly bland book with alphabetical listing, but the examples are ace!

20.03.2022 · Tweet

It inadvertently teaches you to recognize logical fallacies behind arguments, which you can then exploit to your advantage. But as mentioned, it also offers essential tools to recognize bullshit. Highly recommended! https://t.co/dTkDFDsHwO

20.03.2022 · Tweet

@svenja_lohmann Age doesn’t matter, mine are about 15 years old and have had a fair few sets of new wheels over the years 😁. Now the kid is also regularly going out with their friends so I’ve successfully passed on the bug!

20.03.2022 · Tweet

One last note about small angle scattering. I like building my own equipment but I’ve also seen many good X-ray scattering solutions offered by manufacturers. One thing bugs me though. The manufacturers are regularly doing the field a disservice… 1/2

20.03.2022 · Tweet

1/2 they’re selling their equipment with the impression that any monkey could flip the switch and get good results. That gives the impression the technique is easy and doesn’t require a dedicated expert. However, like TEM, such equipment needs a specialist to 2/3

20.03.2022 · Tweet

… to keep it up and running, and who can tell the users what they can (and moreover cannot) tell from the measurements. This misrepresentation has led to more than a few new instruments being left to collect dust not long after they were bought! 3/4

20.03.2022 · Tweet

In the worst case, the instrument is used poorly or incompetently, leading researchers to get disillusioned by the technique itself. So please, manufacturers, give the technique the respect it deserves, admit it needs a specialist, and you might end up with happier customers!

11.04.2022 · Tweet

@Andre_marinho91 Awesome! What kind of layered materials do you work with? TMDs?

11.04.2022 · Tweet

I hope you’ve all decided to have lasagna tonight! 🍴 Inorganic layered materials encompass many different compositions and structural motifs Let me tell you about a few of the awesome variations out there: 💪 Threading🧵

11.04.2022 · Tweet

Graphite and hexagonal boronitride (h-BN): These materials are made of one-atom-thick nanosheets. The individual 2D nanosheets are formed by covalent bonds forming repeating hexagonal structures. Meanwhile, the stack of sheets are held together only by weak Van der Waals forces https://t.co/jDiPFhwBNr

11.04.2022 · Tweet

Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs): TMDs have nanosheets that are typically three atoms thick. The transition metal, (i.e.Molybdenum), is sandwiched between layers of dichalcogenides (i.e sulfur). Here again, only Van der Waals forces hold stacks of nanosheets together. https://t.co/2EJxhYk2ZG

11.04.2022 · Tweet

Layered Double Hydroxides (LDH): 😍 LDHs are a class of anionic clays (i.e. hydrotalcite). The nanosheets have a positive charge and often anions like carbonate or chloride are found in between the layers along with water molecules. H-bonding makes them difficult to exfoliate. https://t.co/SLBF4zgTju

11.04.2022 · Tweet

Intergrowth Structures: A broad class of materials that often includes layered metal oxides and perovskites structures. (also layered oxysulfides, sulfides, and oxyfluorides) Some of these materials can be exfoliated into nanosheets while others refuse to. https://t.co/BkGqNCz3Jc

11.04.2022 · Tweet

Lasagna á la Nano: The most delicious type of layered material. Flexible sheets of pasta are separated by interlayer spaces filled with ricotta or béchamel, and bolognese sauces. Easy to mechanically exfoliate with a fork. 😂 https://t.co/j4aqf3u5aQ

12.04.2022 · Tweet

Today I'm going to be talking about how I synthesize different inorganic layered materials. Not all methods need high temperatures, but this one does! #chemtwitter https://t.co/m0wXhJ3vND

12.04.2022 · Tweet

So, today is dedicated to writing a bit about atomic force microscopy (#AFM) and related techniques for electrochemical analysis and the possibilities in our lab. We were finally able to get our own AFM last October, and I am super happy that we now have all possibilities

26.04.2022 · Tweet

to perform measurements at different temperatures between 0-120 °C and also in different gas environments and also in liquids. This is me in front of the new instrument, looking very relieved that the installation (finished on the previous day) went so well. https://t.co/4Qf5xVAamq

26.04.2022 · Tweet

@Loberd3 I was really lucky to acquire so much money over the years to get my hands on 3 of them. The Keysights (black big box -> 5600 LS, small grey box -> 5500) were purchased during my doctoral studies at the Chemistry department and the Cypher ES is for my new group at @fzj_iek

26.04.2022 · Tweet

@Loberd3 @fzj_iek But you are right: AFM experiments are extremely time consuming...

26.04.2022 · Tweet

Most of you will already have an idea how an atomic force microscope works. Basically, a very small tip with a reflective backside is dragged along a sample surface. An AFM tip is really small. In the image, what you can see is the chip, on which the cantilever https://t.co/EqLtvsryEq

26.04.2022 · Tweet

(the small antenna protruding from the pointy part of the chip) is mounted. At the end of the cantilever, pointing in the direction of the viewer, sits the AFM tip. It is only visible under the microscope.

26.04.2022 · Tweet

This is how it look when we fix the cantilever into the tip holder of our Cypher ES. If you are tired, drank too much coffee, are excited, are clumsy, drank too few coffee… there are 1000 reasons, why mounting the #AFM tip can go wrong. https://t.co/yYgN25P18V

26.04.2022 · Tweet

As they cost between 15-200 € depending on which tip you have, this is sometimes really annoying. After some years, however, you are properly trained to loose only a few tips per year… still makes me angry every time it happens. though. https://t.co/nJqkPRCl9h

26.04.2022 · Tweet

The position of the tip on the sample can be determined with very high accuracy by pointing a laser on the reflective backside and measuring the reflection with a four-field detector. This can either be performed in constant contact with the surface https://t.co/YwyYK6J94x 1/3

26.04.2022 · Tweet

or the tip can be oscillated at its resonance frequency (normally in the kHz range) if the surface is sensitive. This is called tapping mode, as the surface is only touched very gently. The resulting image gives information about the topography of a sample. 2/3

26.04.2022 · Tweet

Here for example, is a Li4Ti5O12 (LTO) thin layer on silicon substrate: each pyramid is a spinel single crystal. Is a typical lithium ion conductive material used in the electrode of lithium ion #batteries. 3/3 https://t.co/9La3TIqBfx

26.04.2022 · Tweet

We usually stick the samples onto simple metal plates with conductive C-tabs. They are then fixed in the specimen holder with a magnet. For electrochemical measurements we have sample holders with a cable attached to them 1/3 https://t.co/qzWO2HcyCR

26.04.2022 · Tweet

or we contact the sample directly with Ag paste and a small Pt wire. The special thing about our approach is that we mostly do not work with samples specially made for the AFM, but get e.g. electrodes from post-mortem analysis directly from a normal cell. 2/3 https://t.co/7hFwcxyDym

26.04.2022 · Tweet

These samples are often very rough and an analysis away from the topography is therefore often very difficult. 3/3

26.04.2022 · Tweet

Apart from getting very nice topography images, we can AFM-based measurements to get information about physical characteristics of a sample. As the institute I am working at is dedicated to Ionics in Energy Storage, obviously we are very interested in 1/8

26.04.2022 · Tweet

ion and electron conductivity of materials. Electron conductivity of materials can be measured very easily with the so called conductive AFM (CAFM) or current sensing AFM (CS-AFM) which both means the same: we take an AFM tip with conductive coating 2/8

26.04.2022 · Tweet

(Au or Pt are common) and apply a voltage between the tip and a back contact which is attached to the sample (I mainly use conductive Ag paste to paint a contact). 3/8 https://t.co/wvOjbLMOz3

26.04.2022 · Tweet

We can then measure exactly the current at each position where the AFM tip is and get corresponding information on topography and current flow. 4/8 https://t.co/hLDxnqMxF3

26.04.2022 · Tweet

Here is an example: the topography and corresponding CS-AFM image of a cathode material with consists of a polymer binder and large graphite flakes. The applied tip bias was +2.5 V. 5/8 https://t.co/aTUueErYBg

26.04.2022 · Tweet

As you can see, the flat areas on top of the flakes are not that conductive but the rims (very dark red, nearly looks black) have a high conductivity. This is to be expected as graphite is only conductive along the basal plains. 6/8

26.04.2022 · Tweet

What you also can see: AFM images do not necessarily have to be in old-school brown images but can actually be in every color you like, which brings me to my next poll: 7/8 https://t.co/pYwiYTvoAC

26.04.2022 · Tweet

What is your preferred color code for #AFM images? 8/8

26.04.2022 · Tweet

So for me, I normally use brown or black and white for topography images and thermal for KPFM/CS-AFM images, so that the attention of the viewer is directly drawn to the colorful image.

26.04.2022 · Tweet

Now we come to my method of choice: Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy or KPFM (sometimes also SKPM). With this method, we can use the AFM to measure the contact potential difference between a metal-coated AFM tip (I mainly use tips with Pt/Ir coating as some of our samples 1/5

26.04.2022 · Tweet

have issues with Au) and the sample with high lateral resolution. In theory, as can be seen on the image, we can precisely measure the Fermi level of a given semiconductor. In a single phase material, this gives us direct information about variations of local defect 2/5

26.04.2022 · Tweet

concentrations (e.g. variations of dopant cation concentrations, vacancies in the lattice or contaminants). There is a very nice, easily understandable paper by Zhang and Yates (https://t.co/Tljab3u7DN) about the situation at interfaces, if you would like to get more details. 3/

26.04.2022 · Tweet

Also, there is another paper by Örnek et al. (https://t.co/MfBJUQRwbu) which explains very well the confusion between electrochemists and physicists, because in electrochemistry the KPFM signal is called surface potential while it is technically the Volta potential. 4/5

26.04.2022 · Tweet

I’ll stick with surface potential though, because my colleagues are mainly electrochemists and speaking about Volta potential tends to confuse them even more than my explanations about AFM-based measurements already do. 5/5

26.04.2022 · Tweet

But of course, measuring absolute value for the Femi energy level (or work function) of a sample with KPFM is not as easy as it sounds: for one, we cannot “see” the local chemical composition, so we have to use methods like XRD, XPS, EDX or EELS to get further information 1/5 https://t.co/ynSJAUw1Sa

26.04.2022 · Tweet

about inhomogeneities. With polymers it becomes even more complicated as compared to semiconductors. Second, even small amounts of adsorbed species on the sample surface (like water from air moisture) can have a small effect on the signal. 2/5

26.04.2022 · Tweet

Absolutely accurate measurements yielding absolute numbers can only be performed with super-clean samples in vacuum. 3/5 https://t.co/UXV84aVFVn

26.04.2022 · Tweet

We cannot measure in vacuum, but as we are often working with Li metal samples from our colleagues, we have the possibility to either assemble the measurement cell in a glovebox (see image) or we even have one AFM which is attached to a mini-glovebox. 4/5 https://t.co/J4SHTFTnqE

26.04.2022 · Tweet

The AFM cell can be completely closed and is then sealed, so we can keep the sample under Ar or we can also switch between different gas environments if necessary. 5/5 https://t.co/YYdIiOfPHs

26.04.2022 · Tweet

Today I would like to talk a bit about #electrolytes and MIEC materials. So let’s directly dive into definitions. An electrolyte is a material that can transport charge not by using electrons but by transporting anions or cations. Typically, if you built a Daniell element 1/6

27.04.2022 · Tweet

during school time or during a practical course at the uni, you probably have used aqueous solutions of some salts to receive a voltage from your system. https://t.co/jgn2sjaqit 2/6

27.04.2022 · Tweet

The interesting point is, that charge transport by ions is not only possible in liquids. There is a plethora of solid electrolyte materials available, ranging from polymers with dissolved salts in them (e.g. PEO with LiTFSI as a typical Li+ conductor) or Nafion 3/6

27.04.2022 · Tweet

(a proton conductive polymer) to Y-doped ZrO2 (high oxygen ion conductivity around 1000 °C, can be found as sensor material in the lambda probe in your car https://t.co/Ow4qpZGtEW). 4/6

27.04.2022 · Tweet

You cannot build energy storage devices without cheap, mechanically and chemically stable and easy to fabricate electrolytes! They are absolutely necessary for getting away from #fossilfuels, 5/6

27.04.2022 · Tweet

so recent events underline the importance of ongoing research in this field to improve #batteries etc. 6/6 https://t.co/uc1RvytP5x

27.04.2022 · Tweet

BTW: There are also some fun possibilities to use "aqueous" #electrolytes... have a look at this video of the Royal Society of Chemistry @RoySocChem where they used 2,923 lemons to generate a voltage. https://t.co/Sf4Xw1EpVj So, if life gives you lemons, make a #battery 🍋🔋.

27.04.2022 · Tweet

Apart from these pure ion conductors, we also find mixed conductors, which exhibit ion conductivity on the one hand, but also a non-negligible electron or hole conductivity on the other hand. These materials are MIECs or Mixed Ion-Electron Conductors. 1/

27.04.2022 · Tweet

MIECs are extremely useful for energy storage applications. Of course, they cannot be used as a standard electrolyte material in batteries or fuel cells, as they would generate a short circuit between the anode and the cathode. But they can be used at the electrodes 2/

27.04.2022 · Tweet

to include and exclude e.g. lithium ions during charging and discharging of the cell (e.g. Li4Ti5O12 or lithium titanate, which is a common material used at the anode of lithium ion batteries) or they can be used for proton or oxygen ion permeation in fuel cells 3/

27.04.2022 · Tweet

(most prominent example would be the oxygen ion conductor Ba0.5Sr0.5Fe0.8Co0.2O3 or BSCF). In the image, you can see BSCF samples glued to the metallic #AFM sample holders with a dip of conductive paste at the edges. https://t.co/rb87y0xLdf

27.04.2022 · Tweet

For my dissertation and until today, I have mainly been dealing with oxygen ion conductors – a bit with BSCF, but most importantly (for me) with doped cerium dioxide. CeO2 is a very versatile material. It has cubic fluorite structure and can accommodate a lot of different 1/5

27.04.2022 · Tweet

elements in comparably high concentrations as partial substitute for the Ce. Depending on the valency of these dopants, we can distinguish acceptor dopants (valency < 4), which increase oxygen ion and hole conductivity in the material, 2/5 https://t.co/53TpgTeQIa

27.04.2022 · Tweet

and donor dopants (valency > 4) which promote electron conductivity. Acceptor doped ceria is cream-colored to brownish, while donor doped ceria is black and has a metallic shine. 3/5

27.04.2022 · Tweet

In the image, you can see a set of ceria-ZnO mixtures from my Ph.D. Zinc serves as slight acceptor dopant, but has a relatively low solubility in the ceria matrix. 4/5 https://t.co/pn7rRj7qbs

27.04.2022 · Tweet

BTW: have you ever seen the gorgeous colors the natural mineral fluorite (CaF2) has? And that it glows when illuminated with UV-light? Also, team #fluorite was in the semi-finals of last-years @MineralCup and you can find a lot of nice Scicomm and images of fluorites there ♥️ 5/5 https://t.co/HdT8P5szFX

Back to our MIEC CeO2… Our main goal was to tailor the electron and ion conductivity of CeO2 by using combinations of different dopants in order to maximize the oxygen permeation under certain conditions. For oxygen permeation, you need a gradient of the 1/4 https://t.co/LR4CGVKRII

27.04.2022 · Tweet

oxygen partial pressure between both sides of a membrane made of acceptor doped CeO2, e.g. by having air on one side and Ar as sweep gas on the other side. Oxygen ions will then move through the material to equilibrate the conditions. 2/4

27.04.2022 · Tweet

As the charge balance has to be kept, electrons have to move in the opposite direction. So, for really high permeation rates you need both good electron and good oxygen ion conductivity. This has already been achieved with BSCF, but his material is not chemically stable 3/4

27.04.2022 · Tweet

against CO2, as the Ba and Sr on the A sites tend to form carbonates. Ceria, in contrast, is chemically really stable and uses much less transition metals (Co is the main issue here as it is toxic, often mined under dubious conditions and also is really expensive). 4/4

27.04.2022 · Tweet

Typical applications for oxygen permeation membranes could be O2 generation for medical or scientific purposes where O2 has to be very clean or for the so-called oxyfuel process (that was the objective of my dissertation). Here, fuels are burned with pure oxygen to achieve 1/3

27.04.2022 · Tweet

maximal heat output. Excess heat from the process could heat a membrane O2 generation plant, as typical solid oxygen permeation membranes need optimal temperatures between 700-1000 °C to work properly. By adjusting the burning process, gas burned with pure O2 would lead to 2/3

27.04.2022 · Tweet

very pure CO2 exhaust, which could then be subjected to sequestration (carbon capture and storage, CCS). Apart from this, ceria can also be used as electrode material in solid oxide fuel cells. https://t.co/AUrFrFSHtw 3/3

27.04.2022 · Tweet

With my change to the Helmholtz Institute Münster @fzj_iek, I also slightly broadened by focus: apart from oxygen ion conductors I now also deal with lithium ion and proton conductors. Most of my colleagues work with #electrolytes (mainly for lithium ion #batteries) and my group https://t.co/KfvC9eJyGX

27.04.2022 · Tweet

adapted to materials with very different characteristics: solid ceramics behave differently compared to thin films which behave differently compared polymers or polymer-particle composites. 3/4

27.04.2022 · Tweet

This is actually what I like most: every series of experiments has a different question and different challenges. I‘ll never get bored! 🥳4/4

Today, I would first like to talk a bit about #AFM-based #electrochemistry. Electrochemistry deals with the connection between electrical and chemical processes in a material. For example, when we apply a voltage on an ion conductive material, we apply a force, which moves 1/6

28.04.2022 · Tweet

the ions, which in this example are the charge carriers, in one direction. This can lead to local depletion or enrichment phenomena or it can trigger chemical reactions. This is the point, where AFM-based measurements come into play: “conventional” electrochemical 2/6 https://t.co/PgRpe5eo3r

28.04.2022 · Tweet

experiments like impedance spectroscopy or cyclovoltammetry normally work with macroscopic electrodes. This means that the results you get when you gather information about processes in your sample generally represent 3/6 https://t.co/6QwdVhYB15

28.04.2022 · Tweet

an average over the whole chunk of the sample which is covered by the electrodes. This is nice, if you would like to get information about your sample as a whole, but if you are after microscopic information e.g. about inhomogeneities or to inform some theoretical models, 4/6

28.04.2022 · Tweet

this can be a problem. #AFM can help here: we have a very small measurement tip which can also be used as an electrode if it is e.g. coated with metal (standard AFMs come with an internal potentiostate). So, we can easily access tiny areas of the sample and 5/6

28.04.2022 · Tweet

have a look on electrochemical characteristics without polarizing the whole sample. Using the AFM, we can for example apply voltages between tip and sample and measure the current flow (local cyclovoltammetry). 6/6 https://t.co/VbzSsLUVOW

28.04.2022 · Tweet

As the AFM tip is so small, the majority of the voltage drop is directly near the tip (if we use a large back contact) and the majority of the sample are unaffected, yielding information about very small areas. 1/5 https://t.co/o3yRzDBxmk

We even have an electrochemical measurement cell to perform in situ measurements with a sample that is covered with liquid electrolyte: the sample is put on a brass counter electrode and covered with liquid electrolyte, the copper working electrode and the silver 2/5

28.04.2022 · Tweet

pseudo-reference electrode (inserted through the small hole in the visible in the plexiglass of the lid) dip into the liquid. The AFM tip in this case is current free and can monitor e.g. changes in the surface morphology during charging and discharging of an 3/5 https://t.co/xEhcOoN00K

28.04.2022 · Tweet

electrode material sample. In theory, this sound very nice. In reality, this often means a lot smaller signal-to-noise ratio compared to “conventional” electrochemical methods and also a higher standard deviation, as the results of 4/5

28.04.2022 · Tweet

AFM are only for the very small part of the sample, while the “conventional” methods already yield an average results and normally are fairly comparable. 5/5

28.04.2022 · Tweet

So, a lot of AFM-based electrochemistry is about finding the right sample preparation procedure, and making many, many measurements to get good statistics. One major problem is the sample surface itself. For ceramic samples, this normally is not a big obstacle, but polymer 1/

28.04.2022 · Tweet

samples can be really tricky as they sometimes tend to be sticky, depending on the material. In some cases, the whole cantilever is covered immediately, so there is no possibility to do any measurements at all. https://t.co/xn511bjzsW

28.04.2022 · Tweet

To all #AFM enthusiasts out there: how do you deal with sticky surfaces, especially with glue- or honey-like polymer layers which you want to measure? Freezing? Functionalized cantilevers? I would be happy for helpful comments! @AFMCommunity https://t.co/FNJISACMOz

28.04.2022 · Tweet

Another point is measuring samples with very low (ionic or electronic) conductivity by using KPFM: the samples tend to accumulate static charge and the signal can be completely changed by this. 1/5

28.04.2022 · Tweet

To the #AFM and #KPFM community: What are your tricks to prevent static charging of the samples during KPFM measurements? Please comment😃! @AFMCommunity 2/5 https://t.co/cOVOD9g0PJ

28.04.2022 · Tweet

In our lab, there are some measures we can take, if the sample shows electrostatic charging: First, it is always a good idea to ground the sample (e.g. by attaching a wire with a little dot of silver paste and attaching this to instrument ground). 3/5

28.04.2022 · Tweet

Second, it sometimes helps (for hard samples) to gently brush them with some aluminum foil. There even is an ion brush available for such issues, but I have never used one so far. Do you have experience with this? 4/5

28.04.2022 · Tweet

A third possibility, which is only the last resort when measuring KPFM, is to increase the humidity in the sample chamber. H2O can then build a monolayer on the sample surface which is quite effective to get rid of surface charge, BUT it also influences the KPFM signal… 5/5 https://t.co/CDi5DoWG3m

28.04.2022 · Tweet

As you perhaps may have heard in the podcast, there is actually one set of studies I am especially proud of 🥰. Already during my Ph.D. I started to develop and further adapt a method, where the diffusion coefficient of my oxygen ion conductive samples can be measured using 1/7

28.04.2022 · Tweet

KPFM measurements combined with a polarization experiment. First, the initial state of the sample’s surface potential is measured using KPFM, second, a certain point on the sample surface is chosen and we apply a defined voltage between the tip and the sample for a certain 2/7

28.04.2022 · Tweet

amount of time. Afterwards, we switch back to KPFM and measure the decay of the introduced potential gradient over time. As the oxygen ion conductors are really bad conductors at room temperature, the surface potential gradient relaxes very slowly 3/7 https://t.co/csaDBOgyLU

28.04.2022 · Tweet

(sometimes taking several hours) so it can be easily mapped. Recently, we were able to show, that it is even possible to address single ceria grains in a composite made of ceria as oxygen ion conductor and a Fe-Co-spinel as electron conductor https://t.co/XHURQu4Kqo 4/7 https://t.co/fMzIXST4Pc

28.04.2022 · Tweet

In the image, the ceria grains have a distinctly higher surface potential than the spinel and can thus easily be contacted.5/7 https://t.co/0yw30KNxxk

28.04.2022 · Tweet

Compared to conventional electrochemistry or permeation experiments, this is a huge advantage. Another way of getting more information about single constituent would be polarizing the whole sample – something we will try for comparison in the near future. 6/7

We were very happy, that our research to apply this technique to #battery materials was awarded with a 3rd place in the poster competition for my PhD student Christina at the #AdvancedBatteryPower Conference this year. 7/7

28.04.2022 · Tweet

to visualize the boundary between ceramic particles and ion conducting polymers in a hybrid lithium battery electrolyte (https://t.co/NP11XEy0Ef). This was my first independent paper as #NewPI and my first all-female authors paper… perfect for #GirlsDay2022 3/3

28.04.2022 · Tweet

So why are these boundaries so important? 3/3 https://t.co/Ky4qVXmHMZ

Hybrid electrolytes are currently in focus of some large investigations, but it is not really clear, which role the particles have and if they really take part in the charge transport themselves. In polyethylene oxide (PEO), which was one of the polymer hosts we 1/8 https://t.co/VwvdsPYko8

28.04.2022 · Tweet

investigated, it is assumed that particles mainly surpress partial crystallization of the PEO which improves conductivity. So it does not really matter, if the particles are able to transport Li ions themselves as long as they interact favorably with the polymer. 2/8

28.04.2022 · Tweet

The other polymer matrix we investigated was MEEP (poly[bis-2-(2-methoxyethoxy)-ethoxyphosphazene]), which does not show crystalline domains. Particle addition (image below) does not have a significant effect on the Li conductivity of this material, so possibly the particles 3/8 https://t.co/B0BRp3nfWD

28.04.2022 · Tweet

just do not take part in the transport processes. A possible reason could be a high resistance for Li ions to transfer from polymer to particle and/or back. Normally, this should lead to very restricted differences of the surface potential directly at the boundary between 4/8

28.04.2022 · Tweet

particles and polymer. We were able to show that both in PEO and in MEEP, there are some small-scale variations of the surface potential visible, which depend on the type of particle (pure electrolyte, typical anode or cathode material) and on the concentration of the 5/8

28.04.2022 · Tweet

conductive salt in the polymer. Why these exists and what they tell us about conduction processes is a topic we are still investigating. 6/8

28.04.2022 · Tweet

28.04.2022 · Tweet

particles by comparing the phase images: the LFP is much harder than the polymer matrix and can easily be distinguished. 8/8

Good morning everyone. Today I would to zoom in a little bit more on materials we discussed previously and talk again about boundaires, in this case about grain boundaries. So, what is a grain boundary (GB) and why are they so important? 1/6 https://t.co/Ihb7Ou8hSZ

29.04.2022 · Tweet

Crystallographically speaking, a grain boundary in a single phase material is a very small area (1-2 nm width) in a crystalline material, where two areas - the grains - with different crystallographic orientation touch each other. There is a certain amount of lattice 2/6

29.04.2022 · Tweet

mismatch and overall confusion in this zone, so it’s the preferred place for single phase materials to dump all the ions which do not perfectly match the lattice. Also, point defects such as voids or “vacancies” in the lattice normally occur in a higher concentration at GB. 3/6 https://t.co/zNMcSXHLvU

29.04.2022 · Tweet

This increased concentration of so-called defects (e.g. vacancies, dopant ions, contaminations) severely change the characteristics of the charge transport at grain boundaries compared to the bulk of the material. In acceptor doped ceria, GB are mainly slowing down the oxygen 4/6

29.04.2022 · Tweet

ion transport in perpendicular direction, while the electron conductivity along the GB is often enhanced, especially when transition metal oxides are added e.g. as sintering aids. 5/6

29.04.2022 · Tweet

This also leads to a difference of the surface potential of the GB compared to the bulk, which can be measured with KPFM and related techniques. 6/6

29.04.2022 · Tweet

In the past, I have worked with other research groups to investigate grain boundaries in a very exciting and versatile material: ZnO. This material normally is not so well known for its ionic conductivity (although there is some proton conductivity possible) but for

29.04.2022 · Tweet

electronic applications. Historically, it has been used as a pigment, but nowadays you can also meet it in sunscreen or ointments for baby butts because it has an anti-inflammatory effect. https://t.co/AvYpVyzjKs

29.04.2022 · Tweet

Regarding the electrochemical aspects of the GB: it has been shown that negative charges represented by missing zinc cations agglomerate directly at the grain boundary, while a positively charged space charge layer (SCL) surrounds the grain boundary. This SCL is produced

29.04.2022 · Tweet

mainly by increased concentrations of oxygen vacancies and zinc on interstitial lattice sites but also impurity donor cations (D) at the place of zinc. D can either be donor dopants (H+ can also be a donor dopant in ZnO) or impurities like Bi or Sb. https://t.co/FiBbazBfqJ

29.04.2022 · Tweet

In a collaboration with @JGonzalez_83, we were able to show by #KPFM measurements, that the potential barrier height at the grain boundaries of ZnO is strongly depending on the synthesis process. https://t.co/4CFXVl1V3g The work was focused on a new sintering method (spark 1/4

29.04.2022 · Tweet

plasma sintering with addition of a small amount of water) that achieved dense, nanocrystalline ZnO pellets at only 250 °C. The densification was even better, when small amounts of zinc acetate were added to the water to manipulate the pH, and the group was wondering how to 2/4 https://t.co/h88Nglxju3

29.04.2022 · Tweet

show what was going on at the GB. By using #KPFM and supported by impedance spectroscopy measurements focusing on the bulk and grain boundary conductivity, we were able to show that the treatment led to very high potential differences between grains and grain boundaries, 3/4

29.04.2022 · Tweet

which means that there are a lot of defects around. For sintering, this is beneficial, as a high concentration of defects lowers the activation energy of the atomic diffusion. This is of course a simplified version, so for more details, please have a look at the paper😃🔬📚4/4

29.04.2022 · Tweet

So far, I have been talking about ZnO pellets, but now we are coming to the promised #AFM measurements of ZnO stars: The Ceramics for Smart Systems group from the Instituto de Cerámica y Vidrio, CSIC in Spain was performing research on ZnO for antimicrobial applications. 1/8 https://t.co/e3NtiwOWfg

29.04.2022 · Tweet

For this purpose, they already had synthesized star-shaped ⭐️ ZnO particles, which were working pretty well against the common germs Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus as well as against growth of the fungus Aspergillus niger 🦠🍄. 2/8

29.04.2022 · Tweet

Cathodoluminescence imaging showed that the tips of the stars had a slightly increased defect concentration compared to the bulk of the stars, but CL cannot see, whether these defect lead to a more positive or more negative potential at the tips. 3/8

29.04.2022 · Tweet

So they asked me to perform KPFM on the particles. In #AFM, the stars look more like little clouds, as you can see in the topography image. 4/8 https://t.co/WrHXANaYb8

29.04.2022 · Tweet

To date that was one of the most annoying samples as the particles kept sliding away as soon as they were touched by the AFM tip, but I was finally able to get some decent images of some. Side effect: I have greatly expanded my repertoire of swear words during this time. 5/8 https://t.co/VNUkUtXTJE

29.04.2022 · Tweet

Finally, by combining our data, we were able to show that the star-shape of the particles which consist of stacked ZnO micro-platelets led to negative charge accumulations at the tips of the stars with an extremely high potential difference of up to 3.5 V between 6/8

29.04.2022 · Tweet

bulk and tips. Apparently, 🦠 and 🍄do not like that. As the antimicrobial effect is due to physical characteristics of the particles and not due to chemical interaction, the major advantage is, that it will not wear off, so these kind of particles could be 7/8

29.04.2022 · Tweet

ideally suited for antimicrobial coatings. For a more detailed analysis, please have a look at the paper https://t.co/OMXpFmc4D6 8/8

29.04.2022 · Tweet

For my dissertation and also afterwards, the main material I worked with are CeO2 (ceria) based materials. Ceria has a fluorite structure. By doping with cations with lower valency than 4+, the material becomes also oxygen deficient. The free oxygen vacancies in the 1/3

29.04.2022 · Tweet

lattice allow for oxygen ions to move through the material by a hopping mechanism. At grain boundaries, this happy hopping is much more difficult. Previous investigations found a much higher surface potential compared to the grain interior, that inhibits the propagation of 2/3 https://t.co/Zb7BtlR7nw

29.04.2022 · Tweet

the oxygen vacancies, which have a net positive charge compared to the rest of the lattice. 3/3

29.04.2022 · Tweet

Last year, I was able to show that we can use #KPFM to not only measure the height of the grain boundary potential barrier in ceria in dependence on grain boundary composition, but we can also us this method to determine the width of the potential anomaly. I used a

29.04.2022 · Tweet

standard material for oxygen permeation (Gd-doped ceria) and added Al2O3 to get a model system. Al2O3 is an insulator and it has already been shown that increased concentrations of Al2O3 in combination with ceria (which is used for catalysis reactions where ceria is

29.04.2022 · Tweet

the catalyst and Al2O3 is the substrate) increase the potential barrier at GB ➡️limited oxygen transport. KPFM measurements showed that the potential barrier at the grain boundaries not only becomes higher but also broader. This was confirmed with EIS https://t.co/sLTDgDaCF8

29.04.2022 · Tweet

The grain boundaries can be easily distinguished from the grain interiors, as you can see here in the graphical abstract of the paper. https://t.co/qXwbm1uBIl

29.04.2022 · Tweet

This can obviously be adapted for a lot of other materials, e.g. #battery #electrolytes where severe band bending or material segregation occurs at grain boundaries, which means that we get a strongly differing surface potential at the GB compared to the grain interior.

29.04.2022 · Tweet

Today I’ll talk about metasurfaces. Below you can see an example of a metasurface I designed few years ago. Metasurfaces are artificial surfaces which are designed to achieve functionalities beyond the natural surfaces. Let me explain simply what is the metasurface below (1/6) https://t.co/Tl9mdIxzJL

03.05.2022 · Tweet

Metallic surfaces reflect the electromagnetic wave in GHz frequencies fully but they apply a 180 degree phase shift (the reflection coefficient is r=-1). We can design an artificial surface which reflects the EM wave with 0 degree phase shift ( r=+1). (2/6)

03.05.2022 · Tweet

These surfaces are called artificial magnetic conductors (AMC). Why do we need a surface which has r=+1 ? There are so many applications for such a surfaces, but one important one is to design high gain and more compact antennas, for example in your mobile phones. (3/6)

03.05.2022 · Tweet

The prototype shown above is an artificial magnetic conductor working on f=11 GHz with 21% bandwidth. I worked on this project during my bachelor and my master studies ( 4/6) https://t.co/hSARMjgpSQ

03.05.2022 · Tweet

You can check the paper below which is published in IEEE R. Rouzegar, A. Alighanbari and O. M. Ramahi, "Wideband Uniplanar Artificial Magnetic Conductors Based on Curved Coupled Microstrip Line Resonators," in IEEE Microwave and Wireless Components Letters, vol. 27, no. 4, 2017.

03.05.2022 · Tweet

If you have questions about metasurfaces I would be happy to answer. (6/6)

Today we will be tweeting about scanning tunneling microscopy! An 'atomically' sharp tip raster scans the surface and can map electron density on a sub-nanoscale size, enabling the visualization of single atoms 🤯 https://t.co/joGCHEWOKV

17.05.2022 · Tweet

For this technique to work, a bias is applied between the tip and the sample - enabling quantum tunneling of electrons between the tip and the sample!

17.05.2022 · Tweet

STM is so sensitive that even music playing nearby is picked up in the tunneling current/topography, enjoy our "acoustic STM" rendition of Queen's "Another Perovskite Bites the Dust" https://t.co/mtwf6N2zTb

17.05.2022 · Tweet

Did you know that you can combine STM and optical absorption spectroscopy? Single Molecule Absorption STM: SMA-STM Adding laser illumination changes the populated electron levels in the sample - resulting in a change in the tunneling current. https://t.co/270zrZGYUQ

17.05.2022 · Tweet

Using this technique, I've looked at 'atomic orbitals of PbS quantum dots during my PhD, and more recently we've applied this technique to #perovskites, stay tuned for more updates soon at @NienhausFSU... https://t.co/ywWhNADj9k

17.05.2022 · Tweet

So... as if adding optical spectroscopy to STM isn't hard enough, why don't we throw some X-rays in the mix? Using XTIP at the 4-ID-E beamline at @argonne National Lab, we do X-ray absorption spectroscopy on the nanoscale, using the STM tip as a local probe. https://t.co/sYcPUAdcVV

17.05.2022 · Tweet

with this, we've been able to track the palladium M2,3 edges when doped into perovskites: https://t.co/J8hwFRXy6E

17.05.2022 · Tweet

In a different study, we've investigated the effect of bias polarity on the local environment of iodide in perovskites: https://t.co/jDkkuu7tc5
