Today - what you've all been waiting for! We will talk about #glowythings. Today's topic is nanocrystals!!! https://t.co/AP2hq7HMHS

18.05.2022 · Tweet

Now that we've seen atoms, let's talk about "artificial atoms", also known as quantum dots! Quantum dots bridge the gap between atoms and bulk materials, they have unique properties due to so-called quantum confinement effects. https://t.co/QtNChyzfcJ

18.05.2022 · Tweet

Quantum confinement occurs when you force an electron-hole pair to be in a box that is smaller in size than its natural size, much like this reddit cat squishing into a box that's too small for it. https://t.co/FrKuWPzBkz

18.05.2022 · Tweet

Therefore, different sized nanocrystals (quantum dots) absorb and emit different colors, as shown here for CdSe https://t.co/7xoyOipapv

18.05.2022 · Tweet

How are these magical #glowythings made? We use the hot injection method where quantum dots nucleate and grow at high temperatures. Injection of precursors looks something like this for CdSe... https://t.co/o4V666DtUs

18.05.2022 · Tweet

Sometimes you can even track the nanocrystal growth directly during synthesis. This is a hot injection process under UV light to see the beautiful glow. https://t.co/3R2goRuWRM

18.05.2022 · Tweet

Sometimes we even invite theorists into the lab for some hands-on experience with #glowythings. This is our "interdepartmental outreach program" 😆 https://t.co/dqbGdwLAiV

18.05.2022 · Tweet

It made our resident theorist @DePrinceFSU so happy! https://t.co/4ClPS55OfF

18.05.2022 · Tweet

Perovskite nanoplatelets can also be made through a ligand assisted reprecipitation method at room temperature, watch them glow! https://t.co/0QyUuw4F8M

18.05.2022 · Tweet

What is a nanoplatelet, you may ask? A nanocrystal that is quantum confined in only one direction, and results in a rectangular shape when we look at them under a transmission electron microscope. Image from @ZacharyVanOrman paper https://t.co/YsrjZUl6P5 https://t.co/SoU87zHQc4

18.05.2022 · Tweet

@sciencenotscary I think you might mean sulfur.... ??? that stinks. Never smelled anything bad using Se...

18.05.2022 · Tweet

@ZacharyVanOrman We can also make nanorods, where the excitons are quantum confined in two directions - sort of like a cat stuck in a tube. Scanning transmission electron microscopy image from @ZacharyVanOrman paper on CdTe nanorods, which we like to call "nanobananas" 😁 https://t.co/e2cCqi3k87 https://t.co/sy2KyAVaG8

19.05.2022 · Tweet

Today we will be talking about bulk perovskites!

19.05.2022 · Tweet

“Perovskite” is a general term for a crystal with an ABX3 structure. A is a monovalent cation, B is a divalent cation, and X is a monovalent anion. The composition can be customized, and you can even make mixed compositions, like the mixed halides we make in our lab. https://t.co/dLwDe84ePj

19.05.2022 · Tweet

We make bulk perovskite thin films by spin coating precursor solutions onto glass and drop casting an antisolvent. The perovskite crystal structure is formed upon annealing, leading to a visible color change as the perovskite forms. https://t.co/j2NvU2JAyB

19.05.2022 · Tweet

This is a mixed halide perovskite thin film in 405nm light. Perovskites are great at absorbing light, which is why they are used in photovoltaics. The blue emission is from the epoxy used to encapsulate the film, since perovskites are sensitive to oxygen and water. https://t.co/UkYoZCfPuY

19.05.2022 · Tweet

Perovskites can be investigated by many different methods...

19.05.2022 · Tweet

For example, atomic force microscopy can be used to determine surface morphology, as shown in our recent collaboration with @toniobuonassisi, @SunShijing and @SarahWi8 https://t.co/DMK7yegngT https://t.co/BOIdmzUm0d

19.05.2022 · Tweet

PL mapping can show heterogeneities in the emission intensity and lifetime across the surface. https://t.co/sELuBfipEp https://t.co/L7zIPetBGc

19.05.2022 · Tweet

You can also make single crystal perovskites, like this MAPbBr3 made by our undergraduate student, @Gregers00. How beautiful! https://t.co/LzlXUYsM8x

19.05.2022 · Tweet

XRF mapping can also be used to determine the location of dopants in the perovskite. https://t.co/sELuBf0OfP https://t.co/ImrqrTsXkm

19.05.2022 · Tweet

Of course, we also investigate perovskites with our old friend STM. STM can give insight into e.g., the effect of an electric field on the soft perovskite lattice. https://t.co/DSciVpV0sQ https://t.co/ztg7k2qlrQ

19.05.2022 · Tweet

Why do we care about perovskites? They're fascinating materials, they glow, they make great solar cells, and they sensitize upconversion - stay tuned!

20.05.2022 · Tweet

Today we will be talking about photon upconversion @Rachel591 https://t.co/G7ygKWr1Cl

20.05.2022 · Tweet

Why do glowy things glow? If a photon (AKA a shiny crumb) is absorbed, an electron is promoted from its ground state to a higher excited state. When this excited electron relaxes back to the ground state, the energy can be released as light. This is called photoluminescence.

20.05.2022 · Tweet

The excited states of our molecules come in two different flavors: singlets and triplets. In a singlet state (vanilla), the electron spins are opposite, while in the triplet state (rocky road) the electron spins are the same. This causes problems when you want things to glow…. https://t.co/D3cAYDSPoi

20.05.2022 · Tweet

“Fluorescence” is photoluminescence from an excited singlet state. “Phosphorescence” is photoluminescence from an excited triplet state. But the optical transition into a triplet state is forbidden by selection rules ☹️.

20.05.2022 · Tweet

Why do we care? We study photon upconversion, a process where low energy light is absorbed and high energy light is emitted. Do you believe in magic??? https://t.co/beWLBVDahe

20.05.2022 · Tweet

Photoluminescence in general involves a loss of energy – higher energy light is input, lower energy light is output. In upconversion, higher energy is output. How does this not violate the fundamental laws of thermodynamics? When two become one…

20.05.2022 · Tweet

Triplet-triplet annihilation (TTA) is our favorite mechanism of upconversion. Basically, two triplet states are smushed together into one higher energy singlet state, just like Kelvin and Fred smooshed into this cuddle puddle. No spin flips are required... https://t.co/RFvLSM2DYx

20.05.2022 · Tweet

Since TTA requires excited triplet states, and triplet states aren’t readily formed by optical absorption, we use triplet sensitizers. The molecules that undergo TTA are often called “annihilators” or “emitters”.

20.05.2022 · Tweet

More info on TTA in a recent perspective with @schmidtim, @drjessalves and @JialeF https://t.co/2aAxRXBo29

20.05.2022 · Tweet

We use bulk perovskites and semiconductor nanocrystals as triplet sensitizers. These materials have two different triplet sensitization mechanisms.

20.05.2022 · Tweet

Nanocrystals generally populate the triplet state of the annihilator by exciton transfer, while perovskites inject free charges to the triplet state. https://t.co/BzK81ge2gv

20.05.2022 · Tweet

In this photo by @ZacharyVanOrman, inputting green (lower energy) light onto the sample leads to blue (higher energy) emission, AKA, upconversion! #FluorescenceFriday https://t.co/ahoJBrx9tM https://t.co/7Gp76Ea8dz https://t.co/aSLC63Ouik

20.05.2022 · Tweet

In these photos by @NienhausFSU, infrared light is upconverted to visible light. #FluorescenceFriday For more on bulk perovskite sensitized upconversion, see https://t.co/opNQes1Dl0 https://t.co/YPXl1O725m

20.05.2022 · Tweet

In addition to looking cool 😎, upconversion has many applications and allows us to learn about energy transfer processes, charge transfer processes, energy levels, fluorescence, etc… https://t.co/GudgAHSiG9

21.05.2022 · Tweet

Today, I'll start things off by telling you a bit about my early days! As a kid, I always had a grand curiosity about everything. I gained a reputation for asking a truly unbelievable number of questions 😅🤷🏻‍♀️ I simply needed to know the how and why for... everything! (1/6)

I have always loved learning new things and finding out whatever I could. Nothing was too mundane to observe, as exhibited by this qualitative study of human versus rabbit hair, from my beloved first furry pet 🐇 (2/6) https://t.co/cQZLJxAIki

24.05.2022 · Tweet

By jr. high school, I was involved in science fairs, competing both regionally and nationally over several years. These were a wonderful experience into performing “real” science in a methodical way, as well as great practice in public speaking! (3/6)

24.05.2022 · Tweet

Here is me around 14, taken at the national competition for Sanofi-Aventis Biotech Challenge (now Biogenius Canada), before giving a nerve-wracking presentation at the NRC in Ottawa! This also unknowingly prepared me so well for many elements of grad school! (4/6) https://t.co/OeELB1bhpA

24.05.2022 · Tweet

From here, I went on to study chemistry and physics in high school, and then went on to complete a BSc in chemistry. After that, a PhD... which I did -not- originally plan to do! I was lucky to have the supports and means to carry through with all of this. (5/6)

24.05.2022 · Tweet

The need to investigate and understand the world around us has always burned in me. Though many steps along the way helped lead me to the next, the passion for this career was always there😊 (6/6) https://t.co/V9bCNiPjrV

24.05.2022 · Tweet

Now that you know a bit more about me, @ChemGallant, let's talk some science! I've been active in research since 2014, mid-BSc at Memorial University 🇨🇦 When meeting w/ the prof for my inorganic course (@merschrod), she offered me a research position for the term! (1/10)

24.05.2022 · Tweet

Her group works in materials and surface science, studying both biological materials and novel sensing methods/materials. I ended up on the sensing side of things! This work involved developing + testing new sensors for Raman spectroscopy. (2/10)

24.05.2022 · Tweet

We were working on enviro. sensors for monitoring polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in water - highly-stable major by-products of oil & gas processes. Since detection at low concs (≤ μg/L) was of interest, we worked w/ surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS)! (3/10) https://t.co/WEHJvXL120

24.05.2022 · Tweet

Raman scattering is an inherently weak effect — only 1 in 1,000,000 photons will be inelastically scattered! SERS uses materials which boost the local electromagnetic field via oscillating surface electron clouds, allowing more photons-of-interest to be collected 😎 (4/10) https://t.co/LqzcLPKTzJ

24.05.2022 · Tweet

These signal-boosters are known as plasmonic materials, where those oscillating e- clouds are referred to as a "plasmon" (a quasiparticle, depending on who you ask 😉) The classic examples of plasmonic materials are roughened silver or gold! 🪙🥈 (5/10) https://t.co/vDC6Fx9Wup

24.05.2022 · Tweet

Whether presented as roughened surfaces or as individual particles, these plasmonic materials all have something in common: nanoscale features! The unique physical and optical properties of nanomaterials in general make them fantastic tools for spectroscopy. (6/10) https://t.co/AkS4z7DbjM

24.05.2022 · Tweet

A quick example fr. my own work of how small nanoscale changes lead to differing properties: The pale pink slides here have an uneven gold film roughly 5 nm in thickness, while the dark purple-pink slide is after annealing the same slide at 300°C for a few hours. (7/10) https://t.co/hq0cT3tR4p

24.05.2022 · Tweet

This image shows height mapping via atomic force microscopy (AFM) of these two gold surfaces, where we can see that the annealed sample is much more consistent (in height variation and pattern across its surface) compared to the freshly sputtered one. Wow! (8/10) https://t.co/YJxOjS8OxV

24.05.2022 · Tweet

Nanoscale and plasmonic materials are clearly fascinating subjects, having so much potential for use in many fields. Most people have observed the beauty of the nanoscale without realizing it — a great example is stained glass, often made with metal NP colloids 😍✨ (9/10) https://t.co/QZsrSXCshy

24.05.2022 · Tweet

I hope you have all enjoyed this little theory lesson and some background of my field 😊 Tomorrow we will take a look at my PhD research which touches on many of these things (+ more)! (10/10)

25.05.2022 · Tweet

[admin] "Nanodetectives Revolutionising Next Level Sensors" Long podcast with the amazing @ChemGallant is out now!🥳👇🎧 #UnderTheMicroscope #sciencepodcast #sensors #sciencetwitter #nanoscience #materialsscience https://t.co/dgR8yQJNP6

25.05.2022 · Tweet

I began grad school in 2016, and was lucky to have the opportunity to design my own project from the ground-up. I chose to study use of nanoscale magnetic metal oxides as the main sensing component of a SERS sensor. Was this an out-there idea? Maybe! Probably! (1/?)

25.05.2022 · Tweet

Plenty of research exists looking at properties and uses of magnetic NPs; some work is specific to SERS/plasmonics, though most of the studies at the time only used the magnetism for easy handling/movement of NPs. (2/?) https://t.co/XNXK0jMq00

25.05.2022 · Tweet

Such “core-shell” NPs are used for SERS where the outer layer of the NPs = classic plasmonic metal (Au, Ag), while the interior NP is made of another material, often magnetic iron oxides for quick manipulation through fluid/tissues/etc. (DOI: 10.1016/j.jmmm.2015.06.012) (3/?) https://t.co/cHLFqOBHQs

25.05.2022 · Tweet

I noted that many of these studies around the time tended to ignore any contributions of the iron oxide nanoparticle (IONP) cores to the SERS activity, despite them often being in local range of the sensing surface! The IONPs: (4/?) https://t.co/GheLOLWVbA

25.05.2022 · Tweet

Many researchers were then beginning to, and still are, looking into new classes/combos of plasmonic materials beyond Au or Ag, studying various metal oxide NPs, semiconductors, graphene/GO, carbon nanotubes, and more! (img DOI: 10.1063/5.0020752) (5/?) https://t.co/XNB43Qaq5U

25.05.2022 · Tweet

It was this exploration of new, "unconventional" materials done by others for SERS which gave me some confidence to explore use of magnetic NPs as a major contributor to the SERS enhancement, and create a new design. A scary but exciting scientific chance! (6/?) https://t.co/iuaL5ZLjVD

25.05.2022 · Tweet

There was a lot of learning and troubleshooting in this new project — I had never even made nanoparticles before this, nor worked in an inert environment — though some of that could just be said about grad school in general 🤔😂 (7/?)

25.05.2022 · Tweet

But eventually, I made reliable magnetic IONPs! Here are some scanning electron microscope images of them 💪🏼🧲 (left: plain as-made NPs; right: organosilane-capped w/ APTES) (8/?) https://t.co/A0kKeQMWgz

25.05.2022 · Tweet

Then the task was to design a "deconstructed" version of the Fe3O4@Au core-shell sensors, using the gold layer in a more background role, and the IONPs at the surface of the design... (9/)

26.05.2022 · Tweet

It turns out the usual film-formation methods are challenging when your particles are magnetic, and you haven't forced colloidal stability and/or discouraged aggregation. Films were too thin at best, uneven and not reproducible at worst! (10/?) https://t.co/2h1hs8Tj0U

26.05.2022 · Tweet

We tried switching our capping silane to a thiol-terminal one for better Au adhesion, but this caused some strange activity of the surface upon irradiation at 830 nm. We’re talking… fully saturated detector @ only 1% laser power🥴 along with changing peaks over time! (11/?)

26.05.2022 · Tweet

New bonds/complexes forming seemed likely; w/ some digging, it turns out research existed showing the catalytic activity of MPTMS, particularly on NP surfaces, including reducing capabilities. In any case, we had to scrap that mystery + head back to the drawing board. (12/?)

26.05.2022 · Tweet

When drying IONP films onto our Au coated substrates, space was limited in the glovebox, so I ended up placing some atop the hot plate inside. When I took the dried samples out, they amazingly looked uniform, which I realized was fr. the magnet of the plate! (13/?)

26.05.2022 · Tweet

Though these films were also too thin, as glass fluorescence still dominated the Raman spectrum (a constant issue!). But the idea was sparked: could I just... use external mag fields to direct the NPs into ordered layers...?! (14/?) https://t.co/sZeXkyHJQa

26.05.2022 · Tweet

Running with this, I tried several iterations, and long story short — it worked! What we ended up designing was a patterned multilayer of IONPs, forming a wheel-and-spoke type shape across the 2D surface, following the radial mag. field lines (atop a cylindrical stack) (15/?) https://t.co/dBxmU5xIVH

26.05.2022 · Tweet

The many layers result in a rippling texture, with “hills” + “valleys” of NPs, where the base Au film can show through. Here is a depth profile of a region on one of the sensors! The sensing spot size for SERS at 20x would take up about a 20 x 20 μm area in the centre. (16/?) https://t.co/VhViqpiDKu

27.05.2022 · Tweet

Testing our new nano/micro-featured surface, we determined a few important things for optimal function of the sensor: 1. Both the Au thin film + mag NPs needed to be present 2. The NPs had to be patterned 3. The laser had to be focused -within- the NP multilayer (17/?)

27.05.2022 · Tweet

Here is our report including all the details for the research I've laid out so far! This covers our inital sensor design, testing/optimising this version, and trials for sensing PAHs in complex real-world samples (validated by GC-MS). https://t.co/zQ8lnqGw20 (18/?)

27.05.2022 · Tweet

I had been continually interested in analogous forms of these magnetic iron oxides (Fe3O4/γ-Fe2O3) where the Fe2+ is swapped out for another transition metal — commonly Co2+ or Ni2+ — and the inverse spinel crystal structure is maintained. (DOI: 10.1002/sia.6568) (19/?) https://t.co/Q7BLPQxVKb

27.05.2022 · Tweet

The type of magnetism does come down to e- counts and geometry, so that is a consideration when planning for a particular product! "Magnetic" = ferro- or ferrimagnetic = must have a net moment across the material. All considered, I chose to explore CoFe2O4! (20/?) https://t.co/ivDikMHijA

29.05.2022 · Tweet

Our big manuscript is still in-progress on a lot of this cobalt ferrite sensor work, but I can share a few snippets! Largely, the tl;dr of it all is that scaling of nanoparticle syntheses are RARELY straightforward, but "bad" products aren't necessarily useless 😉🤔 (21/?)

29.05.2022 · Tweet

Following a very similar synthesis to that of our IONPs, the products were -supposed- to be spherical little darlings... spoiler alert: not at ALL! We got mixed geometries as we scaled the reaction volume, but I decided to try making sensors with these products anyhow. (22/?) https://t.co/kFyNMcWSXM

29.05.2022 · Tweet

All of the CFNPs had fairly different magnetic parameters than the IONPs — significantly larger coercivity and remanance values! This means these behave as permenant mini-magnets themselves, and ALSO respond to an external field. This vid shows how strong they are! (23/?) https://t.co/kZsfyr9fGz

29.05.2022 · Tweet

Excitingly, the sensors patterned with these various CFNPs performed better than the previous version, boasting things like more sensitive signal detection at low concs and better reproducibility across replicate sensors. (24/?)

29.05.2022 · Tweet

These sensors being better in function largely comes down to two factors: (1) The varied geometries + size scales of NPs (2) The large magnetic remanance + coercivity. (25/?)

29.05.2022 · Tweet

(1) Geometry is super important for plasmonics, as we want lots of so-called "hot-spots" where we find the greatest density of electron clouds! Angular shapes can be better (cubes, octahedra), and lots of NPs touching help in coupling their individual e- clouds together. (26/?) https://t.co/6EM61UZBw2

29.05.2022 · Tweet

(1, con't) We have angular morphologies [big octahedra], along w/ round shapes [very small spheres, medium disks], all patterned together on the surface. Lots of opportunities for coupling, especially w/ varied scales — eg. many spheres touching one big Oh crystal (27/?) https://t.co/riFh6g3sTG

29.05.2022 · Tweet

@Orad Fumbling upwards on my own basically -does- describe the trajectory, and I stand by that 😤

29.05.2022 · Tweet

@lukeweston Yes! People are doing similar things currently re: theranostics, and this has been on my mind especially since switching over to biosensing in my postdoc. Lots of potential there!

29.05.2022 · Tweet

On point (2), as their properties allow the NPs to work as mini magnets individually, this means a magnetic field is being exerted (at least) locally on the surface w/o any additional influence. This backs up our original hypothesis that magnetism is impactful for SERS! (28/)

29.05.2022 · Tweet

Optimal analyte sensing happens within the NP layers, so our laser is interacting w/ the particles/their fields + vice versa. While there may be some directional element of the fields to further explore, we are dealing with scattering of light in many directions anyhow! (29/?)

29.05.2022 · Tweet

To further probe the magnetic properties potentially being the most important factor, we did a series of tests applying an external magnetic field to the CFNP sensing surface during spectral acquisition. (30/?)

29.05.2022 · Tweet

While this did boost the signal across all sensors made with various products, the only statistically significant data (between the magnet vs. no magnet tests) was for the sample with the largest permanenet magnetism and biggest octahedral shapes ✅ (31/?) https://t.co/hrgDIBZ9Jr

29.05.2022 · Tweet

The CFNP sensor experiments went above and beyond what I could have expected! As I mentioned, we are still tidying-up the final manuscript contaning all of this data, and working on answering a few final Q's before it's sent out. Tough to do this remotely for sure! (32/?)

29.05.2022 · Tweet

There are many hopes I have for continuation of this work, but as I've moved on to a new role, it's uncertain if or how things will continue. There is so much potential for new variations, futher fleshing out the surface and enhancement model, etc.! (33/?)

29.05.2022 · Tweet

But, aside from papers, we also have a patent for our novel sensors! This process started way back in 2018 with the first publication to the USPTO, and it has reached the final stages before (hopefully) being granted 🤞🏼 https://t.co/YXXYRt2UNp (34/?)

29.05.2022 · Tweet

In my current role, I've switched gears a bit, getting into biosensing! It's a massive field with lots of very interesting, high-impact work, and where much of the groundbreaking SERS/plasmonics are developing. Especially revelant in the times we have been living through! (35/?) https://t.co/jHVNI0xdb8

29.05.2022 · Tweet

Though the physics and chemistry theory is the same, I've had to learn a lot of biochemistry and biology! It's been a huge learning curve for such a physical chemist like myself, just to get basic acronyms and terminology down. Assay, CRP, IgG, PBS, ???? (36/?)

30.05.2022 · Tweet

But! Luckily familiarity is setting in, and I've enjoyed getting to work in tandem with this "new" by working on things I'm more familiar with: Raman sensing, NP synthesis, and other various bits of chemistry. (37/?)

30.05.2022 · Tweet

We are working on continuations of LSPR and SERS nanoprobe work done previously in the group, looking at various biomarkers in tissues and blood. These methods are particularly useful for biosensing as they are quick, affordable, and label-free! https://t.co/ipOk2rTkfo (38/?)

30.05.2022 · Tweet

With this, that about covers the scope of my work thus-far in my early career! Thank you all for reading along this week — I hope you have found it both entertaining and informative 😊 You can always find me at @ChemGallant ✨ Take care!

First off, I wanted to share how I got started in science, because that's really where my journey begins! I did my undergraduate degree at @TuftsUniversity, where I majored in chemistry and math and got involved in undergraduate research almost right away. 🐘👩‍🔬

06.06.2022 · Tweet

My research in Prof. Mary Jane Shultz's lab looked at the surface structure of ice, trying to understand which crystal face dominates when you grow solid ice from liquid water. This is actually a really hard question to answer, because all of the different crystalline faces...

06.06.2022 · Tweet

...are really similar in surface energy! This is why snowflakes are all so unique ❄️ In the lab, I would grow single-crystal ice samples and then etch their surfaces to reveal the crystal structure below. Here, you can see the interface between two crystalline domains! https://t.co/WxGrVcSUNH

07.06.2022 · Tweet

Next up: graduate school! I chose @NUChemistry because I loved how interdisciplinary the department was. You can really tell an NU alum by their work-- it's like everyone is doing materials/nano work! 🤩 Lake Michigan also might have sweetened the deal... https://t.co/kWtnvCyO8T

07.06.2022 · Tweet

At NU, I joined the group of Prof. Richard Schaller, who works jointly between @NUChemistry and the Center for Nanoscale Materials @argonne. I was SO lucky to be able to call these two places my home-- the user staff at the CNM was so kind and was always willing to help me out.

07.06.2022 · Tweet

The focus of my graduate research was the photophysics of CdSe nanoplatelets, which are nanoparticles shaped like playing cards: they are really thin in one dimension, but their lateral dimensions are (relatively) quite large. My thesis aimed to understand... https://t.co/aX3YojsjWJ

07.06.2022 · Tweet

...how this dimensionality mismatch affected the dynamics and optoelectronic properties of these colloidal 2D nanoparticles, which are even more promising than conventional quantum dots for applications like LEDs and lasing.

07.06.2022 · Tweet

On my way to group meeting this morning! All our meetings are at 9am, which is not my cup of tea... https://t.co/RvQ74lSFXH

07.06.2022 · Tweet

Today, I've been in the lab! For my postdoc, I made a pretty big switch from my PhD, moving from ultrafast spectroscopy of semiconductor nanoparticles to self-assembly of polymer nanocomposites 😅 Right now, I am trying to understand how we can use external fields...

07.06.2022 · Tweet

...like magnetic fields to control the hierarchical structure of nanocomposites. For example, by drying iron oxide/supramolecular nanocomposites in a 0.1 T magnetic field, we can produce composites that have the same nanostructure (positioning of nanoparticles, polymers, etc) https://t.co/nqNr4wequ5

07.06.2022 · Tweet

...but that have completely different microstructures (larger scale order when you zoom out). This raises the question, can you make a whole suite of structures where the nanostructure is the same but the microstructure is varied? https://t.co/KDUNdUdfbM

07.06.2022 · Tweet

Making such a big switch for my postdoc has been a massive challenge. But it has also really helped me refine my ideas and expand my knowledge. I definitely wish the community were more tolerant of exploration this "late" in a career!

07.06.2022 · Tweet

For the most part, postdocs are valued for their expertise. Yet the whole point of pursuing a postdoc (from my perspective) is to gain additional training. This dichotomy is something I have really struggled with. On top of that, add in the pressure to publish in a short time.

07.06.2022 · Tweet

@buerviper You could isolate the effect of microstructure on material properties. In a hierarchical material, each layer contributes to the overall properties. To understand how the microstructure plays a role, we need to be able to change the microstructure without changing anything else.

What is @ANSTO’s @ausynchrotron? It is a light source facility - in comparison to colliders (like CERN). We produce electrons with an electron gun and accelerate them to almost the speed of light (99.999987%) before forcing them with magnets on a circular motion. https://t.co/vXfNa6Pvzd

13.06.2022 · Tweet

Those fast electrons don’t really like being forced on a ring by magnets🧲, so every time they are bent, they give of synchrotron light of all wavelength. 💫🌈 This light is extremely bright😎 and can be used by different instrument endstations, so called beamlines for research. https://t.co/ONCp7hBiCS

13.06.2022 · Tweet

We currently have 10 operational beamlines - with another 8 being currently built as part of the BRIGHT program. 👩‍🔧👨‍🔧 But the synchrotron is more than just the science 🧬🦠🔬🩻 We celebrate the connection to Aboriginal knowledge and diversity of international staff and users. https://t.co/JhNoE214f7

13.06.2022 · Tweet

The latest addition, thanks to the endless efforts of our Diversity and Inclusion committee, are rainbow steps. 🌈 Just in time for #PrideMonth, we got them installed in both the NCSS and main Synchrotron building 🤩 I love them and point them out to everyone I meet! #pride https://t.co/JSsqm8UkNP

13.06.2022 · Tweet

Some random facts: - the storage ring (the outer ring where the electrons fly around in circles) has a circumference of 216m. - because we send electrons round and round in circles (it takes them 720 nanoseconds to go around the ring once) we call it the Science Donut 🍩 https://t.co/36K9fiWTLr

13.06.2022 · Tweet

Good morning everyone 🥱 In case anyone wondered why it was quite quiet after all on here yesterday (nobody wondered 🙄😅) - we had a public holiday. 🙂 But today, I have a full on program for you, introducing our shiny toys in a bit more detail. 🤩 But first ☝️ COFFEE ☕️☕️☕️ https://t.co/SJkXFGJGl9

13.06.2022 · Tweet

Freshly fuelled with Melbourne’s finest coffee ☕️, let’s start our walk around our ring 💫/ donut 🍩 and look at the operational beamlines in a bit more detail - shall we? I’ll try and spread them out over the morning - each one as a separate thread 🧵, so you can keep up 😜 https://t.co/6Ncsqx7v1V

13.06.2022 · Tweet

1️⃣ First up: Imaging and Medical Beamline Abbreviation: IMBL Fun fact: size matters - these guys have the world’s widest Xray beam 😉 Coolest gimmick: a monitor showing some examples of their 3D scans 🤩 1/5 🧵 https://t.co/S65005CuWt

13.06.2022 · Tweet

This beamline is one of only a few of its type in the world! 🌏 Researchers use it for dynamic, high resolution, phase contrast 3D Xray imaging for tissues and bones for biomedical investigations 🤓 That’s quite a mouth full. But what does that mean? 2/5 https://t.co/37Zh4NHovo

13.06.2022 · Tweet

The images you get from this beamline are similar to a medical Xray 🩻 BUT IMBL does that much faster and with higher precision. They can also scan in layers through an object and therefore create these lovely 3D images. And all of that in a non-destructive manner 👍🏼 3/5 https://t.co/HmKlwuc9o5

13.06.2022 · Tweet

The team looks at all sorts of samples: shark heads 🦈, rhino skulls 🦏, full grown trees 🌳 and even living animals 🐑🐁. We have a vet and animal pen on site for that, to keep everyone safe and happy! The next step is to treat cancer in humans! 🤯 4/5 https://t.co/9b0itP1eiM

13.06.2022 · Tweet

To get the world’s widest beam, they have a huge distance from the Xray source (🍩) to the detector - measuring in a satellite building 135m away, connected through a tunnel. The result is a beam width of about 45cm! This is also the reason we can’t run laps around the ring!🏃 https://t.co/tlF5550Ur9

13.06.2022 · Tweet

2️⃣ next up: Xray Fluorescence Microscopy Abbreviation: XFM Fun fact: discovering hidden paintings is their speciality 🎨 Coolest gimmick: the most beautiful, coloured images of worms and plants 🌱 1/4 https://t.co/qR96XcCiqa

13.06.2022 · Tweet

This beamline can map a range of elements at low concentrations but with very high resolution in a range of samples. Researchers use it for biological 🪴🪱, geological 🪨, cultural heritage ⛰ and industrial 🏭 samples. 2/4 https://t.co/NJyulW79Fq

13.06.2022 · Tweet

They use the Xray beam from the source (🍩) to raster over a sample - which can be quite large - in micrometer precision to get quantitative elemental concentration maps. 🗺 This leads to these lovely colour 🎨 overlayed images showing where certain elements can be found. 3/4 https://t.co/qxL1DCO6rp

13.06.2022 · Tweet

XFM can therefore reveal features from more than just the surface, demonstrated brilliantly in their collaborative project with the @NGVMelbourne where they revealed a hidden painting under Edgar Degas’ “Portrait of a Woman”. This made the news 🗞 📰 https://t.co/wJBla6UXny

14.06.2022 · Tweet

3️⃣&4️⃣ Macromolecular & Micro-Crystallography Beamline(s) Abbreviation: MX1 & MX2 Fun fact: these are 2 different beamlines but I shall present them as a double up here. Coolest gimmick: @Elamanor’s artwork on their user cabin windows 🎨😍 1/5 https://t.co/maiFw1EIDC

14.06.2022 · Tweet

Both these beamlines use Xray diffraction to determine the atomic structure of crystalline samples. 💎 The difference is that on one of them, samples are usually protein crystals, while on the other researchers are looking at chemical crystals. 🧬🧪 2/5 https://t.co/Bx08ks9Nqo

14.06.2022 · Tweet

These beamlines are the workhorses 🐎 of the @ausynchrotron! Their super-fast and high throughput data collection means they can measure many 100s of samples per day - collecting a full data set of a crystal in as little as 18s!!! 3/5 https://t.co/aDuzfdRQUE

14.06.2022 · Tweet

On top of that they have a sample mounting robot 🤖 for remote access, so researchers from all over Australia 🇦🇺 and the world 🌍 can send samples and run the beamlines from the comfort of their home. 🏡 4/5 https://t.co/lGdw2RguSJ

14.06.2022 · Tweet

During the past pandemic years, MX was essential for a lot of COVID research 🦠, looking into the structure of nanobodies. One of the studies that made it into the news involved Alpacas 🦙 you can read it here: https://t.co/70kENXkmL6

14.06.2022 · RT

RT @Elamanor: Susi is doing a beamline-by-beamline tour of the Science Donut! Follow to learn about the cool stuff we do here <3

14.06.2022 · RT

RT @DrEmilyFinch: Follow along for a virtual tour of the scientific equipment @ausynchrotron!

14.06.2022 · RT

RT @Elamanor: What can I say? You give me chalk markers, I'm gonna chalk-mark...

14.06.2022 · Tweet

5️⃣ Infrared Microscopy Abbreviation: IRM Fun fact: they can run even without the source (🍩) with a separate light source Coolest gimmick: they don’t need lead shielding so they don’t need to search hutches to operate 🙌🏼 1/4 https://t.co/kfdQZOlSlf

14.06.2022 · Tweet

This beamline combines the brilliance of the source (🍩) with a FTIR spectrometer and a microscope 🔬. This way researchers can analyse microscopic samples, like particles, thin layers or coatings. It accesses a wider range than lab IRs in combination with a microscope. 2/4 https://t.co/ttvsauDu5G

14.06.2022 · Tweet

The molecular vibrations detectable with IRM are like signatures or fingerprints of molecules. 👍 Through a spatial mapping feature of the microscope, chemical maps of biological🕷, biomedical🦴 or food science🧀 as well as materials and forensics samples can be analysed. 3/4 https://t.co/iDC9taJmT8

14.06.2022 · Tweet

The team works with researchers to look into the secrets of Australian basket-web spider’s silk 🕷🕸 to develop new biomimetic fibres for textiles, tissue engineering and medical applications. Spiders are definitely friends around here 😉 https://t.co/pRN8UzkUtc

14.06.2022 · Tweet

Btw their neighbour beamline is our number 6️⃣ Terahertz / Far-Infrared Beamline Abbreviation: THz/Far-IR Due to a range of components and accessories available, researchers can do a variety of gas and condensed phase experiments here. https://t.co/oc2epTsRr9

14.06.2022 · Tweet

7️⃣ inching closer to my workplace: Soft Xray Spectroscopy Abbreviation: SXR Fun fact: I call it the “airship” - like spaceship but reverse Coolest gimmick: their Toroidal Analyser on wheels that are controlled by a console controller 🎮 1/5 https://t.co/eS5RmsXEpQ

14.06.2022 · Tweet

The SXR beamline is set up for Xray absorption spectroscopy of surfaces with low atomic number elements. 🆒 And with surface, they mean it as their Xrays only penetrate 10nm to a few Angstrom of the sample surface. 🤩 2/5 https://t.co/dXarUK0ruI

14.06.2022 · Tweet

The wavelength of Xrays SXR uses is so high, that we call them “soft” and they are get completely absorbed by the first ~200nm of material. That’s why their endstation doesn’t need any shielding (no hutch). 3/5 https://t.co/vCiVGNttY5

14.06.2022 · Tweet

That’s also why their endstations need to be under Ultra High Vacuum to be able to measure anything. The vacuum conditions are similar to that in outer space! 🚀 it’s basically an airship - an inverted spaceship 🛸 4/5 https://t.co/qkg3S0Wpqr

14.06.2022 · Tweet

Their Toroidal Analyser for Angle Resolved Photoelectron Spectroscopy (ARPES) is the only instrument of its kind, as it was designed and built in Australia in collaboration with @latrobe. This enables excellent research into 2D materials like Graphene etc. 5/5 https://t.co/MWwEdDf7HA

14.06.2022 · Tweet

8️⃣ welcome home: Small and Wide Angle Xray Scattering Abbreviation: SAXS / WAXS Fun fact: I work here 😂 - no “seriously”: we are known to constantly upgrade our beamline. When you come back, something has changed. Coolest gimmick: our wall of post-it thank you notes 🥰 1/6 https://t.co/d7tjsTVYF6

14.06.2022 · Tweet

This beamline is probably one of the most versatile beamlines at the @ausynchrotron. 🙏 Due to our open sample mounting table, we can accomodate for all types of sample environments and experiments. 🧪🔬💉 And we can look at objects between 0.5 and 500nm. 2/6 https://t.co/M9OOanCf6i

14.06.2022 · Tweet

The motto “everything goes” is sometimes taken quite literally: we can measure basically everything you can get Xrays through. Samples can be solids, liquids, powders, fibres, films, biological or synthetic, wet or dry, stationary or moving, hot or cold etc. 3/6 https://t.co/h03YrrHS2B

14.06.2022 · Tweet

SAXS generally measures elastic scattering from Xrays, similar to diffraction. We talk in scattering angle, which follows a reciprocal rule to the dimension of the sample feature. Small or Wide Angle refers to the angular region of scattered beam to primary beam. 📐 4/6 https://t.co/AlK7PBLJMb

14.06.2022 · Tweet

You might already know quite a bit about #SAXSland if you followed @drheaddamage in his week here. I do want to talk about some things specific to our beamline a little bit later 😉 5/6 https://t.co/e1aMnhJZ6t

14.06.2022 · Tweet

One of the prime examples from our beamline in recent years is the “Malaria Milkshake” 🥛🦠 project we’re working on together with @group_boyd at @MonashUni. They / we recently won a @eurekaprizes for this research. You can read all about it here: https://t.co/qCFmenWFgi 6/6

14.06.2022 · RT

RT @_SuSiSe_: Everything you always wanted to know about SAXS in one 🧵… or is it everything? 🤔😉

14.06.2022 · Tweet

9️⃣ onto the finish line: Xray Absorption Spectroscopy Abbreviation: XAS Fun fact: XAS is a synchrotron-only technique! Can’t do that in the lab 🥼 Coolest gimmick: they currently have a High Energy Resolution Fluorescence Detection setup in one of the hutches 1/4 https://t.co/DpnzGgcK2e

14.06.2022 · Tweet

XAS uses hard Xrays (so the opposite of SXR) to look at different oxidation states and chemical environments of specific elements in samples. They can also get information about the distance to and identify the neighbouring atoms of that element. 💁 2/4 https://t.co/KgJacmQdin

14.06.2022 · Tweet

Samples can be liquid, solid or gas, but most often researchers opt for powders! Our XAS beamline can look at all elements between Titanium (Ti) and Plutonium (Pu), and at very low concentrations of them (100 ppm) 👌 3/4 https://t.co/2vLg1USxO9

14.06.2022 · Tweet

During the pandemic, they worked with researchers from @excitonscience @UniMelb to analyse different batches of magnetic nanoparticles 🧲 for COVID test kits. 🦠 You can read about it here: https://t.co/NFHJULGs5b

14.06.2022 · Tweet

🔟 last but not least: Powder Diffraction Abbreviation: PD Fun fact: they have one of the smallest datasets per measurement- only ~400KB Coolest gimmick: they can heat up and measure samples up to 1600 degrees 🔥 and cool them down to 10K 🥶 1/4 https://t.co/s3x6XSkzVm

14.06.2022 · Tweet

This beamline can be used to look at crystal atomic structure both qualitatively (as a fingerprint) to see what phases are present and quantitatively, to see how much of each phase is present. 👍 2/4 https://t.co/GTaODjfqi5

14.06.2022 · Tweet

PD is invaluable as a vast extension to lab XRD, as it can use different sample environments and has a large angle high resolution Mythen II detector, collecting data simultaneously over 80 degree. 📐 3/4 https://t.co/ktH79pgjqR

14.06.2022 · Tweet

One of the largest community of this beamline use PD to look at batteries and their crystal structure during charge and discharge cycles. 🔋🪫🔌 But that’s not all. They do some excellent space 🛰 rock 🪨 research and indigenous projects too! ✋ https://t.co/27m9sZJ973

14.06.2022 · Tweet

It’s a cold wet and windy morning in Melbourne, so we start the day at the beamline with an extra caffeine shot ☕️ I hope you are excited as throughout today we will take a deep dive into all things happening at #SAXSland @ANSTO https://t.co/2GbnwBdIH3

15.06.2022 · Tweet

Busy day at work at the beamline 🤗 But what does this SAXS beamline actually do 🤨 and how does it work? 🧐 A thread 🧵👇 https://t.co/FUFJMtZmyo

15.06.2022 · Tweet

SAXS is another form of light scattering - similar to blue skies 🏞 or red sunsets 🌅. While they are visible light from the sun ☀️ scattered by gas molecules or dust in the air and atmosphere, SAXS is scattering of Xrays, with a wavelength 1000times smaller than visible light. https://t.co/uC4AiLOyo9

15.06.2022 · Tweet

We use it to analyse the internal structure of solids, liquids or surfaces. 🧊 And with structure I mean how the matter inside a sample is arranged over a wide range of sizes 📏 https://t.co/vS4mbJKtdt

15.06.2022 · Tweet

So what happens when we put a sample at the beamline? 🤷🏼‍♀️ The incoming Xrays are scattered off the electrons from atoms of the sample ⚛️ How they are scattered depends on how the electrons are arranged spatially. They can have different density variations, distances or direction. https://t.co/5LOUYWkuoP

15.06.2022 · Tweet

All of this influences the scattering pattern that comes out the other end. 💠 We use a sensitive 2D detector to collect these patterns. From that we can calculate the internal structure. ✳️ Unlike other instruments, for us samples don’t need to be optically transparent! 🔍 https://t.co/TBXRPqvhZ9

15.06.2022 · Tweet

Let’s talk samples! 🧬🧫🧪 What can we actually measure - and how - at #SAXSland ?! Here is the thread 🧵 for all of you who are thinking of measuring SAXS 🧵👇 https://t.co/NXWFKV7sPy

15.06.2022 · Tweet

The most common experiments and also the majority (so far 😉) are TRANSMISSION measurements. The principle is pretty straight forward: we measure through the sample ➡️➡️➡️🧪➡️➡️➡️ https://t.co/iPHbz0DttB

15.06.2022 · Tweet

A small, highly parallel Xray beam hits the sample, some Xrays get absorbed but most travel straight through. These will be absorbed by a beamstop to protect our detector from being damaged. https://t.co/JZoKJCxIpa

15.06.2022 · Tweet

Some Xrays that hit the sample are scattered in different angles as they pass through, forming a 2D, angle-dependent scattering pattern. ↗️ ↗️ ➡️➡️➡️🧪 These hold all the info about the structure and orientation of the measured sample. https://t.co/dKuv5FJnvV

15.06.2022 · Tweet

Which angles are captured depends on the position of the detector relative to the sample. We can go as close as 600mm and as far as 7m - and everything in between. https://t.co/LnE6Ea2M49

15.06.2022 · Tweet

The other measurement style is called GRAZING INCIDENCE. Here, we look at the surface of a sample by detecting the refracted beam. This is typically used to look at crystalline structures dependent on the incident angle of the beam. 📐 https://t.co/eFBgd7vZDX

15.06.2022 · Tweet

For this method, we usually use a 6-axis motorised hexapod. This piece of equipment enables us to not only move in x-, y-, and z-direction but also precisely control pitch, yaw and roll angle of the samples. https://t.co/1XZdH0OmnB

15.06.2022 · Tweet

Both of these types of measurement can be performed either in AIR or in VACUUM, depending on your sample! We have a super versatile sample table, several standard setups and a vacuum sample vessel, minimising background scattering to basically not existing! https://t.co/fpS2XGroJy

15.06.2022 · Tweet

Oh and before I log off for tonight, I can’t forget to mention that we also do super fancy equipments. As I said, we’re a super versatile beamline and we give almost everything a go… https://t.co/sz3fO7NcL6

15.06.2022 · Tweet

The latest addition is our shiny new @AntonPaar Rheometer. We got it through a collaboration with @SoftMatterHackr and are finalising the installation at our beamline. Soon we can do rheology and SAXS simultaneously 😵‍💫 https://t.co/VkvSpOVZ2X

15.06.2022 · Tweet

My favourite, however, are microfluidic setups. Pushing the boundaries of fluid dynamics. 😍 I have been part of some pretty funky experiments in this field. But I will tell you a bit more about that tomorrow. https://t.co/XhkRNs6yk4

15.06.2022 · Tweet

Too busy running users at the beamline yesterday (because Science 🤩) So we’ll use today to talk about Microfluidics instead 😉 I hope you’re as excited as I am! https://t.co/fcA790piDm

17.06.2022 · Tweet

It’s-a me 🙋🏼‍♀️😉 Let’s jump into the warp pipe of Microfluidics - the Mario Bros. of Science 🧪🔧 (Although I got told I have more of a Princess Peach resemblance 🤔🤷🏼‍♀️) Anyways… here we go… https://t.co/EVLTo2Tn8q

17.06.2022 · Tweet

What has Microfluidics to do with Mario Bros? People working with microfludics are basically tiny plumbers. 🪠 Microfluidics is a multidisciplinary field dealing with the behaviour of liquids 💦 in dimensions below 1mm. 📏 https://t.co/rhyqdLrtAx

17.06.2022 · Tweet

So why warp pipe? Microfluidic systems typically transport, mix, separate or otherwise process and control fluids in small channels on devices. These can also include micropumps or microvalves. https://t.co/xpPOnPKv0Z

17.06.2022 · Tweet

And why do we need this? Microfluidics is an extremely powerful tool to perform quantitative and qualitative analysis of a small amount of sample with high sensitivity and resolution. 🧪 They are also usually quite low cost devices, making testing and adjusting very easy! 🤑 https://t.co/GeH5CeYtcG

17.06.2022 · Tweet

What can they be used for? Applications range across various fields, like analytics 💻, biology 🧬, chemistry 🧪, medicine 🩺 and technology 📱. “Standard” designs are trying to scale down chemistry labs to so-called lab-on-a-chip devices https://t.co/7UHlkJUoyd

17.06.2022 · Tweet

But there is also a lot of development happening to produce efficient microarrays - so-called DNA chips 🧬- and even reproduce complete organs in microfluidics, called “organ-on-a-chip”🫀🫁🧠, which is a significant step away from animal testing! 🐭🐰 https://t.co/9C7oxT1VtA

17.06.2022 · RT

RT @_SuSiSe_: Today I take you on a deep dive down the Mario Bros warp pipe of microfluidics!! Head over to @RealSci_Nano and read the in…

17.06.2022 · Tweet

Now what did I use microfluidics for? I user 3D hydrodynamic focussing devices to look at super fast reaction kinetics during continuous flow. https://t.co/L7vPWkmOKE

17.06.2022 · Tweet

Transferring reactions from batch to microfluidics is particularly useful to transfer a time axis (= fast reaction occuring) onto a distance axis (= measure along the channel of the microfluidic device) https://t.co/ELQJDPdwGw

17.06.2022 · Tweet

When combining this now with a powerful technique like SAXS, we can follow the reaction at very fast timescales, like milliseconds, a measurement at a time = a step along the device at a time. https://t.co/UjltZ5t2FH

17.06.2022 · Tweet

I used this to follow the nucleation and growth of nanoparticles, the shape evolution of nanorods from seeded growth and the assembly of anisotropic, pH sensitive particles. You can also couple this with different optical methods like fluorescence or absorption measurements. https://t.co/BkHgqh7dF1

Hi there! I’m @JulienBarrier, a researcher in condensed matter physics at @UoMPhysics. Sounds vague? Follow the threads and hopefully by the end of the week you will know everything about this field of research!

I'm studying condensed matter physics (CMP), and within this field, I'm working on electron transport in graphene and graphene heterostructures. I'll talk a bit more about the science in the coming days

08.08.2022 · Tweet

The curriculum @ESPCI_Paris is simple: a) it teaches experimental science, 50% of the time spent on hands-on practice at the bench b) it gives a mixed culture: physicists able to carry out basic chemical synthesis, chemists who understand the physical properties of their material

08.08.2022 · Tweet

Halide perovskites are exciting materials, showing promising photovoltaic performances but are prone to phase instabilities leading to degradation and thus performance loss

08.08.2022 · Tweet

08.08.2022 · Tweet

08.08.2022 · Tweet

In the second, we used X-ray diffraction (XRD) to understand the heterogeneity better. Before that paper, it was very hard to monitor structural heterogeneity at length scales between 1nm and 100nm. Drawback overcome with XRD. Published in @EES_journal https://t.co/Y2scygKCWW

.@JulienBarrier back here! Let's talk about some of the particularities of the British research system

08.08.2022 · Tweet

So I said I am currently an @EPSRC Fellow. What does it mean?

08.08.2022 · Tweet

In most academic systems, a typical career path would be PhD > postdocs > assistant prof. > associate prof. > full prof. with naming differences depending on the country.

08.08.2022 · Tweet

In the UK, it is similar, the typical career path follows PhD > postdocs > lecturer > reader > professor. But there's another way: fellowships.

08.08.2022 · Tweet

The idea is that a career move from the lecturer stage would be decided by how much grant money a researcher brings to their institution. Postdocs are not used to apply for grants, so hiring directly at the lecturer stage can be risky for an institution

08.08.2022 · Tweet

Fellowships in the UK are a way for early career researchers (postdoc level) to prove that they can bring grant money and therefore are worth hiring on a permanent contract (tenure)

08.08.2022 · Tweet

There are multiple fellowships awarded after a competitive application process by both public and private bodies: EPSRC, Leverhulme Trust, Wellcome Trust, Royal Academy of Engineering, Royal Society, etc.

08.08.2022 · Tweet

Right after my PhD, I was awarded the EPSRC Doctoral Prize Fellowship. It is a relatively small one but gives me my own research budget (consumables + travel) to manage and pays my salary. I am currently hosted in an existing group, therefore can't get large equipment.

08.08.2022 · Tweet

The next career move would be to apply to other fellowships (longer, more budget). In some of them, the researcher can apply for grants. If granted, this is a very strong case for a lectureship.

08.08.2022 · Tweet

One issue: they are very competitive. Much more than a usual postdoc: a) one needs to find a group to host them b) institutions can usually present only a limited number of applicants: it's competitive at institution level c) there's limited funding: competitive at national level

08.08.2022 · Tweet

The main advantage is that it shows independence. I wrote my own proposal, follow my own ideas, carry out my own independent research, and manage my own research budget

08.08.2022 · Tweet

On the + side, I'm considered a postdoc, therefore don't have teaching or administrative duties, and can focus on my research 100% (and writing proposals for the next step 😰)

08.08.2022 · Tweet

What do you think about such a system? Would you like to have such opportunities? Or would you find it overwhelming?

09.08.2022 · Tweet

Heya! @JulienBarrier here. Today, I want to tell you about the transition from chemical physics in my Master's project to condensed matter physics in my PhD

09.08.2022 · Tweet

As I said yesterday, I worked on X-ray characterisation of halide perovskites at the end of my master's degree

09.08.2022 · Tweet

It would have been a natural way to transition to a PhD in that field. And originally, that was what I did

09.08.2022 · Tweet

In fact, I submitted a research proposal to my PhD supervisor at the interface between his expertise and my experience. This is how I got the PhD position

09.08.2022 · Tweet

So I proposed to exfoliate halide perovskites and make van der Waals heterostructures with graphene and perovskites. For those interested about the proposal: https://t.co/o674j9Ln71

09.08.2022 · Tweet

So I arrived in this lab in September 2018 and tried to do this. The goal was to make halide perovskite monolayers and then contact them with graphene to explore their electronic properties.

09.08.2022 · Tweet

The issue is that these perovskites are already unstable as bulk crystals, I let you imagine how unstable it is when you manage to have a few atomic layers…

09.08.2022 · Tweet

I tried several methods, but the halide perovskite would systematically degrade before it could be encapsulated with any other crystal. After 6 months, we decided I could not achieve the impossible, and we dropped this original project.

09.08.2022 · Tweet

In hindsight, I'm glad I had the chance to try that direction! I think we lacked good chemistry methodology: some other groups focused on chemistry ventured into this direction and obtained pretty good results: https://t.co/LW0D0aQU59

09.08.2022 · Tweet

The exfoliation method, which my group specialised in, yields good quality stable crystals (like graphene) but was not efficient for these perovskites. On that path, I learned a lot in microfabrication techniques!

09.08.2022 · Tweet

After we decided to drop the perovskites, my supervisor suggested I took charge of a dilution refrigerator. The goal: measure electronic devices at temperatures 0.01 degrees above absolute zero.

09.08.2022 · Tweet

I accepted since that was the natural direction I intended to pursue: a) fabricate perovskite, b) measure them in the facilities. Since I couldn't fabricate, I would measure other sorts of devices

09.08.2022 · Tweet

Tomorrow I'll talk a bit more about dilution refrigeration, that's a fascinating technique!

09.08.2022 · Tweet

Since I started measuring electronic devices, I found a few interesting phenomena involving the behaviour of electrons at low temperatures and high magnetic fields. More of this later!

09.08.2022 · Tweet

So... this is how I moved from chemical physics training to being a condensed matter physicist, studying the behaviour of electrons at ultra-low temperatures!

10.08.2022 · Tweet

Good morning everyone! @JulienBarrier here. Let's talk about cryogenics! https://t.co/a0GLa8pGbl

10.08.2022 · Tweet

We use dilution refrigerators to cool down to millikelvin temperatures.

10.08.2022 · Tweet

Why so? At low temperatures, atoms and molecules move around less: they are basically frozen. The only thing that moves are electrons, and we want to study their transport properties

10.08.2022 · Tweet

There is another reason: at low temperatures, you get rid of perturbations from the outside world, and quantum effects can emerge. We expect new physics!

10.08.2022 · Tweet

How low is a millikelvin? That's one thousand of a degree (C) above absolute zero, -273.15°C or about -450°F. Very, very cold! https://t.co/9EAQIbjkoH

10.08.2022 · Tweet

To cool down a device, there are different methods. The easiest: liquefy a gas and place your device inside. Here Liquid nitrogen, at 77K (-195.8°C, -320°F) https://t.co/UrsD4PEVnt

10.08.2022 · Tweet

To cool down further, one can use liquid helium, that boils at 4.2K (-269°C, -452.11°F)

10.08.2022 · Tweet

The method to cool down even further is to pump on a liquid bath of helium. When atoms are pumped away from the vapour phase, the most energetic atoms (the warmest) leave the liquid and replenish the vapour. This effectively cools down the liquid helium

10.08.2022 · Tweet

This method can achieve 1.3K with helium. That's already very cold!

10.08.2022 · Tweet

If we want to cool down even further, we can use 3He, an isotope with 2 protons and 1 neutron (the usual 4He has 2 protons and 2 neutrons). Pumping on a 3He liquid can cool down to 0.3K

10.08.2022 · Tweet

How do we cool down further? We mix 3He and 4He! This is done in a dilution refrigerator, an instrument that was imagined almost 60years ago!

10.08.2022 · Tweet

The working principle is based on the dilution of 3-He in 4-He. To understand it, here is the phase diagram of 3He in 4He https://t.co/CGX0UX1Ibz

10.08.2022 · Tweet

The most important parameter: below 0.87K, there is a forbidden region, and the two isotopes are only miscible for some concentrations

10.08.2022 · Tweet

Close to absolute zero, one can get almost pure 3He (right side) and a dilute phase with 6.5% of 3He in 4-He.

10.08.2022 · Tweet

The magic here is that helium is a quantum liquid, and we use all the properties of quantum physics to cool down! https://t.co/YGszXn2Mq8

10.08.2022 · Tweet

On this left side of the diagram, 4He is superfluid (so has no excitation like phonons), and basically acts as an inert background for 3He. On that side, 3He is a fermion and the interatomic distance is controlled by its concentration in 4He

10.08.2022 · Tweet

Important, below 0.8K, the mixture is phase-separated, like oil in water: the 3He-rich phase (concentrated phase) sits above the dilute phase

10.08.2022 · Tweet

If we take atoms from the concentrated phase to place them into the dilute phase, they will split up but this needs energy. Guess where the energy comes from?

10.08.2022 · Tweet

From temperature! The mixing of 3He in 4He is endothermic. That's how we cool. This technique was first proposed in 1962 and achieved experimentally at @UoMPhysics in 1965

10.08.2022 · Tweet

Here are the first prototypes of dilution refrigerators, created by Prof Henry Hall https://t.co/GlULEejzjs

10.08.2022 · Tweet

Here is a schematic of the inner circuit. The dilution occurs in the mixing chamber (MC). 3He/4He from the dilute phase are distilled in the Still. This pumps atoms from the dilute phase, forcing 3He to move from the concentrated phase back to the dilute phase. https://t.co/Ow7b1yaSml

10.08.2022 · Tweet

This is a closed circuit: 3He atoms pumped away on the top come back to the concentrated phase through the thin line.

10.08.2022 · Tweet

To cool down a device then, we bolt it to the MC and circulate the helium mixture, taking heat from the device to work!

10.08.2022 · Tweet

Here is a picture of the mixing chamber in my setup. It is bolted to a plate, to which we attach all devices to cool down. The blue items are thermometers. The rings are heat exchangers that allow the mixture to flow to the still and the incoming, pure 3He to be cooled down https://t.co/kWhe1VE5Xf

10.08.2022 · Tweet

In practice, the system is a tad more complicated, there are multiple plates that are cooled down to different temperatures, to maintain the whole system cold https://t.co/IwLloRNvkJ

10.08.2022 · Tweet

Of course, we cannot leave the system in the air, it would never cool down. We place it in a vacuum can to isolate each element from one another and prevent heat leaks https://t.co/3E2ACzcpV1

10.08.2022 · Tweet

For those interested in the history of dilution refrigerators at Manchester, there was a conference in 2015 on the 50 years of the first DR. Presentations here: https://t.co/fhKZjwW0GJ

11.08.2022 · Tweet

Hi there! @JulienBarrier again. Let's talk about graphene electronic devices and how I measure them

11.08.2022 · Tweet

I am studying van der Waals heterostructures made of graphene and other 2D materials. The principle: take several atomically-thin materials, stack them together and voilà! https://t.co/2k1l5ucSiT

11.08.2022 · Tweet

For example, we like to work with graphene and hexagonal boron nitride, an insulator that protects a material to study (here graphene). The picture shows the fabrication process of such heterostructure https://t.co/8o5NWxdGnY

11.08.2022 · Tweet

Once a stack is made, it is etched into a shape of interest, and metallic electrodes are added. The structure can be very complicated depending on the project's aim. Here the width of the purple strip is 1.5µm https://t.co/XpFM8qPxIb

11.08.2022 · Tweet

All of this is done in a cleanroom, a highly controlled environment, where dust is minimal, humidity and temperature well calibrated

11.08.2022 · Tweet

Outside of the cleanroom, we "bond" the device to a chip carrier holder. Here the silicon wafer is 5mm wide. This is a very precise activity https://t.co/7hxxiLsBjW

11.08.2022 · Tweet

Under a magnifying lens, we deposit droplets of silver-charged conducting epoxy on the contacts created by lithography. We do this with a sharpened toothpick. Then, we connect these pads with gold wire to the chip carrier. Everything by hand!

11.08.2022 · Tweet

The last step: placing the chip carrier in a sample holder, ready for measurement in the dilution fridge! https://t.co/osd6ozl1cc

12.08.2022 · Tweet

Once the sample is loaded in the fridge, we can measure its electrical properties.

12.08.2022 · Tweet

The principle of our measurement is simple: flow a current throughout the device, and measure a voltage drop at different contacts, using a variety of equipments to tune the properties https://t.co/K8vnF2DG6v

12.08.2022 · Tweet

That way, we can measure a device's resistance and deduce some properties : the mobility (how much electrons are accelerated by an electric field), the mean free path (how far can an electron go before bumping into another electron or a phonon), etc.

12.08.2022 · Tweet

The typical device has a transistor architecture: we connect it to a "gate", which is a metal plate below or above the device, that we can charge with electrons or holes

12.08.2022 · Tweet

Because our devices are atomically thin, applying a gate voltage changes the energy level (the Fermi level) within the device, allowing to study the electronic response for different chemical potentials https://t.co/iH3pP89458

12.08.2022 · Tweet

This technique of gating a device via field-effect is not possible in all materials: 3D bulk crystals will feel the field effect only in the surface, for example

12.08.2022 · Tweet

but for 2D materials and van der Waals heterostructures, this is one of the most powerful tool!

12.08.2022 · Tweet

For example in cuprate high-temperature superconductors (3D), different phases appear with different dopings. To change the doping, one needs to synthesise a new crystal, with a different chemical composition each time! https://t.co/EYhgTmaIuk

12.08.2022 · Tweet

In van der Waals heterostructures, it became possible to change the doping via tuning the gate voltage: the same phase can be described in a continuous measurement! https://t.co/5Hweu55dMa

12.08.2022 · Tweet

The doping level is not the only parameter to vary: we can change the temperature, apply a magnetic field to the device, apply different sorts of electric fields, etc. Some people use lasers as an additional tuning knob

12.08.2022 · Tweet

Later today, I'll talk about our recent results in graphene superlattices, combining variation of the Fermi level (via gate voltage tuning), magnetic field, and ultra low temperatures. Stay tuned!

12.08.2022 · Tweet

Hey folks! @JulienBarrier here! Let's talk about one of my recent projects: Brown-Zak fermions in graphene superlattices

12.08.2022 · Tweet

If you sandwich graphene between two layers of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), you'll get high-quality graphene. If now, one of the two layers of hBN is exactly aligned with the graphene layer, the magic starts

12.08.2022 · Tweet

In fact, hBN has a similar lattice structure as graphene, but 1.8% larger. When aligning them, we get a long-range superlattice pattern, called moiré (like moiré fabrics) https://t.co/zAudK5uD1x

12.08.2022 · Tweet

When measuring the resistance as a function of the gate voltage (therefore doping) of a superlattice device, we observe peaks. They correspond to features associated with the main graphene (0V) and the long-range moiré (other satellite peaks) https://t.co/Uq51TTkXV6

12.08.2022 · Tweet

And in practice, the band structure is changed: the resistance features correspond to new mini-cones at high doping (in blue) https://t.co/RAYkA2DTO0

12.08.2022 · Tweet

The physics is relatively easy to understand with a physics background; it is based on the Bloch theorem.

12.08.2022 · Tweet

If you take free electrons, their band dispersion will be parabolic. If now you add an atomic lattice, gaps emerge, and the band can be folded in a Brillouin zone https://t.co/LhN9XVAMX9

12.08.2022 · Tweet

This is the same when you add an hBN moiré to the graphene layer, the band folds (again) in a mini-Brillouin zone, smaller than the graphene Brillouin zone. Gaps appear, and resistive features are observed

12.08.2022 · Tweet

Now let's add a magnetic field perpendicular to the graphene. If you study 2D electrons in a magnetic field, they will form orbits (quantised!), with a characteristic length scale that is the magnetic length lb: https://t.co/M5r5yZVcEM

12.08.2022 · Tweet

The question we tried to answer is: what happens when lb becomes comparable to the lattice constant a?

12.08.2022 · Tweet

Well, in a usual material, that would be hard to achieve: a magnetic length comparable to a few Å lattice constant would mean a magnetic field of 10 000T. The best magnets on earth achieve around 50T, so it wouldn't be possible

12.08.2022 · Tweet

Not if you use graphene superlattices! With a superlattice constant of a few 10nm, you only need 30T to have a comparable magnetic length!

12.08.2022 · Tweet

We did the experiment: placed a graphene superlattice device at ultra low temperature, in a magnetic field, and measured the resistance

12.08.2022 · Tweet

Usually, the resistance of any metal exposed to an increasing magnetic field, increases as well

12.08.2022 · Tweet

This was not the case in the devices we measured. The resistance increased roughly, but whenever the magnetic length became a fraction of the lattice constant, the resistance dropped

12.08.2022 · Tweet

In terms of physics, that is something unexpected, the resistance should not drop, since the electrons follow circular trajectories, and should not contribute to electronic transport anymore

12.08.2022 · Tweet

So we understood that whenever one orbit had a size of a few superlattice unit cells, the band structure changes. In fact, the combination of the magnetic field and the superlattice results in the emergence of new quasiparticles

12.08.2022 · Tweet

Quasiparticles are a framework we use to describe the electronic behaviour in simple mathematical terms: instead of adding a loads of parameters in the equation, we use a simple equation, where the mass is changed to reflect interactions

12.08.2022 · Tweet

We named these new quasiparticles the Brown-Zak fermions, in honour of two theoretical physicists, Brown and Zak, who studied the "magnetic translation group", a mathematical framework for superlattices in high magnetic fields

12.08.2022 · Tweet

The physics is actually much richer than resistance drops. This is for example a map of the conductance as a function of the gate voltage and magnetic field. The conductance peaks for fractions of the superlattice unit cell, and decreases above https://t.co/PwVMYS03IZ

12.08.2022 · Tweet

If you're interested, more details are available in our paper https://t.co/9OlBeasZ4y, + it's #OpenAccess

12.08.2022 · Tweet

This is 100% fundamental science; it's really hard to think about any application for this

12.08.2022 · Tweet

However, in condensed matter physics, it can take 50 years before blue sky research can be transformed into an application

12.08.2022 · Tweet

Think about, for example, superconductivity. Discovered in 1911, it's only in the 1960s that people started fabricating superconducting magnets, used today in MRI!

14.08.2022 · Tweet

Hi from Hamburg. I am so excited to do this weeks takeover.🥳 My name is Rebecca (@RPittkowski)👩‍🔬 and I am a PostDoc at @UCPH_Research in Copenhagen🇩🇰. But today I am starting with a little impression from our current experiment at DESY @desynews in Hamburg/Germany🇩🇪 https://t.co/mH8Z2JKVLV

03.10.2022 · Tweet

So, what is DESY @desynews? Or more general, what is a synchrotron facility? And what makes our #research so exciting that we happily work #nightshifts and on #weekends? #ScienceNeverSleeps A thread 🧵 1/5 @RPittkowski https://t.co/YU5EOyBbgi

03.10.2022 · Tweet

DESY @desynews stands for "Deutsches Elektronen Synchrotron" and is a large scale research facility located in Hamburg. The PETRAIII ring at DESY, a 2.3 km ring underneath the city, was once the largest particle collider worldwide, but has since been rebuild to supply X-rays. 2/5

03.10.2022 · Tweet

PETRA III is a storage ring generating extremely high energy X-rays. The electrons in the ring are accelerated to 6 billion electronvolts (6GeV) particle energy and race around the ring close to the speed of light. They can provide X-rays with energies up to 200 keV. 3/5

03.10.2022 · Tweet

Scientist can use these high energetic and intense X-rays at ca. 40 end-stations, where different experiments and techniques run e.g. to study tiny objects: proteins, small nano-particles,interactions of matter, or look into thick samples, to study processes in e.g. a battery 4/5

03.10.2022 · Tweet

We are currently sitting with a team from @jensengroup_cph at one of these end-stations (@p021_desy), and are shooting X-rays at small capillaries full of newly synthesized materials, to understand how the atoms are arranged in our nano-particles. 5/5

04.10.2022 · Tweet

We finished this morning! After 48 h of experiments, with two sets of 12 h shifts - running on Chocolate, Cola and Coffee☕️ Nerves always run high at beam time, so the tiredness comes when everything is done. Now we are happy to get home to Copenhagen, just a 5h train ride away🚅 https://t.co/uKULfaSK9y

04.10.2022 · Tweet

I will try to give you a little #glimpse of the experiments we were running the past days at the P02.1 beamline at DESY @p021_desy The experiments did involve a #robot 🤓🤖 and many, many tiny glass capillaries.... A #thread 🧵 with a robot #video 1/6 @RPittkowski https://t.co/ephy7qZXNH

04.10.2022 · Tweet

First, we place capillaries filled with #nanoparticles (small glass tubes) on a holder, which the robot can later grab. This involves a lot of wax and steady hands, to place the capillaries in a straight way. In the picture you can see a sample rack full of capillaries. 2/6 https://t.co/jITlI7KkDx

Here you can see a sample spinning in the lab, to check if the capillaries are straight, or if we need to move them a little to even out any wobbling👩‍🔬- we can melt the wax again and angle them new 3/6 https://t.co/KSfcgLFQLy

The sample racks with capillaries go into the experimental hutch, the place where all the #Xray #action happens. It is closed off with heavy lead and once the X-ray beam is on, you cannot enter. Because we cannot enter with the beam on, there are a lot of cameras 🎥 installed through which we can double check that everything is running smoothly. Here a photo of a camera image, where we watch the #robot arm picking up a sample. 5/6 https://t.co/KkREYdE1L9

When the X-ray beam hits our capillary, the particles inside the capillary #scatter the X-rays. The scattering is detected by a 2D detector, and we can see such a pretty scattering image. We get these beautiful 2D images from where the #scattered #X-ray beam hits the detector plate. What you see below is the scattering recorded for LaB6 - not surprising that we use it as a standard for calibration when you look at the beautiful #rings 2/6 https://t.co/9TybK0Ljem

06.10.2022 · Tweet

By radial integration we get a 1D diffraction pattern, which shows distinct Bragg peaks for each ring on the 2D image. I made a very boring #GIF where you can see how the #rings relate to #peaks in the pattern 3/6 https://t.co/zybBlmw2S8

06.10.2022 · Tweet

Such a a beautiful #diffraction pattern we get for powder #crystalline samples. The #periodic lattice planes reflect the X-rays periodically which leads to interference. Maybe you remember #BraggsLaw 🤓 4/6 (image credit @kirsten_mj) https://t.co/ZLJgxMsBOz

06.10.2022 · Tweet

We can identify many #crystalline compounds based on their #diffraction #pattern which serves as a kind of #fingerprint and can be compared to #database structures. There exist many databases with hundreds of thousand structures - a good start to identify your structure 5/6 https://t.co/I0rEXPwLuQ

06.10.2022 · Tweet

But what happens when we #go #nano ? By downsizing the crystal we lose most of the periodic lattice planes - so no more beautiful rings💍or Bragg peaks 🤔Not to worry, we can still get structural information - from #PDF (not the #fileformat 📰) - but that deserves its own🧵6/6 https://t.co/088BSj3XGA

06.10.2022 · Tweet

@drheaddamage Dioptas

06.10.2022 · Tweet

Finally, the thread (you didn't know) you have been waiting for 🥳 "How can we use X-ray scattering to learn about the way the atoms sit in a #small #nanoparticle?" - lets use the Pair Distribution Function #PDF ! It's all about the neighbors 1/6 /@RPittkowski https://t.co/LzQLBXBwad

06.10.2022 · Tweet

To get information from small #nanoparticles, where periodic lattice planes are rare, we measure the X-ray scattering to very large scattering angles. This is called #Xray #totalscattering. So we need to come veeeery close with the detector to our sample.😱😬 2/6

06.10.2022 · Tweet

Again, we integrate our scattering image (check up older tweets), but we are not done yet. More data treatment is necessary. We use a #Fouriertransform and transform from reciprocal (Q) space to #real #space - and there we have it, our PDF 😍3/6 https://t.co/6Ayj3Q6Oze

06.10.2022 · Tweet

We see that we have distinct peaks at certain distances. These correspond to specific #distances between #atom #pairs . And we can use the distances to characterize the atomic structure in our sample 4/6 https://t.co/Tm5lPix5RZ

06.10.2022 · Tweet

The distances prominent in the example, agree with the atomic pairs in a metal phase, where the atoms are densely packed (face centered cubic). We can also #fit our structural #model to the PDF data to confirm - our particles are #metallic and have an fcc #lattice 5/6 https://t.co/ZqlEl5t5tj

06.10.2022 · Tweet

But we can get more #information from the PDF. As the PDF shows the interatomic distances in the particle, it tells us when there are no longer characteristic #distances, so the particle probably ends. This can give an idea of #size - we have around 1nm metal fcc particles 🥳6/6 https://t.co/Jo9JhRCeZO

Small particles have the advantage that many of the atoms are located on the particle #surface and are not #hidden inside. We want such a large number of surface atoms, because we use the particles for #electrocatalysis 2/8 https://t.co/GqaMfERLNV

07.10.2022 · Tweet

What is an #electrocatalyst ? Basically a catalysts that makes an #electrochemical #reaction easier. So we are talking about reactions where #voltage and #current play a role- #electricity is key 3/8 https://t.co/5WhCLut81e

07.10.2022 · Tweet

One example that highlights the power of #electrocatalysis is splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen. When we talk about #green #hydrogen, renewable electricity is used to power this reaction. #hydrogen can then serve as a #storage for e.g. #solar 4/8 https://t.co/UVm2fWShvY

07.10.2022 · Tweet

To release the energy from the #hydrogen, we can than use a #fuelcell to react #hydrogen with #oxygen - and we are back to #water and #electricity. In this #process we lose some of the #electricity. So my research focuses on making #electrocatalysts #efficient and #stable 5/8 https://t.co/3QgwV2vvTO

07.10.2022 · Tweet

A while back I made a video explaining this #hydrogen #cycle for students, but I still think it is a beautiful resource to explain #electrolyzers and #fuelcells Feel free to check it out: https://t.co/8xyW7QiGfz 6/8

07.10.2022 · Tweet

What I would like to understand is, how does the #structure of the #catalyst relate to its #properties and how can we follow how the structure #changes during #catalysis. And for me #Xrays are my favorite tool. Because #Xrays dont need to work in #vacuum 7/8 https://t.co/WRS1gsyGQb

07.10.2022 · Tweet

With all these beautiful #Xray techniques - #XRD, #PDF, #SAXS, #XANES etc. we can actually #look into real #reaction environments and follow how #nanoparticles change in shape, atomic arrangement or oxidation state. To understand the #structure during the reaction 8/8 https://t.co/1fe34IP4cg
