At @LNM_eth we fabricate and study #nano things. This afternoon I will be showing the tools that allow us to do so and that we are lucky enough to have within 50m of our coffee machine! https://t.co/RIj6voUGHd

01.11.2022 · Tweet

These are our film deposition techniques. Using either very high temperatures or a strong magnetic field, we "transfer" the material to whatever we want to deposit on. This way we are able to deposit layers as thin as 1nm thin. https://t.co/aPXW6ni4dO

01.11.2022 · Tweet

All these machines operate in very high vacuum. Inside these chambers, there is up to 1000000000 times fewer molecules than in normal air. This is achieved by very good isolation + ultra efficient vacuum pumps, making this room quite noisy 👂🙆

01.11.2022 · Tweet

The sound is heard in this (sorry for the bad quality!) video. The purple light that we see is plasma, caused by the acceleration of gas molecules towards our material. The plasma then goes towards our substrate. This becomes apparent in the video when I open the shutter. https://t.co/214Rb6lOX0

01.11.2022 · Tweet

We can also change the material that we deposit by making this plasma react with an atmosphere of a certain gas that we introduce in the chamber. This #blender scheme that I presented on @metaconference tries to illustrate this technique, called "reactive sputtering" https://t.co/fJbV4WPyt0

01.11.2022 · Tweet

We also have a range of #3Dprinters to deposit more exotic shapes. This is our self-made printer. With it, we are able to deposit metals and semiconductors down to 100nm! This work actually made it to a #nanoscale cover: https://t.co/sZGFXCd6gk https://t.co/4HkkIbEeek

01.11.2022 · Tweet

Once the materials are fabricated, it is time to examine them to learn about their properties and structure. We use many different tools for that, and we have many of them in our own facilities! Roughly, they can be divided in: x Optical x Mechanical x Microscopy

01.11.2022 · Tweet

Optical characterization: We can study how light interacts with our materials and structures. Do they reflect light? Or transmit it? How much? We also use light for Raman Spectroscopy, which can tell us what material is it, whether it is crystalline and even if it is stressed! https://t.co/TGBfPPiqJZ

01.11.2022 · Tweet

Stress means something different to material scientists than to the rest of mortals🧐 When one pulls a material (compressing it, for example) we call that stress. We use Reflectance Anisotropy Spectroscopy to study this! https://t.co/rI0FHZuiN3 https://t.co/MwH4nkKgnP

01.11.2022 · Tweet

Our favourite mechanical characterization technique is Nanoindentation! Basically, there is a tip that "pokes" the material with a certain force, and we can see how much of a mark it leaves, indicating how tough the material is. https://t.co/r4yeAJqLck

01.11.2022 · Tweet

This is a great video showing how nanoindentation works from our former senior scientist and micromechanics expert, Jeff Wheeler. https://t.co/G29DRPr3L7

01.11.2022 · Tweet

Finally, there is microscopy! We of course have tons of optical microscopes, the kind of microscopes that one uses at highschool and science toys. However, that is typically not enough to see the very small structures that we fabricate.

01.11.2022 · Tweet

For that, we need an electron microscope, which uses electrons instead of light for imaging. We are lucky enough to have one in-house that can easily image things as small as 5 nm! https://t.co/p0QHxtXFiG

01.11.2022 · Tweet

This great machine also has an Electron Dispersive X-Ray Spectrometer incorporated. When electrons hit our material, they generate X-Rays with an energy characteristic to the kind of material. Therefore, the microscope can tell us the chemistry of the material!

01.11.2022 · Tweet

The machine incorporates a Focused Ion Beam. Ions (electrically charged atoms) are focussed into a very small beam that can be used to draw and cut the sample. This panel from @MingChen101 shows how small these cuts and drawings can be. https://t.co/qPkgm649hy https://t.co/iLmbYUgsEs

01.11.2022 · Tweet

Guten Morgen, Bon hour, Buongiorno, Buen di! Today I wish you good morning in every official language in Switzerland, can u identify them all? Today we have an 'optical metamaterials subgroup' especial breakfast, and I'll be using this opportunity to tweet about metamaterials!

02.11.2022 · Tweet

What is a metamaterial? My humble attempt to explain it in this thread! 👇👇👇

02.11.2022 · Tweet

"Typical" materials derive their properties from their chemistry, from the elements in them. For example, glass is transparent and brittle cos it is silicon and oxygen atoms. In metamaterials, the properties are instead derived from their "designed/engineered structure".

02.11.2022 · Tweet

Look at these images. This is what we mean by "structure". Do you see the periodicity? That a certain pattern repeats? This is the engineered geometry, this is what gives the metamaterials their properties. https://t.co/MUfOVW40V0

02.11.2022 · Tweet

To circumvent copyright issues, I asked @craiyonAI to draw me a "metamaterial". From what I know about artificial intelligence, the fact that it comes up with this kind of structure indicates the kind of images typically published with the marker "metamaterial". https://t.co/Td3RLDGJgP

02.11.2022 · Tweet

However, there are many objects around us that have a "designed structure" and aren't metamaterials. Think about a wheel! On top of that, the structure of a bone looks fairly similar to the images of metamaterials... The "structural" definition is a bit more complex! https://t.co/d16nwE7Gat

02.11.2022 · Tweet

This designed structure needs to be way smaller than the property it is designed for. In the case of optical metamaterials, this is straightforward: the designed geometry needs to be described by distances several times smaller than the wavelength of interest. https://t.co/VWjUacEaeJ

02.11.2022 · Tweet

That is why, although the idea of negative-index metamaterials was developed in the 60s, it wasn't until 40 years later that it was achieved and ONLY with microwaves, which have rather long wavelengths. We need to fabricate fairly small structures! https://t.co/RfyfiFtJc3

02.11.2022 · Tweet

There is still another component to the definition: Metamaterials show properties that are not found (some downgrade it to "not very common") in nature. Let's see some examples:

02.11.2022 · Tweet

Negative refraction. Light changes direction when it goes from one material to the other, aka refraction. In nature, refraction is "always positive". We all know what a straw in a glass of water looks like. With negative refraction, it looks quite different... https://t.co/zJNTiaq3Cq

02.11.2022 · Tweet

To the best of my knowledge, negative refraction metamaterials are what started the field. My personal fav example of how this looks is the example with a swimming pool that I found in @drskyskull, check this blog post for a more detailed explanation: https://t.co/FRVzK7c4JO https://t.co/hsStwYatuG

02.11.2022 · Tweet

Negative Poisson Ratio When you compress a material in one direction, it typically expands in the other one. This is measured by the Poisson ratio. If you compress a negative poison ratio material in one direction, it also compresses in the other!

02.11.2022 · Tweet

The great @TEDxTalks from Bas Overbelde shows this (1:40-2:20 approx) and more about mechanical metamaterials. Some recognition to him, he was the supervisor of @GiorgioOliveri4, who gifted me the metamaterial that I showed at @the_ScienceTalk! https://t.co/tVWkKgGldw

02.11.2022 · Tweet

Following the "negative" properties of metamaterials, there are even metamaterials that behave like they had negative density! This is found in acoustic metamaterials and pretty far away from my expertise, but still fascinating!

02.11.2022 · Tweet

To sum up: Metamaterials are engineered metamaterials that derive their exotic and non-common properties from a designed structure much smaller than the scale of these properties! Next, I will tweet about some metamaterial research in our group!

02.11.2022 · Tweet

This morning I tried to explain what are #metamaterials. Now it is time to showcase the metamaterials that we study at @LNM_eth ! I will begin with some #mechanical #metamaterials before diving into optics. https://t.co/c9b8nQWLwB

02.11.2022 · Tweet

Metamaterials show "abnormal" properties, so to understamd them, we first need to look at "normal" material properties! So, to feel the beauty of this metamaterial, we ned to talk about the stress-strain curve! https://t.co/H4cTf3gOzg https://t.co/EBB0Qote5t

02.11.2022 · Tweet

I touched briefly on what stress means yesterday, and tomorrow I will talk about the stress-strain curve more in detail since I will be with first-year students in the lab during a Praktikum. https://t.co/JpCSp2gFIH

02.11.2022 · Tweet

For now: stress is the force that we apply to a material, and strain is the deformation that it causes. The stress-strain curve shows that and this is how a typical one looks. Initially, the relationship is proportional. Then, it is not, and eventually, the material breaks. https://t.co/QQdfBNgxaM

02.11.2022 · Tweet

Compare both stress-strain curves: the mechanical metamaterial (on the right) shows TWO areas where the stress-strain relationship is proportional! That is our special abnormal property. How is that possible? Because of its topology! https://t.co/tjOW16NNCZ

02.11.2022 · Tweet

What is topology? It is a full field of math that deals with the geometry of continuous bodies. As long as things are connected, it is the same topology. Only "holes" matter. This video summarizes the basics way better than I ever could! https://t.co/05ga0bbKfD

02.11.2022 · Tweet

This video summarizes the two different topologies of the #mechanical #metamaterial, which was produced by #3Dprinting. The paper by Marius and @FabianMrBlack was the group's first excursion into #mechanical metamaterials! https://t.co/if9i6dIiNt

02.11.2022 · Tweet

Now time for #optical metamaterials! Some people in our group, lead by @paunessa, try to look at large-area scalable optical metamaterials. What do we mean by that?

02.11.2022 · Tweet

As mentioned, the designer structure of metamaterials needs to be way smaller than the wavelength of interest. If we talk about visible light, this means patterns of less than 100nm! This typically leads to very long fabrication times. https://t.co/glICjnq5bG

02.11.2022 · Tweet

We look at fabrication approaches that allow us to build #optical metamaterials with this #nano feature sizes in hours and not in days, and which are compatible with the large-scale fabrication used in industry. How? We are looking at two approaches:

02.11.2022 · Tweet

(1) Disordered metamaterials In the metamaterial definition thread, I made you look at the periodicity. But we can also have metamaterials where the features are disordered, meaning that they do not repeat! https://t.co/2UgshgTIDj

02.11.2022 · Tweet

Some examples: Structural colours using network metamaterials https://t.co/ChrrqNJRu6 An outreach explanation on how it is actually #bioinspired: https://t.co/IOP6IwOvyw https://t.co/wwBDiqZrJV

02.11.2022 · Tweet

Tailored super-absorption at different wavelengths by chemical engineering, from @Jelena_Wohlwend. https://t.co/kNLbEn69kk https://t.co/Yu6TTXPlKl

02.11.2022 · Tweet

Zero-index disordered metamaterials https://t.co/WsSTj3xenO The interaction of light with matter can be described by two indexes, for the electric and magnetic fields, respectively. So zero-index=no interaction!

02.11.2022 · Tweet

The examples exposed above were fabricated using various kinds of magnetron sputtering, one of the machines that I showed yesterday. We deposit two elements at the same time and, if the elements don't dissolve or react with each other, we get disorder! https://t.co/LEFsFUNu6h

02.11.2022 · Tweet

But what if instead of doing that we deposit one material at a time and on top of each other? We are getting to our second approach: (2) Multilayered metamaterials

02.11.2022 · Tweet

I will go into detail about them tomorrow since that is my topic AND we do not only do multilayers for #optical metamaterials. For now, I leave you with the thread of @LNM_eth lab about my latest publication! https://t.co/fBJsSo8kBw

02.11.2022 · Tweet

The reason why I decide to wait to explain everything about my beloved multilayers... Today we are celebrating 'october fest' in the department! (Yes, in November. Yes, after Halloween. Material Scientists are confused animals) https://t.co/M5kdiAgEM9 https://t.co/sGRsiWuGbc

What is on the plate today? In the morning I will focus on multilayers and their applications: from hyperbolic optical #metamaterials to self-healing materials! In the afternoon I will show how I teach 1st-year uni students about materials and their stiffness using experiments

03.11.2022 · Tweet

I could be more impressed with how artificial intelligence draws every scientific topic... Here is what @craiyonAI thinks that a multilayer is 😅😅 https://t.co/7cF6CJXGVq https://t.co/RjPVvgBD2D

03.11.2022 · Tweet

Thin films and multilayers! Thin layers (or films) allow to change the properties of an object while only using a tiny bit of another material. e.g? Chip bags! They are made out of opaque plastic, but if you open them, you will see that the inner part is reflective: Aluminum! https://t.co/55fLA5d4x3

03.11.2022 · Tweet

At @LNM_eth we develop and use optical tools to study thin films. https://t.co/rI0FHZuiN3 https://t.co/Co1BTOQa4l

03.11.2022 · Tweet

But what if instead of putting a thin material on top of a thick one we stack thin materials one over the other and repeat it many times? That is a multilayer and turns out that it opens the door for a lot of material property engineering. https://t.co/TmV6MpcRj4

03.11.2022 · Tweet

Many tools are coated with multilayers to make them tougher, resistant to the heat produced by their operation (think about a drill) and more. Multilayers are also used to make good mirrors for X-Rays. And, to some degree, also solar cells are multilayers! https://t.co/tGOPwe0lMp

03.11.2022 · Tweet

A couple of examples of multilayer work at @LNM_eth: (1) Reactive multilayers. If we combine the right materials that "like" each other, upon ignition, the components of a multilayer will react to form a single layer.

03.11.2022 · Tweet

Reactive multilayers have been proposed for a variety of applications, but my favourite one is self-healing films. Thin films can break and then your device is dead. But what if there was a multilayer system that would locally release heat where the fracture happened? https://t.co/PDBaqJrHo4

03.11.2022 · Tweet

Some of our work on reactive multilayers (1/4): https://t.co/FAIbXfC3O6

03.11.2022 · Tweet

Some of our work on reactive multilayers (2/4): https://t.co/p9ScWr7810

03.11.2022 · Tweet

Some of our work on reactive multilayers (3/4): https://t.co/aQNcnCbJkr

03.11.2022 · Tweet

Some of our work on reactive multilayers (4/4): https://t.co/O4IVeO3geN

03.11.2022 · Tweet

This was work on "chemical" multilayers. Now an example on how multilayers can be used for #optics: (2) Hyperbolic metamaterials https://t.co/I0009wClQY

03.11.2022 · Tweet

For an accessible explanation of what hyperbolic metamaterials are, I recommend the first 15 min of this video: https://t.co/5YyyI4WxpP

03.11.2022 · Tweet

There are basically two kinds of optical materials: metals, which reflect light, and dielectrics, which transmit it. Hyperbolic metamaterials close the gap between these two kinds of materials: they are metallic in one direction and dielectric in the other!

03.11.2022 · Tweet

This extreme change in the optical properties depending on the direction can be exploited to get, for example, a specific kind of negative refraction. https://t.co/v2XEwxvbxP

03.11.2022 · Tweet

Hyperbolic metamaterials have lots of proposed applications. They are superabsorbent, blacker than black! They allow us to see and detect very small things with regular light, with no need for electrons! https://t.co/IKo0kqlpA5

03.11.2022 · Tweet

More examples! Hyperbolic metamaterials have been proposed for energy solutions (thermophotovoltaics, radiative cooling) and for disease treatments (hyperthermia). These applications require materials to deal with high temperatures, though. That is a problem for multilayers.

03.11.2022 · Tweet

The components of a multilayer can react with each other at high temperatures if the elements like each other (see reactive multilayers!). If they don't, they can try to get away from each other, which doesn't happen if they don't have enough energy (temperature!)

03.11.2022 · Tweet

So: 1 Hyperbolic metamaterials are kind of a "third state of optical matter" since they behave like dielectrics or like metals depending on how you look at them! This gives them awesome optical properties! https://t.co/lKUB5MNKGR

03.11.2022 · Tweet

2 We can obtain Hyperbolic metamaterials by stacking thin films on top of each other aka fabricating multilayers! This means fast, scalable fabrication! https://t.co/9ij2VOxkzx

03.11.2022 · Tweet

3 Many applications of Hyperbolic metamaterials require working at high temperatures (hundreds to thousands of Celsius). However, multilayers tend to degrade at those temperatures... https://t.co/Tsd2vNFf8Q

03.11.2022 · Tweet

My research focusses on how to solve this compromise! Are there hyperbolic metamaterials stable at 1000C? Why do multilayers degrade? Can we make their optical properties resistant to this degradation? https://t.co/kuu3SPSOwH

A close up of the negative Poisson ratio metamaterial that I showed on @the_ScienceTalk https://t.co/tq8k3yyORK https://t.co/OXgiT6AhfT

03.11.2022 · Tweet

Time to write about the Young's modulus and how I teach it in an experimental exercise. In Spring 2020 I had to give an ONLINE experimental exercise, so why not a TWITTER experimental exercise? https://t.co/FKmlAMtVsa

03.11.2022 · Tweet

This video from @efficiengineer is a very good introduction to Young's modulus (or elasticity modulus, E-modulus). It is basically a measure of how much force one needs to deform a certain material aka how stiff a material is. https://t.co/ikxEMKruqo

03.11.2022 · Tweet

We visualize the E-modulus in the strass-strain curve. As I tell students, it is probably the graph that they are gonna see the most during their #materialscience studies. (Could be an exaggeration though, probably no one measured it). https://t.co/4G2gBrb60O

03.11.2022 · Tweet

The experiment is simple: pull some weights on a beam of material and measure how much it deflects. From that one can calculate the E-modulus. When labs were closed, I sent them this video for them to understand the experiment: https://t.co/2L6WsN2Sy2 https://t.co/LfMnoyAubu

03.11.2022 · Tweet

They typically fit data for the 1st time. Of course, the true objective of the exercise is for them to get an intuition of what a high Young modulus means. That's why they have to compare PVC with steel. And then comes the question: why are some materials stiffer than others?

03.11.2022 · Tweet

It mainly boils down to two things: the kind of atomic bond (covalent? metallic?) and atomic structure (crystalline? amorphous?). To visualize that I always bring along some short experiments. And I have a youtube version of them all!

03.11.2022 · Tweet

1. Simply stretch a plastic bag to see the difference between covalent and intermolecular bonds. The #corona version of it was: https://t.co/xPpzrJBzbv

03.11.2022 · Tweet

2. Cleaving silicon wafers as an extreme example of the importance of crystallinity (and anisotropy)! The 2020 version: https://t.co/2qTYlGJe48

On Wednesday I tried to define a #metamaterial. Now it's time to define #metals, which should be way easier, right? Spoiler: even in a #metallurgy group @LNM_eth, not everyone agrees! https://t.co/oVrvdroruq

04.11.2022 · Tweet

First a list of "high-school science" definitions that don't really help us. The "Metals are reflective": Yes but not all reflective things are metals. Not definition friendly. https://t.co/WWQymNOCY8

04.11.2022 · Tweet

"Metals are ductile and malleable, easy to work with": Not necessarily. Good luck working with Tungsten, which is definitely metal. This article tells a bit about how hard making the Tungsten filaments that we used on lights was! https://t.co/p4O1hDPeOL

04.11.2022 · Tweet

Until the 19th century, a metal was simply "a dense element". The first known metals were #HeavyMetal after all! After 1809, light metals like sodium and later aluminium were discovered. So don't use density as a definition, you are wrong by 2 centuries!

04.11.2022 · Tweet

Actually even nowadays different disciplines use different definitions. Astronomers consider that everything that isn't Hydrogen or Helium is a metal... So you are all metals! And so is the air that you breathe! https://t.co/9Fjj0oWkXx

04.11.2022 · Tweet

https://t.co/jcG0X3nooG

04.11.2022 · Tweet

A pretty popular definition among the #Chemistry community is that metal is a substance whose oxide is basic. (Basic means something else in chemistry! Basically the opposite of acid. Alkaline is a better word, but alkaline #Memes are boring) https://t.co/I6aQCJ06if

04.11.2022 · Tweet

What I call the "bonding definition" seems to be the most popular among material scientists and solid-state physicists: metals are elements held together by metallic bonds aka by the electron cloud. https://t.co/YxNNNcQ7MO

04.11.2022 · Tweet

The problem with the bonding definition is that it is not too compatible with quantum mechanics: the three kinds of bonds are defined by "where the electrons are", something that QM doesn't allow! In reality, most bonds are a mixture. https://t.co/Mzb9ZqBkIk

04.11.2022 · Tweet

In #optics, we define #metals as media with negative permittivity. This requires you to be comfortable with the idea that something might be a metal or not depending on the wavelength. https://t.co/GDOa2DOzvS https://t.co/jcOrMbdeQD

04.11.2022 · Tweet

So far we have covered what are the wrong definitions of metals (reflective, malleable), what are outdated ones (dense) and which are acceptable as long as you only talk to your immediate-field community. What is the agreeable definition of metals then? https://t.co/JW6be4LoyF

04.11.2022 · Tweet

The one that makes the most sense to me and that seems to be accepted by physicists who looked into it is related to electronic conductivity. "Metals conduct, non-metals don't...at 0K" https://t.co/UfDgPfw9Sz

04.11.2022 · Tweet

So only at 0K (-273 C) can we know what a metal actually is. If you are dissatisfied with the answer, you can extrapolate it and say that in metals the conductivity decreases with temperature, while in other "conductive" solids like semiconductors it is the other way around.

04.11.2022 · Tweet

However, this extrapolation fails again to describe metals since: (1) the same happens in electrically conductive liquids. (2) the case of superconductors needs to be taken into account.

04.11.2022 · Tweet

If you made it this far and are disappointed... SORRY! I was too when I found out! Defining metals is far from trivial, but looking into it is a good #science exercise! https://t.co/mvjSNcF0DO

04.11.2022 · Tweet

#SelfPromotion A blog entry on @MasScience, a Spanish-speaking outreach blog, in which I elaborated on this. The images were drawn by #design students based on my text, in a #scienceandart project! https://t.co/onEEQRfheL

06.11.2022 · Tweet

If you have been folowing the account his week, you might have guessed that I have a thing for definitions and debates over definitions. What is a metal? https://t.co/gvdEhVcjwg What is a metamaterial? https://t.co/512aaQLhbN And now: what is a cake? https://t.co/UfZUcJkEYW

06.11.2022 · Tweet

That is the discussion that delayed our lab's (@LNM_eth) baking competitions. Do cakes need to be sweet? Are all cakes flour based? Are all cakes layered? Are all cakes round? (and much more)

06.11.2022 · Tweet

Maybe the reason for this discussion is that we discussed it in Switzerland, a country known for its polyglotism: Turns out that @Wikipedia defines it differently in different languages! In French, for example, salty cakes pass the filter: https://t.co/LLC2wmnVfj

06.11.2022 · Tweet

In german the distinction seems to be what recipient is used for baking. https://t.co/LI45GDTA3E One of the most popular dishes in Switzerland is Flammkuhen, the "Alsacian pizza" (which infuriates Italian speakers, the other big language in Switzerland). Is this a cake? https://t.co/TeFhH5zKaS

06.11.2022 · Tweet

I felt like, if that is a cake, my mum's traditional "tortilla"/Spanish omelette cake should be considered. Some pics of the one I brought to a dinner party yesterday. https://t.co/beXolDx7bb

06.11.2022 · Tweet

Besides definition wars, which illustrate Gedankenexperimenten (thought experiments) quite well, cakes can teach us a lot of science. Later today I will use this amazing #ScienceCake to talk about my paper. https://t.co/lclaMVclJ5

06.11.2022 · Tweet

Imagine that you design the perfect cake. Due to the combination of different layers of ingredients, it will have awesome unrealistic properties. A #meta cake! But: will the structure withstand the temperatures needed during baking? Thread on my paper 👇 https://t.co/IxgRS8aA1x https://t.co/qJ07Qw3Ss4

06.11.2022 · Tweet

Instead of a cake, we designed a near-perfect absorber. Less than 0.1% of the light hitting it can escape it! How is that possible? By disorder! Turns out that having the layers of ingredients intermix a bit makes an even better cake! https://t.co/ZYWO62T585

06.11.2022 · Tweet

1st lesson: it's not always worth it to find a fabrication technique that avoids intermixing. Those techniques are way slower and don't necessarily improve their properties. A step towards scalable, large-area #metamaterials. https://t.co/yz7r83zUWX

06.11.2022 · Tweet

A material with such a high absorption would be great for solar energy solutions such as thermophotovoltaics... if it would withstand high temperatures. That's why the next step was to put it in the oven at different temperatures. https://t.co/nuVaM6u3PQ

06.11.2022 · Tweet

High temperatures mean different things to different communities. In metallurgy, we typically compare the "homologous temperature", which is the temperature divided by the melting point of the material. Everything above 30% of the homologous T is considered high temperature.

06.11.2022 · Tweet

Turns out that our metamaterial still has awesome properties at almost 50% of its melting point, very very hot! However, when we cut the cake baked at that temperature and look at its structure, the lower layers are gone without affecting its properties. https://t.co/sECh1DbeXO

06.11.2022 · Tweet

And when I say "cut and look", that is exactly what we do. This tweet plays with that concept, exemplifying what we do with a focussed ion beam (FIB) and an electron microscope (SEM) at smaller scales: https://t.co/A3i6TTxtxN

06.11.2022 · Tweet

So our cake still has its abnormally cool optical properties at high temperatures, even though the structure has began to degrade. How is that possible? Yet another prove that disorder isn't necessarily a bad thing! https://t.co/Kc0ZaKHdxE

06.11.2022 · Tweet

The structure of the cake only degrades in the lower layers in this regime. The upper layers are untouched! We know because we cut alternated cutting a bit more of the cake with taking pictures, and reconstructed all the images in a #3D tomography! https://t.co/vmbJXtBP8q

06.11.2022 · Tweet

So, why does the cake start breaking at the bottom? Understanding that could help us identify why the degradation is happening and what is driving it. We did simulations on our 3D structures to find out, and we compared how important the different driving forces are. https://t.co/qFayMxsLCQ

06.11.2022 · Tweet

There are basically three reasons for degradation : 1 dissolve in each other (not here) 2 move to try to minimize the area of one element that is in contact with the other 3 move to minimize how stressed they are. Most literature focusses on 2, but we find that 3 is dominating!

06.11.2022 · Tweet

The cherry on top of the cake is to confirm this experimentally: if we change the stacking order, we can change where the instability starts: now it starts on the top cos a different force dominates. And top of that, the evaporation temperature also changes! Double cherry! https://t.co/ICNaWcSsf9

06.11.2022 · Tweet

To find out more about what metamaterials can teach us about baking... https://t.co/IxgRS8aA1x https://t.co/ZdC9lK1iKo

06.11.2022 · Tweet

Today has been full of talks about graph-based machine learning (ML) What is graph-based ML and why is it important for chemistry? 🤔 https://t.co/P3FjIANoP0

29.11.2022 · Tweet

Graph-based ML uses the concept of nodes and edges to represent your data in a different way than traditional ML. For example, a chemical compound can be represented with a graph by assigning the atoms as nodes and the atomic bonds as edges, connecting the nodes.

29.11.2022 · Tweet

Nodes and edges can contain multiple attributes! 😲 For the example of chemical compounds, nodes and edges could contain such attributes as atomic numbers, valence electrons, and atomic distances.

29.11.2022 · Tweet

Here we describe a metallic nanoparticle using graphs. The nodes are assigned atomic positions and numbers, and the edges are assigned distances between neighboring atoms. Edges exist exclusively between nearest neighbouring atoms. https://t.co/ygXmTOaSWx

29.11.2022 · Tweet

Why do we need machine learning to analyse x-ray scattering patterns? 🤔 An x-ray scattering pattern is like a fingerprint of the chemical species. So, let’s zoom into a crime scene and follow the work of a detective…. A 🧵

29.11.2022 · Tweet

What does a detective do when he/she finds a fingerprint? He/she gathers suspects! He/she gathers fingerprints! He/she compares the fingerprints with the fingerprint he/she found on the crime scene :O https://t.co/J4xEQWAKQz

29.11.2022 · Tweet

We can do the same with x-ray scattering patterns! We simulate our suspects' x-ray scattering patterns and compare them to our measured data! 👊 However, if the database is large and we have to go through every entry, this is a very time-consuming process. 😑 https://t.co/K1h6SgU3VK

29.11.2022 · Tweet

Instead, we can use supervised machine learning! From the chemical species and their x-ray scattering patterns, we train an ML model. This ML model can predict the chemical species from a dataset within a second!😲 https://t.co/YjVofoOpYm

29.11.2022 · Tweet

But what do we do if the chemical species is not in our database? 🙃 We have tried to address this issue with our ML model, DeepStruc, which I further explain here: https://t.co/WCxA30cZKs https://t.co/uYDDDZAuMB

30.11.2022 · Tweet

Synchrotrons allow us to measure x-ray scattering data fast! 🥳 In-house instruments are beginning to achieve quality x-ray scattering patterns within hours, but for synchrotrons, we can achieve quality data with second-resolution. 🧵

30.11.2022 · Tweet

A previous Twitter takeover @RPittkowski has explained the use of synchrotrons here: https://t.co/IvWWAVHrSO

30.11.2022 · Tweet

When we measure more data, we need more efficient tools for data analysis! 🤔 This is where machine learning (ML) comes in helpful! ML is super fast analysing data and often orders of magnitudes faster than traditional minimization techniques like least-squares refinements.😲

01.12.2022 · Tweet

Can we understand how the machine thinks? 🤔 While the Machine is finding trends in large datasets that we, humans, cannot find, they are often still a black box. By opening the black box, we can begin to discover new science. This is referred to as explainable ML. 😏 🧵

01.12.2022 · Tweet

In this thread, I explain how we have explored the use of explainable ML to analyse x-ray scattering data. https://t.co/SBXuvocujB

01.12.2022 · Tweet

Whereas we with conventional approaches can refine a structural model to x-ray scattering data, now we can, with explainable ML, get an estimate of how much each atom contributes to the goodness-of-fit. 😲

First though my inbox is calling, and I have a quiet hour to get through some of the messages at least. Coffee at the ready! Back later when I'll tell you about how I ended up as a materials scientist at @warwickuni

05.12.2022 · Tweet

Well, some emails got sent, others got deleted, and in what I feel may be typical for this untypical week I did an interview for a film @wmgwarwick are making about what it's like to work here! Can't wait to see the final version! https://t.co/FEnsY5TrYw

05.12.2022 · Tweet

So, let's tell a bit of my story. I grew up in South Wales, near Cardiff, and knew from quite an early age that I wanted to be either a physicist or an engineer - ending up as a materials scientist seems quite natural now, but I didn't know anything about the subject from school.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

After school I went to the University of Cambridge to study Natural Sciences. This proved to be an amazing thing for me as the course structure there is really why I ended up in materials rather than physics as I'd planned.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

At Cambridge you don't choose your science specialism straight away, in first year you do maths and 3 other broad sciences. I chose physics and chemistry, and then for the 3rd opted for "materials and mineral sciences" - sounds interesting enough for my third choice, I thought.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

It took less than half the first term for me to realise that materials was my subject. We learned about symmetry in crystals, and how they can be studied and understood from the placement of atoms, to the microstructure of grains and defects, up to their macroscopic properties.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

We learned about metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites, and how materials are characterised. And I've never really stopped learning - I find materials science fascinating, and I love how understanding materials helps me understand the world. I have @cumat to thank for that!

05.12.2022 · Tweet

I made some amazing friends at Cambridge, and had the most incredible four years including a summer on an ERASMUS project at ETH-Zurich @ETH_Materials where I decided I wanted to do a PhD, but I wanted a change from the Cambridge bubble.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

So I took the not particularly radical path for of moving to the University of Oxford @OxfordMaterials. Mostly due to the project there which was exactly what I wanted to study, as it had been the subject of my 3rd year project. So what could hold such fascination? More later…

05.12.2022 · Tweet

Back from giving my lecture - one of my favourites! We teach a degree apprenticeship here @wmgwarwick - the students work for their sponsoring companies and come to campus for block teaching a week at a time. Intense but very popular way to study. https://t.co/tiuJq8xoS8

05.12.2022 · Tweet

We have a lovely shiny bright red building to teach them in too. Today I was teaching a 3rd year lecture on ceramics. It focuses on properties of ceramics through the window of their applications - I think it's surprising quite how many variations there are!

05.12.2022 · Tweet

My favourite is probably the ceramic knife. Always quite a surprise to those who haven't encountered these - but they are really excellent knives! And I have this Kyocera video https://t.co/HRtbNg99UC which is excellent for learning about how they are made and how to use them!

05.12.2022 · Tweet

@JoFeanelwa @wmgwarwick It is an easy one to direct people to that's for sure!

05.12.2022 · Tweet

So, returning to my doctoral studies. The material which fascinated me is what I still believe is a genuinely incredible material called magnesium diboride.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

MgB2 sounds like nothing special, but in 2001 a prediction that it was a superconductor was verified experimentally, and the superconductor research community exploded into a frenzy. They're an excitable bunch anyway but this material was quite extraordinary😁

05.12.2022 · Tweet

The reason? That simple formula. Magnesium and two borons. No non-stoichiometric complex oxides. No arsenic or thallium or rare materials. Simple, available to buy from chemical suppliers - and with a superconducting transition temperature of 39K.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

So this seemed like an absolute dream compared to the alternatives! And there was a huge drive to make MgB2 into wires, to use in MRI scanners. So lots of people were doing MgB2 research, and finding good, if not exceptional, performance.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

To me as a materials scientist the microstructures didn't look great, and it felt like this was a material which wasn't living up to its potential. There was a big gap between what was easily achievable, and what would actually be technologically useful enough for industry.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

So with all that activity going on around me I embarked on a project to look at how to process MgB2 to get the best properties. It became apparent in my first year that really the processes being used to make the MgB2 wires and pellets from powders weren't very effective.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

Under the microscope they still just looked like powders, because really they were. The process of solid-state consolidation of ceramics which we call "sintering" wasn't happening at the temperatures being used. But going too high in temperature made it decompose. https://t.co/TesnOLQFgZ

05.12.2022 · Tweet

So the ultimate question of my project became "Does Magnesium Diboride Sinter?" And after a lot of work I came up with an answer - yes! But not easily. And not under ambient pressure.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

To get MgB2 to sinter you need a reducing atmosphere (or at least not an oxidising one), uniaxial pressure, and a moderate temperature. And if you get it right you can get fantastic properties. One of the pellets I made achieved a record magnetic performance at 20K. https://t.co/SmXNz6lJm1

05.12.2022 · Tweet

And so that was where I ended up at the end of my doctoral studies, with a very good understanding of how to process a rather awkward, water and air reacting ceramic which was great for a particular purpose.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

But I was a bit fed up of awkward, and understand ceramics more generally, and to do that I wanted to study some "conventional" ceramics. So while MgB2 was the start, it was by no means the end.

05.12.2022 · Tweet

I'm going to sign off there - but tomorrow I'll tell you more about ceramics and why I've ended up devoting my research career to how to make them more effectively and efficiently. See you tomorrow!

06.12.2022 · Tweet

Today is rather less busy than yesterday; mostly I have meetings with various types of students, so I think I can stay warm in my office and talk to you all about ceramics.

06.12.2022 · Tweet

So perhaps to get started, let's have a little quiz. Which of these is a ceramic? https://t.co/GAVvG0oYyO

06.12.2022 · Tweet

Which of these is a ceramic?

06.12.2022 · Tweet

@philjemmett https://t.co/993XU93YRV

06.12.2022 · Tweet

Well, I have good news for all of you - you are all correct! https://t.co/8PCf4uOxEN

06.12.2022 · Tweet

Yes, these are all ceramic materials - but most people don't think of them all as the same type of material. That's because the ceramic class of materials covers a huge range of materials types, which have really quite varied properties.

06.12.2022 · Tweet

So what makes them a class of materials which we can group together if the properties are varied? Well one behaviour is common to them all: the mechanical properties.

06.12.2022 · Tweet

Ceramics, unlike metals and polymers, are very brittle. This means that they deform only very slightly (and reversibly at that) before they break (fracture). Under normal conditions we do not see the irreversible deformation (plasticity) which we see in metals and polymers.

06.12.2022 · Tweet

Ceramics can also be rather hard to work with because of a statistical scatter in their strength from one sample to another. This is because fracture in a ceramic material is caused by tiny flaws inside it which can't be accurately detected by non-destructive methods.

06.12.2022 · Tweet

The flaw which causes failure will nominally be the largest one, but must also be orientated correctly in the sample to be able to cause a crack to go through the material in the right direction to cause it to crack.

06.12.2022 · Tweet

It is not possible to specify the strength of a ceramic part - I can't say a ceramic will definitely withstand a certain level of force on them, for instance. We can only specify that they will have a 95, 98, 99% chance of failing under that level of load.

06.12.2022 · Tweet

All of which makes ceramics a bit tricky to design with mechanically. And often we need to avoid placing them in situations where cracks are likely to open - i.e. where there are tensile (opening) forces on the cracks.

06.12.2022 · Tweet

But if we can do that we reap the benefits. Ceramics are incredibly durable, and very chemically inert. They can be used in extreme environments where no other material can be. Often the "material of last resort" - but without them we wouldn't be able to do all sorts of things.

06.12.2022 · Tweet

Silicon solar cell - most definitely ceramic, but not much confidence! Teapot - most likely made of porcelain ceramic, as the majority knew. Helmet made of boron carbide, which can be shaped and is very effective. And brick: probably one of the most familiar ceramics around.

06.12.2022 · Tweet

2/8 Sir William Hamiltonian, born 1805 in Dublin, Ireland, laid down an important formalism for quantum mechanics through his formulation of Hamiltonian mechanics. This was a powerful new technique used for working with equations of motion.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

3/8 He also discovered the non-commutative algebraic system known as quaternions: where he famously carved an equation on the Broom Bridge in Dublin. More can be found here : https://t.co/Aw9ijGPoAZ https://t.co/8pit93ItNx

21.03.2023 · Tweet

4/8 Erwin Schrödinger of the famous “Schrödinger cat” 🐈‍⬛ born 1887 in Austria-Hungarian Vienna carried out his work in Ireland for 17 years, a controversial figure who explored a unified field theory whilst in the Emerald Isle. https://t.co/JswbQCcQVX

21.03.2023 · Tweet

21.03.2023 · Tweet

3/24 A: As an undergraduate student, any quantum related modules resonated the most with me. Competition for PhD positions was no where near as high in 2008 so I had some options, but I was most drawn to the quantum related ones.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

4/24 cont’d: At that stage I didn’t know about quantum computers or quantum information, but there were two projects in particular that I found interesting. Unbeknownst to me however, they both offered the chance to work with Prof. Paternostro.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

5/24 Q: What was your favourite part of doing a PhD? https://t.co/t6lGWYbpS9

21.03.2023 · Tweet

6/24 A: I was very fortunate in that I collaborated with many people in my works — I really enjoyed that element. It offered the chance to not only learn from new perspectives but also to travel.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

7/24 cont’d: My favourite thing however, was the feeling I had when I first published a paper. It was really exciting that something I worked on was now out there and ‘good enough’ for others to build on.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

8/24 Q: What was your favourite part of doing a Postdoc? https://t.co/N1tw9ABYhB

21.03.2023 · Tweet

9/24 A: Here I had the chance to really travel a lot and participate in many new cultures, living in Ireland, Japan, and Italy. This was also the time that I managed to develop myself the most as a researcher.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

10/24 cont’d: By joining different groups I learned many new techniques and heard interesting schools of thought. I also had the chance to be more independent, working on two single author projects.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

11/24 cont’d: That was particularly useful in improving my self confidence as an independent researcher. It was also the time I cultivated my most significant collaborators, with whom I still work with closely to date.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

13/24 A: The first year was very tough! I was in a completely different research group, with a different work culture and working in an area I wasn’t too familiar with.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

14/24 cont’d: The level of responsibility was also orders of magnitude different. As a Postdoc you have to be an autonomous researcher, contributing to the development of students, while also developing yourself and career.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

21.03.2023 · Tweet

17/24 Q: Can you give some advice to undergrad students looking to do research? https://t.co/o3lHBfGhWj

21.03.2023 · Tweet

18/24 A: Make sure you find an area you are *passionate about*. Doing a PhD is a massive commitment, and is not immediately financially rewarding, so make sure you choose a topic you love.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

19/24 cont’d: Also, to get accepted to a PhD program nowadays is significantly more challenging than it was in my day. Take every opportunity as an undergraduate student to be as competitive as possible.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

20/24 Q: Could you give some advice to PhD students? https://t.co/3EvSuxHlJA

21.03.2023 · Tweet

21/24 A: DO NOT WORRY ABOUT METRICS‼️ Do not place value on quantity (of papers) and metrics over quality and understanding.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

22/24 Q: What are the biggest challenges as a Prof? https://t.co/aHksBtqHmk

21.03.2023 · Tweet

23/24 A: The time constraints — you have a wider diversity of responsibilities, and therefore less time to dig into the weeds. This is compensated by working more closely with students and teaching undergrads.

21.03.2023 · Tweet

24/24 That is a wrap from Steve, thank you so much for your time! Tomorrow we will dive into some of Steve’s works & discuss life as a Postdoc researcher! You can check out @quantumwizard’s work on the website https://t.co/upXcbfXKkb

22.03.2023 · Tweet

2/9 We begin with work which has a special hold over Steve’s heart 💕, the first work of his PhD “Dissipative scheme to approach the boundary of two-quit entangled mixed states”

22.03.2023 · Tweet

3/9 In this work, they study how dissipation (a typically deleterious process to the coherence of a quantum state) can be used to create “maximally entangled mixed states” https://t.co/QRdPxZFsbf

22.03.2023 · Tweet

4/9 See full details in the paper below: https://t.co/TvtBYbCx0y

22.03.2023 · Tweet

5/9 Through the close collaborations built as a Postdoctorate researcher, Steve has also contributed (with Dr. Sebastian Deffner) to the community with an entry level book 📖🧐 to the field of Quantum thermodynamics & Information https://t.co/MaHjaxnx3o

22.03.2023 · Tweet

6/9 I’ve actually benefited from this text directly as a masters student! https://t.co/6Um0Vatn3D

22.03.2023 · Tweet

7/9 Steve has also looked at alternative representations of how a quantum system interacts with its environment: The collisional model approach. https://t.co/dYHW8V6b2e

22.03.2023 · Tweet

8/9 In this picture, the environment is pictured as a large, discrete set of smaller units (ancillas) which interacts (collides) with the quantum system one at a time (conveyer belt). Image ref: https://t.co/vWRnOufFRC https://t.co/XSASpX5ia7

1/11 Interested in learning about some of the challenges and rewards of being a Postdoctorate researcher? Want to learn about some exciting research in the area of Quantum Optimal Control? We speak to Dr. Anthony Kiely 🧵⤵️ https://t.co/fvVv8VYqvw

23.03.2023 · Tweet

2/11 Q: What is your favourite memory from your time as a PhD researcher? https://t.co/r5zoNthlsl

23.03.2023 · Tweet

3/11 A: In 2014 an opportunity arose for me to attend a workshop in Japan. It was a tremendous experience, meeting new people and travelling to such a different country.

23.03.2023 · Tweet

4/11 cont’d: Alain Aspect (current Nobel prize winner, awarded in 2022) was there and would perform card tricks for the PhD students, with quantum themes like teleportation and entanglement.

23.03.2023 · Tweet

5/11 Q: What has been then been the most rewarding element as a Postdoc? https://t.co/XxWNintnaL

23.03.2023 · Tweet

6/11 A: I’ve really enjoyed being a more central part of a research group. We have a really nice setup in UCD and group dynamic. I’ve most enjoyed having the chance to help develop and mentor PhD researchers in the group.

23.03.2023 · Tweet

7/11 Q: What has been the biggest change PhD -> Postdoc? https://t.co/S0UfBzXln8

23.03.2023 · Tweet

8/11 A: As a Postdoc you have more autonomy and can largely dictate the direction of your own work. You also have added responsibilities, like mentoring PhD students.

23.03.2023 · Tweet

9/11 Q: Does being a Postdoc have any big challenges? https://t.co/ZkBKmTlREp

23.03.2023 · Tweet

10/11 A: One challenge is that you have to be prepared to work in different groups and countries.

23.03.2023 · Tweet

11/11 Thanks so much to Anthony for his time! Later on we will share what his favourite work to date has been, and I’ll share what I think has been his coolest work! 🙀🍍

24.03.2023 · Tweet

What a wonderful day to be alive and enjoy some Physics! Today we will talk about some of the Dr. Anthony Kiely has produced in the Quantum sector 🧵⤵️ https://t.co/CJXEZYFeA5

24.03.2023 · Tweet

1/9 In the review paper, “Shortcuts to adiabaticity: concepts, methods, and applications” Anthony (and collaborators) explore state of the art methods of controlling quantum systems. https://t.co/kBotF0CEIM

24.03.2023 · Tweet

2/9 cont’d: The particular control method they consider, STA’s, are fast routes to the final results of slow changes of a system parameter. https://t.co/vUfiq035Tm

24.03.2023 · Tweet

3/9 These control methods can be designed both numerically and analytically - depending on the conditions and systems explored.

24.03.2023 · Tweet

4/9 STA’s are instrumental in preparing and driving internal and notional states in atomic, molecular, and solid-state physics.

24.03.2023 · Tweet

5/9 I personally love this review paper as it gives a nice introduction explaining what STA’s are — to different methods, and applications in items such as spin and bosonic systems!

24.03.2023 · Tweet

6/9 When Anthony isn’t busy designing methods of controlling quantum systems (which is a really important task in computational tasks, etc) he’s can also be found analysing the cost of implementing them! https://t.co/S0WiHbTNzc

24.03.2023 · Tweet

7/9 In his paper (and collabs) “Energetic Cost of Quantum Control Protocols”, they examine just this! https://t.co/ntddKWwFvU

24.03.2023 · Tweet

8/9 They look at well known control protocols and employ an energetic cost measure in several systems, finding a hierarchy of costs emerging depending on the duration of the protocol itself! https://t.co/3FV82cYlJl

24.03.2023 · Tweet

9/9 Anthony has also looked at disordered quantum systems, some chaotic systems, and statistics of the work distribution! Check out his full research profile here: https://t.co/gpNOkWFmcS

25.03.2023 · Tweet

Tomorrow we will speak closely to a PhD student working on the intersection of machine learning & quantum physics — let’s dive into some of the issues in Ireland if you’re a PhD researcher 😬🧵⤵️ https://t.co/iBsZGqluVT

25.03.2023 · Tweet

This week there was a protest regarding PhD rights in Ireland https://t.co/1tJErgTGUa

25.03.2023 · Tweet

But why protest exactly? (Information from the wonderful @PWO_Ireland)

25.03.2023 · Tweet

PhD stipends are set at the poverty line 😘 Not even minimum wage! An average EU PhD researcher is paid €32,100 - the Nordic countries have their pay start at €50,000. In Ireland, some PhD researchers earn €16,000, the lucky ones earn €18,500 ! https://t.co/2dyZLU7GIQ

25.03.2023 · Tweet

Ireland prides itself as a research hub & world leader; the backbone of this endeavour is based off the work of PhD researchers. Why doesn’t Ireland show love to the PhD researchers? https://t.co/EtkrgXPA0B

25.03.2023 · Tweet

Is it because they work little hours? Is it because they don’t contribute enough to research and the university?

25.03.2023 · Tweet

Well, no. PhD researchers often support professors by providing tutorials, grading assignments + test. They are also the workhorse of the research being carried out in universities. This is far more than a 9-5 job.

25.03.2023 · Tweet

There are many issues and people who cover them better than I can, I’ll highlight the main issues with links to amazing threads.

25.03.2023 · Tweet

There are other issues too, especially for non EU workers and women. There’s some really good threads here: https://t.co/cLkQwoZpMs https://t.co/O5on2gsMuM

25.03.2023 · Tweet

And here: https://t.co/7naOaH9Ymx https://t.co/29DXYPIeO7

25.03.2023 · Tweet

@SimonHarrisTD https://t.co/98BJr4cJ0V

26.03.2023 · Tweet

1/33 Today we speak to Jonas Rigo, a final year PhD researcher in the nanoelectronics group, with expertise in machine learning methods and many body quantum physics :)

26.03.2023 · Tweet

2/33 Q: why did you decide to do a PhD? https://t.co/0BZr0rwdVp

26.03.2023 · Tweet

3/33 A: At the end of my undergraduate degree, although I both enjoyed myself and learned a lot of physics, I still felt there was so much within physics I wanted to learn about.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

4/33 cont’d: So I felt that doing a Masters degree would help satisfy my curiosity and quench my thirst for physics knowledge. Again, at the end of my masters, I still felt there was so much to be explored and to be learned.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

5/33 cont’d: So, this then naturally lead me to pursue a PhD, where research would grant me the opportunity to dig even deeper into the weeds. Coming to the end of my PhD now, I still feel that there is so much physics that I want to explore..

26.03.2023 · Tweet

6/33 Q: Is doing a PhD what you expected?

26.03.2023 · Tweet

7/33 A: In many ways it is how I imagined it would be. I was very fortunate, in the university of Innsbruck (where I did my undergraduate) there is a strong focus on research.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

8/33 cont’d: Here undergraduate students were encouraged to attend seminars, colloquiums, and journal clubs. This was further amplified as a masters student.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

#9/33 cont’d: These experiences helped inform me on how research was conducted, so I had fair idea of what doing a PhD would be like.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

10/33 cont’d: One thing about research that I was very excited about was how collaborative it is, and how it allows one to interact with new people and ways of doing physics.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

11/33 cont’d: Unfortunately , due to the pandemic, I didn’t have the opportunity to collaborate as much as I would’ve liked too with other researchers outside of my group.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

12/33 Q: Coming from abroad, what’s one item that you liked about doing your PhD in Ireland?

26.03.2023 · Tweet

13/33 A: One thing I noticed is that, both in Italy (where Jonas is from) and in Austria, the research groups are larger, with many postdoctoral and PhD researchers.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

14/33 cont’d: In practice, because of group size, this means that the PhD researchers are often guided and trained by the postdoctoral researchers, rather than directly by the supervisor with whom one applied to research with in the first place.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

15/33 cont’d: In this situation, your supervisor is more like your boss. To contrast this, in Ireland I’ve noticed that your supervisor is more like your peer, and directly a collaborator. This is very nice.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

16/33 Q: How was it like settling here, and were there any challenges in doing a PhD here?

26.03.2023 · Tweet

17/33 A: Having moved from Italy to Austria to pursue my undergraduate and masters, I’ve had some prior experience living abroad.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

18/33 cont’d: Logistically speaking, I found moving to Ireland (as an EU citizen) was quite easy compared to Austria. This is because as a PhD researcher in Ireland, you’re technically not employed.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

19/33 cont’d; This means that you don’t have to worry about sorting taxes out etc. However, this is also a huge downside..

26.03.2023 · Tweet

20/33 cont’d: You basically don’t exist in the eyes of the state; for 4 years you don’t have any contribution toward a pension; you have to pay for really expensive health insurance; and you’re paid less than the EU min. wage.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

21/33 cont’d: This is all technically allowed as you’re not an employee! This then ties in with other issues; in Ireland, it’s impossible to find a place to live.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

22/33 cont’d: In reality, to find somewhere to live often requires you “know a guy”. Then when you finally find a place, the rent is untenable given how small the stipends are.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

23/33 cont’d: This is a massive challenge.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

24/33 Q: You’re a final year PhD researcher, how’s that like and do you have any general advice to other PhDs in training?

26.03.2023 · Tweet

25/33 A: Final year is stressful — it’s putting together the largest block of study (in my case 10 years) you’ve done to date into context. It makes you revise all the choices you’ve made along the way.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

26/33 cont’d: But, now is the time to assess if you want to change career or continue down the academic path.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

27/33 cont’d: I’ve done many interviews, both in the industrial sector and the academic one to help inform my future career path. I have many friends working in R&D for companies.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

28/33 cont’d: It’s made me realise that intellectual property has a lot of value nowadays & that, as researchers, we are perfectly positioned to enter this domain. Research is a mindset and skill.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

29/33 cont’d: My biggest advice to people in their latter years of a PhD is to do many interviews. The more the better, as you not only improve in taking them, but it also teaches you to more critically contextualise everything you’ve done.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

30/33 Q: To wrap up, what’s been your favourite work to date?

26.03.2023 · Tweet

31/33 lA: I really enjoyed working on making the NRG differentiable. This is a process inspired from machine learning which we apply to the numerical renormalization group.

26.03.2023 · Tweet

32/33 cont’d: This is a powerful many body computational technique. I’m most proud of this work because it randomly occurred to me that maybe it could be done, and we actually did it! https://t.co/PD8pIHgMf7

26.03.2023 · Tweet

33/33 That’s a wrap! Thank you to Jonas for his time and insights, if you want to learn more about machine learning methods in many body quantum physics or quantum transport, check out his Google Scholar: https://t.co/azq96GuOXY

26.03.2023 · Tweet

Well, that’s me signing off! It was a really fun week. I hope we were able to give you guys a flavour of a researchers perspective & some insights into the booming area of quantum science and technology! May the force be with you all ✌🏼 https://t.co/Fgo80k6dG8 https://t.co/qqF8xgkWUd

But lets first take a step back first. So I am a 'condensed matter physicist'. We make up the LARGEST group of physicists (about 1/3 of us work in this area). It's a big field b/c it underpins many of the technologies we use every day. https://t.co/WFs12FJ4rC

19.04.2023 · Tweet

Never heard of it? Yep - definitely not one of the commonly known sub disciplines of physics (no-one on a TV show like the big bang theory would be a condensed matter physicist!) but its super cool and really overlooked by students IMHO..

19.04.2023 · Tweet

Many students coming into physics want to study astrophysics or quantum.. but often they tell me they don't want to just do theory or analyze data... they want to work in the lab and do experiments.

19.04.2023 · Tweet

Condensed matter physics can be theory or experimental-based (or both). I am experimental and honestly its a LOT of cool experiments, techniques, equipment and tackles lots of real-world problems.
