Evening! My research journey has been pretty varied. I never really knew which areas of chemistry appealed to me most. I was fascinated by building functional molecules and materials, using chemistry to create things which can do something useful. 1/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

For my masters project, I worked with Prof. Howard Colquhoun on developing polymer-supported 'molecular tweezers' for the detection of nitroaromatic explosives like TNT. It was a really interesting project, with a very important application! 2/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

Explosives like TNT go boom because they have a lot of high-energy nitrogen and oxygen atoms forced into a small space. When they detonate, they release N2 and O2 which is a strongly exothermic reaction. 3/30 https://t.co/SCV6xrncVZ

04.05.2023 · Tweet

The molecular tweezers I was working with contained electron rich ‘prongs’ that bound to the electron-poor TNT. This changed the fluorescence of the tweezer, allowing us to ‘sense’ the amount of TNT present by how much they glowed! 4/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

We added the molecular tweezers to a polymer to change the material properties – we wanted to make flexible films instead of a hard solid! Unfortunately, the polymer sensors that I made were worse than the original design. I learnt lots though, including polymer synthesis! 5/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

In my CDT, I did 3 rotations in the Wass, Aggarwal and Davis labs in Bristol. In the @WassResearch lab, I was making new catalysts to upgrade ethanol into butanol – a more advanced biofuel. I learnt lots, especially about organometallic chemistry! 6/30 https://t.co/vXcsDcsBHK

04.05.2023 · Tweet

In the @AggarwalLab, I got a taste of #organicchemistry and learnt how to use their Lithiation-Borylation methodology to make complex organic molecules. Some examples of the molecules they have assembled using this methodology are in this cool paper: 7/30 https://t.co/8d89Rdbajv

04.05.2023 · Tweet

In the Davis lab, I dipped my toes into supramolecular chemistry, learning how to make and test synthetic anion carriers that can deliver chloride across a lipid membrane. These have potential as treatments for diseases like cystic fibrosis! 8/30 https://t.co/oDz3qdELLJ

04.05.2023 · Tweet

By this time I knew that I was interested in building functional molecules and materials, and was increasingly interested in medicinal chemistry. I had considered med school in the past - I saw med chem as a way to combine my chem skills with my desire to help treat disease! 9/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

We had over 30 PhD projects to choose from. @MCGalan_Bristol had a really interesting project in collaboration with @JuanCar77902465, who was based at the CSIC in Seville, Spain at the time. The aim of the project was to develop sugar-based anti-cancer drugs! 10/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

But what is cancer? Well, in short it’s a collection of diseases that lead to uncontrolled growth of the bodies own cells. These mutant cells spread throughout your body, taking over vital functions and ultimately leading to death. 11/30 https://t.co/OND66ZdF3P

04.05.2023 · Tweet

It’s hard to treat because you need to find a way of selectively killing the mutant cells, without also killing the healthy cells! BUT, the mutant cells used to be healthy, so there are few differences between them! 12/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

Cancer research is therefore all about finding these differences and making medications that selectively kill the cancer cells without also killing healthy cells. Common treatments include surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. Chemotherapy is treating cancer with drugs! 13/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

But, many of the older chemotherapy agents like cisplatin are not selective for cancer cells – they kill all cells, so the aim is to kill the rapidly dividing cancer cells before you harm the patient. This is why chemotherapy often has bad side effects like hair loss. 14/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

The story of how the first chemotherapy drugs came about is really cool, and involves mustard gas, and a WW2 bombing! 15/30 https://t.co/qNqHpGWpii

04.05.2023 · Tweet

Nitrogen mustard (aka mustard gas) was the first chemotherapeutic. It was developed into Cyclophosphamide, which remains a frontline chemotherapeutic today! 16/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

Luckily for us, we are entering a new age of ‘precision medicine’, with more specific treatments for cancer appearing all the time. Side note: The first targeted cancer treatment (and my fav drug) is called imatinib. It’s a really cool story! 17/30 https://t.co/330uv46rc7

04.05.2023 · Tweet

The target of my research was a unique 4-stranded DNA structure called a ‘G-quadruplex’ (G4). G4s are very interesting structures, and we are still learning about them. They are involved in key genome functions, and have many links to cancer biology. 18/30 https://t.co/kSfQok0WUB

04.05.2023 · Tweet

Many proteins involved in cancer have G4s in their genes. By stabilizing the G4, you can stop protein production and kill the cell. G4s also affect a key cancer enzyme called telomerase, which is responsible for immortality! 19/30 https://t.co/r6Ait7YBjv

04.05.2023 · Tweet

To stabilize a G4, chemists have been designing and testing small molecules that can bind to G4s and prevent them from unfolding. As G4s are enriched in cancer-associated locations, they should be more specific for treating cancer than the older chemotherapy treatments. 20/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

We hoped that the sugars could be used to bind to G4s in a specific way. I developed some odd molecules with sugars, and showed that they had anti-cancer activity! I tested the anti-cancer activity myself, so I learnt cell culture at this time. 21/30 https://t.co/gk2TNTwmP8

04.05.2023 · Tweet

As I had done all the hard work, I also decided to submit some cover artwork too. I was lucky to have my reimagination of the Beatles Abby Road album cover published! This is a street in Bristol, outside where I used to live. 22/30 https://t.co/oQLfNPYCwm

04.05.2023 · Tweet

This project took most of my PhD, and was the only published paper from my main PhD project when I graduated. Since then, with lots of help from collaborators and coworkers, we have published a further two papers on G4s! 23/30 https://t.co/E9Pz1cn4HE

04.05.2023 · Tweet

We also showed that they can have antiparasitic activity, for e.g. Leishmaniasis. We performed lots of ‘Structure-Activity Relationship’ (SAR) studies, which is varying the structure to see if it works better – a common task in med chem! 24/30 https://t.co/ssdoHsMEFY

04.05.2023 · Tweet

However, the road to getting a drug into the clinic is expensive and fraught with failure – it takes years, and millions of $ to get a new drug through clinical trials, and for every 10,000 drug candidates evaluated, only 1 will make it. So the chance of success is slim! 25/30

04.05.2023 · Tweet

We are still waiting for the first G4 targeting drug to be approved, though several are in clinical trials. It was because of this that when I finished my PhD, I was thinking about what some other promising cancer treatments might be. 26/32

04.05.2023 · Tweet

I had become really interested in nucleic acid therapies like CRISPR, which is a promising gene therapy that won the Nobel prize in 2020. I had also become interested in cancer immunotherapy, as harnessing the bodies immune system seemed an elegant way to treat cancer! 27/32

04.05.2023 · Tweet

I saw that DNA and RNA treatments were very powerful tools for treating disease, however they were both in the realms of biology – I struggled to see how I as a synthetic chemist could contribute to the area. 28/32

04.05.2023 · Tweet

Then I learned that delivering nucleic acid therapies like CRISPR to their target location in the body was actually one of the biggest challenges that this technology faced. THIS was a problem for synthetic chemists! 29/32 https://t.co/o7bADaTIm8

04.05.2023 · Tweet

I knew that polymers were widely studied for therapeutic delivery, and I knew that the Manners lab had been working on precision polymeric nanostructures, so I thought it might be interesting to see if you could use the precision nanostructures to deliver nucleic acids! 30/32

04.05.2023 · Tweet

And so that was how I came to join the Manners lab, working on polymeric DNA delivery systems. My journey as a chemist had come full-circle, and after not knowing what areas of chemistry I liked for a long time, I had returned to functional polymers! 31/32

04.05.2023 · Tweet

This is where we will leave the story for now – tune in tomorrow to find out the rest! Thanks for reading this far. Peace ✌️ 32/32

05.05.2023 · Tweet

How do you image something that’s 1000x smaller than the width of a human hair? You use a microscope! Except we need to use electrons to see things this small (which costs 💵). This is our Transmission Electron Microscope, which I was using today to image some tiny sticks! 1/6 https://t.co/7PDqdbbm8r

05.05.2023 · Tweet

In case you were wondering how small the samples are, this is the sample holder next to my finger. The tiny circles are where the sample goes – inside each is a mesh of 500x500 squares, which are each 0.03 mm in size. You can see one square on the screen in the first image! 2/6 https://t.co/0jKaGp25p3

05.05.2023 · Tweet

This is an example of the images you get. This is actually a nanofiber sample that I imaged today! The white bits are the nanofibers (sticks), and we use Uranium to ‘stain’ the sample to get the dark background. And yep, getting your hands on Uranium is as hard as it sounds! 3/6 https://t.co/caJ1Rw6lL3

05.05.2023 · Tweet

This is part of our lab space. We are quite lucky, as the lab was set up in 2017 so everything is max 5 years old! I even got to see what new clamp stands look like 🤯 (spoiler alert: they don't come rusty...) 4/6 https://t.co/7Z4f8DJvZx

05.05.2023 · Tweet

And this is my fume hood. We use these to do chemical synthesis as the hood sucks all the bad things away (only chemicals, sorry 😅). Mine is quite clean at the moment as I’m not doing much synthesis at present. I also have lots of bench space for doing self-assembly. 5/6 https://t.co/DFAqvFp7T9

05.05.2023 · Tweet

And finally, on the right is what a sample of nanofibers in water actually looks like! The sample on the left is after they have been degraded by enzymes. Whilst some nanofibers can be coloured, usually they are just transparent liquids - so not very exciting to the eye! 6/6 https://t.co/4BKhqdaMQ6

05.05.2023 · Tweet

It’s time to learn about nanomedicine and nano-sticks! Let’s start with the 3 different classes of medicines. First, you have small molecule drugs, such as cisplatin or doxorubicin (both anti cancer drugs). This is the oldest class, which still pulls its weight to this day! 1/25 https://t.co/kCJinIWk5i

05.05.2023 · Tweet

Small molecules typically have a biological ‘target’, which they bind to, to have their intended effect. Designing the ideal drug that works on its intended target without having off-target effects or issues with delivery around the body is a big challenge. 2/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

Next, you have what are called ‘biologics’, which is a fancy name for things which are derived from biology, such as proteins, hormones, and antibodies. These are usually much more complex mixtures, and typically larger in size than small molecules too. 3/25 https://t.co/U5siaTPBxI

05.05.2023 · Tweet

Biologics might also have a biological target that they inhibit (like antibodies), or they might be therapeutics themselves (like insulin). 4/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

The third class is ‘nucleic acids’ (NAs). This includes both DNA and RNA therapeutics. Advances in science mean that this new kid on the block is rapidly growing and becoming a powerful method for treating disease. Examples include mRNA vaccines, and siRNA cancer therapies. 5/25 https://t.co/fQuWKxxyAN

05.05.2023 · Tweet

A separate, but related area is gene therapy, which aims to cure genetic conditions like sickle cell anemia. One popular gene editing method is called CRISPR (it won the nobel prize in 2020). Both NAs and biologics can be gene therapies. 6/25 https://t.co/98nlQGh1I2

05.05.2023 · Tweet

However, all of these classes of medicine suffer from the same problem: It is bloody hard to get them to their desired location inside specific cells in your body. A number of issues have to be overcome, at multiple different stages of the process. 7/25 https://t.co/HpaYjl1gqb

05.05.2023 · Tweet

It’s kind of like trying to pull off the ultimate heist (Oceans 11?). You have many barriers to overcome, and you need to overcome them all otherwise you’ll fail. Evade casino security? Get down into the vault? Open the vault door? All challenges to be overcome! 8/25 https://t.co/fqal7Lno5W

05.05.2023 · Tweet

Sometimes, small molecules and biologics can be designed in a smart way so that they don;t need any help – they have to have the perfect balance between activity and delivery effectiveness. But this is hard, and many small molecule drugs, biologics and NAs do need help. 9/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

The body is especially good at breaking down and recycling materials ♻️. This means we often need to protect the valuable therapeutic cargo from degradation. NAs are especially prone to degradation, which is an issue as they are so useful! 10/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

One solution to this problem is to use a delivery system for your therapeutic. Delivery systems play multiple roles – they are expected to protect the valuable cargo, whilst ensuring that it reaches its intended destination at the right time. 11/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

This is exactly like real life delivery companies! We hope our delivery systems are more like @Amazon, and less like Hermes/Evri! 🚚📦 There are many different delivery technologies, each with their own quirks. 12/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

The most popular are viruses like adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), and lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Viruses are the most common delivery system used, as they evolved to do exactly this job! LNPs were used in the COVID RNA vaccines, and are the major rival system to viruses. 13/25 https://t.co/KWL2XkDbjE

05.05.2023 · Tweet

Polymers are a third important type of delivery system, which is where my research comes in! Polymers and LNPs can both be used to deliver small molecules, NAs, and even biologics! One example of a LNP therapy is Myocet, which contains the anticancer drug Doxorubicin. 14/25 https://t.co/w3LWDQ37g8

05.05.2023 · Tweet

There are MANY factors that affect how good a drug delivery system is. Some of the main ones are: particle size, shape, hardness, surface charge, surface chemistry, and architecture. Most delivery systems are nanoscopic, so they are very small! 15/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

How small you ask? Well, typically they are ~100nm, which is 1000x smaller than the width of a human hair. To put that another way, they are ~100x bigger than the speed your hair grows every second! At this scale, controlling the size and shape of objects is hard. 16/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

This size is too small to physically manipulate, though ‘top-down’ methods such as lithography are used to try and ‘cut’ nanoparticles out! (e.g. look up DeSimone’s PRINT). This size is also much bigger than the molecular world. For example, a glucose molecule is ~1nm wide! 17/25 https://t.co/RDigADTjKZ

05.05.2023 · Tweet

So, we have to try ‘bottom-up’ processes, which aim to make larger structures from molecular building blocks. This is challenging as you have to rely on fundamental physics to get the building blocks to ‘self-assemble’ into the shape you want. 18/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

A sphere has the lowest volume out of any shape, so when these building blocks ‘self-assemble’, they usually form spheres to minimize their energy and avoid unwanted interactions. Making non-spherical nanomaterials is therefore a big challenge! 19/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

Both the AAV viruses and LNPs that are mentioned above are spherical or quasi-spherical. One of the aims of my research is to make non-spherical delivery systems to see if other shapes are better at delivering medicines! 20/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

But, there are limited methods for making non-spherical nanomaterials, and making them all the same size and shape is hard. This is important for medicine though! The study of using nanoparticles in medicine is called ‘nanomedicine’ 21/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

In 2007, the @MannersResearch and Winnick labs pioneered a method for making non-spherical nanoparticles, called ‘Crystallization-Driven Self-Assembly’ (CDSA). CDSA is (literally) driven by the crystallization of polymers. Crystals are rigid and prefer non-spherical shapes. 22/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

We can make sticks, called ‘nanofibers’, as well as ‘platelets’ which are flat, 2D structures. A whole bunch of other different particles have been made through CDSA too, and we are discovering more all the time! 23/25 https://t.co/rlb83nulMR

05.05.2023 · Tweet

One promising aspect of this technology was that you can control the size of these unique shapes too. For example, you can choose the length of nanofibers, or the area of platelets. The resulting particles are all very similar in size, which is good! 24/25

05.05.2023 · Tweet

What happens next? Find out later on in the epic conclusion to this tale! Happy Friday! 25/25

06.05.2023 · Tweet

What is my research all about? Well, I want to turn these tiny sticks from a research curiosity into a useful material for society. I am especially interested in using them to treat diseases, because I think they will be really useful in this area. 1/20

06.05.2023 · Tweet

At the start, these tiny sticks could only be made in organic solvents, and they were not degradable. This was a problem, as for nanomedicine applications we needed them to be biodegradable so they are non-toxic, as well as water soluble, as humans are mostly water! 2/20

06.05.2023 · Tweet

By the time I started, the first examples of water-soluble and biodegradable nanofibers had just appeared in the literature. These works showed that it was possible to make nanofibers that could be useful for nanomedicine! 3/20

06.05.2023 · Tweet

The first thing I worked on was helping to develop a new system with a biodegradable core that was stable in water. We showed they were non-toxic, which was a promising start! But, the polymer wasn’t functional – it couldn’t really do anything useful. 4/20 https://t.co/f0SNLhE5sy

06.05.2023 · Tweet

So, I set about designing a new system that could do something. I thought things would be smoothest if I used ‘off the shelf’ components, so I combined several pre-existing technologies together to come up with nanofibers that I hoped would be able to bind and deliver DNA. 5/20

06.05.2023 · Tweet

The first challenge was making and purifying the polymer. As any polymer chemist will tell you, purifying polymers is usually one of the biggest problems! Luckily I managed to overcome this issue. Next, I had to work out how to get it to self-assemble into nanofibers. 6/20

06.05.2023 · Tweet

Luckily for me, the system that I made was able to undergo CDSA to form nanofibers really easily, which was great for me! I did have to screen lots of conditions to get it to work though. I also examined the degradation and toxicity of the nanofibers. 7/20 https://t.co/4h8XFoErxu

06.05.2023 · Tweet

My next challenge was to work out how to get DNA to stick to them in a way which would let them deliver it to cells. This was hard, as you don’t want your fibers to stick together in a big mess (like below), and adding DNA makes this happen! 8/20 https://t.co/Eo7461OCjV

06.05.2023 · Tweet

After lots of experiments and head scratching, I managed to find out how to get DNA to stick to the nanofibers in a way that would work with delivering the DNA to cells. My next challenge was to test them out! 9/20

06.05.2023 · Tweet

This also proved to be a huge PITA, and I found out the hard way why DNA delivery was such a big challenge! It took many months and lots of experiments to iron out the details and get them working as DNA delivery systems. But, we got there! 10/20 https://t.co/JIQ8zbI439

06.05.2023 · Tweet

And, we tested them out by delivering the gene for luciferase, the protein that makes fireflies glow in the dark! We delivered this to some brain cancer cells (pic of the unedited cells below). We knew our experiments worked as we made glow-in-the-dark brain cancer cells!😅11/20 https://t.co/l7LLSJuvba

06.05.2023 · Tweet

I wanted to see how well our sticks compared to balls as well as normal polymers and lipid nanoparticles, so we tested these out too. It turned out that the sticks were the best delivery system that we studied! 12/20

06.05.2023 · Tweet

I wanted to show that non-spherical nanomaterials were promising for DNA delivery, so I hope they receive more attention in the future. Since then, we have played with some more variables, and managed to improve their DNA delivery even further! 13/20 https://t.co/7xmlRb9XuY

06.05.2023 · Tweet

But, that’s not all that these functional nanofibers could do. I worked with others in our group to see if they could kill bacteria. Our nanofibers were good at this due to their positive charge, which disrupts the negatively charged bacteria! 14/20 https://t.co/b5w4rLOYeY

06.05.2023 · Tweet

I also worked with others in our group to develop a new design of nanofibers that could bind and hopefully deliver small molecules like drugs. This is an ongoing area of research, but the results were promising! 15/20 https://t.co/oIxjq6SwGK

06.05.2023 · Tweet

Lastly, I also worked with others on making glow-in-the-dark nanofibers, which we hope might be used to detect diseases within the body. I got some cool data as part of this project, including some TEM images of nanofibers inside cancer cells! 16/20 https://t.co/lkD7HAjy3Z!

06.05.2023 · Tweet

And in case you were wondering, this is what a cancer cell looks like via TEM. You can see all the things that you find in a textbook in here, as well as a load of other stuff I can't identify😅. Can you see the mitochondria? 17/20 https://t.co/HDaW6v0nPD

06.05.2023 · Tweet

One of my highlights of this project was making cover artwork for @ChemicalScience. I wanted to go with a Star Wars theme, so recreated the opening scene of episode IV using nanofibers and some crudely drawn cancer cells! 18/20 https://t.co/mifDLYn68G

06.05.2023 · Tweet

Whilst these were all promising results, there is a long way to go before nanofibers will be used to deliver the drugs or nucleic acid medicines of the future, be diagnostics or treat bacterial infections. This is what I, and many others are currently working towards! 😃19/20

06.05.2023 · Tweet

I hope you enjoyed this thread on some of my research. Hopefully you found it interesting! If you have any questions about anything I’ve said this week, please ask away! 🤓20/20

This evening I'm going to highlight some of the areas of research from the Gun'ko group, and how my work ties into some of those themes! First up is chiral nanomaterials 🧬🔬

26.06.2023 · Tweet

First of all, what is chirality 🤔 Consider your left hand and your right hand. They look very similar, right? If you place your left hand on a mirror, and you compare the left hand reflection in the mirror to your right hand, you'll notice they look identical! But are they..? https://t.co/mhPx5jc3LA

26.06.2023 · Tweet

The short answer is - no🤯 If you try to place your left hand directly on top of your right hand, you'll find that they don't match up perfectly - they are perfect mirror images of each other. This concept of mirror image symmetry is the key to understanding chirality 🔑 https://t.co/whptw6WcW7

26.06.2023 · Tweet

In chemistry, chirality refers to the property of certain molecules that have mirror-image forms, just like your hands 👐 Just as your left and right hands cannot be superimposed on each other, chiral molecules cannot be superimposed on their mirror images ❌ https://t.co/kqVTE7Gnuy

26.06.2023 · Tweet

Chiral molecules have two forms, usually called enantiomers, which are kind of like left-handed and right-handed versions of the same molecule. They have the same chemical formula, and the atoms are connected in the same way, but their arrangement in space is different 🧬 https://t.co/FBNKZs2fbC

26.06.2023 · Tweet

Our cells are mostly composed of chiral molecules, and they are very sensitive to chiral environments. So for example, when designing a new drug, we have to consider it's chirality - one enantiomer can be beneficial, while the other can be toxic☠️ https://t.co/aS8dG7djkb

26.06.2023 · Tweet

Knowing this, your next question may be - why chiral nanomaterials? 🤔 This question will be answered tomorrow - for now I'm logging off to have my dinner and head to bed! 😴 Check back in tomorrow to hear about the fascinating world of chiral nanomaterials! 🧬🔬

27.06.2023 · Tweet

Welcome to Day 2! We're back to discuss chiral nanomaterials 🔬🧬 Posting will be a bit sporadic today as I'm getting trained on some new equipment (!!!), but I'll try my best! Let's get this show on the road, and pick up where we left off - why chiral nanomaterials? 🤔

27.06.2023 · Tweet

Combining the property of chirality with the already unique properties of nanomaterials, including quantum confinement, high surface to volume ratio, makes for some very cool science!

27.06.2023 · Tweet

27.06.2023 · Tweet

@gunkogrouptcd @Finn_pm @WeAreTUDublin The field has been advancing ever since, with potential applications in biosensing, chiral photonics, asymmetric catalysis and chiral separation! Chiral 2D nanostructures are of particular interest here 👐 https://t.co/59nlACDEBG

27.06.2023 · Tweet

@gunkogrouptcd @Finn_pm @WeAreTUDublin So - where does my research fit in?🤔 As a side project during my PhD, I discovered we could make chiral 2D metal oxides, using very simple green, inexpensive methods 💲♻️ So - how did we do it?

27.06.2023 · Tweet

@gunkogrouptcd @Finn_pm @WeAreTUDublin By stirring layered double hydroxides (LDH) in water with some base (NaOH) and an amino acid (phenylalanine), we found that the LDH can decompose into a chiral oxide, as the chiral molecule attaches to the surface 🧬 https://t.co/2N4I9fyCPw

27.06.2023 · Tweet

@gunkogrouptcd @Finn_pm @WeAreTUDublin These chiral 2D nanosheet assemblies can interact incredibly strongly with circularly polarised light, which we hope can be utilised in the future for chiral/asymmetric catalysis, as well as biosensing! https://t.co/ldoWVtPm21

Good afternoon folks, it's Day 3 of my Twitter takeover 🎉 Today I'm going to focus on a major aspect of my work - tailoring 2D materials for use in water purification 🚰♻️

28.06.2023 · Tweet

Global access to clean water is a huge problem, and is a consequence of increasing industrialisation, climate change, as well as escalating levels of inequality https://t.co/2ZfYpD5Naa

28.06.2023 · Tweet

In 2015, the UN announced their Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with the aim of creating a "shared blueprint for peace and prosperity for people and the planet, now and into the future" https://t.co/fhZhZLSCNB

28.06.2023 · Tweet

SDG 6 deals with water access and sanitation, and one of its goals is access to clean water FOR ALL by 2030. For that goal to be achievable, we need more research and innovation in new, cheap methods of water purification, which is where nanofiltration comes into play ♻️ https://t.co/5iLHwuqILR

28.06.2023 · Tweet

Nanofiltration (NF) membranes are kind of like tiny sieves, which let only some of the smallest of molecules (typically < 3 nm) through @gunkogrouptcd alumna @Nat95gd kicked off the group's work on NF, and explains it in this review wonderfully! https://t.co/0klE27QXHO

28.06.2023 · Tweet

@gunkogrouptcd @Nat95gd Our group focuses on NF membranes made of 2D materials, which look kind of like tiny, irregular sheets of paper. We can tell they are sheets using a scanning electron microscope (SEM), which shines electrons on a sample instead of light, to see smaller features! 🔬 https://t.co/fqItjAKkus

28.06.2023 · Tweet

@gunkogrouptcd @Nat95gd When these sheets are stacked on top of each other, like in a NF membrane, they form hundreds and thousands of channels called pores that the water has to make its way through, and contaminants can get trapped in these pores, making the water cleaner! https://t.co/Q8Zku7hIjY

28.06.2023 · Tweet

@gunkogrouptcd Early work in the group by @Nat95gd made new NF membranes from boron nitride - a cheap layered material, that can be exfoliated into individual nanosheets! These NF membranes could remove up to 100% of a variety of polluting dyes from water ♻️💧 https://t.co/IXssjjK2GE

28.06.2023 · Tweet

Further work on this found that we could slightly change the chemical makeup of the boron nitride, introducing oxygen and hydrogen to make it more reactive🧪 It still performs just as well as normal boron nitride for water purification!💧♻️ https://t.co/FUqdpgaUxz

28.06.2023 · Tweet

This work is so important because boron nitride is famously unreactive❌ If we make it reactive, then we can attach other molecules to the nanosheet surface. This could lead to specialised and targeted applications such as selective separation!

28.06.2023 · Tweet

So then the question is - if these membranes are so good, then why are still working to improve them?📈 What are the drawbacks of these membranes? 🤔 My bed is calling, so the answer will have to wait until tomorrow! 😴😴 See you then for Day 4 and more nanofiltration! 😊 https://t.co/Pp70gGQrXx

Yesterday, we left off with boron nitride NF membranes - why did we feel the need to improve them? The problem was, when testing for dye retention, we could only use them once, before we saw a reduction in performance. The dyes eventually blocked the membrane pores ❌

29.06.2023 · Tweet

These membranes are pretty cheap to produce (around €3 per membrane, only factoring in starting materials and using our setup) But, if you can only use the membranes once, then it turns out it's actually not a very cheap or efficient method of water purification 💔

29.06.2023 · Tweet

Today is my final day curating this account 💔 today I'd like to chat a little bit more about our nanofiltration membranes, and follow it up by chatting a little about the lacking research landscape currently in Ireland...

09.07.2023 · Tweet

I mentioned last week that we needed to think of a way to make our nanofiltration membranes reusable - our innovative solution to this was to add a photocatalyst into pre-existing partially oxidised boron nitride membranes 💡 https://t.co/l6ocq1KFuC

09.07.2023 · Tweet

Photocatalysis is a light-powered chemistry process, which harnesses light energy to trigger a catalyst💡 It has many applications including helping break down pollutants and generating clean energy! ♻️

09.07.2023 · Tweet

We found a suitable 2D material catalyst - copper aluminium layered double hydroxides - to put into the membranes This was important because boron nitride is a 2D material, so we wanted a material that wouldn't disrupt the structure and performance of the membranes!

09.07.2023 · Tweet

As it turns out - this worked pretty effectively! We found that by using a €10 LED from the middle aisle of Lidl as our light source, that we could very effectively degrade a number of dyes which are very persistent pollutants in areas with high textile production ☠️ https://t.co/jpqJ7czLxk

09.07.2023 · Tweet

These membranes perform almost identically to pre-existing BNOx-based membranes, with the additional functionality of being able to degrade the dues after the dye retention! This allows us to regenerate our nanocomposite for re-use ♻️ https://t.co/qa2b6wHMhb

09.07.2023 · Tweet

We were delighted to get this work published #openaccess in @JMaterChem A! Couldn't have done it without support from various funding agencies - @IrishResearch PG scholarship, as well as @scienceirel @biOrbic_centre 🎉 https://t.co/rmuEPSBiQI

09.07.2023 · Tweet

While I am incredibly lucky to have the opportunity to conduct this research and share it with people, it's important to note that the Irish research landscape is currently in turmoil - lack of funding, lack of infrastructure, as well as major exploitation of PhD researchers.

09.07.2023 · Tweet

The top PhD stipend in Ireland is €18,500, which is 22% below minimum wage (source: @PWO_Ireland) For reference, that's about €1540 per month. The average rent in Dublin is currently standing €2324 per month. It is impossible for most to live here under these conditions. https://t.co/TyF2Lh9Thn

09.07.2023 · Tweet

There are many other major problems facing PhD researchers in Ireland. We have zero employee rights, no sick leave, no maternity/paternity leave, and a plethora of issues facing international students regarding visa status and residency issues.

09.07.2023 · Tweet

A recent review of PhD supports by the Department of Higher Education recommended a raise in stipend to €25,000, which is a good first step, but the rest of the report failed to recognise or address other key issues facing PhD researchers in Ireland.

09.07.2023 · Tweet

In addition, this stipend increase will only apply to those funded by our government bodies - Science Foundation Ireland and the Irish Research Council. It seems based on this report that everyone else will get left behind and continue to survive on less than minimum wage.

09.07.2023 · Tweet

The entire research system in Ireland is increasingly under threat due to chronic underfunding. The EU target is that member states should invest 3% of GDP in research and innovation. The average is sitting at 2.3% as of 2020. In Ireland, only 1.2% is invested. https://t.co/EYJVmIlWoa

09.07.2023 · Tweet

Our research equipment is incredibly outdated and increasingly breaking down. Dr. Catherine Day from University College Cork revealed that 52% of equipment at Irish universities is over 10 years old, with 30% being at least 15 years old. https://t.co/7FltFexC2K

09.07.2023 · Tweet

This is just one of the many consequences of chronic underfunding in the Irish research system. I have personally faced so many hurdles to my PhD research from old equipment breaking down because the department can't afford to service and maintain it.

09.07.2023 · Tweet

We recently saw what sufficient funding can do for excelling research. @tcddublin recently jumped from 98th to 81st in the QS world university rankings. This was a result of a significant increase in the 'citations per faculty' metric. https://t.co/8yR7hbCdpW

09.07.2023 · Tweet

@tcddublin As explained by @LindaDoyle and @TCDdeanresearch Prof. Sinéad Ryan, this is a direct result of a short-term boost in research investment. It is proof that this chronic underfunding of research in this country cannot continue if we want to compete on the global stage.

09.07.2023 · Tweet

12.07.2023 · Tweet

Good morning everybody!🌞Hope everyone is ready to get energized by ferroelectrics! ⚡️⚡️ First, I am attaching a previous video I made to briefly introduce ferroelectrics and why they can be important👇 https://t.co/d8d8QOXp4r

12.07.2023 · Tweet

First things first: what are ferroelectrics? 📔Textbook definition: Ferroelectrics are materials with spontaneous switchable electric polarization. Too complicated? No, actually it's not! 👇

12.07.2023 · Tweet

Imagine the magnets (that we also have on our fridges). 🧲They have a magnetic field within them naturally, with two magnetic poles N(orth) and S(outh) indicating the direction of the magnetic field.

12.07.2023 · Tweet

Ferroelectrics are also similar, they have two poles. But this time the poles are not magnetic; instead, they consist of separated electric charges with opposite signs: positive and negative. https://t.co/MMkWFGjXJL

12.07.2023 · Tweet

These separated opposite charges create an electric field inside the material, which is called electric polarization (P). For a polar material to be ferroelectric, the direction of the polarization needs to be switchable. ⚡️⚡️

12.07.2023 · Tweet

🤨: Cool! But how do we switch/control ferroelectrics?? In many ways! That's what makes them amazing! The main ways can be listed as: 1⃣By applying an electric field ⚡️ 2⃣Using mechanical force 🔨 / sound wawes 🔊 3⃣Heating up / cooling down 🌡️🔥❄️ 4⃣Shining light on them 💡

12.07.2023 · Tweet

What does this exactly mean? 🧐 It means that we can convert all of these different energy resources into electrical signals. Having an electrical signal means that we can put them in our electronics or we can make devices from them. 🤩

12.07.2023 · Tweet

Indeed! Actually, we already have ferroelectrics in many devices around us: - Acoustic sensors, electromechanical sensors/transducers, imaging sensors, microphones - Infrared/UV detectors - Memory devices - Capacitors - Energy harvesters 📱💿🎙️📻🔌

There are many types of microscope (as you'll see this week!) but the most widely known type is the light microscope (from https://t.co/2iXIi1ZrZE) https://t.co/RoQy6mgasK

31.07.2023 · Tweet

Light from a lamp or laser is pointed at the specimen. This light is reflected, absorbed, transmitted, or scattered (RATS 🐀) by the sample. A set of lenses collect this light and direct it to a camera or eyepieces.

31.07.2023 · Tweet

Light microscopes have been around for ≈400 years 😮. Here's a sketch of a louse and a Grey Drone Fly from Micrographia by Robert Hooke, 1665 (https://t.co/581VW1b0rH). Most microscope photographs ("micrographs") you've seen are probably from a light microscope. https://t.co/5uZSkY6cCh

31.07.2023 · Tweet

Light microscopy is particularly impactful in the life sciences. Or so I'm told. I'm a physicist so I don't have any of my own biological microscopy images. So here are some entries into the @LightMicroAus 2022 micrograph competition (see https://t.co/ZLrp3iqG9C) https://t.co/ljIqb1Rp1a

31.07.2023 · Tweet

Light microscopes are also valuable in studying materials - this includes alloys, ceramics, polymers, and much more. My research is in materials science, so that will be the focus of my Tweets this week.

31.07.2023 · Tweet

This micrograph (also my Twitter profile header) shows a polished copper-manganese alloy, with dark crosses of manganese oxide and light crosses of manganese-enriched alloy. These features are bad for the application of this alloy, but make for pretty pictures. https://t.co/eqSpfSpQRn

My main weapons are electron microscopes. Here's a scanning electron microscope (SEM) from our labs. An unassuming little white box, but a powerful machine 🧵 https://t.co/i5tJoEsSVr

SEMs scan a focused beam of electrons across a sample, and produce images of the surface. They're capable of amazing things. They can handle many different types of samples...

01.08.2023 · Tweet

For example, here is the face of a moth (from https://t.co/qmg7CtHW8p). Microscale features are resolved in incredible detail. https://t.co/yvvJKmadRt

My research focus recently has been in nanoporous metals as a way to hold water ice for other microscopy. At the nanoscale they're very beautiful... https://t.co/k7Y8U26Js3

The SEM (see yesterday) usually looks at the surface of the sample. The TEM looks through the material. It's basically the same as a light microscope (Monday) but it uses electrons instead. (from https://t.co/5Ev7kPjG7K) https://t.co/m1g6XZglqF

As you might expect, microscope technology has improved a lot in the last 90 years! Today the TEM is used to image all sorts of samples at all sorts of magnifications. The key requirement is the sample be very thin, ideally < 100 nm ...

... if you can make a sample this thin, the TEM is a very powerful instrument. Here are some examples:

A very thin sheet of nanoporous gold - a different view of a nanoporous metal from what I showed yesterday (from https://t.co/aV3QblGANa) https://t.co/mbU7vXHjXj

04.08.2023 · Tweet

When the electron beam in an electron microscope hits the sample, all sorts of signals are produced (see the legendary https://t.co/z3UngyGs9L) https://t.co/2whGM1l5AD

04.08.2023 · Tweet

We can form different images of the sample depending on which signals we collect. The images shown so far have collected secondary electrons (SEM) and direct beam (TEM). But there's so much more to see!

04.08.2023 · Tweet

In the SEM, back-scattered electrons (BSE) can diffract (EBSD) from the crystalline sample. Collecting the diffraction pattern allows determination of the crystal structure and orientation at the beam position ... (see https://t.co/L5UEuAAdBt) https://t.co/JG0bOmxGHM

04.08.2023 · Tweet

Here's (A) light microscope image and (B-D) SEM+EBSD of a martian meteroite. Although some features are visible in the light micrograph, the EBSD data more clearly shows areas that are (B,C) highly deformed and (D) mechanically twinned (from @Daly_Planet https://t.co/NKM6FPJ4FA https://t.co/UnvfKL23tp

04.08.2023 · Tweet

More EBSD, this time comparing grain structure of an (a-c) additively-manufactured and (d-e) wrought titanium alloy (see https://t.co/Oeond66BVh) https://t.co/7pv67aDpwc

04.08.2023 · Tweet

The beam can also knock-out core electrons from atoms. An outer electron can take its place, releasing an X-ray, which we collect in energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Here's EDS maps of a multiple principle-component alloy (see https://t.co/3olqFpNzh4). https://t.co/ERXwJW17MO

04.08.2023 · Tweet

@the_ScienceTalk Caption says "coloured transmission electron micrograph of carbon nanocoils". Very beautiful!

04.08.2023 · Tweet

We can put a saw INSIDE THE SEM CHAMBER to image a surface, cut it off, image the new surface, and repeat. The images can be stacked up to give a 3D view of the sample. Here's the anchoring of spiders silk! https://t.co/zh5gfkxaJ5 (see https://t.co/RdiopvvBo2)

04.08.2023 · Tweet

In the TEM, the electron beam can be diffracted by the crystalline order in the sample. We can configure the lenses to project the image onto the screen. Behold: dots and a cube! (from https://t.co/Naj6jtUEBr) https://t.co/Y2uY3cVsSZ

04.08.2023 · Tweet

The atom probe is a whole other beast. A very high voltage is used to ionise and rip atoms from the surface of the specimen. We time their flight and catch them on a dartboard, and use their score to determine where they started. (see https://t.co/5ihCyKyiB9) https://t.co/jFUAseFVJl

04.08.2023 · Tweet

The result is an "atom map" of the sample. Here is an aluminium alloy showing nanometre-scale rod-shaped precipitates (aka gummy worms) (from https://t.co/wrXOgdS6k4) https://t.co/ffMxv0luBh

04.08.2023 · Tweet

Here's a whole range of geological samples. Nanodiamonds!! (from https://t.co/dtiX8GLTO6) https://t.co/XOKrTajLX0

04.08.2023 · Tweet

Another aluminium alloy, but this one is dripping with hydrogen. Atom probe is one of the few techniques which can detect hydrogen (so long as great care is taken) (see https://t.co/wqcUEXkOrX) https://t.co/Va3z6b5D8p

04.08.2023 · Tweet

This wild three-phase microstructure of a samarium-cobalt magnet (from @bkhm1234 https://t.co/3Yy6OBrns1) https://t.co/LsJYcTagaC

04.08.2023 · Tweet

Some electrons lose energy when they pass through the sample, e.g. they ionise (producing X-rays: see EDS above), or they excite something "optical". We can collect the beam and disperse it to a spectrum: electron energy-loss spectroscopy. (from https://t.co/z3UngyGs9L) https://t.co/k65JbwfkNE

04.08.2023 · Tweet

The low-loss part of the spectrum includes interband transitions and plasmons. Here's surface plasmon mapping of the cube from the other thread (see https://t.co/wDLcALpQMi) https://t.co/76jxwE6DIt

04.08.2023 · Tweet

The high-loss (or "core loss") part includes all the ionisations, and allows for chemical "mapping" similar to EDS, above. Here's distribution of N, O, Ti and Co (cyan) in a semiconductor device (from https://t.co/4mbRRdLLBe) https://t.co/feS4NaDjKi

... giving information about the crystalline phases (and their quantity) in a sample. Here are some examples of the power of powder diffraction.

Powder diffraction can (usually) handle samples containing multiple phases. Here's XRD patterns of samples of W-Al-B showing many different phases, clearly distinguished (see https://t.co/DyFbj99nJZ) https://t.co/w2feBRag7F

Hydrogen is quite mobile so work like this usually requires a cryogenic workflow: samples are prepared, milled, or transferred while at cryogenic (~-200 degC) temperatures ... (e.g. https://t.co/HWMktXazD7 or https://t.co/pJn5bFOnml) https://t.co/1jAT3Cfohk

I'm using these cryo workflows with atom probe to study (frozen) water. Water is hard to make into a sharp needle so the community has come up with some creative sample preparation techniques:

Water separates from its substrate easily. "Dealloy" an Au-Ag alloy to prepare nanoporous Au. Keep it wet, and use the focused ion beam (FIB) to mill-out a needle. (see https://t.co/uO7wBFn0z8) https://t.co/HUM1SOsbcp

Trap liquid between a pre-sharpened tip and individual layers of graphene. This one doesn't even need cryo - the water stays trapped under the graphene, even in air and under vacuum! (see https://t.co/LmPt3qqU9Z) https://t.co/AwOjzXc6q5

15.08.2023 · Tweet

Today we’ll refresh our knowledge of some of the battery terms. Let’s start from the beginning: we call a battery a device that converts chemical into electric energy using redox reactions. To narrow it down, let’s focus on batteries which use Li (Li-ion batteries). image:iStock https://t.co/XqHqXg8qXF

15.08.2023 · Tweet

It is a secondary (rechargeable) battery which uses reversible reactions with Li-ion to store energy. fig:https://t.co/bMWuELalAX https://t.co/P4WUqJLAp4

15.08.2023 · Tweet

Redox (oxidation-reduction) reactions involve transfer of electrons between two substances. As a result of gaining or losing electron, oxidation state of the substances changes.

15.08.2023 · Tweet

Common example from LIB: oxidation reaction on anode: LiC6 → C6 + Li+ + e- (which describes delithiation of graphite); reduction reaction on cathode: CoO2 + Li+ + e- → LiCoO2 (lithiation of LCO positive electrode).

15.08.2023 · Tweet

So far we've mentioned cathode and anode, both of them contain active materials - a chemical which participates in redox reaction. However, they also have inactive materials which also play important role.

15.08.2023 · Tweet

A typical electrode coating consist of mixture of active material, binder (polymer which ensures mechanical stability) and carbon (conductive additive to enhance electric conductivity). doi: https://t.co/wqzXqJXO7O https://t.co/HXrkTlTiIS

15.08.2023 · Tweet

This mixture is coated onto current collector: aluminum for positive electrode and copper for negative (to avoid lithium loss due to allowing with Cu at low potentials).

15.08.2023 · Tweet

Other elements of a typical cell are electrolyte, which lets ion pass form cathode to anode and typically consist of Li salts dissolved in organic electrolytes, and separator - a polymer membrane which isolates cathode and anode from contact (that would short circuit the cell).

15.08.2023 · Tweet

Now let's look at the most popular battery terms: 1. (Nominal) Voltage - is the amount of voltage output a cell gives out when charged. It is defined by cell chemistry, which will depend on redox centers of both positive and negative electrodes. Image: https://t.co/PghKDJw7ku https://t.co/PDquGXYOMt

15.08.2023 · Tweet

2. Capacity: how much current it can provide to a load or how much charge is stored in a battery. A term related to that is State of Charge (SoC) and Depth of Discharge (DoD). Image: https://t.co/Vf2WrRUT2r https://t.co/V2SKesHqZC

15.08.2023 · Tweet

3. Internal Resistance: Resistance of the battery. The higher resistance, the lower efficiency the battery has, and the lower the actual capacity it can deliver as well as it will be problematic to use for high current.

15.08.2023 · Tweet

4. Energy density: how size or weight efficient the battery is. The higher energy density, the more energy can be stored while occupying less space or being more lightweight.

15.08.2023 · Tweet

And that’s main terminology simplified. Tomorrow we will look at how these useful devices degrade.

16.08.2023 · Tweet

How do batteries degrade? Yesterday we checked some important concepts and today we can describe what can go wrong with the device we rely on a lot, especially when it comes to mitigating global warming. image:https://t.co/Kq9YtDTsd4 https://t.co/ce0ISRRHPt

16.08.2023 · Tweet

When we say that a battery reached the end of its life, usually we mean that it lost 20% of its initial capacity. Why 20%? Good question 😉 Generally, the degradation of the battery is not linear. After 20% of capacity loss, it fades much faster with rapidly degreasing safety.

16.08.2023 · Tweet

As we saw yesterday, a battery has many components: metallic, polymer, solid, liquid, crystalline and amorphous, some contain heavy metals and light elements. It must be a headache to analyze, right? Well, some see problems, and others anticipate opportunities 😉 Joking! or…

16.08.2023 · Tweet

To make our lives easier, all degradation mechanisms are split into three types depending on their effect: Loss of lithium inventory, loss of active material, and increase of resistance. Yes, it is simplified but still helpful.

16.08.2023 · Tweet

If you ever heard about the ageing of lithium-ion batteries, the first thing you probably saw is this figure. It quite nicely summarizes the main mechanisms and how they relate to the degradation modes. doi: https://t.co/070uRG9nKa https://t.co/ZdafvoMfOx

16.08.2023 · Tweet

In real systems, degradation depends on cell chemistry, cell optimization, cycling conditions and other factors. Our recent study focuses on testing batteries from an electric car and evaluating degradation based on cycling conditions check it out: https://t.co/QLYJ6WXXF4 https://t.co/6VATBQ5fIW

16.08.2023 · Tweet

As you can see here we highlight some of the mechanisms which are relevant for Ni-rich positive electrode: transition metal dissolution, void formation, formation of CEI (we tested 2 working temperatures and 3 state-of-change windows). Check it out to see more details!

16.08.2023 · Tweet

It was also very interesting to study the negative electrode: blend of graphite and SiOx. These compounds degrade differently and it was fun to be able to decouple that!

17.08.2023 · Tweet

So for now, we saw some degradation modes and a fancy figure with many mechanisms attributing to these modes. Now let’s see how we can analyze a couple of them. Fig: https://t.co/rtEyOFalsK https://t.co/MonTj7moyM

17.08.2023 · Tweet

First al all, it is quite important to take into account testing conditions: ex situ, in situ and operando are the terms we see a lot. They refer to the state of the material we analyze. Let me just put a fun picture so you get the analogy. doi: https://t.co/C54QByTdFA https://t.co/l3XxJ03Dvb

17.08.2023 · Tweet

Then, I would say, the two approach to characterize the batteries are electrochemical and material analysis. My biggest passion is the second one, but with we can’t put apart electrochemistry. Not in battery science 😁

17.08.2023 · Tweet

So let’s start from electrochemistry. One can do many things: cycle batteries, apply pulse techniques or use impedance spectroscopy. All depend on what you actually want to know. Another thing to take into account is the configuration of your cell.

17.08.2023 · Tweet

In some cases, i.e. in real battery systems, we have to look at full cells. Which means that we test both electrodes and their responses vs each other. If we would like to know more about one electrode or the other, the simplest thing is to assemble half cells or 3 ed cells.

17.08.2023 · Tweet

In order to understand changes in capacity, increase in resistance or have an estimation of LAM and LLI, chronopotentiometry and follow-up data analysis can be applied (DVA and ICA).

17.08.2023 · Tweet

In order to follow time-resolved processes, for example, Li diffusion, perturbation techniques can be used: PITT, GITT, EIS, ICI.

17.08.2023 · Tweet

I think my favorite will always be EIS, it’s tricky, involves quite some assumptions, yet, you can learn a lot about your system. I’d also take a change to promote a nice online resource with good educational materials about batteries and electrochemistry: https://t.co/DOd87b6rle

17.08.2023 · Tweet

As for the rest, let’s meet here tomorrow and talk about material analysis!

Yesterday we briefly checked on electrochemical methods for battery characterization. Today is the time for material analysis! fig: https://t.co/hZT5GjMQwa https://t.co/udmX4vH15w

18.08.2023 · Tweet

When choosing a method for analysis, many factors should be considered: - Scale of studied phenomenon and probing depth - Properties of studied species (light/heavy elements, crystalline/amorphous) - Level of analysis (structure/chemical bonds/etc) - In-house/LSF - Operando/etc

18.08.2023 · Tweet

During the previous week, @ljtegg gave a very nice overview of how microscopy and XRD works. Let’s see how it can be applied to batteries.

18.08.2023 · Tweet

SEM and TEM are extensively used to study battery materials. Morphology observations to spot degradation, deposition of side products and particle cracking - it is fun to see it all!

18.08.2023 · Tweet

One thing is that sample preparation is very important: battery materials from LIB are often air sensitive so proper handling is a must.

18.08.2023 · Tweet

As for X-rays, not only XRD can be used: XAS is widely applied to learn about chemical state of atoms, as well as bond and coordination environment. Read more in this nice review: https://t.co/HjAJhaShYE

18.08.2023 · Tweet

My favorite example is the study where we looked at charge compensation mechanisms in actual commercial battery materials using EXAFS, TEM and RIXS (yes, oxygen matters 😉). Read more here: https://t.co/nJY3pf4oYV

19.08.2023 · Tweet

A small break from 🔋 to talk about something important: #equality and #inclusion in #science. During my PhD I was a part of Chemistry Dep Equal Opportunity group and PhD ombudsman. Here is a couple of concepts to be aware of and tools to improve the environment in science:

19.08.2023 · Tweet

#Discrimination - “the unjust or prejudicial treatment of different categories of people, especially on the grounds of ethnicity, age, sex, or disability”. How to understand that you or someone at your workplace are discriminated:

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Check for: - Verbal microaggresions; - Specific attention (being suspected of cheating or not working properly); - Unfair work distribution (academic housekeeping); - Expectation to work overtime; - Oppression: interrupted, devalued, ignored at work-related meetings/conversations

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Microagressions - “brief, sometimes subtle, everyday exchanges that either consciously or unconsciously disparage others based on their personal characteristics or perceived group membership”. How to identify them?

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Sadly, usually just but knowing what has been actually been said. A couple of examples: more examples https://t.co/c3QdXK3Q5K https://t.co/b0EcGI1dfb

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Academic housekeeping - “type of work tasks within university departments that are low-status, time-consuming, largely invisible, and that nevertheless need to be done”. The study published in swedish became a topic of discussion around the world. Sadly, for a reason.

19.08.2023 · Tweet

The article focuses on gender based aspects of how academic housekeeping tasks are distributed and shows “that women carry out a disproportionate share of academic housekeeping tasks”. https://t.co/i4PEVX1q6M

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Just one more concept to see how it is important to act even if you are not personally affected: #Bystander effect “occurs when the presence of others discourages an individual from intervening in an emergency situation, against a bully, or during an assault or other crime”

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Sadly, presence of passive bystanders increase the detrimental effect of the situation. It is important to take an action and it’s also important to know how to do it depending on situation and people involved:

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Active bystanders “are aware of when someone’s behaviour is inappropriate or threatening and choosing to challenge it.” And there some strategies one can use:

19.08.2023 · Tweet

First, access safety using ABC: “A”ssess for safety: what are your risks; “B”e in a group: It’s safer to intervene in a group; “C”are for the victim: Talk to the person who you think may need help.

19.08.2023 · Tweet

If you decided to act, remember there are different ways of doing that. Remember 4Ds: direct, distract, delegate, and delay.

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Direct action - is to call on the negative behavior directly, telling the aggressor to stop.

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Distract - move attention of the aggressor or the whole group from the situation to something else. It lets the target to also move away towards safe environment while attention is somewhere else.

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Delegate - there is no shame to feel to stressed to act right on point, but it is important to ask someone who is in power to change the situation to pay attention to the problem.

19.08.2023 · Tweet

Delay - if the situation is too dangerous to be act upon directly, remember to come back to the problem later, when things feel safer: ask the affected person. If they are ok and whether they need help.

19.08.2023 · Tweet

I believe that little steps lead to big changes. We are not always prepared to challenges we are facing. However, spreading information on what are the signs of discrimination and how to act if you encounter or witness one, can evolve the working culture of #academia for better.

20.08.2023 · Tweet

Today we're talking science! Have you ever thought about how we got from these huge computers in the past to devices that are so small that you can fit in your pocket? What if I say this was possible because of Quantum Mechanics? https://t.co/emt7d5dGuL

03.10.2023 · Tweet

I need to explain roughly how computers work. Can I do it in a single tweet? They are machines that convert a signal (speaking, typing) into a string of 0's and 1's. These digits are called bits. Some math happens in the computer and it returns something else (image, sound).

03.10.2023 · Tweet

"So computers do math?" Yes. But in a very different way. The input signal is converted into an electric signal: - 0's: no electric current passing - 1's: electric current is passing The "math" is how the electric signal travels in the complex circuit inside the computer.

03.10.2023 · Tweet

So we need an electronic device that allows current to pass or not. Something like a water valve, but for an electric signal. These exist, and is how we used to do electronics in the past. https://t.co/3JbLvqBYjU

03.10.2023 · Tweet

But the image in the previous tweet also shows something. These electronic valves are large! Is not very easy to shrink the size of a computer if inside it there are a bunch of empty glass bulbs. That is definitely not how we make a cell phone!

03.10.2023 · Tweet

So let's think again. It would be great if we had a tiny piece of material that we control if it is a conductor or insulator of electricity. That'd make our valve much smaller! So what are really conductors and insulators?

03.10.2023 · Tweet

To answer, we need to talk about atoms. In school we learn that atoms are constituted by two parts: a heavy positively-charged nucleus; and a bunch of light negatively-charged particles, called electrons, orbiting the nucleus. https://t.co/RKRSy9ZOz5

03.10.2023 · Tweet

But these electrons cannot orbit as they wish. Quantum Mechanics says that they can only occupy orbits with a well-defined energy. Also, electrons don't occupy an orbit where there's already another electron.

03.10.2023 · Tweet

So if you put atoms together, the orbits cannot be identical to how they were before. That would mean many electrons occupying identical orbits. As a consequence, the energy of these orbits changes by a bit, forming what we call energy bands. https://t.co/geTgvp9PMr

03.10.2023 · Tweet

That's what happens inside any material. And whether it is an insulator or a conductor depends on where the last electron is. We start populating the bands with lower energy. And if the last electron we put is in the middle of the band, we call it a conductor. https://t.co/XSlOMnnl1r

03.10.2023 · Tweet

If the last electron is at the very top of the band, we need a very large energy to put it in another orbital. And because of this energy gap, we call the material an insulator. https://t.co/J97UeGWEsz

03.10.2023 · Tweet

But there are materials with a gap that is not so large. And these materials we can actually control if they should behave as insulators or conductors. These materials are called semiconductors. We found what we needed! https://t.co/2DyVADOArq

03.10.2023 · Tweet

That's how the transistor was created -- the electronic valve that requires no empty bulb. Since then, there were basically no limits on how small one could make a computer. And that's how you are reading this thread on a much smaller computer!

03.10.2023 · Tweet

Have you heard all the fuzz about #LK99 some time ago? If you didn't: some researchers claimed that they discovered a room temperature superconductor. But what are superconductors anyway?

03.10.2023 · Tweet

More than 100 years ago now, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes was working in a laboratory in city nearby (Leiden) trying to obtain get lower and lower temperatures in his lab. Eventually, he managed to liquify helium. A process that happens at 4.2K (-269 Celsius)!

03.10.2023 · Tweet

And what do you think a scientist do when you get such low temperatures? They (responsibly) throw whatever you can in there.

03.10.2023 · Tweet

He was particularly curious about how metals conduct electricity at low temperatures. Especially if these metals are very pure, their resistance should SLOWLY drop more and more.

03.10.2023 · Tweet

To purify metals, you need to melt them and let all the impurities evaporate. So what are the easiest metals to melt? The ones that are already liquid in room temperature. So Heike choose Mercury. https://t.co/7d6nlWx9j9

03.10.2023 · Tweet

But something unnexpected happened: the resistance dropped SUNDENLY to zero! After many checks, he concluded that this was indeed happening and the phenomenon was coined superconductivity.

03.10.2023 · Tweet

It took from 1911 to 1957 for physicists to find an explanation for this phenomenon. And even today, this explanation only holds for some materials. And guess what: the reason why it happens is because electrons ATTRACT each other! 😱 https://t.co/6mXVw2QK6A

03.10.2023 · Tweet

It turns out that at very low temperatures, electrons don't have a lot of energy. And when atoms vibrate by a tiny bit, they can cause electrons to attract each other. As a consequence electrons move in pairs (called Cooper pairs) inside a superconductor.

03.10.2023 · Tweet

We don't have yet a room-temperature superconductor. But we already use superconductivity in many devices. Stay tuned and you'll learn more about where we use them!

04.10.2023 · Tweet

Today I’m doing something different: I’m in Leiden attending a PhD defense. And the topic of the thesis inspired me to write about my favorite material today: graphene!

04.10.2023 · Tweet

Let's start with graphite. Yes, the same material as the one in your pencil. If you look into the atomic structure of graphite, you will notice that it consists of many layers of carbon. Each layer is organized in a honeycomb structure. https://t.co/CoLJlWUbQS

04.10.2023 · Tweet

In fact, this structure is the very reason we use graphite to write. These many carbon layers detach easily from each other. As a consequence, if you slide it on paper, some layers just stay there.

04.10.2023 · Tweet

It's actually so easy to detach these layers that with scotch tape and some patience you can isolate a single layer. And that is how graphene was made in a lab for the first time. https://t.co/vKDJcRNARg

04.10.2023 · Tweet

But what is so nice about this material? Well, many things. I will list the ones that are quite important for my research.

04.10.2023 · Tweet

1 - It is easy to combine it with similar materials Many materials out there have a similar layered structure. And in the same way that is easy to detach these layers, is also easy to combine them.

04.10.2023 · Tweet

For example, we can encapsulate graphene with an insulating material to protect it from the external environment. This idea is actually what enabled graphene-based devices to work much better than other materials.

04.10.2023 · Tweet

We can also use this property to combine graphene with other materials. For example, we can use a layered magnetic material to make graphene magnetic. Or a superconducting material to make it a superconductor.

04.10.2023 · Tweet

2 - Electrons move as if they don't have mass Electrons inside a material can behave in a very different way to their behavior in free space. In particular, electrons move in a graphene crystal as if they were massless particles.

04.10.2023 · Tweet

3 - It is an actual two-dimensional system Before graphene devices were fabricated for the first time, the only way to confine electron motion in two dimensions was by growing complicated crystals. Graphene is already two-dimensional, so no engineering is needed.

04.10.2023 · Tweet

4 - You can twist! Since these atomic layers are weakly bonded to each other, you can twist them. In fact, that changes a lot of the electronic properties of graphene. For example, with the appropriate twisting angle, you can make it a superconductor! https://t.co/YFPgQF979C

04.10.2023 · Tweet

There's way more, and I could keep writing. But I think you got why I like this material so much!

06.10.2023 · Tweet

To start, insulators and topological insulators have something in common: they both have a band gap. But what happens when we put insulators in contact with each other?

06.10.2023 · Tweet

Well, if all of them are trivial insulators, nothing really happens. For example, nothing really fun happens if my coffee mug is in contact with the table it's sitting on: both are gapped and when they are in contact their interface also has a gap.

06.10.2023 · Tweet

Now if my mug was made out of a topological insulator material something curious would happen. The energy gap of a trivial and a topological insulator is inequivalent. Therefore, as you go from a point inside the mug to a point inside the table, the gap must close and reopen.

06.10.2023 · Tweet

The energy gap closes at the interface between the trivial and the topological insulator. And, as you learned before, if there's no energy gap, the interface becomes an electric conductor.

06.10.2023 · Tweet

Even if you mess up with the table and the mug, they will still have an interface. Since the interface doesn't care about the quality of any of the insulators, this conducting layer is a very good conductor!

06.10.2023 · Tweet

Hi again! I was out yesteday for an event from my department. But now I'm back! I explained to you how an insulator works earlier this week. But what is a topological insulator? https://t.co/KwUoZjQfp8

06.10.2023 · Tweet

To start, insulators and topological insulators have something in common: they both have a band gap. But what happens when we put insulators in contact with each other? https://t.co/cmhK5Xg7UW

06.10.2023 · Tweet

Well, if all of them are trivial insulators, nothing really happens. For example, nothing really fun happens if my coffee mug is in contact with the table it's sitting on: both are gapped and when they are in contact their interface also has a gap.

06.10.2023 · Tweet

If my mug was made out of a topological insulator material something curious would happen. The energy gap of a trivial and a topological insulator are not equivalent. Therefore, as you go from a point inside the mug to a point inside the table, the gap must close and reopen.

06.10.2023 · Tweet

The energy gap closes at the interface between the trivial and the topological insulator. And, as you learned before, if there's no energy gap, the interface becomes an electric conductor. https://t.co/XNFtpxATDX

06.10.2023 · Tweet

Even if you mess up with the table and the mug, they will still have an interface. Since the interface doesn't care about the quality of any of the insulators, this conducting layer is a very good conductor!

06.10.2023 · Tweet

Now that I told you about topological insulators, time to explain what are topological superconductors and Majorana particles! https://t.co/FG45OanGJ4

06.10.2023 · Tweet

So, I just told you that topological insulators have an energy gap different from a trivial insulator. The same applies to superconductors. But how can a conductor have an energy gap and still conduct electricity?

06.10.2023 · Tweet

Well, I also told you earlier this week that electrons inside a superconductor pair with other electrons. So we cannot really put one electron at a time in a superconductor... https://t.co/zqBbnHzlHB

06.10.2023 · Tweet

...unless this electron has enough energy. This energy is what we call a superconducting gap!

06.10.2023 · Tweet

The rest works just like an insulator. At the interface between a topological superconductor and any material with a trivial gap, the gap closes. But differently from a topological insulator, the particles moving at the interface are not electrons, but Majorana particles.

06.10.2023 · Tweet

These Majoranas are part of a family of particles called anyons. And because of that, they can be used to build fault-tolerant quantum computers. https://t.co/qaLRAliov0

06.10.2023 · Tweet

Obtaining Majoranas in the lab is a very complicated task. And is for example what many of my colleagues @qutechNews do! And in fact, they just made a simpler version of these Majorana particles recently. https://t.co/58ewfDQcjl

06.10.2023 · Tweet

These devices are very similar to the ones I simulate at work. And I want to end the science section today by talking about a recent work that I co-authored that was inspired by these experiments. https://t.co/bNOarp1MlQ

06.10.2023 · Tweet

But I already wrote a thread about it when this work came out. So I'll be a little lazy and link it here for you. 😄 https://t.co/7Vofmvhuo3

Why am I starting with this? Because we started planning our @lorentzcenter workshops already in December 2022! Of course, you start slow - by deciding on the topic and finding people to co-organise with you.

16.10.2023 · Tweet

@lorentzcenter We had to write an application to Lorentz Centre for our workshop - and this included description of the workshop, topics we want to cover, tentative planning and list of activities we wanted to have- and list of key participants.

16.10.2023 · Tweet

@lorentzcenter This all goes for the review, and then we got comments from the reviewers and adapted the final draft based on this - similar to the case of an article under review. And once you are awarded a workshop week, that's when the real work begins!

16.10.2023 · Tweet

@lorentzcenter You have to finalise the participant list to know how many people will attend (in our case we had a limitation to 55 participants), and you also need to ensure that all of your key participants can attend. If not, you need to go for a backup plan!

16.10.2023 · Tweet

@lorentzcenter Of course organising a conference costs money, so dealing with funding is an important step. We are lucky that we got some funding from @lorentzcenter and they also provide us with space, office and an amazing organisational support!

16.10.2023 · Tweet

@lorentzcenter We still had to obtain additional funding, in this case it came from our personal grants andour industrial participants. How to get in contact with companies? It helps if you know someone working there. It is also very important that there is a good connection their work.

16.10.2023 · Tweet

What did we use this extra funding for? We are covering costs of our podcast, use it to provide lunch for the participants, and to provide travel support for PhDs and postdocs who needed it!

16.10.2023 · Tweet

What are other things you need to do when organising a conference? Well, you select speakers/key participants. We took great care to cover our key topics well, and to have representation of all the fields, (including theory vs experiments), seniority, gender and nationalities

16.10.2023 · Tweet

You actually need to secure your speakers quite early. Of course, things might change closer to the date, but the sooner you contact your speakers, the better! Especially if they are travelling from far away, or have a heavy teaching load and need to time conferences well.

16.10.2023 · Tweet

Other things we did included making a schedule, selecting a place for conference dinner (with a lot of help from @lorentzcenter ), arranging for poster sessions and preparing questions - and participants for podcast recording.

16.10.2023 · Tweet

My morning has been mainly dedicated to teaching related activities, but I wasn't actually teaching. So, what was I up to? https://t.co/cpFVGwuffZ

I started working as a tenure track assistant professor @ZernikeInst @univgroningen in 2022. My focus is on research, which means that 60% of my time is dedicated to research, 30% to teaching and 10% to academic service.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

Most of the professors in the Netherlands need to obtain a University Teaching Qualification (UTQ, or BKO). How you get it depends on your University. In case of the University of Groningen, we take classes given by education experts, have homework and a final portfolio.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

Today I was taking classes on modes of assessment, advantages and disadvantages different modes and some mistakes that are good to avoid when making exams. The classes are for all of the lectures, so you might end up in a group with people working at a very different places.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

So far I've been in groups with lecturers from economics, law, history of architecture, medical school, computer science- and one fellow physicist. It is an good place meet your fellow colleagues, and see how different teaching can be. But sometimes it can be very difficult.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

We use different language, departments have different lecture modes, and we might not even know anything about the field of the colleague. I'm usually always happy when I end up in a group with colleagues from #science and #engineering faculty, as we can talk easily.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

These course are not completely theoretical. We actually have to time it well, as we need take certain moduels while we are teaching, as we have 2 experienced people to come and observe us while teaching. One is am expected colleagues, another our teaching coach.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

Yes, we got a coach 📢 It is typically an education expert that is supposed to track our progress, and help us with pur portfolio. So far I've completed my teaching and design modules, and only have assessment left. Then I can write my portfolio- and hopefully get my UTQ! 🤞

17.10.2023 · Tweet

How much do I teach? I'd say a lot, bit it is subjective. And depends how you count hours. I am a coordinator and lecturer for 2 MSc courses, Surfaces and Interfaces (it's basically what I do in the lab 😃) and Nanomaterials:Synthesis and Engineering.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

I'm also coordinator and lecturer for a BSc course Physics Instrumentation and #Technology . These latter 2 courses are also brand new, so that makes them quite handful. I also give a couple of lectures in 2 more courses, one BSc level and another MSc.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

Teaching for first time takes a lot of time - at least me. On average, I'd say it takes me 8 hours to prepare lectures, slides included, for 1 lecture (2x45 min). You need to make an outline, check that it fits well with learning goals and student background, make slides

17.10.2023 · Tweet

How long does it take for you to prepare lectures when teaching a course for the first time #AcademicChatter

17.10.2023 · Tweet

I am back in Leiden and ready to do some work before bedtime. But first, a bit more about teaching! https://t.co/MwEar6320o

17.10.2023 · Tweet

Besides my regular teaching duties, I'm also a member of a curriculum committee for BSc in Physics. At the moment we are looking into possible changes we want to make in our curriculum. Being a member of a curriculum committee is actually an excellent way to learn how things work

17.10.2023 · Tweet

Before coming to the Netherlands, I've only been here as a tourist, so I had no idea about the curriculum, how the semesters are arranged, and even what exact courses students take. As a new PI, you don't have much spare time to read up on this

17.10.2023 · Tweet

But as a curriculum committee member, it is kinda your job to read up on these hings - and it counts in your service hours, so it is a good deal. So what do we do in this committee?

17.10.2023 · Tweet

We look at the curriculum as a whole, courses that are offered and input from the students, and can propose changes. We can suggest that courses are rearranged, changes, removed from the curriculum or propose new ones.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

Now, we don't exist in vacuum! We have representative members from each physics track, we work together on a plan - and then discuss it with our colleagues. After that, we either can write our report, or we gotta go back to the drawing board.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

You might wonder how long this takes -and the answer is that it varies. We do need to finish before Christmas as that is when the plan for the next academic year (teaching wise) is made, so we do have a hard deadline!

17.10.2023 · Tweet

You might have noticed that I am mentioning "plan for the next academic year", and that it is basically done almost a year in advance, but what is that? https://t.co/gqTNo7tmjG

17.10.2023 · Tweet

Well, we actually make plans for the courses close to a year ahead! I don't mean that we have a schedule or start working on the lectures, but we need to know which courses are taught and when, so that students are informed in time.

17.10.2023 · Tweet

We also need to make a description of the course, with learning outcomes, what programme are they for, and even modes of assessment. This can be quite a handful if you are teaching for the first time, but it gets easier with time - as long as you are teaching the same course 😅

17.10.2023 · Tweet

These things can be changed every year - and are actually often updated. Maybe you decided to switch from written to oral exam, or you decided to change the book you use, or learning outcomes - you gotta plan it a year ahead!

17.10.2023 · Tweet
