Today's topic - my recent paper that I am super excited about and that I already mentioned in the podcast with @MySci_PK ! In Situ Exfoliation Method of Large‐Area 2D Materials - also known as KISS method (kinetic in situ single-layer synthesis) 💋 https://t.co/8yaj7A6wla

18.10.2023 · Tweet

This is my first work that came out since I joined @ZernikeInst , and it was mainly done when I moved there. And yes, this is the work done with the international team of scientific besties 🥰💜

18.10.2023 · Tweet

@ZernikeInst What is this method about? Well, it is an #exfoliaiton #method that uses atomically clean surfaces as both a substrate for 2D #materials and a sort of a sticky tape for their exfolation

18.10.2023 · Tweet

Method is made to really work well for different #surface #science techniques, as that is my main branch of work, and all of the tools are simply tools you would find in your average surface science #lab!

18.10.2023 · Tweet

How does it work? Well, we take a substrate - in our case often a single #crystal metals, as we like conducting surfaces, such as Au(111)🥇 and Ag(111)🥈and we use sputtering & annealing methods to make them extremely clean. All done in ultra-high vacuum!

18.10.2023 · Tweet

In the meantime, we also prepare a layered crystal that we would like to exfoliate in a 2D form, let's say WSe2. How do we prepare ti? Well, we use a little pin- or a sticky tape (!)- to remove top layers in ultrahigh vacuum, so that crystal also has super clean surface

18.10.2023 · Tweet

And then we simply bring these 2 atomically clean surfaces in contact and make them KISS 💋 We do have a little addition - layered crystal is on a sample holder with a spring- to make it easier to aling things, and to know for sure when things are brought in contact.

18.10.2023 · Tweet

Once you separate them, you are left with your layered crystal AND substrate that has large area 2D film (in our example case of WSe2). Large area is the key here. All methods that I use usually require samples of at least 200 um, preferably larger. and KISS method makes them!

18.10.2023 · Tweet

Sounds quite neat, right? We also tried it on semiconductors (Ge), and also on air sensitive materials such as WTe2, and it works like a charm! We've done these measurements at a couple of places @ZernikeInst @KTHuniversity and @AarhusUni_int and it worked quite nicely!

18.10.2023 · Tweet

@ZernikeInst @KTHuniversity @AarhusUni_int We managed to measure the electronic structure, which is one of the most interesting things to me, and it also seems that it is interesting to other people in the surface science community - which is what we hoped for!

18.10.2023 · Tweet

@ZernikeInst @KTHuniversity @AarhusUni_int There is already a work on @arxiv by M. Bianchi from @AarhusUni_int using KISS method to exfoliate CrSBr https://t.co/l7l5VlDN1R Very exciting thing!

18.10.2023 · Tweet

As today is my last day here, I thought I will tell you a bit about how my career changed since I was here 2-3 years ago (also week 42!)

22.10.2023 · Tweet

Last time I was Tweeting from this profile, I was a #postdoc @KTHuniversity . That was also during COVID19 time, so I have to admit that I did not see too much of #Stockholm and #Sweden. Quite unfortunate as it is a country with beautiful nature.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

I was there on a 2 year postdoctoral fellowship,with a possibility of extension. Not to bad of a deal (no one wants to move during a pandemic...). During that time, I received an email via a mailing list advertising a tenure track position @ZernikeInst @univgroningen

22.10.2023 · Tweet

I've never been to Groningen at that point, but the position looked perfect to me, as it was really in the field that I was interested in - ultrafast #Science And I even had a background in it! I was considering whether to apply or not, as I wasn't sure I really stand a chance..

22.10.2023 · Tweet

But I thought positions that sound perfect don't appear that often, and I can at least use it as a practice. It definitely helped to have a supporting partner -and supportive work #friends who were telling me to definitely apply.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

I took it as a bit of a research project - I checked what is all the information they need, and how it should be written: CV, publications, cover letter, research and #teaching statement... I also asked friends for examples of their applications to have an idea how they did it.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

After being on a hiring committee myself - I can tell you that (at least at my university) all of the requested information is relevant. Yes, we are the most interested in your research (for research position), but we also really care about your teaching, and collegiality.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

When preparing for an application, I also read about the university, and the institute I was applying with. Who works there, can I collaborate with someone? And also, what are some classes I could teach. It is also good to check possible funding you can apply with.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

And then I did my best, sent an application, and got a glass of wine! 🍷

22.10.2023 · Tweet

Some time later, I was informed that I am shortlisted, and that they would like to do an online interview (remember, COVID19 time...). This was both exciting, and a bit terrifying. Luckily for me, I have great friends and colleagues who helped me prepare.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

I was scheduled to give a seminar to the department, and then a 5 min presentation on my research and teaching vision, respectively.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

I made several different versions of each, until I was happy. And I asked people for help. My PhD supervisor is amazing, and he checked my research plan and my seminar. Gave really helpful advice.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

I had a meeting with my former colleague about teaching, and I even had a chat with two former collaborators who work(ed) in the Netherlands to prepare better. If you can, do ask people for advice. Most of the time people are happy to help you, and want to see you succeed!

22.10.2023 · Tweet

I am really privileged to have an amazing #PhD supervisor, and great friends from my PhD time that I consider family at this point who helped and supported me in this journey. If you are not as lucky, you should still try to contact people you know.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

Maybe you collaborated with someone who work at the place you are applying at, or you met someone at the conference some time ago, and you had a great discussion? Do contact them and see if they are willing to meet with you!

22.10.2023 · Tweet

And don't underestimate importance of all the things they asked for in the application. In my interview, everything was covered - from research to teaching and management. One of the committee members was a senior master student and they had a lot of questions about teaching.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

Of course, before doing online or in person interview, check who you will be talking to, so that you can prepare. It is your interview, sure, but you are also interviewing them! You might end up working with these people next 30-40 years so take the opportunity to ask questions.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

I've discussed my research, teaching, even outreach with the committee members!

22.10.2023 · Tweet

If interview is online - plan to have an evening off afterwards. It is an exhausting process even if you have good conversations and never leave your room/office. In person, well, it is even more exhausting, but you do avoid possible internet connections issues 🫣

22.10.2023 · Tweet

Something I will not go in details, but is also important, is the part when you are offered a position and need to negotiate your contract/starting package. It varies A LOT from a place to a place, even in the same country. For this, you do want to talk to someone, if you can.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

And you want to talk to someone from at least the same country - again, as this vastly differs from a place to a place. Did I do a great job negotiating? Don't think so, I kinda sucked at it... But I am happy with there I am. My colleagues are great, and #groningen is nice :)

22.10.2023 · Tweet

Once you start, things are tough. You need to move from your mainly research oriented work and start teaching, figuring out paperwork, policies etc. I am super lucky that @ZernikeInst tenure trackers are amazing, and always help new people. I always have people to ask advice

22.10.2023 · Tweet

@ZernikeInst We work on solving problems together. And if no one has a solution for my problem, at least I can get moral support from them (and more senior colleagues) 😃 They are a really excellent group of people, and I am happy to have them, as otherwise it gets a bit lonely...

22.10.2023 · Tweet

@ZernikeInst I also relatively often work evenings and weekends (today as well a bit). Sometimes it is due to paper deadlines 📰, but often it is simply a bad combination of teaching deadlines/preparing lectures and grant deadlines.

22.10.2023 · Tweet

@ZernikeInst As I've mentioned before, it does take me 8h (on average) to prepare one lecture for the course I am teaching for the first time. This does go down A LOT second time you teach, so I am optimistic about my free time in the future 🤞

22.10.2023 · Tweet

@ZernikeInst I also do think that we need to work on changing our academic culture when it come to this. We love our work, but we also have so many different roles we need to fulfill, that it is simply impossible to do within "normal" working hours https://t.co/1rTaFs5lJh

22.10.2023 · Tweet

@ZernikeInst So sometimes you really need to decide what to prioritise - and also you need to see if there are thins you can delegate and optimise.

"Chemical Bathtubs", where did we get that title? Well, it comes from the technique I (@DrCBrew) use in my work, Chemical Bath Deposition (CBD) of transition metal chalcogenides.

26.10.2023 · Tweet

In simple terms, CBD is a method for depositing a material onto a substrate by placing the substrate into a solution containing a mixture of chemical components. https://t.co/UdyuBuOHco

26.10.2023 · Tweet

Like our other deposition project (PACVD), the substrates that I use here are self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) on Au, which are a model system for depositing onto other organic substrates. https://t.co/40GYOuMCjs

26.10.2023 · Tweet

We use different functionalized SAMs to determine how a functional group influences the deposition of a material.

26.10.2023 · Tweet

Functionalized SAMs also allow us to look at performing area selective deposition of our materials by using patterned SAMs.

26.10.2023 · Tweet

The common components in a CBD bath are a metal source, a chalcogen source, and a complexing agent. Other properties of the bath (like pH) can also be tuned!

26.10.2023 · Tweet

We do all of our depositions at room temperature. So we typically tune amounts/ concentrations of components, the components used, and pH. With this we can modify, the reaction pathways occuring, their kinetics, and some of the surface chemistry. (Likely over simplification!)

26.10.2023 · Tweet

The deposits that we get from CBD are thick enough you can see them with your eye! https://t.co/dfw7ANtBjL

26.10.2023 · Tweet

Our common initial characterization includes optical microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS. https://t.co/2ylTItKaMQ

26.10.2023 · Tweet

My work is not published yet (I do talk a little bit about what I am doing in the podcast though!), but I can share a bit about some of the prior CBD work we have done in the lab.

26.10.2023 · Tweet

Previous lab members done some work on CBD of MoS2 films in the past: https://t.co/YpB2e9dymE

26.10.2023 · Tweet

For a look at area selective deposition of CuS by CBD, check out some of our previous lab member's work! https://t.co/gRMNOT4OCK

26.10.2023 · Tweet

Depending on how you tune your bath pH, you can control the deposit between Cu2S and CuS! https://t.co/hKozU1UWiC

26.10.2023 · Tweet

Hopefully you find chemical bathtubs as exciting as I do now! I'm looking forward to being able to share my work once it is ready

N-S you beauty: At the heart of fluid dynamics lies the Navier-Stokes equations, governing the motion of fluids. These equations are derivatives of basic laws of #physics viz. Mass conservation and Newton's Second law applied to Fluid Flow https://t.co/veHn4E3jk1

14.11.2023 · Tweet

The Clay Institute's problem revolves around proving the existence and smoothness of solutions to these equations. While solutions are available in limited cases, a universal understanding remains elusive. This challenge stands as one of the seven problems.

💰 A $1 million reward awaits anyone who cracks the code! Mathematicians worldwide are drawn to the challenge, making it a pinnacle of mathematical exploration.

Vortex-based #cavitation involves the controlled formation and implosion of tiny bubbles in a fluid, creating powerful shockwaves. This phenomenon is harnessed to enhance processes like #mixing, #reactions, #emulsions, and #crystallization. https://t.co/qOmjtm4gzt

15.11.2023 · Tweet

Unlike traditional #cavitation, where the collapse of bubbles can be destructive, vortex-based devices leverage controlled cavitation. The result? Enhanced mixing efficiency, accelerated reactions, and improved performance in various applications.https://t.co/A0qI6yYuDS

15.11.2023 · Tweet

From chemical processing to wastewater treatment, vortex-based cavitation devices hold promise in diverse fields. These devices can optimize energy transfer, reduce resource consumption, and improve overall process efficiency.https://t.co/B5s8ccqNHR https://t.co/QiOohvikzG

15.11.2023 · Tweet

@VORTA_TECH is a company that uses such a Vortex-based #cavitation for a variety of applications more about them in a separate thread. https://t.co/LgStnG0rp7

Crystallization is a process widely used for purification and synthesis of drugs and biomolecules in the pharmaceutical industry. The critical quality attributes (CQA) of the crystals help us decide whether the crystals produced are fit for our application or not. 💎✨

16.11.2023 · Tweet

Along with purity, polymorphic form, shape of the crystal, and particle size is an important CQA. The crystals formed are not all of the same size and hence we refer to the distribution of the sizes as the particle size distribution (PSD). https://t.co/dNo8o1K7FK

16.11.2023 · Tweet

One of the major goals in the pharmaceutical industry is to achieve a uniform particle size. We need to incorporate tools that help us monitor the process while it is happening👩‍🔬These tools are referred to as PAT tools or process analytical tech tools.

16.11.2023 · Tweet

The focused beam reflectance measurement (FBRM) is one such PAT tool that uses the measurement of the reflectance of a laser beam off the surface of the particles as an indicator of the size and number of particles. 🔦⚡https://t.co/kzVxgiOn7u

16.11.2023 · Tweet

The FBRM measures the length of a random chord (CLD) on the particles and not the actual size. The inversion of CLD to PSD for spherical particles has been discussed before. https://t.co/kT4O5C06kD

16.11.2023 · Tweet

While everything would seem easy-peasy with the instrument telling us the size of our particles as we are crystallizing them, it is unfortunately not so easy for irregular-shaped particles. https://t.co/U1zFcMBmej

16.11.2023 · Tweet

At MRing @VyshnvyH has developed a mathematical model that helps us convert the CLD of needle-like particles to its corresponding PSD. These models are applicable in the case of irregular particles as well as to systems described by bimodal PSDs. @SSPCentre @ChemicalSciUL https://t.co/9oOBQVoPkK

Now that you know how I got here, you may be asking what is or was my work. 🔬 👩‍🔬 Well, if you already listened to the podcast, you may already know, but here is an overview of it😉

28.11.2023 · Tweet

Nowadays, @nanoGUNE, I work with van der Waals (vdW) materials. Have you heard of graphene?✏️Well, it is a vdW material, but since its "exfoliation" (remember this word) a lot of other materials like it have appeared, from magnets, like the ones on the fridge, to superconductors!

28.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE But now you ask me, well but why do you care about them? What is so special about these materials? And what do you do with them?🤔

28.11.2023 · Tweet

And while I let you think about why we care about vdW materials 😉, it is time for a Basque (Euskera) class at @nanoGUNE! Euskera is spoken here in the Basque Country, and the classes are always a fun break to learn and discover more about the region! https://t.co/B3o6aS5kFh

28.11.2023 · Tweet

The vdW materials have a wide range of applications due to some extraordinary properties! 💫 They are made up of layers connected by these vdW forces, which are very weak. Thus, one fantastic property is that we can separate the layers, aka exfoliate, and get very thin flakes!

28.11.2023 · Tweet

In a magnetic vdW material, we can play with its magnetism: we can go from a ferromagnet, like the fridge ones, to different magnetic phases like antiferromagnet 🧲 We can also end up with different magnetic orientations, called anisotropies, which we look for in certain things!

28.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE I am exploring the magnetic and transport properties of these vdW magnets, also called layered magnetic materials.🔎 We study how they behave when we apply magnetic or electric fields and then we try to tune and control their behaviour! 🔧🎮

28.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE And one of the reasons for doing all of this is to create novel Spintronics devices! Listen to the podcast to hear me explain what this thing called Spintronics is, but in a very simple way Spintronics=spin+electronics It is using the spin like we use the charge of electrons!

28.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE Due to the vdW forces magic 🪄 we create these devices like we play with Legos: we stack one vdW material on top of another! 🧱 So we can combine a vdW magnet with another vdW material that, by generating a spin current, controls its magnetism! The possibilities are endless!

28.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE So, some days this is me! (With tiny flakes and in a clean room suit but an accurate representation 😅) https://t.co/OmSeNrsOC0

29.11.2023 · Tweet

I showed you how I play with legos, aka build nanostructures of van der Waals materials, and study the magnetic and electronic properties of these. But, how do we fabricate these materials to be able to explore their properties? Come with me and let's fabricate a device!🧵

29.11.2023 · Tweet

It all starts with a bulk crystal! 🪨 This is a piece of material that is macroscopic that we can hold in our hands. But it is made up of thousands and thousands of layers connected by vdW forces, so if we want just a few layers, what do we do? We exfoliate with scotch tape!

29.11.2023 · Tweet

Yes, you read that right! We put the crystal between two pieces of a special scotch tape and we seperate them. This separates the layers of the material. And if we keep going and going we can reach very thin flakes, aka pieces of the material with very few layers!🤏

29.11.2023 · Tweet

Sometimes these materials don't like being in normal air conditions, too much oxygen and water for their liking🌬️💧 for these we exfoliate inside a Glovebox: a box where the air is controlled to minimise O2 and H2O that we access with gloves (the name is very apt isn't it?)

29.11.2023 · Tweet

So, now we have our thin flakes on the scotch tape, but how do we study it? We need to transfer the material onto a substrate where we can then do all we need. We mostly use silicon substrates with an oxidized layer, aka Si/SiO2. This is what it looks like! https://t.co/ebxnGHN4SS

30.11.2023 · Tweet

We end up with many flakes on the substrate and now comes the best part for some, the worst for others: we need to search and choose the flake we want to study! For that, we use a simple optical microscope🔬and take a📸! What do you think, would you like to search for flakes?

30.11.2023 · Tweet

We now have our flake!🥳But how do we measure its electronic properties? We need to contact the flake with electrical contacts! We use a metal, like Gold or Platinum . But before we use up our Gold, we have to do the part I like the most: design the contacts! ✍️

30.11.2023 · Tweet

For this we use a method called Lithography, which comes from Greek and means writing in stone✍️🪨But if you draw by hand, your design is too big! So we use something else to write: light🔦and if we really want to go small, we even use electrons⚡️!

30.11.2023 · Tweet

This is because the wavelength of light or of electrons is small enough that we can write micro or nanometric things〰️! And this is precisely the size we need for the contacts to our flake! But now you are thinking, if we are "writing" with light, what is our paper (or stone)?📜

30.11.2023 · Tweet

Light sensitive polymers and we call them photoresists! We put a resist layer on the substrate with our flake and then we shine with light to draw our design. If it is a➕resist, the area iluminated can be removed, but with➖resist, this area stays and everything else goes away!

30.11.2023 · Tweet

Here @nanoGUNE we can do it with light in a machine we call the Laser Writer (because it uses an UV light laser) 🔦 or we can use an eBL, which stands for electron beam lithography ⚡️, and uses an electron gun to write our devices!

30.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE Here is an example! You see on the left our flakes on the substrate, and we want to study the thin blueish one, marked with the green line. And on the right, you see the result after we do the lithography and we develop (yes! like an old photographic film) the resist! https://t.co/YOGnhB2EwH

30.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE On the right, the green area and the very big flake are still covered with the resist. In the purple area, the resist has gone away and we are left with holes, that we can fill with gold and thus contact and measure the sample!

30.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE We have our device almost fabricated, only two steps to go! We need to fill the opened resist holes with Gold. For that we deposit a thin film of gold or platinum, with a nanometric thickness, so also very small😉

30.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE We can use an Evaporator: we heat the gold to make it evaporate and it forms a film. Or we use a sputtering: we have a target of platinum at which we throw Argon ions so fast that some platinum is removed and is deposited! Here is a GIF of some sputtering I did in my PhD! https://t.co/4hvlcq9vdy

30.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE Almost there! Now we have or metal on the holes contacting the flake but also on top of the rest of the substrate that had the resist. So, how are we just left with the contacts? Well, we do what we call a lift-off 🏋️and we remove the resist, and thus also the metal on top!

30.11.2023 · Tweet

@nanoGUNE This is the most nerve wracking step for me. After so many steps and effort, everything can be destroyed by a simple bad lift-off! But have no fear! We place our device in acetone and it worked! We get all the resist away and we are left with a nice contacted flake, our device!🥳 https://t.co/UffqDbJ0LQ

30.11.2023 · RT

RT @DrSofia_F_T: Halfway there with the fabrication! We already see some drawn contacts! 👀👀 @nanoGUNE @RealSci_Nano

If you remember, we had our devices, contacted with metal and all ready to be measured. 🥳 Well, what do we actually want to measure here? 🤔

03.12.2023 · Tweet

This material is a magnetic semiconductor, so we can explore its magnetic properties through measurements of its electric resistance and its dependence on temperature 🌡️, magnetic fields 🧲 (Magnetoresistance) or electric fields ⚡️ (Gate dependence)

03.12.2023 · Tweet

We know what we want to measure, so let's get our device ready! We have to connect the metal that is on our flake to all the cables, to apply electric currents and measure voltages. We use a wire bonder: we connect our device with small wires of Gold or Aluminium to a puck! 🪡

03.12.2023 · Tweet

This is what it looks like! I have 2 substrates, the shiny squares each with one device. You can see the squares of gold (or pink in the bottom one, do you know why they have different colours?), the tiny wires connected to them and the gold rectangles on the green puck! https://t.co/vABvME7scO

03.12.2023 · Tweet

And here is a zoom into the puck, with other devices I have measured bonded. You can see how the tiny wires go from the Gold rectangles in the puck to the Gold pads of our devices! 🟨🪡🟪 https://t.co/dkxUYhaUuJ

03.12.2023 · Tweet

Depending on the size of nanometric Gold, its colour changes! In this case the thickness of the metallic thin film is different, the pinkish squares are around 15 nm whereas the other ones are almost 50 nm!

03.12.2023 · Tweet

Devices are ready to be measured! And we do this in a PPMS: a Physical Properties Measurement System! And yes, you read that right, a lot of the physical properties of materials can be measured in these systems, from optical, to thermal, to electrical as in our case!

03.12.2023 · Tweet

They are super cool machines because we can measure things at temperatures all the way down to 2K and with magnetic fields up to 9T! And this is what one of our systems looks like at @nanoGUNE! To me it looks like a tiny space ship🚀, what do you think? https://t.co/R9zoi0O73b

Hello! I’m @xamberlim, and I will be your guest scientist this week! I’m a chemistry PhD student in the @Fredrickson_UW group at @UWMadisonChem by day, and also an art-loving, D&D-playing nerd 24/7! This week I’m going to cover 💎Crystals! 👩‍🎨 Comics! & 💻 Calculations!

18.12.2023 · Tweet

💎 Crystals! I study intermetallic solid state chemistry. In molecular chemistry, the kinds of chemicals we study are often smaller, singular units. In solid state chemistry, our chemicals are linked together in one large unit that extends beyond the atomic scale.

18.12.2023 · Tweet

This is one aspect that makes it challenging to research the solid state. Not only do we need to consider local effects around individual atoms, but also consider long-range or bulk effects.

18.12.2023 · Tweet

Crystals are one type of solid. In science, we describe crystals with a unit cell, which gives us information about how atoms are arranged. These unit cells repeat in 3-D space, very much like a 3-D wallpaper. (Comic excerpt from our group website: https://t.co/l6eUWuWDGK) https://t.co/5zr9h3Ja5n

18.12.2023 · Tweet

I study intermetallic crystals because metals are so diverse! Metal atoms can have varying sizes, electron counts, and electronegativities. As a result, when metal elements come together to form a new intermetallic compound, the bonds between them can have different characters!

18.12.2023 · Tweet

This diversity of bonding in solids can be understood with the van Arkel-Ketalaar Triangle, which shows that bonding is a spectrum rather than a fixed types. https://t.co/THOLpjGL1d

18.12.2023 · Tweet

Intermetallic materials can have bonds that have a mixture of these characters. My job and my passion is to understand the complex bonding in these types of materials, and I do that mainly through computational chemistry. https://t.co/3yvrsyz8UO

18.12.2023 · Tweet

Of course, there's experimental aspects in this field of work too! I used to do experiments as an undergraduate researcher, but I have since turned my focus to pure computational work. I do miss getting pretty crystals though! (CuP2 below) https://t.co/14XmYiCNcG

18.12.2023 · Tweet

Stay tuned this week to learn how I tackle these problems!

18.12.2023 · Tweet

One perspective our group uses to study the formation of intermetallic materials is through the lens of FAST: Frustrated and Allowed Structural Transitions. 🚌💨 Before we talk about FAST, let's dive into some background...

18.12.2023 · Tweet

There are three different factors we use to understand why solid state materials form: (1) Atomic size effects (2) Electronic structure (3) Electronegativity These are often called Hume-Rothery factors. In my research, I will focus on the first two factors! https://t.co/0t9kOycXfk

18.12.2023 · Tweet

Atomic size effects: One way to think of our materials is to think of them as hard spheres in a box. A lot of metallic elements pack in certain patterns (hcp, bcc, fcc). If you’ve seen produce in pyramids at the grocery store, you may be familiar with these ordered packings. https://t.co/Xw1dezaHUR

18.12.2023 · Tweet

When the atoms are different sizes, however, the problem of filling up space in an ordered way becomes more complex, as we can see in this holiday-themed example. 🎄 https://t.co/9jwUyUYJ1D

18.12.2023 · Tweet

Electronic structure: A core part of chemistry is understanding how electrons interact with each other and nuclei. We have so many electron-counting concepts in chemistry (such as the octet rule and formal charges for Lewis dot structures) to rationalize structure.

18.12.2023 · Tweet

In the field of solid state chemistry, we have many models and electron-counting principles as well, including but not limited to the Zintl concept, the Mott-Jones model, and Wade-Mingos rules. https://t.co/iofeU67s8G

18.12.2023 · Tweet

These fundamental principles help us to determine whether systems are "electronically favorable" based on whether they ✅ perfectly satisfy the rules, 🆗 are very close to meeting them, or ⛔ don't fit at all.

18.12.2023 · Tweet

Lastly, Electronegativity! This is the tendency of an element to attract electrons. Electronegativity is intertwined with electronic structure because differences in electronegativity can lead to different kinds of bonding (see the van Arkel-Ketalaar triangle in the last thread).

18.12.2023 · Tweet

We tie these concepts together with the FAST principle. Overall structural stability can be viewed as a combination of these factors. When atomic packing conditions and the electronic structure are both favorable, the crystal structure will easily form. 👍 + 👍 = 👍

18.12.2023 · Tweet

When these factors disagree, the crystal structure will be harder to form. In fact, we may see some ✨interesting, more complex structures✨ (such as intergrowths and modulated structures) as the factors compete on a local and global level. 👍 + 👎 = ⁉😱⁉

18.12.2023 · Tweet

For an introduction to the FAST concept and a cool, modulated structure, check out this paper by my former colleague! It's a long one, but it's a good one! https://t.co/btYfkZzCnB

18.12.2023 · Tweet

Tomorrow, I'll talk more about my specific research project. 👋😉 Signing off for today.

@CycleFunMtl Cousins!! I love your desk companion as well!

19.12.2023 · RT

RT @CycleFunMtl: @RealSci_Nano Moo! https://t.co/bbcpfXxxEZ

19.12.2023 · Tweet

Today, I’ll give an overview of my specific project: ✨ 18-n+m isomerism in T-E intermetallics✨ Whoa, what a mouthful! 💦 Isomerism? 18-n+m? What does that mean?

19.12.2023 · Tweet

Yesterday, I talked about electron-counting rules in chemistry, each useful in specific contexts and bonding. https://t.co/m6wt5zDf3Z

19.12.2023 · Tweet

One domain of bonding we’re interested in is when compounds have both metallic and covalent characteristics. Transition metal (T) - main group metal (E) intermetallics are perfect candidates for this investigation, and furthermore, there's some interesting structural trends...! https://t.co/avXZIBXmKL

19.12.2023 · Tweet

T-T connectivity in the crystal structure can be related to its electron count. We call this concept the 18-n+m rule, though it's also known in one of its forms as the 18-n rule. How does this rule work? We know that closed-shell compounds are electronically stable. https://t.co/zrVabk6hRp

19.12.2023 · Tweet

Transition metal atoms can achieve closed-shell stability with multi-center T-T bonds, which we call isolobal bonds. These bonds are enabled through the support of main group atoms. The number of electrons shared in these bonds correspond to the "n" in the 18-n rule. https://t.co/qtT49WpGyV

19.12.2023 · Tweet

In the case of ScAl3, we have 12 valence electrons, so using the 18-n rule... 18-n = 12 Then n=6! This is exactly what we see in ScAl3, which forms the AuCu3 type. Sc can form 6 Sc-Sc contacts, all supported by Al atoms. https://t.co/jvFocRsczg

19.12.2023 · Tweet

For detailed reading and examples of the 18-n rule, I recommend this excellent article, aptly titled, "Generality of the 18-n rule". https://t.co/p0BS3orTge

19.12.2023 · Tweet

What about the 18-n+m rule? m corresponds to the number of electrons that are NOT associated with the transition metal atoms. These atoms are based in main group-only states. e.g. for Ir3Sn7, 1 electron goes in the isolobal bond, and 1.33 electrons populate the Sn-Sn σ bond. https://t.co/6abvBRX41D

19.12.2023 · Tweet

This electron-counting rule has been helpful for us to rationalize a number of structures! However, you can see in the below example that I can have different (n,m) configurations at the same electron count... https://t.co/eU7bCCYydm

19.12.2023 · Tweet

Herein lies the problem of 18-n+m isomerism. If we can have multiple (n,m) configurations and still be electronically stable, how do we know which structure type is the best candidate? https://t.co/nRj4eKQe6S

19.12.2023 · Tweet

This is where the FAST concept I talked about yesterday comes in! We break down the candidate systems into two analyses. (1) ⚛ Electronics: How does the 18-n+m rule apply? (2) 💥Atomic packing: What kind of packing tensions are present in the systems? https://t.co/8k1vDF2rp9

19.12.2023 · Tweet

That's it for now! Later, I'll talk about the two analyses in detail, then bring them together to solve the conundrum of 18-n+m isomerism. 👋

20.12.2023 · Tweet

Happy Wednesday! ☕ Today I'll be talking about the theoretical methods we use to explore our crystal systems! While I prepare those tweets, have another one of my desk companions 🦆 and a 20 oz. coffee mug for scale. My roommate got me this mug to celebrate this paper! https://t.co/0TtMmwXasa

20.12.2023 · Tweet

As the holiday traveling season approaches, PACKING may be on your mind. How are you going to pack all those gifts and clothes into one carry-on bag? https://t.co/AAnVgljZ2G

20.12.2023 · Tweet

Well, I don’t have an answer for that, but I do have a theoretical tool for understanding packing in solid state materials. Introducing the ✨DFT-Chemical Pressure analysis!✨ (TOC image from https://t.co/v5M8cTzizO) https://t.co/F9fsFWXFKW

20.12.2023 · Tweet

What’s Chemical Pressure? Imagine a 2D lattice of atoms. These atoms are the same element and are placed at their equilibrium distances. If we replace one atom with a smaller one, its contacts must shorten but at the expense of other contacts! We have packing tensions! https://t.co/JWGN6NPnLU

20.12.2023 · Tweet

We encapsulate this concept in calculating "chemical pressures" for our system. To do this, we: (1) Use DFT packages to calculate energies of our system at its normal volume, a slightly bigger one, and a slightly smaller one. (2) Calculate a pressure for every voxel (a 3D pixel) https://t.co/Ak7Qelv19z

20.12.2023 · Tweet

(3) Project the 3D chemical pressure information onto spherical harmonics centered on atoms. This gives us a means to interpret contact-wise chemical pressures. * This is a simplified version of the whole DFT-CP process.

20.12.2023 · Tweet

These spherical harmonics (called CP features) tell us which contacts are too long and which contacts are too short. Black = -CP. Energy DECREASES as the atoms come closer. The contact is too long! White = +CP, Energy INCREASES as the atoms come closer. The contact is too short! https://t.co/eNcTYOEyXU

20.12.2023 · Tweet

These CP schemes are useful, as they can tell us what the local packing tensions are. In general, we can compare two CP schemes of structures of the same composition to identify which structure type reduces packing tensions, and how it does so!

20.12.2023 · Tweet

One way I used DFT-CP was to look at a series of intergrowth structures in the REAl3 series! We combed through literature and found a trend that compounds with larger RE atoms tend to have more of the hexagonal Ni3Sn type than the cubic AuCu3 type. https://t.co/FqxQPBRBPr

20.12.2023 · Tweet

This suggested to us that atomic size and packing effects played a large role in which structure type forms. But why? We could look at tables of covalent and metallic radii, but this wasn't enough for us. DFT-CP came to the rescue! 🦸‍♀️

20.12.2023 · Tweet

We calculated the DFT-CP schemes of a selection of these compounds and found that the Ni3Sn type relieves packing tensions in the AuCu3 type for compounds with larger RE atoms (illustrated below with YAl3). https://t.co/Troza2MLMU

20.12.2023 · Tweet

We can see some problems in the hypothetical AuCu3-type YAl3 packing scheme. The Y atoms have a white positive pressure all around it, meaning it's feeling rather constricted. Expansion of its coordination environment, however, is hindered by negative CPs along Al-Al contacts.

20.12.2023 · Tweet

We can see how replacing the Y atom with something smaller, say a Sc atom, can be more favorable!

20.12.2023 · Tweet

(Side note: Calculations are great! You can get information about hypothetical systems that you can't realize IRL with experiments! But of course, you need to be careful about drawing conclusions because it's a hypothetical system.)

20.12.2023 · Tweet

When we compare this to the CP scheme of the Ni3Sn-type YAl3, we note some key differences: (1) Al-Al negative pressures are reduced within the newly formed columns (2) Positive pressures on Y are reduced in the ab plane, forming an hourglass shape. https://t.co/6lR37QcgUz

20.12.2023 · Tweet

DFT-CP shows us exactly which packing tensions are relieved by the Ni3Sn structure type, and why it's a better arrangement for REAl3 compounds with larger RE atoms!

20.12.2023 · Tweet

If you want to read more about this, plus some interesting electronic considerations, check out my paper in Inorganic Chemistry! https://t.co/CdSP9sMnTU

20.12.2023 · Tweet

I also designed a very cool cover for that issue related to the work, which I think you should look at. 👀https://t.co/GHuBlrSYPX https://t.co/zVdIyGNEw0

20.12.2023 · Tweet

Thanks for tuning into this thread over the DFT-Chemical Pressure method! Stay tuned later today for MORE applications of DFT-CP, including phonons! 😲

20.12.2023 · Tweet

For reading on the Chemical Pressure concept and some advances in the methodology, check out these papers or our publications list: https://t.co/rfmpWr6HqR 1st CP paper: https://t.co/Hlfo0s2aEr 1st DFT-CP paper: https://t.co/sCgkhUKyV0 Latest updates: https://t.co/vw4FnnmcKt

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Earlier today, I talked about the DFT-CP method. Now, let’s talk about a special CP feature, which we call the CP quadrupole! This unique feature is linked to cool phenomena, including phonons, incommensurate modulations, and guest atoms. Let’s dive right in! https://t.co/yRTt3LNQyt

21.12.2023 · Tweet

CP quadrupoles (QPs) are features where the distribution of positive and negative pressures on an atom are perpendicular to each other. As a result, these QPs look very much like d-orbitals! https://t.co/noUZemz8Sw

21.12.2023 · Tweet

QPs are linked to anisotropic motion of atoms. If an atom moves along the negative CPs, that motion or vibration will be relatively unhindered, resulting in soft atomic motions or low energy vibrations. https://t.co/ogt2ZUMV81

21.12.2023 · Tweet

On the other hand, movement along positive CPs, where the contact is already too short, is very unfavorable, and vibrations in those directions will be higher in energy. These energies and atomic motions can be then linked to phonons... But what are phonons?

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Phonons are vibrations for crystal structures. Instead of just one pairwise vibration, now we have concerted motions! (img src: https://t.co/cRFiczIjWw) https://t.co/YVObNRris4

21.12.2023 · Tweet

So if QPs show us the directions of low and high energy vibrations, we should be able to see that in phonon band structures, which we do! The lowest frequency optical mode has displacements along those negative CPs, and the highest frequency modes has them along the positive CPs! https://t.co/97s7BxrlWk

21.12.2023 · Tweet

This is exciting, because we can take this idea even further. One of my projects is the investigation of the polymorphs of IrIn3. The phase transition temperature is approx. 350C, which is pretty low for an intermetallic! Why is that? https://t.co/y3gITfcYBW

21.12.2023 · Tweet

When we compare the CP schemes of both polymorphs, we see CP quadrupoles are present in the CoGa3 type but not the IrIn3 type. These QPs are enabled due to the large void spaces in the CoGa3 type structure, which the IrIn3 type doesn't have. https://t.co/zEQcOxzt65

21.12.2023 · Tweet

And as expected, the atomic motions are correlated to low and high frequency phonon modes. In fact, the separation in frequency of these states is so large we see a phonon band gap! https://t.co/Qa2AoHhSJY

21.12.2023 · Tweet

If we compare the phonon DOS of the CoGa3 type to the IrIn3 type, we see that the IrIn3 type doesn't have comparable low energy modes. This tracks, because any motions along negative CPs will be hindered by positive CPs. The IrIn3 type simply doesn't have as much QP character. https://t.co/L7mHmxA7DW

21.12.2023 · Tweet

And this is a critical point: low energy vibrations are easier to access and thus contribute more to vibrational entropy than high energy vibrations, illustrated by the figure below. The CoGa3 type then must have greater vibrational entropy than the IrIn3 type... https://t.co/X9M65iOyNQ

21.12.2023 · Tweet

We can then use our gen chem knowledge to do a simple calculation to get the phase transition temperature, using ΔG = ΔE -TΔSvib The phase transition should occur when the free energies are the same. Behold! Our calculated phase transition temperature is 410! Pretty close! 😲 https://t.co/FqHzIIMIP0

21.12.2023 · Tweet

To demonstrate how important those low energy phonons (motions into the void spaces of the CoGa3 type), we artificially shift the frequencies in the CoGa3 type up +0.53 THz, and our "new" phase transition temp is now 912C, much, MUCH larger than before! https://t.co/Ki6wBa1Cqy

21.12.2023 · Tweet

From this, I've learned two things! (1) CP quadrupoles are great for anticipating these high and low energy vibrational effects, which is awesome since they're cheaper than phonon calcs. (2) Those void spaces in the CoGa3 type enable entropic stabilization.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

That's partly why the CoGa3 type is the higher temperature phase, and also why the phase transition temperature is so low for an intermetallic!

21.12.2023 · Tweet

There's a lot more that CP quadrupoles can tell us. I won't spoil more for now, but I highly recommend reading this paper by Dr. Kendall Kamp, who did a lot of work in this area! https://t.co/nRX9vzP9ym

21.12.2023 · Tweet

I'm also leaving a lot of cool details out in the IrIn3 polymorphism paper, so go read that too! I'm quite proud of this work. https://t.co/i7W0XEeLlF

21.12.2023 · Tweet

That's all I got for now! See you tomorrow, where we'll be exploring ELECTRONICS and COMPUTATIONS!

Good morning! Today I will be talking about the electronic structure analysis I do. A big part of it is running calculations and writing code! So I thought I'd give you all a sneak peak at what it's like to be a computational chemist. What's on YOUR desk? https://t.co/1rs4dJffUk

21.12.2023 · Tweet

An essential part of being a grad student is running down to the seminar hall when they announce free food up for grabs. 🏃‍♂️💨 https://t.co/Cfyj4IsROv

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Part of my work this week is writing a manuscript! Though writing is not my favorite aspect of research, it's an important process that helps me think deeply about my scientific findings and how it fits into what we currently know. Here's my flowchart with how I approach writing! https://t.co/KhGDPrdxo2

21.12.2023 · Tweet

I start writing highly detailed work first (such as the experimental section), then slowly work towards more generalized or abstract sections. I like to leave the title for last! This allows me to brain dump, organize my thoughts, then form a larger story for my work.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

So what does a computational chemist do to understand solid state structures? How does one even approach computations? Let's have a tour!

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Say you want to know about the electronic structure of a solid state system. You know you can do ab-initio computations somehow! Where do you start? 🤔 You start with the crystal structure!

21.12.2023 · Tweet

We typically use Crystallographic Information Files (CIFs) as a starting point for building crystal structures. I like to look in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD) for CIFs of my system, or if they're not available, CIFs of the same structure type as my system. https://t.co/hKcB8XPCJA

21.12.2023 · Tweet

I typically open these CIFs in a visualization program like VESTA or Diamond to understand what's going on. For the compounds I study, drawing homoatomic bonds is very helpful! https://t.co/4KmdatVMLf

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Next, I put the crystallographic information into the input files for computational chemistry packages. Our group uses VASP and ABINIT, two common DFT packages. Since these calculations can be intense, we use our department's computing cluster to run this software.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

We have to run software from the command line. It's a bit of a hurdle when you initially learn it, but it is very powerful! 💪💻 (Plus it makes you feel like a hacker in the movies...) https://t.co/2UuSQZbphA

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Not only do we need to put in crystallographic information, we have to tell the program what kind of settings we want to use! My input files start to look like some kind of hidden code. 😵 That's why I like to put some comments in my template files. https://t.co/BVOrCUhQJD

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Let's fast-forward! The first calculations we do are for setting certain parameters, like the energy cutoff and k-point mesh. Though we don't get info from these calculations, we need to do this to find the right balance between precision and computational cost! https://t.co/AynZKG7ppD

21.12.2023 · Tweet

This is important, because we can get *super* precise, but if your basic calculation takes months to run, it's not very practical.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Once those are set, we need to optimize our crystal's geometry! For our purposes, need to have our system at the energetic minimum to extract meaningful, accurate data.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

We do this geometry optimization in two steps: (1) atoms are allowed to shift (2) atoms and unit cell shape are allowed to shift This two-step procedure helps the software find the equilibrium geometry efficiently. https://t.co/3GRK6MLf1x

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Once we have our equilibrium geometry, we run static calculations, where the atoms are now locked in place and we can get the data we want!

21.12.2023 · Tweet

For example, we can get info about the electronic density of states, which can tell us things such as whether our crystal is a conductor/insulator or what kind of orbital characteristics our bands have. https://t.co/AM4iFqqyEL

21.12.2023 · Tweet

For my research, the region around the Fermi energy (EF) is of interest! Typically, compounds that follow the 18-n+m rule have a dip in their density of states at the EF in the form of a pseudo- or band gap. Sometimes, they don't, like in the IrIn3 type in the above image.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Why do some 18-n+m compounds not show that band or pseudogap at the Fermi energy? To investigate this, I use one of our group's tools called DFT-raMO! This is a tool that uses the occupied crystal orbitals (which we get from DFT calculations) to make molecular analogies.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

DFT calculations on crystal structures use planewave basis sets to describe the information about the electrons of a system. Think sin and cosine functions! https://t.co/iiiGz55kxV

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Instead of analyzing waves that are spread out, we want to understand the electronics in a localized context. This allows us to understand the bonding in our system by making analogies to molecular orbitals. https://t.co/qV3IBi4kmF

21.12.2023 · Tweet

To do this analysis, we wrote software in MATLAB* that does some BIG matrix math to transform wavefunction information into approximate molecular orbitals! Each of these new functions contains 2 electrons, so we have a way of doing electron-counting for our system.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

* It's in MATLAB, for now, but I'm currently rewriting it in the Julia programming language.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

The plot here shows the output of some DFT-raMO analysis, with one dot representing one reconstructed molecular-like orbital. You can see that we're able to generate atomic- and molecular orbital-like isosurfaces! https://t.co/uyz1QsBRiF

21.12.2023 · Tweet

But what's that on the y-axis? That's Psphere, which is a tool that helps us evaluate the localization of our reconstructed function. It's calculated as the ratio of electron density in a defined sphere over the electron density in the whole unit cell. https://t.co/WlVal4O82W

21.12.2023 · Tweet

What's important to us is that Psphere is consistent, meaning our reconstructed molecular orbitals are well-localized. When it drops sharply, it's an indication of delocalization. Or in simple terms, electrons can't be fully occupying those orbitals!

21.12.2023 · Tweet

This tool helped me with a lot of projects! Remember the REAl3 story? With DFT-raMO, I was able to show which orbitals were associated with electrons n=7 and m=1 in the 18-n+m rule! https://t.co/TbJI0elCDV

21.12.2023 · Tweet

In the story of IrIn3 polymorphism, DFT-raMO helped showed that m electrons were localized in the void spaces of CoGa3! https://t.co/FUOX3470zS

21.12.2023 · Tweet

There's still more we can plan to do with DFT-raMO, and part of my work is expanding its functionality by writing code! I've been working on the newest version of it for almost two years now, and I am pleased to say that it's more efficient and has quality-of-life improvements. https://t.co/XCxmx80BmZ

21.12.2023 · Tweet

... and this is where we get into one aspect of computational chemistry. Coding and software! https://t.co/YZtafUzay7

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Before I begin, a disclaimer: I haven't taken a single coding class since high school, so a lot is learned on-the-job or self taught! 😱

21.12.2023 · Tweet

Not all computational chemists write code regularly, but sometimes they write scripts to automate their tasks or process data! These scripts are relatively simple. When you need a collection of scripts to perform complex tasks, you might consider writing a software package.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

I find myself coding in short bursts rather than on a daily basis! This is because I have other tasks to do, like analyzing data or writing manuscripts!

21.12.2023 · Tweet

But if you catch me on a coding day, my screen might look something like this! https://t.co/HEtXxnEOgl

21.12.2023 · Tweet

I also use Github for version-control, which is something I learned a couple years ago. It has changed my life immensely, and if you are a coder but haven't used any form of version-control, what are you doing!!!

21.12.2023 · Tweet

The coding process is usually: idea -> sketch it out -> attempt to code -> test -> debug -> debug -> debug -> debug -> debug ... -> commit change It's almost similar to writing a manuscript in that aspect. 😅

21.12.2023 · Tweet

It's a challenging (and sometimes painful) process, but I also find it deeply rewarding, and I learn new things all the time! The biggest challenge for me is trying to keep the BIG PICTURE in mind while still minding all the small details.

21.12.2023 · Tweet

I'm still working on my DFT-raMO.jl package, but I'm excited to get it published and shared with the scientific community so anyone can use it! 🤞 Coming soon 2024...

21.12.2023 · Tweet

I'd love to answer any questions you may have about computational solid state chemistry, writing scientific code/scripts, or DFT-raMO if you have any!

21.12.2023 · Tweet

In the meantime, I will close with relevant further reading! The DFT-raMO method: https://t.co/rZQMhYJRt9 Psphere update to DFT-raMO: https://t.co/CdSP9sMnTU

1/n Hey all! Hello from the city of Hyderabad. 👋 I am Narayanan, an experimental material scientist. I am thrilled to be your curator for the week and bring to you exciting news about research from our group. @TnnLab @TIFRH_buzz Stay tuned for our lab updates...😀

25.03.2024 · Tweet

2/n The last 10 years of our research (https://t.co/GebQNF01Vc) at TIFR Hyderabad, India mainly focused on the development and studies of materials for applications, in energy, including renewable energy harvesting, electrocatalysis, & energy storage, as well as, in electronics.

25.03.2024 · Tweet

3/n Our materials engineering approaches reside in the modulation of different mesoscopic interfaces & probing their interfacial properties. For this we study light-matter interactions, electrode-electrolyte phenomena, interfacial electron/ion transport & quasiparticle dynamics.

25.03.2024 · Tweet

4/n We also focus on the controllable development and optimization of atomically thin layers and their heterostructures using different physical and chemical routes.

25.03.2024 · Tweet

Lucas from @TUBerlin and me being fascinated by our new detectors. Superconducting nanowire single photon detectors from @SingleQuantum . User friendly and really fast 🚀. In there it has 1.9 K 🥶❄️ Explanation will follow⬇️ © @DorisEReiter #Quantour #SUPERquantum #QTorch https://t.co/6NyBJ9JnJ2

10.05.2024 · Tweet

The detectors are based on superconductivity. In a superconducter electrons form Cooper pairs below a critical Temperature. The Cooper pairs are able to flow through the material without giving off energy. Therefore the resistance is zero. https://t.co/mAqVVQGKMm

10.05.2024 · Tweet

There is a critical current above which the detector loses its superconducting state. If the detector is operated slightly below this current, a photon hitting the detector will break Cooper pairs and create a resistance region, resulting in a measurable voltage spike.

As Rome has always been a must-stop place in any European tour, our quantum source could not miss the opportunity of spending a couple of spring weeks here, with the Nanophotonics (@QuantumMinions) group @SapienzaRoma University! #QuanTour #QTorch #SUPERquantum https://t.co/cBjjsBg6Ol

27.05.2024 · Tweet

@SapienzaRoma is one of the oldest and most important Universities in Italy. With more than 100000 enrolled, it is the institution with the highest number of students in Europe! People come from all over the country to study here.

27.05.2024 · Tweet

Founded in 1303, @SapienzaRoma has the “Città Universitaria” as its nerve center: the campus, built in the 1930s, features some architectural must-see. Pay a visit to the Math Department, designed by the world-renowned architect Gio Ponti! #QuanTour #SUPERquantum #QTorch https://t.co/rhhpo3Ya0e

27.05.2024 · Tweet

The Physics Department in @SapienzaRoma is one of the most prominent in Italy, both for the cutting-edge research we currently develop here and its bright history. Let’s take a look at the department as it is today!

27.05.2024 · Tweet

Two main buildings, hosted in the @SapienzaRoma campus, are part of the Department of Physics: the “old physics building”, dedicated to Guglielmo Marconi, and the “new physics building”, named after Enrico Fermi, who taught here from 1926 to 1938. https://t.co/OsrzJANG4H

27.05.2024 · Tweet

And look here! A letter from Lawrence to E. Fermi himself. This is the kind of evidence that is carefully kept in the halls and the stunning museum of the department, together with experimental equipment from the last two centuries! https://t.co/rPNg8PCjiP

27.05.2024 · Tweet

But, as we said, it’s not all in the past! Giorgio Parisi, 2021 Nobel laureate, used to work and teach here until a couple of years ago! https://t.co/7iQqgtOqPM

27.05.2024 · Tweet

Ours is a large department, where both theoretical and experimental physics are cultivated in their wide variety: astrophysics, gravitation, superconductivity, quantum field theory, statistical physics, spectroscopy, photonics, and quantum information.

27.05.2024 · Tweet

And here we are too, the @QuantumMinions group. In the next few days, you will learn something more about us: what we do and what we like, how we are so very different, and how, somehow, we manage to accomplish great things together! #QuanTour #QTorch #SUPERquantum https://t.co/ETvjkp2UiB

28.05.2024 · Tweet

If you are following QuanTour from its start, you have already met the quantum dot: a nanostructure made of tens of thousands of atoms. We are interested in how they emit entangled photons. https://t.co/6Q9KqFssxq

28.05.2024 · Tweet

Entangled particles behave as if they were a pair of dice that, after having been entangled, roll and always return the same but random outcome. https://t.co/rSJFzEcLPF

28.05.2024 · Tweet

In our game, instead of a number the information is encoded in the polarization of light https://t.co/VXthaqMuW5

28.05.2024 · Tweet

In fact, we have plenty of ways to control, manipulate polarization https://t.co/oGEPUfzEwq

28.05.2024 · Tweet

Decades passed before this phenomenon was experimentally demonstrated for the first time in the Eighties, which won Alain Aspect the Nobel Prize last year. https://t.co/umflwjHOtg

28.05.2024 · Tweet

Today, the whole research community is making an effort to generate entangled photon pairs fast and on demand, dealing with the many effect that can introduce errors in the process. #QuanTour #QTorch #SUPERquantum https://t.co/BlZjoHyzWt

28.05.2024 · Tweet

One technical approach we develop and use is pulling and stretching our samples. Yes, one can do that even with apparently brittle and rigid materials such as the ones we use! https://t.co/VUqXu2GZAl

28.05.2024 · Tweet

A semiconductor material containing the quantum dots is thinned down to 30 micrometers, a third than the thickness of a typical human air, and glued on a piezoelectric material that can apply stress upon the application of voltage. https://t.co/cOxjVYTE54

28.05.2024 · Tweet

The geometry shown in the picture, developed together with @jkulinz and FH Voralberg and dubbed “the six legs’, allows us to stretch the sample in any given direction in its plane https://t.co/JkdaukEhW0

28.05.2024 · Tweet

We use this to compensate for very small asymmetries in the shape of the quantum dot which are detrimental to the generation of entangled photons (here the sketch of the most recent device developed with the additional contribution of @Uni_WUE) #QuanTour #QTorch #SUPERquantum https://t.co/oEQrQxJ1v0

28.05.2024 · Tweet

As entangled photons become a more exploitable resource, we can use them for practical purposes, such as sharing secret keys between two parties. https://t.co/tyNJvyeNtM

28.05.2024 · Tweet

We have done this with the group @qlab_sapienza, led by Prof. Fabio Sciarrino, linking the two Physics buildings in the main campus of Sapienza University https://t.co/dtxlopJMcp

28.05.2024 · Tweet

Despite these signals being very weak compared to sunlight (a photon flux 20 orders of magnitude weaker!), we are able to transmit them also during the day using smart geometries and spectral filters. https://t.co/Ek3EM87BsF

28.05.2024 · Tweet

The process starts with the exfoliator tools: crystals, gels, and, of course, tape! We peel the crystals from the bulk to get the monolayer, which we transfer on the piezoelectric substrate. https://t.co/kUxyB5YXQm

28.05.2024 · Tweet

With the sample at hand, we cool it down and quantum light appears! We explore how dynamic strain fields affect the exciton energy, intensity, and magnetic response! https://t.co/3lA8ydSaNq

28.05.2024 · Tweet

Quantum light comes from the 0D-world, true, but…we can take it also from Flatland! Deformations and defects induce quantum emitters in 2D semiconductors, crystals one-layer thick. We place them on piezoelectric actuators, which allow us to tune their energy and brightness. https://t.co/FxqMrFiEvJ

28.05.2024 · Tweet

The process starts with the exfoliator tools: crystals, gels, and, of course, tape! We peel the crystals off the bulk to get the monolayer, which we transfer to the piezoelectric substrate. https://t.co/7nXC64iSCe

28.05.2024 · Tweet

We can process them in an anaerobic chamber, which keeps the sample clean from oxygen contamination. https://t.co/RIsBt56DV0

28.05.2024 · Tweet

With the sample at hand, we cool it down in our cryostat and quantum light appears. We explore how dynamic strain fields affect the exciton energy, intensity, and magnetic response! https://t.co/MpbbnHKTxa

29.05.2024 · RT

RT @RealSci_Nano: 😎Stressed for Quantum😎 Please welcome this week's curator: Rinlado Trotta @QuantumMinions of @SapienzaRoma Want to kno…

29.05.2024 · Tweet

Now that you know our work, it’s time to know our people, the actual foundation of any research group. Let’s give a closer look to a day in the life of the @QuantumMinions members, starting from our PI, Rinaldo!

29.05.2024 · Tweet

It’s early in the morning, a little boost is necessary: what’s better to start off a tough day at work than a black espresso? https://t.co/YohIijPuYO

29.05.2024 · Tweet

Office time: checking the inbox, dealing with bureaucracy, pondering over new results and new ideas; but always with a smile! https://t.co/iYYCvkkNdH

29.05.2024 · Tweet

Rinaldo then meets a student from the Erasmus Mundus QUARMEN programme: an innovative EU-funded master course that allows highly motivated scholars to be introduced to the world of quantum technology https://t.co/APhbg3Hw0b https://t.co/7LScZYl5xV

29.05.2024 · Tweet

Students from all over the world spend each semester in an institution among @ParisSaclay, @UofT @UPorto and @SapienzaRoma. @SapienzaRoma is the first destination, where QUARMEN students attend Rinaldo’s Quantum Optics course. #QuanTour #QTorch #SUPERquantum

29.05.2024 · Tweet

Teaching is a very important part of Rinaldo’s activity: here he is, answering questions at the end of an Optics lesson. https://t.co/F1s5SOPBON

29.05.2024 · Tweet

But today’s a very important day, and his presence is required: two @QuantumMinions master students are graduating! Kudos to Leone and Pierpaolo! https://t.co/miIz0MyhPq

29.05.2024 · Tweet

Such a stressful day: time for another coffee. Or maybe two. That’s Italy, what can you do about it? #QuanTour #QTorch #SUPERquantum https://t.co/L8M2i4ionZ

29.05.2024 · Tweet

A special guest arrives and at @QuantumMinions we try to make him at home, welcome Maximilian! https://t.co/0g0Zbnix4u

29.05.2024 · Tweet

Notwithstanding the many duties that keep him busy every day, Rinaldo always finds the time to step in the lab for a little discussion https://t.co/pZrRC9xxHy

29.05.2024 · Tweet

But enough for now about Rinaldo, it’s time to meet the other members of the @QuantumMinions family! #QuanTour #QTorch #SUPERquantum

30.05.2024 · Tweet

How's a day in the life of @QuantumMinions? First of all, we have to get to the Lab. In Rome, that is not straightforward: whether you come by car, bus or train, you know when you leave, but you never know when you'll arrive. #QuanTour #SUPERquantum #QTorch https://t.co/4u90Yi2dfh

30.05.2024 · Tweet

Look, Michele just arrived on his bike! Michele is a Researcher and he has expertise on a wide variety of topica: he can deal with optics and sample growth as well as with hydraulics and electronics (but don't let him get too close to your PC, he likes to open them). https://t.co/C9do6CRqJG

30.05.2024 · Tweet

Francesco is already in his office writing, thinking...he Is a Researcher, too, and he always hands out great feedback to any question: he usually points out how the things you are doing are wrong in this and that regard, but I guess someone has to do that, right? https://t.co/YeSobsKIdV

30.05.2024 · Tweet

Of course, PostDocs need to start their morning with coffee, too; and alongside the coffee machine, we find Alessandro. He is in a complicated relationship with quantum dots, but he is fond of math and writing. Go to him if you need a break: he's always up for that! https://t.co/bici034SOD

30.05.2024 · Tweet

Lab Time! Let's visit our heroic PhDs. Giuseppe is all about 2D materials, a big fan of light polarization and always ready to lend a hand. But sometimes it is hard to keep up and he has to ask for help. Cheer up, Peppe, you're the best! https://t.co/upW3c6Gp98

30.05.2024 · Tweet

We cross the door and, in the other lab, we find Mattia, absorbed in his work. There is no dot he can not excite and he is afraid of nothing. No kidding, he is scary. https://t.co/AaAFp4tL6S

30.05.2024 · Tweet

Time for another well-deserved break. Let's go for a stroll in the beautiful Physics Department "zen garden" and say hi to the turtles! https://t.co/gvroiiBsrk

30.05.2024 · Tweet

Walking back upstairs, we meet Carola in her office, busy as always: she is a natural problem solver and there is no bureaucratic conundrum that she can't handle! https://t.co/ZZxhMgFXXy

30.05.2024 · Tweet

The clock hits 1 p.m. and the @QuantumMinions head for lunch. Well, to be honest, it is hard to get these people out of the lab, and the process of actually going for lunch can get intricate. But, once outside, it's just smiles in the sunlight! https://t.co/PYW3LoVI3T

30.05.2024 · Tweet

Our Master students really give it their all: meet Fabrizio, Silvia and Fabrizio, working hard on their theses! https://t.co/9PTJlREdEb

30.05.2024 · Tweet

Even when the night comes, our activities do not stop! We opened our lab to the public in the context of the European Museums Night, letting the visitors in to discover about our research and, of course, the QuanTour! https://t.co/WNA187XpZh

30.05.2024 · Tweet

Here is Giorgio, another @QuantumMinions Master student, introducing people to the incredible things we do with light and quantum mechanics. https://t.co/ZByef9vKu6

30.05.2024 · Tweet

It's late now and the @QuantumMinions go home. It's been a busy day and tomorrow is going to be another tough one: we will finally show you the QTorch! #QTorch #QuanTour #SUPERquantum

31.05.2024 · Tweet

It’s finally time to see what our QTorch can do! The @QuantumMinions are ready to mount the sample https://t.co/VhcHn64YU6

31.05.2024 · Tweet

Mattia handles it like a pro! A little bit of silver glue and then, with care, the sample is in the stick. https://t.co/ok1lWRvAn8

31.05.2024 · Tweet

Slow and steady, Fabrizio! Don’t drop it! Once in the cryostat, the sample will reach 4 K, close to the temperature of deep space! https://t.co/WcXG0oDrb8

31.05.2024 · Tweet

The sample is cold, let’s get this dot excited! First of all we have to explore the sample, imaging and looking for the bullseye cavities built around the dots. #QuanTour #QTorch #SUPERQUANTUM https://t.co/pMHoQSzVlP

31.05.2024 · Tweet

Lights on! The source is emitting. Giuseppe and Fabrizio couple the signal into single-mode fibers in order to get it to our single-photon detectors. https://t.co/yjvwm9slWj

31.05.2024 · Tweet

Now we want to see if this source hands out single photons. So, we perform a g(2) correlation measurement (as they did in Linz, do you remember?). Look! Almost no coincidences! We are truly observing single photons! https://t.co/Re9qHzNbk0

31.05.2024 · Tweet

We keep characterizing the emission, measuring the lifetime of the excitation and then, we have another idea… #QuanTour #QTorch #SUPERquantum https://t.co/UEACENv9pZ

31.05.2024 · Tweet

Since we have our source up and running, let’s play a little bit. In our AttoDry1000 cryostat by attocube systems, we have the possibility of applying a magnetic field up to 6 Teslas!

31.05.2024 · Tweet

What happens when we increase the magnetic field directed along the z-axis? We induce a Zeeman splitting in the energy levels. We can see them split while we increase the magnetic field! https://t.co/pfJLWKu6AD

31.05.2024 · Tweet

The external magnetic field couples to the excitonic complexes' total angular momentum and removes the degeneracy in the projection along the z-axis. #QuanTour #QTorch #SUPERquantum https://t.co/m4m5jUkYw8
